# GIOVANNI BATTISTA
## DELLA PORTA OF NAPLES,
## TWENTY BOOKS OF NATURAL MAGIC,
<note>original: "Io. Baptistæ Portæ Neapolitani, Magiæ Naturalis Libri Viginti." Giambattista della Porta (1535–1615) was a renowned Italian scholar and polymath. "Natural Magic" in this period refers to the study of the hidden powers of nature—essentially an early form of experimental science—rather than "black magic" or sorcery.</note>

| III | On the production of new plants. |
| IV | On increasing household goods. <note>Latin: *supellectili*. This book focuses on domestic economy, preserving food, and making useful items for the home.</note> |
| V | On the transmutation of metals. <note>An exploration of alchemy and metallurgy.</note> |
| VI | On the counterfeiting of gems. <note>Instructions on how to create imitation precious stones using glass and dyes.</note> |
| VII | On the wonders of the magnet. |
| VIII | On marvelous remedies. <note>A collection of medical cures and extraordinary potions.</note> |
| IX | On women's cosmetics. |
| X | On extracting the essences of things. <note>This chapter deals with distillation and the chemistry of oils and spirits.</note> |
| XI | On the making of perfumes. <note>original: *myropœia*. Derived from Greek, referring to the art of preparing scented ointments.</note> |
| XII | On incendiary fires. <note>Covering pyrotechnics, gunpowder, and "Greek fire" used in warfare.</note> |
| XIII | On rare tempers of iron. <note>Detailed instructions on metallurgy, specifically the hardening and softening of steel.</note> |
| XIV | On the wondrous preparation of banquets. <note>Includes "tricks" for the table, such as making meat appear to crawl or turning wine into water.</note> |
| XV | On catching wild animals by hand. <note>The OCR reads *ferris* (irons), but the context and other editions confirm the intended word is *feris* (wild beasts). This book covers hunting and trapping.</note> |
| XVI | On invisible writing. <note>An early treatise on cryptography and secret inks.</note> |
| XVII | On mirror images. <note>original: *catoptricis imaginibus*. Catoptrics is the branch of optics dealing with reflection.</note> |
| XVIII | On experiments in statics. <note>The science of weights, balances, and equilibrium.</note> |
| XIX | On pneumatics. <note>The study of air pressure and water-driven machines.</note> |
| XX | Chaos. <note>A final "catch-all" chapter for miscellaneous experiments and observations that did not fit into the previous categories.</note> |

# TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS IUNIO BOBALI, SON OF ANDREA, OF RAGUSA.

## GIAMBATTISTA DELLA PORTA, NEAPOLITAN, SENDS MANY GREETINGS.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter 'A' enclosed in a square frame featuring floral and vine patterns.</image-desc>

*I could hardly restrain the other daughter, who was at home, Illustrious Iunio, now excited and rushing toward you: the immense praises which her sister brought back concerning her husband <note>Della Porta is using an extended metaphor here. He personifies his books as his "daughters," and their patrons as their "husbands." The "sister" refers to an earlier, smaller edition of his work.</note> have so filled her mind with a noble envy that, having broken every bond of restraint and propriety, she cannot control herself from crying out that she desires no other husband than you. To you, she says, if she were to be denied, she would rather grow old in her own home <term>laribus</term> <note>original: "laribus." In Roman religion, the Lares were household gods; the term is used here as a classical way to say "within her own walls" or "at home."</note> than risk the danger of others. Indeed, if they are compared to one another, she does not seem to herself less worthy than her sister. If that one probes the causes, this one produces the effects; if that one contemplates, this one—being active enough—proposes that those things which fell under contemplation should come into the light of men; and if that one is proud of discovery, this one, on account of her wondrous operations, does not* <note>The text ends mid-sentence at the bottom of the page; the "wondrous operations" refer to the practical experiments and results described in this expanded edition.</note>

<summary>Giambattista della Porta dedicates this expanded edition of his "Natural Magic" to the Ragusan nobleman Iunio Bobali. Using a playful metaphor, he describes the book as a "daughter" eager to find a patron as distinguished as the one her "sister" (the previous edition) found.</summary>
<keywords>Giambattista della Porta, Iunio Bobali, Ragusa, dedication, Natural Magic, patronage, metaphor of books as daughters</keywords>

*...is less ambitious. In these matters, not only is the mind nourished by understanding, but all the senses of the body are also enticed and refreshed by the practical effects. This Magic, therefore, excels all other sciences (though I exclude divine Philosophy), so that all other arts and faculties seem to serve her as if she were their queen. Cicero writes: No one among the Persians was accustomed to obtain the kingdom who had not first mastered Magic. And Plato in the* Alcibiades: *The sons of the Persian Kings are so instructed, that they might learn to administer and organize their own Commonwealth according to the model of the worldly Commonwealth <note>original: "mundana Reipubl." This refers to the Stoic and Platonic idea of the "Cosmopolis," or the universe as a divinely ordered state. By learning Magic, the king learns how the universe is governed, allowing him to rule his kingdom in harmony with nature.</note>. Why should I mention Pythagoras, Empedocles, Apollonius of Tyana, and Plato—the most famous men in nearly the whole world—who burned with such a desire for it that they traveled the globe to learn it? They undertook journeys that were more like exiles than voyages, and having returned, they preached it and held it among their secrets <term>arcanis</term> <note>original: "arcanis." In the context of the Renaissance, "arcana" were "secrets of nature"—hidden knowledge not meant for the uninitiated.</note>. Why mention the Magi Kings coming to adore Christ, and the many others illustrious in this art, with whose names the monuments of the ancients are filled? But who will fairly weigh my labors, my sleepless nights, and the expenses I poured into adorning this daughter of mine, so that she might finally seem worthy of you? I did this so she would not waste away with envy for her sister while trying to emulate such noble works. The point is, since she is not inferior to her sister, she disdains to marry an inferior man. For you <note>Della Porta is likely referring to Iunio and a relative (perhaps his father Andrea or a brother) to whom the previous edition was dedicated, or simply comparing Iunio to the highest standards of his family.</note> are born of the same blood, adorned with the same gifts of Nature and Fortune, and possess the same character of mind, countenance, and excellence. If in one there is the magnificence of Alexander, in the other there is the magnificence of Caesar. If in one there is the strength of the Fabii, in the other the strength of the Scipiones <note>The Fabii and Scipiones were among the most powerful and storied families of Ancient Rome.</note>: one is no less wise than the other is prudent, and finally—to say it in a single word—such is the integrity of your character, and your incredi-*

<summary>Della Porta argues for the superiority of "Natural Magic" over other sciences, citing ancient authorities like Plato and Cicero, and explains his effort in expanding the work to be worthy of his patron.</summary>

...incredible kindness <note>original: "humanitas." In the Renaissance, this referred to both a refined education and a gentle, civilized character.</note>, and your other virtues compete with one another: so that while each strives to outdo the next in this noble contest of distinguished virtues, each surpassing itself, they crown you with all their splendor <note>original: "pompa." This implies a magnificent, ceremonial display.</note> and triumph. As for myself, I am compelled to admit these things; and since there is nothing I have more earnestly desired in my prayers, I obey most willingly. I send her <note>Referring to the "daughter," a metaphor for this book, as established on the previous page.</note> to you. But amidst such great affection, do not forget me. Farewell, and give my greetings to your brothers, Marino and Michael, in my name.

# TO THE READERS
## P R E F A C E.

<image-desc>An ornamental drop-cap letter 'E' within a square frame decorated with floral patterns and scrolls.</image-desc>

BEHOLD, fair-minded readers, a work on Magic <note>original: "Magiæ." In this context, Natural Magic refers to the study of the hidden powers of nature (science), rather than sorcery.</note> nearly completed. If, when it was first printed by a youth barely fifteen years old <note>Porta published the first version of *Natural Magic* in 1558; while he claims to have been fifteen, records suggest he may have been in his early twenties.</note>, having just left childhood behind, it was received with such great applause and eagerness that it was translated into many languages—namely Italian, French, Spanish, and Arabic—and frequently printed in those same places, flying through the hands and mouths of many; then now, coming forth from a fifty-year-old man, I hope it will be received even more dearly and with greater favor. For indeed, when I saw the first fruits of the work received with such gratitude, I was moved by these favorable omens <note>original: "auspiciis." A metaphor from Roman divination, meaning a lucky start or sign of success.</note> to strive that it might be printed in an enlarged, richer, and more noble form. From that time when it was first published (now thirty-five years ago), if any man has ever felt a heavier burden of care to reveal the secrets of nature, I can plainly profess that I am that man. With my whole mind and all my strength, I have pored over the monuments of our ancestors <note>referring to the classic texts of ancient Greek and Roman scientists.</note>, and if they wrote anything secret or hidden, I have gathered the choice parts <note>original: "defloraui," literally 'to pluck the flowers,' meaning to select the finest or most important excerpts.</note>. Then, when I had traveled through Italy, France, and Spain, I visited libraries and all the most learned men. I even met with craftsmen <note>original: "artifices." Porta famously sought practical knowledge from artisans, alchemists, and laborers to verify scientific theories.</note> so that I might learn if they had discovered anything new or curious, and recognize what things they had proven to be most true and useful through long experience—

->rem.<- <note>This is a catchword, indicating the first syllable of the first word on the following page (likely "removendo" or "remotissima").</note>

<summary>In this preface, Giambattista della Porta introduces the expanded edition of his work on Natural Magic, reflecting on its international success since its original publication in his youth. He describes his decades of research, travel, and consultation with both scholars and craftsmen to uncover the secrets of nature.</summary>

->PREFACE.<-
)( 4

I solicited cities and men, whom I did not have the chance to visit in person, with frequent letters, asking them to share copies of hidden books or anything new they might possess; I did not hold back from prayers, gifts, exchanges, skill, or industry. Because of this, throughout this entire time, whatever was exceptional or desirable anywhere in the world—whether in books or in the most excellent physical objects—was sought out by me most abundantly, so that this equipment of Nature <note>original: "Naturæ hæc supellex." Porta uses the word "furniture" or "equipment" to describe his collection of scientific specimens and knowledge.</note> might be more complete and enlarged. 

Therefore, with the most intense study and persistent experimentation, I tested day and night whether the things I had read or heard were true or false, so that nothing would remain untried. I frequently remembered the sentiment of Cicero, who said: *It is right that those who desire to hand down to memory the most useful, carefully weighed, and explored things for the human race should try everything.* <note>original: "Par est eos, qui generi humano res utilissimas & perpēsas, exploratasq; memoriæ tradere concupierint, cuncta tentare."</note> In testing these things, I spared no labor and no expense; I expended my meager means with grand magnificence <note>original: "res angustas meas, augusta magnificentia impendi." Porta is making a Latin wordplay on "angustas" (narrow/meager) and "augusta" (majestic/grand).</note>. 

Nor was there any lack of labor, diligence, and wealth from most famous heroes, magnates, nobles, and most learned men—especially (whom I mention for the sake of honor) the Illustrious and most Reverend <term>Cardinal of Este</term> <note>Luigi d'Este (1538–1586), a powerful patron of the arts and sciences and a member of the ruling family of Ferrara.</note>; all of these men provided free and kind assistance to this work of ours. Nor was there ever lacking at my home an <term>Academy</term> <note>This refers to the *Academia Secretorum Naturae* (Academy of the Secrets of Nature), a scientific society founded by Porta in Naples. Members were required to contribute a new discovery in natural science to join.</note> of curious men who, by pooling their resources, devoted strenuous and eager effort to investigating and testing these matters, and who were the greatest help to me in organizing and enlarging this work. These things, therefore, with such great expenses, labor, and study...

<summary>Porta describes his exhaustive research process, which involved international correspondence, personal financial sacrifice, and the collaborative efforts of his private scientific academy and noble patrons like Cardinal Luigi d'Este.</summary>

<keywords>scientific method, Cicero, Cardinal d'Este, Academia Secretorum Naturae, patronage, experimentation, book collection</keywords>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's preface to the expanded edition of his work on natural magic. On the previous page, Giambattista della Porta described the great effort and expense he went through to gather secrets of nature from across the world and test them through experiment.</meta>

->PREFACE.<-

With these things prepared, and as I was already "packing my bags" <note>original: "sarcinulas colligens." A metaphorical expression suggesting the author is preparing for the end of his life or the conclusion of his work.</note>, I remained anxious in my mind as to whether I should allow them to come into the light. For there are many things here that are most excellent and worthy of the greatest heroes; yet if ignorant men, not yet initiated into the sacred mysteries of **Philosophy**, were to obtain them, they would surely become cheapened and despised. Plato says to Dionysius: *Those who attempt to hand these things over to unrefined and profane men seem to make philosophy look ridiculous.* <note>original: "Philosophiam videntur ridiculam facere, qui agrestibus & prophanis viris hæc tradere conantur."</note> Furthermore, there are many things that are harmful and malicious, which, if they fell into the hands of wicked and dishonest men, could bring harm to someone. 

What, then, should be done? Let envy be defeated and cast aside; let the pleasure of helping future generations prevail. The most majestic wonders of **Nature** must not be concealed or kept silent, so that in them the supreme power, kindness, and **wisdom** of God may be praised, cherished, and venerated. However small these things may be, I set them out for you; may you recognize that my diligence and most devoted will were directed toward you. Indeed, I feared that I would incur the guilt of a wicked man if I had kept these secrets hidden. Cicero carries over a thought from Plato: *We are not born for ourselves alone, but our country, our parents, and our friends should claim a part of us for themselves.* <note>original: "Non nobis solum nos esse natos, sed partem patria, partem parentes & amici sibi vindicare debent." This is a famous Stoic sentiment found in Cicero's "De Officiis," emphasizing social duty over private gain.</note>

Therefore, let those things which until now lay hidden in the lap of wondrous Nature emerge into the light from the storehouses of the most renowned men, without disguise or deception. We reveal those things about which there has long been silence—whether because of the **envy** of the knowledgeable or the ignorance of the unlearned. Here you will not hear empty trifles, nor riddles, nor the mere authorities of others. Nor did it seem right to us to "err honorably" <note>original: "honeste errare." Porta implies that he prefers finding the truth through his own experiments rather than following the prestigious but incorrect theories of ancient authors.</note> by following even the best leaders. Most magnificent and excellent—

<meta>catchword: —issima (the conclusion of "praestantissima")</meta>

<summary>In this preface, Della Porta grapples with the ethical dilemma of publishing powerful natural secrets that could be misused by the "ignorant" or "wicked," ultimately deciding that the benefit to humanity and the glorification of God's handiwork outweigh the risks of secrecy.</summary>
<keywords>ethics of science, secrecy, Plato, Cicero, natural philosophy, divine wisdom, public good, experimental method</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the preface of Giambattista della Porta’s work. On the previous page, the author discussed the ethical dilemma of publishing "secrets of nature" that could be dangerous in the wrong hands, quoting Plato and Cicero on the duty to share knowledge while protecting it from the profane.</meta>

->PREFACE.<-

...the most excellent things <note>original: "fima," likely the conclusion of "purissima" or "excellentissima" from the preceding page.</note> we have veiled with a certain artifice, such as by the transposition and suppression of words. Those things which are harmful and malicious, we have obscured; yet not in such a way that a very clever person cannot uncover and perceive them. Nor have we made them so clear that they are exposed to the ignorant crowd; not so hidden that the mind of a searcher cannot grasp them, nor so open that they promise the same things in the inner recesses as they do on the surface. We have added some useful and well-known things because they are most true. Sometimes, from the most familiar and even the commonest things, one arrives at useful and lofty matters which the mind can barely perceive. Our intellect, unless it rests upon the truest principles, cannot contemplate high and sublime things. **Mathematical science** <term>Mathematica scientia: here referring to the logical method of starting from simple, self-evident axioms to prove complex truths.</term> rises from certain trite and common starting points to many arduous and sublime heights; hence it seemed better to write true and useful things rather than false and grand ones. True things, however small they may be, provide a handle <note>original: "ansam," a common Latin metaphor for an opportunity or a starting point for further discovery.</note> for thinking out greater things. 

The incomprehensible and infinite multitude of things extends to infinity, and it is greater than can be considered by men. In our writing, we will set down the works of our ancestors or more recent authors; next, we reveal whether they were true or false as tested by our own experience; afterward, we present our own discoveries, so that the learned may see how remarkably the age of the moderns has surpassed antiquity. For there are many who have written about things they had never seen, and did not even know the simple components entering the work, but described them through the traditions of others with a certain innate and troublesome zeal for adding more. Thus, errors are successively propagated, and finally increase so immensely that not even the footprints <note>The text cuts off here, likely leading to "not even the footprints of truth remain."</note>...

<meta>This page continues Giambattista della Porta’s preface to "Natural Magic." On the previous page, the author discussed the importance of building knowledge upon simple, true principles rather than grand falsehoods, mentioning how he intended to record the works of the ancients.</meta>

->PREFACE.<-

<note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing from the previous page's discussion of the writings of the ancients.</note> ...indeed, those of the first rank appear in such a way that they can be read not only with difficult experimentation, but not even without frequent laughter. Furthermore, we omit many who, while they transmit wonderful things to be known by posterity and promise **mountains of gold**, write something different from what they actually believed. Hence, those endowed with a more sublime talent and more eager for learning are held back by the longest interval of time; because they distrust that they can attain those things, and they realize they have wasted their **labor and oil** <note>original: "operam & oleum contriuiſſe," a Latin proverb meaning to waste one's time, effort, and money on a fruitless task, referring to the oil burned in a lamp while working late.</note>, they are driven by despair and regret it too late. Others, then, made wise by the danger of another, learn to hate these things before they even know them. 

We have divided these **Secrets** into their own classes, so that everyone may have what pleases them. Finally, I would have gladly passed over offending your ears if I did not care to refute the slanders of detractors and the envious, who tear me apart quite immodestly, thinking me to be a <term>Magician</term> and a <term>poisoner</term> <note>original: "Magum veneficum." In the 16th century, "veneficus" referred to a sorcerer who specifically used harmful potions or "black" magic.</note>, a name I have dreaded and thought vain from my **tenderest years** <note>original: "à teneris vnguiculis," literally "from my tender fingernails," a Latin idiom meaning from earliest childhood.</note>. 

For my part, I have always considered myself a man, subject to fallacies and errors; I have entreated all the most learned men to refute me if I have interpreted anything unfaithfully. But what I always dreaded has happened: I have fallen among a most vile and hated kind of men, who snatch up a sordid little glory and a vulgar, popular breeze from the injury of others, whether just or unjust. Those wounded by their virulent bites do not waste away, but rather, by twisting the poison back upon the attackers, these men cast down their own reputation instead. A certain **Frenchman** <note>This refers to the French jurist and philosopher Jean Bodin (c. 1530–1596).</note> in his book on <term>Demonomania</term> <note>original: "Dæmonomania," referring to Bodin's famous 1580 work "De la démonomanie des sorciers," which was a treatise on the prosecution of witches.</note>, called me a <term>Magician</term> and sorcerer...

<meta>catchword: sorcerer [neficum]</meta>

<summary>In this portion of the preface, della Porta defends his work against critics and "mountains of gold" charlatans, specifically addressing accusations of black magic made by the French philosopher Jean Bodin.</summary>

He is responding to critics who labeled him a sorcerer due to his previous writings on the "witches' ointment"—a recipe he claimed had natural, rather than demonic, effects. ->PRÆFATIO.<-

<note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing the author's defense against his critics.</note> ...considers me a **poisoner**, and thinks this book of mine, printed long ago, is worthy of the fire, because I wrote about the **ointment of witches** <note>original: "lamiarum vnguentum." Porta famously investigated recipes for "flying ointments" used by suspected witches, arguing they were actually pharmacological hallucinogens rather than magical substances.</note>, which I had brought forward to expose the detestable deceits of demons and hags; so that those things which occur by nature itself should not be misused in superstitions; which I had excerpted from the books of highly praised theologians. In this, how have I sinned, or why have I deserved the name of a **poisoner** <term>veneficum</term> <note>In the 16th century, "veneficus" referred to someone who used potions for harmful magic; it translates to both "poisoner" and "sorcerer."</note>?

But when I asked many noble and learned Frenchmen, who deign to meet with me with great honor, "Who is this man?" they responded that he is a heretic, and one who, on the feast of **Saint Bartholomew** <note>Referring to the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre in 1572, a targeted group of assassinations followed by a wave of Catholic mob violence directed against the Huguenots (French Calvinist Protestants).</note>—on which day a slaughter was declared against all such impious men—escaped danger by throwing himself headlong from a lookout point. 

Meanwhile, I shall pray to God Most High (as becomes a noble and Christian man) that, having been converted to the Roman Catholic faith, he himself might not be condemned to be burned alive. Another Frenchman, while unworthily condemning all the learned men of his age, attaches me to them: he thinks only three physicians, his friends, are worthy of praise as if they were the most learned of our time; among whom he includes himself, even though his own book is circulated without the author's name. 

Oh, immortal God, what sort of trick to seize praise has this man devised? He who, since he has no one to praise him, nor is judged worthy of being praised, praises himself. I pass over others of that same sort, who also consider me a **sorcerous magician** <term>Magum veneficum</term>; whereas nothing has ever been treated by me here or elsewhere that is not contained within the **boundaries of nature** <term>Naturæ promœria</term> <note>Porta uses "pomoeria" (or "promœria"), a term for the sacred boundary of a city, to define the limits of natural science vs. forbidden magic.</note>. Receive...

-># PREFACE<-

<note>The text continues directly from the previous page's prayer for the author's critic.</note> ...that he may be restored to his senses. Therefore, **eager readers**, receive with that same generous spirit with which we offer these long labors, undertaken with no small zeal, sleepless nights, great expense, and many hardships. Cast aside the blindness of mind and soul, as well as the envy that is so often accustomed to dull the edge of the intellect and block the path of truth. Weigh these matters with upright judgment as you examine what we have written; for once you discover both the **truth** and the **usefulness** of this work, you will perhaps be more favorable toward my studies. 

Although it does not escape me that there will be many ignorant men, idle in any serious matter, who will look upon these things with hatred and envy. They will rashly claim that some things are not only false, but even impossible. While they strive to overturn the truth with arguments and empty debates, they truly act in such a way that by "understanding," they understand nothing at all, and thus their own ignorance is laid bare. 

Such men, like the **profane** <note>original: "prophani." Here meaning those uninitiated into the secrets of nature or those who lack the proper intellectual reverence for the subject.</note>, ought to be barred from the boundaries of our **Natural Magic** <term>Magia Naturalis</term> <note>Porta defines "Natural Magic" not as demonic sorcery, but as the highest part of the natural sciences—the practical application of the hidden "virtues" or powers of plants, minerals, and animals.</note>. For those who do not place faith in the miracles of Nature are, in a way, attempting to abolish **Philosophy** <note>In the 16th century, "Natural Philosophy" was the precursor to modern science, involving the study of the physical universe.</note> itself. 

But if we have omitted anything or spoken clumsily: I know that nothing is so well-adorned that it cannot be further polished, nor so full that it cannot

# GIAMBATTISTA
## PORTA OF NAPLES,
## ON NATURAL MAGIC,
### BOOK ONE,

->Which investigates the causes of things, from which marvelous<-
->effects flow.<-

### *What Magic Signifies.* CHAPTER I.

Among the Platonists, Porphyry and Apuleius testify clearly in the speech for <term>Magic</term> <note>Referring to Apuleius’s *Apologia*, a famous legal defense against charges of practicing sorcery.</note> that Magic took its name and origin from Persia. Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine Greek encyclopedia and lexicon.</note> the Greek thinks the name was derived from the *maguseis*. Cicero, in his book *On Divination*, says: "A <term>Magus</term> <note>original: "Magus"</note>, in the Persian language, is nothing other than an interpreter and servant of divine things; it is a class of wise men among them." Jerome, writing to Paulinus, says that Apollonius of Tyana <note>A first-century philosopher and reputed miracle-worker often compared to Jesus or Pythagoras.</note> was a Magus (as the common people say) or a Philosopher (as the Pythagoreans assert). Pliny stated that among authors it is certain without doubt that it arose in Persia from Zoroaster, son of Oromasius; more diligent scholars say there was another Zoroaster of Proconnesus shortly before him. Osthanes <note>A legendary figure considered the first writer on magic who allegedly introduced the art to the Greeks.</note> was the first to write comments on it, having accompanied Xerxes, the King of the Persians, in the war he brought against Greece; he scattered the seeds of this wondrous art in passing, infecting whatever part of the world he traveled through, which drove the Greek people not just to a greed for this knowledge, but to a frenzy. <term>Magic</term> therefore is accepted by everyone as wisdom and the perfect knowledge of natural things; and they call those men <term>Magi</term> whom the Latins call "Wise Men" and the Greeks call "Philosophers."

<summary>This opening page of Giambattista della Porta’s "Natural Magic" defines the term "Magic" not as sorcery, but as the pinnacle of wisdom and the study of nature, tracing its origins to ancient Persia and the figure of Zoroaster.</summary>
<keywords>natural magic, definition of magic, Zoroaster, Persian wisdom, ancient philosophy, history of science, Magi, Osthanes</keywords>

--- Page 40 ---
<meta>This page continues the introductory discussion of the history of magic from page 1. It completes the list of historical figures associated with ancient wisdom and begins Chapter II, which establishes the crucial distinction between "Natural Magic" and "Sorcery." The catchword "derunt" from the previous page completes the word "prodiderunt" (they have put forward) in the final sentence here.</meta>

<page-num>2</page-num>
<header>NATURAL MAGIC, BOOK I.</header>

from the one Pythagoras, the first of that name, as Diogenes writes; the Indian Brahmins, and the Gymnosophists in Greek (as if you were to say "naked philosophers"), the Babylonians, as well as the Assyrian Chaldeans named after Chaldea, a region of Asia; the Celtic Gauls have their Druids, Bards, and Semnotheoi; the Egyptians their Priests; the <term>Kabbalists</term> <note>original: Chabalistæ; practitioners of Jewish mysticism</note> their Prophets: and so Magic overflows with different names among various nations. But we find that most of these were men highly skilled in the things of Nature, such as Zoroaster, son of Oromasius, among the Persians (as we have said); Numa Pompilius among the Romans; Tespion among the Gymnosophists; Zamolxis among the Thracians; Abaris among the Hyperboreans; Hermes among the Egyptians; and Buddha among the Babylonians. Furthermore, Apuleius mentions Carimondas, Damigeron, Hismoses <note>Likely a reference to Moses.</note>, Apollonius, and Dardanus after Zoroaster and Osthanes.

->What Magic is. CHAPTER II.<-

They divide <term>Magic</term> <note>original: μαγείαν (mageian)</note> itself into two parts. One is infamous and ill-omened due to its dealings with unclean spirits, constructed and fashioned by incantations and the art of wicked curiosity; this they call <term>Goeteia</term> <note>original: γοητείαν; sorcery or low magic, often associated with fraud and malevolence</note>. All learned and outstanding men oppose this, for beyond mere imaginings, it offers no truth of reason or essence, and no trace of it remains afterward, as Iamblichus holds in his book *On the Mysteries of the Egyptians*. The other kind is Natural Magic, which every wise man receives with joyful applause, cultivates, and honors; nothing is higher, nothing more pleasing to those devoted to good literature. To learn and investigate this, we read that the most eminent leaders in Philosophy—Pythagoras, Empedocles, Democritus, and Plato—departed from their homelands, undertaking what were more like exiles than travels. Upon their return, they preached this magic and held it among their secrets. Men most skilled in hidden literature call it the very pinnacle of the natural sciences and its most perfect faculty; so much so, that if anything nobler or closer to a miracle can be fashioned or imagined in the natural sciences, they would call it Magic. Others have put forward that it is the active portion of natural Philosophy...

<summary>Porta traces the diverse names for magic across global cultures before defining the essential difference between "Goeteia" (dark sorcery) and "Natural Magic," which he defends as the highest form of scientific inquiry studied by ancient philosophers.</summary>
<keywords>Brahmins, Druids, Gymnosophists, Pythagoras, Plato, Goeteia, Natural Magic, Philosophy, Science, Ancient Wisdom</keywords>

--- Page 41 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the definition of Magic from Chapter II. Having previously distinguished "Natural Magic" from "Goeteia" (dark sorcery), the author now defines Natural Magic as a legitimate science rooted in the observation and application of nature's own laws. It cites the authority of the Platonists and classical authors to frame magic as a "royal" science of harmony and attraction.</meta>

# ON THE CAUSES OF THINGS. #

<sig>A 2</sig>

...put forward, producing its effects from a mutual and timely application. The <term>Platonists</term>—as Plotinus, following Mercury <note>original: Mercurium; referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of hermetic philosophy</note>, writes in his book *On Sacrifice and Magic*—believe it to be a science by which lower things are subjected to higher, or earthly things to celestial; and by certain charms sought out by art, it allures the quality of the universe. For this reason, the Egyptians called Nature itself a "Magician" <note>original: Magam</note>, because it possesses a power in alluring and attracting similar things through things similar to themselves, and that this power consists in "love"; those things drawn together by a kinship of Nature, they called "magical attractions." 

To us, however, Magic seems to be nothing other than the contemplation of all Nature. For from the consideration of the motions of the heavens, the stars, the elements, and their transmutations, as well as the hidden secrets of the birth and death of animals, plants, and minerals, the whole of this science seems to depend upon the "face of Nature"—as we shall see more broadly. Plato seems to indicate this in his *Alcibiades*, where he says the Magic of <term>Zoroaster</term> seemed to him nothing other than the science and worship of divine things. The sons of the Persian Kings are imbued with this among their royal duties, so that they might learn to govern and administer their own Commonwealth <note>original: Remp. (Republicam)</note> according to the image of the worldly Commonwealth <note>the Cosmos or the Great World</note>. 

And Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note>, in his book *On Divination*, says that no one among the Persians obtains royal majesty who has not been imbued with magical science; for just as Nature governs the world by mutual disagreement and agreement, so they themselves may learn to govern their own state. This science, I say, being master of great power and overflowing with hidden mysteries, bestows a knowledge of the qualities and properties of hidden things and of all Nature. It teaches how to separate or join things by mutual and timely application based on their agreement <note>original: consensu; also called "sympathy"</note> and disagreement <note>original: dissensu; also called "antipathy"</note>, so that it performs those works which the common people call "miracles"—works exceeding all admiration or human understanding. 

Therefore, it flourished in Ethiopia and India, where there was an abundant supply of herbs, stones, and other materials pertaining to it. Wherefore you, who come to witness Magic, should believe the works of Magic to be nothing other than the works of Nature, where Art serves as a diligent handmaid. For wherever Art recognizes something missing from a natural kinship, it restores it through vapors and numbers at the proper times, just as in Agriculture...

<summary>This page defines Natural Magic as the "contemplation of all Nature," distinguishing it from sorcery by framing it as a royal science practiced by Persian kings and ancient philosophers. It explains that magic works by applying the natural "sympathy" (love) and "antipathy" between things to produce effects that appear miraculous to the unlearned.</summary>
<keywords>Natural Magic, Plotinus, Hermes Trismegistus, Egyptian magic, Zoroaster, Plato, Cicero, sympathy and antipathy, royal science, wonders of nature</keywords>

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on the definition of magic as the contemplation of nature. Having established that magic is a natural science rather than a dark art, the author now transitions to the practical requirements and education necessary for a true magician.</meta>

->ON THE NATURAL MAGIC, BOOK I.<-

...Nature herself produces herbs and crops, but art prepares them. For this reason, the poet <term>Antipho</term> <note>Antipho of Rhamnus, a 5th-century BC Athenian orator and poet</note> used to say that by art we overcome those things by which we are conquered by nature; and <term>Plotinus</term> <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 204–270 AD) who viewed the universe as an interconnected living being</note> calls the Magician a servant of Nature, not its master <note>original: artificem; literally "artificer" or "craftsman," implying one who makes something from scratch rather than working with nature's existing materials</note>. You superstitious, profane, and impious men—begone from here! We have nothing in common with you; the door is closed against you. We believe you should not only be expelled from these borders, but from the city and the world, punished, and brought to ruin. But what duty and learning this "servant" should possess, we intend to demonstrate in the following.

### *On the Instruction of a Magician, and What Kind of Teacher of Magic is Required. CHAPTER III.* ###

It is now proper to instruct the Magician, and to show what he ought to know and remember, so that being equipped in every way, he may undertake wondrous and marvelous effects. Since we have described active Magic itself as a portion of <term>Natural Philosophy</term> <note>The historical study of nature and the physical universe that was the precursor to modern science</note>, I would rightly desire a Magician—who ought to possess such great majesty—to be exact and perfected in Philosophy, and most highly skilled. For Philosophy itself teaches:

> *What heat accomplishes, what the earth, the soil, and the air,*
> *What the waves generate, the origins of the great heavens,*
> *From whence comes the tide of the sea, and how the rainbow shows various colors,*
> *What causes the echoing thunder and the spheres to return,*
> *What secrets bring forth torches* <note>original: faces; referring to meteors or celestial lights</note> *in the night, and what cause produces comets,*
> *And what hidden power shakes the swelling earth,*
> *Where the seeds of gold and iron lie,*
> *And the entire ingenious force of hidden Nature.*

Let him also not be ignorant of Medicine, for it is related and very similar to this science. They say it crept in under this guise and so enticed the minds of men, and it provides many protections for us. For it teaches the mixtures of temperaments <note>The "temperament" or "complexion" was the specific balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—within a person or substance</note> and how to compose and apply them in a proportionate way to achieve results. Next, in the identification of herbs, we do not require a simple botanist, but a most keen investigator of plants <note>original: stirpium vestigatorem</note>; for we have labored long and hard over some works because of the vague naming of plants and their indistinguishable similarities. Nor is anything more unsuitable for the practitioner than [the lack of] instru-

<meta>catchword: ments [instrumenta]</meta>

<summary>This page defines the magician as a "servant of nature" and outlines the broad scientific education required for the practice, including natural philosophy, medicine, and botany. It explicitly distances natural magic from superstition and impiety, framing it as a rigorous academic pursuit.</summary>

<keywords>natural magic, education, natural philosophy, medicine, botany, Plotinus, Antipho, temperaments, secrets of nature</keywords>

--- Page 43 ---
<meta>This page continues the curriculum of the Magician. Following the requirement for mastery in Philosophy, the author now lists the specific scientific disciplines—Chemistry (Distillation), Mineralogy, Astrology, and Optics—that serve as the "handmaidens" of Natural Magic.</meta>

# ON THE CAUSES OF THINGS. #
->A 3<-

...to be ignorant of the elements with which nature works, and we judge this so necessary that everything depends upon it. Nor is it less fitting to know metals, minerals, stones, and gems. Furthermore, we think there will be no one who doubts how much value one should place on the art of **distillation**—an imitator and, as it were, the offspring of heavenly rains. For it daily brings forth marvelous inventions, most ingeniously devised, and many things useful to the lot of mortals. It allows one to draw out dewy vapors from things, as well as misty and fatty spirits, clumps, and gummy liquids, and to elicit the essence hiding in the innermost chambers, raising it to a sublime state so that we may enrich its powers. However, let the student learn to do this not with a **crude or thick wit** <note>original: "crassa Minerva"; a Latin idiom referring to a plain, unrefined, or uneducated intellect</note>, but by its own causes and reasons.

One must also master the mathematical disciplines, and especially **Astrology** <note>In the 16th century, "Astrology" encompassed both the mapping of stars (astronomy) and the study of their influences</note>; for it demonstrates:

> *By what motion the lofty stars of heaven are swept along,*
> *What force now compels the darkening Moon to grow dim,*
> *How the golden Sun, according to fixed and measured parts,*
> *Guides the orb through the twelve constellations of the world.*

Indeed, through the many-wandering curves and habits of the heavens, many celestial gifts are bestowed upon the earth; they draw forth many powers for both being acted upon and for operating, and various properties of things flow from them. For this reason, the inquiry into how the heavens receive these influences long tormented and anxious the minds of the **Platonists** <note>Followers of Plato who believed the physical world was a reflection of a higher, spiritual reality connected by "influxes" or "emanations"</note>. 

Let him also be instructed in the faculty of **Optics**, so that he may know how the eyes are deceived, and how visions are formed in water or in mirrors of various shapes—even so that they project images hanging outside in the air. Let him know how to make those things which are far off be seen clearly, and how to hurl fire a very long distance; upon these things a great part of the secrets of **Magic** depends. 

Magic has adopted these sciences as its followers and helpers, and whoever is ignorant of them shall be held unworthy of the name of **Magician**. Let him be an artisan and a mechanic by the gift of Nature: for a scholar without craftsmanship, or an ignorant artisan (so closely are these things joined), will spend his labor in vain and never possess his heart's desire. Some, by the gift of heaven, are so skillful in these matters that they seem to have been molded by God for them. Nor do I say this to suggest that Art cannot polish anything, or that good things cannot be made better, or that things which are not the best cannot be sharpened and corrected in some way.

...to be able to do so. With a knowing mind and diligence, let the practitioner first consider and prepare the matter, then soon set about the work, doing nothing rashly. I wished to say this so that if an ignorant man is deceived, he does not turn it into a fault of ours, but blames his own ignorance; for this is a weakness not of the teacher, but of the one attempting the work. For if these matters are handled by a novice, faith in science will be undermined, and it will happen that things which are most true and result from necessary causes appear to be accidental. 

If you wish the things you perform to seem more marvelous, remove the knowledge of the cause; for that is a wonder whose cause is hidden from the spectator. He who knows the causes greatly diminishes the authority of the work; a thing will be held as rare and unusual only so far as its causes are concealed. Aristotle says in the *Mechanics*: "Architects construct instruments, concealing their principles to provide admiration." <note>original: "Architecti instrumenta fabricant, celantes principia illius, quæ admirationem præstant."</note> Someone once extinguished a lamp and, by moving it back toward a wall or a stone, lit it again as if it were a miraculous thing; and then, as Galen says, it ceased to be a wonder once they found it had been touched with sulfur. <note>original: "sulphure contactum reperiere." Sulfur has a very low ignition point; Porta is describing a common "magic" trick where a recently extinguished wick is relit by the heat of a surface or a hidden spark.</note> Ephesius says: "A miracle is dissolved by the same means from which it appears to be a miracle." <note>original: "Miraculum inde soluitur, vnde videtur esse miraculum."</note> 

Let the practitioner also be wealthy in fortune; for we work with difficulty if resources are not available. Indeed, one must grow rich to philosophize, not philosophize to grow rich. <note>This is a play on a common proverb; Porta argues that experimental science is an expensive pursuit that requires significant funding for materials and equipment.</note> Let him not spare expenses but be lavish in his inquiries; and while he searches more attentively and thoroughly, let him not be reluctant to repeat his efforts, nor spare his labor. For the secrets of nature are not opened to the idle and the ignorant. Whence Epicharmus used to say rightly:

> The gods sell everything to mortals for the price of labor. <note>original: "Deos mortalibus omnia laboris pretio vendere."</note>

And if the effects do not match the description, know that you have failed in some part; for we have written briefly not for the unrefined and for beginners, but for craftsmen and the ingenious.

...they established first principles, as **Hippasus of Metapontum** and **Heraclides of Pontus** chose fire; **Diogenes of Apollonia** and **Anaximenes** chose air; and **Thales of Miletus** chose water. These they established as the original seeds of Nature—namely the elements, which are simple bodies. (Nowadays, however, they are considered illegitimate, <term>spurious</term> <note>Porta implies that the "elements" we see around us are no longer pure but are mixed and "adulterated" versions of the theoretical prime elements.</note>, and corrupted, being changed as they are mixed more or less with others.) These elements are the material principle of the natural body; they are agitated and subject to change through a perpetual cycle of transformation. They are so gathered together within the vast arches of the heavens that they fill this entire **sublunary world** <note>The "sublunary" realm refers to everything below the orbit of the moon, which in ancient cosmology was the region of change, decay, and the four elements.</note>. 

For **Fire**, being the lightest and purest, raises itself upward to escape our sight and claims the highest place for itself, which men call the **ether**. Closest to this is the element of **spirit** <note>original: "spiritus". In this context, it refers to the element of Air.</note>, which is a little heavier than fire. Spread out with immense breadth and passing through all things, it returns us to its own quality; at times it thickens into clouds, is forced into mists, and flows. Following these is **Water**. Then, finally, there is that which is scraped and condensed from the dregs of the elements, which is called **Earth**. It is spread beneath all else, thick, very solid, and impenetrable, so that nothing solid can be touched that lacks earth, and nothing is empty without spirit. Earth itself, balanced in the center of space, is walled in by all the others; it alone remains motionless, while the other elements are carried around it in a rotating whirl. 

**Hippon** and **Critias**, however, said that the "vapors" of the elements were the first principles. **Parmenides** declared them to be "qualities," for he said that all things consist of the hot and the cold. **Physicians** say things are made of the **four qualities**—hot, cold, moist, and dry—arising from the victory of one when they are mixed together. For each individual element embraces its neighbor as if with its arms, yet they disagree with those elements of contrary qualities. Nature, a wise architect, designed this machine with a fixed measure and wonderful fitness. Since there were two qualities in each element, in some there is a "joinable fellowship" <note>original: "iugabilis societas". This refers to the Aristotelian idea that elements share a quality with their neighbors, allowing them to transform into one another.</note>, while in others there is a disagreement. Nature gave to each a second quality shared with its neighbor, so that whatever it clings to, it has a quality akin and similar to itself. For example, **Air** and **Fire**: one is hot and dry, while the other is hot and moist. While "dry" and "moist" are contraries, they are nevertheless coupled by the conciliation of their shared "heat." Likewise, **Earth** is cold and dry, while **Water** is cold and...

### NATURAL MAGIC, BOOK I. ###
->8<-

...moist things, which although they are opposites through dryness and moisture, are nevertheless connected by the fellowship of cold; otherwise their agreement would be difficult. Thus **fire** gradually passes into **air** through heat, air into **water** through moisture, water into **earth** through cold; and earth is joined to fire through dryness, and so they proceed most providently. From there, they are transformed again in reverse order and are made from one another; for the transition is easy when they have obtained a common quality, such as fire and air through heat. However, those that are opposite in both qualities, like fire and water, are converted with more difficulty. 

Therefore heat, cold, moisture, and dryness are called the **primary qualities** <term>qualitates primae</term> <note>In ancient and medieval science, these four qualities were the "building blocks" of all physical matter.</note>, since they flow first from the elements, and from them secondary effects emanate. Two of these are active—heat and cold—which are born more to act than to be acted upon. The others—moisture and dryness—are passive, not because they are entirely idle, but because they are preserved and induced by the others. 

**Secondary qualities** are so called as if serving the first, and are said to work in the second place, such as to soften, to ripen, to dissolve, or to thin. For instance, when heat acts upon some mixture, it draws out the impure parts; and while it attempts to make it suitable for its action—so that it may become simpler—it ends up thin. Likewise, cold preserves, constricts, and congeals. Dryness thickens and roughens; for while it consumes the moisture on the surface that it cannot destroy, it hardens it; hence a roughness of the surface is induced, for when emptiness is depressed and hardness is elevated, a roughness and prominence of the parts occurs. 

Likewise moisture increases and corrupts, and mostly acts as one thing through itself and another through accident; as from ripening, constriction, expulsion and similar things, it calls forth milk, urine, menses, and sweat. These are called **tertiary qualities** by Physicians, serving the secondary just as those serve the primary. And sometimes they operate in certain limbs, such as strengthening the head or providing for the kidneys; these some also call **quaternary qualities**. These, therefore, they declared to be the foundations of all mixtures and wonderful operations; and whatever experiments they brought forward, they believed could be composed of these and their causes found. But **Empedocles of Agrigentum** <note>A Greek pre-Socratic philosopher (c. 490–430 BC) who is best known for originating the cosmogonic theory of the four classical elements.</note>, using the elements...

...examples are read in the process. And now, about to speak clearly on where they originate, I must begin a bit further back. In the composition of every **natural substance** <note>Porta defines "substance" as the union of matter and form—the physical stuff and the organizing principle.</note>, matter and form emerge as the primary principles. Nor do we exclude the functions of the qualities, which lay hidden in the elements from the beginning; these three together fill the total number of causes. 

When the elements themselves come together in the formation of an object, the formed object retains certain prevailing qualities. Although all qualities work together to produce an effect, it is believed the whole proceeds from the superior ones, since the object takes on the powers of the rest. For if all qualities competed equally, their power would be unnoticeable. 

Nor is matter entirely devoid of powers. I am not speaking of that primary and simple matter <note>This refers to "Prime Matter" (*materia prima*), a philosophical concept of pure potentiality without any physical characteristics.</note>, but that which is born from the elements and substances—especially from the two most "passive" elements, namely **earth** and **water**. These are what Aristotle sometimes calls "secondary qualities" and "bodily effects." Let us call them the functions of matter, or its powers, or whatever other name is pleasing—such as being rare, dense, rough, light, hard, or splittable. Though these are rooted deep within the lap of matter, they all come from the elements nevertheless. 

I have therefore judged it more correct, lest they be confused, to say that the effects of qualities flow from the **temperament** <note>In Renaissance science, "temperament" or "temperature" refers to the specific balance or mixture of the four primary qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry).</note>, while the effects of matter flow from its **consistency**. 

But so much power exists in the **form** that everyone knows the effects we observe are produced primarily by it. It has a divine origin; being superior and most excellent, it uses the other factors as instruments by itself, without the help of any other, to carry out its actions more quickly and easily. Anyone whose mind is not devoted to or practiced in speculation might think everything is achieved by temperament and matter alone, since things happen through them as if through tools. 

For if a craftsman uses a stylus or a chisel in the construction of a statue, he does not use it as the primary agent, but rather employs it to work more effectively. Since there are three efficient causes in every thing, do not think they are idle or at rest. All are productive: one more mildly, another more strongly, but above all the **form** itself accomplishes the work, strengthening the others,

### *From whence form arises, and concerning Homer’s chain and Plato’s rings. CHAPTER VI.* ###

Form, being the most excellent of all things, originates from a place of equal excellence. It comes directly from the highest celestial rotation, then from the **intelligences** <note>In Renaissance philosophy, "Intelligences" were the spiritual or angelic beings believed to guide the movements of the planets and stars.</note> to the heavens, and finally from God himself to those intelligences. Thus, the origin of forms is the same as the origin of properties. **Zeno of Citium** <note>original: *Zeno Cirticus*; likely an error for *Citieus*. Zeno was the founder of the Stoic school of philosophy.</note> joined God to matter, making one the active principle and the other the passive principle. For God—as **Plato** believes—when he had first established the heavens, the stars, and the very beginnings of things (the elements, which wither by the alternating cycle of birth and death) through the omnipotence of his divinity and with fitting harmony, then assigned the types of animals, plants, and inanimate objects. So that they would not share the same eternal condition as the heavens, he summoned the powers of the heavens and elements and assigned them through ranks; he decreed by a fatal law that lower things should serve the higher, and instilled in each its own form, filled with powers through the celestial influence. And so that the continuous procreation of things would not cease, he commanded each to bring forth seed and to lend its form to those prepared to receive it. Thus you will necessarily proclaim that forms coming from heaven itself are divine and celestial. In this consists the archetype of forms and the most noble cause, which Plato himself (the prince of philosophers) calls the **World Soul** <note>original: *mundi anima*; the vital spirit that Neoplatonists believed permeated all of nature.</note>, the great **Aristotle** calls **Universal Nature**, and **Avicenna** calls the **Giver of Forms**. God, drawing not from any perishable thing but from himself, imparts form first to the intelligences and the stars; then, he gives shape to the elements through their **aspects** <note>In astrology, an "aspect" is the angular relationship between planets that was believed to transmit specific influences to Earth.</note>, which act as instruments to prepare matter. Who then is so insane, so poorly formed by nature, that if these [powers come] from the elements, the heaven, the intelligences, and finally...

...that it comes from God himself, should one not call it celestial, since it does not savor of that [earthly] nature, and in a certain way reflects divine majesty? This combination of things, therefore—this series and order serving divine providence—ensures that all these lower things which are governed proceed originally in succession from God himself and receive the power of operating. For God, as **Macrobius** <note>Ambrosius Theodosius Macrobius (fl. 400 AD), a Roman provincial whose works on Neoplatonism were highly influential in the Renaissance.</note> says, who is the first cause, the prince and origin of all things, created **Mind** <note>original: *mentem*</note> from the abundance of his majesty. This Mind, in turn, created the **Soul** <note>original: *animam*; the author notes that "Christian truth holds otherwise," likely distancing himself from the Neoplatonic idea that the Soul was created by the Mind rather than directly by God.</note> which imparts **Reason** <note>original: *rationem*</note> to divine things, such as the heavens and the eternal fires (which is why they are said to be animated by divine minds). It also bestows the power of sensing and growing upon fragile, earthly things. **Maro** <note>The Roman poet Virgil (Publius Vergilius Maro).</note>, sensing this, calls the Mind the "Soul of the World" in these verses:

> *Spirit nourishes from within, and Mind, infused through all the members,*
> *stirs the mass and mingles itself with the great body.* <note>Virgil, *Aeneid*, Book VI, lines 726-727. A classic description of the "World Soul" animating the physical universe.</note>

Man, therefore, stands in the middle of both; while he falls away from the nobility of heaven, he yet shares in reason, by which he deserves to surpass the other animals. He also retains the power of sensation. The remaining animals, as they degenerate from him, retain only two remaining powers: to sense and to grow. Trees, however, because they lack sense and reason and require only the function of growing, are said to possess this alone—to grow and to live in this capacity. The Poet expresses this shortly after:

> *From here comes the race of men and beasts, the lives of birds,*
> *and the monsters the sea bears beneath its marble surface.* <note>Virgil, *Aeneid*, VI, 728-729.</note>

Since, therefore, Mind proceeds from God himself, and Soul from Mind, and the Soul itself animates all that follows, there is a harmony: the plant agrees with the beast in growth, the beast with man in sense, and man with the rest in intellect. Thus, from the first cause, like a cord stretched from heaven down to these lowest depths, there is a mutual binding and continuity. The superior power, by spreading its rays, reaches down to these things; so that if one end is touched, it trembles, and the rest is moved. Justly, then, might we call this connection "rings" or a "chain," corresponding to the **rings of Plato** <note>A reference to Plato’s *Ion*, where he uses magnetized iron rings to explain how divine inspiration passes from the Muse to the poet and then to the audience.</note> and the **Golden Chain of Homer**. <note>The *Catena Aurea*. In the *Iliad*, Zeus speaks of a golden chain suspended from heaven to earth; for Renaissance magicians, this symbolized the "Great Chain of Being" connecting all levels of reality.</note>

### *On sympathy and antipathy, and how through them the virtues of things can be discovered and tested.* CHAPTER VII.

From these <term>hidden properties</term> <note>original: *proprietatibus occultis*; qualities of a substance (like magnetism) that cannot be explained by the four physical elements (hot, cold, wet, dry).</note>, there exists in animals, vegetables, and all species a certain (if I may say so) compassion, which the Greeks call <term>sympatheia</term> <note>sympathy: a natural attraction or "agreement" between two different things.</note> and <term>antipatheia</term> <note>antipathy: a natural repulsion or "disagreement" between things, such as the supposed enmity between a lion and a rooster.</note>, and which we more commonly call **consensus** and **dissensus**. For certain things are joined together in a mutual marriage and bound as if by a treaty; others, however, are hostile to each other, disagreeing in enmity and struggling in blind discords. Some even possess something horrible and destructive, which cannot be sought out or constrained by any probable reasons. Nor is it the part of a wise man to try to prove the causes of such things, except to say that Nature herself was delighted by that spectacle. She did not wish anything to exist without a peer, and nothing exists among the secrets of Nature that does not thrive with some hidden and peculiar property. From these enmities and friendships, many **remedies** for human uses and needs were contemplated. For if one thing is seen to have enmity with another, that thing can be used as a remedy for the harms the other might inflict. Success favored this conjecture, and having discovered many things by this method, they handed them down to the memory of posterity, as can be seen from their records...

For while the vine is accustomed to embrace all things with its twisting tendrils, it flees from the cabbage alone. Sensing it nearby, the vine turns itself in the opposite direction, as if someone had warned it that an enemy was close at hand. Furthermore, while cabbage is being cooked, if you drip in even a tiny amount of wine, it will neither cook properly nor will its color remain consistent. **Androcides** <note>A physician to Alexander the Great who famously advised the king against excessive drinking.</note>, using this very example, deduced a remedy against wine: namely, that cabbage is able to drive away drunkenness, as **Theophrastus** <note>A Greek philosopher and the "father of botany."</note> says, since the vine itself flees even the scent of cabbage. 

This same vegetable, which puts the vine to flight, withers away when near the **cyclamen**; it is necessary that when one flourishes, the other dries up, and when planted together, they are often seen both withered. Cyclamen added to wine increases intoxication, whereas cabbage takes it away, as we have said. **Ivy**, although it leads all trees to their destruction, is especially opposed to the vine and harms it; for this reason, it also drives away drunkenness. 

There is also a marvelous discord and stubbornness between the **reed** and the **fern**, so much so that one kills the other. Because of this, the root of a fern, when crushed, draws out reed splinters that have been fixed into the body. If someone wishes for reeds to never grow again, the place should be plowed with a fern placed upon the plowshare, and he will find that they hardly grow back at all. 

**Orobanche** <note>Also known as broomrape; a parasitic plant.</note> loves to grow among legumes, especially near beans and bitter vetch, and it strangles them—which is how it earned its name <note>original: *orobanche*; from the Greek *orobos* (vetch) and *anchein* (to strangle).</note>. However, **Dioscorides** <note>The most famous ancient authority on herbal medicine.</note> records that when added to legumes, it speeds up the cooking process. 

**Hemlock** and **rue** are mutually opposed to one another. Rue should not be weeded or handled except with a gloved hand; unless you cover your hand, it will produce harmful ulcers. If, through ignorance, you weed it with a bare hand and itching or swelling occurs, the hand should be smeared with the juice of hemlock. Rue, if eaten in large quantities, possesses the harm of a poison, which is extinguished by the juice of hemlock—so much so that they are the "poisons of poisons." Dioscorides also recorded that rue is effective against the drinking of hemlock. 

A fierce **bull** tied to a **fig tree** will grow mild and is tamed, as **Zoroaster** says <note>Porta refers here to the *Geoponica*, a collection of agricultural lore often attributed to ancient figures like Zoroaster.</note>. From this, it was discovered that if the shoots of a wild fig <note>term: *caprificus* (the wild fig tree, whose fruit is used to ripen domestic figs through a process called caprification).</note> are added to beef while it is boiling—as **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, the Roman encyclopedist.</note> writes—they cook it thoroughly with a great saving of firewood. # ON THE CAUSES OF THINGS.

**Wild figs** <note>original: *olynthos*</note>, swollen with milky sap, when mixed with vinegar-water, serve as a remedy against a draft of bull’s blood <note>In antiquity, bull's blood was widely, though incorrectly, believed to be a lethal poison.</note>. The **elephant** fears the **ram**; for even while it is carried away by its own wildness, once it sees a ram, it grows tame and its force withers away. By using such machines, the Romans put the elephants of **Pyrrhus**, King of the Epirotes, to flight and gained an ample victory. From this very opposition, many remedies for <term>elephantiasis</term> <note>A skin disease, likely leprosy or a similar condition in this context, named for its resemblance to the thick, wrinkled hide of an elephant.</note> have been discovered using the elephant's own body parts, as the disease mimics the surface of an elephant's skin. 

The **monkey** dreads the **turtle** beyond measure. The monkey is prone to drunkenness, for it is often captured after being intoxicated with wine; however, a wash made from the turtle provides a remedy against drunkenness. **Man** and the **serpent** conflict with such irreconcilable enmity that man shudders and grows pale the moment a snake is seen. If a snake crosses the path of a pregnant woman, the shock may cause a miscarriage. From this fact, a practice arose: for a woman struggling with a difficult birth, a <term>suffumigation</term> <note>The practice of inhaling or exposing the body to medicinal smoke.</note> is made from the discarded skin of snakes (<note>original: *anguium senecta*</note>), which expels or kills the fetus; however, it is better if the opening of the womb is anointed with the snake's own fat. 

The sight of a **wolf** is so harmful to a man that if the wolf sees him first, it steals his voice. Having been anticipated by the predator's gaze, the man lacks the use of his voice even if he desires to cry out. If the wolf feels it has been seen first, it falls silent, its ferocity numbs, and it suffers a heavy loss of its power. From this came the proverb: "The wolf is in the story" (<note>original: *Lupus est in fabula*, a Latin equivalent to the English 'speak of the devil'</note>), recorded by **Plato** in the *Republic* <note>original: *Politis*</note>. The wolf fears the **hedgehog**; hence, the blood of a hedgehog used as a gargle makes a hoarse and muffled voice clear and sharp again. 

The **dog** is the wolf's enemy. If a dog's skin is hung over someone who has been bitten by a rabid dog, it drives away the <term>water-swelling</term> <note>A reference to the symptoms of hydrophobia (rabies).</note>. The **hawk** is a hostile enemy to the **dove** family. The **kestrel** <note>original: *tinunculus*</note> protects them; the hawk dreads the kestrel's sight and voice. The doves themselves are not unaware of this, for wherever the kestrel resides, they do not leave the place, trusting in their protector. On this subject, **Columella** <note>A Roman writer on agriculture.</note> says, regarding the expulsion of hawks from the dovecote: "There is a kind of hawk that country folk call a kestrel, which indeed builds its nests in buildings. Its chicks are placed individually in earthenware jars, and tight-fitting lids are applied; these vessels, sealed with plaster, are hung in the corners of the dovecote. This practice wins the birds' affection for the place so that they never desert it." # NATURAL MAGIC, BOOK I.

As Plutarch noted, and C. Ptolemy after him, the **loadstone** <note>original: *magnes*; a naturally magnetized mineral</note> possesses a destructive power, and **garlic** <note>original: *allium*</note> acts against poison; although no one has yet described garlic as being effective specifically against the loadstone, we can nevertheless conjecture it to be true, as it is effective against vipers, rabid dogs, and poisonous changes in water. In the same way, animals that maintain enmities with poisonous enemies—fighting them and devouring them without harm—can serve as evidence for us that those animals’ parts are effective against the venomous bites of their rivals. There is a continuous struggle between **stags** and **serpents**: upon seeing a stag, the serpent hides itself in a cavern, but the stag draws it out with the breath of its nostrils and devours it. For this reason, the fat and blood of stags, and the **stones formed in their eyes** <note>original: *lapides in oculis concreti*; likely referring to "stag's tears" or bezoars, which were highly prized as antidotes in the early modern period</note>, are offered as a drink against serpent bites. The breath of **elephants** also draws serpents from their hiding places, and they fight with **dragons** <note>original: *draconibus*; in natural histories of this era, "dragon" often referred to large pythons or legendary serpents</note>; the smoke from burning elephant limbs puts serpents to flight from afar. **Storks**, in the regions they inhabit, drive away lizards, water-snakes, spotted snakes <note>original: *cenchros*</note>, and other pests of the meadows; all their limbs are adverse to these creatures. The **ibis** does the same in Egypt. The **ichneumon** <note>The Egyptian mongoose, famous in lore for its battles with cobras.</note> armors itself with mud <note>original: *loto*; referring to the silt of the riverbanks</note> and wages war against the asp. The **weasel** <note>original: *mustela*</note> fights with serpents, and its bite is fatal even to the **basilisk**, the most poisonous of snakes. The crowing of a **cock** also terrifies the basilisk, and the cock fights with serpents on behalf of the hens; its broth is given as a remedy against the venom of serpents. So too the **turtle** and the **eagle**. **Star-lizards** <note>original: *stelliones*; likely geckos or spotted lizards</note> are enemies to **scorpions**; for this reason, they are steeped in oil to be smeared upon places stung by scorpions. The **mullet** devours the **sea-hare** <note>original: *lepus marinus*; a toxic marine mollusk</note> and is effective against its poison. The **sow** hunts the **salamander** without harm and provides a cure for its plague. The **hawk** is an enemy to the **chameleon**; as an antidote to the chameleon's poison, the hawk's dung is drunk in wine. 

Thus, by observing the sympathies of plants, one should not fail to hunt for some hidden secret that possesses allied powers to expel some evil. **Wild asparagus** <note>original: *corruda*</note>, from which garden asparagus comes, is best sown where the **reed** <note>original: *harundo*</note> grows, because they enter into a great familiarity with one another; both render people prone to **Venus** <note>Both plants were considered aphrodisiacs, stimulating sexual desire.</note>. The **vine** and the **olive** enjoy a mutual fellowship, according to Africanus; both offer friendly powers for the benefit of mankind. Likewise, **francolins** <note>original: *attagenes*; a type of game bird</note> love stags, as both possess a luxurious nature; the limbs of both make one more ready for coitus. There is a mutual love between **partridges** and **goats**,

### *That power is born from the Heavens and the stars, and many things result from them. Chapter VIII.*

I believe there is no doubt that these lower things serve those higher ones, and that a certain power flows down from that ethereal nature, so that those things subject to change may be destroyed and born again by a fixed law and a continuous sequence. The **Egyptians**—who it is clear were the first who dared to examine and measure the effects of the heavens—since they lived in the flat plains of open fields under the indulgence of perpetual clear skies, where nothing rose up from the earth that could obstruct their contemplation of the sky, observing the eternal stars, always bright and clear, they placed all their care into the knowledge of the stars' **influences** <note>original: *influxuū*; the "influx" or astrological flow of power from the stars to the earth</note>. 

And since the pursuit of causes greatly frightened those at leisure, they ascribed everything to the heavens and the stars, so that each thing might draw its fate from there. They produced wonderful effects through the movements of the stars and the influence of the heavens at the hour of birth and death; from this, all things began to be prepared and gathered at specific hours, fixed times, and **aspects** <note>original: *aspectibus*; the relative positions and angles between planets which were believed to determine their power</note>, and they went no further in defending their opinion. **Ptolemy** <note>original: *Ptolemæus*; the famous 2nd-century astronomer and astrologer</note> confirms this, he who dared to explain celestial influences according to a rule and predict many things from them; he says it does not require a wordy proof. 

No less, by the striking of all the stars, all living creatures and sprouts grow and decrease—more frequently and clearly from some, but more uncertainly and at rarer intervals from others. **Aristotle** <note>original: *Aristoteles*</note>, when he contemplated the higher motion as the cause and principle of all things, noted that if it were to cease, these lower things would immediately perish. He said that by necessity this world was connected to the higher motions, so that the universal power might be governed from there. He knew such a great power was diffused from the **Sun**, which he elegantly explained again: the winding path of the Sun in the **oblique circle** <note>original: *obliquo circulo*; referring to the ecliptic, the Sun's apparent path across the sky throughout the year</note> is the source of the birth and death of all decaying things, and its approach and withdrawal cause the intervals of the seasons. **Plato** <note>original: *Plato*</note> says that certain celestial circuits are the cause of fertility and sterility. The Sun itself governs the seasons...
