...is the governor and the rule of life. Hence **Iamblichus** <note>original: *Iamblicus*; a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on Egyptian mysteries and theurgy</note>, relying on the doctrine of the **Egyptians**, says: "Whatever good is present, it is certain that it exists by solar power; and if we have anything from others, it is nevertheless fulfilled by him." **Heraclitus** calls him the fountain of celestial light, **Orpheus** the light of life, **Plato** the celestial fire, the eternal animal, the animate star, the greatest and diurnal, and the **natural philosophers** <note>original: *Physici*; scholars who studied the laws of nature</note> call him the heart of heaven. **Plotinus** brings forth from the ancients that the **Sun** was worshiped in the place of God. Nor does the **Moon** work with any less power of her own and of the Sun, since she is more akin and particular to us. **Albumasar** <note>original: *Albumasar*; the influential Persian astrologer Abu Ma'shar</note> said that through the Sun and the Moon power is infused and instilled into all things; the most learned **Hermes** <note>original: *Hermes*; referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of alchemy and the Hermetic arts</note> said that after God, the Sun and the Moon are the life of all living things. She [the Moon] is closest to the earth, surpassing the other planets in her proximity; she is the mistress of moisture and a mediator, and things have such an affinity with her that both animate and inanimate things feel her increases and losses. Seas, rivers, and the flows of waters increase and fail, now fluctuating rapidly, now carried in a slow course. The tide of the sea is agitated by a perpetual alternation in receding, nor have all men ascribed this to anything but the motion of the Moon: so that now it absorbs with a greedy gulp, now indeed swelling, it flows back by retreating; nor does it appear how it could happen otherwise.

She [the Moon] provokes animals more generously, as if binding them to her; for filling her orb, as **Lucilius** says, she nourishes oysters, sea urchins, mussels, shellfish, crabs, and the rest, because by night she softens them with a warm glow; however, when she is hunched or curved into horns on both sides <note>referring to the crescent phases of the moon</note>, she empties them and renders them exhausted. The cucumbers, gourds, and melons—and those which have the most watery humor—also feel the same star that we just mentioned, so that they grow thick when she is young <note>the waxing moon</note> and decrease when she is aging <note>the waning moon</note>, as **Athenaeus** reports; the greatest changes can be seen when they are opposite the Sun, and their increases and decreases are contrary. Nor do the buds of plants reject the state of the heavens: which farmers know, since they have often tested it in grafting: for the growing wood does not thicken the fruit, but when the moon is **silent** <note>original: *silens*; the "New Moon" phase when it is not visible in the sky</note>, the fruit thrives while the wood is languid and lean. Hence those more skilled in Agriculture have judged both the circuit of the year and the monthly course of the Moon so necessary for plants, that this part of Agriculture is exceedingly necessary...

...was deemed necessary. The Moon also, while she travels through the Earth signs of the Zodiac <note>The Zodiac is divided into four elements: Fire, Earth, Air, and Water. Earth signs include Taurus, Virgo, and Capricorn</note>, causes planted trees to strike deep roots and throw out their underground parts. If she lingers while migrating through the Air signs <note>Gemini, Libra, and Aquarius</note>, the tree will spread its branches, luxuriating in leaves, and growing more upward than downward. Indeed, what more certain sign can be found than what is seen in the pomegranate tree? For however many days the Moon has moved away from the new moon <note>original: *interlunio*; the period of the month when the moon is invisible</note>, for that many years the tree will bear fruit. And it is said that garlic, if it is planted while the Moon is positioned beneath the earth, and likewise harvested while she is hidden beneath the earth, will be free from its foul odor. All felled wood, such as beams and timber, when the Moon receives her new light [the waxing moon], abounds with much moisture; being softened as if by the conception of moisture, they become worm-eaten and decay. Hence **Democritus** <note>An ancient Greek philosopher known for the atomic theory and observations on nature</note> commands, and it does not displease **Vitruvius** <note>A famous Roman architect and engineer who wrote on the practicalities of building materials</note>, that by a fixed rule it is safer to fell wood during the Moon's wane, so that the material, being cut at the right time and not failing through rot, may attain longevity.

Furthermore, by changing her ages [phases], the Moon demonstrates various effects: for from her meeting with the Sun until she becomes crescent-shaped and then halved, she moistens and warms, though she moistens more; a sign of this is that all moist things swell and receive a moistening power from her. But when she becomes quite swollen and rounded into a circle [the full moon], she possesses heat and moisture equally; trees and minerals feel this. Then waning until she is cut to a half-circle again, she is warm and moist, yet with more heat because she has more light <note>The author likely suggests that the residual solar light reflected by the Moon carries a "hidden warmth"</note>; hence it happens that fish travel through the surface of the waters. Yet in this state there is a hidden warmth, because she diffuses moist things, and with increased moisture, rot arises; thus she dissolves things into decay. When, however, her meeting <note>original: *synodus*; the conjunction of the Sun and Moon at the new moon</note> with the Sun occurs again, and being bereft of light she ceases to appear, the **Chaldean** <note>original: *Chaldæi*; ancient Mesopotamian sages renowned for their expertise in astrology and astronomy</note> sages assert she is warm, and that the state of the heavens is then more excellent.

Thus they also record that there is a "lunar herb" with round, circular, and blue leaves, which knows the days of the Moon: for as she waxes, it produces one leaf a day, and as she wanes, it drops them. We may observe this more widely and frequently among our domestic animals and plants, and we experience it continuously with our own sight. The ant, that smallest of animals, feels the changes of the stars, so that during the new moon <note>original: *interlunio*</note> it ceases and rests, while at the full moon <note>original: *plenilunio*</note> it works through the nights. The onion (which is much more wonderful) alone among all vegetables knows the adverse changes of the stars and possesses contrary powers of increasing and decreasing: for it revives and sprouts as the Moon wanes, but conversely decreases as she waxes. For this reason, the Egyptian priests do not eat it, as I read in **Plutarch’s** fourth commentary on **Hesiod**. One kind of spurge <note>original: *Tithymali*</note>, which they call the "sun-watcher" <note>original: *helioscopium*</note> as if it were a "sun-follower," turns its foliage according to the sun’s rule, so that it wakes up and lies down at twilight as if put to sleep, stirred by a certain longing; it watches the sun's rising in the morning, but at night closes its flower.

There are many solar herbs, such as the heliotrope: for when the sunbeam rises, it always watches with a tilted head during the day, so that it never seems to have twisted its flower head <note>original: *folliculum*</note>; by a kind of bond of love, it inclines itself in the same direction as the star [the sun] travels. The flowers of mallow and chicory do the same. The lupine also gazes at the setting Sun, so that it never twists its stem; every day it shows the hour to farmers even when clouds cast shadows, acting as a pointer of the hours, and it serves as a sign to them of the star's [the sun's] completed course. Selenite <note>original: *Selenites*, literally "moon-stone"</note> (just as if you were to say "the brightness of the moon" <note>original: *Lunae iubar*</note>) is a stone which others call *aphroselinon* <note>from the Greek for "moon-foam"</note>; it contains an image of the moon and reflects it, increasing and decreasing through the individual days. The baboon <term>cynocephalus: literally "dog-head," referring to the sacred baboon of Egypt associated with Thoth</term> greets the Moon at her rising, for it stands and lifts its hands to heaven and wears a royal emblem on its head. It has such a harmony with the Moon that during her conjunction—when she is accustomed to being affected, and during her monthly period when she does not shine all night nor illuminate everything with a soft color, but is dark and silent—the male baboon will not look at anyone nor eat; instead, with its face cast down to the ground, it mourns miserably, grieving the Moon's disappearance <note>original: *raptu*, literally her "seizure" or "theft" during the dark moon</note>. However, the female, not satisfied with the moonless night and never turning her eyes away, suffers the same as the male and sheds blood from her genitals. For this reason, even to this day, baboons are raised in sacred rites so that from them the time of the conjunction of the Sun and Moon can be known, according to **Horus** <note>referring to Horapollo, a 5th-century author on Egyptian hieroglyphs</note> in his work on hieroglyphics.

Arcturus rising brings storms and rain. Dogs know the rising of Sirius <note>the Dog Star</note> because they are driven to madness; vipers and serpents rage, ponds are stirred, wines in the cellars fluctuate, and the greatest effects are felt on earth. Sweet basil <note>original: *ocimum*</note> turns pale at its rising, and coriander dries up, as recorded by **Theophrastus**. They used to observe the rising of the Dog Star <note>original: *Canicula*</note> diligently every year and took from it a conjecture (as **Heraclides Ponticus** writes) as to whether the coming year would be healthy or pestilential. For if the star was dimmer and as if cloudy, it meant the sky was thick and curdled, so that its quality would be heavy and pestilential; if the star appeared bright and clear, it signified that the sky was thin and pure and therefore healthy. The ancients feared it so much that they established the sacrifice of a dog to it. **Columella** wrote:

> *Hence, so that the evil blight does not scorch the green herbs,*
> *It is appeased with the blood and entrails of a suckling pup.*

**And Ovid:**

> *This dog is placed upon the altar in place of the celestial dog.*

### *On the Attraction of Superior Virtues.* CHAPTER IX.

We have spoken of the effects of the heavens upon these inferior things, and of the agreement <note>sympathy</note> and disagreement <note>antipathy</note> of things; we shall now add, based on the kinship of nature, how we may attract the virtues of the superior [celestial] things. The Platonists called Magic the attraction of one thing by another, out of a certain kinship of nature. For the parts of this world, like the limbs of a single animal, all hanging from one author [the Creator], are joined together by the bond of a single nature: therefore, just as in us the brain, lungs, heart, liver, and other limbs draw something from one another and help each other mutually—so that when one of them suffers, the others suffer with it—so the limbs of this huge animal (that is, all the connected bodies of the world) likewise change their natures by turn and are changed; and from a common kinship, a common love is born, and from love a common attraction. This is truly Magic. 

From the concavity of the Moon’s sphere, fire is drawn upward because of a natural fitness; from the concavity of fire, air is drawn; from the center of the world, earth is drawn to the lowest parts, and water is snatched from its place. Hence also the magnet draws iron, and amber <note>original: *electrum*</note> draws straws, sulfur draws fire, the Sun draws many flowers and leaves to itself, and the Moon draws the waters. Plotinus and Synesius <note>Neoplatonic philosophers who wrote on the soul and the interconnectedness of nature</note> say: Nature is great everywhere, clearly baiting certain things everywhere with certain foods, no differently than drawing heavy things to the center of the earth, light things to the Moon's concavity, leaves by heat, roots by moisture, and other things likewise. ...that the world is an animal, everywhere male and female at once, and through the mutual love of its members, it joins with itself everywhere, and so remains stable. The order of the [Zodiac] signs declares that the masculine sex is everywhere mixed with the feminine, where the preceding sign is masculine and the following is feminine. In this way, trees and herbs, like animals, possess both sexes. I pass over how fire relates to air, and water to earth, as the male relates to the female; thus it is no wonder that the members of the world desire a mutual marriage among themselves. The planets are partly male and partly female; Mercury is a hermaphrodite <note>original: *hermaphroditus*; possessing both male and female characteristics, reflecting Mercury's role as a neutral or dual-natured planet in astrology</note>.

Truly observing this, Husbandry <note>original: *Agricultura*</note> prepares the field and seeds for celestial gifts. Medicine effects similar things in our body, both to nourish our own nature and to more fully align it with the nature of the universe. So too the Philosopher skilled in the stars, whom we usually and properly call a Magician <term>Magus: in this context, a "Natural Magician" who uses the hidden laws of nature rather than demonic or supernatural power</term>, by certain allurements, joins celestial things to earthly ones at the right moment—doing so in no different a way than a diligent farmer who grafts a new shoot onto an old trunk. The Magician subjects earthly things to celestial ones—indeed, everywhere lower things to higher ones—just as iron is drawn to a magnet, crystal is illuminated by the Sun, or an egg is warmed by a hen.

Furthermore, just as some people warming eggs even without animals win life for them from the universe, and often, by preparing certain materials at the right time, procreate animals without eggs or visible seeds—such as bees from a bull <note>original: *ex boue*; referring to *bougonia*, the ancient belief that bees were spontaneously generated from the carcasses of oxen</note>, or a scorpion from basil <note>original: *ex ocimo scorpionem*; a common folk belief that basil, when crushed and left between bricks, would transform into scorpions</note>—by applying life from the world to specific materials at opportune times; so too the Magician, once he has learned which materials (whether begun by Nature or perfected by art, even if scattered) can receive a celestial influence <term>influxum: the "flowing in" of astral or divine power into material objects</term>, gathers, prepares, and applies these especially while that star is reigning, and through them claims celestial powers for himself. ...glass [responds] to a face, or a wall opposed to a voice is suddenly affected from above, by a most powerful agent and by a power—both of which are wonderful and present everywhere. Proclus <note>Proclus Lycaeus (412–485 AD) was a Greek Neoplatonist philosopher whose works on "theurgy" or divine magic were foundational for Renaissance thinkers</note> indeed, in his book *On Sacrifice and Magic*, says that when the philosophers considered a certain kinship and mutual connection in natural things—of some things to others, and of manifest things to hidden powers—and found "all things in all things," they established Magic. They recognized the highest things in the lowest, and the lowest in the highest; in heaven, earthly things exist, though not in their own form, but according to their cause and in a celestial manner; and in the lower things, celestial things exist, but in an earthly manner. 

For from where else do we think those plants move, which they name heliotropes <note>original: *heliotropias*; sun-turning plants, such as the sunflower or turnsole</note>, toward the motion of the Sun? Or the selinetropes <note>original: *selinetropias*; literally "moon-followers"</note>, which turn toward the Moon? For this reason, one may look upon the Sun and Moon on the earth, but according to an earthly quality; and in heaven, one may see all plants, stones, and animals according to a celestial nature. The ancients, having contemplated these things, applied some to celestial beings and others to earthly ones, whereby they drew down divine virtues into a lower place because of a certain similarity: for indeed, similarity itself is a sufficient cause for binding individual things to one another. 

If someone warms a piece of paper <note>original: *papyrum*; though translated as paper, in this context it refers to any flammable plant-based material used as a wick or fuel</note> and then places it near a lamp, even if it does not touch it, he will see the paper suddenly ignited, though it has not touched the fire, with the flame descending from above to the lower parts. Let us therefore compare the warmed paper to a certain kinship of lower things to the higher; its approach to the lamp to the opportune use of things according to time, place, and matter; the movement of the fire into the paper to the presence of divine light to that which is capable of receiving it; and the approach of the paper to the deification of mortals <note>original: *deificationi mortalium*; the process by which a human or material object is infused with divine essence</note> and the illumination of material things, which are then carried upward like burning hemp <note>original: *accensæ cannabis*</note>, because of a certain participation in the divine seed.

...we believe it depends. For the constant investigator and contemplator of natural things, as he sees Nature herself producing and destroying all things, so he also learns to do the same. ### NATURAL MAGIC, BOOK I

[Ser]pents protect themselves with parsnip <term>elaphobosco: likely the wild parsnip or "deer-grass," which was believed to repel snakes</term>. Likewise, wood-pigeons, jackdaws, and blackbirds use laurel leaves. It has been discovered that the nature of the bedbug <note>original: *cimicis*</note> is effective against the bite of asps; the proof, according to Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the *Natural History*</note>, is that chickens are not killed by an asp on the day they have eaten them. Goats shun basil <note>original: *ocimum*</note> because it induces lethargy, according to Chrysippus <note>a Stoic philosopher who wrote on the nature of plants and animals</note>.

Animals have even demonstrated the use of wound-healing herbs themselves. Deer cast out arrows from their bodies with the herb dittany <note>original: *dictamo*; a famous medicinal plant from Crete</note>: for the Cretans, who are skilled in wounding, strike wild beasts grazing on the mountain peaks; once wounded, the animals seek out this herb, and immediately the arrowheads fall out. Goats do the same. Elephants wounded in hunts seek the "tear" of the aloe <note>the bitter sap or resin of the aloe plant</note> and smear it on their wounds.

They also discovered medicines for themselves to purge harmful humors <term>humores: the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—believed to control health</term> from their bodies, and they have taught these to us. Donkeys eat the spleenwort herb <note>original: *asplenum*</note> to expel black bile; having been taught by them, physicians prepare the same herb for the same use. Does [female deer] are purged with the herb seseli <note>meadow saxifrage</note> before giving birth, making the use of the womb easier. Bears eat wild arum <note>original: *arum*</note> to relax their intestines, according to Aristotle. Pigeons and poultry use wall-pellitory <note>original: *helxine*</note> to overcome their annual lack of appetite. Dogs, having eaten grass, vomit up everything that afflicts them, along with phlegm and bile; this vomiting brings them health, for it prevents madness <note>rabies</note> which occurs if the bile is not removed.

And by applying specific remedies to the specific diseases with which they are infested, humans—having been reminded by these animals—use the same remedies for our own ailments. A lion suffering from a quartan fever <note>a fever that recurs every four days, often associated with malaria</note> devours monkeys to be cured: from this, we know that the blood of a monkey is effective against fever by strengthening the body. Also, by drinking the blood of dogs, one is freed from the same disease.

Pain in the belly and intestines is soothed by the sight of geese and ducks; for if the sick look upon them, they are immediately freed from griping pains <note>original: *torminibus*; intestinal cramps or colic</note>, according to Vegetius <note>an author on veterinary medicine</note>. According to Columella <note>a Roman writer on agriculture</note>, the same duck heals the equine race [horses] even more effectively by its mere presence. Hence Pliny says: "What is reported regarding griping pains is marvelous: that by placing a duck against the belly, the disease passes into it, and the duck dies." Marcellus <note>Marcellus Empiricus, a late antique medical writer</note> writes that the flesh of a duck eaten as food benefits those suffering from these pains. Goats and gazelles <note>original: *dorcades*</note> do not suffer from bleary eyes because they eat certain herbs. Hawks eat hawkweed <note>original: *hieracium*</note> when they feel a mist over their eyes. In cases of eye disease, elephants drink milk.

# ON THE CAUSES OF THINGS.

...[will find their cure]. Fennel <note>original: *Foeniculum*</note> was made famous by serpents, who use it to cast off old age <note>referring to the shedding of their skin</note> by tasting it, and to refresh their eyesight with its juice. From this, it was understood that human "cloudiness" of the eyes <note>likely cataracts or blurred vision</note> could also be relieved by it. Hares eat "milky" herbs, and because of this, they have rennet <note>original: *coagulum*; a substance used to curdle milk</note> in their stomachs; shepherds learned from this to use many milky herbs to curdle milk. Partridges eat leeks because it aids in creating a resonant voice, according to Aristotle's book of *Problems*. For this reason, the Emperor Nero, for the sake of his voice, would consume nothing but oil on certain days of every month—not even bread.

Furthermore, animals even discovered many medical instruments. In cases of eye-clouding <term>suffusione: an early term for cataracts or a "pouring down" of humors behind the lens</term>, a she-goat drains blood with the prick of a rush, or a he-goat with a bramble. When the animal feels its eye is darkened with mist and not fit for seeing, it moves its eye to the thorn of a bush and allows it to be pierced. As soon as it is pricked, the phlegm <note>original: *pituita*</note> is drawn out, and with no damage to the pupil, it recovers its sight. It is believed that humans learned this type of surgical cure from them.

The Egyptians proclaim that they did not learn about enemas <term>clysteres: a procedure where liquids are injected into the rectum for purging</term> through human invention, but that the Ibis bird taught them this medicine and practice for purging the bowels. From this bird, they also learned about diet: to increase the amount of food as the Moon waxes and to decrease it as it wanes. The eyes of bears often grow dim, which is the main reason they seek out honeycombs; by having their faces stung by bees, they relieve that "heaviness" through bloodletting. This is why physicians today use bloodletting <term>phlebotomia: the surgical opening of a vein to withdraw blood</term> for dimness of the eyes. The wolverine <note>original: *Gulo*; a creature famous in early natural histories for its gluttony</note>, filled with excessive greed, squeezes its belly between two trees to force out its excrement.

### NATURAL MAGIC, BOOK I.

...they recognized, as well as the properties of stars, metals, stones, and gems; from these, Hippocrates, Dioscorides, Pliny, and others, once they recognized them to be true, transcribed them into their own books—with the exception of those who quite foolishly (not to say enviously or even rabidly) tried to reduce everything to the standard of "manifest qualities" <note>In traditional medicine, "manifest" qualities are those directly felt, like hot, cold, wet, or dry. The author is criticizing those who ignore "occult" or hidden natural sympathies.</note>. It will be of no small value to record some examples of this kind. 

Theophrastus, speaking of herbs that resemble the images of scorpions and octopuses, says: "There are some plants that are observed for a certain peculiar form, such as the so-called *scorpion-root* <note>original: *scorpij radix*</note> and certain ferns; for one represents the appearance of a scorpion and is useful against its sting, while the other is hairy and full of hollow suction-cups, like the tentacles of an octopus <note>original: *polyporum cirri*</note>. This latter plant is fit for purging the lower parts, and where he affirms a polyp <note>the term *polypus* refers to both the sea creature and a medical growth, such as a nasal or uterine polyp</note> might grow, it destroys it." 

And elsewhere: "Nor do the things attributed to the powers of plants seem to be recorded absurdly—for instance, the capacity for generating seed or causing sterility—such as the plant called the *testicle* <note>referring to *Orchis* species, named for their twin tubers</note>. For since there are twins, one large and one small, they say the large one is effective for sexual intercourse, while the smaller one is a hindrance." 

Certain plants are said to be effective for procreating a male or a female, such as the herb they call the *male-maker* <note>original: *marificam*</note> and the *female-bearer* <note>original: *foeminiparam*</note>. Both are similar to one another, but the fruit of the female-bearer is like oily moss, while that of the male-bearer is twin-like, in the manner of a man's testicles. 

To prevent the seed from being fertile, they say the fruit of white ivy is effective; conversely, to make it prolific, they use the fruit of the *hawthorn* <note>original: *crataei*</note>, which produces fruit like millet. A person is said to become utterly sterile by the leaf of the herb *hemionitidis* <note>Mule-fern or Hart's-tongue fern, which produces no visible seeds</note>. For those plants that are fruitful and very fertile they call "life-giving," while those that are sterile they say make humans sterile. 

And elsewhere: "Notable is the *burdock* <note>original: *lappa*</note>: a flower is born within that very hairy and rough exterior, not emerging nor visible, but conceiving within itself and bringing forth seed, so that it is similar to what happens in sharks <note>original: *galeis*, referring to dogfish or small sharks which were believed to give birth to live young</note> and vipers; for those, once they have produced eggs within themselves, soon give birth to live animals; and this plant, containing the flower within itself and ripening it, then brings forth the fruit. Thus they share mutual virtues." 

Dioscorides writes that the herb *scorpioides* <note>Scorpion-grass</note> has the likeness of a scorpion's tail and is effective against the bites of a scorpion. Likewise, the greater and lesser *serpentaria* <note>Snakeweed or Dragon-root</note>, which on the outermost surface of their bark are marked with various spots—dark, red, saffron, and blue—like a snake...

He said that a herb grown on the head of a statue, if collected in a piece of someone’s garment and bound in linen, would immediately settle a headache. 

Many have handed down the *eriphia* <note>A legendary plant mentioned by Pliny</note>: this has a beetle in the oats, running up and down with the sound of a kid goat—from which it also received its name <note>The Greek word *eriphos* means 'kid' or 'young goat'</note>—and he records that nothing is more excellent than this for the voice. 

Orpheus <note>The legendary poet and musician, to whom several ancient texts on the magical properties of stones were attributed</note> hunted for the virtues of stones based on their inner nature. The milk-stone <term>galactites|A stone that, when ground, produces a milky liquid</term> is of a milky color; if you sprinkle its powder over the backs of goats, they will provide abundant milk for their young, and if given in a drink to nurses, it increases the milk in the breasts. Crystal bears a resemblance to water: held in the mouth and rolled around during fevers, it extinguishes thirst. Amethyst reflects the color of wine; it repels drunkenness. In agate, one can see crops, trees, meadows, and gardens: its powder thrown around the horns or shoulders of oxen while they plow causes Ceres <note>The Roman goddess of agriculture and grain</note> to bestow the greatest abundance of crops. 

The serpent-stone <term>ophites|A spotted stone, likely serpentine</term> mimics the spots of serpents and helps against their bites. The bronze-sound stone <term>calcophonos|From the Greek for 'bronze' and 'sound'</term>, when struck, gives back the ringing of bronze; they say it should be worn by tragic actors because it makes for an excellent voice. Hematite <note>original: *haematites*; literally 'blood-stone'</note>, when ground up, is useful for those spitting blood and for eyes bloodshot with gore; so too cinnabar, which is of the same color and power. We have decided that the remaining things should by no means be brought in here, since they are treated more diffusely in our *Phytognomonica* <note>Giambattista della Porta’s famous 1588 work on the "Language of Plants," which used the Doctrine of Signatures as its primary framework</note>.

# NATURAL MAGIC, BOOK I.

Let us teach how we may apply these things. There is no principle that will be more useful in what is to be said, nor a root from which the operations of secrets and wonders sprout forth more abundantly; therefore, you should apply as much diligence as we find the ancients most accurately applied in their writings, so that the greater part of these secrets may be established from this: that you learn to recognize and match them in composition. We see that all species and qualities of things are able to incline, draw, allure, and convert to their own likeness everything according to their total power; and if they are preeminent in action, this happens more easily; just as fire moves toward fire, and water toward water. 

Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath and one of the most influential physicians of the Islamic Golden Age</note> asserted that if anything stands in salt for a long time, it will take on the taste of saltiness; and if anything stays in something foul, it becomes foul; and if one is with the bold or the timid, one becomes bold or timid. If any animal is accustomed to living with humans, it turns out human-like and tame. Many dogmas of the Physicians <note>Referring to the established medical authorities of the classical and medieval world</note> affirm this: that certain parts of bodies delight in similar parts, such as brain for brain, teeth for teeth, lung for lung, and liver for liver. 

The brain of a human or a hen contributes to memory and wit, and a fresh skull of the same <note>Referring back to the human</note> mixed into a feast helps with epilepsy <note>original: *epilepsiæ*; a common treatment in Renaissance "corpse medicine" where parts of the human body were used as remedies</note>. If you eat a hen’s gizzard <note>original: *ventriculum*; literally the stomach</note> before dinner, even if you otherwise digest with great difficulty, it nevertheless strengthens the stomach. The heart of an ape prevents palpitations of the heart and increases boldness, which resides in the heart. If a wolf's penis <term>virga|Literally 'rod' or 'branch', a common Latin euphemism for the male organ</term>, roasted and sliced, is eaten, it excites Venus <note>A poetic reference to sexual desire or libido</note> if the strength is languishing. If you place the skin from the right heel of a vulture upon the right foot of a person with gout <term>podagrici|A person suffering from 'podagra', the historical term for gout, particularly when it affects the foot</term>, or the left on the left, it soothes the pains of the joints; and finally, any limb benefits its similar limb. 

You will learn most of these things from the books of the Physicians, for it is not our plan to mention everything they have already recorded. Furthermore, much must be collected and noticed: in which things there exists a quality, or an excess of some property that is not common, or an affection, or disturbances of this kind, and whether that excess is implanted by chance, nature, or art—such as heat-producing, cold-producing, love, boldness, sterility, fertility, sadness, talkativeness, or anything else we wish to achieve—let them work from these, and I think not at all without success. For example, if a fertile woman...

Likewise, a human, or any individual who has never been sick, provides a remedy for all illnesses.

If you place their tongues upon the breast or head of a sleeping woman—because these animals are more talkative at night—she will reveal the secrets of the night. Many other things [might be said], which would be more for indulgent reading than for profit, since these are treated more fully in our *Phytognomonica* <note>Referring to Porta’s own 1588 work, *Phytognomonica*, which explores how the appearance of plants reveals their hidden virtues</note>.

### *That peculiar gifts exist in individuals, in some in the whole body, in others in parts. CHAPTER XIII.*

Individuals are by no means lacking in bright and wonderful gifts; rather, they retain great power in their operations—even greater than what they might have from their species itself, or from a hidden property, or from the celestial position of the stars. As Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a medieval scholar whose works on "Natural Magic" were a primary source for Porta</note> believed, they draw a marvelous energy for receiving and acting that is not common to the species, but is proper and peculiar to the individual. From this, various effects and inclinations are ascribed to individuals, arising from various influences and celestial alignments, all of which a Magus <term>Magus: in this context, a "Natural Magician" or scientist who seeks to understand and use the hidden laws of nature</term> must know.

### **_On the powers that exist only during life, and those after death. CHAPTER 14._**

**I**t is fitting to weigh and observe certain remarkable functions—indeed, the greater part of them—which operate only during life, but after death are dulled, vanish, and rarely serve any purpose. The eyes of wolves take away the voice <note>A common ancient belief (found in Virgil and Pliny) that if a wolf sees a person before the person sees the wolf, the person is struck dumb.</note>, while the <term>catoblepas: a legendary Ethiopian beast with a heavy head whose gaze or breath was lethal</term> and the basilisk instantly snatch away life; the <term>echeneis: the remora or "ship-holder" fish, believed to have the power to stop a sailing ship in its tracks</term> slows the momentum of ships; the ostrich <note>original: *struthio camelus*</note> digests iron. These creatures do not perform such feats once they are dead, for they then act in no clear way at all. For that power dies and perishes as life vanishes; indeed, if parts are to be chosen from them for use, they must be sought from the living. Therefore, I believe it was not rashly decreed in the precepts of Natural Magic: if any benefit can be obtained from animals, take those parts while they are still alive. It would be even better, if possible, for the animal to survive the removal, for the power of a creature already expiring is weakened and withers.

For the soul, says Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a medieval polymath who wrote extensively on the "virtues" or hidden powers of minerals, plants, and animals.</note>, contributes much to those things produced in animals; for death or decay perverts them, especially if the death is natural, occurring when they die from corrupted humors. Living things are accustomed to act in a far different manner and possess more radiant powers. This is frequently observed with the agreement of Physicians and others who devote their labor to this kind of study. If tongues are extracted from frogs, or stingers from <term>stingrays: original *pastinacis*, the common stingray</term>, or stones from the heads of animals, or eyes, or anything else—so that they may work effectively, these must not be taken from the dead, but from those still enjoying life. Let the animals be thrown back alive into the water so that they may live, lest their innate power perish and wilt; instead, through the abundance of their vital power, they become more ready to act. You should imitate this in all things which, to spare words, we omit here.

No less may one perceive properties in things lacking life; for some qualities remain so closely joined that they do not cease to work—indeed, they work much more strongly. Wolves are so fatal to sheep that they preserve their hatred even after death. For if you prepare a drum <note>original: *tympanum*</note> with a wolf skin, you will hear it [resound] among other drums made from sheep skins; it will cause all those sheep-skin sounds to remain silent and strike them mute, if the drum is fashioned from the hide of a bear or a wolf.

### ***All simples must be gathered at fixed times, and prepared accordingly. CHAPTER 15.***

**W**e have said that power is bestowed by the heavens upon lower things, and especially upon plants; therefore, we believe that we must prepare everything at fixed times, and this must not be overlooked. ...if they waste away through weakness. Thus all roots must be pulled up in autumn, for it is then that they abound most in moisture and power. Know that some things retain their power for a long time, while others lose it in a short span, as anyone can see; this is cautioned in the **rules of the Physicians** <note>original: *Medicorum regulis*. These are the established guidelines of classical and medieval medicine regarding the shelf-life of "simples" or herbal ingredients.</note>, which note which things may be kept for many years and which are to be considered useless. Because of this, experiments that are handed down are often deemed empty and vain, when perhaps they have simply fallen into one’s hands after they have collapsed and been consumed by old age.

But if herbs are collected at specific times, they receive a certain singular virtue from the **celestial configurations** <note>The alignment of planets and stars which was believed to "infuse" plants with specific spiritual or physical properties.</note>, and a capacity far nobler than that from the heavens, since it flows from the most excellent nature and quality of the stars. Thus roots, stalks, flowers, leaves, and seeds gathered this way receive the greatest efficacy and far more potent strengths. This should be done in the evening, for the dewy moisture is driven away by the rising of the Sun and is pulled back to the depths through the "siphon" of the stalk. This is the fitting time, they say, when the wrinkles and folds of the root vanish and are smoothed out because of the increase in sap; indeed, they develop small cracks, gaping like a woman girding and striving for a future birth, and already the inner crack widens into fissures and threatens to burst.

It is beneficial to cut the leaves shortly after they unfold from the shoots and show themselves clothed; but not when they are wet with the night dew, but rather at the first appearance of the Sun. For at midday, their moisture is exhausted by the heat of the Sun, and they thirst. Flowers are gathered when they are eager and striving to bring forth their fruit, before they fall away limp, and while they are still moist with dewy humidity.

<note>"Simples" (*simplicia*) refers to medicinal herbs or minerals used in their natural state, rather than as part of a complex chemical mixture.</note>

It is clear, by the authority of **Dioscorides** <note>Pedanius Dioscorides (c. 40–90 AD), a Greek physician and the father of pharmacognosy.</note>, that it matters greatly if the places where plants come forth are hilly, exposed to the winds, breezy, cold, and lacking in water. For in such places, the powers of the plants are understood to be far more potent. Conversely, those that grow in plains, well-watered and shady spots, and other places sheltered from the wind, usually degenerate and have less strength in their virtues. Therefore, if plants seem to differ greatly from their originals due to their region and do not retain equal strength, they should be brought to a place where they seem most likely to obtain that power.

### Some properties of places and springs which may contribute to our work. CHAPTER XVII.

**N**or does the diversity of locations work any less in the various effects of things. For a location also holds many miracles of lands and waters, which it is proper for a **Magus** <term>Magus: a practitioner of "natural magic," which in this period was considered the highest form of natural science and philosophy.</term> to rightly understand and know. Indeed, we often see that the soil works by some logic of its site and brings about miracles due to the inclination of the heavens and the force of the **Sun** as it approaches and recedes. For if one land did not differ from another, then not only in **Syria** and **Arabia** would there be scents and incense-bearing trees among the reeds, rushes, and herbs—nor would they alone give pepper berries or clumps of myrrh—but in all places of the earth, all the same things...

### *That compounds work more powerfully, and how simples ought to be mixed and composed when entering into our mixtures. CHAPTER XVIII.*

NOW it seems necessary to add how we ought to compose many <term>simples</term> <note>Individual, unmixed ingredients, usually herbs or minerals.</note> into one, so that the mixture may work more powerfully. **Proclus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on the "hieratic art" or theurgy.</note>, in his book *On Sacrifice and Magic*, teaches that the ancient priests mixed several things together because they saw that simples possessed some property of a divinity, but were not individually sufficient for the summoning of that divinity. For this reason, by the very mingling of many things, they attracted heavenly influences; and because by composing they made one thing out of many, they made it resemble that "One" which is over many.

...many things. They would also establish statues composed of many materials, and by their art, they gathered blended scents into a single whole, producing something that exists as divine in its very essence, encompassing many powers. I wanted to present these examples so that we might recognize how the ancients very often used mixtures of <term>simples</term> <note>In traditional medicine, a "simple" is a single medicinal herb or ingredient used on its own.</note> so that the resulting mixture might work more vigorously.

We ourselves have frequently composed a mixture from herbs, land animals, birds, sea creatures, metals, and stones—an <term>alexipharmacum</term> <note>original: "alexipharmacum"; a defensive medicine or "counter-poison" intended to neutralize venom or toxins.</note> against all poisons. We were led by the principle of similarities to use dragon-wort herbs, the dragon-fish, vipers, and the <term>ophite stone</term> <note>A type of green, spotted marble or serpentine stone, named for its resemblance to snake skin (*ophis* is Greek for snake).</note>. 

The greater <term>dracunculus</term> <note>original: "dracunculus"; likely the Dragon-arum (*Dracunculus vulgaris*).</note> has a stalk with multicolored spots like those of dragons, as does the smaller variety. It is claimed that if someone rubs the leaves of the greater or smaller dragon-wort in their hands, or eats the root, they cannot be struck by a viper. The sea-dragon, when dissected, opened, and placed upon the wound from its own spine, serves as a cure, according to **Aetius** <note>Aetius of Amida, a 6th-century Byzantine medical writer.</note>. 

The viper itself, when skinned with the head and tail cut off and all the internal organs removed, can be cooked in the manner of an eel; when eaten by those who have been bitten, it offers the greatest protection. Alternatively, the head cut from a living viper and placed upon the bite while the part touching the neck is still warm, extracts the poison marvelously. The ophite stone, having the color of serpents, is useful against the bites of serpents. You will find many similar compound medicines made from land, water, and winged animals, herbs, and stones in the book of the <term>Cyranides</term> <note>original: "Kirannidis"; a famous ancient Greek text on the magico-medical properties of plants, stones, and animals.</note> and the works of the ingenious **Harpocration** <note>Valerius Harpocration, an author associated with natural magic and herbals.</note>.

But now we shall describe how simples ought to be mixed, and the method of compounding which I see is most diligently observed by physicians. Because we often require not a single effect, but a double or triple one, we must use a mixture of simples so that it may bring forth the desired results; I judge the art of mixing was invented for this very purpose. For it often happens that ingredients work too weakly; we, therefore, are accustomed to strengthen them with multiple defenses so they may act more promptly and finish their action more quickly. Conversely, if they produce an effect too intensely, we can dull and extinguish their strength. Most often, however, it happens that when we wish to target a specific limb—such as the head, the heart, or the bladder—we associate certain ingredients so that they may wound that part directly and provide for the needs of all.

...whence it happens that contraries are also mixed together. Let us therefore follow through with the discussion we have begun. When you undertake any work, first consider that which we most intend <note>That is, the primary goal or effect of the magic/medicine.</note>, and toward which we direct that <term>simple</term> <note>A single medicinal herb or ingredient.</note> or mixture; let us establish the base or foundation of the composition, from which the compound takes its name, and let it be of such a quantity as the actions of the material form require. For in order to act, they demand a proper and determined quantity; others, however, are added as assistants and "seasonings" of the first [base ingredient], so that without them they might not work so easily, or might work too slowly or too quickly. 

Thus, something fragrant is mixed with something foul-smelling, and bitter with sweet, for the sake of flavor or scent. For if a bitter or foul mixture is to be administered, it is rejected by those to whom it is directed, and the <term>animal spirits</term> <note>In early modern physiology, these were subtle fluids that traveled through the nerves to facilitate movement and sensation.</note> flee and abhor it, so that once it is absorbed, a loss of power follows. Likewise, thick and hard parts are mixed with thin and soft ones for the sake of pleasantness. 

It sometimes happens that a part is so small that, before it can warm the body, it is consumed by the body's own heat; then we add some bulk. For while not hindering the operation, it provides suitable <term>fuel</term> <note>original: "pabulum"; literally fodder or nourishment.</note> for the heat, so that the material is not consumed sooner than is necessary, and it remains fit for the operation. If, for example, we attempt to catch birds by putting them to sleep, the **methel nut** <note>original: "nux methella"; likely the *Datura metel*, or Thorn-apple, known for its narcotic properties.</note> provides this convenience for us. It possesses such powers that it induces sleep, renders them dazed, and by a heaviness of the brain, they are given over to sleep. We lay this down as the base of the mixture for the rest; so that it might work more vividly, we add **opium** and the **dregs of unmixed wine**. 

If the ingredients are hard and we want them to flow—so that legumes or other things may be more aptly saturated (as we shall say in the section on preparations)—we will also bait the birds with them. Therefore, let them be dissolved in the juice of **mandragora** <note>The mandrake plant, famous for its sedative effects.</note>, or **hemlock**, or **ox gall**. Lest they seem foul or bitter, we mix in honey, cheese, or flour, so that the thing becomes more edible, and the legumes become soaked and are offered to them to be eaten. ## *How the weight of a mixture ought to be investigated.*

### CHAPTER XIX.

It must also be most carefully observed that the correct dose of a mixture be understood and the ratio of weights be discovered, because the goodness of operations in all things exists only in optimal proportion and right harmony. Nor will mixtures provide the effects they promise unless they are perfect in every respect <note>original: "omnibus numeris absolutæ"; a Latin idiom meaning complete, perfect, or finished in every detail</note>. Hence we find that the ancients were always accustomed to use things not so much in their mixtures as by themselves as <term>simples</term> <note>Single, unmixed medicinal ingredients, usually herbs</note>, recording for us nothing except what was proven by selection, weight, and experience.

Therefore, you who devote the greatest effort to these things, first find the weight of the simple medicine, as much as the matter requires, according to your conception of the proportion of the thing sought. Imagine to yourself that medicine as being made of any of its components, considering what proportion it has to the whole. For that which is found in the parts ought also to be in the whole; and if you find that more than its proper dose has been placed there, once the components are considered, it should be subtracted from the whole. Once the weight is known in this way, let it be established as the foundation, and let it stand for other weights; and let as much be removed from it as would equal the fair dose of the others combined with it, since many things must enter into a medicine, and these are understood from the practitioner's judgment. Thus, you should never give a compound mixture that exceeds the dose, even if it were a simple in its <term>virtue</term> <note>In this context, "virtue" refers to the inherent power or medicinal efficacy of a substance</note>. 

But once all the <term>degrees</term> <note>A system used by Galenic physicians to measure the intensity of a quality—like heat or moisture—on a scale of one to four</note> have been calculated, the mixture should not be greater in quantity or power such that it possesses a different quality or virtue; for we do not add ingredients to increase the dose, but so that the medicine may carry out its work more easily. This also is especially worthy of notice: that in mixtures and medicines, the proportion of weights ought to vary just as regions and climates differ, for in their operation they acquire a different power. For in one place it works more vividly, but here more weakly, as we have warned. You, balancing with an even mind, should change the ratio of weights according to the operation of the simples—by taking away, by adding, and by adapting with the skill of your own intellect—so that they perform that which is intended.

It also emphasizes that a medicine's weight must be adjusted based on the local climate and the practitioner's judgment.</summary>

...that which we seek. Moreover, in our work, we have very often used the best method in the description of experiments by describing weights in parts. ### On the preparations of simples. Chapter XX.

We have already taught how to compose a mixture and how to investigate its weight; it remains now to describe certain preparations of <term>simples</term> <note>Single, unmixed medicinal ingredients, usually herbs, minerals, or animal products</note> which seem most suited and necessary to the work. These preparations require far greater skill than the other steps. Indeed, the success of the operations does not depend so much on the simples themselves as it does on their preparation, without which they will perform little or nothing at all.

Simples, therefore, are usually prepared by many methods so that they may be more fit and convenient for use. Those which we use most frequently are maturation, <term>elixation</term> <note>The process of boiling or decocting a substance in a liquid</note>, burning, reduction to lime <note>original: "in calcem reductio"; also known as calcination, where a substance is heated to high temperatures to remove volatile parts</note>, <term>incineration</term> <note>Reducing a substance to ash</note>, distillation, drying, and other similar processes.

We <term>macerate</term> <note>Soaking a solid in a liquid to soften it</note> something when we immerse it in a liquid so that the substance becomes moist and softened both inside and out, as we have said. In this way, the finer part may be drawn out through pressing, while the earthy part is left behind, allowing the substance to absorb the desired moisture into its very core.

We use <term>elixation</term>, however, when the juice cannot be drawn out of a substance easily. For by boiling, we extract the essence from the center to the outside, which does not happen through simple maceration or infusion; boiling itself releases thin vapors.

Likewise, we use scorching, roasting, and reduction to lime so that we may utterly deprive the parts of all moisture. This occurs when we reduce a substance to lime so that it may be more easily dissolved, or turned into a liquid, and mixed with other things. We roast things when they cannot be easily ground, so that they may be turned into powder. In this, one must take care that the thing is not entirely burned up, for a burned substance loses its sought-after powers; rather, it should be parched so that it may achieve a fine consistency. Finally, things or simples are distilled so that water of a more powerful virtue may be drawn out...

<header>NATURAL MAGIC, BOOK II.</header>

*is found, we will conclude within the boundaries of this volume. But so that we may perform and complete this, we will arrange these secrets in their proper places; and to ensure nothing is displaced from its category, we will follow the order of the sciences. We will first divide them into the natural and mathematical sciences, and we will begin with the natural ones, for we judge it fitting that we move from the simpler, less laborious, and more familiar things toward the mathematical ones. We shall begin, therefore, with animals, then move to plants, and proceed as if by steps toward metals and other works of Nature. We will describe the most important points—the very fountainheads from which the origins of things flow—and at the same time we will add the reasons and causes, so that the industrious reader, knowledgeable in the subject, may discover other things for himself. Because there are two ways that animals and plants are generated—spontaneous and through mating—we will first speak of those born spontaneously, and then of those born from the mixing of different kinds, so that we may produce new animals unseen in previous centuries. We will therefore begin with putrefaction* <note>original: "putrefactione" — in early modern science, decay was not seen merely as death, but as a creative process that released the "vital heat" necessary for new life to emerge.</note>*, because it stands as the principle for producing new things, not only from various simple substances but from a mixture of blendable ones. Nor did we think anything should be omitted, even if it were base, since there is no thing in Nature, however lowly it may appear, in which something admirable is not to be found.*

## *On putrefaction, and on the wondrous power of producing animals. CHAPTER I.*

It seemed fitting that, before we teach how new animals are born from decay, we run through the opinions of the ancient Philosophers regarding what they thought of it. Even though we have spoken of this matter in our <term>Phytognomonica</term> <note>Phytognomonica: Porta’s 1588 work on the "signatures" of plants, which argues that a plant's physical appearance reveals its medicinal virtues.</note>, it is necessary to preface some things here, lest the reader’s mind be distracted elsewhere, so that we may see how from decay not only "imperfect" but even "perfect" animals are born.

<meta>This page continues the transition into the study of animals, specifically focusing on the theories of "spontaneous generation"—the ancient belief that life could arise from non-living matter like mud, water, or decaying remains under the influence of the sun or stars.</meta>

<page-num>47</page-num>
<header>ON THE COMMINGLING OF ANIMALS.</header>

Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> believed that the various kinds of animals were created from the "bowels of the earth" when they were moistened with water and the power of the Sun was thrust into them. Archelaus of Athens, Anaxagoras of Clazomenae, and his disciple Euripides <note>The famous Greek playwright, here cited as a student of natural philosophy.</note> also held this same view. But Theophrastus, following the opinion of Cleodemus, judged that animals are born from <term>putrefying water</term> <note>original: "aqua putrescente" — in this context, putrefaction refers to the breakdown of matter that releases vital energy for new life.</note> and a certain mixture it forms with the earth; he believed that the more they are born from turbid and cold substances, the more they are deprived of the nature and stability of true animals. 

Diodorus <note>Likely Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian.</note> and a significant number of other philosophers say that all animals arose from putrefaction. They claim that at the beginning of the world, once the sky, earth, and elements had been settled into their proper places, the earth was left muddy and soft in many regions. When struck and dried by the rays of the Sun, the earth produced certain swellings on its surface in which the "seeds" of decay were fostered bit by bit. These were covered by thin membranes which contained that putrid matter within them. Moistened by dew at night and warmed by the Sun during the day, they were brought to maturity at the right time; and when these "little bags" <note>original: "vtriculis" — describing primitive gestational sacs or bubbles in the mud.</note> broke open, all the kinds of living creatures were excluded. Those that obtained a greater heat became birds; those that favored the earth became reptiles; those with a higher proportion of water became fish swimming in the sea; and those with a middle nature became the animals that walk on feet across the land. 

But as the Sun warmed the earth daily, the ground no longer produced animals spontaneously; instead, those already produced brought forth their own likeness through mutual coupling. Avicenna <note>The influential Persian polymath Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037).</note>, however, in that work he composed regarding floods, dared to assert that after immense floods of the earth—when no human seed remained—man and the other animals were generated solely from decaying corpses by the provision of <term>celestial influence</term> <note>The belief that the alignment of stars and planets provided the "soul" or "form" to matter.</note> alone. For this reason, he argued that neither the womb, nor the vulva, nor other such places seem strictly necessary for the generation of man, provided the infant is "better formed" by nature. 

He brings an argument for this assertion: not only are mice produced from the earth in some places (which soon multiply wonderfully through mating), but snakes are especially conceived from the hair of women <note>A common folklore belief that a woman's hair, particularly during menstruation, would turn into a snake if left in water or soil.</note>. Furthermore, in his book on animals, he claims he had a friend who bred scorpions in a marvelous way, from which many others were born—not as imperfect or "monstrous" creatures, but as complete beings capable of producing their own kind. And if this opinion

Our ancestors, believing that all animals were produced from the earth, called her the Mother of the Universe; the Greeks, changing the name slightly, called her <term>Demeter</term> <note>original: "Dimiteram" — referring to the Greek goddess of agriculture and the earth, whose name likely derives from "Mother Earth."</note>. ## *Certain land animals that are born from decay. CHAPTER II.*

Animals have this in common with plants: some arise from seed, and others arise by Nature spontaneously, with no preceding seed of their own kind. This is because some are made from the ground or from rotting wood, such as insects; others from the dew that sits on leaves, such as caterpillars; others from mud, such as shellfish; and others are born from the animals themselves and the excrement of their parts, such as lice. We shall record some of these as described by our predecessors, so that once they are clearly understood, we may learn to create new ones from them. And first, let us see:

People are greatly amazed by this, for they see that the front part of these mice, as far as the chest and the front feet, is animated and moving, while the rear part is not yet formed, remaining nothing but shapeless mud. *Pliny* says: "When the Nile recedes, little mice <note>original: "musculi"</note> are found, the work of the generative water and earth having just begun; they are already living in one part of their body, while their newest extremity is still only made of earth." They wander far and wide through the fields, causing the greatest calamity by attacking the harvests; they cut them down and ruin the piles of sheaves." He notes that the same thing happens in the region of Pontus <note>A region on the southern coast of the Black Sea.</note>, and such plagues are only averted by many prayers offered to God. Likewise, *Macrobius* and *Avicenna* say that mice born from rain increase miraculously through mating. They also state that mice are produced in great abundance from the rotting matter found in ships, and that these too go on to generate others by mating. *Aristotle* observed the wondrous origin of an overflowing race of field mice; for in many places, they are known to arise in such an unheard-of manner that very little of the grain is left. They consume it so quickly that some modest farmers, having decided the day before that it was time to harvest, arrive the next morning with their reapers only to find the entire crop destroyed. Their disappearance, however, happens in a way that defies reason, for within a few days they vanish entirely. It escaped *Pliny's* notice how that multitude dies off so suddenly, for their bodies are not found lying dead, nor has anyone ever been found who dug up a field mouse in the winter. Indeed, the incursion of field mice drove certain peoples of Italy from their ancestral homes, according to *Diodorus* and *Aelian*. Mice destroyed the city of *Cosa* in Etruria <note>An ancient Roman colony in modern Tuscany.</note>. Great numbers of them arrived at the Troad <note>The region around the ancient city of Troy.</note> and drove away the inhabitants from there. *Theophrastus* and *Varro* relate that they drove out the inhabitants of the island of *Gyaros*; the same is told of *Heraclea* in Pontus and other places. ### *How a scorpion may be born from basil.*

Florentinus the Greek <note>A 3rd-century author on agriculture often cited in the *Geoponica*.</note> claimed that basil <note>original: "ocimum"</note> that has been chewed and placed in the Sun generates scorpions. Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), author of the monumental *Natural History*.</note> adds to this: if ground basil is covered with a stone, it produces a scorpion; and if it is chewed and placed in the Sun, it brings forth worms. Indeed, some even report that a handful of basil ground with ten crabs, either from the sea or from rivers, is sufficient to draw all nearby scorpions to that spot. Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath and one of the most significant physicians of the Islamic Golden Age.</note> writes that he had a friend who possessed, as we have mentioned, a marvelous secret for producing scorpions. Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician and philosopher in the Roman Empire (129–c. 216 AD).</note> denies this, but notes that the plant’s sap is harmful; this fact impelled some to spread falsehoods about it, asserting that the plant could generate a scorpion in a few days if ground and placed in an empty jar—especially if one warmed the jar daily in the Sun—but that is certainly false. However, the body of a crab is wonderfully transformed into a scorpion. Pliny says: they say that when the Sun passes through the sign of Cancer <note>The astrological sign of the Crab.</note>, the bodies of crabs, once they are dead and left on dry land, are transfigured into scorpions.

->Ovid.<-

> *If you remove the hollow claws from a shore-dwelling crab,*
> *And bury the rest in the earth, from that buried part,*
> *A scorpion will emerge, threatening with its hooked tail.* <note>original: "Concaua littoreo si demas brachia cancro..." from Ovid's *Metamorphoses*, XV.369-371.</note>

### *The ephemeral is born in vinegar.*

According to Aelian <note>Claudius Aelianus (c. 175–c. 235 AD), a Roman author and teacher of rhetoric who wrote on nature.</note>, such animals are called <term>ephemera</term> <note>From the Greek meaning "lasting only a day."</note> because they live for such a short age that they complete the course of their life in a single day. They draw life from the dregs of wine that is turning sour; when the jar is opened, as soon as they are caught in the light, they depart from life. The river Hypanis <note>The modern Southern Bug river in Ukraine.</note> near the Cimmerian Bosphorus <note>The Strait of Kerch, connecting the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov.</note> brings down, during the solstice, things like little pods larger than grape seeds, from which four-legged winged creatures burst forth. This kind of animal lives only until the afternoon; it flies, but soon, as the Sun descends, it languishes until it dies at sunset. Its life lasts no longer than one day, so it is called a <term>hemerobion</term> <note>From the Greek *hemera* (day) and *bios* (life), meaning "day-liver."</note>, that is, a "daily creature." ...immediately seal the door and windows with thick mud, so that no entrance or breath of air or wind is open. They say that kings <note>Ancient writers, including Aristotle and Virgil, believed the leader of a beehive was a male "king" rather than a queen bee.</note> are born from the brain, but other bees from the flesh; a king also comes from the marrow, yet those born from the brain surpass the others in size, beauty, and color. They sit by the windows, pushing against them impetuously because of their desire for light. But it is better to open the windows on alternating days. ## ON THE COMMINGLING OF ANIMALS

> *Meanwhile the moisture, warmed within the tender bones,*
> *Seethes; and creatures wonderful to behold,*
> *At first lacking feet, soon buzzing with wings,*
> *Mix together, and more and more they seize the thin air.*
> <note>original: "Interea teneris tepefactus in ossibus humor / Æstuat..." These lines from Virgil’s *Georgics* describe the miraculous transformation of decaying matter into a swarm of insects.</note>

But just as the best bees are generated from a tender and noble calf, so base bees are generated from the flesh of a worse and cheaper animal. For this reason, Aelian <note>Claudius Aelianus (c. 175–235 AD), a Roman teacher who wrote about the habits of animals.</note> relates that

->**Wasps are generated from horses.**<-

When its carcass has rotted, wasps fly out from this putrefying marrow; truly an avian offspring from the horse, the swiftest of animals. Ovid calls them wasps and hornets.

> *The war-horse pressed into the ground is the source of the hornet.*
> <note>original: "Pressus humo bellator equus, crabronis origo est." From Ovid's *Metamorphoses*.</note>

Isidore says the hornet <term>crabro</term> is named after the word <term>cabus</term>, that is, a horse <term>caballus</term>, because they are created from it. Hornets are also born from the rotting flesh of horses. Pliny, on the authority of Virgil, says that wasps and hornets are generated from the dead body of horses, as nature transforms certain things into others. In the same way

->**Drones are made from mules.**<-

This is on the authority of Isidore, who said that drones are generated from a mule. The drone <term>fucus</term> is so named because it eats the labors of others, as if it were a "glutton" <term>phagos</term>; for it feeds on what it did not work for. <note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636 AD) frequently used "etymology"—explaining the origin of a word—to explain the nature of the thing itself. Here he links the Latin *fucus* to the Greek *phagein*, meaning "to eat."</note> But others have said that not drones, but locusts, are generated from the flesh of mules. Finally, the most worthless of all arises from the most worthless of animals:

->**The beetle arises from the donkey.**<-

Pliny wrote that beetles are born from the corruption of the bodies of donkeys. Isidore says beetles are generated from swift dogs. Aelian says the race of beetles is devoid of the female sex; therefore, it injects its seed into a ball of dung, which it rolls and warms for a space of twenty-eight days <note>The twenty-eight day period reflects the ancient belief in the influence of the lunar cycle on biology.</note>, and then produces offspring.

...they bring forth, which when they fall into the water below at the opportune time, they come back to life and are turned into a living bird, which they call the **tree-bird**. Indeed, the ancient cosmographers, especially **Saxo Grammaticus**, <note>Saxo Grammaticus (c. 1160–1220) was a Danish historian. But more recent authors report that not only in Scotland, but even by the **Thames river**, where it flows past London, there are bivalve shells with thick, wrinkled stalks attached to the hulls of old ships. These are small, almost circular in shape, white on the outside, shiny, smooth, and fragile, much like a pressed almond nut. From the bottom of these shells, small bellies grow out as if from mucus and half-rotten slime, hanging by a single fungal stalk as if they were sucking nourishment from it. Some say these are created from little worms; others say they are the offspring of tree shoots and branches cast into the sea by the tides. Those that fall on dry land die, but those swept up by the sea's flow are released from the shell and grow into a duck, or a bird of a similar kind.

->*Birds from the putrefaction of wood*<-

**Gesner** <note>Conrad Gessner (1516–1565), a Swiss naturalist whose multi-volume "History of Animals" was the standard reference of the era.</note> relates that these are also born in the **Hebrides islands**. If you throw wood into the sea, in the course of time, worms are first born from the hollowed-out wood; these gradually grow a duck’s head, feet, and wings, and finally produce feathers. Eventually, they equal geese in size, and when they have reached their proper magnitude, they seek the sky, carried through the air by the rowing of their wings <note>original: "alarum remigio"—a poetic Latin phrase for flight.</note> in the manner of other birds. When the wood begins to rot, a huge multitude of worms appears immediately; some are still unformed, others have certain limbs shaped, and some are in the perfect form of birds, among which some have fully formed feathers while others remain featherless. **Paracelsus** <note>The famous 16th-century Swiss alchemist and physician.</note> says that just as the heat of a hen animates the mold and phlegm of an egg into a chick, so too a bird burned in a sealed glass vessel and kept buried in dung <note>Dung was used by alchemists as a source of steady, low-intensity heat for "digestion."</note> is turned into a mucous phlegm; and by that same heat, it is animated and restored into a small bird, just like a **phoenix**. **Ficino**, <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), a central figure of the Italian Renaissance who translated Plato and wrote on "Natural Magic."</note> citing **Albert**, <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a medieval scholar famous for his works on natural science.</note> says that from the putrefaction of sage, a bird is born similar to a blackbird, which is animated there by the "life of the world." <note>original: "à mundi vita"—referring to the *Anima Mundi* or World Soul, a concept where the universe itself is a living being that grants life to matter.</note>

### On fishes that are born from putrefaction.
## CHAPTER IV.

It remains for us to mention several types of fish that are born from putrefaction <note>The theory that living organisms can arise from decaying matter without parents.</note>, now that we have spoken of those belonging to the earth and the air; and first,

->*How eels are generated.*<-

Among eels, there is no female or male sex, nor are they generated through mating, nor do they lay eggs. Indeed, none has ever been caught that possessed either genital seed or eggs, nor does any internal opening show a structure suited for a womb. This is proven by the fact that in certain muddy ponds, even after all the water has been drained and the mud cleared away, eels are born anew once the rainwater returns. For they cannot be born in dry times, even in a perennial pond, since they are born and nourished by rainfall—according to **Aristotle**. <note>Aristotle (384–322 BCE) was the primary authority for the idea that eels emerged from "the guts of the earth" (worms).</note> They are also generated from rotting things. For it has been discovered that when a dead horse is thrown into a pond, countless eels are seen shortly thereafter; this also happens from the carcasses of other animals. Aristotle said they arise from the "guts of the earth," <note>original: *intestinis terræ*. This refers to earthworms, which were thought to spontaneously generate and then transform into eels.</note> which arise both in the sea and in rivers, and in ponds of decay, especially by reason of heat; but in the sea, they arise where there is seaweed, and in ponds and rivers near the banks, for the heat causes those parts to undergo more putrefaction. Because of this, we know of a friend who, having filled wooden vessels with water, added seaweed and certain river weeds and weighed them down with a stone in the open air; in a few days, he would generate eels. Similar is the

->*Origin of anchovies from foam.*<-

The Greeks call the small fish *aphye* <note>original: ἀφύην (*aphyē*), a term used for various small fry, anchovies, or sardines.</note> because this little fish is born from rain. There are many kinds of them which are born "from foam" <note>original: ἐκ ἀφροῦ (*ek aphrou*). This is a folk etymology linking the name *aphyē* to *aphros*, the Greek word for foam.</note>, that is, from froth, and not from mating. Instead, they arise from sandy earth; they neither grow in size nor produce offspring, but perish over a span of time and are born anew. For this reason, they are generated at almost all times of the year and are born in shady, lukewarm places whenever the ground grows warm, such as in the land of **Attica** near **Salamis**, and near the **Themistocleum** in **Marathon**. <note>Locations in Greece famous for these small fish.</note> They also appear elsewhere whenever water falls from the sky.

This little fish <note>Referring to the *apua*, a term used by ancient naturalists for various small fry, often identified as anchovies or sprats.</note> arises in the foam; it is sometimes carried through the surface of the sea and floats in the foam, just as little worms do in dung. **Athenaeus** <note>A Greek rhetorician and grammarian (c. 200 CE) known for his work *The Deipnosophistae*.</note> says it is sacred to Venus, because she herself was also born from foam, from which she earned the name **Aphrodite**. <note>The name Aphrodite was traditionally derived from the Greek word *aphros*, meaning "foam."</note> **Aelian** <note>Claudius Aelianus (c. 175–235 CE), a Roman author and teacher of rhetoric who wrote in Greek about natural history.</note> writes that small fry do not procreate, nor are they procreated [by others], but are born from mud; for when the filth in the sea has thickened and become very muddy and black, it grows warm through a miraculous and vital nature, and is transformed into a great many animals—specifically, small fry. Against the more numerous surges and the rock-breaking waves, they find refuge in the winding hiding-places of the cliffs, and they require no food. **Oppian** <note>A Greco-Roman poet (2nd century CE) who wrote the *Halieutica*, a poem about fishing.</note> describes it most elegantly thus:

> *The foam-born are a defenseless race, not born of blood,*
> *A tiny multitude generated without any parent;*
> *When the mind of Jove <note>original: "Mens Iouis," referring to Jupiter/Zeus as the source of weather.</note> draws heavy rains from thick clouds,*
> *The sea is immediately stirred with a roar,*
> *Waves are lifted, mixed in a swift whirlpool,*
> *Which creates white foam, and the water swells;*
> *And these shoals, gathered from unseen unions,*
> *Emerge from the deep, appearing suddenly nourished.*
> *They are born from foam, and from foam they take their names, etc.*

### Small fry of mullets from putrefaction.

The hottest period of summer, associated with the rising of the star Sirius.</note> and the mud was parched, as soon as the rains began to flood the places again, little fish of the mullet kind were born, the size of small sea-bream, <note>original: "mænarum." The *maena* was a small, salted Mediterranean fish.</note> and in these fish, nothing of either eggs or milt <note>original: "feminis," referring here to the reproductive seed or milt of the fish.</note> was contained. ### Earth-born fish from putrefaction.
