### Shellfish from foamy mud.

If we consider those <term>shellfish</term> <note>original: ostracoderma; from the Greek meaning "shell-skinned."</note> covered by a shell, we see they are procreated either from the power of maritime moisture, without seed, and without male or female. For since they are covered everywhere by a hard shell, no contact or rubbing of the internal parts—which are designed for generation—can conveniently occur. **Aristotle** <note>The Greek philosopher who wrote extensively on the history and generation of animals.</note> says that all shellfish are born spontaneously, the proof being that they arise on ships from rotting foamy mud. Furthermore, in many places where nothing of the sort existed before, when a location became muddy due to a lack of moisture, shell-dwellers were born. Indeed, there is proof that nothing of a genital nature is emitted by them: for when certain people of **Chios** had brought various oysters from **Lesbos** and distributed them in muddy places near the sea, after some time they were no more numerous, though their size had increased. Therefore, oysters are generated in the sea, rivers, and lakes, and for that reason are called "mud-oysters" <note>original: limnostrea; from the Greek *limne* (marsh/mud) and *ostrea* (oyster).</note>, and they take their origin where there is mud. **Oppian** <note>A Greco-Roman poet known for his work on fishing.</note> says:

> *Now even in the damp places of the sea that have liquid paths,*
> *Sprouts are born spontaneously in the whirlpools, a race lacking a mother:*
> *The oyster, the weak small fry <note>original: apuæ</note>, and various kinds of shells,*
> *And the shell-covered, the sea-snails <note>original: turbines</note>, and those born in the sand.*

And elsewhere:

> *Those who do not lie together, nor produce offspring by unions,*
> *Are born by themselves, foul as oysters from the mud:*
> *The oyster is always smooth, without a distinct sex,*
> *Among these fish neither male nor female is known.*

# NATURAL MAGIC, BOOK II.

*Sea-nettles, purple-fish, and razor-clams are born spontaneously.*

Like limpets, scallops, sea cucumbers, and all those that cling to their fixed places. For how could a meeting and mingling of bodies occur among them, since they live in the manner of plants? Therefore, purple-fish <note>original: purpuræ; the sea snails from which the famous Tyrian purple dye was harvested.</note> and shellfish <note>original: ostracoderma; a general term for hard-shelled sea creatures.</note> are born from putrefying matter and mud. Trumpet-shells <note>original: buccinis; often referring to whelks or shells shaped like trumpets.</note> have the same origin. The origin of oysters exists in the mud of swampy places. Shells, razor-clams <note>original: vngues; literally "nails," referring to the long, narrow shape of the razor clam.</note>, and scallops are formed in sandy places. Upright fan-mussels <note>original: pinnæ</note> tied with sea-silk <note>original: bisso; the strong, silky fibers these mollusks use to anchor themselves to the seabed.</note> are found in sandy and swampy places. In short, all shelled creatures are made spontaneously from mud, varying according to the type of mud. In swampy mud, oysters; in sandy mud, shells; in the small hollows of rocks, sea cucumbers and barnacles <note>original: balani; literally "acorns," describing the shape of the barnacle.</note>; while limpets and nerites <note>original: neritæ; a type of sea snail.</note> adhere to the very tops. Mussels <note>original: mytulis</note>, purple-fish, and trumpet-shells have the same origin, which is the putrefying matter in certain ponds. When wooden hedges were set out for the sake of fishing and had rotted through age, an abundance of mussels flourished; but once these were torn away, the place lacked mussels.

->*That new animals can arise from the mixing of different animals.* CHAPTER V.<-

**W**E HAVE spoken of animals that were born from putrefaction; now we shall not deny that various animals can arise from the mixture of different species, and from these, other new ones are generated, so that the opportunity is never lacking for procreating infinite animals and unseen monsters. For no other reason did **Aristotle** <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BCE) whose biological works dominated scientific thought for centuries.</note> say in his book on animals that "**Africa always brings forth something new**," <note>original: Africam semper aliquid noui parere; a famous ancient proverb regarding the biodiversity and "monsters" of the African continent.</note> except because, due to the scarcity of water in those regions, various kinds of animals would gather at the rivers from nearby and neighboring places. There, compelled by force or the drive for pleasure, they would mate, and shapeless offspring and monstrous animals were born. Many things were described by the ancients, and many have been recently devised and found by chance; whether these are possible in the future, I leave to the judgment of ingenious and wise men. But the persuasions of certain philosophers should not divert or deter the ingenious—the idea that from two different kinds, a nature of a third kind is made which is similar to neither parent, and that these very things, once born, do not reproduce within their own kind, simply because they see that the mule does not reproduce, whereas many animals

### ON THE MIXTURE OF ANIMALS

...now they are seen, born from different kinds, which bear young, and others generated from them bear young in turn, so that the species may be preserved forever. Nor is it proper for a law to be established based on the example of a few cases to prevail over all others, since in our own homes and villas, through the mixing of different animals, different species are often generated, which in turn generate others. Their faces and bodies vary from their original ancestors in proportion to how many numerous mixtures they have been mingled through, so that they hardly retain any of their former likeness or appearance. 

It is not entirely true that those born from the mixing of different kinds are imperfect and dissimilar, and that nothing more can be born from them. From these mixtures, we obtain various properties for use in Medicine; and in domestic uses and in hunting, we correct defects and introduce various virtues. 

We shall first recount those things devised and described by the ancients, then those by more recent authors, and finally those things we ourselves have seen in various regions. From these, any ingenious person will be able to discover other things for himself. But before we descend to the practical experiments, it seems worthwhile to recall certain precepts worthy of observation, which are recorded by Aristotle and various others, so that animals may be more easily joined in mutual mating and become pregnant. 

**First**, they should not differ much in size from one another, but there should be little or no difference between them; for if a great difference intervenes, they cannot be mixed together. The size of a dog and a wolf is equal, as is that of a lion and a panther, a donkey and a horse, and among birds, a hen and a partridge, or a falcon and a hawk. For one would quite foolishly attempt to associate a horse with a dog, or a mare with an elephant, or sparrows with hens. 

**Furthermore**, there should be an equal gestation period <note>original: gestationis tempus</note>, meaning they must carry the womb for an equal length of time. For if one animal carries its young for a year and the other for six months, at the time when one is ready to give birth, the other still has a half-formed fetus. A dog carries its young for two months, a horse for twelve; and as the Philosopher <note>Referring to Aristotle, often called "The Philosopher" in Renaissance texts.</note> says, an animal is not born except at the proper time. For this reason, a dog is not born from a human, nor a horse from an elephant; they must not differ in their time of gestation.

# NATURAL MAGIC, BOOK II.

Those that are chaste, and are hardly incited to mating once a year, will let the time for mating pass before they turn their mind to another species if a female of their own kind is missing. But those subject to lust, driven by furies, rush blindly toward animals of their own and other kinds. Among quadrupeds, the dog, the goat, the pig, and the donkey are lustful; among birds, partridges, quails, pigeons, and sparrows. It is also necessary that they be joined at a time suitable for mating: for Nature has fixed and established certain times and ages for **Venus** <note>Used here to mean sexual desire or mating</note> for each animal. The common time for mating is when the harshness of winter ceases and the mildness of spring rises, at which point I might say almost all animals are incited and burn for mating. Let the ages also be appropriate: for at a fixed time, that prolific power reaches the animals; for the first emission of seed from young ones is either infertile or weak, which is why a convenient age for prolific mating is established for each species. Let the age be youthful and almost always nearly equal for both, neither worn out by age nor weak. But if the animals are not naturally lustful, we shall make them so through various arts.

->*That animals may more ardently apply themselves to mating*<-

And if the female does not retain the seed, we must act in various ways so that she does not reject it. Many incentives for **Venus** <note>aphrodisiacs</note> exist among authors, and many are used among us. **Aelianus** <note>original: "Aelianus"; referring to the Roman author of 'On the Nature of Animals'</note> writes that so animals may indulge more in mating, shepherds of sheep, goats, and mares rub their genitals at the time of mating with hands smeared with salt and nitre <note>potassium nitrate or mineral soda</note>, so that a vehement desire for mating arises in them. Others rub them with pepper, others with the fruit of the nettle, others with myrrh and nitre; for from such rubbing, the female's libido is excited and she sustains the males. And they make goats more inclined to mating if they rub their nostrils and chin with scented ointment; and conversely, they restrain them from a desire for more vehement mating by tying linen around the middle of their tails. **Absyrtus** <note>A Greek authority on veterinary medicine</note> makes males more eager for **Venus** by wiping the genitals <note>original: "natura"</note> of a mare and smearing it on their own nostrils. **Didymus** says that rams are rendered strong for mating by frequently offering them the herb called **polygonum** <note>knotgrass</note> in their fodder; from which they and other cattle are incited to mating. **Pliny** offers onions to cattle to increase the power of mating, no less than **eruca** <note>rocket or arugula</note> does for man. ### *How very strong dogs, possessing various virtues, can be produced from the commingling of different animals. CHAPTER VI.*

We shall begin with **DOGS**, since no animal is more familiar to us, and since many animals are equal to them in size and in the duration of the womb’s gestation. The dog is also lustful and always ready for mating; it mixes both with its own kind and with those of a very different nature. Through this, one may change its habit and form, correct its other faults, and adapt it for guarding, hunting, and various other uses and pastimes. First, we shall see how they may be produced.

### *The very strong Indian dog produced from a tiger.*

This dog is called a **mastiff** <note>original: "mastinus"</note>, a robust warrior, and is named **Hyrcanian** <note>original: "hircanus"; referring to Hyrcania, a region near the Caspian Sea known in antiquity for its wild beasts</note> by others. **Aristotle** says they are generated from a dog and a tiger, and are called "Indians." Elsewhere, he says they come from a dog and a certain wild beast, though he does not specify the name. **Pliny** <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, author of the 'Natural History'</note> writes that the Indians desire dogs conceived by tigers; for this reason, they tie up female dogs in the forests during the time for mating. They believe that the offspring of the first and second litters are produced with too much ferocity, and they only raise those from the third litter. From the writings of Indian affairs, **Aelian** <note>Claudius Aelianus, a Roman author who wrote in Greek about animal biology</note> describes the history of this robust dog. Shepherd’s dogs of a very noble breed—excellent at tracking wild beasts with a keen sense of smell and very swift in the chase—are led out to places where tigers are known to live. The shepherds tie them to trees and depart. Tigers, happening upon them and suffering from a lack of prey or hunger, may tear them apart; however, if the tigers are inflamed with lust and have already eaten their fill, they join with the dogs in a sexual embrace. From this habit of tigers with dogs, a tiger is not actually produced, but the seed, falling toward a lower state <note>This reflects the ancient belief that the "stronger" parent determines the species, but "weaker" seed results in a dog-like hybrid</note> and reflecting the maternal kind, becomes a dog. These dogs born of a tiger father utterly despise hunting deer or boar, but when they encounter a lion, they leap with joy. An Indian man of the highest nobility once made a trial of the strength of these dogs for **Alexander** <note>Alexander the Great</note>, the son of King Philip, in this manner: first he sent out a deer; the dog from that...

# NATURAL MAGIC, BOOK II.

In the place where it was resting, holding the [deer] in the lowest contempt, it did not move at all; then, when a wild boar was released, just as it had been affected by the stag, it remained unmoved. But when a bear was sent in, holding both this and the others in disdain, it restrained itself from attacking. Finally, when they brought a **lion** into the midst of them, as soon as the dog saw it, it flared up with rage, and truly, as if a worthy foe had descended into the arena, it attacked without delay and without fear. Holding the lion gripped in a most fierce embrace, it pressed upon its throat and began to suffocate it. Then the **Indian**, who was presenting this spectacle to the **King** <note>Alexander the Great</note>, and who well knew the strength of the dog's spirit and its constancy, first ordered its tail to be cut off. The dog, because of the lion which it held in its bite, easily allowed its tail to be severed. Then he even commanded one leg to be broken; yet the dog pressed on just as he had from the beginning, and likewise yielded nothing, as if someone else’s leg—pertaining nothing to itself—were being broken. After that, a second was broken, at which the dog was not at all moved, but held on tightly; then he ordered a third to be cut into. The dog, just as before, did not relax its hold on the lion. Then he even wanted the fourth leg to be cut off; the dog, becoming no less intense and holding the lion no less firmly, leaned in with its greatest strength toward the lion's destruction. Finally, even though its head was severed from the rest of its body, its teeth remained hanging together from that part of the lion where they had first been fixed; and although the one who had first sunk them in was now dead, even then its head, hanging from the lion, was carried aloft. At this, **Alexander** was affected by no small grief, being struck dumb by admiration for such virtue <note>original: "virtutis"; here meaning "valor" or "manly courage"</note>, because the creature who had given such a specimen of courage had preferred to depart from life rather than yield from the strength of its spirit. Seeing this, the Indian gifted him four dogs similar to that one. The King accepted them as a gift with a grateful and pleasant mind, and then rewarded the one who had given them with as great a price as was fitting for a most excellent King. **Philes** <note>Manuel Philes, a 14th-century Byzantine poet who wrote on the characteristics of animals</note> records these same things. **Diodorus Siculus** <note>A Greek historian of the 1st century BCE</note> and **Strabo** <note>A Greek geographer and historian</note>, however, write that it was **King Sopithes** who gave those one hundred and fifty dogs to Alexander, which were extremely large and robust, and were said to be mixed with tigers.

The same history is related by Pollux <note>Julius Pollux, a 2nd-century Greek grammarian</note>. The **Indian dog** described by Plutarch does not seem different from this one. He says that a dog, which held the first rank among the Indians and had fought against Alexander, was brought into the arena. As long as a deer, a boar, or a bear was released, they say it lay motionless in contempt. But indeed, when a **lion** was sighted, it was stirred in a moment, scattering the sand with its feet as if it judged this antagonist worthy of itself, while looking down upon all the deer. 

**Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, the Roman natural historian</note> records that when Alexander the Great was heading to India, the **King of Albania** gave him a dog of unusual size as a gift. Delighted by its appearance, Alexander ordered bears, then boars, and finally fallow deer to be released; but the dog lay motionless in contempt. The Emperor, offended by such laziness in so large a body, ordered the high-spirited creature to be killed. Fame reported this back to the King; and so, sending a second dog, he added instructions that Alexander should not wish to test it on small things, but on a lion or an elephant. He noted that he had only possessed two such dogs, and with this one killed, no other would remain. 

Alexander did not delay, and immediately saw a lion broken. Afterward, he ordered an elephant to be brought in, and he was never more delighted by any other spectacle. Indeed, with the hair bristling over its whole body, the dog first thundered with a massive bark, then rushed forward attacking. It rose up against the beast on this side and that, harassing it with a skillful style of fighting where it was most needed, and then evading it, until by a constant whirling motion like that of a wheel, it wore the beast down, the earth shaking at its fall. **Gratius** <note>Gratius Faliscus, a Roman poet of the Augustan age who wrote on hunting</note> wrote of this kind of dog:

> *But the ferocity of the Hyrcanian race is not enough*
> *To suffice: of their own accord, the fierce females seek the woods,*
> *Venus grants them access, and joins them in a seductive covenant.*
> *Then the wild adulterer wanders safely among the tame*
> *Stables, and the female dog, daring to yield to the heavy tiger*
> *Of her own will, bore an offspring from a greater lineage of blood.*

### A strong and swift dog from the Thoe.

**Aristotle** said that the **thoe** <note>original: *thos*; generally identified as the golden jackal</note> has internal organs entirely similar to those of a wolf; it is a robust animal, fights with lions and dogs, and is very swift. **Pliny** says it belongs to the wolf family, and **Hesychius** also calls it similar to a wolf. **Herodotus** records that they are born among the Africans, while **Solinus** calls them "Ethiopian wolves." **Nearchus** calls common tigers *Thoas* and notes that they are of various kinds. From these, **Gratius** <note>Gratius Faliscus, a Roman poet who wrote on hunting</note> asserts that dogs born from *thoes* are strong and fit for hunting; he calls them "half-wild" because they are born from one parent that is a tame dog and the other a wild animal, the *thoe*.

> *Here he also produced a half-wild offspring from the blood of the thoe,*
> *no greater courage exists in any other heart.*
> *Whether it learns commands or is called to the contests of naked War,*
> *the thoes (so says the famous report) have even attacked lions*
> *by cunning and mastered them with their small limbs.*
> *For one would be ashamed to admit how small and shapeless the breed is.*

### A dog from a wolf and dog: the Crocuta.

**Pliny** calls those conceived from a wolf and a dog **crocutas** <note>original: *crocutae*; a legendary creature often associated with the hyena, though here described as a canine hybrid</note>; they crush everything with their teeth and immediately digest what they have swallowed in their bellies. Just as they bred dogs from tigers, the **Gauls** do the same with wolves; each of their packs has its own leader and guide chosen from the dogs. **Aristotle** says that wolves mate with dogs in the region of Cyrene, and **Pollux** follows him in this; they therefore call the wild beast conceived from a dog and a wolf a "crocuta." **Galen**, in his book *On the Use of the Parts*, affirms that a male wolf can conceive with a female dog, and a male dog with a female wolf, receiving the seed, retaining it, and bringing it to the mixture of a living animal. **Diodorus** says: "That which the Ethiopians call a crocuta is a mixture of the natures of a dog and a wolf." When **Niphus** <note>Agostino Nifo, a 16th-century Italian scholar</note> was hunting, a dog pursued a female wolf with great effort; when he caught her, he began to mate, his hatred and ferocity having subsided in favor of his desire for Venus <note>Meaning sexual desire</note>. **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus, the medieval polymath</note> said that from a wolf and a dog is born a large dog called a **mastiff** <note>original: *mastinus*</note>. I have seen a dog sired by a wolf in Rome, and a female wolf sired by a dog in Naples. **Ovid** writes:

> *And Nape, conceived from a wolf,*

### Swift Laconic dogs can be bred from a dog and a fox.

**Aristotle**, and **Galen** following him, say that animals can mate whose genus is indeed different but whose nature is not far apart, provided that a similar physical size allows for equal gestation periods, as is certainly the case with dogs and foxes. From a fox and a dog, **Laconic dogs** <note>original: *Laconici*; a famous breed from the Laconia region of Greece, known for scent and speed</note> are produced. The first offspring are born with a physical appearance common to both types, but as time proceeds, different individuals emerging from different pairings eventually result in a form restored to that of the female. **Pollux** relates that Laconic dogs born from foxes and dogs were primarily called **alopecidae** <note>original: *alopecidas*; from the Greek *alopex*, meaning fox</note>. According to **Xenophon**, these "fox-dogs" are born from dogs and foxes, and their nature is blended over a span of time. He identifies these fox-dogs as hunting dogs; and indeed, certain swift hunting dogs, such as those called greyhounds, appear to resemble the fox, with their heads tapering to a sharp point and the shape of their snouts. **Hesychius** and **Varinus** call them **cynalopecae** <note>original: *cynalopecas*; literally "dog-foxes"</note>. But if we wish to know

### How a swift and strong dog may be bred.

Mixed and hybrid <term>bigeneres: "of two kinds," referring to cross-bred animals</term> dogs are those born from two dog parents but of different breeds. For example, in **Aristotle**, from a **Molossian** <note>a large, heavy-set ancient breed used for guarding and war</note> and a **Laconic** dog, a puppy is born that will be both swift and strong. There are also those born with one parent being a dog and the other a wild beast, such as a wolf, a lion, or similar animals. Hunters devised this mixing for two reasons: with the first kind of breeding, they sought to correct certain flaws and prevent them in the offspring, or to add certain desirable traits; with the latter kind, they aimed to produce more robust dogs for hunting against larger wild beasts.

### *How small puppies are generated.*

In former times, puppies were highly prized for the delight of women; these were born on the island of **Melita** <note>The author likely refers to the island of Mljet in the Adriatic, though "Melita" is also the ancient name for Malta; both were famous for small dogs.</note> situated in the Adriatic Gulf not far from Ragusa <note>Modern-day Dubrovnik, Croatia.</note>, and called the *Melitean* dog by **Callimachus**. **Aristotle** seems to teach how they are generated in his book of *Problems*, asking: Why in the genus of animals are some composed of a small body and others a large one? ### That a mimic dog may be born.

One that plays willingly, jumps here and there, barks gently, nips without biting, and stretches out its front legs like hands, and brings back what has been thrown with its snout. Let us make these live with a monkey <note>original: "simia"; could refer to an ape or monkey</note>, and as it becomes accustomed to being around it, it will learn to do many humorous things worthy of laughter. If it even mates with the monkey, the dog born from them is the most fit of all for the tricks which mountebanks <note>original: "agyrtæ"; itinerant performers or quacks</note> and street-performers <note>original: "circumforanei"</note> show their dogs performing for the sake of games, mimicry, or the works of actors. The best may also be born from a fox, as is held from the writings of **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus, the 13th-century polymath</note>.

But **Oppian** <note>A Greco-Roman poet of the 2nd century AD known for his work on fishing and hunting</note> prescribes that dogs to be trained for hunting should not be suckled by the teats of domestic dogs, nor goats, nor sheep; for he says they will become sluggish and weak. Instead, they should be nursed by a hind, a tame lioness, a gazelle, or a wolf, so that they may become robust and swift. For he says:

> *But if the skillful rearing of puppies is a care to you,*
> *Never let the pups be suckled from the fresh teat*
> *Of goats, or sheep, nor of domestic dogs:*
> *For they grow heavy, sluggish, or of no value.*
> *But rather the teat of hinds, or a tame lioness,*
> *Or of gazelles, or the night-wandering wolf.*
> *For thus you will make them both strong and very swift,*
> *Similar to those milk-bearing nurses themselves.*

**Aelian** <note>Claudius Aelianus, a Roman author and teacher of rhetoric who wrote "On the Nature of Animals"</note> says the same: if you strive to rear puppies correctly, beware that they do not suck the teats of goats, sheep, or domestic dogs, for they will be made sluggish and weak; rather, let them suckle from hinds, or a tame lioness, or deer, or a wolf, for in this way you will make them both robust and swift. For when they remember that they were nourished by such animals, they will be ashamed not to exist as robust and swift creatures. **Pollux** <note>Julius Pollux, a Greek grammarian whose "Onomasticon" served as a multi-volume dictionary and encyclopedia</note> said that mother’s milk is especially suitable as food for puppies; after that, the blood of the animals which the dogs have caught, so that they may gradually become accustomed to a hunter's diet. **Ctesias of Cnidus** <note>A Greek physician and historian from the 5th century BC</note> in the books he wrote about Indian matters, says that the race of the **Cynamolgi** <note>term: Cynamolgi; literally "dog-milkers," a legendary tribe of Ethiopia described by ancient geographers</note> nourish many dogs on cow's milk, which, when set against Indian cattle, overcome them and kill even the most ferocious. And the Cynamolgi themselves press milk from the dogs into a milk-pail, and then indeed drink it just as we drink either sheep's or goat's milk; this is from Aelian. **Solinus** <note>A 3rd-century Latin grammarian and compiler</note> says that because of this, the Ethiopian Cynamolgi are said to have dog-like muzzles and protruding mouths. We shall also have it in this way, how

->*A noble donkey may be produced.*<-

If, immediately after it is born, it is removed from its mother and placed under an unsuspecting mare: she is best deceived by the darkness; for when her own offspring is removed in a dark place, the aforementioned [donkey]...

### How different kinds of mules can be produced.
#### CHAPTER IX.

We shall teach the mixings of donkeys, horses, and others; and although these are known to everyone, we will perhaps add other things that will not be unpleasing to readers. **Aelian** <note>Claudius Aelianus, a Roman author of the 2nd century AD who wrote about the natural world</note>, citing **Democritus** <note>An Ancient Greek philosopher best known for his atomic theory, but who also wrote on biology</note>, says that mules are not a work of nature, but an "adultery" and a "theft" invented by human machination. He claims it began when a Median donkey <note>Referring to Media, an ancient region in modern-day Iran</note> forced itself upon a mare, accidentally making her pregnant; humans, becoming students of this violence, afterwards brought it into a custom of procreation. According to the commentator on **Homer** <note>Homer's Scholiast; an ancient commentator on the Iliad or Odyssey</note>, the breeding of mules was first devised in the city of the Veneti in Paphlagonia <note>An ancient region on the Black Sea coast of Anatolia</note>. We read in the books of **Genesis** <note>Genesis 36:24</note> that **Anah**, the father-in-law of Esau, found mules while pasturing his father’s donkeys in the desert. But

->*A mule is produced from a mare and a male donkey.*<-

Mules do not come from a root of their own kind, but are "double-natured" and "grafted," according to **Varro** <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a prolific Roman scholar and writer on agriculture</note>. Therefore, one ought to prepare a mare of large body and solid bones if one seeks strength rather than speed; in this way, she will bring forth a large and strong mule. However,

->*a hinny is produced from a horse and a female donkey.*<-

For this, one must choose a female donkey of the largest form and with strong limbs, who is most patient of labor. She contributes to the offspring not only the goods of the body, but also those of the character. For although the offspring take their name from the father—being called **hinnies**—they will be similar to the mother in all respects. They have a mane and tail like those of a donkey, yet they bear equine ears; they are smaller in body than a mule, unruly, and of an indomitable slowness <note>referring to the stubbornness typical of donkeys</note>. The most excellent of all are

->*Swift mules generated from a wild donkey and a female donkey.*<-

For there is nothing in this herd more excellent in either spirit or form than what a donkey <unclear>p̄</unclear> will seed, although that which a wild donkey <note>original: "onager"; the Asiatic wild ass</note> procreates can be compared to it to some extent.

...except that it will display the wild habits of its father—untamed, resistant to service in a wild manner, and lean in appearance. Whatever is produced from this match reflects the paternal form and modesty, while retaining the strength and speed of its grandfather, according to **Columella** <note>Lucius Junius Moderatus Columella, a Roman writer whose work *De Re Rustica* is a major source on ancient agriculture</note>. These are perhaps the mules that **Aristotle** writes are unique to Syria; they are outstanding in speed and are not sterile, yet they share a common name with others because of their similar shape, just as wild donkeys took on the name of the domestic ones. But this genus is not so unique—

### *The strongest mules from a bull and a donkey.*

For a fourth kind is found, which is located in Grenoble <note>original: "Gratianopoli"</note>, as it is written, and is named a *Jumar* in the French tongue. **Gesner** <note>Conrad Gessner, a 16th-century Swiss naturalist often called the father of modern zoology</note> heard from trustworthy sources that a "horse" was seen at the base of Mount Splügen <note>original: "montis Spelungi"</note> in Rhaetia <note>a region in the central Alps</note> that was born from a mare and a bull. We, however, saw some in Ferrara <note>a city in Northern Italy</note> with the form of a mule but the head of a calf, which had two small bumps in place of horns; they were of tireless and untamed ferocity, black in color, with the eyes of a bull, and we were wonderfully delighted by that sight. We have heard they are common in some parts of France, although I did not see them myself while traveling through that country.

### *How goats and sheep may be mixed.*
## CHAPTER X.

To correct certain defects in a ram and to instill better traits, we can achieve our desire either by mixing them with wild and forest-dwelling animals, or with those similar and not far from their own kind. The closest kind is the goat and the sheep; therefore, by mixing them—

->*A musmon is produced from a goat and a ram.*<-

In Spain, and especially Corsica, there is a kind of animal not unlike sheep called the musmon <term>musmon: likely referring to the mouflon, a type of wild sheep</term>, says **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the encyclopedic *Natural History*</note>; it has a goat-like hair rather than a sheep's fleece. The ancients called those born from this kind and domestic sheep "Umbri," while **Strabo** <note>A Greek geographer and historian</note> called them the *musmon* <note>original: "μυσμόν"</note>. <page-num>73</page-num>
<header>ON ANIMAL CROSSBREEDING</header>

**Albert** <note>Albertus Magnus, a 13th-century philosopher and scientist known for his work on natural history</note> calls those *musmones* which are born from a goat and a ram. Among the Rhaetians <note>the people of Rhaetia, a Roman province in the central Alps</note>, who are allies of the Swiss, I hear that in Alpine places goats are sometimes born with the hind part of a goat and the front part of a sheep or ram; however, they cannot live and die shortly after birth. For when rams grow old, they become strong and lustful, and sometimes come upon goats. From the mating of sheep and wild rams, it is said the offspring reflects the father's color, and that this trait continues through the lineage and grandchildren. The wool in the first offspring is shaggy, but in the grandchildren and thereafter it becomes soft. On the other hand,

### *a cinirus is generated from a sheep and a buck.*

The same Albert says that a *cinirus* <note>a name for a specific sheep-goat hybrid</note> is the name for the offspring born of a sheep and a buck <note>original: "hirco," a male goat</note>. But the most excellent method of crossbreeding <note>original: "adulterium," implying a violation of natural boundaries</note> ever devised is

### *to generate offspring from wild and domestic goats.*

Whatever species exists among wild beasts, writers report that their wildness can be softened through successive generations of offspring until they become tame. I will cite the example of **Columella** <note>Lucius Junius Moderatus Columella, a Roman writer on agriculture mentioned on the previous page</note>. In the municipality of Cádiz <note>original: "Graditanum"</note>, wild and fierce rams of extraordinary color were brought from nearby Africa, just as other wild beasts are brought for those who provide public games. Marcus Columella, the uncle of Junius Columella, purchased some of these, brought them to his fields, and once they were tamed, he allowed them to mate with domestic sheep. These first produced shaggy lambs that retained the father's color; these lambs were then put to Tarentine sheep <note>sheep from Tarentum, famous in the ancient world for having the finest, softest wool</note>, and they procreated rams with a finer fleece. From these, whatever was conceived reflected the mother's softness along with the father's and grandfather's color. The same was experienced in swine, for

### *we can procreate hybrids from wild and domestic swine;*

for the wild boar is most inflamed with the lust of Venus and burns with the frenzy of mating; if his female resists the mating of one so raging with lust, he either overcomes her by force or strikes her dead to the ground. And while some say that wild animals do not conceive when tamed—such as geese, boars (which are slow to do so), and deer raised from infancy—in no genus is the mixing with a wild animal as easy as it is with swine. The ancients called those born this way "hybrids" <note>original: "hybridas"</note>, as if they were half-wild. It appears the name was derived from the Greek word for "outrage" or "excess" <note>original: παρὰ τὴν ὕβριν (para tēn hybrin)</note>, perhaps because the name was hurled as an insult against those born from an "adulterous" crossbreed.

### *That various animals are born from the crossbreeding of different animals.* CHAPTER XI.

We shall point out the mixtures arising from animals of different species, and then, by experimenting with other mixtures from those already born, we shall attempt to establish the sought-after species. We will consider which offspring retain more of the mother or the father, so that we may achieve our desires; and first

->*to generate a leopard from a panther and a lioness.*<-

A leopard <note>original: "leopardus"</note> is born from a lion and a panther <note>original: "pardalis"</note>. They say the lioness is fervent for mating, but the lion is not quite able to mate due to the excessive heat of his temperament. Therefore, the lioness admits the panther into the lion's dens. However, when the time for giving birth approaches, she flees to the mountains and places familiar to panthers. For they give birth to spotted cubs, and for that reason, they nourish them hidden in the densest forests, pretending to be away from the males for the sake of hunting. For if the lions discover the cubs, they tear them apart and destroy the offspring as being adulterous, according to **Philostratus** <note>Flavius Philostratus, a 3rd-century Greek scholar who wrote on the lives of animals and heroes</note>. In the wild places of Hyrcania <note>a region southeast of the Caspian Sea</note> there are panthers—the second kind after the panther species <note>original: "pantheris," suggesting a distinction between different large spotted cats</note>—well enough known and not needing further description, from whose adulterous matings with lionesses the breed is degenerated; they do procreate lions, but they are ignoble <note>lacking the characteristic mane and stature of "pure" lions</note>. **Solinus** <note>Gaius Julius Solinus, a 3rd-century Roman geographer known for his collection of curiosities</note> says: From the adultery of the panther and the lioness, the leopard is born, creating a third origin. **Isidore** <note>Isidore of Seville, a 7th-century archbishop and encyclopedist</note> says: The lions which panthers create remain destitute of manes. **Pliny** and **Solinus** note: The lion senses the mating by the scent of the panther on the adulteress, and rises up with all his strength for punishment; for this reason, the lioness either washes herself in a river or follows the lion from a long distance. But if the lioness conceives by the panther, she gives birth to a creature like herself in body, but different in spirit; likewise, if a pantheress conceives by a lion, she produces a spotted offspring. Thus there are two types of leopards, just as with the mule: one from a horse and a female donkey, the other from a male donkey and a mare. For all hybrids <note>original: "bigenera," animals of two races</note> seem to take more from the mother, especially regarding size and the form of the body. **Claudian** <note>Claudius Claudianus, a late 4th-century Roman court poet</note> wrote:

> *The river-dwelling panthers hasten to face wounds,*
> *Born of mixed seed, when by chance a vigorous* <note>original: "viridis," literally green, but here implying youthful or wild</note> *adulterer*
> *Once again corrupted a noble lioness;*
> *They resemble their fathers in their spots, and their mothers in their backs.*

->*a crocuta is born from a hyena and a lioness.*<-

We have said that the lioness is driven by the greatest provocations, and when

From the mating of a hyena, the Ethiopian lioness gives birth to a **crocuta** <note>A mythical beast often described as a hybrid between a hyena and a lion or dog, said to mimic human speech</note>, as **Pliny** says, and **Solinus** after him. The panther is also an extremely lustful animal, so much so that it mates even with different species. Hence

In the season of lust, the panther is quite vocal, and animals of its own kind or of various species run toward its voice. A scholion on **Homer** says it is similar to a hyena; others call this a *chaos*. **Pliny** states that the games of **Pompey the Great** first displayed the *chaus* <note>original: "chaum," likely referring to the jungle cat, Felis chaus</note>, which the Gauls call a *raphium*, with the image of a wolf and the spots of panthers. But an admirable adultery <note>In this context, "adultery" refers to the "corruption" of a species through crossbreeding</note> is reported by the Greeks:

**that from a pig and a camel, the Bactrian camel is born.**

For **Didymus**, in the Greek *Geoponica* <note>A 10th-century collection of agricultural lore</note>, declares that in those mountains belonging to India, the Bactrian camel conceives from wild boars grazing together with them: the camel born from a pig, or boar, and a female camel is born with a double hump <note>original: "geminatum tuber"</note>. But just as the mule bears most of the father's traits from horses and donkeys, so the camel arising from the seed of a pig acquires strength and density of hair as a sign of its power; it does not slip in the mud as easily as other camels do, but stands up immediately by its own strength and carries double the weight of the others. They call them, and rightly so, **Bactrian**, because they were first born in Bactria <note>An ancient region in Central Asia, roughly modern-day Afghanistan and Uzbekistan</note>.

To condemn and cast down the memory of these impious men, we shall recall some examples. **Plutarch** <note>Plutarch (c. 46 – 119 AD) was a Greek philosopher and biographer whose works were frequently cited by Renaissance naturalists</note> denies that beasts contract love with other species, but that man indeed goes mad with wicked pleasures, so that some are not ashamed to most disgracefully mate with mares, goats, and others. Plutarch relates that in the *Banquet of the Seven Sages* held in the house of **Periander** <note>The Ruler of Corinth and one of the Seven Sages of Greece</note>, a story was brought by a shepherd:

Having inspected this, **Thales** <note>Thales of Miletus, often considered the first philosopher in the Greek tradition</note> said to Periander that to him it did not seem a prodigious thing, or a portent sent by the gods to signify seditions and discords (as **Diocles** judged), but that it was a natural occurrence. Therefore, he advised that either he should not have grooms, or he should provide them with wives. The same author records in his *Parallels*, citing **Agesilaus** from the third book of *Italian Affairs*, that **Fulvius Stella**, out of a hatred for women, shared himself with a mare, which then gave birth to a very beautiful girl, timely named **Epona** <note>Epona was the Gallo-Roman goddess of horses; here the author treats the myth as a historical biological event</note>. ### *A girl born from a man and a donkey.*

For **Ariston Aristonymus of Ephesus**, the son of Demonstratus, utterly loathing the female sex, joined himself to a certain donkey, which then in its own time gave birth to a girl of most honorable appearance; her name was **Onoscelis** <note>original: "Onosceli". ...conceived and brought to perfection, this animal might be born. By what nutrients would it be fed once born? But it does not seem impossible to me, though difficult, since not all men consist of the same temperament <note>Latin: *complexio* — the balance of bodily humors or qualities that define a person's physical nature</note>, but it is possible to find some men who are somewhat similar in temperament to the horse; and there are those who possess a longer member, and among mares, those who have a short neck of the womb. Aelian <note>Claudius Aelianus (c. 175 – 235 AD) was a Roman author whose "On the Nature of Animals" was a primary source for Renaissance naturalists</note> tells another story,

### *A half-wild offspring born from a man and a goat*

In Sybaris, a certain young goatherd named Crathis <note>original: "Crachis"</note>, who burned with the lust of goat-love, joined with the most beautiful of all in a venereal embrace. He held her in the place of a mistress and gave her gifts; he would toss her ivy and rushes to eat, making her mouth smell sweeter for kissing. He would spread soft and tender herbs for her so that she might sleep more comfortably. When the buck, the leader of the flock, saw this while they were asleep, he made an attack and crushed the youth's skull. In due time, the goat gave birth to an infant having the legs of a goat and a human face. The same author writes that

### *Women mate with he-goats and baboons.*

Herodotus <note>A 5th-century BC Greek historian often cited for his descriptions of foreign customs</note> writes in his second book that a he-goat mated with a woman openly, so that it became a public spectacle. Strabo <note>A Greek geographer and historian of the Augustan era</note> says: In the inland region above the Sebennytic and Phatnitic <note>original: "Pharnicum"</note> mouth of the Nile is the island of Xois, and a city in the Sebennytic province, and Hermopolis and Mendes, where Pan is worshipped, and the he-goat is a sacred animal; and (as Pindarus <note>Pindar, the famous Greek lyric poet</note> says) in this place goats mate with women.

### *That various birds can be generated from the diverse intermixing of birds. CHAPTER XIII.*

**B**EFORE we descend to the intermixing of birds, we shall mention certain observations regarding the ease of the process; so that if it happens in practice that some defects need to be corrected, making them more suitable for our conveniences, we might be able to accomplish this more quickly. We have said, following Aristotle <note>Aristotle (384–322 BC), the Greek philosopher whose biological works provided the framework for understanding animal reproduction in this era</note>, that for animals capable of intermixing, there should be an equality of size, an equal time of gestation in the womb, a similar incubation of eggs, a similarity of color, and among other things, a very fervent lust <note>original: *luxuriæ præferuidæ* — referring to intense sexual drive or being "in heat"</note>, so that they may easily mate with those of a different kind. If a fowler <note>original: *aucupi* — one who breeds or catches birds</note> desires to produce pugnacious hawks, roosters, or other birds, it is necessary to have pugnacious, strong, and robust males, so that they may produce such sons. Nor should he require any less robust and noble mothers; for if only the father or the mother is noble <note>original: *generosa* — of high quality or good breeding stock</note>, the son will retain the father's laziness and sloth rather than the mother's nobility. When you have chosen the best parents, before you mix them together, ensure that they become accustomed to the domestic quarters and first enter into some degree of familiarity, which you will best achieve through living together and through food. Therefore, let a small house be built, more or less ten feet wide and long; in it, let all the little windows face the south, so that light may be supplied sufficiently and copiously from the top of the roof. In the middle, let wicker partitions divide the cell. The gap between the wicker bars should be just open enough to allow the bird's head and neck to pass through; on one side of the chamber, let the single bird rule that we wish to make tame <note>original: *cicurem* — tamed or domesticated</note>, while the other side should hold those with which we seek to join and intermix the guest bird. At the beginning of spring, therefore (at which time all animals are provoked by the sting of lust), you should have birds of known fertility, and let their feathers be similar to the one you are striving to tame. ### *How ospreys, bone-breakers, and vultures are born from various eagles.*

## On the mixing of fish. CHAPTER XVI.

If different kinds of fish were to mingle with one another, it would be difficult for a person to become aware of it, since fish live under the water; nor can their actions be easily observed, especially those that occur outside the normal laws of Nature. But if you consider what we have said above, you will easily master the subject—namely, which species are the most lustful, which have equal gestation periods, their relative size, and so on. Furthermore, Aristotle says in his *History of Animals*: The seeds of different fish do not mix, and no one has ever seen different kinds of fish mating, with the exception of

->the angelshark and the ray, which produce the guitarfish.<-
<note>original: "Squatina & raia, quæ rhinobaton gignunt." The angelshark (*Squatina*) and the ray (*Raia*) were thought to produce the *Rhinobatos*, known today as the guitarfish.</note>

For the name *rhinobatos* <note>Greek: $\rho\iota\nu\acute{o}\beta\alpha\tau\omicron\varsigma$</note> is derived from both. Regarding this, Pliny says: Different kinds of fish do not mate except for the angelshark and the ray, from which is born a creature resembling a ray in its front part, and it takes its name from a composition of both among the Greeks. Beyond these, nothing is read or accepted anywhere else regarding the guitarfish. Theodore Gaza <note>A 15th-century Greek humanist and translator of Aristotle.</note> translated *rhinobaton* as *squatinoraia* <note>a compound word of monkfish and ray</note>, and although some deny its existence, it was revealed to us through the diligence of Simone Porzio <note>Simon Portius, a 16th-century Neapolitan philosopher and physician.</note>, a most learned Neapolitan philosopher; a depiction of it is still preserved, and it is found in the Strait of Naples.

## How new and miraculous births are produced. CHAPTER XVII.

Miraculous births <note>original: "prodigiosi partus"</note>, whether they be monsters or miscarriages, are produced from animals through the methods mentioned above: the mixing of seeds, imagination, or other causes. We shall speak of imagination later. For now, let us hear the reasoning of our ancestors regarding how miraculous and monstrous births are produced, so that by considering these, an ingenious person might devise for themselves ways to bring miraculous offspring into the light. Democritus, as Aristotle says, believed they arise from the mixing of many seeds; when one portion is cast into the womb first and another later, they enter the parts of the womb and are confused together, and their limbs become disjointed—which is how two-headed humans and many-limbed animals are born. Empedocles <note>A Greek Pre-Socratic philosopher who proposed that the world was made of four elements and moved by Love and Strife.</note>, however, by anticipating all possible answers, seems to have grasped the truth. He claims that monstrous animals are born because of an excess or deficiency of the female seed, or because of the starting point of movement, or due to its distribution into several parts, or because the process has strayed from its path. 

Straton <note>Straton of Lampsacus, a Greek Peripatetic philosopher known as "The Physicist."</note>, on the other hand, teaches that these things happen through addition, subtraction, transposition, or inflation. But certain physicians have attributed it to the womb, which, being frequently filled with gas, is overturned. 

Aristotle says: it happens more frequently to animals that produce many young at once, and even more so to those with "multifid" feet <note>meaning animals with paws or divided toes, rather than solid hooves</note>, to bear monsters; for since they otherwise produce young that are almost imperfect, they more easily slide into a monstrous division. This occurs most especially in those called *metachoera* <note>original: "metachœra." An Aristotelian term for "after-pigs" or offspring born with slight defects, often smaller than their siblings.</note>, which are affected by a monstrous blemish to some degree; for to lack something, or to have something in excess, is a "monster" <term>monstrum: a biological wonder or deviation from the natural pattern</term> and is contrary to nature. 

Indeed, in the book of *Problems* <note>A work traditionally attributed to Aristotle consisting of questions and answers on various scientific topics.</note>, it is said: Small four-footed animals produce monsters, but humans and all large living creatures do so less, such as horses and donkeys. This is because small animals, such as dogs, pigs, goats, and sheep, are far more fertile than large ones; for among the large ones, some always bear only one offspring, and others for the most part produce few. Monsters, however, are usually created when many seeds stick together and are mixed—either when they come from the male, or when they mingle within the female. 

For this reason, even birds can produce monsters: for they lay eggs with a double yolk <note>original: "vitello geminato"</note>, and monsters consist of those doubled yolks when no intervening membrane separates them. Nature, being wise in the shaping of animals, first forms the limbs that hold the primary command in the body; afterwards, from the remaining material, she works sometimes sparingly and sometimes profusely, following her own lead. Thus, hindered by a deficiency or overcome by an excess, she is blocked from the work she began. From this, she produces births affected by a monstrous blemish, as is often seen in art: sometimes mutilated, such as the lame or the one-eyed; sometimes superfluous, such as hermaphrodites, or those with four eyes, four arms, and four feet. In this way, Nature herself aids those things arranged by chance or by art, and brings to completion what was only just begun. 

But you, who are eager and desire to bring monsters into the light by some art, so that you may learn from examples, let us hand down many principles of these things, which you must consider...

### *Monstrous Births in Humans.*

These occur either through disordered intercourse—where the seed falls into improper places—or if two fetuses become cramped in the womb due to the narrowness of the space, or if the internal membranes <note>original: "pelliculæ aliæ mediastinæ," referring to the dividing membranes within the uterus</note> are corrupted, much like how apples growing too close together on a tree branch often fuse into one. Thus, at the proper time of incubation, they are hatched with four feet and four wings; you must take care that they are raised diligently. ### How monstrous births can be produced in other ways.

->CHAPTER XVIII.<-

We are now able to shape births already brought forth into monstrous forms at will, and in another way than what we said above: for just as we produce growing fruit according to the shape of a vessel—such as quinces in the likeness of a human head, or cucumbers in the shape of a snake, by applying molds <note>original: "typos"</note> to them while they are still growing—so too can it happen in the offspring of animals. Hippocrates shows the precise method in his book *On Airs, Waters, and Places*, and how those who live near the Phasis <note>A river in the ancient region of Colchis, modern-day Georgia</note> do it, all having heads longer than is normal, since there is no other race that has similar heads. In the beginning, custom <note>original: "consuetudo"</note> was the cause of them having such heads: but now nature itself has conspired with custom, since among them he is thought most noble who has the longest possible head. This was the beginning of the custom: when an infant is newly born, its head being still tender and soft, they squeeze it with their hands as quickly as possible and, fitting it, force it to increase in length; they even bind it with bandages and tie it with suitable instruments so that the roundness of the head is prevented and the length increased. This custom achieved so much that such a nature of heads existed. Indeed, with the passage of time, Nature also produced such children, so that it was no longer necessary to force them by the earlier custom. When...

### On the power of the wonderful imagination, and how various offspring can be conceived. Chapter XIX.

Plutarch, in *The Opinions of the Philosophers*, says that Empedocles believed the infant is formed by what is seen during conception; indeed, women often held images and statues as objects of delight, and gave birth to offspring similar to them. Hippocrates, defending the reputation of a woman who had born children quite unlike their parents, derived the reason from a painting that was in her bedroom. Quintilian defended a woman by the same reasoning who, being white, had given birth to a person of color <note>original: "æthiopem"; historically used to refer to a person of Black African descent</note>, whom everyone thought was the child of a slave. Damascenus <note>Likely referring to St. John of Damascus</note> relates that a girl gave birth to a hairy child, and investigating the reason for this, found a hairy image of Saint John in the view of her bedroom. Heliodorus begins his most beautiful history <note>The "Aethiopica," a famous ancient Greek novel</note> with the fact that the wife of the King of Ethiopia had given birth to the white Chariclea because, in the home where she lay with the king, the story of Andromeda was depicted. Elsewhere we read of women giving birth to horned sons because they had contemplated the story of Actaeon <note>A mythological hunter turned into a stag</note> during sexual intercourse. We see everywhere children with cleft lips <note>original: "labra bifida"; literally "split lips"</note> because their mothers, while carrying them in the womb, looked upon a hare.

### How peacocks may become white.

In Cologne <note>original: "Coloniæ"</note>, white peacocks were once so rare that they were marveled at as a rare thing. But later, they became more frequent there through merchants from Norway <note>original: "Noruegia"</note>. For when black or multicolored peacocks were brought into that region for the sake of spectacle, they all became white. This is because, while the males were incubating the eggs in the open air, they saw those snowy mountain ridges perpetually before their eyes, and they hatched white chicks from the already living eggs. ### How shaggy dogs may be born.

Women desiring this <note>The author likely means the owners or breeders of the dogs</note> should strew the bedding with the fleeces and skins of sheep in the places where those dogs lie, mate, and move about. Thus, by always having such things before their eyes, they bear "maned" offspring, just as lions do. We have heard of this happening by chance: a little bitch, by lying daily on soft ram fleeces, produced shaggy pups which were conceived afterward.

### To produce white pigs and livestock

Herdsmen and swineherds wanting this have constructed and decorated the bedding and stables with horse skulls on the ground and with surfaces made white by rainwater <note>original: "compluviis exalbificatis," perhaps referring to sun-bleached or lime-washed areas near water catchments</note>; from there, the pigs and cattle born were white.

[The seed] that migrates from the right parts of the body flows into the right parts of the womb, and likewise that from the left into the left. But if this descent happens in reverse, females are born. **Leucippus** <note>A 5th-century BCE philosopher often credited with early atomic theory.</note> held that it depends on the transformation of the offspring, through which the male has a penis <note>original: "colem"</note> and the female a womb. Thus far Leucippus. **Democritus** believed that shared parts come from both parents, and the specific sex is born according to which parent's influence prevails. **Hipponax** thought that if the generative seed prevailed, a male is born; but if the nourishment prevails, a female. 

However, all physicians have said that the right side is the warmest; thus, if a woman retains the semen discharged into the right side, she will conceive a male, but in the left, a female. This can be seen in animals that bear many young: for if you open a pregnant sow, you will find males on the right side and females on the left. Therefore, they instruct women to lie on their right side after receiving the seed. For this reason, if the right testicle of a ram is tied off, only females are born. 

**Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the massive 1st-century "Natural History."</note> wrote: When a bull mounts a heifer, one can understand by certain signs which sex he has sired; for if he dismounts on the right side, it is clear he has sired a male; if on the left, a female. For this reason, the **Egyptians**, when intending to represent a woman who has borne a daughter, paint a bull looking toward the left; if a son, a bull turning toward the right. 

Furthermore, if you desire the offspring to be a male, at the time of mating, bind the left testicle with a cord; but if a female, bind the right in the same way, according to **Columella**, **Africanus**, and **Didymus** <note>Famed agricultural writers of the Roman and Byzantine eras.</note>. But because this is laborious in large herds, let us try it another way. 

Males are conceived when the North Wind <note>original: "Aquilonis"</note> blows, and females when the South Wind <note>original: "Austro"</note> blows, according to Pliny. The force of the North Wind is so great that it even changes those who would otherwise bear only females toward the procreation of male offspring. The females ought to face the North Wind when they mate. Those who are mated in the morning produce a male; if you admit them late in the day, they do not. 

**Aristotle**, a man most expert in the Nature of things, instructs that at the time of breeding, one should observe the northern breezes on dry days, so that we pasture the herd against the wind, and the cattle be admitted facing it. Likewise, if females are to be generated, they should catch the southern blasts, so that by the same reasoning...

## *On various experiments with animals.* CHAPTER XXII.

There remain certain experiments regarding animals, neither unpleasant nor to be despised, which we have decided to bring here so they need not be sought elsewhere. And first:

### *How white spots may be induced on horses.*

In the <term>cosmetics of horses<note>original: "equorum cosmetica." This refers to the grooming and aesthetic modification of livestock, often for trade.</note></term> there is a discussion on what should be done if you desire white hairs on horses. For <term>horse-dealers<note>original: "mangones." Chance shows how this works: for when the skin of a horse is accidentally stripped away, white hairs grow back in that place. But those who wish to produce them on purpose wound the skin where the hair has been shaved, and the hair will grow back white. **Oppian** <note>A Greco-Roman poet known for his didactic poems on hunting (Cynegetica) and fishing (Halieutica).</note> achieves this through fire:

> ->*For them, the skin is divided into round circles,*<-
> ->*Like a panther, it turns white among the black spots;*<-
> ->*Thus first, the skilled groom shapes the tender [foals],*<-
> ->*When, having been taught, he burns the hair with a hot iron.*<-

Now we shall relate the fellowship of a <term>magpie<note>original: "pica." When it was fully grown, he left it free at home, and it flew wherever it liked, but at feeding time it always returned home. It so happened that my friend left home to set out on a journey of more than fifteen days' duration. The magpie was his constant companion: now flying far ahead and sitting upon a branch until he reached it, then flying onto his cap and shoulders, leaping with joy and gladness; then flying back, if he had proceeded further, it would run to catch up to him; it always slept with him at night, and even to this day it enjoys his company.

### PREFACE

We have already reviewed the new and various births of animals; now those of plants are at hand, which, through their singular delight and wondrous elegance, provoke the minds and eyes of beholders into admiration. These bring more profit, and by these the Magician <term>Magus<note>In Porta's view, a "Magus" is not a sorcerer, but a "natural magician"—someone who understands the hidden properties of nature and uses that knowledge to perform seemingly miraculous feats of science and agriculture.</note></term> can appear more wonderful. For the yield <note>original: "fœneratio." Literally "past childbearing." Porta argues against the common contemporary fear that the world was "aging" and becoming less fertile.</note>, but luxuriates everywhere of its own accord, remaining of insatiable fertility and perennial yield for receiving new seeds and producing new ones. Not only can every tree be grafted onto every other tree, but one single tree will be able to sustain the matings and adulteries <note>original: "adulteria." A standard botanical term in the Renaissance for the "unnatural" or artificial mixing of species, particularly through grafting different fruits onto a single trunk.</note> of all others. ### *How new herbs can be generated from putrefaction.*
#### CHAPTER I.

To maintain the order we established from the beginning—having already said that new animals can be born from putrefaction <note>Porta refers here to Book II of *Natural Magic*, which deals with the spontaneous generation of insects and small animals.</note>—we shall likewise demonstrate that new herbs can arise spontaneously. Our ancestors felt, beyond any doubt, that many plants arose from the mixtures of earth and water, and that specific places generate specific herbs. We have said, according to Diogenes <note>Diogenes of Apollonia, a 5th-century BCE philosopher who believed all things were modifications of air/breath mixed with moisture.</note>, that plants are born from water as it putrefies and takes on a certain mixture with the earth. Theophrastus says that certain rains cause decay and changes in the ground, and that plants can be nourished and increased by them. When the sun warms and dries, and the earth is stirred, it always produces the plants familiar to that place. On the island of Crete, wherever someone moves the earth (unless other earth is brought in), the cypress is born and immediately springs forth; and in semi-damp crops, if they are hoed, the caltrop <note>original: "tribulum." A thorny, spreading weed.</note> arises. Likewise, <term>Silphium</term> <note>original: "laser." A medicinal plant highly prized in antiquity, which supposedly disappeared during the Roman Empire.</note> appeared in Libya after a certain pitch-like and thick rain fell, and its herbal nature immediately emerged. ### How asparagus may be produced.

Didymus <note>Didymus of Alexandria, an ancient author on agriculture.</note> relates that if you wish much asparagus to grow, you should commit the horns of wild rams, pounded very finely, into furrows and water them. *ivy is born from the horns of stags.*

### *That hyphear and polypody are generated.*

For various herbs are born, such as *hyphear* <note>original: "hyphear," a parasitic plant similar to mistletoe</note> and *stelis* <note>original: "stelis," another type of mistletoe or parasite found on trees</note>, which grow on the fir, the pine, and others. For in these places, a certain phlegmatic and pituitary humor <note>The "humors" were thought to be the vital fluids of plants and animals; "phlegmatic" implies a cool, moist, and thick substance.</note> rots, which, from its abundance, spreads itself over the outermost surface of the branches and the trunk. There, having found some decay of the bark and being warmed by the Sun, it easily transforms into herbs of this kind.

## *How plants are changed so that they pass from one form into another. CHAPTER II.*

We think that performing miracles is nothing other than turning one thing into another, or accomplishing things that seem to go against the norm of nature; therefore, we shall hand down the instructions for how we might do this. We can force plants to depart from their own nature and pass into another kind through neglect, or through the "cheating" of cultivation <term>mangonio: the art of artificial manipulation or "faking" a plant's qualities through clever gardening</term>. This is done not only so that they degenerate in flavor, color, size, and form—which will easily happen if you apply care to neglected plants, or neglect those that were once cultivated—but furthermore, every plant has its own methods of sowing. For some are sown by seed, others by the trunk, or by the root, by tearing away a branch <note>original: "auulsione"</note>, or by a small shoot <note>original: "furculo"</note>. Hence, if you sow by seed that which is usually planted by roots, or if you plant with a shoot or trunk that which is usually preserved by seed, things will be born that are quite different from those that would have come forth in the usual way, according to the author Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus (c. 371–287 BC) was the primary ancient authority on botany and a student of Aristotle.</note>. So also, by changing the site, the climate, and the soil, you will overturn everything, and it will happen that the tree born there counterfeits the figure, the face, and the appearance of a foreign tree. All these things are clear in the books of the rustics <note>Porta refers here to ancient Roman agricultural writers such as Varro, Columella, or Cato.</note>, from which we shall bring forward some examples. If you wish

### *That a white vine should turn out black, and a black one white,*

Sow the seed of a white vine in a refined manner <note>original: "vrbane," meaning with careful garden cultivation</note>, and a black and wild one will be born; and if you sow the seed of a black vine, a white one will be born, as Theophrastus taught. For we know for certain that the vine is not usually sown from seed, but from roots; its genuine sowing is from a branch or shoot. Whence, if you do something different from what is required, it is necessary that something different will also be born. In the same way

From the pit of an olive grows a wild olive, and they often assert that from a female cypress, a male comes forth; and finally, nothing cultivated at all, but clearly a wild thing is produced, and sometimes to such a extent that it can hardly ripen its fruit. Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a Roman scholar and writer on agriculture</note> says that

->*Cabbage is changed into a turnip, and a turnip into cabbage.*<-

In some cases, old seed is so powerful that it changes the plant's nature: for he says that if old cabbage seed is sown, a turnip is born, and conversely, cabbage is born from turnips. With preparation and labor

->*Typha and Zea are turned into wheat, and vice versa,*<-

and this happens if they are sown after being crushed, and not immediately, but in the third year, according to Theophrastus <note>The "Father of Botany," a student of Aristotle</note>. Pliny writes that after two years, winter wheat <note>original: "siligo"</note> changes into common wheat. Thus all seeds <note>original: "femina," likely a corruption of "semina" (seeds), though it could refer to the "feminine" or reproductive nature of the plants</note>, through neglect, or through the opposition of the sky and soil, pass away into faults and corruptions. Virgil says:

> ->*I have seen things long chosen, and watched with great labor,*<-
> ->*still degenerate; unless human force every year*<-
> ->*picks out the largest by hand. Thus all things by fate*<-
> ->*rush toward the worse, and falling backward are carried away.*<-
<note>original: "Vidi lecta diu..." These lines are from Virgil’s *Georgics* (Book I, 197–200), a famous Roman poem on agriculture. It reflects the historical belief that nature naturally tends toward decay or "degeneration" unless actively managed by people.</note>

Galen’s father <note>Galen was a celebrated 2nd-century Greek physician whose ideas on medicine and biology were standard for over a millennium</note>, in his old age, became very fond of farming and applied diligent effort to become more certain whether the pests of crops were born by their own nature, or if the seeds themselves degenerated into other species. Therefore, he committed pure wheat and barley to the earth, thoroughly cleaned of all foreign seeds. When he saw that much darnel <term>lolium: a weed (ryegrass) that often grows among wheat and was once thought to be wheat that had "gone bad"</term> had come forth in the wheat, and a little in the barley, he made the same experiment with other grains as well. He finally discovered that in lentils, the round vetch <note>original: "aracum"</note> and axewort <note>original: "securidacam," a type of medicinal herb in the pea family</note> are born by a certain degeneration of the lentil. Unless cultivation restrains it,

### *Water-mint is turned into mint.*

For this reason, it must be transplanted more often so that this does not happen, as Theophrastus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher and the "father of botany"</note> says. For this occurs when one does not cultivate it, nor apply care so that the roots are drawn down deeper; the upper part, having been made weaker, loses the intensity of its scent, and a faint odor is left behind which approaches that of mint. When I had sown mint from its own seed, it turned into catmint <note>original: "nepeta"</note>—that is, in its scent—though in form it remained mint. On the authority of Martial <note>A Roman poet known for his epigrams</note>:

### *Basil weakens into wild thyme.*

If it is exposed to strong Sun, it will produce flowers sometimes purple, sometimes white, and sometimes rosy; and it will degenerate not only into wild thyme <note>original: "serpillum"</note>, but even into water-mint <note>original: "sisymbrium"</note>. So too Galen reported that the small branches of cassia are changed into cinnamon. Likewise:

### *Gillyflowers, roses, violets, and purple wallflowers are changed into white*

By age and neglect: for Theophrastus reports that if violets, wallflowers <note>original: "leucoia," referring to white violets or stock-gillyflowers</note>, and roses are neglected, they turn white in the third year, and we have clearly seen this in all of them. But this happens not only where a kinship of natures exists, allowing one plant to turn into another, but even when it departs entirely from its own kind.

#### *That an oak is changed into a vine.*

Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus, a 13th-century philosopher and scientist who wrote extensively on botany in *De vegetabilibus*</note> reports this, if the matter is as true as it is wonderful—but the credibility rests with him. For he tells that oak or beech forests, when cut down, have passed into trees called tamarisk and aspen, which are lowlier; and in the land of Alumnia <note>This likely refers to the Almunia region in Spain, historically noted for its fertile soil</note>, if oak branches are fixed into the earth, they are transformed into vines bearing good wine. He also notes that sometimes old trees, when cut back, degenerate into vineyards. However, this does not happen because the oak shoots remain as they are, but because, as they rot and mix with the nature of the soil, they pass into the nature of the vine.

---

### CHAPTER III.

#### *How fruit composed of diverse parts may be made.*

Just as we mixed diverse animals into one through mating, so now through grafting—which is the "intercourse" of plants—we shall compose various fruits into one. We do not deny that this can be done in other ways as well. We praise grafting enough for this purpose, though we shall praise it far more hereafter, once we create an indissoluble bond through the mutual embrace of different species, providing a reason for wonder. Even if someone considers these graftings laborious or impossible, let the result be the relief of the labor; for skillful care will remedy even the nearly impossible grafts. Do not let the sayings of the unrefined farmer or the ignorant craftsman dissuade you from what experience demonstrates. Consider in your mind what has been handed down to memory by the ancients: that the fig is grafted onto the plane tree and the mulberry; the mulberry onto the chestnut, the terebinth <term>terebinth: the turpentine tree (*Pistacia terebinthus*), often used as a hardy rootstock in antiquity</term>, and the white poplar (from which white mulberries are born); chestnuts onto the nut tree and the oak; that the pomegranate enjoys various "adulteries" <note>original: "adulterijs" — a common classical metaphor for grafting different species together to "marry" them</note> and is mixed with all; and that the cherry delights in the terebinth. Finally, so that we do not weary the readers with a longer speech, Columella <note>Lucius Junius Moderatus Columella, a Roman writer whose 1st-century AD work *De Re Rustica* was the most important source on Roman agriculture</note> maintained that every kind of shoot can be grafted onto every kind of tree. From this comes every composition of fruits, from this every adoption of them, and from this come unusual fruits. Virgil says:
> ->*Marveling at new leaves and fruits not its own.*<-
<note>original: "Miratāq; nouas frondes..." From Virgil's *Georgics* (Book II, line 82). This famous line describes a tree's "surprise" at seeing foreign fruit growing from its branches after grafting.</note>
And Palladius <note>A 4th-century Roman agricultural writer</note>:
> ->*To join happy forests under the appearance of a wedding chamber,*<-
> ->*So that a mixed beauty may grow from both offspring.*<-
