# NATURAL MAGIC, BOOK III.

> *To clothe the joined grove with related shadows*
> *And to ennoble the offspring with twin foliage,*
> *To blend sweet juices with seductive treaties,*
> *And to nourish a wide fruit with double flavor.*
<note>original: "Connexumq; nemus vestire affinibus umbris..." These verses, likely adapted from classical agricultural poetry such as Columella's *De Re Rustica*, poetically describe the art of grafting.</note>

But we shall add some rules so that the grafts, by uniting more easily, may bring forth new and mixed fruits, following the same principles we spoke of regarding animals. Let the nature of the bark <term>cortex: the outer protective layer of the plant</term> be the same, and let them possess the same timing for flowering and the budding of shoots <term>surculus: a young twig or sprout used for grafting</term>, lest one flowers and buds sooner and the other later—much like the period of gestation in the womb for animals. It is also a contrary thing whenever dry parts resist moist ones, or soft barks resist hard ones. Let the union <term>coalitus: the growing together of the graft and the host</term> be made in the healthiest part, and let nothing in it be ulcerous, scarred, or shriveled.

It matters greatly if the shoots are taken from a favorable spot on the trees; specifically, from the "shoulders" of the trees looking toward the summer sunrise <note>The northeast</note>. Let them be from fertile trees, well-known for their quality, and from new growth. Let the shoots be "pregnant"—that is, swollen with budding—and those that expect to bear fruit that year; namely, two-year-old shoots. The favorable age for the trees to be grafted is youth, for the hardness of old trees is inhospitable to newcomer shoots—and you will find similar advice in our *Agriculture* <note>Porta refers here to his own extensive writings on farming, likely his work *Villae*</note>. Furthermore, we shall not omit birdlime <term>viscum: a sticky substance, often made from mistletoe berries, used here as a botanical adhesive</term>, by which

->*the grafted cutting may take hold more easily.*<-

For it is excellent for gluing together the layers of the bark, and the union will bud more easily, even between those that are not of a related nature and would otherwise unite with difficulty. The first benefit is that, just as human flesh is united more quickly when sticky substances are applied to wounds, so the bark of plants or wounded branches will take hold more rapidly with this glue. For if the bark is stripped from the wood, or a shoot <term>thermes: a bough or cutting</term> is cut from its mother, and it does not adhere perfectly to the host tree on all sides, it fails; the moisture expires, and the natural sap is drained away. To prevent this, the glue ensures that a union occurs. Furthermore, if a gap opens between the bark and the wood, a vacuum is created where entering air prevents any joining; to remove every doubt of a successful union, we shall add birdlime. And if there be any trees that reject a foreign guest, through the benefit of birdlime—

### *To compose a fruit from a peach and a nectarine.*

This mixture and offspring were unseen, unheard of, and entirely unthought of by our ancestors. You shall achieve this through grafting, which farmers call "budding" or "shield-grafting" <term>emplastratio: a method where a bud and a small patch of bark are moved to a new tree</term>. Take young, fertile branches from a nectarine and a peach—those that give a great sign of maturing and budding. Mark them off with the width of two fingers in such a way that the buds are placed in the middle. Then, with a sharp knife, gently peel the bark from the wood so they are not damaged. Split these patches down the middle so that, when joined together <note>Joining the half-bud of a peach with the half-bud of a nectarine</note>, they may grow together properly, and the site of the scar does not appear, but looks like a single bud. Insert it into whichever tree you choose, on that part of the tree which looks most polished and especially vibrant. Prune away the remaining branches so they do not steal the nourishment, ensuring everything serves the graft. Open the bark of the host tree, taking care that the iron blade does not wound the wood itself, and cut an area the size of the bud; then fit the hybrid bud so that it matches the cut part. Tie it round without causing injury, and the wound must be protected with mud, placing something over it so that rain does not wash it away. Thus it will sprout and produce offspring, retaining a nature midway between both parents—a thing trees have never produced before. For it will be a fruit that represents both the peach and the nectarine with a shared appearance. In this same way, we are able

### *How fruits may also be composed together in other ways.*
## CHAPTER IV.

We can also compose fruits together in another way, and that by a different kind of grafting. For example, if we want various and composite pomegranates <term>Punica</term> to grow together. This is taught by Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus (c. 371 – c. 287 BC) was a Greek philosopher and the successor to Aristotle; he is considered the father of botany.</note>. Softening the twigs as if with a hammer, so that they may more easily stick together where the part is bruised, they then plant them bound very tightly. Then one tree arises from the union of the composed twigs: but each individual keeps its own kind, and draws and digests <note>original: "excoquunt," literally "cooks out," referring to the internal metabolic process of the plant</note> its nourishment for itself: nor do they have anything else in common between them than that mutual embrace and joining. The same author says in the same place:

### *How the same vine-shoot may bear black and white grapes at the same time, and in the same bunch, some berries are black and others white.*

They bruised the upper half of both cuttings <term>maleoli: a vine cutting with a piece of the older wood at the base, resembling a small hammer</term>, then they planted them equally composed and bound together: for in this way a single joint is formed from both. Since every living thing is sociable with other living things—and especially those that share a common nature—when they are joined they melt into a single nature, but each transmits its nourishment through itself without confusion. Thus it happens that the fruit is rendered varied, according to what is suitable for each. For it is as the rivers do when meeting one another, like the Cephisus and the Melas in Boeotia <note>A region in central Greece; the author uses the metaphor of two rivers sharing a bed but keeping their distinct waters</note>: for each keeps its own course. Columella <note>A prominent Roman writer on agriculture from the 1st century AD</note> teaches in this way. There is a kind of grafting that creates such grapes, in which berries <term>acini: individual grape berries or seeds</term> of various kinds and colors are found; this is achieved by the following method. Take four or five, or even more if you wish, twigs of different kinds, and bind them together carefully and equally composed: then insert them tightly into a small clay tube <term>tubulum fictilem</term> or a horn, so that they stick out somewhat from both...

### To make a vine bear white clusters and black berries,

The Greeks assert it can be done in this way: If black and white vines are growing near each other, when the shoots are pruned, you shall join the different cuttings together in such a way that you can unite the middle eyes <term>oculos: the buds or nodes from which new growth emerges</term> of both kinds by making them flush against one another. You shall then bind them tightly with soft papyrus and take care to smear them with moist earth. Every three days, you must adjust them until the buds of the new foliage burst forth. After some time has passed, if you wish, you can produce this variety through several more cuttings. 

We ourselves chose two shoots from neighboring vines; where the buds were to be joined, we divided them so that about a third of the eye remained. We then caused them to stick together and tied a binding around them, so that they would not be separated by the growth of the buds. One bud should rest upon the other so that they produce a single shoot, and in that same year, they will produce berries split into two parts <note>original: *bifidos vuarum acinos*; referring to berries that appear physically divided or split in color/flavor</note>. We added this resulting shoot to another, and so on continuously, so that we might create clusters of as many varieties as possible. Indeed, we produced a grape that consisted of the Muscat <note>original: *apiana*; literally "bee-grape," a sweet variety like Muscat that attracts bees</note> and the scentless variety, with berries shaped like little horns, like fingers, and round, and all the berries were distinguished by various colors. But Pontanus <note>Giovanni Gioviano Pontano (1429–1503), a famous Italian humanist and poet who wrote on agriculture and gardening.</note> describes this elegantly:

### *How Citrons may bear different fruits.*

> There are those who join different branches, but with the bark scraped away,
> And bind them together, so that with the glue mixed
> They grow equally, and soon, once the trunk is fixed, they are joined
> And implanted together. Then they duly crown the wound,
> And protect the deceptive work with applied skill,
> So that from one branch, and from one shoot, the fruits
> That come are not of one kind, and there is honor and glory for the countryside
> As nature, aided by unusual favor, rejoices.

### The Golden Apple, so that it may bear a fruit of which half is sweet and the other sour.

In our case, chance created the union. There were two branches of a Golden Apple tree <note>original: *mali aurei*; in this context, most likely referring to an orange tree</note>, one of which, having been grafted, bore sweet fruit, while the other bore sour. When the opportunity arose for the tree to be transplanted, and it was being cut through the middle—as is the custom for farmers when planting such trees when they are already old—the cut happened by chance...

### CHAPTER V.

We shall also bring forward another device by which fruits can be mixed and combined together at the same time, a method handed down by the ancients, even if it seems to me not only difficult, but impossible. But because these things have been described by men of greater weight, I shall not disdain to report them; and even if they did not succeed for me in my own testing experiments <note>original: *periclitanti experientiae*; Porta often expresses skepticism when he cannot replicate the "miracles" of ancient science</note>, we shall not for this reason take away the opportunity from more diligent men to try them; perhaps fortune will favor diligence. The method is that many seeds of different trees and fruits are gathered together in cloth strips <term>lacinijs: small pieces of fabric or strips used for binding seeds together</term> and sown: for from all of them growing up together from many little stalks bound together, so that they cannot be pulled or torn apart, they grow together into one; and thus one tree will produce diverse fruits, and a single fruit will be combined from diverse ones at once. 

Perhaps they were taught this by Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus (c. 371 – c. 287 BC), a Greek successor to Aristotle and the foundational author of Western botany</note>, who wrote that in a palm tree one should sow two seeds placed next to each other, and as many again on top, all however face down. For they do not send out a bud from the supine and hollow parts, but from the upper parts; four joined together grow better. Indeed, the roots of these, connected in a mutual embrace, grow together into one trunk from all of them at their first promiscuous birth. If this were true, the greatest and innumerable experiments would come from it. Therefore—

->*How berries of different colors may be produced at once.*<-

If many white, black, or red berries are sown mixed together, from their various stalks, if they were bound together and grown into one, berries of two colors will be born. Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), whose *Natural History* was the standard encyclopedia of the natural world in the Renaissance</note> records a method discovered by birds, saying: "Nature also taught how to graft by seed, when it has been swallowed in haste by hungry birds, and made soft and moist by the warmth of the belly, and then dropped with the fertilizing medicine of dung <note>original: *fimi medicamine*; Pliny’s observation that bird droppings act as both a delivery system and fertilizer for seeds</note> into the soft beds of trees, and often carried by the winds into some cracks in the bark." Wherefore we have seen a cherry on a willow, a plane tree on a laurel, a lau-

## *How a doubled fruit can be made, and one enclosed within another.* CHAPTER VI.

There is also another way of composition by which fruits can be combined together—not in the manner we recounted above (namely, that one part of a fruit belongs to one species and the other part to another, or that two or three different fruits are seen on the same branch), but rather that one fruit is contained within the other, so that it is truly doubled; we are the first to bring this method forward. But let us see how our ancestors accomplished it, and first:

### *How the olive-grape is made.*

Diophanes <note>An ancient Greek writer on agriculture</note> teaches that an olive grafted into a vine bears a fruit called *elæostaphylon* <note>from the Greek: *elaia* (olive) + *staphyle* (bunch of grapes)</note>, which is to say, the "olive-grape." But Florentinus, in the eleventh book of his *Georgics* <note>Florentinus was a Roman agricultural author; the *Georgics* refers to his collected writings on farming</note>, recorded it thus: if someone grafts an olive into a vine, it will produce not only clusters of grapes but also the olive. Therefore, we bore into the vine close to the ground and insert a small branch of olive, so that it may draw sweetness from the vine and native nourishment from the ground at the same time, so that we may finally enjoy its more pleasant food. Finally, if the fruit-bearing shoots of a vine that has not yet borne fruit are transferred, they will preserve the mixture of their parents. Furthermore, the fruit adopted the name of both parents from this promiscuous condition of grafting, called *elæostaphylos* by the Greeks. Marius Maximus <note>A Roman consul and historian</note> claims to have seen such a tree...

### *The Almond-Peach, which is a peach on the outside, and contains a sweet almond within.*

The methods of the ancients which we have discussed thus far are characterized by a certain "Greek vanity" <note>original: *græca vanitate*; a common Renaissance trope suggesting that ancient Greek writers were prone to exaggeration or fanciful claims</note>. They are not only false, but impossible to achieve in the manner described. For instance, if you were to graft myrtle into a grape vine, as we mentioned in our work on *Agriculture*, the plant would bear no fruit. It is likewise impossible to graft an olive onto a vine; even if it were to take hold, it would not produce grapes. Pliny <note>The Roman naturalist Pliny the Elder</note> mentions apple-plums, almond-plums, and those produced from nuts, but he does not teach the method, which is perhaps unknown to everyone. 

Through this example, we reveal the method to the world: this fruit is called the "almond-peach" <note>original: *amygdaloperficum*</note> by more recent authors because it is born of both parents. Since this offspring possesses a nature shared between both progenitors, it is through the diligence of grafting—a new kind of cross-breeding <note>original: *adulterij*, literally "adultery," used here as a metaphor for the mixing of species</note> discovered by us—that a lineage unknown to previous centuries arises from the almond and the peach. It reflects the character of both parents while simultaneously adopting their appearance. This is a fruit that, on the outside, deceptively mimics the face of a peach, yet on the inside, it represents a sweet almond in both form and taste. The tree itself is a hybrid between the almond and the peach.

This is achieved by placing one bud upon another <note>term: *oculum oculo superponendo* — a technique known as "budding" or "shield grafting," where a bud from one tree is inserted into the bark of another</note>, either by removing both from the mother tree or just one. This technique was discovered by us in our old age. We can even place a third bud upon a shoot that is already growing, and we shall have a triple hybrid. These trees have flourished in our pleasure gardens for many years. In this same way, we can produce a portentous fruit that fills the eyes and mind with wonder: namely,

### *that a citron should have a lemon inside.*

This is done by placing a citron bud upon a lemon tree. Among the people of Calabria <note>original: *Brutios*</note> and Sorrento, these varieties are commonly found; they produce a different kind of citron in the place where the sour pulp usually is, yet both are contained by the same stem. Similarly, there is produced the

### *doubled golden apple,*

<note>original: *malum aureum*; in this period, "golden apple" was the standard term for an orange</note>

This variety is also common among us, characterized by having doubled rows of seeds. It is a form so rare and beautiful that you will never cease to marvel at it.

### *How unseen fruits, both better and worse, may be generated by another artifice. CHAPTER VII.*

**W**e have pursued the praise and excellence of <term>grafting</term><note>original: *insitionis*; the process of joining a piece of one plant (the scion) onto the stem of another (the rootstock) so they grow together</note> elsewhere with a longer encomium; here it should suffice to say that by grafting alone new fruits can arise, both better and also worse. We will record some experiments discovered by the ancients and by us. What must be done

->*to make the best chestnut.*<-

The rarity of one example must not be omitted. Corellius, a Roman knight born at Ateste <note>Modern-day Este in northern Italy</note>, grafted a chestnut with its own <term>scion</term><note>original: *surculo*; a young shoot or twig of a plant used for grafting</note> in the Neapolitan territory; thus was produced the chestnut which took its name from him among those most praised. Later, his heir (a freedman), grafted the "Corellian" chestnut again. This is the difference between them: the former is more plentiful, but this second Corellian one is better. These things were done in ancient times, and such is the excellence of grafting that a tree grafted with its own shoot always turns out more excellent. Thus also the cherry tree <note>original: *cerasus*</note> delights most in grafting, nor will it ever give good or sweet fruit unless it has been grafted to another tree, according to Pamphilus <note>An ancient Greek writer on agriculture</note>. By an example of this kind

->*To change the fruits of the hawthorn into medlars*<-

we have attempted, and I do not think the hawthorn <note>original: *oxyacantham*</note> is anything other than the medlar tree <note>original: *tuberum arborem*; likely referring to the *Mespilus* or a similar fruiting tree</note> having degenerated in the woods. Whence, if someone, following the example of Corellius, were to graft the hawthorn tree many times with its own scion, it would be changed back into a medlar tree; for the neglected medlar tree reverts into a hawthorn. In our gardens <note>original: *viridariis*</note>, we have grafted it three or four times with its own scion, and unless death prevents us, we shall continue grafting it until it produces medlars; even now it brings forth both larger and sweeter fruit. Now we shall speak of those which are grafted with a foreign scion, where the powers and forms are mixed, and we will teach a new discovery of our times:

# How to produce early fruits and flowers.
## CHAPTER VIII.

Art is both the rival and the imitator of Nature; by following her, it accomplishes even more sublime things. Thus the **Magus**—acting like a fertile Nature himself and clothed in her habits—uses the evidence of his eyes and the conjectures of his mind to investigate those things which Nature, in her hidden majesty, carries out. Nature often dwells in many-sided detours and obscure coverings, sometimes hindering her own work or causing it to regress; she may bring forth a "precocious birth" <note>original: *præcoci partu*; refers to fruit that ripens much earlier than usual</note> late, or compel something that usually works slowly to ripen early, finally forcing it to obey him. The Magus knows that fruits and flowers are produced by the restless circuit of celestial heat <note>The Sun's warmth and the influence of the stars</note>, as are all living things seen in the world. If it is his heart's desire to delay these things or to bring them forth more hastily so they might be more valuable, he accomplishes this by manipulating the intervals of time—changing spring into winter, and winter into summer. Furthermore, <term>grafting</term><note>original: *insitio*; the practice of joining a stem of one plant to the roots of another</note> brings no small advantage to this business. Let us therefore see, through the skill of grafting, how to:

### Produce grapes in the spring.

If we see the cherry tree bearing its fruit in the springtime and we desire grapes at that same time, we shall not lack a plentiful supply, according to the **Tarentine** <note>Methods attributed to Tarentum, an ancient Greek city in Southern Italy famous for its gardens</note> fashion. If you graft a black vine into a cherry tree, you will have grapes even in the spring; for it will produce grapes at the same time the cherry tree normally bears its own fruit. However, this grafting can only be done through "boring" <note>drilling a hole through the trunk</note>, which **Didymus** <note>Didymus of Alexandria, an ancient writer on agriculture</note> teaches. You must pierce the trunk of the cherry tree with what is called a **French borer** <note>original: *terebra gallica*; a type of auger or drill</note>. Then, take a branch from a superior vine located nearby, pull it toward the tree, and insert it into the hole—but do not cut it away from its original "mother" vine. In this way, the shoot survives, being nourished both by its old parent and by the cherry tree which has received it and grown together with it. Within the space of two years, the inserted shoot will be united; then, once the scar has formed, you must cut away the part of the shoot still held by the old mother vine. You should then use a saw to cut off the trunk of the cherry tree in which the graft was made, as far as it stands above the drill hole, so that henceforth the grafted shoot exists as the principal part of the vine. Meanwhile, the original vine into which the graft was made does not remain idle, but bears fruit in the same way, and the united shoot grows at the same time...

<margin>*How cucumbers may hasten their fruit.*</margin>

<margin>*Cucumbers maturing their fruit more rapidly.*</margin>

Anticipating the usual time—specifically at the beginning of spring—they plant the seeds. When there is Sun and heat, or irregular rain, they set the baskets out in the open air; around sunset, they carry them into a sheltered house. They do this diligently, sprinkling water when necessity demands it. After the cold and ice of spring have ceased and the weather becomes milder, they carry the baskets or jars to a tilled and cultivated spot and bury them so that the rims are level with the earth; and thereafter they apply their usual care. They do the same with gourds. Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and the "father of botany"</note> teaches that one may have an early cucumber if the cucumber seeds are kept during the winter time, moistened with lukewarm water, exposed to the Sun, and moved near a fire; then, when the sowing time arrives, the entire baskets are committed to the earth. In this way, they grow far faster...

### How we may have cucumbers all year round,

both early and late, as Aristotle teaches in his *Problems* <note>a collection of scientific and philosophical questions attributed to Aristotle</note>. When they have grown, let them be lowered into a well near where they were born, and let the well be covered. In this way, the overflowing Sun cannot dry them out, and the rising vapor of the water below ensures they feel no dryness, but remain green as if in a fresh state. Theophrastus <note>a Greek philosopher and the "Father of Botany"</note> follows him in this. To the same effect are those things which happen to cucumbers and gourds in terms of softness and growth if someone hides the small fruits away. For in this way, no part of the nourishment is destroyed by the Sun’s harm, nor dried out by the winds—factors that prevent the bulk from increasing, as also happens to trees standing in places exposed to the Sun and wind. But so that

### Citron trees may always be weighed down by the burden of their crop,

and stay on the tree all year round: you shall observe that custom which is peculiar to Assyria <note>frequently cited in antiquity as a land of legendary fertility</note> and frequent in many other places. When the time for harvesting arrives, you should cut back part from the reproductive stem <note>original: *genitali stirpe*</note> and correct the overgrowth with iron <note>meaning a pruning knife</note>, leaving a part behind. On the part where you have pruned the tree's shoots, it will substitute other fertility; and when those are grown, the earlier ones can be picked, and a new "brood" <note>original: *fœtura*; a term comparing plant growth to the birthing of offspring</note> invited. > *While the large ones remaining enjoy their full size.*

> *A fresh blossom, and fills the boughs with rich hope:*
> *Thus the grove will grow rich with alternating metal.* <note>The "metal" refers to the golden color of the citrus fruit, often associated with the golden apples of the Hesperides.</note>

### *To produce late-ripening figs.*

If you wish to make a fig tree late-fruiting, even if it is not so by nature, Columella <note>Lucius Junius Moderatus Columella, a Roman writer on agriculture from the 1st century AD</note> teaches us: when the small green figs <term>grossuli <note>original: *grossuli*; the early, small, unripened fruits of a fig tree</note></term> are tiny, strike the fruit off; the tree will produce a second crop, which will delay its ripening until late winter. Pliny follows him, saying: late figs are produced if the first green figs are struck off once they have grown larger than a bean; new ones then grow beneath, which ripen later. In the same manner, Tarentinus <note>A Greek writer on agriculture, often cited in the *Geoponica*</note> teaches us

### *To yield autumnal grapes.*

One must remove the clusters that first sprout, and others will grow in their place; moreover, if you take great care of the plant, it will produce clusters again, and these, once mature, will be late-ripening. In this way also

### *To make roses bloom later.*

By striking off its first tender buds when the little "vases" <note>original: *alabastrule*; a metaphor for the flower buds before they open</note> indicate that the flowers are about to burst forth. This succeeds especially well with musk roses, and best of all with the hundred-leaved musk roses <note>likely the *Rosa centifolia* or cabbage rose</note>; for in the countryside, and in clay vessels kept in windows, we have them blooming throughout the entire winter. If you wish

### *To make carnations flower late.*

Snap off the little stalks and the first cups <term>calices <note>the sepal structure holding the flower</note></term> of the flowers about to sprout with your fingers, and expose them to the burning summer sun, but nourish them with constant watering so they do not dry out. For by producing other stalks and other cups, we have delayed the late flowers until winter and even until spring, so that in the country and at home we may have winter carnations <term>garyophyllos <note>original: *garyophylli*; while this word can mean cloves, in early modern horticulture it usually refers to the carnation or clove pink (*Dianthus caryophyllus*)</note></term> continuously. By nearly the same artifice—not by cutting back the buds, but by planting later and guarding against the cold—we ripen fruits in winter. For instance, if we wish

### *To produce late cucumbers.*

In this way, they will best withstand the cold and will not be killed by it. > *And the fruit rejoices to surpass the size of the leaf.*

### *To make pomegranates as large as huge pears*

Later, in the months of October and November, we uncovered the parts of the pomegranate roots, wrapped them in this mixture, and finally covered them again with earth. In their own time, they will yield larger fruit than the tree ever gave before; and if you do the same for the two following years, you will produce pomegranates to the point of wonder, so that they almost equal gourds in size.

We smeared beans with this same ointment and sowed them, and we obtained huge beans in huge pods.

I 4

Those plants also respond in the same way which are enclosed in a giant fennel stalk <note>original: *ferula*; the stalks of the giant fennel were often used in antiquity as lightweight, hollow containers.</note> or a clay tube; for more nourishment is provided to them because no part of it evaporates or dries out. Following this same reasoning, we shall now teach

->***How to make Celery grow large***<-

from the same Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus (c. 371–287 BC), the "Father of Botany" and successor to Aristotle.</note>. Digging around the plant down to the root, they cover it almost entirely with parched husks <note>original: *cachrylio*; likely referring to the chaff or the winter-buds of certain plants used as a warming mulch.</note>, and soon after they heap earth over it. The reason is that the roots consume the entirety of the nourishment and do not transmit any of it to the sprouts; if the plant is thus divided, it must necessarily follow that there will be more growth. These husks are warm and dense; they help in drawing nourishment by the power of their density, and they retain that same nourishment without letting it pass upward. At the same time, through the benefit of their own heat, they are able to ripen <note>original: *concoquere*; a classical biological term referring to the "cooking" or processing of nutrients within a plant to make them useful for growth.</note> the nutrients. Thus, when nourishment is added in large quantities and is fully processed, a large increase in size follows. He took this from Aristotle. It is also said that celery becomes even larger if, when it is transplanted, you drive a stake into the ground as deep as you wish the celery to grow; for the root can easily fill that entire space. And

->***To make Radishes grow huge***<-

it seems this happens in cold places, in the same way that Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), author of the *Natural History*.</note> says: for the radish so enjoys the cold that in Germany it exceeds the size of infant children. Some have recorded that if a stake is driven into the ground and the resulting hole is lined with straw to a depth of six fingers, and then the seed is covered with manure and earth, it will grow to the size of the pit itself. Florentinus <note>A 3rd-century AD Greek writer on agriculture whose work is preserved in the *Geoponica*.</note> teaches a trick not much different from this

->***To make Lettuces large.***<-

If, after being transplanted, they are watered, and when they have reached the height of a small palm <note>A unit of measure based on the width of a human hand, roughly 3 inches.</note>, you dig around them so the roots appear, cover them over with cow manure, and water them immediately. When they have grown larger, split the sprout with a very sharp iron tool and place a potsherd <note>A piece of broken ceramic or pottery.</note> that has not been treated with pitch upon it, so that they take their growth in width rather than in length. Likewise,

->***to make a Beet grow large***<-

Sotion <note>A Greek agricultural writer.</note> says: If you wish to make beets large, cover the roots themselves with fresh cow manure, split the sprout, and place a wide stone or a potsherd upon it.

->*How to make leeks grow large,*<-

While you are transplanting leeks, place a potsherd <note>original: *testam*; a piece of broken pottery often used in ancient gardening to direct root growth.</note> or a large stone underneath them, and do not water them. By this same artifice, Anatolius <note>Vindanius Anatolius, a 4th-century writer on agriculture.</note> teaches 
->*how to make bulbs larger*<-
if, in the same manner as with leeks, potsherds are placed beneath them around their roots. Slightly different from this method, Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus, the Greek "Father of Botany."</note>

->*To make a radish grow larger*<-

demonstrates a practice commonly used by the gardeners of his time: If the leaves are removed in winter, when they are most vigorous, and the plants are covered with earth, they can endure and grow until summer; for they do not sprout again nor send out leaves unless you remove the heaped-up soil. The same thing happens with the turnip, as Palladius <note>Rutilius Taurus Aemilianus Palladius, a late Roman author of a popular farming manual.</note> teaches: so that

->*Larger turnips are produced.*<-

Once the turnips are dug up, you clean them of all leaves and cut the stem down to the thickness of half a finger; then, you bury them in carefully prepared furrows, spaced eight fingers apart, throw earth over them, and tread it down; in this way, they will grow large.

->*How arum may grow larger.*<-

Theophrastus advises doing this same thing to increase its growth: when the plant <note>original: *arum*; likely the Cuckoopint or "Lords-and-Ladies" plant, valued for its starchy root.</note> flourishes with leaves that spread out quite widely, they usually bend the leaves and bury them around the plant, so that it does not expend its energy on new sprouts, but draws all its nourishment into its own head <note>the bulbous root or corm.</note>.

->*How an onion may become more swollen.*<-

Theophrastus suggests pulling the leaves off all of them, so that they communicate their strength to the base and do not waste energy going to seed. Sotion <note>An ancient writer on farming whose works are mostly lost except for fragments.</note> says: When about to plant onions, if you remove their tails and extremities, they will turn out large. Palladius: If we wish their heads to be larger, we must remove all the leaves, and thus the sap <note>original: *succus*</note> will be forced to the lower parts. Likewise, so that

->*garlic heads may become more massive,*<-

it is fitting to twist all the green growth and lay it flat on the ground before the garlic produces a stalk. Now we shall teach another artifice for making herbs and roots reach a giant size...

...we shall learn from the testimony of the ancients, though this does not entirely satisfy me, as I have said: namely:

### How the leek may become large.

The technique handed down by Columella <note>Lucius Junius Moderatus Columella, a prominent Roman writer on agriculture from the 1st century AD.</note>: to make the leek's growth greater, many seeds are tied in loose linen cloths and buried in that way. Palladius <note>Rutilius Taurus Aemilianus Palladius, another late Roman agricultural author.</note> says: if you plant many seeds tied into one bundle, a grand leek will be born from them. But all these authors follow Theophrastus <note>The Greek "Father of Botany."</note>, who stated that if one sows many seeds tied in a linen cloth, it will make the roots and sprouts larger; for this reason, they were accustomed to sow leeks, celery <note>original: *apium*; which can refer to celery or parsley.</note>, and certain other things in this manner. For several seeds joined together have more power, and from all of them a single nature is established. Furthermore, seeds taken from certain locations cause larger fruits to grow.

### The gourd will achieve a vaster growth,

if you plant using the middle part of the gourd with the top inverted. Columella writes in his poem *On Gardening* <note>original: *Hortulo*; refers to Book X of Columella's De Re Rustica, written in dactylic hexameter.</note>:

> *Whether it be of a globose*
> *body, or one that swells too vastly in its womb:*
> *if you gather from the middle belly, it will give a capable offspring.*

And we have observed this not only in this case, but in all fruits: for the seeds which are in the "belly" <note>The middle or central part of the fruit.</note> are more perfect and produce more perfect plants, while those at the extremities are weak and imperfect. Grains in the middle of an ear of corn will provide the best wheat, while those at the ends degenerate and bear imperfect ears; because the gourd produces such a large fruit, the example is seen more clearly. The Quintilii <note>Two brothers, Sestus Quintilius Condianus and Sestus Quintilius Valerius Maximus, who wrote on farming in the 2nd century AD.</note> promise to produce large cucumbers if their seed is planted "into the head" <note>original: *in caput*; likely referring to the orientation of the seed or the top of the planting bed.</note>, or if a vessel full of water is buried beneath them and you hide the roots in it; we know they become sweeter and larger this way.

The Arcadians, however, oppose this opinion. For they say that every tree from which the pith has been partially removed lives, but if it is taken away entirely, it is inevitable that not only will the fruit fail to develop its kernels, but the tree will be robbed of life and dry up completely. They support this reasoning because that part is the most moist and vital; for the nourishment provided by the soil runs through it until it reaches all the parts. Indeed, by a natural spirit, all the nourishment of a living thing is drawn up through the pith of the trunk, as if through a siphon, like a kind of soul. This is shown by wood that lacks pith: it warps and twists into a circle until it is entirely dried out, a thing which the ancients persistently dreaded. We, however, must hold a different view from Theophrastus and the others who have written on Agriculture, since trees can live without pith, and those living without it still bear fruit with inner kernels, as I have discussed more extensively in my books on *Agriculture*. But lest we seem to have omitted anything, we will set down their examples so that everyone may have the freedom to experiment; perhaps those more diligent than ourselves will meet with better success. Almonds and chestnuts may be covered with a softer skin. If we wish to pre-soften and change the fruit, we shall use swine dung <note>original: *stercore suillo*</note>, for such dung is among the most powerful varieties. Likewise, frequent digging <note>original: *fossio*</note> ensures that the trees themselves are invigorated by better and more abundant nourishment, and thus they bring forth better fruit: for the stones <note>original: *nuclei*</note> will become smaller, and those fruits covered by wood or a crust—such as almonds and Euboean nuts <note>original: *nuces euboicæ*; a common Roman name for walnuts</note>—will certainly have thinner shells, while the inner flesh will become larger. ### *If you wish to produce the Tarentine nut.*

Damageron <note>An ancient writer on agriculture and stones whose works are largely lost but preserved in later compilations.</note> demonstrates the same. The nut will acquire a thin shell and easy fruit, as will the almond, if you continually pour ash over the trunk and the roots. This also applies to other types of fruit that have a shell on the outside, if they are cultivated in the same manner. Palladius says if you wish to make a Tarentine nut <note>original: *nux tarentina*; a variety of walnut or almond from Tarentum famous in antiquity for having a shell so thin it could be broken with the fingers</note>, you should water it three times a month for a full year with lye <note>original: *lixivio*; a solution of wood ashes and water</note>. Others "chastise" <note>original: *castigando*; a metaphorical term for severe pruning or root-cutting to redirect the tree's energy</note> the trees by cutting away the tops of their roots. Or, if the nut is hard and knotty, the bark must be cut around to draw off the vice of the bad humor, according to Damageron. The reasoning for this is that, just as we improved the inner kernels by removing the pith, so by cutting and scarring the bark, we render the bark or shells soft; the pith corresponds to the bone, just as the bark corresponds to the shell. We have observed this in another example: for when a peach was grafted upon a bitter almond, the skin was bitter, so that it could not be eaten unless it was peeled. Use this secret in other matters. We have a variety planted in our own garden <note>likely referring to the author’s experimental garden in Naples</note> with a skin so fragile and membrane-like that the husk falls off at a mere touch, leaving the nut naked. Florentinus <note>A Greek author on agriculture from the 10th-century *Geoponica*.</note>

### A gourd may bear fruit without internal seeds.

From the teaching of the Quintilii <note>The Quintilii were two brothers, Sextus Quintilius Condianus and Sextus Quintilius Valerius Maximus, who wrote a famous but now lost work on agriculture often cited in the Renaissance.</note>. A gourd will not nourish its seed if, once the first sprout or shoot of the gourd has grown, you bury it in the ground in the manner of a vine <term>layering: a technique where a branch is buried while still attached to the parent plant so it develops its own roots</term>, so that only its head sticks out and remains prominent. When it has grown again, let more earth be heaped over it, but care must be taken that the offshoots that sprout are pruned away, leaving only the third. Thus, the fruits that are born—whether gourds or cucumbers—will be without internal seeds. They will also be born without seed if, for three days before sowing, the seeds are soaked in sesame oil; in this way, they will indeed bear offspring deprived of seeds.

And **a white fig will turn out red** if you graft it into the same mulberry, according to Diophanes. From the same kind of grafting will be born

### Apples stained with a blood-red hue,
which blood-red color is derived from the mulberry graft, as Avicenna teaches. But Beritius <note>Anatolius of Beirut, also known as Vindanius Anatolius, a 4th-century author on farming.</note> and Diophanes wrote that for the mulberry, from which all red apples are made, if you wish

### To make the mulberry produce white fruit,
you should graft it into a white poplar, for then white fruit will result. But Palladius <note>Rutilius Taurus Aemilianus Palladius, a 4th-century Roman writer on agriculture.</note> does not graft into a white poplar so that

### The mulberry may bear snowy-white fruit,
but rather into fig trees; he teaches that from this graft it acquires such a white color, as he writes in these verses:
> The fig persuades the mulberry to change its dark color,
> And gives its own laws to the captured leaves. <note>original: *Persuadet moris tetrum mutare colorem / Ficus, & inuasis dat sua iura comis.*</note>
From these examples, we ourselves have seen

### A white vine produce red wine.
This happens if you graft a white vine into a black one: for it will vary the color somewhat from the tree beneath it <term>subiecta arbore: the "subject tree" or rootstock onto which the graft is joined</term>, as I saw in the "bee-grapes" <note>original: *apianis uuis*; likely Muscat grapes, which are attractive to bees</note> and those called "Greeks" by us. For vines grafted onto the so-called "Ellanic" <note>Hellenic or Greek vines</note> vines produced a darkish wine, and with repeated grafting it will turn out even darker. On Mount Vesuvius, Aminean vines <note>Aminean vines were highly prized in antiquity for producing top-tier wine.</note> grafted onto the aforementioned vines produce a wine more deeply colored than the rest.

### That red fruit may be born
if you wish, but through the cultivation of *mangonium* <term>mangonium: the art of artificial enhancement or manipulation to improve the appearance of goods; here, horticultural trickery</term>, namely by the application of rich and warm substances. For there are two elements of colors...

## *How the colors of flowers may likewise be changed.*
### CHAPTER XV.

In the varied mingling and transformation of flowers, they are so variegated with pleasant colors that nothing more delightful meets our eyes—now those which glow with a deep purple may turn into blue; now those which are milky-white may fade into yellow, green, or crimson, and delight us with a mixture of different colors. In the contemplation of these, the sharpness of the mind is soothed with pleasant fruit, and, overwhelmed by the greatness of these things, it marvels that its own ability to perceive such excellence is seen to be far inferior. For this reason, we shall set down rules for how we may change the colors even in flowers. What we have done with fruits, we believe should also be done with flowers. And first, we shall achieve this by grafting <note>original: "infitione"</note>, so that

->*Purple and white carnations may turn blue.*<-

Take endive, or cornflower, or bugloss <note>original: "buglossum," a plant in the borage family</note>—but wild endive is better—of an old, thick variety exceeding the size of a thumb. We cut it down to the root and split it through the middle, as is done in cleft-grafting <note><term>encentrismo</term>: from the Greek *enkentrismos*, meaning the process of grafting by insertion or inoculation.</note>, and we insert a shoot of the flower pulled up by the root. We bind it with a vine-shoot and heap the earth around it with rotted dung. In this way, it produces a flower which

# *How fruits and flowers can be made more fragrant.*

## CHAPTER XVI.

IF the fruits and flowers have pleased by the allure of their color, now their fragrant scent should not be despised; we shall achieve this in various ways—through grafting, irrigation, and other artifices. And for the sake of example, let us teach how

### *To make lemons more fragrant.*

If we graft that smallest kind of lemon, commonly called the *little limoncello* <note>original: "limoncello piccolo"</note>, onto a citron tree <note>original: "citrium"</note>, it will receive the greatest scent from the trunk below; and the more often you repeat the grafting upon the same tree, the more sweetly it will vibrate with scent—a fact proven by our continuous experience in Neapolitan gardens. ### *To make pears smell more sweetly,*

We shall make fruits sweeter first by grafting, and then by drilling, or cutting, and by other methods. By grafting

### *To make laurel-cherries*

we are able to do this: for we have said that one may correct the faults of plants and add certain virtues through grafting. If a fruit is rejected because of excessive sweetness, by grafting it onto a slightly bitter tree, a more flavorful fruit will be produced from that mixture. Pliny said that the cherry could be grafted onto the laurel, and that from this the "laurel-cherry" was born. Palladius writes:

> *The cherry is grafted to the laurel, and by a forced birth,*
> *An adopted blush tints the face of the virgin.*
> <note>original: "Inferitur lauro cerasus, partuq; coacto, Tingit adoptiuus virginis ora pudor." The "blush" refers to the red fruit appearing on the laurel, which was sacred to the virgin Daphne.</note>

In our own times in Naples, there have appeared what are called "laurel-cherries," which possess a not-unpleasant bitterness. This is a most noble variety, far surpassing others; they are clearly large, blood-red and juicy, and within their great sweetness there is a certain slightly bitter flavor. This ensures they are not rejected for too much tartness, nor do they cause distaste through excessive sweetness. There are also produced

### *Sweet apples from the grafting of a quince.*

If you graft an apple onto a quince tree, they will take on a honey-like flavor. According to Diophanes, these were called *honey-apples* among the Athenians, as if they had the flavor of honey <note>original: "melimela," a term for a sweet apple variety</note>. Now, with the help of Agriculture, we shall pass on how fruits may become sweeter by drilling through the trunk, by scarring around it, and by other "chastisements" <term>castigationibus: the practice of wounding or pruning a tree to improve its output</term>, as farmers are accustomed to call them; thus, by sweating out the harmful and superfluous humor, they grow sweet. For example, if

### *You wish for almonds to produce sweet fruit,*

Aristotle teaches: that if a nail is driven into the almond tree so that the gum distills out for a long time, the tree is rendered "urban" <note>original: "vrbanam," meaning refined or domesticated as opposed to wild</note>.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of plant modification from the previous section. While the previous page focused on grafting different species together (like the "laurel-cherry"), this page transitions into techniques for "correcting" the natural bitterness of wild trees—specifically almonds and citrons—through physical wounding, draining of sap, and the introduction of sweeteners like honey.</meta>

<page-num>134</page-num>
<header>NATURAL MAGIC, BOOK III</header>

And through this artifice, wild trees become domesticated. **Theophrastus** <note>Theophrastus (c. 371 – c. 287 BC) was a Greek philosopher and the successor to Aristotle; he is often called the "Father of Botany."</note> says that if one digs around the trunk and bores a hole into the lower part a nine-inch measure deep, allowing the "tears" <note>original: "lachrymam"; referring to the sap or resin that exudes from a tree's wound.</note> flowing from all sides to drain away, the tree will grow sweet. Indeed, the almond tree is corrected by being perforated. If you wipe away the flowing moisture from the cut peg and do this for two or three years, you will turn a bitter tree into a sweet one. For bitterness arises from an excessive abundance of nourishment and a wealth of <term>humors</term> <note>The "humors" were the vital fluids believed to regulate the health of all living things; the author suggests that "bleeding" a tree removes excess, bitter sap.</note>, which is corrected by the perforation. Once freed from that moisture, the tree passes into a state of fertility producing better and more pleasant fruit, as the remaining moisture can be more easily "cooked" or digested by the plant. **Africanus** <note>Likely referring to Sextus Julius Africanus, a 3rd-century traveler and writer who recorded agricultural practices.</note> asserts that sweet fruits are made from bitter ones if, after digging around the trunk, a small cavity is pressed in four fingers' width from the root, through which the harmful moisture may sweat out. **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the 1st-century "Natural History."</note> says: Almonds become sweet from bitter if, after digging around the trunk and perforating the bottom part, the flowing "phlegm" <note>original: "pituita"; here used to mean a thick or sticky sap.</note> is wiped away. But there are some who, so the cavity does not remain idle in the meantime, pour in honey; they believe it is drawn through the <term>marrow</term> <note>original: "medullam"; the pith or central core of the plant tissues.</note> as if through a siphon, all the way to the fruit. We shall have an example of this if we wish.

### To make citrons sweet.

This fruit <note>The citron (*Citrus medica*), a large, thick-rinded citrus fruit that was one of the first citrus species known to the Mediterranean.</note> was not usually eaten in the age of **Theophrastus**, nor in the memory of **Athenaeus's** ancestors (as he himself reports), nor in the time of **Pliny**. Therefore, **Palladius** taught how to change its sharp pith into sweet. These are his words: It is said that sharp piths can be changed to sweet if the seeds are soaked for three days in <term>honey-water</term> <note>original: "aqua mulsa"; a mixture of water and honey, often used in ancient medicine and agriculture.</note> or in sheep's milk, which is better. Some people, in the month of February, drill an oblique hole into the trunk from the bottom, such that it does not come out the other side, and they allow the moisture to flow from this until the fruits begin to form; then they fill the hole with mud. They confirm that in this way, the center of the fruit becomes sweet. **Pontanus** <note>Giovanni Pontano (1426–1503), a famous Neapolitan humanist and poet known for his work "The Gardens of the Hesperides."</note> describes this in his *Gardens of the Hesperides*:

> *Where does art not penetrate? Let the branch itself*
> *Be cut thicker, and hollowed out a palm’s breadth, and everywhere*
> *Led in a circle with its edges, no thicker than a thumb. Into that place*
> *Pour melted honey, and cover it with a great stone*
> *Which might turn away the Sun. After the thirsty tree has sucked up*
> *The enclosed moisture, and thirsting, longs for new cups,*
> *Take care that you imbue the yellowing fruits by immersing them in honey.*

*Again, fill the empty storehouse with honeyed nectar <note>original: "Thymbraeo nectare"; literally "Thymbraean nectar." Thymbra was a place famous for savory herbs, which produced high-quality honey.</note>, and sprinkle the fluids poured from a human body <note>original: "latices humano è corpore fusos"; the author is referring to the use of human urine as a nitrogen-rich fertilizer, a common practice in Renaissance and ancient agriculture.</note> upon the tender roots. Meanwhile, do not neglect to pluck the leafy buds from the whole trunk, unless the Attic honey <note>original: "mopsopius liquor"; Mopsopia was an ancient name for Attica, the region of Athens famous for its honey.</note> fills them, and the lips themselves draw the sweet liquid from the source of the honeyed wine.*

### *How sweet almonds may be made from bitter ones.*

**Palladius** <note>Rutilius Taurus Aemilianus Palladius, a 4th-century Roman writer on agriculture.</note> bores through the middle of the trunk and drives in a wedge of wood smeared with honey.

### *How cucumbers may become sweet.*

If you soak the seeds in sweet liquids while they drink them up, they will bring forth sweet fruit. **Theophrastus** <note>The "father of botany" (c. 371–287 BC).</note> teaches that sweet cucumbers are produced if the seed, before it is sown, is soaked in milk or honey-water <note>original: "melicrato"; a traditional Greek mixture of honey and water.</note>. **Columella** <note>A prominent Roman authority on farming (4–70 AD).</note> says: The cucumber will become tender and most pleasant if you soak its seed in milk before you sow it. Some also do the same with honey-water so that it might come out even sweeter. From these authors, **Pliny** and **Palladius** take their instruction.

### *That sweet artichokes may come forth.*

If the seeds of the thistle <note>original: "cardui"; referring to the cardoon or wild thistle, the ancestor of the artichoke.</note> are soaked in milk and honey and planted after being dried, they will draw sweetness into their moisture. **Cassianus** <note>Likely referring to Cassianus Bassus, compiler of the *Geoponica*.</note> cites **Varro** <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC), a prolific Roman scholar.</note> on this. Likewise,

### *Sweet fennel will come forth.*

If its seeds are sown after being soaked in honey-wine <term>mulsum</term> <note>A common Roman beverage made of wine and honey.</note> and milk, they will bring forth sweeter fruits in their season. Or, if the seed is inserted into dried figs and then sown. In the same way,

### *How melons are made sweeter*

**Palladius** teaches: their seeds are to be soaked in honey-wine and milk for three days, and then planted once dried; from this, they are made delicious.

### *Lettuces grow sweet,*

If one waters them in the evening with honeyed wine, and they are sated by this drink for three days until they have drunk their fill, they will be sweet; this is what **Aristoxenus of Cyrene** <note>A philosopher and music theorist who famously "seasoned" his garden with mead to produce pre-flavored vegetables.</note> taught, as recorded by **Athenaeus**. To ensure

### *That the radish is rendered sweet.*

You shall soak the seeds for a day and a night in honey, or in raisin wine <note>original: "passo"; a sweet wine made from partially dried grapes.</note>, according to **Palladius** and **Florentinus**. Radishes will be sweet if their seed is soaked in honey-wine or the juice of raisins...

The cause is a peculiar softness found in the roots. From **Anatolius** <note>Vindonius Anatolius, a 4th-century writer on agriculture whose work was a source for the later *Geoponica*.</note>. For the apple tree <note>original: "malus"</note> rejoices greatly in urine, and it should be irrigated with this constantly. Some have applied goat manure and poured the dregs of old wine over the roots, making the fruit sweeter. **Theophrastus** says that if an apple tree is watered with boiling water in the spring, it improves. The same treatment applied to herbs makes them sweeter; for example:

### *to make endives sweet.*

There are many things which, when watered with salt water, lose their bitterness and take on a sweetness. **Theophrastus** <note>Theophrastus (c. 371–287 BC) was a Greek philosopher and the successor to Aristotle; he is often called the "Father of Botany."</note> orders that for endives <note>original: "intuba"; likely referring to chicory or endive.</note> to shed their bitterness, they must be watered with salt water or be planted in salty places. The same

### *to make cabbage more pleasant,*

occurs. And for this reason, the Egyptians sprinkle cabbage with <term>nitre</term> <note>original: "nitro"; in antiquity, this usually referred to natron (sodium carbonate) or saltpeter, used here as a fertilizer or soil amendment.</note> mixed with water so that it turns out sweeter, which is why cabbage sown in salty places is best: for it washes away the sharpness and the natural saltiness inherent in the cabbage. And likewise,

### *so that the Beet might turn out sweeter,*

he irrigates it with salt water, and thus thinks it turns out better; **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, the Roman naturalist and author of *Natural History*.</note> reports the same things from him. Finally,

### *Rocket is made more pleasant,*

if it is watered with salt water, and it puts forth more edible leaves. They use another trick of cultivation so that vegetables might come forth more pleasant for eating, by cutting back the stalks. Thus, therefore,

### *so that Basil may grow more pleasant,*

they cut back the stalk, for the stalks are sweeter and more pleasant after regermination; **Theophrastus** provides a most evident reason for this. By the same reasoning,

### *Lettuce regerminates more pleasantly,*

**Theophrastus** also says that after the first stalks are picked, those that come forth in the first sprouting are considered more pleasant; those earlier ones were "milky" and unpleasant, as if they were less <term>concocted</term> <note>The ancient theory that heat "cooked" or "concocted" the raw sap of a plant into sweet, ripe fruit or leaves.</note>, but the second ones are perceived as sweeter as long as they are tender. By the same reasoning,

### *to make the Leek turn out sweeter,*

the same author relates that it will germinate better if it is trimmed and re-trimmed: the reason for which he gave in his book *On Causes*, for the first germination exists as something weak. The same should be done with other vegetables.

### *That growing fruits may take on all shapes or impressions.* CAP. XVIII.

Chance often demonstrates many things (as we frequently see in citrons, which, through the encounter of branches, holes, or carved objects, abound with various images, impressions, and seals). These things are increased by no small amount of labor by those with powerful intellects, and through frequently conducted experiments, they are adapted for use. Whence the poem:

> *Experience itself, through the varied nature of things,*
> *And labor, the master of practice, has shown new arts to those in need.*
<note>A variation on Virgil's *Georgics*, emphasizing that human ingenuity arises from necessity and observation.</note>

And since the cause remains hidden to most people, these things instill a great deal of wonder in those who behold them, so that they are judged to have occurred outside the norms of Nature. For if you fit earthenware vessels <note>original: "testacea vasa"; clay molds or pots.</note> to growing fruits, they will fill the molds as they grow vigorously and will take on whatever form you wish. Furthermore, if any colors have been painted inside and concentrated in the proper places, they will stain the fruit as if they were natural. For this reason, one often sees a human head in <term>chrysómelis</term> <note>original: "chrysómelis"; literally "golden apples," a term used in antiquity for quinces, apricots, or yellow plums.</note>, with white teeth, reddening cheeks, and darkening eyes, so that—all greenness being cast aside—it imitates a human head. But the method of **Africanus** <note>Likely Sextus Julius Africanus, a 3rd-century author known for his "Cesti," a collection of "magical" and practical knowledge including agriculture.</note> for achieving this is clear:

->*The method by which a citron may take on*<-
->*the form and image of a human head,*<-

## How all fruits may shine more tenderly, more beautifully, and with a broader form. CHAPTER XIX.

Finally, lest we omit anything, we shall write down many modes of cultivation concerning fruits and herbs, so that they may not only be sweeter, larger, more tender, and more flavorful, but also shine with a more elegant form and gleam more cheerfully. 

And first:

### So that the apple tree and the myrtle may improve.

Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus (c. 371 – c. 287 BC) was a Greek philosopher and the successor to Aristotle; he is often called the "father of botany."</note> reports: If they are irrigated with boiling water, they improve; even the myrtle is rendered hollow, with its inner seed removed. This was discovered by chance, while they stood neglected near a bathhouse. But if you wish 

### Fig trees to sprout broader fruits.

Columella <note>Columella was a Roman soldier and farmer who wrote "De Re Rustica," a definitive work on Roman agriculture in the 1st century AD.</note> demonstrates this. To make the trees more fruitful and firm, do thus: When the tops of the fig tree begin to leaf out, it is beneficial to cut off the highest tips with iron. It will always be appropriate, as soon as the fig begins to push out leaves, to pour red ochre <note>original: "rubricam"</note> diluted with olive dregs <note>original: "amurca" — the bitter, watery liquid that settles out of unfiltered olive oil</note> and human manure onto the roots. This makes the fruit more abundant, fuller, and better. From him, Pliny and Palladius <note>Pliny the Elder and Palladius were both famous Roman encyclopedists and agriculturalists whose works were foundational to Renaissance science.</note> agree: When the fig begins to produce leaves, to ensure they bear much and rich fruit, let us strike off the very highest tips at the start of the budding, or at least that tip which proceeds from the middle of the tree.

Palladius writes that some have recorded that if we pierce the trunk here and there and insert wedges into each hole—using terebinth <note>The terebinth or turpentine tree</note> on one side and lentisk <note>The mastic tree</note> on the other. ### *To make cucumbers long and firm,*

### *A tree which alone produces the fruits of all,*

It was three-forked; on one branch it bore a grape empty of seeds <note>original: "vinaceis vacuam"</note>, variegated in color and medicinal, of which one type caused sleep and the other a purging of the bowels. Another branch gives cherries—seedless, sour, and sweet—and it gives golden apples <note>original: "mala aurea," a term used in this period to refer to citrus fruits like oranges or citrons</note>...

## How various fruits and medicated wines are made.
### CHAPTER XX.

Those ancients strove with the greatest zeal and diligence to find out how they might season wine with various antidotes <note>In this context, "antidotes" refers to medicinal mixtures or additives meant to counteract ailments, not just poisons</note> and adapt it for use if needed. This was not done without reason, as nothing is more excellent for one's well-being. This is shown by the fact that the majority of them recorded many such things—more curiously than was perhaps fitting—wonders to tell and easy to perform, which Theophrastus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher and the "father of botany"</note> mentions. Near Heraclea in Arcadia, a wine is made which, when drunk, makes men lose their minds and renders women infertile. A similar wine in the territory of Troezen is confirmed by Athenaeus <note>A Greek rhetorician and grammarian, author of the *Deipnosophistae*</note>. And at Thasos, a wine is produced that induces sleep, and another is crafted by a certain art which makes the drinker more alert. You will find various seasonings for wines among the more diligent physicians and writers on agriculture; these are not difficult to know, nor do I believe it will be hard for those who know the powers of simples <note>original: "simplicium," referring to "simples"—medicinal plants used on their own rather than in a compound</note>. By reasoning, it follows that they finally achieve those things that result from the property of the place. I think it would be most useful to apply these methods for those who fear and dread medicines, so that they may swallow them pleasantly before they have a chance to hate them. Let the first be:

### *How the theriac vine is made.*

A shoot should be planted, as Florentinus <note>A 3rd-century author whose agricultural writings are preserved in the *Geoponica*</note> teaches in the first and second books of his *Georgics*. It should be split at the bottom to the depth of four fingers, the pith <note>The soft, spongy center of the plant stem</note> removed, and in its place, hellebore <note>original: "veratrum," a plant used in antiquity as a powerful purgative</note> should be inserted. Then, having bound it carefully with a willow twig, let it be committed to the earth. In this way, it will produce grapes whose eating softens and empties the bowels. Or if—

->*How a vine may make for a good bowel movement.*<-

If you wish to keep the wine for a long time, save it specifically for moving the bowels, and do not mix it with the rest of the wine. Take a small cup <note>original: *cyathum*; a Roman liquid measure approximately equal to 0.045 liters</note> of that wine, mix it with water, and drink it before dinner. It will move the bowels without danger. More modern practitioners clean the roots of the vine and apply the juice of a purgative medicine, irrigating them and repeating this for several days—especially when the bud is swelling. Once this is done, they heap earth over the roots. Above all, they take care that the roots do not lie uncovered while the North Wind <note>original: *Aquilone*</note> is blowing, for that wind exhausts the potency of the medicine. A grape will be born whose clusters will be purgative. 

->*The same result in another way*<-

is achieved by us. Drill through the plant as far as the pith using a French drill <note>original: *terebra gallica*; a specific type of auger or boring tool</note>; or we have placed ointments beneath the bark here and there in various places around the whole circumference of the trunk. This is done during the time of grafting <note>original: *inoculationis*</note>, when the tree swells with sap. As the moisture rises, it carries the antidote to the fruits and infects them—whether for plague, purging, childbirth, death, or life.

# NATURAL MAGIC, BOOK III.

...let us gather, and wine from the vineyards. This is a matter of truly immense utility, that from one measure <term>modius</term> <note>original: *modius*; a Roman dry measure roughly equivalent to two gallons or 8.7 liters</note> more than a hundredfold might come forth. But I would not want anyone to think, because I have said one will receive more than a hundredfold, that I mean this exact number of measures will always be collected from a single sowing; for if the year, the weather, the soil, and the stars <note>referring to the astrological timing and seasonal influences believed to govern plant growth</note> are unfavorable, the harvest will be smaller. Yet it will not be so much smaller that it does not exceed the usual harvest by five times; while if these factors are favorable, one hundred and fifty measures will be returned from a single one.

But this promise of ours will seem a paradox to some; yet if they were of sound mind, it should indeed seem the greatest paradox why we do not receive two hundred measures from a half-measure sown, since we see that from a single sown and germinated grain, the root sprouts into multiple and numerous stalks—more or less fifteen—and that sixty grains are contained in each ear. I pass over the soil of Byzacium in Africa <note>a region in modern-day Tunisia famous in antiquity for its extreme fertility</note> mentioned by Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, the Roman author of *Natural History*</note>, which produced nearly four hundred sprouts from a single grain; and from that same place, a procurator sent three hundred and forty stalks from one grain to Nero <note>the Roman Emperor</note>.

But let us hunt for the cause <note>catchword: *Vnde*</note> from which this might happen. There are those who say it happens because the greater part of the sown grain is devoured by birds, moles, worms, and other subterranean animals. But that is proved false by the fact that from a measure of lupin <note>original: *lupinum*; a bitter legume used for soil enrichment and food</note> sown, no more than fifteen or so are harvested, even though the lupin lies abandoned with impunity, safe from all animals due to its unpleasant bitterness, and in its pods and husks, more or less a hundred grains are contained. There are others who ascribe it to the heavens—to the injuries of cold and heat, or the frequency of rains—so that now the fields grow numb with frost, now they are infested by drought, now they grow lush with a surplus of weeds, or now they waste away from thinness. But this also proves to be a false argument, because even with the greatest favor of the heavens, not even thirty are returned from one. 

But lest we wander too far, we say that not all the grains of the ear and the husk grow, for God destined some for the food of animals, and others for seed. There are grains in the ears, like miscarriages and degenerate offspring, which do not bear fruit but decline into defects; [while] there are others that shine forth more robustly from the husks in the ears, which are produced for propagation. Furthermore, they are neither sown at the proper time, nor are they supported by the proper work of the farmers.

<summary>Della Porta explores the discrepancy between the biological potential of grain—which should yield hundreds of seeds per grain—and actual harvest yields. He refutes common theories about pests and weather, suggesting instead that seed quality and farming techniques are the primary limiting factors.</summary>

Therefore, if we meet these conditions, everything will follow according to our wishes. For seeds with more extended, interwoven roots, creeping far and wide beneath the earth, bring forth more numerous stalks, surrounded on all sides by ears of grain. 

Therefore, let the bride <note>The author uses a marriage allegory where the "bride" is the seed and the "husband" represents the soil or the elements that fertilize it.</note> be led to her husband, chosen not from the first-born or the last-born, but from those in the middle, because the others are weak. Let her be sequestered in a bath, anointed with ointments, fed with the fatness of old goats, and associated with Vulcan <note>original: *Vulcano*; the Roman god of fire, here representing the application of heat</note> and Bacchus <note>original: *Baccho*; the Roman god of wine, representing moisture or steeping the seeds in liquid</note>. Let the soft bed, optimally prepared, be warmed; for by life-giving heat they join in a friendly nature, and are bound and cling together in sweeter embraces. Thus the woman, animated by the man, may grant not a degenerate but a legitimate offspring. 

Let the Moon preside with her fertile light, for the fruitful makes the seed fruitful. One thing remains to be warned: the wife to be led to Bacchus should not be entirely destitute of hair <note>A metaphor for the outer layers or awns of the grain</note>, for a bride deprived of the beauty of her head is scorned by her husband, nor would she have a way for harmful impurities to be purged; rather, let her only be shorn of her curls. Thus, less adorned, she will please herself and her husband more.

# JOHN BAPTISTA PORTA OF NAPLES, NATURAL MAGIC, BOOK FOUR,

## PREFACE.

<image-desc>A decorative square woodcut initial letter 'E' surrounded by floral and vine motifs.</image-desc>

From animals and plants we have moved on to Domestic Economy; for there we prepared animals and fruits that were remarkable, varied, and suited to our needs. Now, it would seem we have accomplished and produced nothing if—having served and brought forth these things at such immense expense—we did not here teach by what means they might be preserved, and rendered resilient against the injuries of a freezing or sweltering sky, so that they might be brought out in their proper season. It would be the mark of a godless and lazy man to allow those things which you prepared with such great labor and diligence to rot and perish through utter neglect. Therefore, it is necessary that just as you were skillful in generating them, you should appear equally diligent in preserving them. And the head of the household <note>original: *paterfamilias*; the male head of a Roman or Renaissance household, responsible for its legal and economic status.</note> who stores away his fruits will have no small portion of his provisions throughout the winter, for they serve as a main dish. As **Marcus Varro** <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC), a prolific Roman scholar; his work *De Re Rustica* is the primary source for ancient agricultural techniques.</note> says: "No one stores away fruits except to bring them out, and he brings them out..."

Afterward, we will declare those things which we have found to be true, mixing in our own findings throughout, which seemed more important to the matter and which we have more frequently put to the test <note>original: *periculum fecimus*; in this context, it refers to empirical testing or experimentation</note>. But let us begin the business.

### How fruits can be preserved on their own tree.
### CHAPTER I.

To begin then with fruits: both these and flowers are preserved either on their own parent <note>referring to the parent plant or tree</note> or after being gathered from it. We shall first say how they can be preserved on their own tree, and we shall relate those things found by the ancients, and then those discovered and tested by us. When our ancestors wished for fruits to endure on the trees, they first bound them to the trunk or the branches, lest they be shaken by storms or damaged. Furthermore, they would intercept the sap <note>original: *succum*</note> which brought them to maturity: for there are certain fruits which, once they have achieved ripeness, do not linger on the tree, but fall off as windfalls even if no one has shaken them; yet there are also those which remain longer on the tree. Also, to protect them from the injuries of the sun and frost, they covered them with certain defenses, or to prevent them from being eaten by animals. Whence if...

### *How pomegranates may remain for a long time on the tree,*

Some people twist the stalks <note>original: *pediculos*; the small stems connecting the fruit to the branch</note> of pomegranates just as they are on their own tree, so that the fruits are not split open by rains and perish from the gaps. They tie these to the larger branches so that they remain motionless, and then they enclose the tree with ropes made of esparto grass <note>original: *sparteis restibus*; a tough fiber used in antiquity for cords and nets</note> so that the fruit is not mangled by crows, jackdaws, or other birds. Some fit earthenware vessels around the hanging fruits and allow them to remain on the trees, sealed with mud mixed with straw. Others wrap individual fruits in hay or stalks and, moreover, coat them thickly with straw-mud and tie them to the larger branches so that, as I said, they are not shaken by the wind. According to Columella <note>Lucius Junius Moderatus Columella, a 1st-century Roman writer on agriculture</note>, all these tasks ought to be performed under a clear sky without dew. 

However, Beritius <note>Anatolius of Berytus, a 4th-century writer on farming</note> allows the fruit to stay on its parent tree in this manner: having wrapped the fruits individually in sand starting from the blossom, they bind them with small cords so that they do not gape open into cracks as they ripen; they leave them protected in this way. Others place individual fruits into small earthenware jars and, once they are carefully covered, they stabilize them so that they cannot be broken by hitting the trunk or by colliding with one another. In this way, they will always obtain fruit that is both more abundant and more mature. Marcus Varro <note>A famous Roman scholar and agriculturalist</note> says: if you take immature pomegranates while they still hang from their branch and place them into a pot without a bottom, then sink the pot into the earth and bury the area around the branch so that no air can blow in from the outside, the fruits will not only be taken out whole, but even larger than any that ever hung on a tree. Palladius <note>A late Roman agricultural writer</note> also teaches
