And you will be able to keep them in this way for almost the entire year if you enclose them in certain small vessels. But if we wish 

### *How grapes may remain in their vigor on the vine until spring.*

Beritius commands it thus: near the vines, in a very shady place, dig a trench two cubits deep, and having thrown in sand, fix stakes <note>original: *ridicas*; wooden poles used to support vines</note> into it. Then, gently bending the vine-shoots once or twice, carefully turn and twist them together with the clusters of grapes; then cover them, bound to the stakes, so they are not moistened by any dampness. Care must also be taken that the clusters themselves do not touch the ground. When I had tried this quite often, the outcome did not favor me correctly: for I found them discolored and half-rotten...

#### *to do the same in another way.*

But when doing the same thing in the same way for many years became tedious, we thought a better and more wonderful plan was devised. As the time for pruning approaches, choose two shoots on the vine which promise a certain hope of bearing fruit; clear the tops of both, leaving two or three eyes <note>original: *oculos*; the nodes or buds on a grapevine from which new growth emerges</note>, yet do not cut them from their mother plant. And if you desire to do this more surely and quickly, as far as possible, in summer place a vessel full of water above it, so that through a woolen tongue <note>original: *laneam linguam*; a strip of fabric acting as a wick to provide slow, steady irrigation via capillary action</note> it may drip water little by little and continuously into the vessel. Thus it will strike roots more vigorously and clothe itself in leaves and fruit. After the harvests <note>original: *vindemijs*; the grape-gathering season</note>, cut the shoots below the vessel and carry them into a covered house, in a dry place safe from storms—namely, wine cellars. Cover the windows with nets so birds do not devour them. On clear winter days let them bask in the sun; where frosts are shivering, keep them in warmer places, and you shall keep them until August, so that on one single vine-shoot both new and old grapes may thrive, with their color and vigor preserved.

## How fruit-storehouses should be made, in which fruits are preserved. CHAPTER III.

WE SHALL NOW SPEAK of how they are preserved once cut from the tree. Because we desire to rescue fruit from the stain of rot, we will not be able to achieve this unless we first learn the causes of decay. Philosophers relate that such is the force of the inconsistency of celestial heat <note>original: *syderi caloris*; the heat influenced by the stars or the sun</note> that all things which the sublunary world <note>The region of the universe below the moon, which in Renaissance science was believed to be the only realm subject to change, decay, and the four elements.</note> surrounds and embraces tend toward an end, nor do they cease from motion; for the air, permeable through all things, by the kinship of the hot nature which it finds in the fruit, entices it, so that the poor thing, first harassed by its innate coldness, feels itself emptied of its natural heat which has been snatched away, and as it withers, it dries up. But the minds of men are not so clouded, nor their senses so dulled, that they cannot escape into harmlessness; they act so that they render fruits constant against the course of cold or heat, and this in various ways. And first, we will establish <term>fruit-repositories<gloss>oporothecas; from the Greek 'oporotheke', a place for storing autumn fruits</gloss></term>, from which we will exclude the injuries of heat. Soon we will choose times in which heat prevails less, afterwards gathering them so that they do not contract a blemish from touch, and thence the beginning of putrefaction; finally in various places

### *That wheat may be preserved longer.*

Varro says it ought to be stored in elevated granaries, which are blown through by the wind from the sunrise and the Northern region, and where no damp breeze from nearby places can reach. Some have underground granaries, like caves, as in Cappadocia and Thrace; others, as in Nearer Spain, use pits. In these, they spread straw on the bottom and take care that neither moisture nor air can touch the grain, except when it is taken out for use; for where the air does not reach, the <term>curculio</term> <note>original: *curculio*; the grain weevil, a beetle known for destroying stored crops.</note> does not arise. Wheat stored in this way remains for fifty years, and millet for more than a hundred years. Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and "father of botany."</note> states that dusty wheat, when stored, rots; the cause is external heat found in the dust, for the grain's own internal heat is trapped and suffocated, causing it to grow hot and rot, which produces even more heat. Florentinus <note>A 3rd-century author on agriculture whose works were collected in the *Geoponica*.</note>, following Varro, says that grain is properly stored in places above ground that receive light from the East. Let the place also be moderately aired by the North Wind and <term>Favonius</term> <note>The West Wind, associated with spring and mild weather.</note>, but turned away from the South Wind and similar winds. It should also have dense and frequent channels through which hot vapor may escape and a cooling breeze may enter.

### *Beans are best stored,*

If they are moderately toasted, it contributes more to their longevity, for in this way less moisture remains. According to Theophrastus, they are preserved unprocessed at Apollonia and Tarentum. Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus (Pliny the Elder), author of the "Natural History".</note> sa—

->*To preserve meat and fish.*<-

We ourselves have seen meat and fish kept for nearly a month without rotting in extremely cold places, without any artifice other than the coldness of the location. In subterranean and very cold places, where all heat and the southern wind are excluded, and where there is perpetual dryness and cold, all things are preserved without rot. In the monastery of Mount Parthenius <note>Now known as Monte Vergine, near Naples, Italy.</note>, near Naples, we saw the bodies of men preserved whole for many years. This mountain is covered with snow almost perpetually. And on the summits of mountains where snow is kept in pits, we have found pears, sorb apples, apples, and wild chestnuts that had been collected by chance and stored together with the snow; when the snow was removed after a year, we found them as moist, fresh, and beautiful as if they had just been picked from the tree. In short, nothing is more effective for the preservation of things than the dryness or coldness of a place.

First, that which I judge must be observed in this business is the time when the fruits that are stored for long-term use are gathered: for if we wish to exclude that heat and moisture which spoil our fruit and induce the waste of rot, there is no more suitable way than the selection of the time in which the principal stars, which [possess] such a quality...

Therefore, when the Moon is waning <note>original: *deficiente Luna*; referring to the period between the full moon and the new moon</note>, it is cold and dry: for when the Moon abounds in moisture and heat, and fruits are gathered then, being pregnant with moisture and heat they easily rot; nor do I consider a man who is ignorant of this to be of sound mind. For this reason, all writers on Agriculture prescribe that fruits should be gathered when the Moon is waning. 

Furthermore, night and day, and the morning or evening twilights, impart moisture and dryness to fruits. The day, by the presence of the Sun, is hot and dry; the night, by its absence, is cold and humid. Evening twilights are hot from the departing Sun, and humid from the approaching night; morning twilights are cold from the departure of the night, and hot with the arrival of the Sun. Once these two have passed, for two or three hours of the day, there will be dryness from the Sun’s brief stay and cold from the proximity of the night; this time they proclaim as the best for the collection of fruits. 

Lest we increase the difficulty with astrological precepts, we believe we should favor a more exact doctrine regarding the position in which the other planets may be found, so that the sky might be more dry and cold, and the fruit might endure longer. Without sparing thoroughness, we bring forward experiments and authorities to confirm this, since all animals grow faster when the Moon is waxing <note>original: *crescente Luna*</note>, and twice as much as those when it is waning. ### The time for harvesting and storing wheat

Authors report that barley, or grain <note>original: *frumentum*</note>, ought to be left out for one or two days, or at least one full night, and then carried away before sunrise, so that the crop is placed in the granary while still cooled by the night air. This contributes greatly to its long-term preservation. Columella <note>A prominent Roman writer on agriculture whose works were rediscovered during the Renaissance.</note> also teaches this.

### At what time the bean is gathered and stored

He confesses that he has tested this through experience: Pick the bean during a "silent Moon" <note>original: *Silente Luna*; this refers to the New Moon, when the moon is not visible in the sky.</note> before dawn. Then, once it has dried on the threshing floor, and immediately before the Moon begins to wax <note>increase in size</note>, thresh it and, once cooled, bring it into the granary. Stored this way, it will remain unharmed by weevils <note>original: *curculionibus*; small beetles that are notorious pests in stored grain.</note>. Palladius <note>A 4th-century Roman agricultural writer.</note> records the same. And—

### The pea is laid up for the use of the whole year,

If it is stored once the sun has exhausted its moisture and it has been released from its pods <note>original: *valuulis*</note>, it is thus protected longer from the stain of rot.

## On the method of gathering fruit and treating the stems, so that we may ward off the beginning of rot. CHAPTER V.

Furthermore, since our ancestors saw that the beginning of decay in fruit typically starts at the stem <note>original: *pediculis*; literally "little feet," referring here to the fruit stalk.</note>, or the spot where the stem is joined to the fruit, they took precautions in many ways and modes to ensure no harm arose from them. It was considered fitting that the very place from which the beginning of life and nourishment flows should also be where the onset of death arises.

In addition, fruits intended for storage must be gathered with great care so they are not bruised or crushed together; for rot is born from such bruising. It is necessary that the fruit be in the best possible condition when plucked; specifically, all should be gathered before they are fully ripe, so that they are neither entirely sour nor have reached total maturity. Those intended for storage must also be inspected diligently to ensure they are whole, without blemish, and free of small worms. But let us look at specific examples. First—

Those fruits born endowed with moisture and heat possess within themselves the principle of decay. The opposite occurs with wild plants, and those that grow on the peaks of mountains, in dry and arid places, facing the South, and those destitute of all cultivation; these produce fruits that are solid, dry, and bereft of excess moisture and heat. Hesiod <note>An ancient Greek poet, whose work *Works and Days* serves as a foundational text on farming and morality</note> makes no mention of manure <note>original: *lætaminis*</note> in his work on agriculture, not because he forgot such a necessary part of cultivation, but so that the fruits grown in rich soil would not be subject to putrefaction and disease. Apples that grow in wild places, swept by the wind and in stony ground, are preserved by their own nature without any other artifice; thus, if other techniques are added which aid in conservation, they become much more long-lasting. But let us see if the elders remembered such things, and let us hear from Theophrastus <note>The "Father of Botany," a successor to Aristotle</note>, for he mentions:

### *From what place the fruits of the palm are long-lasting*

Dates <note>original: *palmulæ*</note> that can be pickled and preserved must grow in sandy places, as in the region called "Hollow Syria" <note>Coele-Syria; the valley between the Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon mountain ranges</note>. He says that only in three sandy locations are those produced which can be pickled and stored away; the rest, however, which come from other places, do not last at all but rot immediately. And a little later: they say that of those fruits born in Syria, only those produced by the "Palm Valley" can be stored. Those indeed which are born in Egypt, Cyprus, and elsewhere, are all consumed while fresh. Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the *Natural History*</note> agrees: "Only those are preserved which grow in salty and sandy soils, as in Judea and Cyrenaica in Africa. Not so in Egypt, Cyprus, Syria, and Seleucia of Assyria." The same Theophrastus, speaking of beans, teaches:

### *From what place beans are born that they may be best stored.*

Saying: "One countryside differs from another, and one climate from another, regarding the corruption and preservation of seeds." Therefore, at Apollonia <note>An ancient Greek colony in modern-day Albania</note> on the Ionian Sea, they say the bean is in no way eaten away <note>likely referring to weevils or rot</note>, and therefore should be set aside for storage. ### How fruits should be enclosed to exclude the air. CHAPTER VII.

We have stated that heat and moisture must be excluded if we wish to preserve fruit for a longer time, as these qualities are found most abundantly in the air. Therefore, we shall demonstrate the efforts our ancestors made to exclude the air, and then present our own discoveries. First:

#### To keep apples uncorrupted by enclosing them.

We shall begin with Aristotle, who, in order to exclude external air, said in his *Problems* <note>A collection of questions and answers on various scientific and philosophical topics attributed to Aristotle</note> that fruits are preserved in skins filled with air in this manner: "Why do things remain uncorrupted when contained in inflated skins, or in well-covered vessels that have been sealed all around, such as orchard fruits, meats, and others of that kind? Is it because all things tend to rot when they are moved, whereas those that are full remain unmoved? For it is impossible for movement to occur without empty space; and these things which are so enclosed are held full on all sides, and therefore are kept uncorrupted by reason." It is as if he were saying that air enclosed in this way, experiencing fewer seasonal changes of the atmosphere, lasts longer. Or perhaps if the apples were able to breathe out heat and moisture, they would be restrained by the full skins. But let us see what the masters of Agriculture teach. For instance:

#### To keep citrons uncorrupted by sealing them.

Palladius <note>A 4th-century Roman writer on agriculture</note> protects citrons <note>term: *citria*; large, thick-skinned citrus fruits, ancestors of the lemon</note> from the air in this way. He closes individual citrons in individual vessels, coats them with gypsum <note>A soft sulfate mineral used as plaster</note>, and places them in an orderly fashion in an orderly place. Sotion <note>An ancient author whose works on farming are largely lost but preserved in later compilations</note> commands that the citron fruit be carefully smeared with kneaded clay, so that throughout the entire course of the year it may be kept safe from every blemish with its integrity unimpaired. Let us also see how others have attempted

#### To keep apples enclosed.

Columella <note>The most important Roman writer on agriculture, author of *De Re Rustica*</note> stores each kind in its own small boxes, for when different types that disagree with one another are stored together, they spoil more quickly; truly, when the apples have been carefully arranged, they should be covered with the lids of the boxes, and the lids should be smeared with clay mixed with straw <note>original: *luto paleato*</note>, so that no breath of air can enter. **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman author and naturalist</note> encrusts the finest apples in gypsum or wax; however, if the fruits are not yet fully ripe, they will break the casing as they grow. Others assign individual earthenware vessels to each apple or pear, then place those jars—their lids sealed with pitch—inside a larger storage vat. **Apuleius** <note>Possibly referring to the author of 'The Golden Ass', though here cited as an agricultural authority</note> keeps apples in a clay jar that has been coated on the inside with wax. They also preserve them in earthenware jars wrapped in seaweed, ensuring they are covered on all sides so they do not touch one another; then, lids are added to the jars and they are stored away. **Columella** <note>A prominent Roman writer on agriculture</note>

### How to enclose quinces so they last through the year

teaches the following method. Some people wrap them in fig leaves, then knead potters' clay with <term>amurca<note>the bitter, watery sediment or dregs of olive oil</note></term> and smear the apples with it. These same fruits are then buried in dry gypsum in new pans, arranged so that they do not touch one another. **Palladius** <note>A 4th-century Roman elite who wrote a manual on farming</note> places the fruit between two wooden slats, seals them on every side with mud, and buries them separately in dry gypsum within a new pan. **Democritus** <note>The Greek "laughing philosopher," often associated in this period with "natural magic" and secrets of nature</note> covers them with leaves, then kneads together clay-like mud or potters' chalk with hair, and smears the apples; when these have been dried in the sun, they are stored away. When use requires it, the clay casing is broken, and the <term>quinces<note>original: "cotonea"; a tart fruit related to apples and pears, highly prized for preserves</note></term> will be found just as they were when first put in. But **Pliny** gives the briefest instruction: for quinces, every single "breathing hole" or vent must be removed. Thus also

### All things are best preserved when tightly sealed.

**Mago** <note>A Carthaginian writer known as the "father of agriculture"</note> carefully buries the fruit in potters' chalk and dries them in the sun; then, if the chalk develops any cracks, he smears them with mud and keeps them once they are dried. Alternatively, he spreads poplar or oak sawdust at the bottom of a new earthenware jar and arranges the fruit so that the sawdust can be packed down between them. Then, having completed the first layer, he spreads sawdust again and arranges the apples similarly until the jar is full. When it is filled, he puts on a lid and carefully seals it with thick mud. Or, according to **Palladius**, they are arranged inside a storage jar so they do not touch each other, and the jar is then covered. **Africanus** <note>Likely Cassius Dionysius of Utica, who translated Mago's work</note> also teaches

### How to keep figs preserved by enclosing them,

in this manner: if individual figs are enclosed inside a green gourd, with little compartments carved out for each one, and likewise those that have been sliced and pressed <note>original: "spleniata," referring to figs sliced and flattened like a medical compress</note> are enclosed in a checkered pattern and hung in a shady place.

### *Medlars and truffles are preserved enclosed in little pitchers*

### *That myrtle berries are best preserved,*

### *Walnuts are preserved enclosed in chests*

### *Lilies are kept enclosed for a whole year,*

if they are taken with their little branches while not yet open, but still

### *How grapes may last throughout the year when enclosed*

<meta>catchword: How</meta>
According to **Didymus** <note>a Greek writer on agriculture, often cited in the *Geoponica*</note>. Some people store them in small pitched boxes with dry shavings <note>original: scrobe; likely referring to wood-scrapings or sawdust</note> of pitch-pine, or fir, or black poplar, or with millet flour. You will preserve them for a long duration if, immediately after the vintage, you place the clusters themselves, uninjured and unshaken, into a large jar <note>original: dolium</note>, and diligently block the mouth of the jar and seal it with a coating of **gypsum** <note>a mineral used to create a plaster-like seal</note>. Similarly, they are preserved if they are immersed and suspended in potter's clay that has been well-kneaded until liquid; then, when they are taken out, they are washed of the clay. **Columella** <note>Lucius Junius Moderatus Columella, a premier Roman authority on agriculture from the 1st century AD</note> says that when you have cut **bumastos** <note>original: vuas bumastos; a variety of grape with large clusters, literally "cow-teat" grapes</note>, or hard-berried, or purple grapes from the vine, you should immediately dip their stems in hard, melted pitch. Then, fill a new earthenware basin with the driest possible chaff, shaken so that it is free of dust, and suspend the grapes there; cover it with a second basin and seal the edges with clay mixed with chaff. Once these joined basins are arranged on a very dry floor, bury them under dry chaff.

### *How stored wheat may remain unspoiled*

Inside caves or pits, as we have mentioned from **Varro** <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a prolific Roman scholar</note>. The Cappadocians and Thracians store grain in caves, and the Spaniards in pits; they take care that neither moisture nor air can touch it, except when it is taken out for use. For where the air <note>original: spiritus; referring to the circulation of air</note> does not reach, the **weevil** <note>original: curculio; a beetle that infests and destroys stored grain</note> does not arise. Thus stored, it can remain unspoiled for fifty years.

->*That they also placed closed vessels floating in large jars.*<-

### CAP. VIII.

Even if they excluded air from closed vessels, as it is the source of all rot, they did not for that reason exclude it from the places where the vessels were stored. At the slightest external alteration—namely becoming damp, drying out, heating up, or cooling down—the air trapped inside was changed, and with it, the fruit. Therefore, to avoid these variations of the weather, they would submerge the smeared vessels in various liquids. This was done with good reason and experience; indeed, we ourselves, keeping watch with such study, have noticed that if the air remained uniform, fruits and flowers enclosed in glass vessels would stay unfading. But when it varies, mold <note>original: situs</note> and the beginning of rot are immediately seen on the fruit. For this reason, vessels should be submerged in cisterns, wells, or underground places, so that the motions of the shifting air are felt less. To proceed to the experiments, we will teach

->*How quinces may be preserved for a long time when enclosed and submerged,*<-

**According to Democritus** <note>an ancient Greek philosopher whose name was often associated with early agricultural and scientific "secrets"</note>. Put quinces in a new earthenware vessel, cover it, and seal it with pitch. Close it in a wine cask <note>original: dolium</note> in such a way that they float; thus they are kept fresh, and the wine in which they float will take on a pleasant aroma. In the same way

->*Apples last through the year when closed and placed in cisterns.*<-

**Palladius** <note>a 4th-century Roman writer on agriculture</note>: when you have enclosed apples in earthenware vessels, and these are carefully pitched and closed, the apples are committed to them; for they sink the earthenware vessels in a cistern or a well. **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, the Roman author of Natural History</note> puts floating apples in earthenware dishes, by which method he believes an aroma is also acquired by the wine. **Apuleius** <note>likely referring to a Roman agricultural source attributed to Apuleius</note> says that apples placed in a new pot, and the pot submerged in a wine cask so that it floats, and the cask is then sealed, will keep the apples fresh and the wine fragrant. Thus

->*That closed figs are preserved floating in wine*<-

is promised by **Africanus** <note>Sextus Julius Africanus, a 3rd-century traveler and historian who wrote on agriculture</note>. Having put fresh, less ripe figs, picked with their stems, into a new earthenware vessel, and [separated] from one another...

...they enclose them separately, and allow the vessel to float in a jar full of wine. We also have experienced that

*Peaches, enclosed in wooden cisterns and submerged, are preserved,*

in which the fruits are suspended so they do not touch the liquid, and the jar is closed so that the wind does not breathe into it. Hence Columella <note>a prominent Roman writer on agriculture from the 1st century AD</note> demonstrates that

*Service berries, enclosed and placed underground, live longer.*

During the harvests, carefully pick service berries <note>original: sorba; the fruit of the service tree, which requires "bletting" or over-ripening to become edible</note> by hand, place them into small jars smeared with pitch, put on lids smeared with pitch, and seal them with gypsum <note>a mineral plaster used for airtight seals</note>. Then, in pits two feet deep made in a dry place under a roof, arrange the small jars so that their sealed mouths face downward; then pile up the earth and stomp it down moderately from above. However, it is better to arrange fewer vessels at a distance from each other in more pits, for in the process of removing them, if you disturb the rest while taking one out, the service berries are quickly spoiled. Pliny, citing Cato: Service berries are preserved in earthenware vessels smeared with pitch in pits, with a lid sealed with gypsum, with two feet of earth brought over them in a sunny place, with the vessels turned upside down. From these sources, Palladius [writes]: Picked when quite hard and set aside, when they have begun to ripen, they are enclosed in earthenware jars until full, covered with gypsum from above, and submerged in a two-foot pit in a dry place, under the Sun, with the mouth turned over, and the earth is stomped down more thickly from above. The same author said that

*Pears placed in vessels and positioned underground are preserved for a long time,*

specifically those which are hard in flesh and skin; placed in a heap, when they have begun to soften, they are put into an earthenware vessel smeared with pitch and sealed with a lid placed over it. The vessel is submerged in a shallow pit in that place where it may be touched by the Sun daily. Others have stored them immediately after being picked with their stems <note>original: tenacibus</note> in jars smeared with pitch, and the mouths of the small vessels with gypsum, or...

->*Apples, when enclosed and buried in the earth, endure,*<-

->*protect chestnuts also in this manner*<-

stored in new ceramic vessels and buried in a drier place. The same author

*renders roses perennial by enclosing and burying them*

in this fashion. He stores them in an unrefined pot, well-fortified, and buries them in the open air, preserving them for use. We, however, teach

->*how all things may be preserved for years when enclosed.*<-

Fruits, as we have said, are stored in glass vials, and with the glass opening closed by the furnace or a small tube <note>referring to the process of melting the glass neck to seal the container</note>, we submerge them under cisterns and keep them uncorrupted for years. In the same way, we keep flowers fresh for a long, long time by enclosing them in an elongated vessel with the neck closed as we described—namely, by a "Hermetic seal" <note>original: Hermetis sigillum; an airtight seal created by fusing the glass of a container's neck with heat</note>, as they say—and submerging them under water.

...we preserved. Likewise, we have found that grape must <note>Freshly pressed fruit juice, usually from grapes, that contains the skins, seeds, and stems.</note> stays fresh for a year when enclosed in a glazed clay vessel and submerged under water with a weight, as we have described. By an artifice similar to this, we are able:

#### *To keep closed things preserved for a lifetime,*

If we wrap them in some mixture so that the passage of air is entirely denied, and especially if that mixture is itself incorruptible. We have proven this with amber <note>original: succino</note>; for we wrap the object after the amber has been softened. Since it is transparent, it allows the sight entry and demonstrates that the thing is preserved. We store bees and lizards this way, and we have mockingly deceived many into believing they were the very bees and lizards of Martial <note>Marcus Valerius Martialis, a Roman poet famous for his short, witty epigrams.</note>. We see everywhere animal hairs, leaves, and fruits, wrapped in this kind of liquid, rendered eternal. Martial says of the bee:

> *Both hidden and shining, she is preserved in a drop from the daughters of Phaëton,* <note>original: phaëtontide gutta. According to Greek myth, the sisters of Phaëton (the Heliades) wept tears of amber after his death.</note>
> *So that the bee seems enclosed in her own nectar.*
> *She has received a worthy reward for such great labors;*
> *It is believable she herself wished to die thus.*

The same author says of a viper enclosed in amber <term>electro: here meaning amber, rather than the gold-silver alloy</term>:

> *While a viper crawled upon the weeping branches of the Heliades,*
> *The amber gem flowed over the obstructing beast.*
> *While she marveled at being held by the rich dew,*
> *She suddenly stiffened, all of her, in the congealed frost.*
> *Do not take pride, Cleopatra, in your royal tomb,*
> *If a viper lies in a nobler grave.*

As for how amber may be made soft, although there are many ways, you can be satisfied with this: if you throw it into boiling and skimmed wax, it is made so soft that it is easily handled with the fingers and can be adapted to individual uses. Just remember it must be fresh.

### How apples submerged in honey can also be preserved for a long time. CHAPTER IX.

Seeing also that the ancients knew things enclosed in vessels, and even vessels submerged in water, could avoid corruption, they immersed items and fruits in various liquids. They believed they would be preserved longer when submerged in honey, wine, vinegar, brine, and others, since the power to ward off rot is shared with these substances. For in honey, not only fruits but even the bodies of animals may be kept without putrefaction, and

Elsewhere, we have made mention of the body of Alexander <note>Alexander the Great. Historical accounts, such as those by Strabo, suggest his body was preserved in honey before being moved to Egypt.</note> and of a centaur <note>original: hippocentauri. In antiquity, "centaurs" were occasionally reported as biological wonders; here, likely a preserved curiosity or a malformed animal.</note> being preserved in honey. They did not use simple water, which, being moist, seemed to induce rot. But above all, they praised honey, believing that all things could be protected from corruption by honey. Columella <note>Lucius Junius Moderatus Columella, a prominent Roman writer on agriculture from the 1st century AD.</note>

### *Quinces can be preserved in honey without rotting*

said, stating: We have experienced nothing more certain or better than this: let quinces <note>original: cydonia; a tart fruit related to apples and pears, often used in preserves.</note> be arranged in a new, wide-mouthed jar, placed lightly and loosely so they cannot be bruised. Then, when they have been arranged right up to the neck, let them be held down with transverse wicker branches so that they press the fruit moderately, preventing those that have received the liquid from floating up. Then, let the vessel be filled to the very top with the best and clearest honey, so that the fruit is entirely submerged. This method not only guards the fruit itself but also provides a liquor of a honey-wine flavor <note>original: mulsei saporis. Mulsum was a popular Roman drink made of wine and honey.</note>, which can sometimes be given as a remedy without harm. But care must be taken that the fruit you wish to keep in honey be stored while still unripe; for if they are gathered raw, they harden so much that they are of no use. This method is so certain, indeed, that even if there are small worms inside, the fruit is no longer corrupted once it has received the aforementioned liquid. For such is the nature of honey that it restrains defects and does not allow them to spread; for which reason it also preserves the lifeless body of a man for many years without harm. Palladius <note>Rutilius Taurus Aemilianus Palladius, a 4th-century Roman agricultural writer.</note> says: Quinces are chosen when sufficiently ripe and lowered whole into honey, and thus they are preserved for a long time. Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, author of the *Natural History*.</note> submerges them in honey after they have been coated in wax. Apicius <note>Marcus Gavius Apicius, a Roman gourmet and supposed author of a famous cookbook.</note> stores flawless quinces with their twigs and leaves in a vessel, pouring over them honey and boiled-down wine <term>defrutum: grape juice boiled down to a thick, sweet syrup</term>. Quinces prepared in this way were called "honey-apples" <note>original: melimela</note>, as if prepared with honey. Whence Martial <note>A 1st-century Roman poet known for his epigrams.</note> says:

> ->*If quinces saturated with Athenian honey* <note>original: cecropio melle. Cecrops was the mythical founder of Athens; Athenian honey from Mount Hymettus was considered the finest in the world.</note><-
> ->*are served to you, you may call them honey-apples.*<-

Martial <note>Marcus Valerius Martialis, the Roman poet known for his Epigrams, who often wrote about daily life and food.</note> demonstrates that

### *Walnuts can be kept green for a year in honey,*
and he claims to have tested this himself. Only green nuts, freed from their shells, are submerged in honey; the honey itself then becomes so medicinal that a drink made from it heals the windpipe and the throat. Palladius

### *Clingstone peaches do not rot in honey*
he said, if they are preserved with the stones removed, and they are of a pleasant flavor. He also said they can be preserved in oxymel <note>original: oxymelle; a traditional medicinal and culinary mixture of honey and vinegar.</note>. And finally, Columella instructs that there is no kind of fruit that cannot be preserved with honey. But he thought it should be taught as a general rule that they be kept separate by species; for if you mix them, one kind is spoiled by the other. Thus also

### *The grape remains unharmed in honey,*
according to Didymus <note>Likely Didymus of Alexandria, a grammarian and agricultural writer.</note>, and is preserved. But we shall declare

### *which fruits are preserved in honey.*
For while we were applying ourselves to this business, so that fruits could be preserved from advanced decay, we placed them all in honey within glass vessels so that the opportunity might be given to observe which were preserved longer from the rot of decay. We found that some lasted longer, while others lasted less. More moist fruits spoil the pure honey, and it [itself] <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence here as indicated by the catchword.</note>

### *How fruits submerged in wine, grape-must syrup, boiled wine, vinegar, and wine dregs may last through the year.* CHAPTER 10.

Finally, seeing that wine preserved everything, and that grape berries which had fallen into the wine when it was put into jars remained uncorrupted in the jars throughout the entire course of the year, they <note>Referring to ancient agriculturalists like those cited on the previous page.</note> believed that things preserved in wine would remain immune to all decay. Nor were they content with wine alone, but used *defrutum* <note>original: defruto; grape must boiled down to half or a third of its volume to create a thick, sweet syrup.</note>, *sapa* <note>original: sapa; a similar syrup to defrutum, often boiled down even further; both were used as sweeteners and preservatives.</note>, vinegar, and wine dregs, because they smelled of the substance of wine. But we, knowing that a most subtle and unfading liquor can be extracted from the substance of wine <note>A likely reference to the distillation of alcohol or "spirit of wine," which was a major focus of Della Porta’s chemical experiments.</note> (for even wine is sometimes spoiled), are able with its help to preserve things uncorrupted for an age. But to come to examples, Palladius teaches:

#### *Quinces submerged in wine are kept uncorrupted.*
For if we place them into small vessels full of the best wine, or if an equal mixture of wine and boiled wine is made, we will keep quinces <note>original: cydonia / cotonea; the quince was highly prized for its scent and was frequently preserved in honey or wine.</note> for a long time. Others submerge them in jars of must and thus seal them, which also makes the wine fragrant. Democritus <note>Democritus of Abdera, though the agricultural writings attributed to him in the Roman era are often considered apocryphal.</note> submerges gathered quinces in jars of must and thus seals them, which also makes the wine more fragrant. The same author

#### *teaches that apples floating in wine are preserved;*
they put some apples floating in earthenware dishes, by which method they think a scent is also acquired by the wine. Apuleius <note>Likely referring to a Roman author of agricultural texts, not the author of "The Golden Ass."</note> says: Fruit is submerged in jars of must, and thus sealed, it endures; and being preserved by the dregs, they greatly enhance the sweetness of the wine. But if put into a new pot, and the pot is submerged into a jar of wine so that it floats, and the jar is sealed with clay, the apples will be fresh and the wine fragrant. One can also

#### *preserve figs submerged in wine for a longer time.*
As Africanus <note>Sextus Julius Africanus, a 3rd-century writer.</note> teaches: When the wine jars are covered, fresh figs that are not quite ripe, along with their stalks or stems <note>original: vmbilicisve; literally "navels," referring to the bottom end of the fruit.</note>, are put into a new earthenware vessel—not round, but rather squared according to choice, and supported at the bottom—so that they [are separated] from each...

Fresh grape marc <term>vinacea; the skins, seeds, and pulp left over after pressing grapes for wine</term> should first be placed in a vessel together with olives, arranged in alternating layers, and then sealed up. By this method, Columella

### *Cornelian cherries to be preserved in dregs*

prescribes that we may use these in place of olives. Ovid, in the 8th book of the *Metamorphoses*:

> And autumn cornelian cherries <note>original: *corna*; the fruit of the Cornelian cherry dogwood, which tastes like a mix of cranberry and sour cherry</note> preserved in liquid dregs <note>original: *fece*; the sediment or "lees" of wine</note>.

### *Grapes to remain green in wine dregs*

is demonstrated by Columella. Let them be gathered when moderately ripe, then placed on grates in such a way that one does not bruise another; only then are they brought under a roof, and any dry or defective grapes are clipped away with scissors. When they have cooled a little in the shade, three or even four bunches—depending on the capacity of the vessels—are lowered into jars, and the lids are carefully sealed with pitch so that they do not let in moisture. Then, the mass of grape marc, having been well-pressed by the wine-press, is brought forward; once the stalks have been moderately separated and the mashed skins loosened, a layer is spread in a large vat <note>original: *dolio*; a very large earthenware fermenting vat</note>. The jars are then arranged facing downward, spaced far enough apart so that the grape marc can be packed between them. When they have been carefully packed down to form the first layer, other jars are arranged in the same way, and a second layer is completed. Then, the vat is similarly filled with layers of jars, and they are packed tightly with the marc. Soon, the marc is stored all the way to the top rim, and once the lid is immediately placed on top, the vat is sealed with ash. But it will be necessary, when the jars are brought out for use, to remove the entire individual layers at once; for once the packed grape marc has been moved, it quickly turns sour and ruins the grapes.

### *To keep cucumbers fresh in vinegar*

and in a vigorous state: if you suspend them in a vessel containing a little vinegar, so that they do not touch the vinegar, and seal the vessel so that it does not breathe, you will have them fresh in winter by this method, according to the Quintilii <note>The Quintilii were two wealthy Roman brothers and authors known for their agricultural writings</note>. All things can also be preserved in vinegar: but because it ruins the flavor, we shall omit that. But from these methods we cannot

->*That fruits are best preserved in salt waters.*<-

### CHAPTER XI.

**A**fter wine, salt waters <term>falsæ aquæ; specifically brines or saline solutions used for pickling</term> were to be used for the purpose of preserving, for things submerged in them remained free from rot. For they saw that everything preserved in salt persisted without decaying: whence they also declared that fruits immersed in salt waters could protect themselves against putrefaction. Homer used to call salt "divine," because it was effective against rot and preserved bodies for eternity; Plato called it a "friend of God," so that no sacrifices were made without salted meal <term>salsa mola; a mixture of toasted grain and salt sprinkled on sacrificial victims in Roman ritual</term>. Plutarch said the ancients also called lightning "divine" for the reason that bodies struck by heaven's fire remained free from rot. Indeed, salt binds, dries, and constricts; it so reclaims decaying bodies that they endure through the ages, as proven by the customs of the Egyptians, whose habit it was to preserve bodies with salt, as Herodotus writes. Coming now to examples, Beritius relates

->*That pomegranates are preserved in salt waters.*<-

For he heats boiling sea water, or causes brine to boil, and places the pomegranates in it; afterward, they are cooled in the shade, dried, and hung up. When they wish to use them, they soak them in water for two days beforehand. Columella, following the opinion of the Carthaginian <note>original: *Pœni*; referring to Mago of Carthage</note>, writes: Mago <note>A famous Carthaginian agricultural writer whose lost works were frequently cited by Roman authors like Columella and Pliny</note> indeed commands that sea water be heated vigorously, and that pomegranates, tied with flax or broom-twine, be lowered into it for a short time until they lose their color; then, once removed, they are to be dried in the sun for three days and afterward hung up. When the occasion requires their use, they are to be soaked in fresh cold water for one night and the following day, until the hour they are to be used. Pliny, following him, says: Pomegranates dipped in boiling sea water...

[The author] bruises the *radiolum* <note>a small, shutter-shaped variety of olive</note> and puts it into brine; then he takes them out of the brine, squeezes them, and mixes them in a vessel with crushed seeds of mastic and fennel. Then he adds two parts of fresh must and one part of strong brine and preserves them; or he puts them whole into a jar, then adds strong brine until it reaches the very lip of the jar, and when the occasion requires, they are taken from the jar. Cato <note>Cato the Elder, a Roman statesman and author of *De Agricultura*</note> preserves black olives in this way: When the *orchites* <note>an oval, meaty variety of olive</note> are black and dry, rub them with salt for two days, then shake off the salt and place them in the sun for two days. Marcus Varro <note>a prolific Roman scholar and satirist</note> says the same thing. 

But Columella <note>a prominent Roman writer on agriculture</note> says: When the olives have turned black and were picked while immature, it is proper to pick them by hand in clear weather and separate the spoiled ones from the good; then add three *heminae* <note>about 0.5 pints or 0.25 liters</note> of whole salt to every *modius* <note>a Roman dry measure, roughly 2 gallons or 9 liters</note> of olives, and pour them into wicker baskets; let them sit for thirty days to sweat and let the *amurca* <term>the bitter, watery, dark liquid that drains from olives during pressing, distinct from the oil</term> drip out. Afterward, spread them in a trough, clean off the salt with a sponge, and put them in a jar, filling it with *sapa* <note>must boiled down to one-third its volume</note> or *defrutum* <note>must boiled down to one-half its volume</note>. 

Didymus <note>likely referring to the Greek agricultural writer of the *Geoponica*</note> teaches how to make "swimming" olives <note>original: *Colymbades*; olives preserved in liquid so they float</note> in this way: Pick olives when they are nearly ripe with their stems, wash them in cold water, and dry them for a day on wicker racks. Then, by bruising them lightly, place twenty *choenices* <note>a Greek dry measure, roughly 1 quart or 1 liter</note> into the bottom of a vessel, mixed with salt, four *congii* <note>about 3.2 gallons or 12 liters</note> of brine, and three *heminae* of vinegar. Shake the filled vessel so the liquid rises above them. Others put olives into sea water, take them out after seven days, and store them in a vessel with brine. So say Columella, Palladius, and others.

->*That things can be best preserved in oil and amurca.*<-

### CHAPTER XII.

Oil preserves things most effectively, and especially *amurca*, so that it defends them not only from the damage of the air, but also from animals <note>referring to pests like insects and rodents</note>. But let us not linger with too many words; Cato teaches the greatest virtues of *amurca*. *Amurca* prepares the threshing floors for harvesting crops, so that ants do not cause harm, and also
->*so that grain may last through the years in the granaries.*<-
He smears the floors of these rooms and the plaster of the walls with mud made from *amurca*; in this way
->*clothing is not eaten away by moths.*<-
He sprinkles *amurca* against woodworms and harmful animals; so also when poured out...

## *To preserve fig branches with their fruits in amurca,*

## *Olives to be preserved in oil:*

For when they are harvested as they begin to lose their color, they are picked with the stem and kept in oil, so that after a year they still present a fresh green flavor; when sprinkled with ground salt, they are served as if they were new.

### *How fruits buried in sawdust, leaves, and straw may be stored for a long time.* CHAPTER XIII.

The ancients also devised various trees whose sawdust, when fruits were submerged in it, would keep them for a long time due to its dryness—or because the trees themselves were resistant to rot, such as cedar and cypress. Furthermore, fruits are preserved among their own leaves and straw, for every thing is better preserved among its own kind than among foreign materials; just as we said regarding mulberries in their own wine, olives in oil, and grapes in wine. ### *That wheat may be preserved with herbs.*
<note>original: "Triticum cum herbis asseruetur"</note>

Tarentinus <note>referring to Hemitheon of Tarentum, an ancient Greek writer on farming</note> places dry twigs of wormwood <note>absinthium</note> or southernwood <note>abrotanum, a flowering plant in the sunflower family</note> among the grain, and furthermore uses the dry leaves of the houseleek herb <note>sempervivum, literally "ever-living," a succulent known for its resilience</note>. It is also beneficial to have dry pomegranate leaves, prepared with sifted sand; when the grain is being stored, one should sprinkle a choenix <note>a Greek unit of volume, roughly one liter</note> of these leaves for every medimnos <note>a larger Greek measure, roughly 52 liters</note> of grain. It is also very useful to spread flea-bane <note>conyza, a plant often used in antiquity to repel insects</note>, which has been partially cooled, on the floor beneath the grain; after ten medimni have been spread out, cover them again with flea-bane, and sprinkle more grain on top, continuing until all of it is stored. For grain stored in this manner not only remains free from rot for many years, but it will also retain the same weight when it comes time for bread-making.
We are also able

### *To keep barley unharmed with laurel leaves*
<note>original: "Hordeum incolume seruare lauri folijs"</note>

that are dry, provided they are from a fruitful tree; similarly, the dried houseleek herb preserves barley when mixed with calamint <note>an aromatic herb in the mint family</note>. When mixed with gypsum <note>a soft sulfate mineral</note> and barley, even flour remains unharmed for a time if resinous pine torches <note>tedis pinguibus, literally "fatty torches," referring to pitch-heavy pine wood</note> are crushed and cast into them. Some people grind equal parts of cumin and salt, making dry cakes from the mixture, and place them into the flour. This is according to Florentinus <note>a 3rd-century author whose agricultural writings were later collected in the Geoponica</note>.

## How other things may remain uncorrupted.
### CHAPTER XV.

We shall also review in this chapter those things which are effective for preserving other items, so that they may protect themselves from putrefaction: though these methods may seem common, they are nonetheless true. They also provide a pathway for investigating other matters. Furthermore,

### *All things can be preserved in quicksilver*
<note>original: "argentum viuum"—literally "living silver," known today as mercury</note>

Such as fruit and the like: for we have quite often arranged fruits in a suitable vessel so that, once quicksilver was poured in, they could not be carried upward <note>the high density of mercury would cause the fruit to float, so the author suggests a way to keep them submerged</note>; by keeping them buried in this way for many days, we preserved them unharmed. Likewise,

### *Meat is preserved when pierced by a copper nail*
<note>original: "Carnes æreo clauo infixæ asseruantur"</note>

<margin>from Plutarch</margin> if a copper nail is driven into meat, it preserves it unharmed from rot by its styptic, drying faculty. From many experiments that are circulated, we have learned a method by which

### *Corpses may be preserved for a long time*
<note>original: "Cadauera diu possint conseruari"</note>

First, the side being opened, the body is disemboweled, and the skull being cut open, the brain is removed; the pupils of the eyes, the testicles, and the spinal marrow are also taken out. Then, let the body be hung by the feet for three or four hours, according to the thickness and fatness of the body. Soon after, let it be washed with sponges soaked in distilled vinegar and "water of life" <note>original: "aquę vita"—an early term for distilled alcohol or brandy</note>, and allow it to dry. After drying, let it be sprinkled with quicklime <note>original: "calce viua"</note>, alum, and salt, and let it remain hung for two days in the smoke of herbs—namely, myrtle, laurel, rosemary, and cypress—in a dry and open place. Finally, let a mixture be made of five pounds of unslaked quicklime, one pound of burnt alum, two pounds of the best salt, a pound and a half each of aloes and myrrh, half a pound of aloe wood, three ounces of oil of spikenard, five ounces of ashes of rosemary flowers, and two ounces each of burnt verdigris <note>original: "viridis æris"—a green pigment/corrosion product of copper</note> and vitriol <note>original: "calchãti"</note>, and theriac... <note>original: "theriacæ"—a famous ancient poly-pharmaceutical "universal antidote"</note>

## *In what ways various kinds of bread may be made.*

### CHAPTER XVI.

We have spoken of preserving fruits and other things; it remains for us to teach how we may use those things we have preserved. Among other things most necessary for daily use, we shall demonstrate the many kinds of bread, wine, vinegar, and oil, so that not only the head of the household <note>original: "paterfamil."</note> may provide for his family with little loss to the family estate, but also that in times of high prices <note>original: "caritatis annona" — literally "the high cost of the yearly harvest," referring to times of famine or scarcity</note> in the mountains and wildernesses, he may prepare such things for himself with little labor from almost everything we have mentioned. But let us begin with bread and see what our ancestors used in times of necessity. I omit those kinds most familiar for household use made from spelt, its grits, emmer, cattail, millet, sesame, and from legumes, as these are well known. But first:

### *Making bread from water caltrop.*
<note>original: "Panem ex tribulo conficere"</note>

Dioscorides <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note> teaches that a type of caltrop <note>original: "tribulus" — specifically the water caltrop or water chestnut, *Trapa natans*</note> is common to the waters, which, growing in rivers, brings forth a certain seed the size of a chestnut; it is three-pronged, membranous, and filled with white pith. It tastes like chestnuts, and the common people call it the "water chestnut." Those living nearby use it for food, just like chestnuts. Those who travel abroad make small prayer-beads from them. The Thracians, who live near the Strymon River, fatten their horses with this green caltrop...

### *To make bread from the lotus*

Theophrastus teaches this. The lotus <note>The "lotus" described here is the Egyptian water lily (*Nymphaea lotus*), not the lotus tree.</note> grows in the plains where the countryside is flooded. The fruit is similar in nature to a bean, but smaller and more slender; it grows on a head in the same manner as a bean, emerging in great, dense clusters. When the sun sets, it closes itself; when it rises, it opens and lifts itself above the water. In the Euphrates, the head is as large as a poppy. The Egyptians let these heads rot in heaps, and once the husks have decayed, they wash them in the river to separate the fruit. After drying and grinding them, they make bread, which they use for food. Pliny writes: There is also the *lotometra*, which is made from cultivated lotus; from its seed, which is similar to millet, the shepherds in Egypt make loaves, mostly kneaded with water or milk. It is claimed that nothing is more healthy or lighter than that bread while it is warm, but once cooled it is harder to digest and becomes heavy. It is well known that those who live on it are troubled neither by dysentery, nor by tenesmus <term>tenesmus: a distressing and constant urge to evacuate the bowels</term>, nor by other diseases of the belly. Therefore, it is held among their remedies. There was also an ancient custom

### *To make bread from palm dates,*

which is found in Pliny. The Thebaid <note>The region around Thebes in Egypt</note> and Arabian palms are entirely dry, thin of body, and scorched by constant heat; they have a crust rather than a skin. In Ethiopia itself, these are crushed (so great is the dryness) and thickened into bread in the manner of flour.

### *Bread from the sycamore.*

In Caria and Rhodes, and in neighboring places that are not very fertile for wheat, there is a great yield of the Egyptian fig, or sycamore. During a shortage of grain, the people satisfy themselves with this in place of bread and corn, so great is the abundance and supply of this perennial fruit. The bread is indeed friendly to the stomach, but provides very little nourishment; we could also prepare the same from our own local trees. It is recorded among the writers on Agriculture,

## *How to make bread without leaven,*

From Didymus <note>Didymus of Alexandria, an ancient author on agriculture.</note>. Some people add nitre <term>nitre: in this context, likely "natron" or sodium carbonate, which acts as a chemical leavener to make the dough rise</term>, for indeed nitre makes breads more brittle <note>original: "friabiliores" — meaning crumbly, light, or crisp</note>, just as it does with meat. Others, the day before they make bread, throw grapes into water; the following day, when they wish to make the bread, they remove the ones that are floating and squeeze them, using the resulting liquid instead of leaven, which makes the breads more pleasant. If you wish to have leaven throughout the whole year, when the must <note>freshly pressed grape juice</note> boils in the vats, take that foamy part which has bubbled up, mix it with millet flour, and having ground it diligently, form it into small cakes <note>original: "offas"</note>. Once these have been dried in the sun, store them in a damp place; then, taking a sufficient quantity as needed, you may use it as leaven.

## *Various kinds of bread made from roots and fruits.* CHAPTER XVII.

Now we shall proceed to other kinds of bread, discovered in our times, which can be of no small use to us during a grain shortage <note>original: "annonae caritate" — referring to the high price or scarcity of the official grain supply</note>. And first:

### *How bread may be made from the arum root.*

The arum root <note>The root of *Arum maculatum*, also known as cuckoo-pint or lords-and-ladies. The raw plant is toxic and extremely acrid; it requires careful preparation to be edible.</note> is eaten because of its milder sharpness and is sought after in foods. For Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and the father of pharmacology.</note> said it should be swallowed after being boiled, as it is then less pungent. Galen <note>An influential Roman-era physician.</note> says it is eaten in the manner of a turnip, though in some regions it grows somewhat sharper. When you wish to prepare it correctly, it is proper to pour off the water from the first boiling and immediately throw the root into fresh hot water. In Cyrene <note>An ancient Greek colony in modern-day Libya.</note>, the arum is different than in our region: for there it has very little medicinal quality and very little sharpness, so much so that it is even more useful than turnips. In times of grain scarcity, even the ancients used the root of this plant effectively for food. Caesar, in *On the Civil War*: "There is also a kind of root discovered by those who were with Valerius, which is called *chara*; this, mixed with milk, relieved the soldiers' want and created something resembling bread." There was a great abundance of it; when the followers of Pompey taunted our men with hunger during parleys, they would commonly throw loaves made from this at them to diminish their hope. And a little later: "The army maintained excellent health." And in Dioscorides, among the spurious names of simple medicines, arum was called chara anti- <note>The text cuts off mid-word, continuing to the next page.</note>

In our region, it is of such a sharp nature that it can hardly be tolerated by the tongue. But we will reveal the method by which the best bread can be made from it—one might even say more beautiful than wheat. Large roots are cleaned and cut into thin slices; for the thinner they are, the more quickly they lose their bitterness. A very white flour will be produced, which, either on its own or with a third part of wheat flour added, will make the whitest and most savory bread. It can also be prepared in other, quicker ways: when you have mastered it, you will surely rejoice in the result. It is also eaten with the greatest pleasure.

### *Bread made from asphodel is eaten.*

In our land, these bulbs <note>original: "bulborum" — referring to the root of the asphodel</note> are so prolific that no other plant is more numerous; one often finds eighty bulbs clustered together. Furthermore, the mountains and shores are so fertile with them that Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, the Roman author of *Natural History*.</note> says the plant seems born for human food. Asphodel is eaten from the toasted seed and the bulb. The bulb is prepared in hot ashes with oil added; moreover, when mashed with figs, it provides exceptional pleasure, as Hesiod <note>An ancient Greek poet who famously praised the simple diet of "mallow and asphodel."</note> notes. The bulbs are similar to small turnips. Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire who wrote extensively on the properties of foods.</note> says the same. But among us, they are so unpleasant and sharp in flavor that they do not serve as food for man; indeed, swine will hardly eat them even when dug up with their snouts, let alone being fit for greedy gluttony in times of grain shortage. It was once the potherb of ancient frugality. However, by boiling it, its power is made much weaker and its heat milder, just as we said regarding the arum. This will be enough to satisfy hunger, as Pliny testifies was done in ancient times. We have provided a very healthy bread made from these when kneaded with flour, especially for those with wasted bodies and for the consumptive <term>consumptive: those suffering from "phthisis" or tuberculosis, characterized by physical wasting</term>. Also—

### *Bread is made from turnips, rapes, and skirrets.*

From these—when they are cooked, boiled, and cleaned of all waste—a most commendable bread can be made.

### *Excellent bread from squashes.*

Because of this, it is not only useful in times of scarcity, but can even be considered a delicacy. The method of preparation is as follows. Take squashes that are swollen, round, and ripened by the sun; cut them into several slices and clean away the harder and tougher skin and the inner pulp with a knife. You should then take care to boil them by immersing them in a pot of boiling water. Through long cooking, the squash sheds its green plant-like color, its foul smell, and its unpleasant taste, and it acquires a more agreeable scent, a pleasing flavor, and a certain peculiar nourishing power; furthermore, it lasts as long as bread does. Once it has been reduced to the consistency of a paste <note>original: "vnguinis formam" — literally the form of an ointment</note>, let it be pressed by hand through a linen sieve so that if any undercooked parts or woody fibers remain, they are caught by the narrow holes of the fabric. To this mass, you will add a third part of flour and mix it into bread, which will be pleasing for daily eating. We know that in great quantity it is not harmful when eaten to the point of fullness, but rather beneficial when taken in moderation. It is best when fresh; when old, it is less attractive and less delicate. We have revealed the method to be used with related plants; now learn to act skillfully.

## How weight may be added to bread. CHAPTER XIX.

Now we shall teach how bread may be increased—a truly marvelous thing, useful, and very profitable—not only to relieve the dearness of poverty, but it benefits the master of the house, for a small amount of flour can feed many to fullness. And this in a three-fold way: for there are things which, added to grain, increase the substance of the bread itself; others are of a dry and glutinous nature, which thicken the broken element into the substance of bread. There is also the final way, which by the spirit of its own heat, enlivens and grows, like a living thing. Just as much as is lost by the removal of the bran, so much will the water sprinkled in the grinding and the rest of the craft add back. Furthermore, the baking of the bread itself carries away a tenth and a half part <note>Approximately 15%</note> of the weight. Let us see how our ancestors were able to provide:

->*Weight and whiteness to bread with a certain earth, or chalk*<-

Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, the Roman naturalist whose "Natural History" was the primary source for such Renaissance experiments</note> teaches that *alica* <note>A type of groats or porridge made from emmer wheat</note> is whitened with a certain chalk in this way. *Alica* is made from *zea* <note>Spelt or emmer wheat</note>, which he called "seed." The grain of it is pounded in a wooden mortar; for it is worn away by the hardness of stone; more nobly, as is known, by the penal labor of those in chains with a pestle. ### *Rice adds weight to bread,*

It does not spoil the flavor or the goodness of the bread; rather, it increases both the flavor and quality, and forces the portion to grow eightfold. For by continuous stirring, it retains the "flying" moisture, so that you will see it thicken; add leaven to the thickened mixture. However, it must be allowed to cool, so that the power of the thickening is not lost. Let the wheat substance be added to bind and glue the "fugitive slave" <note>a metaphorical term for the volatile elements like steam and air that escape during baking</note> until you see it has become sufficient and grown to the desired weight. <meta>This page continues the technical instructions on grain preparation. While the previous page discussed adding external substances like rice or minerals to bread, this section explores how to increase the volume and weight of wheat using its own internal properties and "vital heat."</meta>

ON HOUSEHOLD ECONOMY

### *To increase the weight of wheat with wheat,*

This is done without any outside addition. Indeed, if we wished, we could accomplish this work with many—almost infinite—additions of any small thing. But in this method, a ferment is drawn out from the true substance of the wheat; once this is separated, purified, and added back to the same wheat, it will increase its own substance by expanding its volume, or by breaking down the elements into its own mass. We must warn you beforehand: do not let the prolific heat <note>original: "prolificus calor" — the vital warmth or life-force that allows the grain to ferment and rise</note> be diminished, but rather let it be preserved and increased, for everything depends on this. Yet it is an extraordinary work of nature and full of wonder, how this might be done.

### *How wheat may grow from itself,*

My mind somehow shrinks from manifesting this secret, lest it be laid bare to the lowest commoners and ignorant little men. However, so that we do not deprive the ingenious, we deny it to the former but shall open it to the latter. This was unknown to the ancients, as evidenced by the fact that they mention no such method of bread-making in their writings. The whole matter is this: the wheat flour must be treated with the "soul of its own heat." This is the offspring of celestial fires, and its nature is of such thinness that, carried up by its own fervor, it renders the mass so swollen that it reaches the very brim of the vessel. On the following day, you shall cast it into the kneading trough <note>original: "mactram" — a large wooden tub used for mixing and rising dough</note> and add flour again. This flour, likewise raised by its own fervor, meets the mass and, like a receding tide, unites with the broken-down elements, turning them into floury lumps. You shall do this three or four times, and you could even propagate the matter infinitely. This should be done in a heated room <note>original: "hypocausto" — literally a Roman underfloor heating system, here referring to a warm room or stove area</note> so that the warm spirit <note>original: "coridus spiritus"</note> may be nourished. We also felt we must warn you not to "throttle" the dough mass <note>original: "ne massam fauces" — meaning to avoid over-kneading or compressing it too tightly</note>, lest the life-giving breaths <note>original: "genitabiles halitus" — the gases produced by fermentation</note> expire and vanish into the air, for then your hope will be frustrated. Nor should there be a lack of dewy vapor, which, carried up to the heavens and turned into droplets, moistens the mass. Thus you will rejoice in a portentous harvest; but there is a need for skillful manual operation. I pray you do not destroy through negligence what has been discovered by the skillful wit of those who take risks.

These matters are primarily necessary, both in times of scarcity and during military expeditions. Pliny says: "Certain substances, when tasted in small amounts, settle hunger and thirst and preserve strength, such as butter, horse-cheese <note>original: "hippace" — a cheese made from mare's milk</note>, and liquorice <note>original: "glycyrrhizon" — from the Greek meaning "sweet root"</note>." And elsewhere: "Scythia produces the foremost among them, which is called the 'Scythian plant' <note>original: "Scythica"</note>; it grows near Boeotia and is very sweet. Another is most useful for what are called spasms. It is highly recommended because those holding it in their mouth do not feel hunger or thirst." The same is provided among those same people by the plant called *hippice* <note>meaning "horse-plant"</note>, because it has the same effect on horses. They report that by using these two herbs, the Scythians can endure hunger and thirst for up to twelve days; Pliny translated all of these details from the first book of Theophrastus. It is sweet and "Scythian," and indeed some call it simply "sweet"; it grows near Lake Maeotis. Among other things, it also extinguishes thirst if held in the mouth; for this reason, they affirm that by using both it and the so-called "equestrian" plant, the Scythians can tolerate thirst for eleven or twelve days. From this, it appears that Pliny translated these accounts from Theophrastus.

But I believe Pliny was mistaken: for *hippace* signifies horse-cheese; it is not a herb. Theodorus <note>Theodorus Gaza, a 15th-century translator of Theophrastus</note> translated it as "equestrian," as if it were a root of liquorice with a similar nature for driving away thirst and hunger. For Hippocrates says: "The Nomadic Scythians eat *hippace*, which is horse-cheese." And elsewhere: "The Scythians pour mare's milk into hollow wooden vessels and shake it; while it is being agitated, it foams. The fatty part, which they call butter, stays on the surface; the heavy part sinks to the bottom. They separate and dry this, and call the dried substance *hippace*." The reason for this is that horse milk is greatly nourishing and corresponds in proportion to cow's milk, according to Dioscorides. The *Western Indians* <note>original: "Occidentales Indi" — referring to the indigenous peoples of the Americas</note> also use another preparation

-> *to endure hunger and thirst,* <-

From the herb called tobacco—specifically from its juice—and the ash of snail shells, they compose pills and dry them in the shade. On journeys lasting three or four days, they place one pill between the lower lip and the teeth, sucking it continuously and swallowing the juice; in this way, throughout that entire span of days, they feel neither hunger, nor thirst, nor exhaustion. ### *The Epimenidean composition for enduring hunger and thirst.*

For there was a certain medicine that was very nourishing and prevented thirst, which was eaten both by those besieging cities and by the besieged; it was called the "Epimenidean composition" <note>named after Epimenides of Crete, a legendary 7th-century BCE seer said to have lived in a cave for decades without food</note> because of the Epimenidean squill <note>original: "scilla" — the sea onion, often used in ancient medicine</note> that enters into its composition. It was made in this way: after the squill is boiled, washed in water, and dried, and finally cut into very small pieces, a fifth part of sesame and a fifteenth part of poppy are mixed in. All of these are then softened in honey—the best available—which acts as a binding agent to form a mass. The whole mixture is to be divided into pieces about the size of large olives; by taking one around the second hour <note>approximately 8:00 AM</note> and another around the tenth hour <note>approximately 4:00 PM</note>, they will suffer no ill effects from hunger. 

There is another composition of the same kind: take a half-sextarius <note>an ancient Roman unit of volume, roughly a pint</note> of Attic sesame, a half-part of honey, a cotyle <note>about half a pint</note> of oil, and a choenix <note>about a quart</note> of cleaned sweet almonds. After drying the sesame and almonds, they must be ground and sifted. Then, after peeling the squills all around, cutting away the roots and leaves, and slicing them into small pieces, they must be placed in a mortar and pounded until they are perfectly smooth. Next, mix an equal part of honey with the pounded squills along with the oil, and by pouring it into a pot and placing it over coals, it must be stirred here and there with a wooden spatula until everything is blended. Once the mass has become solid, it will be worthwhile to divide it into small mouthfuls; by taking one in the morning and another in the evening, a person will have sufficient nourishment. This medicine is particularly useful for an army, for being sweet, it brings a sense of fullness and takes away thirst. We have excerpted these details from a certain manuscript commentary on the book of Heron <note>likely Hero of Alexandria, a mathematician and engineer</note> in the Vatican Library. We saw the same composition in Philo <note>likely Philo of Byzantium, an author on mechanics and siege warfare</note>, in the fifth book of his work *On Warfare*, where he describes other similar things of this kind.

### *Wine from palms*

Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, the Roman author of *Natural History*</note> said that in the East, wine is made from these, and he recounts fifty types of palms and the differences between the wines made from them. Among these, the *cariotae* <note>original: "cariotæ" — a variety of date palm</note> are most celebrated, being very rich in juice. From these comes the principal wine of the East, though it is "hostile to the head" <note>likely a reference to its high sugar content causing headaches; the name *caryota* may derive from the Greek word for "head"</note>, which is how the fruit got its name. Their chief quality is a rich, milky juice with a certain wine-like taste, and they are extremely sweet, like honey. The wine intoxicates, just as the fruit does if eaten in too large a quantity. Having spoken of wine, it follows that we speak of vinegar. First, we shall discuss how it was made by our ancestors, and then by the more recent age—specifically how it may be made very sharp. NATURAL MAGIC, BOOK IV.

->*To turn wine into vinegar, and the reverse,*<-
Cassianus <note>Cassianus Bassus, a 6th-century Byzantine compiler of agricultural lore often cited in the "Geoponica"</note> maintains that if one puts a crushed beet root into wine, it will become vinegar after three hours. If, however, one wishes to restore it to its original state, he should put in a cabbage root. Thus also

->*to achieve the same thing*<-
we will be able to do it in another way, and quickly. Throw salt, pepper, and sour leaven <note>fermentum acidum — a sourdough starter or fermented yeast</note> into the wine, mixed together, and it will quickly be converted into vinegar. If you wish to perform this even faster, plunge a brick or glowing-hot steel into it several times. You may also prepare for this purpose unripe medlars <note>a small fruit that resembles a crabapple, edible only after it decays or "blets"</note>, cornel cherries, mulberries, and plums. But from Sotion <note>an early agricultural writer whose works are mostly preserved in later compilations</note> we have:

->*The preparation of sharp vinegar from must.*<-
Dry grape skins <note>original: "vinacia" — the pulpy residue remaining after grapes are crushed</note> in the sun and throw them into the must <note>unfermented or partially fermented grape juice</note>, adding a few sour grapes, and you will make a sharp vinegar which you may use after the seventh day. Or, put in pellitory <note>original: "pyrethrum" — a plant with a pungent, burning root</note>, and it will turn out sharp. Furthermore, if you boil a fourth or fifth part of the vinegar over a fire and add it to the rest, and expose it to the sun for eight days, you will have a very sharp and pleasant wine. Old roots of grass, raisins, crushed leaves of the wild pear, blackberry root, whey of milk, roasted acorns, glowing coals, a decoction of chickpeas, and glowing potsherds—each of these thrown into vinegar makes it sharp. Apuleius teaches:

->*How vinegar may be doubled.*<-
Take a known measure of vinegar, such as a jar <note>original: "metretam" — an ancient liquid measure roughly equal to nine gallons</note>, and to it add a half-measure of sea water that has been boiled down, and a grape; store these together in a vessel. Some soak barley, strain it, and mix in a measure of the cream, shaking it together; then they throw over it a sufficient portion of roasted salt while it is still hot. Once this is done, they cover the vessel with a lid and leave it for eight days. We, however, are accustomed to do it this way:

->*Vinegar from pressed grape clusters.*<-
After the vintage, we throw the already-pressed clusters into a wooden vessel and add a certain quantity [of water] over them, and it turns into vinegar after a week. Moreover, we add the tendrils cut from vines and crushed to water, and it turns into vinegar. Also in this way:
