HOUSEHOLD MANAGEMENT.
P 3

->*Spoiled wine is turned into vinegar.*<-

Place the grape clusters that have been squeezed in the press into two wooden vats <note>original: "tinas" — large tubs or fermentation vessels</note> and arrange them together. Let them ferment for four days; then pour over them as much spoiled wine <note>original: "perversum vinum" — wine that has begun to turn sour or go bad</note> as is enough to cover them. Let it sit for a full natural day <note>a 24-hour period</note>, and soon after, strain it into another vat. After the same number of hours, place it into another, and continue this until it is turned into a very sharp, white vinegar. If you wish to make more using the same grape clusters, pour a little very sharp vinegar over them and wait until they become extremely sour; then, after removing that, pour spoiled wine over them and apply the same process. Finally, squeeze the clusters in the press <note>original: "prælo"</note>, and you will recover the quantity of wine that was first lost.

# How the defects of wine are corrected and restored. #
# CHAPTER XXIII. #

Our ancestors, to prevent wine from spoiling, discovered many remedies, and the modern age has labored no less at this; for wine spoils easily and takes on many different qualities. Paxamus <note>an author of agricultural works from the late Roman or early Byzantine period, often cited in the "Geoponica"</note> says that wine either turns sour or changes into flat wine <note>original: "vappam" — wine that has lost its spirit and flavor, becoming "dead"</note> around the solstices, the setting of the Pleiades, or under the heat of the dog star <note>Sirius, associated with the hottest part of summer</note>, as well as in the extreme abundance of cold, heat, rain, wind, and thunder. For all these things, we shall apply remedies. First, we will write down the forewarnings of Africanus <note>Julius Africanus, a 3rd-century writer whose agricultural notes appear in later compilations</note> regarding wines that will last or those that will spoil. Once you have stored the wine in the jar <note>original: "dolio" — a large earthenware vessel</note>, transfer it to another vessel after some time and carefully inspect the dregs <note>original: "fæce" — the lees or sediment</note>. We will take evidence of the wine’s condition by testing the smell; if it smells of rot, or if gnats <note>original: "culices"</note> are generated, these are signs that the wine is about to be corrupted. Others take wine from the middle of the jar, boil it, and taste it once it has cooled, judging the wine by its flavor. Others judge by the smell of the lids. A wine-like flavor is the best sign; a watery one is the worst; a harsh <note>original: "austerum" — dry or astringent</note> taste is a sign of safety; and a loose <note>original: "laxum" — limp or lacking structure</note> taste is a sign of one about to spoil. These signs should be observed during those times which we said were to be feared. But let us proceed to the remedies, and we shall teach

*How weak wine may be mended.*

Wine will be weak when that power of its heat begins to expire...

once the spirit <note>original: "anima" — literally "soul." In alchemy and early chemistry, the "soul" or "spirit" of a liquid refers to its volatile alcohol content.</note> has expired, the wine immediately departs; vinegar is the corpse of wine. In that case, we can intervene immediately by adding "water of life" <note>original: "aquam vitæ" — distilled spirits or high-proof alcohol</note>, for that is able to introduce a new soul. The measure will be a quarter of a pound for each barrel <note>original: "dolio" — a large storage vessel</note>. There is another remedy

### *to keep wine from boiling over.*

During the summer solstices, wine boils over and is ruined by excessive heat. In this case, you should put quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum" — mercury. The author believes the "cold" nature of mercury will counteract the heat of summer.</note> into a glass vial and, having sealed it properly, hang it in the middle of the barrel so that it suspends in the center. Its coldness prevents the wine from becoming agitated by the heat. The measure is two pounds for large barrels; for in the heat of the sky, the external warmth draws out the internal heat, and thus, when the spirit has exhaled, the wine is ruined. We

### *to prevent wine from exhaling*

shall use this remedy. Once the barrel is filled, we add oil on top and seal it. Indeed, the oil ensures the spirit does not evaporate; I see this is now commonly practiced with all liquors to prevent them from spoiling. Sometimes wines tend to become cloudy, but

### *to make wines clear*

this must be done according to Fronto <note>Marcus Cornelius Fronto, a Roman grammarian and author, though these agricultural tips are often attributed to him in later compilations like the *Geoponica*.</note>. Take the whites of three eggs put into a wide bowl and beat them until they foam; then add white salt so that they become as white as possible. Once the wine vessel is filled, pour the mixture into it. Salt and egg white together make all cloudy liquids bright. However, mix as many egg whites and as many ounces of salt as there are barrels in the vessel; the mixture must be stirred inside with a wooden rod, and it will become clear in four days. It is also done

### *to prevent wines from rotting,*

We have said that salt prevents all things from rotting. Therefore, for each barrel, grind an ounce of alum <note>original: "aluminis" — a mineral salt used historically as a preservative and to clarify liquids.</note> and cast it into the wine vessel with the wine, for it will prohibit them from rotting. The result will be the same if we add an ounce of common salt, or half of one and half of the other. Sulfur also prohibits rot; hence, if you add four ounces of sulfur to eight ounces of alum or salt, you will perform a not unwelcome service. To prevent this, it was the custom of the ancients to add salt or seawater to the wine, which preserved it for a long age...

->*How oil may be prepared from various things.*<-

### CHAPTER XXIV.

**I**t is a most excellent thing to pass down the various ways of preparing oil, so that if there should ever be a lack of olives, there will still be an opportunity to extract it from countless other fruits and seeds. We shall present some of these from the ancient authors—specifically the more outstanding ones—as well as those we have discovered ourselves. To begin, then, we say:

->*That oil is made from the castor bean, called "cicinum."*<-

According to Dioscorides <note>Pedanius Dioscorides (c. 40–90 AD), a Greek physician and botanist whose *De Materia Medica* was the precursor to all modern pharmacopeias.</note>, it is prepared in this way: Take as many ripe castor beans <note>original: "ricini" — seeds of the *Ricinus communis* plant.</note> as you wish and let them wither in the hot sun. Spread them out on hurdles and leave them in the sun until the outer husk <note>original: "cortex"</note> that covers them breaks and falls off. The pulp <note>original: "caro" — literally "flesh."</note> is gathered and thoroughly pounded in a mortar. It is then placed in a tin-lined cauldron containing water. Once a fire is lit beneath, they boil, and when they have yielded up all their moisture, the vessel is removed from the heat. The oil floating on top is skimmed off with a shell and stored away. But in Egypt, where its use is more widespread, it is usually done quite differently: for they send the cleaned castor beans to a mill, and once carefully ground, they squeeze them through a basket in a press. Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), author of the encyclopedic *Natural History*.</note> boils them in water and skims off the floating oil. However, in Egypt, where it is abundant, it is prepared without fire or water, but sprinkled with salt; it is foul for food, but useful for lamps. We, however, gather them in the month of September, for that is the proper time for harvesting when the seed detaches from the prickly husk and the skin covering it. It is very easily cleaned in a warm bronze pot. The weight of the oil produced is half that of the seeds, but it is pounded twice and pressed twice. Palladius <note>Rutilius Taurus Æmilianus Palladius (4th century AD), a Roman writer on agriculture.</note> teaches how it may be made:

Collect as many ripe berries of the lentisk <note>original: "lentisci" — the Mastic tree (*Pistacia lentiscus*), common in the Mediterranean.</note> as possible and allow them to sit in a heap for one day and night. Then, place a basket full of these berries over any small vessel, add hot water, and tread upon and press them. Then, from that li-

### *Almond oil*

The oil from sweet almonds is best for food, while that from bitter almonds is best for medicines, and in ancient times it was prepared with the greatest care. Dioscorides <note>Pedanius Dioscorides (c. 40–90 AD), a Greek physician and botanist whose "De Materia Medica" was the primary pharmacological text for 1,500 years.</note> demonstrates the method of making it. A half-modius <note>About 4.4 liters or roughly one gallon.</note> of bitter nuts, cleaned and dried, is gently pounded into a paste in a wooden mortar with a wooden pestle. A sextarius <note>Approximately 1 pint or 0.5 liters.</note> of water that has been boiled is added, and once it has absorbed the moisture for half an hour, it is pounded more vigorously than before. Soon after, it is pressed with boards, and whatever has stuck to the fingers is gathered with a shell. A hemina <note>Approximately half a pint or 0.25 liters.</note> of water is sprinkled again over the pressed nuts, and after they have soaked it up, the same process is followed. Each modius yields one hemina of oil. Commonly among us, it is extracted in the same way. These are the oils of the ancients. Now we shall proceed with our own. Next is

### *Hazelnut oil,*

Which pours forth a copious, fragrant, and excellent oil, which we may even use for culinary purposes. One pound of cleaned nuts yields eight ounces of oil, a fact which the previous age was ignorant of. Also extracted is

### *Pistachio oil*

for food and for remedies. From the

### *fruit of the stone pine, oil*

is drawn out. For they select the defective and rotten ones for lamps, and the whole ones for general use and for remedies; a great deal of it is extracted. We have seen this done in Ravenna <note>A city in Northern Italy famous for its vast pine forests, the Pineta di Classe.</note>. But

### *oil from the beech tree*

is expressed as the best and most abundant of all, used both for food and for lamps. It produces a clear light and has the flavor of sweet almonds. Almost the entire nut <note>original: "glans" — refers here to the beechmast or nut.</note> turns into oil, much like the walnut <note>original: "iuglādis" — the Persian or English walnut (*Juglans regia*).</note>. The older the nut, the more copiously it yields oil, and the dregs <note>original: "fraces" — the solid remains of the nuts after the oil has been pressed out.</note> from the pressing are exceptionally good for fattening cattle and pigs. They are collected with very little effort.

### *How the householder can obtain for himself several kinds of thread. CHAPTER XXV.*

Now we shall speak of several kinds of thread, because they seem to be of no small benefit to the **Householder** <note>original: "Oeconomo" — the manager of a domestic estate or household.</note>, since the mistress of the house uses them for constant needs. Our ancestors used flax and hemp. For they produced it in this manner:

### *Thread from flax.*

And even if there is no need for an example, since it is a most common practice, we shall speak of it for the sake of uncovering subsequent things and other inventions. **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman author whose "Natural History" was a primary source for Renaissance science.</note> says: The ripeness of flax is understood by two signs: the swelling of the seed, or a yellowing color. Then, having been plucked up and tied in hand-sized bundles, it is dried in the sun, hanging for one day with the roots turned upward; then for five more days, with the tops of the bundles turned toward each other, so that the seed falls into the middle. Then, after the wheat harvest, the stalks themselves are submerged in water warmed by the sun, held down by some weight, soaked [macerated], and then, having been turned over, let them be dried again in the sun. Once dried, they are beaten on a stone with a tow-mallet. That which was closest to the bark is called **tow** <note>original: "stupa" — the coarse, broken fibers of flax or hemp.</note>, a poorer grade of flax, better suited for the wicks of lamps; and yet even this is combed with iron hooks until all the skin is stripped off. Regarding the art of combing and sorting: It is right that from fifty pounds of bundles, fifteen pounds should be carded out. Then, once it is thread, it is polished by being struck frequently against a flint stone in water, and once woven, the fabric is beaten again with clubs—it is always better for the rough treatment.

### *Thread from hemp.*

Hemp is most useful for ropes. The hemp itself is plucked after the grape harvest, and, stripped of its bark, it is cleaned during night-work <note>original: "lucubrationibus" — tasks performed by lamplight after the sun has set.</note>. There are three kinds of it: that closest to the bark or the pith is rejected; the most praised is from the middle, which is called **mesa** <note>original: "mesa" — the middle layer of the hemp fiber.</note>. Another

...the time of maturity. Once plucked and gathered into bundles, it is left to sit for two days; on the third day it is loosened, spread out in the sun, and dried, before being returned to the bundles under a roof. Afterward, it is soaked in water—sea water is best, but fresh water may be used if sea water is lacking. Once dried in the sun, it is moistened again; if a need for it arises suddenly, a shortcut in the labor is found by soaking it in warm water in a tub and letting it stand to dry. It is then beaten so that it becomes useful, being particularly invincible in water and the sea. For use on dry land, they prefer ropes made of hemp; however, esparto grass <note>original: "spartum" — likely *Stipa tenacissima*, a Mediterranean grass used for high-quality cordage</note> is actually nourished by being submerged, as if it were compensating for the thirst of its place of birth. The upper part of Egypt turning toward Arabia makes thread from cotton <note>original: "gossipio"</note>; Asia makes thread from broom <note>original: "genista"</note>, especially for fishing nets because of its durability in water, after the shrub has been soaked for ten days. Thus, every region has its own thread made from various herbs and shrubs. We know that

->thread from nettle<-

is made among the Northern peoples, being very fine and exceptionally white. There is also made

->thread from American aloe<-

which is hard, white, and of the most perfect quality; we shall describe it exactly as we have received it. Because the edges are armed with thorns, we knock those off so they do not hinder us, and we cut the leaves into long strips lengthwise so that the pulp inside can be more easily removed. Then, two wooden sticks are fixed into the earth, crossed in the middle to form the shape of a cross; these are gripped tightly with the left hand to keep them firm, while the right hand takes the strips by one end and pulls them over the cross-joint. In this way, the pulp remains on the wood, and the wood is stripped of the pulp. They are combed in this manner until they appear white, pure, and strong, like the strings of a lyre or a cithara <note>A stringed instrument of the harp family used in classical antiquity and the Renaissance.</note>; soon they are washed, dried, and stored away. In the thirteenth year after planting, the leaves become very long—up to twenty feet. A stalk rises from the middle forty feet in length; soon the top is crowned with flowers and teems with fruit. I saw this in Rome, and I do not remember ever seeing anything more beautiful. Finally, we shall also describe

### *How to hatch eggs without a hen sitting on them.*
### CHAPTER XXVI.

NOW we shall teach how eggs can be hatched without the brooding of a hen—including those of other birds—whether in summer or winter, so that if there are sick people who desire chicks at such a time, they may not be frustrated in their longing. The eggs of birds are hatched by heat, either from the same animals or from different species; for example, we have seen hens sit upon the eggs of ducks, geese, and peacocks, and we have seen pigeons and the hedge-sparrow <note>original: "currucam"</note> hatch the eggs of all sorts. We have also seen women keep eggs warm and hatch them between their breasts, under their arms, or in their bosoms. Livia Augusta, in her early youth, when pregnant with Tiberius Caesar by Nero, and being very desirous to give birth to a male child, used this "maidenly" omen: she kept an egg warm in her bosom, and when she had to set it down, she passed it to her nurse through her own bosom so that the warmth would not be interrupted—as recorded by Pliny. But Aristotle says: the eggs of both birds and egg-laying quadrupeds <note>original: "quadrupedum ouiperarum" — in the biology of the time, this term referred to egg-laying reptiles like crocodiles and lizards</note> are matured by the brooding of their parents; for all these lay their eggs in the ground, and the eggs are matured by the warmth of the earth.

Intense heat cooks the eggs, while low heat makes them fail. For this reason, you will make the heat equal by adding or reducing the light of the lamp. Another egg should be substituted in the place of the failed one. # *On tin, and how it may pass into a more noble metal.*
## CHAPTER I.

Tin is a rival to silver <note>original: "argenti emulum"</note>; they share much in color and they bond closely. By its very nature, tin possesses such a color that it whitens other metallic bodies most effectively, but it also makes them brittle and prone to crumbling—except for lead. Anyone who knows how to mix it with some skill will obtain a secret of no small value. Therefore, we shall strive to imitate silver to the best of our ability, which will be easily accomplished if we abolish and utterly root out the weaknesses that infect it: namely, its screeching, its dullness, its leaden hue, and its softness. For it does not become red-hot before it melts, but instead, clinging to the fire, it flows into a liquid state with exceptional speed. These flaws are marks impressed upon it, not joined within its very core, but are such that we can strip it of these external qualities. And first we shall teach

### *To remove the screeching and softness from tin.*

Reduce it to a lime <term>calcem</term> <note>In early chemistry, a "calx" is the powdery substance, usually a metallic oxide, produced by heating a metal in air (calcination).</note>, as we shall teach, and then restore it to a solid body. If this does not succeed after the first or second attempt, repeat it a third time in turn until you achieve your desire. In this way, it will become so hard that it will appear glowing red in the fire before it melts. Thus we can harden all soft bodies so that they may be heated to a glow, but this is more evident in tin than in other metals. We can also remove the screeching <note>The "cry of tin" is the distinctive crackling sound made when bending a piece of tin, caused by the friction of its internal crystal structure.</note> if it is melted and quenched seven times in the urine of a boy <note>A common reagent in early laboratory work, prized for its ammonia content.</note>, and just as many times in hazelnut oil. By this, you will recognize that it loses its screech. We have already described the method of extraction. But we shall now explain how it may pass into silver, provided we have first taught in such a manner

### *To turn tin into powder.*

Let the tin boil with fire; throw the molten metal into a mortar, and when it is close to solidifying, stir it restlessly with a wooden pestle. It will congeal into a very fine powder. Sift it through a fine sieve, and whatever has not been perfectly ground down, let it be ground further by the same effort. Now we shall strive

### *To turn tin into silver.*

Throw it into a clay vessel resistant to fire...

[...of a vessel] with a wider mouth <note>original: "patentioris oris"</note>, so that it may glow white among burning coals. It is necessary to stir it incessantly with a small iron rod <note>original: "ferrea rudicula"</note> until it becomes entirely incandescent without melting. If you stop and it returns to a solid body, you must apply the same labor again, until for a quarter of a day it remains as a powder, glowing red without fusion. But if one part melts by the heat of the fire while the other remains, you must turn the part that melts back into powder and repeat the same work in the same vessel. Afterward, place it in a glassmaker's furnace or a reverberation furnace <note>A furnace that reflects or "reverberates" heat onto the material being treated.</note>, and let it be tormented by a fierce fire for three or four days until it whitens perfectly like snow; for the more perfectly it is reduced to a lime <term>calx</term> <note>A powder produced by heating a metal to high temperatures, essentially an oxide.</note>, the better your work will have been. Soon, put it in a vessel with distilled vinegar so that it rises three fingers above the substance; let it boil until the vinegar is colored and becomes thicker. When it has finished, let it settle; pour off the vinegar and add new, and place it in the ashes and repeat the work until it dissolves into the vinegar. If it does not, return it to the reverberatory fire again so that it is more perfectly reduced to a lime and dissolved in the vinegar. After the vinegar has evaporated, let the remaining powder be placed in a vessel made of ash, which they call a <term>cupel</term> <note>original: "cupellam"; a shallow, porous dish used in assaying to separate precious metals from base metals.</note>. Once lead has been melted within it, the powder will rise and then sink; throw in pills made of soap and lime, or saltpeter, sulfur, or another fatty substance, and everything that is received by the lead bath will be changed into the finest silver. But it is hard labor. Thus also:

### To turn tin into lead

Anyone will be able to do this if they reduce it to a lime more often, and especially if you apply a suitable fire during the reduction; for, losing its screeching sound <note>Tin is famous for its "cry"—a crackling sound it makes when bent—which alchemists sought to remove to make it more like silver or lead.</note>, it is easily turned into lead.

### To turn lead into tin,

Which happens through a simple washing; for while it is washed repeatedly so that the earthy part is abolished, it is transmuted into tin...

### *To transmute antimony into lead.*

Antimony—which the chemists call a <term>regulus</term> <note>The pure, metallic part of a mineral that settles at the bottom during smelting.</note>—if you cook and burn it frequently, you will turn it into lead. We have seen this noted by Dioscorides <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and botanist whose works were foundational to pharmacology.</note>, who says: "If antimony is burned a little more, it is turned into lead." But

### *To make lead heavier*

is taught by Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician and philosopher whose theories dominated Western medical science for over a millennium.</note>. For proving that lead partakes of an airy substance, he brings forward this experiment: Of all things we know, lead alone increases both in its mass and in its weight if it is stored in underground rooms having thick or murky air, so that whatever is placed there quickly gathers mold <note>original: "situm"</note>. Furthermore, the leaden bonds of statues, by which their feet are fastened, have often been seen to grow, and some have swollen so much that warts like crystal hung from the stones. This metal contains much quicksilver, which is proven by the fact that it seems, by an easy mastery,

### *to extract quicksilver from lead.*

Let lead be filed into the finest dust, and to two pounds of this powder, add an ounce of salt of tartar <note>original: "salis tartari"; potassium carbonate, often used as a flux in alchemy.</note>, the same amount of common salt, and a little antimony. Let everything be ground together, and once beaten and passed through a sieve <note>original: "incerniculo succreta"</note>, place them in a *twisted* glass vessel <note>original: "vas vitreum obtortum"</note>, as they call it—a retort—but well protected on the outside with a clay mixed with straw <note>original: "paleato luto"</note>. Let the vessel be fitted to a reverberation fire <note>A furnace where the heat is reflected or "reverberated" onto the material being treated.</note>, under which a large receiver is placed half-filled with cold water; with the openings closed, let the fire grow hot gradually for two hours, then increase it, until the vessel glows. Then for four hours let the bellows do their work, and you will see the mercury <note>original: "hydrargyron"</note> fall into the receiver, driven out by the force of the fire; and sticking in bubbles to the sides of the neck, you will gradually shake it down with your hands so that it falls below. From each pound we have shaken out nearly an ounce, or more when we worked more diligently. This was no small source of wonder to us.

*To convert lead into quicksilver* <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note>
is something often seen. But this fraud is the reason why everything brought to us is adulterated, as it mixes with it so easily. Let a pound of lead be melted in a new earthen vessel, to which you should add an equal amount of what they call tin marcasite <note>original: "stanneæ marchesitæ"; likely bismuth or a similar sulfide mineral used in alchemy.</note>; when these are melted, mix them with a wooden rod. Upon this, pour double the amount of quicksilver, which should be heated in another vessel so that it is not spat out <note>original: "disjiciantur"; refers to the dangerous splashing that occurs when cold liquid hits molten metal.</note> by the contact of the cold. Mix it for a short time and immediately throw it into cold water, and it will not solidify; for the whole mass will flow like liquid. This has the disgrace, however, of being lead-colored and not flowing like the true substance, but rather moving slowly and "leaving a tail" <note>original: "caudatum"; a term used by alchemists to describe impure mercury that clings to surfaces instead of forming perfect spheres.</note>. Store it in a glass vessel and put it away; for the longer it remains, the more fluidly it will run.

## On copper, and its transmutations.
### CHAPTER III.

We shall now bring forward some experiments regarding copper <note>original: "æs"; this term can refer to copper, bronze, or brass depending on the context.</note>, which, however small they may be, shall not be omitted by us, so that the eager reader may approach their study and be drawn in. Here we teach those things which color, stain, and adulterate metallic bodies—not permanently, but fading away little by little. These do not withstand the tests of the assayers, yet they are neither to be entirely lusted after nor altogether disregarded. And because there are so few books that do not overflow with such matters, and many things are circulated, we shall write down only those which are easy to prepare and beautiful to see, so that by their luster and the allure of their form, they may occasionally deceive the eyes of the highest judges <note>original: "optimatis censuræ"; referring to those who inspect and value metals.</note>, making it difficult to discern the true from the false. Let them, however, be valued at what they are truly worth. But these require the hands of a most skilled craftsman; those who lack such skill should at least consult the best masters, lest they be frustrated. Copper is whitened chiefly by arsenic, quicksilver, <term>sublimate</term> <note>original: "sublimatum"; likely mercuric chloride.</note>, and the "foam of silver," which the Greeks call <term>litharge</term> <note>original: "lithargyron"; a mineral form of lead monoxide produced during the refining of silver.</note>: also pyrites, tartar, <term>sal ammoniac</term> <note>ammonium chloride</note>, common salt (which the Arabs call <term>alkali</term> <note>original: "alchali"</note>), saltpeter, and alum. If the copper is heated in fire and quenched in a liquid solution of some or all of these, or if it is beaten into thin plates and placed in a melting vessel layered with these substances reduced to powder, and kept in the fire for a long time...

### *Make copper that rivals silver.*

This is worthy of notice in these matters: for if it stays in the fire longer than necessary, the color expires, and its strength having been exhaled, it grows faint and returns to its original state. Therefore, let it be kept in the fire for as short a time as you can; in this way it will produce white copper and a deceptive silver, but it blackens over time: for arsenic always discolors and darkens the appearance. ### Another Method

We shall also attempt to work with orpiment <note>original: "auripigmentum"; arsenic trisulfide, a yellow mineral used as a pigment and in alchemy for its sulfur content</note>, which is not ineffective in operation, though we must take care to wipe away any dark stains that may appear over time. Take the finest orpiment—the kind that flakes apart and shines with a golden color—and let it descend <note>original: "descendere facias"; a term for a type of distillation or melting process where the material flows downward</note> three or four times with copper shavings, sprinkled with tartar. Use an equal weight of each so that it may shine perpetually and remain most brilliant. Let silver be dissolved in strong water <note>original: "forti aqua"; nitric acid, the primary solvent for silver</note> that is not diluted with excess moisture, and let it be dried in a bubbling vessel. Repeat this seven times, or fewer if the task is complete; mix it all together and grind it upon a porphyry stone. While grinding, sprinkle it drop by drop, or like a light rain, with oil of tartar <note>original: "tartari oleum"; a concentrated solution of potassium carbonate</note> or fixed sal ammoniac. When the hot Sun shines, expose the mixture to it to dry; then add more oil and let it dry again, continuing until it reaches the weight of the silver. Store this in a glass vessel and bury it in dung <note>original: "fimo"; horse manure was used by alchemists as a source of gentle, steady heat for digestion</note> until it dissolves. Once dissolved, let it be coagulated, and cast ten or eight parts of copper upon it; it whitens the metal remarkably well. If, however, you seek

### To make copper look like silver by rubbing it with your hands.

As boys and street performers <note>original: "circulatores"; traveling peddlers or mountebanks who performed "miracles" or sold medicines in public squares</note> often do to make vessels instantly take on the luster of silver, this is the method of preparation. Mix equal weights of sal ammoniac, alum, and saltpeter with a small amount of silver filings produced with a fine file. Set them over a fire so they boil together; when they cease to smoke, you may handle the mixture. By sprinkling the powder—moistened either with saliva from the mouth or by adding a little water—and rubbing it with your fingers, you will see it imitate the color of silver. There is another, even brighter way of whitening: dissolve a little silver in strong water and submerge enough tartar and sal ammoniac into it until it mimics the thickness of a paste. Form this into little disks and let them dry. If you rub copper or a similar metal with these, using frequent handling of the fingers and the moisture of saliva, it will appear like silver to the one rubbing it. The same effect occurs no less with quicksilver <note>original: "argento vivo"; mercury</note>, which whitens marvelously. These "silvered" items must be guarded lest they suffer damage from acidic things—such as urine, vinegar, lemon juice, and the like—for they easily lose their color, and the deception is caught and proven.

### *Concerning iron.* CHAPTER IV.

The order of our work now prompts us to speak of iron: for the wise Indians valued it highly, as it retains much good within itself and is easily transmuted into a nobler metal. Yet by some, it is rejected as useless because it melts in the fire with great difficulty owing to its fixed sulfur <note>original: "sulphur fixum"; in alchemical theory, sulfur represented the principle of combustibility and "fixity" referred to its resistance to heat</note> and its great quantity of earthy parts. Whence, if we wish

->*To change iron into copper,*<-

So that it retains no trace of iron at all, this can easily be done with shoemaker’s ink <note>original: "sutorio atramento"; a term for vitriol or metal sulfates, specifically copper sulfate in this context of transmutation</note>. Indeed, in the Carpathian mountains of Pannonia <note>modern-day Hungary and surrounding regions</note>, at the town of Smolník <note>original: "Smolinitio"; a famous mining town in Slovakia known for its "cementation" waters that appeared to turn iron into copper</note>, it is said there is a pit into which water is drawn and poured into three channels; iron placed in these is turned into copper. If the pieces are thin, they turn into a sort of mud which, when smelted in the fire, turns into the purest copper. But it is also changed by this active method: cast iron into a melting vessel, and when it has become white-hot from a fierce fire and begins to flow, saturate it gradually by sprinkling with live sulfur <note>original: "viui sulphuris"; naturally occurring, high-purity sulfur</note>. Remove it, cast it into rods, and let it be ground, for it will crumble easily. Then let it be dissolved in strong water <note>original: "forti aqua"; nitric acid</note> made from vitriol and alum; let it boil in hot ashes, and once dissolved, let it evaporate into vapors. The remaining powder may then be reduced back into a metal body, and you shall have your result. If you wish

->*To whiten iron,*<-

You may do so by many skillful means, yet you may be satisfied with this one. First, we shall cleanse it of slag and the poison of rust, for it is more earthy than other metals; therefore, as often as it is smelted, it produces drossy filth from itself. You shall often quench very thin plates in a strong lye <note>an alkaline solution made from ashes</note> and vinegar where common salt and alum have been boiled, until they glow white. Grind its filings with salt in a mortar, changing the salt from time to time until it shows no sign of blackness and the dross of the iron is washed away; by this means you will whiten the plates. Prepare an amalgam <note>original: "malagma"</note> from quicksilver <note>mercury</note> and lead, grind it, and place its powder in a ceramic vessel interleaved with the plates. Let it be closed and sealed with luting <note>original: "luto muniatur"; a paste used to hermetically seal alchemical vessels</note> so that no vent is left; let it remain in the fire for a day, and finally let it be melted with a fierce heat; for the amalgam [gives] it whiteness and an easy...

The same is done with gold using royal water <term>original: "aqua regia"; a mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids capable of dissolving gold</term>.

### To extract gold from silver,

Nor in such small amounts that you will not, after covering your expenses, gain a great profit. This is the rule for its preparation. Put fine filings of iron <note>original: "elimata ferri scobs"</note> into a melting vessel, and let it glow with a fierce fire until it melts; then gradually sprinkle in artificial gold-solder <term>original: "chrysocollam"; a flux used by goldsmiths to join metals, often involving borax or copper salts</term>, which goldsmiths use for soldering gold, and red arsenic <note>original: "rubeum arsenicum"; likely realgar, a natural arsenic sulfide</term>. You shall collect it; we have found no method more truthful among many, nor more profitable, though it is laborious. Do not spare your labor, and manage it rightly, lest you waste your time and oil <note>original: "ne tempus, & oleum teras"; a classical idiom meaning to waste effort for no reward</note>. Or otherwise: Let fine iron filings be moistened for a day in sea water; let them dry, and let them glow in a melting vessel with fire until they melt. Then, an equal weight of silver having been cast in, let it be poured through half as much copper into a hollow place. Then let it be refined exquisitely in a cupel <note>original: "cineritio vase"</note>; for once the iron and its dross are excluded, sink it into the water of separation, and you shall collect what falls to the bottom, and it will be the finest gold. ### On the separation of metals without strong water.
### CHAPTER IX.

BECAUSE it is quite difficult to extract acids from salts <note>original: "ex salibus aquæ"; referring to the distillation of mineral acids like nitric acid from nitrate salts</note>—and not without the loss of labor, time, and expense—it seemed right to teach the separations of gold from silver and copper, and of silver from copper, without "strong water" <term>strong water (aqua fortis): nitric acid, the standard chemical used by assayers to dissolve silver while leaving gold untouched</term>, but rather by certain very easy operations with little expenditure of time and money. First, we shall demonstrate

->*the separation of gold from silver.*<-

Let a mass of gold mixed with silver be cast into an earthenware vessel resistant to fire, together with an equal weight of antimony, in the following manner: When the vessel, glowing in the fire, has melted the injected mass, and it begins to swirl in a circle by the force of the fire, add a little more antimony. After a brief delay, it too will be carried around in the circulation. When you see this, throw in the rest of the antimony and cover the vessel with a lid. Allow the mixture to cook for as long as it takes to mutter the Lord's Prayer <note>original: "dominicam orationem"; before the prevalence of pocket watches, reciting standard prayers was a common way for craftsmen and alchemists to time chemical reactions</note>. ## A brief separation of gold or silver from other metals with nitric acid. CHAPTER 10.

We shall indeed teach in this way a sufficiently concise method to separate gold from silver, and silver from other metals. No small profit will be gained by anyone who understands what we write perfectly, as we have seen some acquire no meager wealth through this craftsmanship. Let the example be a mixture of copper and silver; we shall dissolve it in common nitric acid <term>fortem aquam: literally "strong water," the historical name for nitric acid</term>. Once it has been dissolved, pour in spring water so that the harshness of the liquid is diluted, and the power of corrosion <note>original: "vis rosionis"</note> no longer remains upon the metal. Pour the liquid into a wide-mouthed earthen jar and submerge thin plates of copper; for the silver will adhere to them in the form of clouds, while the copper is left behind in the water. Place the liquid into a glass retort flask <term>ampullam: a bulbous glass vessel used in distillation</term>, apply a gentle fire beneath it, and the spring water will gradually drip out. When you recognize that the known measure of spring water has finished distilling—or when a saffron color tints the flask and the scent of salts hits the nostrils—remove the receiver and put another empty one in its place. Seal the vents with clay <note>original: "lutato spiramenta"; "luting" was the practice of sealing laboratory apparatus joints with a paste of clay or lime</note>, increase the fire, and you will receive the nitric acid as strong as before, and you will have copper at the bottom of the flask. The nitric acid will be as strong as before; you will be able to use it many times.

### PREFACE.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'E' set within a square frame decorated with floral and vine patterns.</image-desc>

From metals, we shall pass to the counterfeiting of gems, for they follow the same principles; both arts are related, and both use the craftsmanship of fire. Concerning these matters, the ancient age is praised not a little. "Nor is there any fraud in life," says Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman author whose *Natural History* was the primary encyclopedia for Renaissance scientists</note>, "more profitable," and thus the desire for money has lit the torch of luxury so brightly that very often even the most skilled judges of these things have not been safe from deception. Gems are counterfeited by many techniques: either by cutting gems through the middle, inserting colors, and gluing them back together <note>This refers to "doublets," a common historical method of creating fake jewels</note>; or by dyeing a whole crystal; or by fashioning "crystal" <note>Here referring to high-quality glass</note> from various materials. We shall also attempt to make true gems deviate from their own natural color—all with such a fitting excellence of colors that they appear to be natural gems. Finally, we shall teach how to fashion what they call enamels <note>original: "smaltos"; smalt or enamel is a colored glass used for decoration</note>.

### On certain salts that enter into the compositions of gems. CHAPTER I.

**NOW** let us set forth some operations that are highly necessary for the making of gems, so that we are not forced to repeat them too often; and first,

#### *How the salt called soda is made.*

The common people call the *Kali* plant <note>original: "Kali herbam"; likely *Salsola kali* or glasswort, a plant that grows in salty soil and was historically burned to produce soda ash</note>, once it has been turned into ash, "soda." Grind this soda in a mill, then grind it again, and sift it through a fine sieve into a thin powder. Place it into copper kettles so that it may be boiled, diluted in water. The measure shall be this: for every pound of soda, pour in one jar <note>original: "amphorae"; an ancient Roman unit of volume, used here as a general measure for a large vessel</note> of water. Let it boil for four hours, until the water is reduced to a third of its volume. Soon after, remove it from the fire and let it sit for a period of twelve hours so that the dregs may settle. Once all the sediment has been removed, the water will become very clear. Then, let it be separated drop by drop into a large vessel placed below using woolen wicks <note>This describes a "capillary siphon," an early method of filtration where liquid travels up through fabric strips and drips into a lower container, leaving impurities behind</note>. Pour fresh water into the kettles and boil it again; once it has cooled, as we have said, and every impurity has been wiped away, we drip the clear liquid out again. They do the same a third time, taking care to test it with the tongue to see if the salt no longer has any taste. Finally, they place a ceramic pot full of the strained water over a fire, piling up and supplying coals until, the moisture being almost entirely consumed, the water becomes thicker and more substantial, and hardens into salt. This is soon removed with an iron spoon. From five pounds of soda, one pound of salt is squeezed out. In almost the same way, one learns

#### *How salt of tartar is made.*

The dregs from old wine must be chosen and carefully dried; this is commonly called tartar <note>original: "tartarum"; the potassium bitartrate crystals that precipitate out of wine during fermentation and aging</note>. Place it in a furnace constructed with such skill that the flames break out in the upper chambers and, by reflecting back, create the greatest heat. Allow it to be burned there, and you will see it turn white. Turn it over with iron tongs so that the top part, which has already become glowing white, is flipped and the back is exposed to the fire. When the smoke has ceased, break the part removed with the tongs to see if it has taken on a snow-white color in every part; for that is the proof—

->*How flint or crystal are prepared, and how the pellets*<-

The material from which gems are fashioned is either crystal, or flint (of the kind from which fire is struck), or round river pebbles. The chief place is held by those found at the River Thames and elsewhere, which are clear and the size of an egg; for from these, gems are prepared, and they all serve the same function. There are some who think crystal should claim the first prize, but they are mistaken simply because it shines with a bright clarity. The method for preparing the stone is as follows: The river pebbles are placed into furnaces in the spot where the flames seethe in the curves of the upper chamber. When you see them glowing white-hot, pull them out and throw them into cold water. Dry the collected stones and grind them in mortars or a hand-mill <note>original: "trusatili mola"</note> until they are reduced to the finest dust. Put this into a basin with a wide mouth containing rainwater and stir it here and there with your hands; in this way, the finest part will seek the surface and the earthy part will sink. Pour off the liquid that floats, then soon pour new water over the dregs and stir the powder again. Do this repeatedly until the coarse powder, weighed down by its own weight, no longer sinks to the bottom <note>This describes "elutriation," a process used to separate particles by size and weight using water</note>. Allow the waters already removed to settle, and a muddy layer will lie at the bottom. Collect and store these powders, which are so fine they escape the touch. ### How the pellets are cooked.

Artisans call the lumps made from salts, the aforementioned powder, and water "pastilli" <term>pastilli: small, round cakes or pellets, used here as a way to pre-mix and stabilize the ingredients before the final melting</term>. Take five parts of salt of tartar <term>salt of tartar: potassium carbonate, a fluxing agent made from burnt wine lees</term>, and an equal amount of soda salt <term>soda salt: sodium carbonate, a flux derived from the ashes of maritime plants</term>. Take twice as much (ten parts) of the stone powder already mentioned, and mix them thoroughly in a jar. Sprinkle with a spray of water and moisten them so that, when squeezed by the hand, they solidify like dough. Form them into lumps the size of a fist. Set them in the sun to dry as much as possible, then place them in a reverberatory furnace <note>a furnace designed to reflect or "reverberate" heat from the roof back down onto the material</note> for six hours, gradually increasing the fire until the lumps glow red, but do not melt; for this reason, keep away the bellows <note>original: "folium flatus"; literally "the leaf of the breath," referring to forced air that would raise the temperature too high</note>. Once cooked, let them cool; they will become so hard that they can almost withstand a blow from an iron hammer.

## On the furnace, and vessels necessary for the work. CHAPTER III.

Now a furnace must be built, which will be very similar to a glassmaker’s furnace but smaller, according to the scale of the work to be done. Let the furnace be eight feet high and consist of two chambers, the vault <term>testudo: literally "tortoise shell," referring to the arched ceiling of the furnace chamber</term> of the lower one being a span and a half thick. The chamber itself should have a small door below ground level so that wood can be placed in the fire on its floor. In the very top and center of that vault, let there be a hole one foot wide, through which the flames can penetrate into the second chamber and reach the top vault, from which the returning flames stir up a great heat. In this upper chamber, the wall itself is pierced through, with holes cut a palm’s width wide, so that through these openings the small pots or basins can be moved in and out and placed on the floor of the chamber. These small pots or basins are called *padellas* <note>original: "padellas"; a term likely borrowed from the Italian or Spanish word for a pan or shallow pot</note> by the craftsmen, and they are made from clay, which Valen— <note>The text likely refers to Valencian clay, famous in the period for its heat resistance</note>

For when these gems are fashioned, by the sudden encounter with water, the salt is spat out and breaks forth, as it were, and is spread over like a little cloud. Yet this work must be executed with the greatest diligence, lest while the glass is being drawn out, it touches the walls of the furnace; for it clings like birdlime <note>a sticky substance used to trap birds; here describing the extreme viscosity of molten glass</note>, making it difficult to pull away without taking part of the walls with it. One must also take care that it does not fall back into the basins, for it is then separated only with difficulty, and the transparency of the glass is dishonored. Once the glass has cooled, they place it back into the pots so that it may glow white-hot for two days, until it is thoroughly cooked into perfect glass.

When the glass mixture has been heated for two days, some—in order to render the glass purer and more transparent, and to prevent it from swelling with certain little bladders or vesicles (for glass is prone to this kind of defect)—add an equal amount of white lead <term>cerussæ: lead carbonate, used here as a clarifying agent to remove bubbles</term> to the basins; for it reddens immediately, then soon melts with the glass and renders it clear. Then a test must be taken with the hooked iron, for if it lacks those vesicles, it will be perfect, and thus the mass for the gems will be complete. Now we shall teach the colors with which we may dye the gems: saffron-yellow, green, or blue.

### How colors are fashioned. CHAPTER IV.

While the crystal is being cooked in the furnace, the colors are prepared by that same fire, and first, we shall instruct how to make the saffron of iron <term>crocus ferri: a reddish-brown powder, typically iron oxide, used as a pigment</term>. They take three or four pounds of filed iron shavings, which are washed thoroughly by immersing them in water in a wide vessel; they assume that the iron, by the weight of its own nature, will sink to the bottom, while wood, lint, and that sort of filth will rise to the surface. Thus, they obtain pure shavings, removed and washed with water. Then, when it is perfectly dried, it is placed into a glazed earthenware vessel with a wide mouth, into which three or four jars <term>amphorae: here referring to large liquid measures or containers</term> of the best, sharpest vinegar are poured. It is left to macerate for three or four weeks, stirring and shaking it seven times or more each day with an iron rod. When the time has passed and it has settled, the vinegar must be strained into another vessel. Then they pour new vinegar onto the iron shavings for as long as it takes until the vinegar has consumed all the iron. The collected vinegar is poured into an earthenware pot and moved to the fire, where it should boil until the vinegar evaporates into a vapor <note>original: "in halitum expiret"</note>, and a silty, muddy part remains at the bottom. By continuing the fire, a certain "fatness" of the iron will catch flame within; let it finish burning, and the remaining powder that stays behind will be the saffron. Others scrape the rust from iron nails and extinguish them, glowing hot from the fire, in very strong vinegar; they strain it through a vinegar-sieve, expose the dried rust to the fire again until it glows, and sprinkle it again with vinegar. They repeat the same business three or four times; finally, they make the vinegar evaporate from the pot, and the settled saffron is collected from the bottom. Now it remains to teach

### *How copper is burned.*

The desired sheets of copper <note>The OCR reads "luna" (moon/silver), but in the context of coloring glass and "aes," it almost certainly refers to "lamina" (thin plates) of copper</note> are exposed with an equal amount of salt in an earthenware jar within the prepared furnace. Every two or three hours you shall turn them with an iron hook so that they are burned by the fire on all sides; let them glow there for a natural day <term>dies naturalis: a full 24-hour period</term>, then take them out and divide them into two parts. Put one part aside and put the other back in the fire with salt for an artificial day <term>dies artificialis: the period from sunrise to sunset</term>. Perform this work a third or fourth time so that it is more perfectly turned into lime <term>calcem: a powdered metallic oxide</term>, taking care that it glows with the fire but does not melt, and becomes black from the burning.

## *How gems are colored.* CHAPTER V.

Now that everything is prepared, I think nothing remains for us to put the finishing touch on the gems, except to begin the coloring of each specific gemstone. And we shall begin,

### *How the sapphire is tinted.*

For craftsmen begin with this one: for once it has been tinted, unless it is removed from the fire quickly, the color is diluted; yet the longer it remains in the fire, the clearer the color with which it is infused. In a crucible <term>catinum: a melting pot or crucible</term> full of glass, a small amount of what is called Zaphara <term>Zaphra: cobalt oxide or "zaffre," the primary mineral used to produce deep blue glass</term> is added; specifically, two drams are sufficient for a pound of glass. Then it must be stirred restlessly with an iron hook from top to bottom. When it seems best mixed, an experiment must be conducted by taking a tiny bit out of the small pots; if the tint responds to your wish, it is done. If it is too pale, add more Zaphra; if it is too concentrated, add glass from another pot, and allow it to boil for six hours. In this way you will be able

## *How gems may be fashioned in another way.*
### CHAPTER VI.

The method which we have previously described is one peculiar to and commonly used among our craftsmen; however, it is also kept hidden by them. But I subjoin another method, which I had determined would always remain a secret with me; for with small expense, in a short time, and with much lighter labor, gems are prepared that are far more brilliant, more richly colored, and more cheerful. Finally, this method ensures that the passage of a longer span of time will not dishonor the surface or the brightness with salt <note>original: "sal," likely referring to "efflorescence" or the "sickness" of glass where salts leach out and dull the surface</note>. Although those gems found in the ruined masonry and on the shores of Puteoli <note>Modern Pozzuoli, near Naples; a site famous for ancient Roman ruins where glass fragments were often found</note>, fashioned in ancient times, still shine within and possess an unoffending transparency—so much so that it seems impossible for our people to perfect anything similar—we shall nevertheless strive in this way to fashion not only similar gems, but far better ones. Listen closely then, and keep this in a faithful heart. The mass <note>original: "moles," the base glass or "frit" before coloring</note> is fashioned así: 

Let a "Cockscomb" <term>Crista galli: likely a local name for a high-quality, translucent quartz or flint stone found in a specific shape</term> be taken, and having cut away the "helmet," keep the "head" and "neck." Once prepared, as we have indicated, place it in a vessel for a hard fire and put on a lid, so that no coals, or rising ash with smoke, or soot may fall into the vessel and contaminate the brightness. Kindle the fire, and you will hear it crackling; once it is buried in coal and ignited, grasp it with tongs and quench it in clear water. Dry it, and repeat the work three times, changing the water so that no filth appears. Then, let it be ground on porphyry marble <note>A very hard purple stone used for grinding materials without contaminating them with stone dust</note> so very finely that it might be blown away by a breath, and then store it. You may then consider it the "Philosopher’s Stone" <note>Porta uses this term metaphorically to mean the perfect "foundation stone" or base material for his work, rather than the legendary substance that turns lead to gold</note>, most burning in the fire and surpassing in its triple nature. He who is ignorant of this stone shall learn of it from these verses, which we found in a very ancient manuscript codex:

> *Narrow is the way of man, which consists of the elements,*

> *This shall be our enduring bronze, the stone of the Philosophers.*

### On various dyes for crystal. Chapter VII.

WE HAVE SPOKEN of the dyes for glass—not the common or unreliable ones, but those known to few, sought out at great expense of labor, and well-tested. Now we shall recount some ways of dyeing crystal, and especially noble ones, which are still known to few, if not to me alone—namely:

#### To dye crystal the color of jacinth or ruby,

Without breaking or grinding it. Take for yourself six parts of antimony <term>stibij: antimony sulfide, used in early chemistry to produce yellow or orange hues</term>, four of orpiment <term>auripigmenti: arsenic trisulfide, a bright yellow mineral used as a pigment</term>, three of crystalline arsenic, an equal amount of sulfur, and two parts of tutty <term>tutiæ: zinc oxide, a powder collected from the flues of smelting furnaces</term>. We grind each separately and sift them through a fine sieve; we place them in a pot. The small pieces of crystal, either suspended by bronze wires or submerged in the powders, we place on the fire so that they may glow white-hot for four or five hours, but without the blast of bellows, lest they fly apart into pieces or melt. The proof of proper coloring will be if the piece, when removed, is of a most blazing and glittering color; if not, let it be consigned to the fire again and, after some delay, removed in the same manner. Careful attention must be paid, however, so that they are not cooled suddenly while being removed from the fire, for then they crumble and fly apart into many pieces. If a jacinth color is desired, remove it quickly from the fire. If a deep, glowing purple is desired, allow it to remain longer in the fire. We may make a jacinth using orpiment alone. # NATURAL MAGIC, BOOK VI.

*How a blue sapphire may be changed into a diamond.*

This gem, like all others exposed to fire, loses its color; for the force of the fire causes the pigment to vanish. Many people achieve this in various ways. Some melt gold in the fire and place the sapphire in the center of the molten metal; others place it upon an iron plate and set it in the middle of a reverberatory furnace <note>A furnace designed to reflect or "reverberate" heat onto the object rather than heating it by direct contact with the flame</note>; others burn it buried in iron filings <note>original: "scobe"</note>. We are accustomed to doing this more safely: we fill a pottery vessel with quicklime <note>original: "viua calce," calcium oxide, a caustic alkaline substance</note>, in the middle of which we place the sapphire, and bury it in charcoal. Once these are lit, the bellows-operator and the bellows themselves should cease their work; for if you disturb the stone with a blast of air, it will shatter into many pieces. When we think it has changed, one must observe carefully that the fire is allowed to extinguish itself. Once removed from the fire, consider whether it has taken on a white color. If this has happened, they set the imitation <note>original: "adulterium"</note> aside to cool with the fire; if it has not yet progressed, they bury it again, checking more frequently until all color is consumed and vanishes by the power of the fire, which usually happens in five or six hours. If you see that the color has not faded, begin the work again until it turns completely white. 

The greatest care must be taken so that the fire heats up gradually and cools down gradually; for by a sudden encounter with cold, it very often happens that the stone either cracks or shatters into pieces. All other gems, like the sapphire, lose their color—some faster, some slower, according to their hardness. The amethyst is easy, and a light fire should be used for it; in a more vehement fire, it may crack or be turned into lime <note>original: "calcem," referring to a powdery residue or ash</note>. We use this artifice when we turn precious stones into diamonds <note>In this period, "diamond" often referred to any exceptionally hard, clear, colorless stone used in jewelry</note>; when these are cut through the middle and colored in the center, another type of counterfeit gem arises. ### On the foils that are placed under gems. CAP. X.

Metallic foils are fitted under gems; since the gems are transparent, these foils cause them to shine through more purely or brightly, as the heart desires. For if one wishes them to shine more brightly, they place foils of a clearer luster underneath; if more richly <note>original: "meratius"; meaning a more saturated or concentrated color</note>, then they use darker ones. Furthermore, gems shine through with an unbounded transparency and reflect the bottom of the ring, which diminishes the value of their quality. This is an invention of the moderns: to make certain foils of the most colorful, splendid, and pleasant hue, so that they may limit that transparency and accommodate, replenish, or improve the color. Since we have been greatly delighted in making these, we shall describe the process bit by bit.

Foils are made either from copper alone, or from a mixture of copper, gold, and silver; we shall speak of those fashioned from simple copper. They purchase small sheets <term>bracteolas <gloss>very thin plates or leaves of metal</gloss></term> from the copper-smiths' workshops, with the thickness of sturdy paper, so that their thinning may be easier. We shall cut these into pieces three fingers long and two fingers wide, so that two pounds of the plates are divided into one hundred and thirty parts. We shall divide these in two so their hammering is easier; therefore, we will take forty of them and strike them with a hammer, as craftsmen do who beat gold into the thinnest leaves. Let there be a flat, polished anvil and a hammer, lest the copper be marked or broken by heavy blows...

### NATURAL MAGIC, BOOK VI.

Alternating the work, so that while they are being tempered <note>The process of heating and cooling metal to make it workable</note> by the fire and are hot, they are struck; once cooled, let them be put back into the fire. If you do otherwise, they will shatter into pieces, which you must immediately remove from the company of the rest, for the broken pieces will break the others. 

But so they may be tempered more easily, once they have begun to thin, we use this invention. Prepare two iron plates, a palm's length and width, and of the thickness of paper. Let the first be folded so that it receives the other within its folds, so that they hold the copper plates in their "belly" <note>The hollow space created by the folded iron</note> and close them on all sides. This is done not only to prevent them from slipping out, but to stop ash or any dirt from sticking to them. 

When you have enclosed the copper plates thus, expose them to the fire, and with burning coals, make them red-hot. Soon remove the fire and take them up with iron tongs. Shaking off the ash from every side, let them cool, and then strike the same with a hammer so that they are thinned and reduced into fine plates. 

But while you are performing this work, let other plates enclosed in iron be heating, repeating the same process eight times until you have thinned them into the thinnest foils <note>original: "bracteas"</note> and rendered them suitable for the work. It will be worth the effort to inspect the plates often, lest any be broken by the strikes; for when grouped together, the broken ones damage the others. 

However, because they tend to turn black and become fouled while they are being thinned by the hammer—often deceiving the inspector—it is necessary that you have a small pot ready, full of water, with tartar <note>original: "tartaro"; potassium bitartrate, used here as an acidic cleaning agent</note> added along with an equal amount of salt. Let this boil over the fire; put the small leaves in and stir them continually until they turn white through the boiling. Soon they should be removed from the fire and washed in a vessel full of clear water until they are perfectly cleansed, after which they should be wiped with a white linen cloth. Then let them be struck again under the hammer and heated as before, until they are thinned into very fine foils, like gold. 

The anvil <note>original: "incus"</note> and the hammer, while you perform this work, must be flat, clean, and shine like a mirror. They are prepared by such an artifice: first, let them be applied to the wheels on which knives are polished, until they are leveled and smoothed. Next, let them be polished with fine sand and pumice, until they are polished with a wheel-shine. Then, let them be rubbed with a leaden plate and emery powder <term>smiri <gloss>emery, a dark granular rock used as an abrasive for grinding and polishing</gloss></term>. If you use any artifice other than this, you will waste your time and labor. 

Thus, in two days the work will be finished—namely, by exposing the foils to the fire eight or ten times for tempering—and four times [with] salt—

### How the foils are polished. CHAPTER XI.

Afterward, let the water settle; strain it through a sieve, changing the water and straining it repeatedly until nothing coarse settles. Finally, having stretched a cloth loosely over the mouth of a receiving vessel, let us strain it so that we are certain nothing but the finest material has passed through. Afterward, we squeeze out the water and store the clay. We can also announce pressing matters to a friend far away, even one shut up in prison, which I am confident can be done with two nautical compasses <term>pyxidibus; literally "boxes," referring here to the housing of a mariner's compass</term> inscribed with the alphabet. ->On the name, kind, and birthplace of this stone.<-

## CHAPTER I.

Plato writes in the *Ion* that this stone was called a magnet <gloss>μαγνήτην</gloss> <note>original Greek: *magnētēn*</note> by Empedocles, but Lucretius claims it is named after the region of Magnesia:

> Which the Greeks call "Magnet" from the name of its fatherland,
> Since it had its origin within the ancestral borders of the Magnetes.
> <note>original Latin: "Quem Magneta vocant patrio de nomine Graij, / Magnetum quoniam patrijs in finibus ortus." From Lucretius, *De Rerum Natura*, Book VI.</note>

The same Plato says it is called "Heraclion" by some. Theophrastus, in his book on stones, calls it *hērakleion* <gloss>ἡράκλειον</gloss>, that is, "Herculean," because its discovery was near the city of Heraclea. Others suspect it is named after Hercules: for just as he conquered and tamed all wild beasts and men, so this stone conquers and tames iron, which itself conquers and tames all things. Nicander—and Pliny following him—asserts that the name was given to the stone from its discoverer, the herdsman Magnes; it is said he found it when the nails of his sandals and the iron tip of his staff stuck to the ground while he was pasturing his herds. He was a shepherd on Mount Ida. But I think that the magnet...

...is called, as if it were "great" <note>original: *magnus*</note>, by changing or inserting a single letter. He calls it *Siderite* <term>Sideritim; from the Greek word for iron</term> by another name after iron, which is called *siderios* <gloss>σιδήριος</gloss> <note>original Greek: *sidērios*</note> among the Greeks. It is also called by the Latins the magnet, the Heraclean stone, and the siderite. Hesychius makes the siderite stone different from the Heraclean stone: for he records that one has the color of iron and the other the color of silver. Pliny demonstrates five types of it, according to Sotacus <note>an ancient Greek writer on stones</note>: the Ethiopian; the Magnesian from Magnesia bordering Macedonia, on the right as you head toward Lake Boebeis; a third in Echium in Boeotia; a fourth near Alexandria in the Troad; and a fifth in Magnesia in Asia. 

The first difference is whether it is male or female; the next is in color. For those found in Macedonia and Magnesia are red and black. But the Boeotian stone has more red than black. That which is found in the Troad is black and of the female sex, and therefore without strength. The worst, however, is in Magnesia in Asia; it is white, attracts no iron, and resembles a pumice stone. It is found that the more blueish they are, the better they are. The highest praise is given to the Ethiopian stone, and its weight is balanced against silver <note>meaning it was as valuable as silver by weight</note>. It is found in Ethiopia in Zimiri, which is what the sandy region is called. The proof of the Ethiopian stone is that it attracts another magnet to itself. Again, in the same Ethiopia, not far away, a mountain produces the *Theamedes* stone, which drives away and rejects all iron. 

Dioscorides describes it thus: the best magnet is that which easily attracts iron, with a color leaning toward blue, dense, and not excessively heavy. Pisaurensis <note>likely Camillo Leonardi of Pesaro, who wrote on gems</note> identifies three types: one attracting iron, another flesh <note>referring to the "haematite" or bloodstone</note>, and another both attracting and repelling iron; this is quite unlearned, for the "flesh-attracting" stone is different from this, and it is one and the same stone that attracts and drives iron away from itself. Marbodius said it is born among the Troglodytes and the Indians. Olaus Magnus <note>a Swedish historian and geographer</note> says there are mountains in the North of such great attracting force that they must have ships fastened with wooden nails, lest the iron nails be pulled out of the wood when passing the magnetic cliffs. Between Corsica and Italy is the island of Ilva, commonly called Elba, in which the magnet is mined, but of an exhausted power. It is found in Cantabria in Spain, in Bohemia, and in many other places.

->## ON THE WONDERS OF THE MAGNET.<-

...lest we be longer than intended by bringing up the opinions of others, especially since they rely on nothing but words and vain subtleties <note>original: *capriunculis*; refers to trivial or hair-splitting arguments</note>, so that they do not seem to be accepted by philosophers, we have decided to pass over them. Instead, we will present our own [opinion], born from certain experiments. However, we will not omit the opinion of Anaxagoras <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher</note> cited by Aristotle in his book *On the Soul* <note>original: *De Anima*</note>, who, through a certain similarity, calls it an "animated stone" <note>original: *animatum lapidem*; a stone possessing a soul or life-force</note>, and for that reason it attracts iron, as well as for other peculiar powers which are properly said to proceed from the soul, as we shall see. Epicurus <note>the Greek philosopher who founded Atomism</note> tries to provide the cause of its effects, as Galen and Lucretius report. For they say that atoms which flow from the iron and from the magnet match each other in shape, so that they easily embrace one another; therefore, when these [atoms] strike against the solid masses of both the stone and the iron, and then leap back into the middle, they turn toward each other in passing and pull the iron along with them.

Galen <note>an influential Roman physician and philosopher</note> inveighs against these ideas, saying he cannot believe that the tiny bodies <note>original: *corpuscula*</note> that leap back from the stone could be entangled with other similar tiny bodies of the iron and pull such a heavy substance in their embrace. Furthermore, if you move another piece of iron toward one that is already hanging, it also sticks, and another to that one, and so a third and a fourth; if the atoms that flow from the stone, where they encounter the iron, leap back and are the reason why the iron hangs, he argues it is not possible for atoms that have entered through the iron to leap back through empty passages to the former ones and embrace others. This is especially true since he himself has seen five iron styli <term>styli; pointed metal rods or writing instruments</term> hanging from each other in a continuous line. And if the atoms are spread through the iron in a straight line, why should those we hang from the sides also stick, since that force is spread everywhere? Hence, if a tiny magnet touches many tiny bodies of iron, and these touch others, and those likewise others, and it must fill all those bodies, the tiny stone would be almost consumed and dissolved into the outflow of atoms.

But to me, the magnet seems to be a certain mixture of stone and iron, like an iron stone or a stony iron. But I would not want you to think the stone has been so changed into iron that it has lost its own nature, nor the iron so immersed in the stone that it does not protect its own being; rather, while one strives to overcome the other, the attraction of the iron results from this struggle. There is more stone than iron in that mass, and therefore, lest the iron be overwhelmed by the stone...

# NATURAL MAGIC, BOOK VII.

...[it] desires the strength and company of iron, so that what it cannot do alone, it may provide with the help of another. For every created thing protects its own existence. Therefore, so that it may enjoy friendly assistance and not be deprived of its own perfection, it does not unwillingly seize the iron to itself, or even moves toward the iron of its own accord. The magnet does not attract stones because it has no need of them, since there is enough stone in its own mass; and if a magnet attracts a magnet, it does not attract it because of the stone, but because of the iron enclosed within the stone. 

What we have said rests on these arguments. There are magnet mines where there are also veins of iron; these are described by Galen <note>a famous Greek physician in the Roman Empire</note> and writers on metallurgy, and they are born at the boundaries of both stone and iron; magnets are seen in which there is more stone, and in others more iron. In Germany, the magnet stone is dug up from which the best iron is extracted, and while the magnet lies in <term>iron filings</term> <note>original: *scobe*; small particles of metal</note>, it gains more vigorous strength, and if forgotten or neglected, it loses it. 

We have often seen, not without great pleasure of our mind, a magnet buried in burning coals belch out a blue, sulfurous, and irony flame; once this was dissipated, along with the departure of its <term>soul-like quality</term> <note>original: *animæ qualitate*; the vital principle that gives the magnet its power</note>, it lost the benefit of attraction. I have judged that the stench of iron and sulfur—as those who reduce iron to <term>lime</term> <note>original: *calcem*; a chemical residue left after heating a metal</note>, destroy it, or occupy themselves with other <term>alchemical</term> <note>original: *chymisticis*</note> operations easily experience—is that very same soul, and that when it is instilled into another, it necessarily achieves the same power.

### *That the magnet has two opposite poles, northern and southern, and how they can be distinguished. CHAPTER III.*

Since the effects of the magnet are various and manifold, we shall begin our distinction from its effects, so that readers may receive more instruction and benefit. The effects of the magnet belong either to the stone alone, or to iron rubbed by the magnet, or to both the stone and the iron together. The simple effects of the stone are to attract stone, to show the vertices of the heaven <note>referring to the celestial poles</note>, and similar things; there are also mixed and composite effects. 

We shall say first, therefore, that in the stone there are two points, positioned opposite each other—in a large part of the stone as well as in the smallest fragment—which we call poles. One of these is directed toward the North <note>original: *Boream*</note>, the other toward the South <note>original: *Austrum*</note>; namely, if the stone is left hanging freely, without the hindrance of its own weight, it turns of its own accord toward the North...
