...is directed toward the North, and the opposite part toward the South. The method of testing this shall be as follows: Take a small piece of cork, reed, or some other light wood, and fashion it into the shape of a little boat, which is sufficient to support the weight of the stone. Place the stone in this vessel so that it lies level with the bottom. Then, place the boat in a vessel full of water, so that it may move back and forth freely and not be hindered by anything. Once released in this way, the boat will never come to rest until the point of the stone is turned directly toward the North, and the opposite toward the South. When the little ship has stopped by itself, spin it around two or three times with your finger; once it ceases its motion again, it will return to the same spot, and you will be more certain of the Northern point of the stone and its opposite. You may become aware of this same fact in many other ways, such as by balancing it as in a <term>nautical compass</term> <note>original: *pyxis nautica*; the early mariner's compass</note>, for where it is free to move on its own, it will spontaneously direct itself to the aforementioned point. The same thing happens if it is suspended by a thin thread. From this, we can easily learn:

### *How one magnet may be known to be more perfect than another.*

By inspecting this same phenomenon, one can easily be aware of what kind of magnet it is—whether it is exhausted or possesses a sharper <term>virtue</term> <note>original: *virtutis*; in this context, the inherent power or "strength" of the magnet</note>. For the one which turns the little ship more quickly and readily toward its point and comes to rest once it is found, can be taken as an argument for a more valiant and powerful virtue. However, the one which completes its work with more difficulty—namely, that which returns to its place sluggishly and slowly and gets stuck more often—is of a more languid and duller power. We can also be made certain in another way: for the magnet which, while seeking to adhere to the aforementioned point and perform its office, can turn a larger mass of wood or a larger boat—not sluggishly or with hesitation, but quickly—is clearly to be judged more lively. And although there are many methods, you may be content with these for now, as we shall discuss others in different places.

### *The force of the stone spreads through a straight line from the North to the South throughout its length.*

Let there be, for example, a magnetic mountain *A B C D*, and let the line from the North to the South be *A B*. If, however, we break the stone across its width, each fragment will preserve its own line. Let the stone *A B* be split across its width *C F*; there will now be two stones, *A C D* and *E F B*. I maintain that once they are cut through the line *C D*, each one will possess its own <term>poles of the world</term> <note>original: *mundi vertices*; the points aligned with the North and South poles of the Earth</note>. In stone *A C D*, *A* will be the North and *G* will be the South. In stone *E F B*, *H* will be the North and *B* will be the South. This surpasses all wonder: that the points *G* and *H*, while the stone was whole, were actually a single point—joined, as it were, by a mutual treaty—and shared the same powers. But once the stone is divided, each part will hold its own separate powers, which are greatly contrary and discordant with one another. For *G* is drawn toward the South...

### *That the polar line in the magnet is not stable, but moving.* CHAPTER V.

But this similar prodigy of Nature will not lack the greatest admiration; among the many things the parent of all has created, this is remarkable and full of wonder, and for that reason, I would wish it to be hidden from no one. This polar line of which we spoke is not stable in the same place, nor does it always remain fixed, but it changes and moves to different parts; yet it has this constant quality: that it always claims the middle place in the stone for itself. It emulates a Prince, who establishes a citadel or royal palace for himself in the middle of his kingdom. For residing in the center, from which the extremities are curved in a fitting circumference, it easily meets all parts and protects its own power <note>original: *vires*; the inherent magnetic force or "virtue"</note>. But these things will become clearer through an example.

Thus, if we divide the part **A E D** into other parts, and break them into the smallest pieces, every single piece that is separated from its neighbors will possess that lively virtue extended through its length in its own center; this continues until it is divided into the tiniest grains of sand. But what is even more wonderful: if all the parts previously separated are joined back with their neighbors exactly as they stood before, the power of them all becomes one, and retreats back into the center of the whole.

### *That the North and South power flourishes at the extremities.*
### *CHAPTER VI.*

BUT what could be more marvelous? Although the power retreats into the middle of its stone, it does not actually stay in the middle, but spreads itself out toward the ends of the line; it rests sleeping in the middle, but wakes up at the extremities, where it is intensified and comes out into the open. If anyone breaks the stone, he will recognize this fact more exactly by sight. We will provide an example for those who are more scrupulously engaged in investigating every single effect of this stone.

Let the Herculean stone <note>original: *lapis herculeus*; a classical name for the magnet or lodestone, named for its "Herculean" strength or for the city of Heraclea</note> be **A B**, in which point **A** is northern and **B** is southern. ### *That those points do not change their powers by the contact of other stones.* CHAPTER VII.

And because we have said that a magnet does not always possess equal strength, but that one may be stronger in its operation and another more sluggish and dull, a reason for doubt arises: whether by the contact and rubbing <note>original: *adfricatione*</note> of stronger stones, those powers are changed, or whether they remain stable in their own places? For instance, if a magnet performs its duty of indicating the pole with difficulty, could another stronger one bring it help by rubbing its own northern part against the first's northern part? Or, if we rub the southern point of one against the northern point of another, whether that northern part, having been rubbed...

will it depart from its nature and take on a southern character, or will it remain in its own strength? Where the logic of the cause might fail us, experience and the outcome of the matter indicate the opposite. For if a magnet, however small, possesses any amount of strength, even when rubbed by another of sharper <term>virtue</term> <note>original: *virtutis*; in this context, the internal power or strength of the magnet</note>, it never departs from its own property, but persists immovable; and when left free in its little boat <note>a common method of the time: placing a magnet on a piece of wood or cork in water to allow it to rotate freely like a compass</note>, it voluntarily turns toward its own pole, recoiling from the opposite direction. And if we cannot fully grasp this by hunting for causes, it nevertheless does not seem far from reason. We shall say that in a greater mass of stone there is a greater power of the same species of stone; and when one magnet is rubbed against another, it leaves behind certain <term>hairs</term> <note>original: *pilos*; Della Porta describes the microscopic fragments or "filaments" of magnetic material left behind after friction as "hairs"</note>, which are nothing but the smallest crushed parts of the stones adhering in the form of hairs. It is these that grant the power of attracting and turning toward the pole to iron and other things. If, however, the stone that receives the rubbing is larger than those "hairs," it could never happen that the greater power is overcome by the lesser (speaking of the same type of stones). Since those hairs have almost no proportion to the stone's size, and just as the hairs are negligible compared to the magnitude of the stone, so it is impossible for them to twist its power in the opposite direction.

->That a magnet attracts and repels a magnet.<-

### CHAPTER VIII.

Now we shall speak of its other operation, which is that of attracting and repelling. Here it presents to the eyes and mind a spectacle no less pleasing than it is admirable: how one part of one stone so successfully seeks, allures, and draws a part of another, as if to enjoy a friendly companionship and cherish it in its own bosom; yet another part burns with such hatred for its fellow, and exercises such mutual natural enmity, that when the opposing points are brought together, it so abhors the face of its adversary that it turns itself away. Specifically, the northern part of one does not indifferently seize just any part of another toward itself, but only a distinct and determined one. Nor does it drive away every part, but only that which it recoils from by a natural discord, turning away from it as if it were alien and contrary. The northern part of one snatches up the southern part of another, but drives far away and rejects the northern part of the same stone. Likewise, the southern part of this stone does not resist the pull of another's northern part, but opposes the southern. This will become clearer through an example.

# ON THE MARVELS OF THE MAGNET.

Let there be two stones, ACD and EBF. In the first stone, point A is the <term>North</term> <note>original: *Borea*; the northern pole</note> and G is the <term>South</term> <note>original: *Auster*; the southern pole</note>. In the stone EFB, the Northern part is H and the Southern is B. I say that if you move the Southern part G of stone CAD toward the Southern part B of stone EFB, it immediately drives it away and puts it to flight. The same will also happen if you place the Northern A opposite the Northern G <note>The text here reads "Boreali G," though G was previously defined as South; this may be a printer's error for H, the North pole of the second stone</note>.

-> [Illustration: A woodcut showing two magnets. The upper rectangular stone is labeled with A at the top, G in the center, and C and D on the sides. Below it, a crown-shaped stone is labeled with B at the bottom, H in the center, and E and F on the points.] <-

On the contrary, if you show the Northern A to the Southern H, or the Southern B to the Northern A, the stone—as if seized by a shared pleasure—snatches the other part toward itself, and that part is not unwilling. The cause of this does not escape me; for since the Southern part G had previously been joined with the Northern H <note>original: *hessisset*; refers to the stones' original orientation in the earth</note>, once they have been severed, the parts always seek the same union for the protection and preservation of the same body, as the <term>Philosophers</term> <note>refers generally to the Aristotelian tradition of natural philosophy</note> say.

But if the Southern point G is brought near the Southern point B of the other stone, B immediately flees and departs from it; or if you show the Northern A to the Northern H, the same will happen. For they reject one another because in their <term>ore</term> <note>original: *minera*; the natural mineral bed or mine where they formed</note> they did not come together in that way.

At this point, we must not fail to mention the error of <term>Pliny</term> <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman naturalist whose *Natural History* was a standard reference</note> and his followers, who think this power is present only in the <term>Ethiopian stone</term> <note>a variety of lodestone considered by ancients to be the most powerful</note>, when in truth it is common to all <term>Herculean stones</term> <note>original: *herculeis lapidibus*; a classical name for the magnet or lodestone, named after the city of Heraclea</note>. Pliny says the proof of the Ethiopian stone is that it also draws another whole stone to itself. <term>Cardano</term> <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), a famous Italian polymath and contemporary of the author</note> also falsely asserts that a magnet is not attracted by a magnet, but...

...to pull, because the iron secretly clings, which it had previously drunk in. The point is this: dissimilar points <note>the opposite poles</note>, through a similarity of substance and by equal desires, meet and unite together; while similar points, through a dissimilar contrariety, take on enmity. That is, the <term>North</term> <note>original: *boreus*</note> seeks the <term>South</term> <note>original: *austrinus*</note>, and the South seeks the North; likewise, the North and South repel the North and South respectively. We thought it necessary to advise, however, that when we bring stones together for an experiment, they should not both be large or huge, lest, being hindered by their own weight, they be unable to perform their duties. Instead, let one be large and the other very small, or let both be small, so that they may mutually repel and attract each other. The trial will be easy if they are hung by a thread, or placed in little boats <note>referring to floating magnets in water to allow free movement</note>, or adjusted as pendulums in equilibrium.

### *The Magnet's Game.* Chapter IX.

We shall not omit the "magnet's game," with which we have often cheered our friends, so that we may provide for those who are more scrupulously engaged in investigating the reasons for individual things. We shall show how, in a short interval of time, two types of sand mixed together and piled into a heap may be separated from one another; if there be any bystanders who cannot grasp the trick of this cause, it will be impossible for them not to marvel. 

The game will be thus: Let a magnet be ground into a very fine sand, and to it we shall add another sand that is white or notable by some other difference. Let them be mixed together and formed into a heap. For when a magnet is brought near—either bare or wrapped in linens so that the bystanders do not recognize it—immediately the magnetic sand, joined as if by some treaty, runs together in clusters like hairs <note>describing the way iron filings stand on end in a magnetic field</note> and will cling tenaciously to the stone. By shaking it off, you will put it aside in another place; then approach again, and that which remained will run to the stone, until you separate the whole mixture. Nor will it cause little wonder when, as the magnet's touch approaches the mixture, the "divorce" of the clinging sands occurs. 

But so that you may grind the magnet more easily, do this: Put the magnet into an iron <term>mortar</term> <note>original: *pila*</note>, and place it upon blankets or something else soft. For by yielding to hard blows on a soft surface, it is immediately crumbled; otherwise, you will strike and mangle both the bottom of the mortar and the smoothness of the pestle. This same thing also happens with a certain sand which is brought to us from <term>Prochyte</term> <note>The island of Procida, near Naples</note> from...

...iron ore: for it reflects the color and luster of iron. By bringing a magnet near, it is quickly separated from the other sand, to the great wonder of those standing by. Perhaps this was the experiment handed down from the memory of the ancients, that the magnet draws iron, sand, oil, and everything <note>original: "magnetem ferrum, arenam, oleum, & omne trahere." ### *A larger magnetic stone possesses greater power.*
### *CHAPTER X.*

It certainly should not be overlooked that a magnet that excels in size hurls out an <term>effluence</term> <note>original: *effluuium*; early scientists believed magnetism was a physical "flowing out" of invisible particles</note> of its power from a distance, vibrating it so as to entice and seize an opposing magnet with greater violence—provided they are of the same type of stone. For example, if a magnet weighs a pound and another magnet seen from afar immediately leaps across and meets the one drawing it, should we take away half of its mass, the power languishes; it grows sluggish as if breathing its last, and its vigor is diminished in proportion to the part removed. 

If anyone gives little credit to this matter, let a stone be called forth for an experiment: for when a part is dragged away, the vigor is also dragged away; if one joins the removed part back to it, the forces are strengthened and made more lively. They return to their former vigor, so that it may leap toward a meeting magnet from a distance and embrace it immediately. This argument confirms for us that a larger stone possesses greater power within the same species of stone; for we have observed various magnetic stones brought from different parts of the world to be endowed with varying strengths. 

In Rome, we saw a magnet of a one-ounce weight <note>original: *vncialis ponderis*</note> which could pull two ounces of iron, and it embraced what it had pulled so tenaciously that it could hardly be pried away. We have seen others weighing forty pounds that were of such exhausted virtue that they could hardly move a single ounce. But so that we might better serve the curious with a fuller benefit, we shall teach in the following chapters the method by which the power of a stone can be weighed on a <term>balance</term> <note>original: *trutina*; a weighing scale</note> and measured with an equal scale.

### *That the power of stones flows into another, so that a dangling chain of stones may sometimes be seen. CHAPTER XI.*

This same stone comes to be commended by us for another gift: for when it has seized another stone, it not only embraces it stubbornly, but it belches and spits out <note>original: *eructat, expuitq;*; the author uses vivid, almost biological metaphors for magnetic induction</note> an effluence of its own powers into that stone's body...

# NATURAL MAGIC, BOOK VII.

But once it has claimed richer powers for itself, grasping another magnet in its hands, it discharges and spreads that same faculty. This third one, affected by that same force, seizes others from nearby or far away, hurling and vibrating that same <term>virtue</term> <note>original: *virtutem*; in this context, it refers to the inherent power or "essence" of the magnet</note>. And this one holds others so that, by a reciprocal hurling, it holds the others by the same force it is held by; and from each one, as if javelins of power smeared with this essence rush into the other, and raised high, they seem to hang as if chained together. They do not easily allow themselves to be pulled away, so that one might greatly wonder how that internal, invisible force is mutually transmitted and flows through them all. And this power slips out and spreads into more pieces the more potent the original power is. 

We thought this should be forewarned, however, lest you be deceived by experiment: the stones must cohere to each other by their related parts, not by opposite ones. For in such a way, one does not delegate its powers to the other, but by the meeting of an "enemy" part, they are restrained as if hindered by adversaries, and they cease their duties. That is to say, the Northern point of one must stick to the Southern point of the other, as we have said, and not the reverse. For if South meets South, or North meets North, the faculty languishes as if suffering from discord, and falls silent and numb in the presence of its adversary. 

Nor shall we omit this for those testing more carefully: the stones should succeed each other by size, so that the larger draws the smaller, and the smaller draws the tiny one, so they stick more tenaciously and are not so easily pulled apart.

### What that crushed "shagginess" on a magnet might be.
### CHAPTER XII.

From this arises that shagginess of "hairs" which we mentioned above, which sticks so tenaciously to the stone that it can hardly be torn away. For when one stone is rubbed by another, or a tiny piece is knocked off by a light blow of a hammer, those tiny rubbed-off parts do not fall to the ground by their own weight, but are retained by the power of the stone. And so that one part can stick to another, it turns a "friendly face" <note>An early way of describing magnetic polarity; "friendly" faces are opposite poles that attract.</note> toward its neighbor. It cannot conveniently stick to a companion part in any other way, nor be bound to it, except in the manner of a thread or a hair. If you rub stone against stone for a long time, that heap of "sands" grows so much that the stone becomes entirely bristly with hairs,

->*The pulling force is more powerful than the repelling force.*<-

### C A P. XIII.

**A**nother point must be made as a warning so that, having laid the foundations of what is to be said, we may proceed to greater matters. The part that attracts does so more passionately, while the part that repels <note>original: *expellit*; literally "expels" or "drives out," here referring to magnetic repulsion</note> does so more sluggishly. This refers to the opposing parts: for if the Southern part of a stone is joined to the Northern part of another, it attracts across a greater distance and with a more valiant <term>virtue</term> <note>original: *virtutis*; the inherent power or "essence" of the magnet</note>. Conversely, if you turn the "enemy" parts toward each other—namely, Southern to Southern and Northern to Northern—the natural force is blunted. It grows dull, as if starved and diluted, so that it cannot properly perform its duty; unless they are extremely close, this "besieged" force does almost nothing. If anyone wishes to test this for themselves, using a thread, a balance, or hanging stones in little boats <note>referring to the practice of floating magnets on wood in water to allow them to rotate freely</note>, they will find a readiness in attraction but a foolish, lazy softness in repulsion.

---

->*The contrary parts of stones are mutually opposed to one another.*<-

### C A P. XIV.

**T**he parts themselves that we have mentioned, if joined in a friendly fellowship, act as if bound by a sacred treaty. They bring aid to one another and achieve a far more effective and powerful strength. On the other hand, if they are set against each other, they exercise such mutual hatred of their natures and burn with such blind discords that, when brought together in a hostile clash, they cease their duties and are stripped of their power, as if in the presence of an enemy. For example, if you hold stones in your hands that have their opposite parts united (the Northern and Southern poles together), then upon meeting another stone, there will be no movement or "honor" <note>original: *honos*; here meaning the stone's characteristic dignity or display of its natural power</note> from either stone. They will neither entice nor repel, especially if the strength of both is equal. But if one [is stronger than the] other...

...should [the force] be stronger, the stone presented will nod with the motion, and prepare itself for either retreat or approach. But if you remove the opposing companion, it either offers no resistance to the pull or flees without reluctance; that is, it will either join with the friendly part or withdraw from the enemy part. Thus, by this evidence, you will recognize that one is an obstacle to the other. 

We can also be made more certain of this same matter through another experiment. If you attract a magnet with another magnet and keep it hanging in the air: if, at the spot where they joined, you oppose the "enemy" face of a third magnet, the power of both will wither and grow sluggish from this hostile encounter. If this new stone is of more vigorous <term>virtue</term> <note>original: *virtutis*; the inherent power or strength of the magnet</note>, it causes the attracted stone to let go so that it falls. 

Indeed, one may behold with pleasant wonder a chain of many magnetic parts hanging in the air; if we bring the opposing face of another magnet toward the third or fourth stone of that chain, the bond is immediately dissolved. The parts slip from their grip and fall away, yet the other parts, to which that hostile force did not reach, still cling together in their mutual link until you bring the "enemy" face near them as well.

### *How the polar points in a magnet may be recognized.*
## CHAPTER XV.

In another way, entirely more certain than what we described before, we shall recognize the vertical points <note>original: *verticales punctos*; the poles of the magnet</note> in the stone: which turns toward the North <note>original: *Aquilonem*</note> and which toward the South <note>original: *Austrum*</note>. The precise point from which that pulling force emanates will be indicated in this manner. That point, I say, which most vehemently snatches the Southern part of another stone to itself and clings to it persistently, that very point will be Northern <note>original: *boreus*</note>. And the point to which the Northern part of another stone approaches without reluctance will be Southern <note>original: *austrinus*</note>. 

The same can also be distinguished by repulsion. The point that drives the opposing Northern part of a stone far away from itself and rejects it will be the Arctic <note>original: *arcticus*</note> point; and that which puts the Southern parts to flight is the Antarctic <note>original: *antarcticus*</note>. 

Anyone seeking to find the point with even greater precision should use this clever trick: we shall present a tiny fragment of a magnet, slightly larger or smaller than a grain of millet, to the stone. If it is immediately seen to be attracted from a distance and more quickly, and once attracted is more stubbornly torn away, it is proof...

...then it will grant you knowledge of the true point from which that force flows. ### *That the point diffuses its force in a sphere*

we have learned it spreads as if from a center to a circumference. Just as the light of a candle is scattered everywhere and illuminates a room—shining more faintly the further it recedes, and vanishing a little further out, yet shining more vividly the closer one approaches—in the same way, that force emanates from that point. If an object clings closer, the magnet will pull more vigorously; the further away, the more remissly. Indeed, if it recedes too much, the force vanishes and becomes nothing. Therefore, for the things we are about to say, that point must be recognized as diffusive of its power and must be marked; and we shall call the sphere of its power the **range of its forces** <note>original: *virium longitudinem*; literally the 'length of forces' or its reach</note>.

->*That this force of attracting and repelling can be restrained by no obstacle. CHAPTER XVI.*<-

BUT this surpasses all wonder—so much so that you cannot marvel as much as is fitting—that this force of pulling and pushing can be enclosed by no barriers, nor hindered or restrained by any obstacle. Instead, it penetrates invisibly and moves and agitates related stones <note>i.e., other magnets or iron objects</note> placed in its way. It displays its powers as if no intermediary object forbade it, provided they are within the sphere of its power. Truly, if you place stones hanging or balanced in equilibrium above a table made of wood, stone, or metal, and you move a magnet beneath the table, the outflow of <term>virtue</term> <note>original: *virtutis*; the inherent power or strength of the magnet</note> rushing forth from its body—leaping through the associated and solid body of the table as if by some spirit—moves and agitates the stone upon it according to its own motion. When the magnet moves, the stone moves; when it rests, the stone rests. But if the table should be made of magnetic stone or of iron, the power is hindered and will be nothing. We shall provide the reasons for this in their proper places. Among so many and such prodigious miracles of Nature, one can surely see none more wonderful than this.

# How you may see an army of sands fighting.
### CHAPTER XVII.

**N**o less pleasant than it is a wonderful spectacle, we have presented it for the sake of entertainment to friends, who, with the greatest admiration, watched an army of sand—divided into its wings—fighting upon a flat table. Many, being ignorant of the method by which it was moved, imagined it to be the work of demons. I used to crush a magnet <note>original: *magnetem*; Porta likely refers to magnetite or lodestone here, though the effect is most easily achieved with iron filings</note> into a powder, some of it very fine, some a bit coarser, and another portion made of small fragments, so that they might more conveniently represent infantry armed with spears <term>hastatos</term> <note>soldiers armed with the *hasta*, or long spear</note>, or squadrons of cavalry. I would then set up the army here and there; there were wings on the right and left, and the main army in the middle accompanied by the cavalry squadrons. Beneath the table, with my left hand, I moved an excellent magnet. Once moved, the left wing began to march; from the other side, using another stone <note>another magnet</note> with my right hand, the right wing moved. When they were closer together, by clinging more closely to the magnet, the little grains of sand would stand on end <note>original: *inhorrescebant*; literally "shuddered" or "bristled," describing how magnetic filings align with field lines</note>, and as they gradually raised themselves, they imitated spears. When the magnet was tilted, the spears were also tilted, as if they were threatening death and destruction in battle. The more perfect the magnet, the further the bristles would stand up. By moving my hands little by little, the army was moved step by step; and as the stones were brought closer together, the hands of the combatants engaged and were mixed together. Thus the remaining wings and squadrons, as they approached, represent the likeness of a battle: you will see them now retreat, now advance, now conquer, and now be conquered, now raising their spears and now lowering them, according as the magnet approaches more or less, and as its force extends its sphere more or less vehemently. But this is even more marvelous: although it is seen on a flat table, it can also be done hanging in the air, so that the combatants appear to be Antipodes <note>original: *antipodes*; a reference to the classical geographical concept of people living on the opposite side of the Earth, who would appear "upside down" from the perspective of the observer</note>. For if paper or a board is stretched out on high, magnets moved above the board represent that same thing which we have described <note>The filings would cling to the underside of the paper, appearing to hang and move "upside down" like people on the other side of the world</note>. Indeed, if someone ingenious manages it, he will work more and greater things than can be written.

ON THE MARVELS OF THE MAGNET.

### *Position yields contrary virtues in stones.*
#### CHAPTER XVIII.

Nor will it be void of wonder—as it is of reason—that position <note>original: *situs*; referring here to the physical orientation or placement of the magnet relative to another object</note> reveals contrary powers, as we have said of all these things. For a stone performs one way if you move it from above, and another if from below. For if you arrange a stone in equilibrium <note>balanced so it can move freely</note>, or in a small boat, and move a magnet toward it from above, it draws or rejects it, as we mentioned before. But if you move the magnet from below, it will perform the opposite: for that part which drew it from above, will repel it from below; and that which rejected it from above, will draw it from below—specifically if you place the magnet perpendicularly <term>ad perpendiculum</term> <note>perfectly vertical, aligned with a plumb line</note> above and below. By these experiments, it can be clearly seen that position produces contrary effects and changes the turns of the forces. Therefore, in its operations, position must be most carefully observed, whether you approach the magnet from above or from below.

### *How the drawing force of a magnet can be weighed on a scale.*
#### CHAPTER XIX.

We are able to measure that attractive and repulsive force of the magnet, or weigh it with scales, which will be of no small importance in the following speculations—especially regarding perpetual motion <term>perpetui motus</term> <note>a theoretical machine that runs forever; a major obsession of Renaissance science</note> and the suspending of iron hanging in the air <note>original: *in aere pendulum ferrum sistendi*; this likely refers to the legendary "tomb of Mahomet" which was rumored to be suspended in mid-air by magnets</note>, where an equal and measured force of drawing from the circumference to the center is sought. The artifice shall be of this sort: We place a piece of magnet in a scale pan, and in the other pan an equal amount of weight of another material, so that the pans hang level. Soon we arrange a piece of iron lying upon a table so that it clings to the magnet placed in the pan, and according to their "friendly points" <note>original: *amica puncta*; the poles that naturally attract one another</note>, so that they may cohere most perfectly. Into the other pan, you shall cast sand <note>original: *harenam*</note> little by little, until the pan is separated from the iron. Thus, by weighing the weight of the sand, we shall have the magnetic force we sought. We can also arrange the iron fixed in the scale pan and the magnet lying on the ground.

### *On the mutual attraction and repulsion of the magnet and iron.*
#### CHAPTER XX.

Now we have come to the second part of our treatise, in which the mutual partnerships <note>original: *consortia*; attractions</note> and divorces <note>original: *diuortia*; repulsions</note> of magnets will be discussed.

whose effects are so well-known that they fly through the mouths of men <note>a Latin idiom, *per hominum ora volitent*, meaning "everyone is talking about it"</note>, so that there is almost no one who does not profess to be knowledgeable of this matter. This operation is as follows: there is such a natural concord and sympathy between iron and the magnet—as if a treaty <note>original: *foedere*; common in Renaissance science to describe natural laws as "treaties" or "compacts"</note> had been entered into between them—that when a magnet approaches iron, the iron immediately nods and goes to meet it, seeking to be embraced by the magnet. It receives the magnet into its own embrace so stubbornly that it can hardly be pulled away, even when tossed about by many distractions. Nor is the magnet’s own meeting with the iron, its conciliation, mutual love, and assembly any less; for neither of them resists the pull, but the gentler of the two always voluntarily conveys itself to the meeting of the other. So that you may have faith in this matter, you may test it by this argument: either suspend both by a thread, or place them in little boats, or set them in a nautical compass. Pliny, speaking of this, says:

> "For what is more wonderful? Or in what part of Nature is there greater perversity? What is more sluggish than the stiffness of a stone? Lo, Nature has given it senses and hands. What is more combative than the hardness of iron? But it yields and allows delays: for it is drawn by the magnet stone, and that substance, the tamer of all things <note>referring to iron, which harvests crops and wins wars</note>, runs toward some void, and as it comes closer, it stands still, is held, and clings in an embrace." <note>original: Pliny the Elder, *Natural History*, Book 36, Chapter 25</note>

Lucretius, seeking the cause of this kind of effect, asks:

> "By what treaty of Nature it happens that this stone is able to draw iron." <note>original: *Quo foedere fiat, Naturae lapis hic ut ferrum ducere possit*; from *De Rerum Natura*, Book VI</note>

Orpheus, in his poems <note>likely the *Lithica*, a poem on gems attributed to the mythical Orpheus</note>, relates that iron is drawn by the magnet just as a bride to the embraces of her groom; indeed, the iron is so troubled by the desire to marry it, and strives with such fervent desire to meet and cling to the magnet, that when it is hindered by its own weight, it raises its peak <note>the tip or end of the iron piece</note>: like a hand, nodding to the stone and gently stroking it. Impatient that its stability is weighed down, the iron confesses it is not content with its lot unless, at least joining in a kiss, it rests as if its desire were refreshed. And they burn with such mutual love that unless the power of touching one another is granted, it is held hanging in the air. Whence, rather ignorantly, Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus, the 13th-century philosopher</note> tells a wonderful story: that a companion of Emperor Frederick showed him a magnet that did not draw iron, but instead the iron drew the magnet,

### *That the love of iron and magnet is greater than that of magnet with magnet.* CHAPTER XXI.

Nor should we conceal the great mutual love between iron and the magnet: it is more efficacious and far stronger than the love of a magnet for another magnet, and this can be shown by a simple proof. For if you place small pieces of magnet and iron of the same weight upon a table, and another magnet is gradually brought near, when it has come to the proper distance, the iron immediately nods and voluntarily brings itself to the magnet and embraces it. A more certain belief in this same thing will be held by another proof: Let a magnet hold a piece of another magnet in its embrace, and let it gradually approach some iron; when the force of its sphere <note>original: *vis orbis*; referring to what we now call a magnetic field</note> reaches the iron, the magnet immediately casts away the other magnet and embraces the iron. But if it has once received the iron into its fellowship, it will not be moved from its embrace by any attachment of another magnet.

### *That the magnet does not attract from everywhere, but from a fixed point.* CHAPTER XXII.

Yet it certainly must not be thought that the magnet attracts iron with every part of itself, but from a fixed and established point, which must be sought with great labor and the investigation of reason. In this way you will obtain your wish <note>original: *voti compos fies*; a Latin idiom meaning to succeed in one's goal or prayer</note>. Either suspend the iron, or arrange it on a balance above a board, from which it can immediately spring back into an embrace. Then move the magnet all around it, and when you see the iron tremble and run to the contact, that very place is the point of attraction. From that point, the rays of power <note>original: *radij virtutis*; early scientists envisioned magnetic force as rays emanating like light</note> are scattered to the circumference of its sphere; thus, the further the iron is from that point, the more weakly and sluggishly it will move, for in the center, as if on its throne, a more vivid force makes its nest.

### *That the same magnet which attracts also repels iron from the opposite side.* CHAPTER XXIII.

But lest anyone be deceived without forewarning, thinking that one stone is that which attracts and another is that which rejects the iron, we shall dispel this cloud <note>original: *nubilum*; a metaphor for confusion or intellectual darkness</note> with experiments.

Pliny mentions <note>original: *Plinius*; referring to Pliny the Elder’s *Natural History*</note> a magnet stone pulling iron toward itself, and another stone driving it away. And elsewhere: "Again, in that same Ethiopia, a mountain not far off produces the stone **Theamedes**, which drives away and rejects all iron." Since Pliny did not understand this phenomenon, he erred shamefully, thinking there were two different stones that possessed these contrary effects. In truth, it is one and the same stone; from one side, by a certain likeness and **sympathy**, it snatches the iron toward itself quite willingly; yet from the contrary and opposite side, by unlikeness and a mutual discord of natures—or **antipathy** <note>Della Porta uses these terms to describe what we now understand as magnetic poles (North and South)</note>—it drives the iron away and rejects it. 

You can be made more certain of this by a simple device: for if iron is placed in a state of equilibrium <note>such as on a scale or balanced on a pivot</note>, and it is drawn to one side of the magnet, if the magnet is then turned around, the iron immediately flees and withdraws to the opposite side. These points are laid out along a straight line through the middle of the stone itself. This, however, must be remembered: iron that has been drawn by one side of a magnet, or has remained within its **power** <term>virtue: the inherent active force or "field" of the magnet</term> for some time, immediately acquires that same power. Thus, what was drawn by one side is now fled and driven away by the other. You will recognize the distinctions of this attraction more clearly by the following experiment.

## *How iron may dance upon a table, with no visible stone moved toward it. CHAPTER XXIV.*

From this very harmony and discord of the stone, we are often accustomed to show a not unpleasant spectacle to our friends. When iron is cast upon a table, with no visible stone nearby, it seems to roll around and dance by itself, which cannot be witnessed without great amazement from everyone. The spectacle is performed in this way: 

Let a needle be divided through the middle, and let one half be cast upon the table; but first, let the base of the magnet be rubbed against one part of it. You will secretly place your hand with the magnet under the table, and in that spot where the base of the needle rests, the magnet will take hold. Immediately, the needle stands upright, and once standing—to the great admiration of the bystanders—it walks across the table, following the movement of the hand moving beneath. When it has traveled a little way, by quickly flipping the stone, you present the opposite side of the magnet to the needle. Immediately (a wonder to see!), the needle flips over; if it was previously walking on its base, it now walks on its point, and wherever...

### That the power of the magnet is transmitted through pieces of iron. CHAPTER XXV.

This same **power** <term>virtue: the inherent active force or "field" of the magnet</term> which is impressed upon the iron by the magnet does not remain and persist in that iron alone, but is transmitted and propagated into one piece after another. For if you draw an iron needle by the touch of a magnet, and then touch another needle with the opposite end of the attracted iron, that part will pull the needle, embrace it, and snatch it up to hang suspended in the air. And if you bring that part near to another piece of iron, it will snatch that one too, and hold it suspended in the air.

You may repeat this same work with others, until the circle of magnetic force is stretched so far that it grows weak and immediately drops what it had seized, as if it were not strong enough for the weight of the needle, so that a long series of needles may be seen hanging together in the air like a chain. Plato <note>The Greek philosopher (c. 427–348 BC)</note> knew of this power, for he says in his *Ion*: "This stone not only draws iron rings, but also pours power into the rings themselves, so that they can do this very same thing, and just like the stone, draw other rings." Hence, a long chain of iron and rings often hangs from one another, and the power is drawn into all of them from that single stone. Lucretius <note>Titus Lucretius Carus (c. 99–55 BC), Roman poet and philosopher</note> also knew of this power:

> *Now men marvel at the stone: for a chain*
> *Often hangs from rings suspended from one another,*
> *Indeed, one may sometimes see five, or even more*

Who would not marvel at this power of the stone? Which not only resided within it, but also passed through so many suspended things and bound them with invisible bonds?" 

But the sharper the **power** of the magnet is, the more needles it will suspend from the rings; we ourselves have suspended ten needles using a one-pound stone. But he who wishes to attract more needles should rub them only against the magnet at the part with the hole <note>The "eye" of the needle</note>; then, in order, let them all pull by the base from the point <note>original: *ex cono omnes basim trahant*; describing the alignment of the needles in the chain</note>.

### *How a magnet may suspend iron in the air.*
### *CHAPTER XXVII.*

To make iron hang in the air without any contact with the magnet, and without being tied from the lower part: we have labored long and hard to achieve this, and we now judge it to be almost impossible. Pliny says: "Dinocrates the Architect <note>An ancient Greek architect often associated with Alexander the Great and the city of Alexandria.</note> had begun to vault the temple of Arsinoe <note>Arsinoe II, the sister and wife of Ptolemy II Philadelphus.</note> with magnets, so that her iron image might appear to hang in the air within it; death intervened for both him and Ptolemy, who had ordered it to be built for his sister, and so what he had begun, he did not finish." The Greeks say that in the vaults of the temple of the god Serapis in Alexandria, a magnet was fixed which held up a hanging bronze statue, because it had iron in its head. That Muhammad's <note>original: *Mahometi*</note> chest <note>A common European myth claimed the Prophet Muhammad's coffin floated in mid-air via magnets at Mecca or Medina.</note> also hangs in the vaults of a temple is false. Peter Peregrinus <note>original: *Petrus Pellegrinus*; a 13th-century scholar and author of the first extant treatise on the properties of magnets.</note> says he taught how this could be done in another work, but that work is nowhere to be found. Why it seems most difficult to me, we shall explain further below. Now, however, we say it can be done [in a certain way], as we have already done: to hold it suspended in the air from the upper part by an invisible bond, provided that from the lower part it is restrained by a thin thread so that it does not fly upward; and while it strives to cling to the stone above, it will appear to bob and tremble as it hangs in the air.

### *How a wooden man may move a little boat, and other toys. CHAPTER XXIX.*

No small deceptions arise from this principle. The trick is set up as follows: Let a bowl be filled with water, and a wax or wooden boat be placed in it. Then, when a woman seeks answers regarding uncertain matters, the little wooden man—as if he were about to give a true response—will row the boat to those letters which spell out the answer. For the person who holds a magnet in his hand under the table will lead the boat wherever he pleases, and by combining the letters in this way, he delivers the answers. ### *The magnet does not move iron when placed over an iron plate.*

->CHAPTER XXX.<-

We have said that the magnet’s powers are hindered by no intervening material, except for iron. Because of this, if a needle is placed upon a thin iron plate <note>original: *lamellam*</note> and you move a magnet either above or below it, the virtue <note>original: *virtus* — the "power" or "force" of the magnet</note> fades away, and the magnet will not perform its usual tasks. This is not without reason. For it is consistent that if iron is placed upon iron, the two become as one and the same; the portion of the metal acts as part of the whole. Since the plate and the iron filings are of greater weight than can be moved by the magnet’s force, they remain immobile. Thus, if iron sand or magnetic filings are placed upon an iron plate, and a hand moves a magnet beneath it, the sand will not be moved here and there, but will remain motionless upon the iron. Nor if iron or a magnet were placed upon an iron table would they come into contact with a stone moved near them; instead, they rest as if asleep, as if deprived of all power or changed in their very nature. Indeed, if a flat piece of iron is placed opposite a magnet, and on the other side a piece of iron is held in equilibrium <term>equilibrium: a state of physical balance</term>, it will not be moved nor even nod at the magnet’s approach, as if the whole power of the magnet were caught and hindered in the plate's embrace. Lucretius <note>Titus Lucretius Carus (c. 99–55 BC), a Roman poet and philosopher. ### The position of the iron changes its powers. CHAPTER XXXI.

Whatever the magnet performed on its own, the iron will also perform once it has been touched by the magnet. We have previously stated that when a magnet is placed in equilibrium <note>original: *æquilibrio* — a state of balance, likely referring to the magnet being floated or suspended so it can move freely</note>, if a southern magnet is brought near its upper part, the northern part is attracted, and north is repelled by north. However, at the lower part, its nature is changed: what previously attracted now refuses, and what it previously refused, it now attracts. We believe the same must be judged regarding iron that has touched a magnet. For in a nautical compass <note>original: *nautica pixis* — literally a "nautical box," referring to the early mariner's compass</note>, that part of the iron which attracts and repels from the upper side will, when moved to the lower side, repel what it previously attracted and attract what it once repelled. I thought this should not be omitted from its wonderful properties: that its position should produce such different effects. From this, we may conjecture that just as the stone has an arctic and antarctic pole, it follows that it likewise has an east and west, and an upper and lower part in accordance with the heavens. Where the northern and lower part of the stone attracted the southern and lower part of the iron from the upper side, now, with the position changed, it is consistent with reason that the upper part of the stone should attract the lower part of the iron.

---

### *Iron rubbed with the northern point of a magnet turns toward the South, and rubbed with the southern point, toward the North.*
### CHAPTER XXXII.

WE MUST MOVE ON to the third part, namely to treat iron that has been touched by a magnet, all of which will not be lacking in wonders. We say, therefore, that after we have identified the northern point <note>original: *borealem punctum*</note> of the stone and have rubbed one part of the iron with it, if we leave that iron to its own free power—whether placed in equilibrium, suspended by a thread, or placed in a small boat <note>original: *cymba* — a common experimental method where the magnet was floated on water using a piece of wood or cork</note>—it will turn of its own accord toward the South <note>original: *Austrum*</note>. This is not without reason, because the magnet imparts its own force <note>original: *vim*</note> to the iron. For it was the innate power of the magnet that, when placed in equilibrium, it would turn its northern part to the North and its southern part to the South. But while it is rubbed against the iron, the upper part of the magnet is fixed to the iron, and the nearby lower part is related to it; hence, if you rub the northern part on the iron, that which clings to the iron and the topmost surface <insert>of the iron</insert>

By its convenience and use, such vast seas are plowed, with it showing the way. Indeed, our ancestors navigated by observing the Sun by day and the stars by night, for otherwise, wandering in the middle of the sea, they could not perceive the regions of the world. Nor can we only avoid the hidden rocks lurking under the water, but on a cloudy day and in dark nights, the poles of the world become known at every moment. 

The invention of this was by an Italian originating from Amalfi in our own Campania, as is handed down by Flavio <note>Flavio Biondo (1392–1463), a Renaissance historian. He popularized the belief that Flavio Gioja of Amalfi invented the compass in 1302.</note>. He, being ignorant of the nautical wheel, used to fix a needle through a piece of straw or wood crosswise, and would submerge the needles in a bowl full of water so they might float freely; then by moving a magnet around, the needles followed it; when the magnet was withdrawn, as if by some natural motion, the points of the needles turned toward the arctic pole, and having found it, they came to rest. Thus, having pre-determined the location, they directed their journey according to their wishes. 

Now, with the nautical wheel <term>nautical wheel: the compass rose or card marked with directions</term> drawn around, and the iron having been touched by the magnet and fitted to it, from the identification of the pole, the remaining parts of the heavens immediately become known. The wheel is secured upon a brass pivot <note>original: *orichalceo vmbilico* — literally a "brass navel," the central point on which the compass card balances.</note> above a point of the same metal, so that it has the power to revolve itself freely. Hence, from the contact of only one point, the iron not only acquires the virtues of that aforementioned part, but from the other side, even against its will, it acquires the virtues of the other: for if you rub it against the northern part of the stone, that part immediately turns toward the South, and the opposite part of the iron turns toward the North; nor can one force be granted without the other. Thus, iron touched by the southern part of the stone turns toward the North, and the other toward the South: hence the touched part of the iron always receives a power unlike <note>original: *dissimilem* — referring to the law of magnetic induction where the point of contact takes on the opposite polarity of the magnet's pole.</note> that of the stone.

### *Iron touched by a magnet imparts its power to another piece of iron. CHAPTER XXXIII.*

Iron touched by a magnet receives the same power of the magnet from that contact, so that it becomes almost the same in its ability to attract, repel, and turn itself toward the pole. Thus, if a piece of free iron <note>original: "ferrum liberum," meaning iron that is balanced or suspended so it can move easily.</note> is rubbed with the southern part of the stone, it will spontaneously move toward the North; if you then show it the same southern part of the stone, it immediately turns toward the South. But if you touch another piece of iron with that first magnetized iron, it will move toward the South, and if shown the same point of the iron, it turns toward the North. Nor is this power transmitted only to a second piece of iron, but to another, and another, in proportion to the strength of the magnet; for if the virtue is powerful enough, it can be transmitted through as many as eight or ten pieces of iron.

### *The force received in iron is washed away by a stronger one. CHAPTER XXXIV.*

We also thought it necessary to warn you that the power received in iron should not be considered stable or perpetual, but rather that it can be stripped away by a more powerful force and "clothed" in a new one. For example, if iron has been touched by the northern part of a weak <note>original: "ignavi," literally "lazy" or "sluggish."</note> magnet, and you then rub that same part of the iron with the southern part of a stronger magnet, that original power of turning toward the South vanishes and is dulled; it instead assumes the southern force and turns toward the North without resistance. But if the strengths of the magnets are balanced equally, they become "intoxicated" and so clouded <note>original: "inebriantur, offuscanturque," a vivid metaphor suggesting the magnetic orientations become confused or cancel each other out.</note> that they either cannot receive both forces, or they possess neither.

### *How the southern or northern point in a stone may be known. CHAPTER XXXV.*

Among the other methods we mentioned above, we will also teach this one—which is perhaps superior to the rest—for how we may truly recognize the <term>Arctic and Antarctic points</term><note>The North and South poles. These terms were commonly used in the Renaissance to describe the magnetic poles of the Earth or a magnet.</note>. Using lapidary wheels, let the magnetic stone be rounded into a sphere <note>A spherical magnet was often called a "terella" or "little earth," as it was thought to model the planet's own magnetism.</note> and polished; then, let a slender piece of iron be prepared, the length of which is equal to the axis of the ball, and that...

...is placed above the stone: for it will follow and align itself along the line passing through the southern and northern points. ### *How the iron needle of a nautical compass is rubbed.*
## CHAPTER XXXVI.

I know that some are tormented by anxiety while waiting to learn the method by which the iron needle <note>original: "obelus," a Greek-derived term for a spit or pointed rod, here used for a compass needle.</note> in a nautical compass <note>original: "pyxide," a box or casing, from which we get the word "pyx" and eventually "compass box."</note> is rubbed against the magnet so that it might receive the power to turn itself toward the northern pole. It is done in this manner: once we have found the points on the stone, as we described just before, those points are struck with a light blow of a hammer. Then the "hairs" <note>original: "pili," likely referring to the magnetic filaments or the points of strongest attraction that seem to "bristle" like hair.</note> of those spots will stand stiff; if you rub the iron needle against them, it immediately acquires the virtue of turning toward the poles. One must be warned, however, that if you desire the iron to turn toward the North, you must apply the southern part of the stone; but if you wish it to turn toward the South, apply the northern part. For when the needle stands free in equilibrium, it will turn itself toward the aforementioned quarters of the sky. 

But so that it may perform its task more vigorously and fulfill its duty more precisely, we will add a few rules which it will be useful to have taught. If you strike both polar parts of the stone with a hammer so that the "hairs" bristle on both sides, and both ends of the iron needle are touched to them, the iron will perform its duties more swiftly. Furthermore, the greatest care must be observed: after the iron has been rubbed against the magnet and received its "hairs," it must be touched by no other iron or magnet. Indeed, it should be kept far away from them and kept shut in a small box, for by the contact of others, the iron becomes intoxicated <note>original: "inebriatur," a vivid metaphor suggesting the iron's magnetic orientation becomes confused or "drunken" if it encounters competing magnetic fields.</note>.

...and the power is obscured, so that it never perfectly shows the regions of the heavens. Let the needle <note>original: "obelus," a pointer or small rod</note> also be proportional to the stone; for if the magnet is small, but the iron is large, it certainly cannot receive much power, nor can it show the pole. Conversely, a tiny body of iron cannot hold a great power, for it is overwhelmed by the immense force of the magnet. Furthermore, the point intended to show the pole ought not to be sharp, but rather somewhat flat, so that it might best receive and hold those particles of the magnet; for on a very sharp point, hardly any part of the power will cling. The more purified the iron is, the more tenaciously it will receive the power, for it joins itself with difficulty to dirty or rusty iron. For this reason, sailors make their needles from pure steel, since steel <note>original: "chalybs"</note> is made from refined iron. If you observe these things, once the iron has been rubbed, it will retain its force even for a hundred years, and through that time it will clearly and without error demonstrate the most certain directions of the heavens.

Not only for showing the poles for nautical use does the iron needle in the compass box <note>original: "pyxide," the housing for the needle</note> offer its help, but for almost infinite uses which everyone knows are spoken of everywhere; we shall touch upon some of the principal ones. The most well-known use of the magnet in iron needles is in shadow-tracking clocks <note>original: "sciotericis horologijs," referring to sundials that use the sun's shadow to tell time</note>; for when the needles are at rest, they immediately show a line drawn from North to South, from which the shadows falling from the gnomon <note>The upright rod on a sundial</note> will demonstrate the hours of the day. Miners also use a magnetic indicator to track the extension of veins; for in subterranean caves, they know that in whatever position the indicator (which has touched a magnet) stands, the veins of metals will extend from that part of the heavens. Furthermore, it provides a wonderful use for those who describe the floor plans <note>original: "ichnographias"</note> of buildings—indeed of cities, and even of whole regions—while the angles of the sites are captured and transferred onto paper. We use it, moreover, in conducting water, in aqueducts which are excavated underground, and in boring through caves. It is used in excavating tunnels <note>original: "cuniculis," often used for military mining</note> in which piles of gunpowder are placed, and when the vents are obstructed...

## How the longitude of the world may be tracked by the aid of the magnet.
### CHAPTER XXXVIII.

Nevertheless, we shall not omit among the principal uses of the magnet the fact that the longitude of the world can be thoroughly investigated by its help—an outstanding feat that has troubled the minds of many most excellent men. It has long been noticed by our people that an iron needle rubbed against a magnet does not always rest upon the meridian line <note>The true north-south line determined by the sun or stars.</note>, but declines from that line by nine degrees toward the East. Nor does it keep the same position in all places, but shows various and diverse declinations <note>original: "declinationes," now commonly called magnetic variation.</note> in various places. 

But this error seems to follow a specific order: the closer it is to the East, the more it will deviate from the meridian line toward the East; and the further you proceed toward the West, the more the iron needle will incline toward the West. For by finding the meridian line (as Ptolemy and other geometers teach) and erecting the needle upon it so that the iron pointer <term>obelus|a small rod or needle</term> turns freely upon its center, we find that in Italy it declines from the meridian line by nine degrees toward the East—measured by the standard where a quarter-circle consists of ninety degrees. This has already been noted and described in the sun-dials <note>original: "scioterics horologijs," instruments that tell time by shadows; portable versions often included a compass.</note> brought to us from Germany. 

Furthermore, it is reported by men famous for their travels that in the Fortunate Isles <note>A classical name for islands in the Atlantic, often identifying the Canaries or Madeira.</note> there is one called the Azores <note>original: "Afforas."</note>, in which the iron placed in the compass box rests truly upon the meridian line. Navigators toward the West Indies <note>The Americas.</note> have also observed the needle in the compass box nodding toward the West. Therefore, these things being established as true, we can easily know the longitude of the world: for if we make a compass box of unusual size, about ten feet in diameter, and subdivide the degrees and minutes into finer parts, we may then observe the principal movements and declinations of the pointer while sailing under the equator and adapt them to the proportions of the journeys.

<summary>Porta discusses how the magnet's deviation from true north (magnetic declination) varies by geographic location, proposing that this phenomenon could be used to solve the great scientific problem of determining longitude at sea.</summary>

...[find the meridian line] we will easily recognize the longitude of the world, beginning from the Fortunate Isles <note>The Canary Islands, which were used as the Prime Meridian in ancient and Renaissance geography.</note>. From there, latitude, longitude, and our position in the dead of night or during the greatest storms of the heavens easily become known to us. Therefore, what is reported by Cardano <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), an influential Italian physician and mathematician.</note> is false: that the iron in the compass <term>pyxide|the box or housing containing a magnetic needle</term> deviates from the meridian line because it inclines toward the pole star from the tail of the Bear <note>The constellation Ursa Major.</note>; for the deviation <note>original: "inclinatio," here referring to horizontal variation or declination.</note> of the iron is nine degrees, and the polar inclination is not so great.

->*Whether the nautical compass remains still and the stone moves, or vice-versa, they move in opposite directions.*<-

### CHAPTER XXXIX.

If a magnet stands upon a table, and you bring the northern part of the nautical compass's iron toward the southern part of the stone, moving it in a circle toward the right, the iron needle <term>obelus|a small pointed rod or needle</term> will be drawn toward the left. But by moving the compass toward the left, the iron will move back toward the right, and it stays away until it reaches a middle position between those two opposite points. The same will happen with a sundial <term>vmbratili horologio|literally, a "shadow clock"</term> if it remains stationary while the magnet is moved around it; for if you turn to the right, the iron will follow that same direction, and likewise to the left. From this, it is clear that the iron of the compass is drawn by the northern pole: for when traveling toward the East, it turns toward the East; likewise toward the West, it will shift toward that same point in the heavens. And if the magnet is rotated, the iron will also rotate, like a pair of compasses <note>original: "circinus," the drafting tool used to draw circles.</note> around its own center.

### *Two needles clinging to a magnet acquire contrary powers.*
## CHAPTER XLI.

We shall also relate a thing worthy of wonder, even if its cause does not stray far from its own principles. If you bring two needles toward the stone at once, and at the same part, the other ends hanging away from the magnet will recoil from and flee one another. If you force them together with your hands, as soon as you let them go, they will immediately return to their original places, distancing themselves as much as they are able. The reason for this is as follows: if two needles stick by their tips to the single northern point <term>septentrionali|the north-seeking pole</term> of the magnet, they must be considered to have received the southern virtue <note>The author is describing how a needle touched by the North pole of a magnet becomes a South pole at the point of contact.</note>; and since they are similar faces, they will naturally recoil from one another. Because they are bound to the magnet, they cannot flee entirely, even when forced by greater power; but the opposite parts of the iron, because both are similar northern parts <term>boreales|referring to Boreas, the North Wind</term>, must necessarily flee one another, and because they are more free, one will be dissociated from the other. Indeed, while they are thus hanging, if you bring the southern part of another magnet near, they immediately flee, and they struggle to distance themselves so much that they are sometimes torn away from the magnet, propelled by an invisible spirit.

### *Iron touched by a magnet on one side does not always receive the force on both ends.* 
## CHAPTER XLIII.

If iron is touched by a magnet at one end, it receives power in that part, and the contrary power in the other end. However, this is not to be understood as an absolute rule, but applies only to iron of a proportionate length. For if it is quite long, the force will not reach the other end. If we desire to know how far that virtue reaches, we must know the extent of the <term>sphere of influence<note>original: "orbis," literally "circle" or "orb." Porta imagines the magnet's power radiating in a defined physical circle around it.</note></term>, as we have said. Thus, if that "circle of rays" is one foot in diameter, the power will extend one foot into the iron. If you wish to put this to the test: let a piece of iron three feet long be touched by a magnet on one end; if you touch the other end of the iron [with another piece of iron], the touched iron will not move from its place. But if we touch it at one foot, or at two—that is, as far as the known sphere of power reaches—and touch the iron there, it will be immediately snatched up and moved.

### *Iron touched by a magnet in the middle spreads the force to its ends.* 
## CHAPTER XLIV.

If the iron is somewhat longer than is fitting, and we touch it in its center with the stone, the powers of the stone’s side are spread to the ends, but they are somewhat faint <note>original: "obscuriusculæ," meaning the polarity is dim or difficult to detect.</note>, for it will be unknown which [pole] is which. However, if it is touched slightly away from the center, the part closer to the point of contact will take on the powers of the side of the magnet that touched it, whether it be <term>northern<note>original: "borealis."</note></term> or <term>southern<note>original: "australis."</note></term>.

### *An iron plate touched in the middle spreads the force to the ends.*

### *Whether the power of the magnet is hindered by garlic.*
### CHAPTER XLVIII.

Now we must pass on to other properties of the magnet, and first, whether the magnet receives any hindrance in its attraction. Plutarch says that there is a very great disagreement between it and the magnet, which he calls <term>antipathy</term> <note>A traditional scientific concept meaning a natural "hatred" or repulsion between two substances, the opposite of "sympathy."</note>, and such a great hatred between these deaf and senseless things, that it drives iron away from itself if the stone is rubbed with garlic. Ptolemy confirms the same: that the magnet does not draw iron if it is smeared with garlic, just as <term>amber</term> <note>original: "succinum." Ancient writers often compared the magnetic properties of lodestone to the static electricity of rubbed amber.</note> no longer entices chaff or even the lightest things to itself if it is first soaked in oil. It is a common opinion among sailors that onions and garlic are opposed to the magnet; and those who are occupied with such duties—namely, the navigation charts and the <term>compass</term> <note>original: "pyxidi," referring to the nautical compass box.</note>—are kept away from eating onions and garlic, lest the indicator be tainted <note>original: "pollinebrietur." This suggests the "breath" of the garlic might muddle or "intoxicate" the needle's sense of direction.</note>. But when I put all these things to the test, I found them to be false; for not only did the breath and belching of garlic not distract the magnet from its duty of drawing iron, but when it was entirely smeared with garlic juice, it performed its functions just as well as if it had never been touched by garlic. Indeed, almost no difference was noted—I will not even say a minimal one—lest we seem to make the efforts of the ancients appear so utterly useless. Furthermore, when I inquired into the rumor of whether those who have eaten onions and garlic are expelled from the observation of the compass, they replied that these were old wives' tales and ridiculous reports; and that such men would sooner lose their lives than abstain from eating garlic and onions.

---

### *How a "drunk" magnet may return to its duty.*
### CHAPTER XLIX.

If the magnet should become "drunk" <note>original: "ebrius." Porta uses this metaphorically to describe a magnet that has lost its strength or has had its polarity confused.</note>, and should depart far from the performance of its duty—not, as we said, by the breath of garlic and onion, but rather by contact with other parts of a magnet, or because its old and faint power had vanished—we shall compel its vigorous and pristine strength to be restored in this way: by burying it in iron filings <note>original: "ferrea scobs."</note> for many days, until, from the company or the "breath" of the iron, it rightly performs its office once more.

### *How the power of the magnet may be increased.* 
### CHAPTER L.

There are very many and eloquent men who have attempted to increase the strength of the magnet, and in various ways, so that having obtained more vigorous powers, it might be useful for the greatest purposes.

<page-num>327</page-num>
->ON THE MARVELS OF THE MAGNET<-

Alexander of Aphrodisias <note>A famous Greek commentator on Aristotle (c. 200 AD) who often wrote on natural "problems."</note> asks at the beginning of his *Problems* for what reason the stone called the <term>magnet</term> <note>lodestone</note> attracts only iron, and is nourished or helped by iron filings. It is as if he were saying the magnet draws iron because it is fed by it; and the more a thing is nourished, the more vigorous it becomes, and for that reason, it is made stronger by iron filings. But when I wished to test this, I took a magnetic stone of a specific weight and buried it in iron filings of a known weight. When I had left it there for many months, I found the stone to be of greater weight and the filings of lesser weight; but the difference was so small that I am doubtful of the truth of it. Though the stone and the iron filings were of great weight, they caused an imperceptible tilt in the scale. 

**Paracelsus** <note>A famous Swiss-German physician and alchemist (1493–1541) known for his often controversial and mystical scientific claims.</note>, being well-acquainted with the art of distillation, attempted to achieve this in another way. He says that if one were to extinguish a red-hot stone in "oil of iron" <note>An alchemical preparation, likely a solution of iron salts or a concentrated acidic extract of iron.</note> multiple times, it would gradually resume its strength and increase so much that it could easily pull a nail fixed in a wall. Since this idea pleased me, I extinguished a red-hot stone in oil of iron and discovered that not only did it not gain strength, but it lost its own entirely. To ensure I had not performed the work poorly, I tested it many times and realized he had described a detestable falsehood. For a magnet, once made red-hot, loses its power, as we shall say hereafter.

### How the magnet loses its strength. CHAPTER LI.

I myself have found this single method to be the truest among the many handed down by writers: by piling the magnet with glowing coals. For once it is red-hot, it immediately loses its power. A spirit of a bluish-black color is seen, like that of sulfur, with a foul odor like that of coals. When the vapor itself and the flame have ceased to exhale, and it is removed from the fire, it has breathed out all its power. I have always judged that <term>soul</term> <note>original: "animam." Early scientists often used the word "soul" or "spirit" to describe the invisible force or "virtue" that gave a substance its unique properties.</note> to be the cause of the attraction of iron. Since iron consists of imperfect sulfur (according to **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the "Father of Chemistry," whose works laid the foundation for medieval alchemy.</note> and others who write on metals), that "soul" is the reason why it runs so rapidly to the iron and so greatly enjoys its company. Once that vapor has breathed out, the stone is then stripped of all its vigor; and where it has once lost that virtue, it is now a corpse that one attempts to revive in vain.
