### *How iron touched by a magnet loses its power.*
### CHAPTER LII.

In this very same way that a magnet does, iron also loses its power; for even if it has received power from a magnet in the best possible way, once it has been made red-hot <note>original: "ignitum"</note>, it also loses that virtue. Nor is the reason for this lacking: for, as we have said, that part of the magnet adhering to the iron <note>The author refers to the "magnetic quality" transferred to the iron as a physical substance or "part."</note>, when it loses its strength through fire, the iron, being stripped of it, also loses its power. Therefore, in a nautical compass <term>pyxide nautica</term> <note>Literally "nautical box"; the standard term for the mariner's compass in this period.</note>, or in other applications, when the iron has been saturated or tainted by contact with other things and does not possess its legitimate powers, we apply fire to it to free it from this imperfection. 

From this, the error of many is revealed, who, when they prepare an iron needle for a compass, first heat it to a glow and then rub it against the magnet, thinking that the magnet’s force will attract it more vehemently. But they not only do the opposite, they render the magnet so ineffective that it cannot even perform its duty; rather, that force is driven out of the iron by the fire, and only the natural power <note>original: "faciei virtus"</note> remains which it had before contact with the magnet. Thus, whenever that force is destroyed by fire, we can restore the same virtue to it by a new contact.

---

### *That it is false that a diamond hinders the powers of a magnet.*
### CHAPTER LIII.

We have said it is fabulous and false that a magnet rubbed with garlic loses its power; but it is far more false that its powers grow sluggish or dull in the presence of a diamond <term>adamantis</term> <note>The Latin *adamas* referred to the hardest known substances, specifically diamonds.</note>. For they say there is such distrust and contrary qualities, or dissimilarities, between the magnet and the diamond, and that they exercise such mutual hatred of their natures and burn with such blind discord, that when a diamond is brought near, the powers of the magnet are hindered as if by an enemy, and cease as if their duties were ended, and that the magnet faints in this hostile encounter until it lies silent and sluggish. 

**Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), whose *Natural History* was the primary source of scientific myths in the Renaissance.</note> says: *The diamond is at such odds with the magnet that if placed nearby, it does not allow iron to be pulled away; or, if the magnet has already seized the iron, the diamond snatches and carries it off.* <note>original: "Adamas diffidet cum magnete in tantum, vt iuxta positum ferrum non patiatur abstrahi, aut si magnes apprehenderit, rapiat, atque auferat."</note> **Saint Augustine** <note>Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), who often used the magnet as an example of God's mysterious power in *The City of God*.</note> says: *I will tell you what I read about that magnet: How, when a diamond is placed next to it...*

...it does not seize the iron, and if it has already seized it, as soon as the diamond approaches, it is immediately released. Marbodeus <note>Marbod of Rennes (c. 1035–1123), author of a famous medieval lapidary (a book on the properties of stones).</note> says of the diamond:

> All stones have an equal <note>original: "aqua," likely a transcription error for "aequa"</note> power to draw iron.

> For when the diamond is present, it takes away from the magnet that which it seizes.

When I had tested this many times, I found it to be a hollow claim, nor did it taste of even a small amount of truth. But there are many men of letters <note>original: "literatores"</note>—whom I have always considered ignorant and inept—who are forever striving to reconcile ancient writers and excuse their lies. They do not foresee how great a loss they inflict upon the Republic of Letters <note>The "Republic of Letters" refers to the long-distance intellectual community of the late 15th to 18th centuries.</note>. For more recent writers, leaning upon these foundations and believing them to be true, add their own ideas, write commentaries, and deduce other experiments from them. Since these are based on false principles, they produce the falsest results; the blind lead the blind, and both fall into the ditch. Truth must be investigated, cherished, and professed by all; nor should the authority of the ancients or of learned men turn people away from confessing the truth everywhere. 

But let us return to where the laziness of those "reconcilers" distracted me. Through experimentation, I took a small piece of magnet that weighed scarcely four grains <note>A grain is a traditional small unit of weight, roughly 65 milligrams.</note> and fixed iron filings <note>original: "scobem"</note> to it very tenaciously. Then I moved a diamond near it, which exceeded the size of both the magnet and filings three or four times over. In the diamond's presence, the magnet did not cast off the iron; I soon pulled the iron filings away from it, separated them by a fair distance, and even with the diamond still present, the magnet seized them back to itself. I have said this specifically so that those men would not think I was mistaken in my testing—perhaps by using a magnet of twenty or thirty pounds with an inch of iron attached, and then bringing a tiny diamond near it while I made trial of this matter.

## *That goat’s blood does not free the magnet from the diamond’s spell.* <note>original: "veneficio" – can mean poisoning, spell, or neutralizing effect.</note>

# CHAPTER LIV.

**W**e have said that the falsest things arise from false principles. It has already been stated above that a magnet smeared with garlic <note>original: "allio"</note> loses its power to attract iron, and that in the presence of a diamond, it drops the iron it has seized or fails to seize it at all. But because they say that goat’s blood <note>original: "hircinum sanguinem"</note> breaks a diamond, they claim that a magnet smeared with such blood recovers its strength...

...to hope for. Cassianus <note>Cassianus Bassus, a 6th-century Byzantine author who compiled the *Geoponica*, an encyclopedia of farming lore.</note> in the Greek *Geoponica* [says]: The loadstone <term>Magnes lapis: a naturally magnetized piece of the mineral magnetite</term> draws iron to itself, and conversely drives it away from itself if it is rubbed with garlic; but so that its nearly extinguished power might revive and be restored, it is washed in goat's blood. Rhennius, the translator of Dionysius <note>Referring to the Latin translation of Dionysius Periegetes' geographical poem.</note>:

> That which iron is least able to overcome, nor fire,
> Is broken only when soaked in goat's blood—
> But only when warm—after many anvils have been shattered before.
> This [stone], placed nearby, keeps the magnet from its powers;
> Having once seen it seize or draw iron toward it,
> It then draws it away, defending [the iron] with wondrous strength.

Marbodeus <note>Marbod of Rennes, whose 11th-century work *De lapidibus* was a standard text on the magical properties of stones.</note> says of the same:

> Its most solid hardness knows not how to yield,
> Despising iron, and tamable by no fire,
> Yet this stone, warmed by goat's blood, cracks—
> To the ruin of the anvil and the labor of the strikers.

Since, therefore, there is an antipathy <term>antipathy: a natural "dislike" or repulsion between two substances in nature</term> between the magnet and the diamond, and there is a similar sympathy between the diamond and goat's blood and the magnet, it was concluded from this argument that when the virtue of the magnet grows dull—either by the presence of a diamond or the stench of garlic—it recovers its former and more vigorous strength if it is washed in goat's blood. All of these claims have been found to be utterly false. For the diamond does not possess the hardness that is proclaimed, since it yields to iron and even a modest fire; nor does it soften with goat's blood, nor with camel's or donkey's blood. Our own jewelers consider these things to be fables and ridiculous. Nor is the lost power of a magnet restored by the blood of a goat. We have said all this so that we might show how false conclusions are born from false principles.

### *Iron touched by a diamond turns to the North. CHAPTER LV.*

But this is very true, which we discovered by chance while we were testing whether the diamond had the power to weaken the magnet by its presence, as we have mentioned. For if we rub an iron needle upon a diamond, and then arrange it fixed in a small boat <note>A common experimental setup involving a small piece of wood or cork floating in water to allow a needle to rotate freely.</note>, or stuck into a piece of straw, or suspended by a thread, it immediately turns toward the North, almost like iron touched by a magnet, though perhaps a bit more faint...

...much further. Nay, what is worthy of note, the opposite part, like the magnet itself, drives away iron toward the South <note>original: *Meridiem*</note>; and when we tested this with many iron needles <term>obelis: small pointed rods or needles</term> placed in water, they all showed the North <note>original: *Aquilonem*</note>, remaining parallel to one another. ### The Powers and Remedies of the Magnet. CHAPTER 56.

From this wonderful operation of the magnet's attraction, our ancestors devised many stories and derived many remedies, which were noted not at all unskillfully nor without reason. From this wondrous power, I say—which snatches and allures iron and magnets so they may seize each other—they attributed to it the character of Venus <note>the Roman goddess of love and attraction</note>. They believed that one followed the other with love, and that this "insane love" could not be dispelled unless one enjoyed the embraces of the other. Then, when they turn their backs and are seen to pursue each other with hatred, to shudder, and to expel one another, they believed even the hatred of a woman was contained therein. From these ideas, Marbodeus <note>Marbod of Rennes (c. 1035–1123), a bishop whose poem on the properties of gemstones was widely cited in the Middle Ages.</note> wrote:

> It can reconcile wives to their husbands,
> And in turn recall brides to their grooms:
> For he who desires to know if his wife be an adulteress,
> Should place the stone beneath the head of the sleeper.
> Soon she who remains chaste seeks to embrace her husband;
> Yet, without waking, every adulteress falls from the bed,
> As if pushed by a hand, compelled by a sudden stench,
> Which the stone emits as a witness to the hidden crime.

And for this reason, the ancients, to hint at this, very often engraved Venus upon the magnet, or fashioned her from the magnetic stone itself. Hence Claudianus <note>Claudian (c. 370–404 AD), a Latin poet whose poem *Magnes* describes a temple containing a magnetic statue of Mars and a diamond statue of Venus.</note> says:

> —The magnetic gem depicts Venus. <note>original: *Venerem magnetica gemma figurat.*</note>

I remember, moreover, many of the ancients saying that if a magnet is ground up and scattered over glowing coals in the corners of a house so that the smoke flies upward, those staying in the house will immediately flee; for the house appears to be collapsing, and terrified by these phantasms <term>phantasmatib.: illusions or hallucinations</term>, they leave everything and fly from the house...

### Marbod of Rennes:
<note>original: *Marbodeus*; a 12th-century bishop and poet known for his work on the properties of gemstones.</note>

> *If a thief, entering the enclosures of a house*
> *Filled with spoils and treasure, should place*
> *Burning coals throughout the rooms,*
> *And place fragments of a magnet upon those coals,*
> *So that the vapor of the smoke rises high through the four corners,*
> *With their minds overturned as if by an impending collapse,*
> *All who remain within shall flee in terror.*
> *And the thief shall safely seize whatever he pleases.*

The reason for this is that the magnet is "melancholic" <note>associated with the humor of black bile, which was thought to cause gloom and madness</note> as is inferred from its color. Its vapors, when inhaled and carried to the brain, induce terrible and melancholic phantasms in those who are sleeping; burning coals are known to produce the same effect. The weight of a *dauic* <note>original: *dauic*; likely a corrupted reference to a specific weight or a botanical substance like *daucus* (wild carrot)</note> combined with the fat of a serpent and the juice of a nettle, if given to someone to drink, makes them insane and drives them away from their people, their homeland, their dwelling, and their region; it works by exaggerating "black melancholy" <term>melancholy: one of the four ancient humors, believed to cause depression or madness when in excess</term>. Or, for those who hold it in their mouth, it will make them lunatic and melancholic. Furthermore, due to its ability to draw iron, physicians have believed that the magnet is effective for extracting iron arrowheads from the human body.

We also use the magnet in the making of glass. Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, the Roman naturalist</note> says: "After the origin of glass, as clever and ingenious skill was not content to have mixed in nitre <term>nitrum: a mineral salt, often soda or potash, used as a flux in glassmaking</term>, the magnet stone also began to be added; for it is believed to draw the liquid of the glass to itself just as it draws iron." Indeed, a small piece of magnet is added in the making of glass; certainly that singular power is believed in our times, just as in ancient ones, to draw the liquid of the glass to itself as it allures iron. Once drawn, it purifies the glass and turns it from green or yellow into a bright white; however, the fire later consumes the magnet, according to Agricola <note>Georgius Agricola, a 16th-century German scholar and "father of mineralogy"</note>. We also read that the magnet removes all pains from the head. Galen <note>the famous Greek physician of the Roman Empire</note> says it has purgative powers, which is why it is given in a drink to those with dropsy <term>hydropicis: people suffering from edema or fluid retention</term>, as it draws all fluid out from the belly. Finally, we shall not omit the error of Hadrian <note>likely referring to the Emperor Hadrian or a collection of questions attributed to him</note> in his inquiries concerning the magnet; for he says that iron adds no weight to the magnet by its own gravity. For naturalists say that if a strong magnet is weighed on a scale, and afterwards it attracts iron...

### On sleep-inducing medicines. CHAPTER I.

In order to describe the experiments we have mentioned in an orderly fashion, we have decided to begin with those ailments that occur in the head, and first with sleep. Indeed, hidden hypnotic secrets are sought after with great eagerness and are held in the highest esteem among Physicians for easing the pains of patients by means of sleep. They are of no less value to Leaders and Commanders of soldiers when they are devising stratagems against their enemies. These sleep-inducing medicines consist of things that are extremely cold and moist. Plutarch <note>Plutarch (c. 46 – 119 AD) was a Greek philosopher and biographer; his *Symposiacs* (Table Talk) discusses various scientific and philosophical questions.</note> says in his *Symposiacs* that sleep is caused by coldness, and for this reason, hypnotic drugs are thought to possess very great power. We shall first teach:

->*To induce sleep with Mandrake.*<-

Dioscorides <note>Pedanius Dioscorides (c. 40 – 90 AD) was a Greek physician and the author of *De Materia Medica*, the primary pharmacopeia of the ancient world.</note> says that men will fall asleep immediately in the same position they were in when they drank the mandrake <term>Mandrake (*Mandragora*): A plant in the nightshade family whose roots often resemble human limbs. In antiquity, it was used as an anesthetic, though in high doses it is toxic.</term>, with all their senses stripped away for three or four hours from the time they were dosed. Physicians use this when they wish to burn <note>original: "vrere" - referring to cauterization.</note> or cut someone. Skilled men also report that mandrake growing near grapevines transmits its sleep-inducing power into them, so that those drinking wine made from those grapes fall into a deep sleep more easily and readily. Here we shall recount stories of the mandrake from the authors of military stratagems, which are not unpleasant to hear. Julius Frontinus <note>Sextus Julius Frontinus (c. 40 – 103 AD) was a Roman civil engineer and author of *Strategemata*, a collection of military tricks.</note> records: Hannibal, sent by the Carthaginians against the rebelling Africans, knew that the nation was greedy for wine; he mixed a large quantity of mandrake into their supply—a substance whose power lies somewhere between a poison and a sedative. Then, after engaging in a light skirmish, he retreated by design. In the dead of night, leaving behind certain baggage and all the tainted wine in the camp, he feigned flight. When the Barbarians occupied the camp and, overflowing with joy, greedily drank the medicated wine <note>original: "merum" - unmixed or pure wine, which the Barbarians were known for drinking without dilution.</note>, they lay scattered about like dead men. Hannibal returned and captured and slaughtered them. Polyaenus <note>A 2nd-century Macedonian lawyer who wrote *Stratagems in War*.</note> relates the same. Also, Caesar, while sailing toward Nicomedia near Malea, was captured by Cilician pirates. When they demanded a great ransom for his release, he promised double the sum. They landed at Miletus, and the people rushed out from beyond the walls. Caesar [sent] Epicrates...

Its bark, drunk in wine in the weight of a drachm <term>Drachm: An ancient unit of weight, roughly equivalent to 3.5 grams or about a teaspoon of powder.</term>, possesses a sleep-inducing power, though it is gentle and wonderful. Indeed, they can be made into waters without smell or taste, inducing sleep so that the trickery cannot be detected, provided a small quantity of it is administered. When I had recently prepared such a water in a certain way and entrusted it to a friend for certain uses, [instructing] that he should administer no more than a drachm, he instead gave an ounce. The drinker lay for four days without food or movement, so that he was judged dead by everyone; nor could he be awakened by any efforts. Once the vapors had been digested <note>In early modern medicine, "digesting vapors" referred to the body processing and expelling the fumes produced by drugs or food that were thought to cloud the brain.</note>, he woke up, although Dioscorides warns that death may result from immoderate use. Therefore, we have judged it not unreasonable that when the sleeping faculty languishes, swollen by excessive drink, vapors are raised from the nature of the food. Then, from those things which abound in the body, images exult and are tossed about immoderately during sleep—such as various fires, darkness, hailstorms, and decay arising from yellow and black bile, or from cold and putrid humors <term>humors: the four fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) once believed to determine a person's health and temperament</term>. For the arteries of our body, says Galen, draw into themselves whatever closely surrounds them while they are continually dilating. It also helps to anoint the liver; for by evaporating upward from the stomach, the blood permeates to the liver, and from the liver suddenly to the heart. ## *Some most excellent remedies for the eyes.*

Therefore, since we see these things happening before our eyes, let us reason by the same principles that those suffering from stones can be similarly cured by nature through acids because of the sharpness of the juice." ### *A Remedy for Conceiving.*

When the menstrual flow has ceased, take a freshly laid egg, cook it, and mix in musk the weight of a grain of wheat; let the woman swallow this when she goes to bed. In the morning, put old beans—at least five years old—into a new pot and let them boil for a long time in water. As the woman rises from bed, she should receive the steam into her feminine parts, as if through a funnel, for the space of an hour. Soon, after drinking two soft-boiled eggs, she should return to bed, dry away the moisture with warm linens, and then have intercourse with her husband. Afterward, she should rest. Then, let her mix two egg whites with Armenian bole <term>Armenian bole (*bolus armenus*): a reddish medicinal clay used as an astringent.</term> and dragon's blood <term>Dragon's blood (*draconis sanguine*): a bright red resin obtained from certain plants, used in ancient medicine to stop bleeding.</term>. She should soak a linen cloth in this mixture and apply it to her kidneys <note>original: "renibus". In early modern medicine, the kidneys/loins were often associated with reproductive strength.</note>. Because it sticks with difficulty, it must be bound with bandages to prevent it from falling off. Soon she may rise from bed, but at night she should renew the same plaster. When sleep creeps in, she should keep ginger in her mouth. This should be carried out for nine days.

For this reason, we forced half a drachm of **theriac** <note>A famous ancient "polypharmacy" antidote consisting of dozens of ingredients, including viper flesh.</note> or **mithridatium** <note>A semi-mythical panacea named after King Mithridates VI of Pontus, who supposedly made himself immune to poisons.</note>, diluted with **aqua vitae** <note>original: "aqua vitæ." The balsam which they say is brought from the West Indies is especially effective against them; for when we smeared their throats and mouths with it, they died within the space of half an hour. **Aetius** <note>Aetius of Amida, a 6th-century Byzantine royal physician and medical writer.</note> says that the Eastern balsam is a prompt remedy for poison applied as an ointment, or for the bite of serpents. In Arabia, where it grows, all fear of poison is absent, and no one is killed by a bite; rather, it acts like a most precious ointment for the serpents that have fed on it, and the harm of the lethal poison is converted into a milder condition. 

But we have found nothing more excellent than the **earth of the island of Malta** <note>original: "terra insulæ Melitæ." Also known as "St. Paul’s Earth," this fossiliferous clay was highly prized as an antidote because of the legend that St. Paul blessed the island's soil after being bitten by a viper there.</note>; for even a tiny bit of the powder thrown into the mouth kills very quickly. We have found almost the same power in *lithoxylon* <note>original: "lithoxylon." Literally "stone-wood" or petrified wood, used in early medicine for its supposed astringent properties.</note>, which physicians use for children's worms. 

Then there is the toadstone, also called *chelonites* or what the French call *crapaudine* <note>original: "borax, siue chelonites, Galli crapodinam vocant." This "toadstone" was a mythical gem thought to be found inside the heads of old toads. In reality, these were often the fossilized button-like teeth of the prehistoric fish Lepidotes.</note>. They say it is found in the head of a large, old toad, and that if one extracts it while the toad is still alive, it is effective against poisons. They say it is taken from the living creatures by using a scarlet cloth, a color in which they take great delight; while they relax themselves as if on holiday, they set down the burden of their head. The stone then falls through a hole into a box placed beneath; otherwise, the toad swallows it back. 

However, I have found no one truthful who has actually extracted it this way, nor was I ever able to find one myself, though I have dissected many toads. Yet I affirm as true that those stones said to be extracted from bramble-toads are mineral in nature. I remember seeing in Rome a large piece of stone that consisted of many other small stones; they adhered to its back like **limpets** <note>original: "lepades." A type of aquatic snail that clings tightly to rocks.</note> to rocks, small and large, of various sizes. But its true power is this: if someone swallows it along with poison, it keeps them safe from harm, for it moves through the body with the poison and dulls its strength.

And its operation is wonderful. In the month of May, the flowers of **clove pinks** <note>original: "garyophylli flores." Meanwhile, let sugar be cooked: for every pound of petals, add three pounds of sugar into a bronze basin. Let them liquefy and boil in as little water as possible—distilled orange blossom water <note>original: "aqua... è floribus aranciorum stillatitia."</note> is best, so that it may be quickly consumed—until it is brought to the proper consistency. Pour in a sufficient amount of beaten egg white, which will serve for both the boiling and the **skimming** <note>original: "despumationi." The process of removing the "scum" or impurities that rise to the top of boiling sugar.</note>. Stir it and wipe away the swollen foam of the egg white with brushes until all impurities are removed by skimming.

Then, the weight of the crushed petals having been added, let them be stirred with a wooden spatula until they achieve a blood-red color. When we are near the end of the cooking, add two drachms of **cloves** <note>original: "garyophyllorum indicorum." Literally "Indian cloves," the dried spice buds, added here to reinforce the scent of the carnation petals.</note> ground into a very fine powder, along with a little **musk** <note>original: "moscho," a potent aromatic fixative derived from the musk deer.</note>, which by a friendly fellowship may add to and awaken the scent and grace of the flowers. Then let it be placed in earthenware vessels and preserved. If you add a few drops of lemon juice, they will please the eye with a more vivid blood-red color. We can also shape the mixture into diamonds or round **lozenges** <note>original: "placentulas."</note> by throwing it onto cold marble.

If anyone wishes to do this in a more excellent way, let the color be extracted from the flowers with water, and let the sugar be cooked in that dilution, for it will breathe more fragrantly. There are some who do not pound the flower petals but cut them with scissors into very thin hairs and preserve them with sugar, but they do not find favor with the palate. This confection finds great favor with the palate and will please most greatly with the most fragrant scent of clove pinks.

The powers we have experienced are these: it excels in all afflictions of the heart, namely **fainting** <note>original: "animi deliquium."</note> and tremors of the heart; for dizziness, for poisons, and the bites of venomous animals; and especially against the contagion of the **plague** <note>original: "pestilentiæ."</note>. A vinegar and a wash are also made from them; if anyone rubs their nostrils with these in the morning, it is useful for warding off the contagious air. This remedy also has value against nightly **catarrhs** <note>original: "distillationibus." Literally "distillations," referring to the fluid or "rheum" believed to flow from the head to the chest or throat.</note> and melancholic effects.

# NATURAL MAGIC, BOOK VIII.

### *Against the plague.*

In the month of May, you should gather **ivy berries** <note>original: "corymbos hederae."</note> and **wild poppies** before sunrise, so that they do not fly open; in April, gather **goat’s rue** <note>original: "galegam, siue rutam caprariam." *Galega officinalis*, traditionally used to treat infectious diseases.</note>. Let them be dried in the shade and ground into a powder; one drachm of this, swallowed with wine, is effective against the contagions of the disease. The **bezoar stone** <note>original: "Lapis bezoar." A mass found in the digestive tracts of certain animals, highly prized in the Renaissance as a universal antidote.</note> brought from the West Indies, if hung from the neck so that it dangles near the heart, or its powder administered in wine at a weight of four grains, is powerful against the contagions of the plague and pestilential fevers, as we have known; it also removes **syncope** <term>syncope: a temporary loss of consciousness caused by a fall in blood pressure; fainting.</term> and brings cheerfulness to the heart. Water or oil extracted from **citrus seeds** is a most powerful antidote against the plague. The oil of **Apparitius the Spaniard** <note>original: "Apparitij Hispani." Likely referring to a specific Spanish practitioner or a widely traded proprietary oil of the time.</note> has also been found by experience to be most excellent against the plague.

## *Remedies for wounds and blows.* CHAPTER XI.

There remain some remedies for wounds and blows which shall not be omitted, since I have experienced some of wonderful operation among them. First, we shall describe the **Spanish Oil** and many other remedies.

### *Spanish Oil.*

Take two pounds of new wax, four ounces of **sage**, the same amount of **linseed**, two ounces each of **rosemary flowers** and **laurel berries**, the same of **betony**, three ounces of **chamomile flowers** or its oil, an ounce and a half of **cinnamon**, the same amount of **St. John’s wort** <note>original: "hiperici."</note> or its oil, and two pounds of old oil. Let the flowers and herbs be dried in the shade, and when they have become dry, let them be pounded and passed through a sieve. Let the wax be melted by fire, then the oil is poured in, and soon after the powders, always mixing them with a **small rod** <note>original: "rudicula."</note>; finally, pour it out onto marble and cut it into small pieces. Place it in a curved glass vessel protected with **lute made of straw and clay** <note>original: "luto paleato." A common sealant for chemical apparatus to prevent cracking under heat.</note>, and let it be set to the fire with its receiver. Seal the joints tightly, removing every vent from those things enclosed within, so that the power does not fly away and vanish. At first, the water is received with a slow fire; soon, with the heat increased, you will receive the **red oil** in separate vessels; store these in covered containers for use. Its power is heating; it heals **callouses** <note>original: "callum."</note> that have grown hard from cold by bathing them, consolidates wounds by smearing, and is beneficial for contractions of the nerves...

## CHAPTER XIV.

It has been of no small benefit to some to have feigned illnesses, so that they might escape the hands of enemies, or be ransomed for a small price, or avoid the punishments of torture; a practice frequent among the ancients and accepted by modern use. We shall teach

### *How one may fake a flow of blood.*

**Amphiretus of Acanthus** <note>A figure mentioned in Polyaenus's "Stratagems"</note>, captured by pirates and taken to **Lemnos** <note>An island in the northern Aegean Sea</note>, was kept in chains, as the pirates hoped for a great sum of ransom money. When he therefore emptied his bowels, the pirates, thinking he had fallen into a **bloody flux** <note>original: "sanguinis fluxum"; a term for dysentery or internal hemorrhaging</note>, released him from his chains, lest he depart from life due to the disease, and thus their hoped-for money perish. Being freed, he fled by night, and having boarded a fishing boat, reached **Acanthus**. This is from **Polyaenus** <note>original: "Poliano"; a 2nd-century Macedonian author known for his "Stratagems in War."</note>. The fruit of the **Indian fig** <note>likely the prickly pear cactus, *Opuntia ficus-indica*</note>, which like mulberries stain the hands when ripe, if eaten, return bloody urine, which has struck terror into many, believing they were about to perish on the spot. The fruit of mulberries, or cooked and eaten pig’s blood, tints the stool with gore. ...whose marks, he says, are a **double pupil** <note>original: "pupillā geminam"; a physical trait often associated in folklore with the ability to bewitch.</note> in one eye, and in the other the image of a horse; of which Didymus also makes mention. Nor is he of a different kind: Damon described a medicine in Ethiopia whose sweat brings wasting to bodies it touches, and it is evident that all women who have double pupils also bewitch with their sight. Cicero also writes of them, as do Plutarch and Phylarchus regarding the bewitching people of the Paletheobei <note>A group mentioned in classical texts, likely referring to the Thibii or similar tribes of the Black Sea region (Pontus) reputed to have the evil eye.</note> inhabiting Pontus; they are pestilential not only to little children, whose nature is weak, but to adults who are composed of a solid and more compact body; and by their gaze and mere appearance, they cause others to languish into diseases that destroy them and dissolve them into wasting. Not only those nearby, but even strangers and those most distant from their dealings are shaken; such is the power and fascination of the eyes. Although it is often initiated through contact and mingling, it is nevertheless completed through the eyes; so that it is a certain emission of **spirit** <term>spiritus: in early medicine, these were "animal spirits," thin vapors in the blood that carried sensation and motion through the body.</term> reaching through the eyes to the heart of the bewitched person, infecting the whole.

For so it happens that a young man endowed with thin, clear, warm, and sweet blood gives off such spirits when they arise from the purer blood by the heat of the heart; because the lightest spirits arrive in the higher part of the body and fall forth and are darted through the eyes, which are the most porous, veiny, and bright of all parts. And together with the spirit itself, a certain fiery force is emitted in rays, so that those looking at red and bleary eyes are forced to suffer from a similar disease. This happened to me and brought me harm: for it infects the air, which being infected, infects another; thus, that which is closest to the eyes carries with it the vapor of corrupted blood, by whose contagion the eyes of the beholder are affected with a similar redness. 

Thus the wolf takes away the voice, and thus the **basilisk** <term>regulus: literally "little king," the classical name for the basilisk, a mythical serpent said to kill with its gaze.</term> takes away life; it stirs up poison by its sight and strikes virulent blows with its rays, yet with a mirror they are thrown back upon their author by a reciprocal darting. Thus the polished mirror dreads the gaze of an **unclean woman** <note>original: "immundæ mulieris"; a reference to the Aristotelian belief that a menstruating woman's gaze could stain a mirror.</note>, as Aristotle reports, and by her look it grows filthy and its brightness is dimmed. This happens because the bloody vapor unites on the surface of the mirror due to its smoothness, so that it is covered with a certain small stain and is clearly shown; indeed, if it is a new mirror, you will wash it off with great difficulty—which does not happen on cloth or stone because...

<meta>This page continues the scientific and philosophical explanation of fascination—the "Evil Eye"—started on page 357. Having established that certain people possess a physical power to bewitch through their gaze, the author now explains the physiological mechanism: how "spirits" emitted from the eyes of one person physically enter and corrupt the blood of another.</meta>

<page-num>358</page-num>

...receives <note>The word begins on the previous page as "exce-"; "excepit" means "receives" or "catches."</note> it, because it creeps into him and descends into the depths; whereas in the other, it is scattered by the disharmony of the parts. But a mirror, because it stands as a stubborn obstacle, and because it is polished, preserves the reflection unbroken; and because it is cold, it generates droplets from the condensed air. In much the same way, if you breathe upon a clear glass, the surface is moistened by a spray of saliva-like dew, which, gathering together, flows back into a liquid. So too is the flow of rays from the eyes, which, acting as vehicles for the **spirits** <term>spiritus: in Renaissance medicine, these were thin, vaporous substances that linked the soul to the physical body.</term>, reaches the eyes of the one they meet. It pierces through and strikes the inner parts of the man, affecting him and seeking its own home. Since these spirits originate from the heart, they are compressed into blood at the edges of the victim's heart. This foreign blood, being discordant with the nature of the bewitched man, consumes the rest of the body with wasting, from which he falls ill. The contagion remains as long as the force of the warm blood thrives in the limbs. And since it is an affliction of the blood, he is tormented by a never-ending fever; if the illness were in the bile or phlegm <note>The "humors" of the body; illnesses caused by bile or phlegm were thought to be intermittent, like malaria, rather than constant.</note>, it might perhaps subside at intervals.

But so that all things may be made more clearly manifest, it must first be known that two kinds of fascination are found among authors: one of love, and another of envy and malevolence. If, indeed, it is provoked by a longing for beauty and the harmony of form, although the "dart" is shot from a distance, the poison is drunk in through the eyes. The specter of the beautiful form resides in the heart of the lover and kindles little fires, from which he is constantly afflicted. And because the softest blood of the beloved wanders there, it represents their face and shines back with its own blood; the lover finds no rest in himself and is thus drawn to the other, just as the blood of a wounded man flows toward the one who struck him. **Lucretius** <note>Titus Lucretius Carus (c. 99–55 BC), a Roman poet and philosopher.</note> rightly suggests this:

> *That body it seeks, from whence the mind is wounded by love,*
> *For almost all fall toward their wound: and in that direction*
> *The blood spurts out, from whence we are struck by the blow:*
> *And if the foe is near, the red humor occupies the face.*
> <note>original: "Idq; petit corpus, mens unde est saucia amore, / Namq; omnes plerunq; cadunt in vulnus: & illam / Emicat in partem sanguis, unde icimur ictu: / Et si cominus est, os tum ruber occupat humor."</note>

If, however, it is a matter of envy and malevolence, whoever is infected by such a virus suffers a very harmful bewitching, found most often in old women. Nor can anyone deny that a distressed mind may cause the body to fare poorly, while a determined mind strengthens the body's powers and makes them more potent. Not only does it change its own body, but it renders another's different; and it does this all the more when the interior fires of vengeance or desire in the heart...

...they stir <note>The Latin "corde cient" completes a sentence from the previous page: "spirits... stir from the heart."</note> from the heart. Does not greed, sorrow, or love change one's colors and appearance? Does not envy clothe the body in a distinct paleness and extreme thinness? Does not the craving of a pregnant woman infect the tender fetus with the mark of the desired thing? <note>A common Renaissance belief that a mother's strong desires or fears could physically mark her unborn child.</note> Thus, when a person turns eyes burning with envy and grim looks, and the ruinous desire to harm flashes more sharply from the eyes, and an internal fire proceeds from them, they inflict evil upon the bodies of those standing nearby—especially the beautiful ones. The sharp gaze of the eyes pierces like a weapon, scorches the vitals, and causes wasting, especially if the victims are of a **choleric** or **sanguine** temperament <note>Two of the four "humors" or personality types in ancient medicine. Choleric people were thought to be hot and dry; sanguine people were hot and moist.</note>: for because of the opening of the pores and the thinness of the humors, the disease easily consumes them.

Nor is it only from passion that the body becomes so, but it is easy to find that poison can exist in the human body, as **Avicenna** <note>original: "Auicenna"; a 10th-century Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard European textbook for centuries.</note> proves: many are endowed with such a nature, which should not seem strange, since it has often been seen that this can be done by art. A girl of remarkable beauty was sent to **Alexander** <note>Alexander the Great.</note> by the Queen of the Indians, smeared with and fed upon the venom of serpents, as **Aristotle** relates and Avicenna writes on the testimony of Rufus. **Galen** <note>A prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire.</note> however, mentions another woman who could consume **henbane** <term>hyoscyamus: a highly poisonous plant in the nightshade family used in small doses as a sedative.</term> without harm, and another who took **aconite** <term>aconitum: also known as wolfsbane or monkshood, an extremely lethal poison.</term>, so that even a hen would not approach her. 

And by frequent use of it (as we have learned from the records of the ancients), **Mithridates**, King of Pontus, rendered himself so immune to poison that when he wished to commit suicide by poison to avoid surrendering to the Romans, he felt no harm from the poison he took. <note>This practice of taking small, non-lethal doses of poison to build immunity is still called "mithridatism."</note> If you give a hawk hens fattened on the flesh of snakes and lizards, or on wheat boiled in their broth, it accelerates the shedding of feathers; many other things happen besides, which would take too long to list. 

Thus, many men are by their very nature able to cure certain illnesses by touch; many who eat spiders and oleander treat snake bites as nothing, nor do they feel any decay, if they share a similar nature. Their gaze or the breath they exhale emaciates not only humans but also small plants, herbs, and other things, so that they wither away completely; and often where such animals dwell, parched crops are seen dried up, having partaken of the poison, by nothing other than the power of the eyes and the belching forth of a certain vapor. Do not women, during the time of their monthly periods, <insert>spoil</insert> cucumbers and melons by touch...

### ON MEDICINAL EXPERIMENTS

...having slipped through my eyes to the innermost parts, they kindle a most sharp fire in my very marrow. Now, we have provided no small root for those seeking the truth; unless you are completely out of your mind, you will be able to prove this with many examples. 

If it should perhaps seem a wonder to some—when considering diseases that arise from contagion, such as the itch, the mange, or epidemic eye-inflammation <note>original: "lippitudinem epidimiam," likely referring to contagious conjunctivitis.</note>—that if a disease infects a bystander through touch, sight, or speech, and easily spreads its decay, why should "amatory contagion" <note>The idea that falling in love is a literal infectious disease passed through the eyes.</note>, the most serious plague of all diseases, not immediately invade men and consume them within? Nor does this fall back upon others alone, but upon the senders themselves as well, for they attract the very spell <note>original: "fascinum"</note> they have sent out. 

It is also recorded in the writings of the ancients concerning Eutelidas, who, through reflections—whether in water, a mirror, or springs leaping back and twisting the image back toward the viewer—brought the destruction of a spell upon himself. As the author says:

> Eutelidas, seeing his own form in the swirling river, 
> fell into a grievous and painful sickness.
<note>original Greek: "Ευτελίδα ἀνἀγ' βκαίρειν ἰδῶν ὀλόφισις αἵνης / Δινή ἐντι ποταμῷ..." This refers to a legend where a man named Eutelidas fascinated himself after seeing his reflection.</note>

He appeared so beautiful to himself that he fell under the same spell as others, and thus he lost his former healthy appearance and paid the penalty for his peculiar death. In the same way, children often harm themselves with their own "fascination," though parents usually attribute the cause to sorcerers and bewitchers. Now, however, receive:

Remove the cause from which the affection usually grows: interrupt your habits, shun idleness, and apply the mind to serious cares. Furthermore, expel blood, sweat, and excrement in large amounts, so that the harmful vapor <note>The "aura" or spirit of the other person that has infected the blood.</note> may be cast out at once. And there also exist the opposites of the first things. Now, however, receive:

->*An Amulet against the Spell of Envy*<-

If it be the witchcraft of the envious, you shall recognize it thus: the victim will lose their color, raise their eyes with difficulty (always looking downward), and heave frequent sighs. ## How blonde or golden hair may be dyed.

### for making hair golden

Let an oil be extracted from honey by the art of distillation, as we shall teach; first a clear water will come out, soon a saffron-colored one, and finally a golden one. We shall use this by smearing the hair with a sponge, but let it not touch the skin, for it will be stained saffron-yellow and the color is not easily washed off. This remedy is more noble than the others because the dye lasts for many days and even colors gray hair, which is a property granted to few. Let all these be put into an earthenware vessel and boil until the water subsides by three fingers' breadth; let the hair be thoroughly washed with this. You shall then expose the hair to the sun, and afterward, placing sulfur over hot coals, you shall fumigate the hair; while it burns, let the hair receive the breath of the smoke through a narrow vent at the bottom, being covered all around with a cloth so the smoke does not escape.

## To turn the hair red

### *How gray hair may be dyed black.*

If you smear your hair in the sun with **leeches** <note>original: "sanguifugis"</note> that have been left to rot in the darkest possible wine for sixty days, the hair will become pitch black. Alternatively, let a **sextary** <note>A Roman unit of volume roughly equivalent to a pint</note> of leeches rot for the same number of days in a lead vessel with two sextaries of vinegar, and apply it to the hair as we described. **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), a Roman author and naturalist</note> stated that this mixture has such a powerful staining force that unless those who are applying the dye keep oil in their mouths, it will even blacken their teeth. If you wish, however,

### *To make the hair long and black.*

Take a green lizard and, having removed the head and tail, boil it down in common oil; then anoint the head with such a mixture. You shall also have

### *Another method.*

With this method, you can conveniently dye just the beard or the hair if they are turning gray. Mix **litharge** <gloss>tamen</gloss> <note>original: "argentea spuma", literally "silver foam," a term for lead monoxide</note> and burnt copper with four times the amount of strong **lye** <term>Lixivium: A strong alkaline solution made from wood ashes, used as a caustic or a mordant</term>; while it is bubbling over gentle coals, wash the hair with it, and once dried, rinse it with warm water. We have used this according to the desire of the ancients. We made a lye from oak ashes and quicklime, which the common people call **capitellum** <note>A technical term for the strongest, most concentrated form of lye</note>; in this, we boil down silver **litharge** <gloss>lithargyrum</gloss>. Then, we test it with a piece of white wool: for if the wool is dyed black as desired, remove it from the fire; if not, keep boiling it. If it eats away at the wool, add water; if it does not dye it enough, add more litharge. Wash your hair or beard with this; it dyes gray hairs a shiny black color, and the **trick** <note>original: "fraus", referring to the cosmetic deception</note> is never detected, for the more you wash it, the more brilliantly black it becomes.

### *A common depilatory.*

This is used everywhere in the public baths. ->*to delay the growth of hair,*<-

The same thing happens with **hemlock** <note>original: "cicutæ"</note> juice. In olden times, by rubbing the root of a **hyacinth** on the pubes of boys, they prevented hair from growing. Because of this, it is well known in the trade of **slave-merchants** <note>original: "mangoniciis vænalitijs," referring to those who "beautified" slaves to increase their sale value</note>, for when smeared with sweet wine, it restrains puberty and does not allow hair to break out. ->*for hair to grow back no more,*<-

In which matter we have certainly labored not a little, and have tested many things which we found to be false. The area must first be bathed with hot water, and the hairs plucked one by one with women’s tweezers; then **saltpeter** <note>original: "salnitrum"</note> must be dissolved in water and smeared into the hair follicles. Thus we make women's foreheads broader, and we have depilated even "hotter" <note>likely referring to more sensitive or private areas</note> regions.

->To remove the moths that cut the hair. CHAPTER VI.<-

**T**here is a certain plague of the hair which, by invading it, wears it down and cuts it so as to leave the head bare. I will immediately list the remedies by which it may be removed. It will be beneficial for these effects to add bitter medicines so that the moths <note>original: "tineæ," referring to hair-eating mites or fungal infections like tinea capitis</note>, also called "sirens" <note>original: "sirenes," a historical term for hair-boring parasites or mites</note>, may be slaughtered. ## How a radiant or silvery face may be produced.
### CHAPTER XII.

A face is rendered not only radiant, but silvery, by those things we have mentioned which possess a silvery color—even if they are not truly made of silver, they shine as if with a silvery luster. There is a herb commonly called <term>silverweed</term> <note>original: "argentaria" or "argentina," likely *Potentilla anserina*, known for the silvery down on the underside of its leaves</note>, the leaves of which are green on top but shine with a silvery brightness on the reverse. Women drink the distilled water of this plant for facial spots and to induce a silvery glow. <term>Snails</term> <note>original: "cochleæ," specifically land snails known for their mucin</note>, which are found in damp places and leave silvery tracks behind as they crawl (Dioscorides said they mend defects in the face), are greatly sought after by women. For when they are placed in a distilling vessel, a water is drawn out which excellently polishes the skin and contracts it, so that it seems to shine with a silvery brightness. Also the <term>sea-ear</term> <note>original: "auris marina," the abalone shell</note>, whose shell is silvery or the color of pearls inside, and many species of snails which, when soaked in vinegar, lose their outer crust and become clean and shining like <term>pearl-bearing oysters</term> <note>original: "cochleæ margaritiferæ"</note>. There are also shells which we call <term>mother-of-pearl</term> <note>original: "vnionum matres," literally "mothers of unions," where "unio" refers to a large, unique pearl</note>, which are silvery and shining on the inside like pearls. Women use all of these in their <term>cosmetic washes</term> <note>original: "fuços," refers to preparations used to color or beautify the face</note>, for they make the polished face shine with a silvery splendor. But the best among all things...

But no water is prepared more excellently than that made from talc or quicksilver, as we shall describe in what follows.

### How talc may be dissolved for women's cleansers.
### CHAPTER XIII.

Although in the work dedicated to this subject we shall speak more broadly on how talc is dissolved into water or oil, here we will teach only how to prepare it for the use of women. From the methods that are circulated, we will set down those we have found most useful. Crush the talc with a metal pestle, then arrange it in a pot made of very strong clay; with a lid placed on, bound with iron wires and smeared with mud, the vents must be fortified so that nothing escapes. Set it in the sun to be dried. Afterwards, place it in a stone furnace where flames burst forth, or elsewhere, provided the fire is most violent. When the furnace has ceased to burn, take it out and break the vessel; if you find it is already reduced into <term>lime</term> <note>original: "calcem," the powdery residue left after a mineral is "calcined" or burned to remove impurities</note>, you will know it is best. If not, do not be reluctant to do it again and spend equal effort until the whiteness sought for lime appears. When the lime has become perfectly white, grind it on <term>porphyry marble</term> <note>original: "porphyretico marmore," a very hard purple stone used by apothecaries for grinding fine powders</note>, put it into a small bag, or let it remain for a long time on marble in a very damp place—such as a very deep well or a cistern—and you will see it flow out drop by drop from the excessive humidity. For it is dissolved into water more easily and perfectly if it has been burned longer and turned into lime; for parts reduced to lime and dried by the force of fire draw in water. It is also done in

-> another way <-

which is not useless. Reduce the talc to lime, and having put it in a pot, let it remain for six days in a glassmaker's furnace, where the fire rages most. ## The preparation of sublimated quicksilver. CHAPTER XIV.

We have said that no thing can be found more excellent for women’s <term>cleansers</term> <note>original: "smegmata," a Greek-derived term for soaps or detergent unguents used to scrub the skin</note>—specifically for both scouring away impurities and bestowing a luster—than <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argentum viuum," known today as mercury. While highly toxic, it was prized in the Renaissance for its ability to aggressively "whiten" the skin by peeling the top layers</note>. Therefore, we will set down several ways of preparing it, so that you may enjoy them as you desire. Take an ounce and a half of legitimate quicksilver, not adulterated with lead; for if lead has been mixed in, you will waste both your oil and your labor. We have stated elsewhere how it may be purified and recognized. Mix this with half a pound of <term>sublimated quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argenti viui sublimati," likely mercuric chloride, a white crystalline powder</note> and place it in a marble mortar. You shall stir it with a new wooden pestle, rubbing it in a circle. At first it turns black; within six hours it becomes white, if you do not cease your rubbing. Then add an ounce and a half of white salt, always rubbing with the pestle, for the longer you grind it, the more perfect you will make it. When it is thoroughly ground, it must be washed. Sprinkle boiling, clear water into the mortar and stir it up; let it rest for a moment until the muddy part settles. Then, by tilting the vessel sideways, slowly pour off the water along with the filth which is lighter and has risen to the top. Pour more water over it and do the same five or six times, until a pure and unadulterated powder remains, free from filth. You shall gather this into small cakes and see that they are dried in the Sun. There are some who, while they are grinding, sprinkle on water so that the powder does not fly away from the friction...

Then, when water is poured on, whatever dross there is will rise to the surface and flow out more easily. Then, when the sublimated mercury has been washed so that it settles, the previous water is poured off and new water is added, and they wash it; they do this repeatedly until it seems sufficient to those washing it and no blackness floats on top. But none is more excellent, as we have said, than

### *Mercury water.*

There are those who cannot endure sublimated quicksilver because of the harm it usually inflicts upon the teeth <note>Mercury poisoning causes the gums to recede and teeth to loosen or fall out</note>, but they use the water instead. Truly, no better water is prepared than that extracted from quicksilver, clear and transparent. For when the face is smeared with it, it shines, becomes white, and glows with a silvery brilliance; it tightens the skin and immediately makes it soft, nor has it been my lot to see any more excellent. The method of extraction has already been made clear.

...so that women may achieve their desired appearance. Finally, we come to the business of <term>white lead</term> <note>original: "cerussas," a white pigment made from lead, highly valued for its opacity but known today to cause lead poisoning</note>. Take some hog’s fat, well-washed and cleansed with common water at least ten times; place it in a lye of fresh water, and after fifteen days, submerge the fat in a jug or a wide-mouthed earthenware basin filled with the sharpest possible vinegar, so that the vinegar stands three fingers' breadth above it. Then, fix a lead plate over the mouth of the earthenware vessel, sealing the joints with glued linen cloths so that the vinegar's vapor does not escape. Every fifteen days, the seal is loosened and it is inspected to see if the lead has been dissolved; scrape off what has formed (as if a layer of mold had been laid upon it), replace the lid, seal it around, and leave it for the same amount of time. Perform the rest as we have described above until all the lead has been dissolved into white lead. The white lead must be washed in this way: pour water into a basin, submerge the white lead, and move it back and forth so that any impurities, if there be any, rise to the top. Because white lead is heavy, it seeks the bottom; pour off the liquid floating on top into a vessel, add new water, and do this repeatedly until the pure white lead is found to be free of dross, then store it once dried. Then, let the vessel be blocked with a lead plate—ideally arched or at least not flat—and let it have no vent. Let it sit in the sun, half-buried in sand. After the tenth day, when the lid with which you blocked the vessel is removed, the white lead clinging to it is brushed off with a feather and scraped away. Caesar writes of those about to go into battle, who stained themselves with the herb woad <note>original: "glasto," the plant *Isatis tinctoria*, famous for its blue dye</note>, which was called *isatis* by Theophrastus and is called *guado* by us. ## *To wash away excessive redness of the face.*
### CHAPTER XVIII.

We have spoken of how the face may be colored; now, however, we speak of how it may be de-colored—specifically when an excessive redness takes over the body, as is experienced by very ruddy women. Take this method, by which we are able to
->*wash away excessive redness of the face.*<-
Take four ounces of peach kernels and two ounces of cleaned pumpkin seeds; grind them and press them strongly to draw out an oily liquid. With this, touch the red spots <note>original: "carbunculos," here referring to inflamed blotches or pimples rather than deep infections</note> and redness of the face morning and evening, and they will gradually disappear and be corrected. Take
->*another.*<-
Let purple violets, eggshells, glass foam <note>original: "vitri spuma," the dross or scum collected from molten glass, often used in early modern recipes for its mineral properties</note>, and camphor, diluted with water, be distilled. Keep the water under the open sky <note>original: "sub dio," a common practice in alchemy and pharmacy to "charge" a liquid with celestial influence or dew</note>, and wash the redness with it. Furthermore, we know that the distilled water of white lilies extinguishes redness.

## *How you shall restore a face burned by the sun to whiteness.*
### CHAPTER XIX.

When women walk about in the open air and make journeys in the summer, a darkness <note>original: "nigredo," referring here to a sun-tan or sun-scorch</note> is induced in the skin from even a single day’s exposure to the sun, which is very difficult to dispel. For this, we have devised this
->*Proven Remedy.*<-
Beat about ten egg whites until they turn to water; to these, add an ounce of sugar candy <note>original: "sacchari cadi"</note> in a sealed glass vessel. When you go to bed, smear the face with it, and in the morning wash it off with spring water. Pliny also records...

->**Another.**<-

The face itself, when smeared with the white of eggs, is not burned by the sun. Among us, women who are busy defending their faces from the heat of the sun so that they do not become dark, before they walk under the sun, they "armor" <note>original: "loricant," implying a protective coating or breastplate</note> their faces with egg whites beaten with a little starch <note>original: "amyli"</note>; once the journey is finished, they wash off that plastered work with barley water. There are those who achieve the same thing 
->*in another way.*<-
By rubbing the skin with melon rinds, you will easily wipe away sunspots and other blemishes made upon the surface of the skin. Even the seeds, crushed and rubbed on, will perform this more effectively. Also, the liquid found in the follicles of the elm <note>original: "folliculis vlmi," referring to the small galls or pouches formed on elm leaves by aphids, which contain a sticky fluid</note> at the first bursting of the buds, when smeared on the skin, brings about a luster, makes the face more spendid, and removes spots contracted from the sun.

### How spots may be removed from the face. CHAPTER XX.

Spots very often disgrace the faces of beautiful women; this sort of disgrace must be countered by using cleansers, just as one uses detergents in the whitening of faces. Therefore,
->*to remove spots from the face,*<-
Smear the spots with oil of tartar <note>original: "tartari oleo," a concentrated solution of potassium carbonate, not a true oil</note> and allow it to dry; protect the area from all washing for ten days, then wash the place with lye <note>original: "lixiuio"</note>, and you will see the spots no longer. If the area is not yet polished, do not be loath to bestow similar effort again. If this does not please you, take
->*another.*<-
Plunge quicklime <note>original: "Viuam calcem," calcium oxide</note> into hot water, mix it, and stir it ten times a day; after two days, pour the clear water into another copper vessel. Afterward, take sal ammoniac <note>original: "salem ammoniacum," ammonium chloride</note> with your fingertips and rub it against the bottom of the vessel for so long until you see the water colored with a cyan hue; and the more you rub, the more it will be colored, and it will change into a sky-blue and sea-colored <note>original: "halurgum," likely from the Greek for sea-purple or salt-dyed</note> hue, than which nothing more pleasant could be seen by the eyes. Moisten linens with this water and apply them over the spots until they dry, moistening them again and again until the spots are abolished.

### For polishing the face.

Take three parts of sowbread root <note>original: "Cyclamineæ radicis," a plant in the primrose family traditionally used in medicine and cosmetics</note>, six parts of peeled barley, one part of tartar reduced to lime <note>potassium bitartrate collected from wine barrels and burned into a white powder</note>, two parts of powdered wild cucumber root, and as much wheat bran as can be held in the hands. Let them all boil in water until a third of the liquid is consumed; afterward, wash the face.

## How skin eruptions <term>impetigines | a general term used in the Renaissance for various scaly or weeping skin conditions, including eczema, psoriasis, or ringworm</term> are removed from the face or other parts of the body. CHAPTER XXII.

Skin eruptions disfigure the face so much that nothing more foul or hideous can be seen. Sometimes they invade other parts of the body, such as the armpits and thighs, dripping a foul water that stains the clothing. Against these, we have found:

### For skin eruptions.

From the roots of sharp-pointed dock <note>original: "oxylapathi," also known as monk’s rhubarb</note> let water be extracted drop by drop; to each pound of this, you will add half an ounce of musk melons and saltpeter <note>original: "halinitri"</note>, and two ounces of white wine tartar. Let them soak for several days, then distill it. Wash the face with this in the morning, and in the evening, smear it with oil of tartar and almond oil mixed together. Nor will the application of oil of eggs be useless for driving these away. But sometimes skin eruptions are so wild that they can be healed by no medicine; we shall add:

### Another.

Which we have very often used with wonderful success, even in long-standing cases. In a vial of harsh red wine, boil down a drachm of mercury sublimate <note>original: "argenti viui sublimati," or corrosive sublimate, a highly toxic mercury compound used historically as a powerful, though dangerous, disinfectant</note>; then wash the area in the evening and the morning, and allow it to dry by itself. This should be repeated three or four times, and the eruptions are abolished, never to return anywhere. You will also have:

### Another.

Take three ounces of saltpeter, two pounds of bitter almond oil, half a pound of squill <note>a medicinal sea-onion</note>, and one pound of lemon pulp. Mix them and let them sit for three days until they break down; then, with chemical instruments <note>original: "chymisticis organis," referring to a distillation apparatus or a press</note> extract the oil. By smearing the skin eruptions with this, they are abolished, even if they seem ready to turn into leprosy <note>original: "lepram," which in this period often referred to any severe, scaly skin condition rather than specifically Hansen's disease</note>.

### How warts may be destroyed. CHAPTER XXIII.

Warts, calluses, and other such skin deformities are accustomed to occupying the forehead, nose, hands, and other exposed places; women especially tend to loathe them. Against these skin defects, we have discovered these remedies. First:

->against warts,<-

The ancients used the "greater helioscope" <note>original: "helioscopio maiore," likely a species of spurge such as *Euphorbia helioscopia*, known for its milky, caustic sap</note>, the juice of which, when smeared on with salt, removes them; for which reason they also called it the wart-herb <note>original: "verrucaria"</note>. There is also a species of chicory called "wart-weed" from its effect: for those who have eaten it in a salad only once, all warts are abolished from whatever part of the body, or if a drachm of the seeds is swallowed. But we

->another<-

will provide another remedy, and with it we are satisfied. There is a type of beetle <term>scarabei | likely an oil-beetle of the genus Meloe, which produces a blistering agent called cantharidin</term> that is found during the summer in the dusty sands of roads, and it is oily. If you rub this against warts, they are destroyed immediately, so that not even a trace of them remains; they can be sought out and preserved for when needed.

### On Tooth Powders. CHAPTER XXV.

Among the cosmetic arts <note>original: "mangonia", referring to the "tricks" or "deceptions" of a trade, here meaning the art of beautification</note> of women are tooth powders; for they think nothing more shameful in women than when they laugh or speak, they show rough, rusty teeth covered in stains. ### How the growth of the breasts may be prevented.
### CHAPTER XXXVI.

Among the ornaments of women, this is considered especially excellent: to have small, round, solid breasts, not loose or wrinkled from childbirth. Thus we are able to

#### *Prevent the growth of the breasts,*

if we wish. Let hemlock <term>cicuta | a highly poisonous plant used in antiquity as a topical cooling agent to suppress growth</term> be crushed, and its pulp <note>original: "magmata", the residue of a crushed plant after the juice is expressed</note> be applied to the breasts of young girls with vinegar; thus they restrain them so that they do not allow them to grow, especially during maidenhood—although this may deny the milk at the usual time. But if you wish

#### *To firm up soft and sagging breasts.*

White clay, egg white, unripe oak gall <term>omphacitis galla | oak galls harvested while green, valued for their high tannin content</term>, mastic, and frankincense should be ground, mixed with warm vinegar, and smeared on the breasts; let them remain there for an entire night. If it is not effective enough, repeat the work. To this end, the following also help: medlar seeds, unripe serviceberries, wild plums, acacia, pomegranate rind <term>malicorium | the thick, astringent skin of the pomegranate</term>, pomegranate flowers <term>balauſtium | the flower of the wild pomegranate</term>, unripe pine nuts, wild pears, and plantain; if all these are boiled in vinegar and applied to the breasts, according to some authors. In ancient times, the Naxian whetstone <note>original: "cos naxia", a sharpening stone from the island of Naxos</note>—which we use for sharpening iron—was praised for this purpose, to restrain the breasts of virgins, and it did not allow them to increase in size, according to Dioscorides. Galen, however, said it not only prevents the growth of the breasts, but also prevents the testicles of boys from growing. # BOOK TEN OF THE NATURAL MAGIC OF GIAMBATTISTA DELLA PORTA OF NAPLES,

->*It distills, and raises distilled things to the height of their powers.*<-

## PREFACE.

<image-desc>A decorative drop cap 'I' enclosed in a square frame with elaborate geometric and floral strapwork patterns.</image-desc>

NOW we have reached the arts, and we have decided to take our beginning from distillation. This is an invention of the moderns <note>original: "neotericorum" | referring to the "new" school of chemists and alchemists, as opposed to the ancient Galenic doctors who relied primarily on raw herbs.</note>, a wondrous thing, to be praised beyond the lot of mortals; it is not to be used as it is by dabblers <note>original: "sciolis" | those with superficial or "pseudo" knowledge</note> and the common folk—for they corrupt and destroy the truth of the matter—but rather handled by those who understand causes. For this art teaches by admirable means how heavy bodies may become spirits and sublimate <term>subliment | the process of heating a substance into vapor and then collecting it as a solid or liquid</term>, and thus thicken once again and turn back into bodies. 

We can elicit the powers of things—which, overwhelmed by their own mass and trodden down, lie hidden as if in their own little caskets—making them purer, thinner, and without any addition of impure matter, whether from plants, metals, stones, or gems. We can lead these powers, as if they were not content with their own lowly lot, to a nobler state in the heights, and raise them as if into heaven itself. With chemical apparatus <note>original: "chymisticis organis"</note>, we will be able to investigate the virtues of plants far better than the ancients did through the sense of taste. What greater thing, therefore, could be devised? It is the nature of Nature to produce things and endow them with powers; it is the nature of Art to [refine] those produced...

<summary>This page introduces Book X, focusing on the art of distillation as a revolutionary "modern" technique for extracting the pure, spiritual essence of physical materials. Della Porta argues that distillation allows the scientist to transcend the physical limitations of plants and minerals, raising their hidden "virtues" to a higher state.</summary>
<keywords>distillation, alchemy, chymistry, sublimation, Giambattista della Porta, natural philosophy, extraction, essence</keywords>

<meta>Continuity note: This page continues from the preface of Book X on page 397. The previous page ended mid-sentence with "pur...", which completes here as "purify."</meta>

...purify them, mobilize them, and enrich them with manifold powers. Let the reader who is a lover of learning <note>original: φιλομαθὴς (*philomathēs*)</note> and a searcher of nature’s secrets approach, for he will handle distillations in a manner that is by no means inglorious. First, we shall extract waters and oils; soon there will be tinctures, elixirs, salts, and other similar things. This art allows us to dissolve a mixture, as it were, into its constituent elements, to render each part purer, and to separate and draw out its various and opposing faculties so that we may use them as we wish—along with other things which you will not regret having known and learned.

---

### *What distillation is, how many kinds there are, and what we intend by it. CHAPTER I.*

I will not pause to decide whether distillation was known to the learned men of antiquity; however, one may read in the works of Dioscorides <note>Pedanius Dioscorides, a 1st-century Greek physician and author of *De Materia Medica*</note> of a different device than the one we use today. He says: "Catch the oil which is called pitch-oil; once the watery part has been separated, this floats on top, like whey in milk. It is gathered while the pitch is being boiled by spreading pure fleeces of wool over the steam; when these have become thoroughly soaked, they are squeezed out into a vessel, and this is continued as long as the pitch is boiling." Geber <note>An influential 8th-century alchemist, often identified as Jabir ibn Hayyan</note> defines it thus: "Distillation is the elevation of aqueous vapors in their own vessel." However, a true definition will be given elsewhere. He establishes a threefold definition: by ascent, by descent, and by the wick <note>original: *laciniam* | a method using a strip of cloth to move liquid by capillary action</note>. But I cannot pretend that the "wick" should be placed among the species of distillation. We say the methods are by ascent, by descent, and by inclination—the latter being a middle path between the two and very necessary. For when a substance is stubborn against rising, we "incline" it so that it may learn to ascend, elevating it little by little until it becomes thinner and capable of climbing.

The rule for distilling shall be as follows: First, let a vessel be prepared of glass or bronze, usually shaped like a spinning top or a pear, and swelling in its belly like a gourd <term>cucurbita | a rounded, gourd-shaped chemical flask</term>. Over this vessel, let a piece be fitted like a cap, which receives the neck of the vessel placed below; a channel runs around the inside of this cap, from which a spout projects outward. Another vessel is placed beneath this to receive the liquid as it is cast out, and is therefore called the receiver <term>receptaculum | the vessel used to collect the condensed product</term>.

<meta>Catchword: Obsti-</meta>

<summary>Della Porta introduces the practice of distillation as a means to isolate the pure powers of nature and describes the fundamental apparatus—the cucurbit and receiver—while distinguishing his methods from ancient and medieval predecessors.</summary>
<keywords>distillation, Dioscorides, Geber, cucurbit, alembic, chemical apparatus, alchemy, purification, liquid extraction</keywords>

### OF DISTILLATIONS.

The vents are sealed with clay mixed with straw <note>original: *luto paleato* | a common "lute" or sealant used in early chemistry to make vessels airtight</note>, or with linens, so that the gaseous or spirituous matter being produced is not blown away into the air. Once fire is placed beneath the vessel, the matter is dissolved into a rolling vapor by the force of the heat and is lifted into the upper air of the vessel. Encountering the cold arches of the cap <note>original: *pilei* | the "alembic" or head of the still</note>, the vapor settles there, thickened by the cold, and swells into bubbles; thus it bedews the chambers and walls. Soon it gathers into drops, and having become a distillate, it flows back, turns into liquid, and glides through the channel and beak into the receiver. 

However, the vessel and receiver are selected according to the nature of the thing to be distilled. For if the substances are vaporous or gaseous, they demand large, low-positioned instruments and a more bulging receiver; for when these gases are stirred up by the force of the fire and pervade the narrow cavities of the containers, they become compressed there. Otherwise, these flaming gases burst the vessels and escape with a great boom and crack, and shards fly out not without danger to those standing by. In this way, the gas forced out of the narrow spaces will liberate itself by doing harm. But if the substances are hot and thin, they require a long and slender neck, and thus moderate substances seek moderate vessels. 

An industrious craftsman can learn these things from those which Nature has sketched out. In an angry animal prone to rage, such as the bear or the lion, the body is swollen, and it has contracted its neck into a short length, as if its gaseous nature could be exploded from the vessel of a wider belly while the thicker parts settle. On the other hand, the deer, the ostrich, and the giraffe <note>original: *camelopardalis*</note> are long-necked <note>original: μακρόχηλον (*makrochēlon*)</note> animals of a mild and thin spirit with slender bellies; they have retained long necks so that through a much narrower and longer passage, the thin and subtle spirits might be vented into the heights. 

Yet we have deemed that this principal point must not be ignored: a threefold moisture can be drawn out of plants. First, the **nutritional** moisture by which it lives, the loss of which causes it to wither; this differs very little from spring or well water. Second is the moisture of **consistency**, from which the mixture is glued together; this possesses a harder virtue. The third is the **radical moisture** <note>the "root" or essential life-fluid of a substance</note>, which is fatty and oily, and in which the medicinal powers lie hidden. 

Nor should it be passed over in silence—as these are the principles of the art which I have learned by experimenting on many things—that some mixtures first exhale thin and hot vapors, and later wetter and thicker ones. Conversely, some exhale earthy and phlegmatic <note>watery or sluggish</note> vapors first, and afterwards...
