### *On the extraction of waters, and especially those that are sweet-smelling.*

## CHAPTER II.

Since the methods for extracting waters are common knowledge, we shall explain them briefly. If you have a heart for extracting scented waters from hot, earthy plants that retain their fragrances throughout their entire mass in internal cavities, these may be cast into vessels without any special trickery; once fire is placed beneath, they yield their scents. Just so, 

->*from flowers of roses, oranges <note>original: *aurantii mali* | literally "orange apple"</note>, myrtle, and lavender, scented waters*<-

may be extracted, as we have said, and from similar plants. One may use either hot ashes or a water bath <note>original: *balneo* | likely a *balneum Mariae* or bain-marie, providing gentle, indirect heat</note> as desired, though the fire must be applied gradually so the plants are not scorched. There are also fragrant leaves on certain plants, such as myrtle, lavender, citrus, and the like; if you mix these with the flowers, they do not dull the scent of the blossoms, but rather grant a certain grace to the waters. In places lacking such flowers, we have seen excellent scented waters extracted from their young shoots <note>original: *turionibus*</note>, especially if we first place them in a closed vessel for several days to be warmed in the sun. A pleasant and by no means to be despised scent is drawn from the leaves of basil, especially the lemon-scented or clove-scented <note>original: *garyophyllati* | referring to *Gillyflower* or cloves</note> varieties, if the light heat of a water bath, applied gradually, coaxes and draws it out, and if it is then left to be seasoned in the sun. From the flowers of the Chinaberry <note>original: *azadarat* | the Persian Lilac or *Melia azedarach*</note>, or "false sycamore," a sweet-smelling water is elicited, thin and breathable. 

The proof for discovering whether odors reside in the whole mass of a plant, or only on the surface, or are scattered elsewhere, is this: let the leaves or flowers be rubbed between the fingers. Those which, when smelled, keep the same odor or smell sweeter, have their scents hidden throughout their entire mass. On the contrary, if those you rub are not only deprived of their native scent but actually smell worse, it is a sign that the odors reside only on the outermost surface; these, once mixed with the other foul-smelling parts of the plant, are not only dulled...

### *how to extract scented water from clove-pinks, musk roses, violets, jasmines, and lilies,*

How it ought to be done. From wild musk roses, let the first vapor be extracted with the gentle heat of a water bath <note>original: *balnei* | refers to a *balneum Mariae*, a vessel of water in which the still is placed to ensure even, indirect heating</note>. Once these flowers are removed, let others be cast in on top; for if you cook them too long, the scent produced is not the delicate one spread upon the surface, but a sluggish one that comes from the internal part of the plant’s body and breathes less fragrance. In this distilled water, let other fresh roses be macerated <note>steeped or soaked</note> for several hours, then drawn off, and new ones added; the more frequently you do this, the more fragrant the water smells. But this must be done with the vessel well-closed, lest that delicate odor be blown away and perish into the air. In this way, you will have a most sweetly smelling water from the scent of musk roses. If one grows weary of macerating them in their own specific water, the same result can be achieved in rose water. In this manner, we have presented waters fragrant with a profound scent from these flowers to admiring craftsmen and to those of no small reputation. ### *how the stench of burning is corrected.*

Because the materials sticking to the bottom of the vessel experience more heat than those at the top, they are scorched before the ones at the top feel any perceptible heat. Very often, the water then offends the nostrils with a hostile, heavy stench of burning. You shall distill that same water again in a water bath with a light fire, so that the pure water rises and the dregs settle at the bottom along with the oil, which is the cause of the heavy smell. ### On extracting the water of life. CHAPTER III.

The WATER, which we call the water of life <note>original: *aqua vitae* | high-proof alcohol or brandy, considered the "soul" of the wine</note>, is extracted in this way. Let a strong and noble wine be taken, produced in dry places—such as from Mount Vesuvius <note>original: *Vescruivo* | likely a variant of Vesuvius</note>, which the common people call Greek wine, or *protropon* <note>Greek: "the first juice" | wine made from grapes that have leaked juice under their own weight before pressing</note>, or "tears" <note>original: *lachryma* | likely referring to the famous *Lacryma Christi* wine</note>. Distill this in a twisted glass vessel, using a water bath, or ashes, or through a long neck, of which you will catch the third part; keep the remainder, for it is converted into a perfect and sharp vinegar. It is, in effect, the corpse of the wine, since the soul—the subtle part—has been removed. 

Distill the distillate again, and this once more, always taking the third part. Then let a vessel with a longer and narrower neck be prepared—namely, one three cubits high <note>about 4.5 feet</note>, which the common people call a *matarazzo* <note>a tall, narrow distillation flask used to further purify spirits</note>—and let this be distilled again. Finally, let it be placed upon the highest mouth of the vessel and covered with parchment, and a cap put on. With the fire lit, the most thin spirit of the wine, pervading everything, glides down into the receiving dish placed below; the phlegm <note>original: *phlegma* | the watery residue or impurities left after the spirit has been drawn off</note>, to which passage is denied, remains at the bottom. 

The proof of its perfect cleansing from the phlegm will be if a linen cloth is moistened in it and, when lit, is entirely consumed; or if it is poured onto a flat board and, the flame being lit, it leaves no moisture, indeed not even a trace. But the whole business depends on this: that the extreme mouths of the vessels be exactly sealed and glued, lest the most subtle spirits escape through any tiny vent and resolve into the air. 

Nothing will be more suitable for gluing than the bladder of an ox or other animals; for if cut into somewhat wide strips and moistened, and wrapped and tied where the mouths of the vessels meet, it alone can restrain the escaping vapors. You shall observe this in its distillation: as the coals grow hot, the vessel boils, and through the neck of the vessel the most burning spirit of the wine ascends; below it boils, above it is cold, until it has ascended into the cap; then cold...

### How we ought to distill by the Sun. CHAPTER IV.

We can distill not only by fire, but also by the power of the Sun and by dung. However, dung infects the distilled liquids with a foul and loathsome odor. The Sun, conversely, draws out the best water, which is useful for many remedies. The force of fire changes the essence of things and imparts hot and burning qualities; therefore, for eye remedies, we ought to provide waters drawn out in the Sun. For when produced by fire, they sting and pierce the eyes, whereas solar waters are milder and sweeter. More water is collected in the Sun, for the vapors descend immediately upon being dissolved; whereas with fire, while they are driven upward by the force of the heat, they often cling to the sides of the vessel and flow back down into the dregs. There are other benefits as well, to be explained in their proper places. Furthermore, it benefits the household economy, for the work is completed without wood, charcoal, or the constant presence of an artisan; indeed, once the vessels are filled and placed against the Sun, they require no further labor. To summarize the matter briefly: let a bench be prepared three feet high, two feet wide, and of a length that corresponds to the amount of material to be distilled—that is, if you wish to distill much, make it longer; if less, shorter. The side of the bench facing away from the Sun should be closed with boards, lest the Sun heat the receivers and force the water to evaporate and ascend again. In the middle of the length of the board, holes should be carved out, large enough to receive the necks of the vessels. When the Sun enters Gemini... <note>This refers to the Sun entering the zodiac sign of Gemini, typically late May, signifying the start of the stronger summer heat needed for this process.</note>

### On oil, to be extracted by pressing.
### CHAPTER V.

We have spoken of waters; now we shall speak of oils, and later we shall speak of essences. These require the industry of a most ingenious craftsman; for many of the most excellent essences of things reside within oils, as if in their radical moisture <term>radical moisture | original: humido radicali: In Renaissance science, this was the essential, life-sustaining fluid inherent in all living matter, thought to be the seat of its vital power</term>. They are so deeply hidden that they do not come to light except through the greatest art, ingenuity, effort, and skill—so much so that the entire art of distillation depends upon this.

The first method depends upon the press <term>expression | torcular: The process of squeezing or pressing substances, like seeds or olives, to extract liquids without using heat</term>, and although it is considered separate from the art of distillation, because it is so necessary for these matters, it would not be inappropriate to say a few words about it first. The method common to almost all such things is as follows: The seeds from which we intend to extract oil must first be cleaned of their skins and husks. These are removed either by beating them with the hand or by prying them with the fingernails until the little pods that surround them fall away. Once cleaned and gathered into a marble mortar, they are diligently [crushed] with a wooden pestle...

### *Oil of eggs.*

Take fifty or sixty eggs and boil them until they become hard. Strip away the shells and pick out the yolks from the middle. These should be placed in a <term>tinned cauldron</term> <note>original: "lebetem stanno perlitum" — a vessel lined with tin to prevent the metal from reacting with the contents</note> over hot coals. Stir them with a wooden spatula until they exhale all their moisture. Then, once the fire is made more violent, they must be stirred tirelessly so that they are not burned. Thus you will see the oil sweat out. When they have yielded all their oil, withdraw the fire and pour off the oil that flows out; or, when the oil begins to sweat out as we have said, they may be placed into a press, and by heavy pressure, you will force out a copious amount of oil, though it will not be quite as pure.

## *How oil is extracted with water.* CHAPTER VI.

Now we shall set forth the method by which oil may be extracted without the help of a press—first from spices, seeds, leaves, woods, and various other things. Because oil is only drawn out by the violence of fire, and since, being fatty, it rises upward only with great difficulty, aromatic seeds are thin, subtle, and delicate things; if they experience even a little too much fire, they are immediately tainted by the smell of burning <note>original: "cremati nidore" — literally the "reek of the burned"</note>. Therefore, so that they may endure a more vehement fire and be safe from scorching, we achieve the work only by the medium of water. I say that seeds of this kind consist of a spiritual essence that is remarkably thin and volatile, and by an innate property of their nature, they are carried upward. Whence, in distillation, with water as a companion, they are easily led upward and carried into the <term>cap</term> <note>original: "pileum" — the "helm" or top part of a still, also called an alembic, where vapors condense</note>...

### *How we may separate oil from waters.* CHAPTER VII.

When we extract oil, it flows together with the waters into the <term>receiver</term> <note>original: "receptorium" — the vessel that catches the condensed liquid in a still</note>; they must be carefully separated from one another, lest the oil, being diluted by some <term>phlegm</term> <note>original: "phlegmate" — a term used by early chemists for the watery, tasteless byproduct of distillation</note>, lose its potency. It must therefore be purified so that it can exercise its most excellent powers, and we shall achieve this through distillation and separation. For if that mixture is put back into a <term>retort</term> <note>original: "vas retortum" — a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck</note>, or a glass vessel, and well-positioned in the gentle heat of a <term>water bath</term> <note>original: "balnei tepore" — referring to a *balneum Mariae*, or bain-marie, which provides steady, indirect heat</note>, the water will distill off, and the liquid remaining behind will be the oil. However, the management of this separation is laborious. Vessels have been devised with enough ingenuity for this task, by whose help the pure oil remains once all the water or phlegm has been drained. Therefore, let a glass vessel be prepared: it should be wide at the top, gradually narrowing itself until it is reduced to a slender shape, in the manner of a funnel. When the distilled water (which flowed out as a mix of watery phlegm and oil) is poured into it, let it sit for a little while; the oil will float on top, and the water will settle at the bottom. We close the opening with a finger; by relaxing the finger, the water comes out first, and the oil will gradually descend. When the oil has reached the narrow part and is right next to the finger, close it again, and with the opening only half-open, let the water flow out drop by drop until it is all exhausted: then you shall pour the oil into another small vessel. Another separating vessel has been most ingeniously devised for the same purpose: the belly of the vessel is swollen, but the neck is narrow, and in the middle of the neck a <term>spout</term> <note>original: "rostellum" — literally a 'little beak'</note> is attached. Let the oil mixed with water be poured into the vessel; the water occupies the bottom, and the oil stays above in the neck. You then add water drop by drop until the oil rises to the spout...

->*How a vessel may be prepared for extracting oil without fear of burning, and so that more oil may be drawn out.*<-

### CHAPTER VIII.

We are also able to bring into use various extractions of oils and waters by using vessels fashioned in different shapes. Among these, we have discovered one by which we can draw out oil even with a very fierce fire without the danger of burning <note>Burning or "empyreuma" was a constant risk in early distillation, as it ruined the scent and flavor of the oil</note>, and in greater quantity than by any other means, adaptable to various uses. Let a bronze vessel be fashioned, therefore, in the shape of an egg, with a capacity of half a common barrel. At the top, it should have an open mouth of such width that it is convenient for an arm to enter and exit, should it ever need washing or when we are about to refill it with alternating layers of things to be distilled. Let it be lined inside with tin <note>Tinning the inside of copper or bronze vessels prevented the metal from reacting with the botanical ingredients</note>. A bronze cap <term>pileus</term> <note>The "head" or "alembic" that sits atop the boiling pot</note> a foot high is then placed upon the vessel; at the bottom, it should have a hole suitable for receiving the neck of the lower kettle <term>ahenum</term>, and its mouth should exactly enclose the outer edge of the kettle's rims. From the top of the cap, a bronze pipe <term>canalis</term> should run out, fifteen or twenty feet long, winding back on itself in serpentine coils <note>This is an early description of a "worm" or "coil" condenser, used to cool the vapors over a long distance</note> so that it may be moved more easily and occupy less space. This pipe is fixed into the "belly" of another vessel; this second vessel, bulging at its middle, is not of such great capacity as the first, and its uppermost part tapers into a narrow neck. Upon this neck a second pipe sits, of the same length and retaining the same snake-like coils; the final mouth of this pipe enters another straight pipe which, penetrating through the middle of a barrel, finally falls into a receiver. This apparatus is put to use in the following manner: leaves, stems, or seeds, cut into small pieces, are placed into the kettle, and clear spring water is poured over them...

...poured over, until it rises above the materials to the height of a palm or five finger-widths. Then the caps <note>original: "pileos" — the domed lids or alembic heads placed atop the boiling vessel</note> are placed on top, and the joints must be perfectly fitted together. The end of the pipe is placed into another vessel, the openings properly joined; then, once the second cap is fitted, the end of the curved pipe is inserted into another straight one, which, passing through a vat <note>original: "vegetem" — likely a cooling cask or tub filled with water</note>, leads into the receiver. If the joints gap at any point, they should be tightly stuffed with tow <note>original: "stupa" — coarse hemp or flax fibers used for sealing</note>, then glued with wheat flour and egg white, with small strips of animal bladder wrapped over them and tied tightly. For when the vapors are forced by the power of the fire, they become so refined that they break through any cracks or the smallest joints, escaping almost every effort to hold them back.

The tub should be filled with cold water, and if it becomes warm over time, it should be drained through the lower tap <note>original: "epistomio"</note> and fresh cold water poured in, so that by the addition of new water, the pipe remains constantly chilled. Finally, the fire should be lit so that the contents of the bronze vessel boil and bubble; at first slow, then gradually increasing, until it grows so fierce that the vapors passing through the curved turns, driven by the force of the fire, will make a noise as if they would burst the vessel. In this way, the water separated from the phlegm <note>original: "phlegmate" — a term in early chemistry for the watery, non-essential part of a distillate</note> in the lower vessel is carried upward through the curved pipes, and passing through the cold pipe, it is condensed into a liquid and flows into the receiver. 

If the water is exhausted by continuous boiling, the bronze vessel should have a small pipe on its side with its own tap, through which hot water may be replenished, keeping the tap tightly closed afterward so it does not vent. Afterward, the oil is separated from the water using a separator, and it can then be purified and refined in another vessel. Of all the apparatuses we have seen so far, we have observed no vessel that extracts oil more abundantly, or with less labor and effort. In this way, from flowers, leaves, spices, resins, and woods, we can extract oil with a very strong fire without fear of burning—as one can do with juniper berries and laurel.

In the lower vessel, near the middle at a space of half a foot from the mouth, a transverse partition made of a brass plate should be fitted, so that it can be easily placed in and drawn out. From the sides of the vessel, let three holes be fitted through which the necks of the retorts can be inserted, joined with their own small channels, so they may be aptly stuffed with **tow** <note>original: "stupa" — coarse flax or hemp fibers used for caulking</note> and bound with **bladders** <note>original: "vesicis" — animal bladders used to create airtight seals</note>, lest even the smallest amount of air—not to mention water—should escape. 

When we prepare for the work: let the glass retort vessels be filled with the things to be distilled, let the necks hanging outside be inserted through the channels, and let the bottoms rest in the holes of the partition. Let them be slightly elevated, and if any empty space gapes between the neck and the channel, let it be filled and packed with tow, and bound above with strips of bladder. Let the vessel be filled with water so that it sits three broad fingers below the partition. 

Finally, having covered the vessel with its lid and having the joints very well stuffed, smeared with paste, and bound—lest the violence of the rising vapors lift the lid on high and the heat **scald** <note>original: "excarnificet" — literally "to tear the flesh from"; a warning about severe steam burns</note> the faces of those standing by—with the fire lit, let it gradually heat up until it becomes very vehement: the water boils, and the converging spirits hiss among themselves so as to strike terror. First the water will distill out, and soon the oil along with the water.

### How oil is extracted from resins. CHAPTER 10.

The extraction of oil from resins is unique. Although they follow nearly the same method as those mentioned before—namely, by mixing them with water and macerating <note>soaking a substance to soften it and extract its properties</note> them for many days, so that at last, with a fierce fire urging the bronze vessel, the oil is pushed out along with the water—only a small quantity is drawn out. Yet, it possesses a superior scent and is without the stench of burning, as is commonly done with opoponax <note>original: *opoponaco* — a gum resin from the Hercules-all-heal plant, used in perfumery and medicine</note>, galbanum <note>a bitter-smelling gum resin from Persian plants</note>, styrax <note>a fragrant resin from the *Styrax officinalis* tree</note>, and others. But they are also distilled in another way through ashes <term>distilled through ashes (*per cineres distillantur*) — a method using a bed of hot ashes to provide a more even, intense heat than a water bath</term>. However, in this way they demand the presence of a craftsman, a certain singular cleverness, and the skill of a provident hand, so that it deserves to be called an ingenious rather than a laborious administration. We will provide an example of how we can:

->Extract oil from laser.<-
<note>original: *lasere* — This refers to a pungent resin, often identified as asafoetida, which was used as both a spice and medicine in the ancient world.</note>

Let the laser be macerated in rose water, or without it, let it be placed in a twisted glass vessel of the lowest ascent, which craftsmen call "slow" <term>lowest ascent (*minimæ ascensionis*) — a vessel designed with a short neck so that heavy oily vapors do not have to travel far upward to condense</term>. Then let the vessel be placed in a pot with sand, but let sand come between the sides of the pot and the belly of the vessel. Let the neck be inserted into a receiver with a more swollen belly. Let the fire be lit gradually, putting aside all haste and violence of the fire; with diligent work alone, the water will drip out. Soon, with the fire increased so that the oil flows—yet not so strong that it threatens the forces of burning, but observing a middle ground between the two—the oily vapors will fill the entire receiver. From there, having turned into a certain thick substance, they will depart into little clusters similar to fleeces <note>original: *glomusculos velleribus similes* — a vivid description of the cloudy, white vapors condensing into "wool-like" tufts on the glass</note>, and clinging to the sides and the middle of the vessel (so that nothing more beautiful can be seen), they are soon converted into bubbles and oil and fall to the bottom. Keep the heat at the same level until the dregs are dried out; then you shall remove the fire, for the danger of burning is imminent. In the same way is pushed out:

->Oil from storax.<-

->*Oil from turpentine resin.*<-

->*Oil from olive and linseed.*<-

If common oil is distilled, it passes through with great difficulty; it will come forth after at least six hours with an increased fire, yet with the greatest diligence lest the ashes and the vessel ignite; for by catching flame inside, it breaks the vessels and leaps upward so that it can be extinguished only with the greatest difficulty—indeed, it shoots a flame so far that it reaches the ceilings. Therefore, the oil must be extracted in **vaulted rooms** <note>original: *testudinatis cubiculis* — rooms with stone or brick arched ceilings, which were more fire-resistant than wooden beams</note>. From this, **masters of fire** <note>pyrotechnicians or creators of "Greek Fire" and fireworks</note> have learned to mix it into their compositions, since it catches a violent flame and is difficult enough to put out.

->*How oils may be prepared from things by various techniques.*<-

### ->CHAPTER XII.<-

Because the natures of things to be distilled are diverse, oils must be drawn from them by various techniques. For some, when urged by fire, **sublimate** <note>turn directly from a solid into a vapor</note> and are not dissolved into liquid; others cannot endure the force of fire without being suddenly burned. Thus, from the various differences in things, various techniques for obtaining oils have been discovered. We shall offer some examples of these, so that skillful distillers may never despair of being able to extract oil from any substance whatsoever. In this way is prepared

->*Oil from honey.*<-

Oil is extracted from honey with considerable difficulty: for at even the slightest heat it swells and rises in bubbles, so that it climbs up the neck of the vessel—no matter how long it is—into the cap, and flows back entirely into the receiver before it can be dissolved into a liquid or oil. Many clever tricks have been devised for this purpose. 

Take a glass or glazed vessel with a wide, short neck and put the honey inside. You will arrange **tow** <note>original: *stupa* — coarse, unspun fibers of flax or hemp, used here as a physical barrier</note> over it with your hands, fitting it well on all sides so that it sits two fingers high. Thus, when the honey boils and swells, the tow presses it down from above and makes it subside. It will first drip clear water; when the liquid begins to take on color, remove the receiver and put another in its place, and keep both liquids separate. 

Or, put the honey in any vessel so that it rises four thumb-breadths from the bottom, and cover it as is customary. Next, dig a pit in the floor and bury the bottom of the vessel (the part occupied by the honey) in the earth. Above the ground, coat the vessel with a layer of clay four fingers high to protect it, and let it dry. Let charcoal be lit all around it, gradually moving it closer to the vessel; the honey boils, and because the heat is *above* it in the open air, it is prevented from swelling upward. It will very easily distill water, and then oil—first golden, then reddish—until the honey is turned to charcoal. 

Even a simple housewife could perform the work in another way. Let honey be poured into a new earthenware jar, and with the lid put on, let it be buried in a pit dug outdoors so that it lies a **cubit** <note>an ancient unit of length, roughly 18 inches or 45 centimeters</note> deep beneath the surface. Let it sit to rot for ten days. Then you will take it out and pour the crystal-clear water standing on top into another vessel. Cover the jar and bury it again in the same way. After a week, check the jar again and pour off the floating water; do this a third and fourth time until all the honey has turned to water, which can be seen by loosening the stopper. Distill the saved water in the usual manner, and it will yield water and oil to you quite easily. 

By a different artifice from this, one obtains

Place the vessel in a warm bath, or a **hypocaust** <note>original: *hypocausto* — a heating chamber or under-floor furnace used here as a gentle heat source</note>

### Oil from paper and linens.

You will catch a yellow oil from the edges of the rims, smelling of the vice of burning, used for the same purposes. For reviving fainting spirits, it is prepared in another way.

## How oil is extracted by descent.

The method is common and well-known to everyone, for the oil is forced out by the scorching <note>original: *ustulatione*</note> of materials, but it has a most foul odor, and we cannot use it except in medicines applied externally; for such oils cannot be taken into the body. ### *Oil from guaiacum.*

They fill a glass vessel with sawdust of guaiacum wood <note>original: *guaiaci* — a resinous "holy wood" from the Americas, famously used in the 16th century to treat syphilis</note>, and the belly of the vessel is sealed over with clay mixed with straw <note>original: *luto paleato* — a common insulating sealant made of clay and chaff</note>, and it is protected with a double or triple crust of this. When it has been dried in the sun, let brass wires <note>original: *fides orichalceæ*</note> be placed inside the neck, the vessel is inverted, and the receiving vessel is fitted to the opening where the neck passes through, and the vents are sealed. Above the bowl, a fire is lit around the glass—at first somewhat gently, but soon it should heat up more vehemently with closer contact, though it should not glow white-hot, until you believe everything has been burned. Afterward, once the fire is removed, let it rest until it cools, and you will find in the inner dish <note>original: *paropside*</note> a black, burnt, scentless oil. In this same way, oil is forced out from juniper, cypress, and aloe, but in the case of aloe, greater skill and diligence must be used, and a light force of fire, since it enters into ointments.

## On the extraction of the quintessence. CHAPTER XIII.

We have handed down various extractions of oils; now we have come to the quintessence, which it is necessary for us to explain, and how it may be extracted. The quintessence...

...the Paracelsians <note>Followers of Paracelsus, the 16th-century physician who revolutionized medicine by using chemistry and minerals</note> define it to be either the form, the spirit, the virtue, or the soul separated from all impurity and from the elementary condition of its body. We call it "soul" because it cannot be extracted from the bones, flesh, marrow, blood, or other members of animals; since these things lack spirit, they also lack this same **quintessence** <term>the "fifth essence," a highly purified substance believed to be the most potent medicinal part of a material</term>. We say it is separated from all impurity of the elements, for once the quintessence is extracted from things, only a mass of elements remains, stripped of all its powers. For force, virtue, and medicine are not derived from the elements themselves, but from its own specific property. Yet the quintessence itself is an element, and it contains the powers of the elements within itself in an eminent degree; it is led out from the ruder body, far removed from the elements and their strength, and is made spiritual. While it remains within its mass, the spirit is dull; when it is torn away from that company, it exerts and intensifies its powers more strongly. It is smallest in mass, but enormous in its operation.

The powers by which one quintessence surpasses another are not to be judged by the levels of their qualities <note>such as the traditional Aristotelian qualities of hot, cold, moist, or dry</note>, but by the degrees of their operations; for that which roots out and banishes disease more quickly reaches the highest degrees. The quintessence of **juniper** removes leprosy solely by purging the blood; therefore, the first degree in operation is assigned to it. That of **amber** <note>original: *Ambaræ* — likely referring to ambergris or fossilized amber resin</note> removes the poison of disease by purging the heart, lungs, and limbs; for this reason, the second degree is given to it. **Antimony**, besides the aforementioned powers, also purges the body; thus the third degree is its own. But **gold**, by itself alone, performs all operations and renovates the body; because of this, the fourth degree and a more powerful virtue must be attributed to it.

But how these quintessences are to be extracted—"this is the task, this the toil" <note>original: *hoc opus, hic labor* — a famous quote from Virgil’s Aeneid regarding the difficulty of a journey</note>; since they can be an oil, a liquor, or a salt, and are various and manifold. Therefore, they must be extracted by various and manifold ways: some by **sublimation** <term>the process of heating a substance into vapor and then collecting it as a solid again</term>, others by reduction into lime <note>calcination</note>, or using vinegar, wine, corrosive waters, and the like. Thus, various **solvents** <term>original: *menstrua* — specialized liquids used in alchemy to dissolve or extract substances</term> must be prepared according to the logic and nature of each thing. In choosing these solvents, we shall add some rules: that the solvents be made from suitable things, and be as simple as they can be; for the quintessence ought to be simple, defiled by nothing and unmixed, but simple and immaculate. And if it is necessary to add anything, immediately after its separation let them be...

### *To extract the quintessence from musk, ambergris, civet, and spices.*

You shall then gently distill the essence after the *aqua vitae* by means of a water bath, so that the *aqua vitae* evaporates, and the quintessence remains separated at the bottom in the form of an oil. 

If you work with *aqua vitae* alone: Let roots of zedoary be sliced and crushed, and in a glass vessel pour *aqua vitae* over them so that it stands three fingers high above them. Keep the small vessel in digestion for ten days. Move that which is extracted by distillation to a water bath; by a light fire the *aqua vitae* will evaporate, and the quintessence of the zedoary will remain at the bottom in liquid form.

Set the dregs, dried again, in a potter's or glassmaker's furnace to a most fervent fire, so they are burnt into whitening ashes. Let them be gradually moistened with water and placed in the warming room of their oven, so they are converted into salt <note>In early chemistry, 'salt' refers to the solid, purified mineral residue of a substance after calcination (burning to ash).</note>. The proof of an excellent operation will be precise if, when you throw it upon a glowing hot plate, it melts and dissolves into the air; if not, work more correctly. Here the water is remixed and placed in a glass vessel with a long neck, with a cork and parchment added and a cap fitted; when this cap feels the force of the fire, it penetrates everything, and a sort of contracted residue is seen in the chambers of the cap. The water remains unmoved unless the spirit itself has ascended <note>The Latin text says *ascenderis* ("unless you have ascended"), but this is likely a typographical error in the original for *ascenderit* ("unless it has ascended"), referring to the vapor rising.</note>; that spirit, best remixed with the waters, is placed in a circle of perpetual rotation, so that it is drawn out into itself by frequently repeated turns. Thus it removes and lays down all the thickness of its substance and receives a thinner and far more subtle power.

## What magisteries are, and how they are extracted.
### CHAPTER XIV.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a chemical distillation apparatus. It features a tripod stand supporting a wide, bowl-shaped vessel. We have stated that while quintessences <note>original: *quintas essentias*; the most purified and potent form of a substance, believed by alchemists to be a "fifth element"</note> of properties follow the nature of the compounds, a magistery <note>original: *magisterium*; a chemical preparation where a substance is refined into a usable form—often a precipitate or powder—without losing its elemental character or being turned into a volatile spirit</note> on the other hand follows the qualities of the elements. Thus, they extract neither the spirit nor the tincture <note>original: *tinctura*; the concentrated color or medicinal essence</note>, but a certain middle ground between the two. Therefore, a magistery is that which can be extracted from things beyond the mere separation of the elements. Quintessences very often follow colors, and tinctures always do, but magisteries do not follow colors. The method for extracting magisteries varies according to the diversity of natural things. ->*The Magistery of gems, coral, and pearls.*<- <note>original: *uniones*; literally "unions," a term used for large, high-quality pearls</note>

Add saltpeter <note>original: *salnitrum*; potassium nitrate, used as a flux to help substances melt or break down</note> to it as a companion in equal weights. Dissolve this lime in the "water of life" <note>original: *aqua vitae*; high-proof distilled alcohol</note>, and pour off whatever dissolves into the water. Let the remaining powder be exposed to the fire again, and once it is better reduced to lime, [add it to the] water...

A TINCTURE is the purer and more effective extracted part of a colored thing, and the most noble part of its compound. It is extracted indeed from gems, stones, the flowers of plants, roots, seeds, and the rest. ### To extract the tincture from gold.

If men knew the most commendable gifts that this metal, gold—which can never be praised enough—brings to the human body, they would perhaps pursue it with a fuller devotion for health than they do for the comforts of life. The most skillful investigators of the secrets of Nature have observed in gold a transparency, a radiance, and a certain attractive and, so to speak, <term>magnetic</term> power <note>The author compares the visual allure of gold to the physical pull of a magnet, suggesting it has a natural "spirit" that attracts the human soul.</note>. As soon as it is seen, it immediately invites the eyes to contemplate its majesty and beauty, the hands to touch it, and finally our human spirit to desire it. Even infants rejoice at the sight of it; they stretch out their hands with laughter and applause, snatching it toward themselves, and cannot be pulled away from it. Observing this, these investigators conjectured that no small riches were to be found in it for the preservation of the human body. 

The <term>Astrologers</term> <note>At this time, astrology and medicine were closely linked; physicians believed planets influenced specific organs.</note>, seeing that gold rivals the Sun in its rays, brightness, and splendor, and that it holds a certain prerogative and majesty among metals just as the Sun does among the stars, believe that for this reason it benefits the heart, and removes <term>melancholy</term> <note>The "black bile" humor; in this period, melancholy was seen as a cold, dark condition that the "solar" heat of gold could cure.</note> and its followers. The <term>metallurgists</term> say that in its mixture, the elements agree with such a proportioned harmony, and are so purified and compact, that they judge it to be perfectly tempered and far removed from corruption. It is a substance in which nothing is lacking and nothing is superfluous; it is so dense and compact that, remaining in the fire for a very long time, it is not only not consumed, but is daily rendered far nobler and more radiant. For this reason, even if buried for a [thousand]...

It is especially effective against poisons and the contagions of the plague.

Now, however, we must examine whether the ancient or modern physicians knew how to prepare it correctly, so that it might perform these most excellent works. ...[the gold] itself remaining incorrupt and untouched, and even being boiled with honey. Marsilio Ficino <note>A famous 15th-century Italian philosopher and physician who sought to reconcile Hermetic magic with Christianity.</note> says it possesses great substance, but it must be refined into a subtle form so that it may penetrate the body; but he is ignorant of the method. He suggests that, having finally been reduced into the thinnest leaves, it should be administered with cordial waters <note>Medicinal waters intended to stimulate the heart.</note>, for in this way, the water may draw out its powers, or by quenching hot gold in wine. There are others, taught by the words of Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, the Roman author of Natural History.</note>, who say that chicken parts should be cast into the molten metal, and that the gold is absorbed into them, for chicken parts are a poison to gold. Because of this, Ficino mixes gold leaf into capon broth. Thus far have the Greeks, Latins, and Arabs spoken on extracting the virtues from gold, but they have strayed far from the truth; for they quite foolishly believe that gold quenched in water imparts its virtue to it, and that even if they converted it into a drinkable liquid, it could be digested by human heat—something which **does not yield to the powers of the most violent fire, but rather remains untamed against it.**

We have experienced gold standing melted and exposed to a most violent fire for the space of three months, and in the end, it was found to have lost not the slightest bit of its weight; rather, it was found increased in color and quality, and the fire, which consumes all things, only makes it more perfect. How then shall it be digested by human heat, which can barely digest bread? And how can gold quenched in water impart its powers, if even purified "water of life" <note>original: *aqua vitæ*; high-proof distilled alcohol used as a solvent.</note> or other strong waters can scarcely change its flavor or color? We describe what we have seen. More recent, most learned, and skillful investigators of Nature have said that their secret, mastery, "fifth essence" <note>original: *quintam essentiam*; the purest element, also known as the quintessence, thought to be the soul of a substance.</note>, and everything else consists in the tincture of gold—namely, that the strength, power, soul, and energy of gold is the very color of gold itself. 

He who knows how to draw out its tincture attains no small secret. But "this is the task, this is the toil" <note>original: *hoc opus, hic labor*; a famous quote from Virgil’s Aeneid emphasizing the extreme difficulty of a task.</note>. Those who speak of extracting the gold tincture have spoken so concisely and perplexedly that they seem to have hidden it, or to have known nothing, rather than wishing to teach anything. Know that its tincture cannot be drawn out unless it is most perfectly dissolved in the strongest water; it is not dissolved by "strong waters" <note>original: *aquis fortibus*; nitric acid.</note> or "royal waters" <note>original: *regijs*; aqua regia, a mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids.</note> in the manner required, because the corrosive salts are not perfectly or absolutely dissolved in the water, but only release their watery part <note>original: *phlegma*; the watery, less active byproduct of distillation.</note> during distillation. Let them learn, therefore, by long-lasting solution and mixing—

->*How salts are to be extracted from things.*<-

### CHAPTER XVI.

**N**o small part of a substance's power resides in its salt. We use this not only for seasoning the food of the sick, but in other ways, as it possesses the greatest power of penetration. It was long debated by the ancients whether salts retain the properties of the things they came from, or whether they lose some through fire and acquire others. Through countless experiments, it has been shown that they preserve the powers of the substances from which they were extracted, and often these powers are even sharper. We will set down examples that we ourselves have seen; and first,

->*to make salt from lemons*<-

### *Salt from Cumin.*

The root, herb, and flowers are cast into a vessel, which is then thoroughly <term>luted</term> <note>Sealed with a paste of clay and other materials to make it airtight.</note>, dried, and placed into a brick furnace so that the ashes may be burnt. Meanwhile, distill the root, herb, and flowers—or if you prefer, boil them down—and with this water make a very sharp <term>lye</term> <note>An alkaline solution made by leaching ashes with water.</note>. When you have filtered this three or four times through linen cloths until perfectly clear, it is reduced back to salt by boiling in a glass vessel. If you seek it to be purer and brighter, spread the salt upon a porphyry marble slab and set it in a damp place, with a small vessel placed beneath so that whatever is dissolved by the moisture drips into it. Always strain out any impurities that remain, doing this a third time until it appears shining with a crystalline color; then store it. ### *Salt from Saxifrage.*

...in the same way we have described. If you season food with it, it renders one immune to the harm of poisoned food or bread, and protects against the contagion and infection of pestilential air. The same can be made from other things that excel against poisons, which Princes might use in their food instead of common salt, as its flavor is scarcely distinguishable. From <term>thapsia</term> <note>Also known as "deadly carrot," used in traditional medicine as a purgative.</note>, a salt is prepared to expel stones from the kidneys and bladder, and it dissolves hardened deposits of <term>tartar</term> <note>A buildup of minerals in the body, often associated with gout or kidney stones.</note> or viscous humors; it kills intestinal worms and purifies the blood. Taken frequently, it provokes sweating, and is wonderfully effective in the treatment of the <term>French disease</term> <note>original: "morbi gallici"; a common historical term for syphilis.</note>. If one consumes the extract of <term>pimpernel</term> <note>original: "bibinella" (likely Burnet saxifrage or a similar species).</note> for three days every third month, he shall live secure for his entire life from <term>dropsy</term> <note>edema or swelling</note>, <term>consumption</term> <note>original: "phthisi"; tuberculosis</note>, and <term>apoplexy</term> <note>stroke</note>. It effectively preserves the body from the pestiferous air of spreading contagion. It is also beneficial to the stomach when, with failing strength, it cannot digest consumed food. But in this, as in others, it must be noted that one should not eat these salts every day, lest the stomach become so accustomed to them that it treats them as ordinary food. A salt may also be made from the filed shavings of <term>guaiacum</term> <note>A hard wood from the Americas, famously used in the 16th century to treat syphilis.</note>, which is marvelously powerful against the venereal plague when taken in the same way we described. You have now learned how to prepare the rest in your own fashion.

## On Elixirs. CHAPTER 17.

**Elixirs** are preservatives for bodies; they maintain a body in the exact state in which they find it. Their power lies in guarding against corruption <note>In this context, corruption refers to the natural decay or aging of the body and its humors.</note>, not by correcting a defect, but by preserving what is there—though sometimes, by happenstance, their subtle nature may remove diseases. This power is twofold: guarding against illnesses and conserving the body in the state it was found. This applies not only to the human body but also to plants; an elixir emulates the powers of **balsam**. It primarily targets the heart, the brain, and those members in which the **spirit** <note>The "vital spirit" was believed to be a subtle substance that carried life and sensation through the body.</note> is most active. 

An elixir is of three species: **metallic**, **gem-based** (from precious stones), and **plant-based** (derived from roots, herbs, flowers, seeds, woods, resins, and the like). It differs from essences, tinctures, and all the other substances we have discussed. Because it is made from many components, it does not retain the form of a tincture (which lacks "fatness" or oily substance); nor is it an oil, for it lacks clarity and transparency; nor can it be a pure essence. Rather, it is a certain medium between all of these, appearing in the form of a liquor rather than anything else; hence it claims the name **elixir** <note>The word "elixir" comes from the Arabic *al-iksīr*, originally referring to a powder for transforming metals, but here used for a liquid medicinal preservative.</note>. An example would be

->*to compose an elixir from Burnet-saxifrage.*<-
<note>original: "è bibinella elixir componere." Bibinella refers to *Pimpinella saxifraga*, a plant highly valued in Renaissance medicine for its warming and protective properties.</note>

The root is dug up at its proper time and macerated in its own distilled water. With weights placed upon it, it is left to **putrefy** <note>A controlled process of fermentation or breaking down organic matter using gentle heat and moisture.</note> until the flowers have reached their full vigor. At that time, the flowers are picked and macerated in the same way, but in a separate vessel. The same must be done with the seed. It is then placed in an <term>alembic</term> <note>A classic distillation apparatus consisting of a boiling vessel and a cap with a downward-sloping beak.</note> to draw off the **phlegm** <note>The watery, non-active part of a distillate.</note> and the oil, until only dry dregs remain. The separated liquid is placed in a <term>pelican</term> <note>A specialized alchemical vessel with two side-arms that return the distillate back into the base, allowing for continuous "circulation."</note> and is **circulated** <note>A process of continuous redistillation where the vapor condenses and flows back into the liquid to further refine it.</note> for two months; finally, it is taken out and stored. Now we shall describe another,

->*Elixir from many things.*<-

Many compositions of elixirs are circulated which we have found to be faulty and inconsistent. Furthermore, in the extraction of the oils and waters, the work is so difficult that time and expense are wasted rather than any good being achieved. These are often practiced by Princes for the sake of pomp and magnificence, rather than for any benefit to men...

### *What "clissus" is, and how it is made. CHAPTER XVIII.*

Lest we omit anything, we shall teach what a <term>clissus</term> <note>original: "clissus"; a term used in Paracelsian alchemy to describe the unified essence or "specific power" of a plant, containing all its various parts (salt, sulfur, mercury) combined</note> is, and how it may be produced. A clissus is the extraction of the subtlety of all parts of a plant coming together into one common being. In a plant, there is a root, the herb, the flower, the fruit, and the seed, and within each of those parts, a peculiar nature dwells. The preparation shall be thus: the root is collected when its maturity is complete; the leaves when we suppose them to be gathered and picked at the proper time; the flowers when they are already blooming; and likewise the fruits and seeds. From all of these, the subtleties—or essences—are to be extracted by distilling, <term>putrefying</term> <note>the process of allowing organic matter to decay or ferment to release its active principles</note>, and <term>calcining</term> <note>reducing a substance to ash or powder through high heat</note>, or by any other method already taught. But when the essences have been drawn out from each part separately—one in the form of an oil, another as a salt, or another as a liquid—then all are joined into one, so that by their meeting and mutual fellowship they unite and come together into one body, whether it be a salt, an oil, or a liquid; then we shall have the "clissus" of the thing. There are some who unite them by distilling in vessels prepared for this purpose in the following way: they cast the liquid, the oil, and the salt into three <term>cucurbits</term> <note>gourd-shaped glass vessels used in distillation</note> of equal size and length, and they insert the three necks, tied together into one, into a <term>cap</term> <note>original: "pileum"; the head of the still or alembic</note> which faithfully receives and encloses the necks of them all. Once they are properly <term>luted</term> <note>sealed with "lute," a clay or paste used to make joints airtight</note>, fire is applied beneath, which draws up the thinner essence from the contents of each; they meet in the cap, and it discharges them through the opening into a small vessel placed beneath, where it is received and stored. This substance, united from many virtues, searches out the hidden passages of the body and provides remarkable utility in healing.

We have spoken of many ways of extracting oil; now, however, we shall speak of how it is extracted from salts, so that they may operate more powerfully, more thinly, and more piercingly. Furthermore, they could not be prepared in any other way. They seem to have something of fatness in them, yet they do not burn, nor do they seem to have any other oil, as if they were a kind of medium. First...

### To extract oil from tartar.

Let it be burned and reduced into a salt, as we have said; afterward, let it be exposed upon a marble slab in a damp place, for in a few days it turns into oil, and let it strain into a dish placed beneath it. But if you seek a different way, you shall prepare it most easily in this manner: Let the <term>tartar</term> <note>original: "tartarum"; the hard crust of potassium bitartrate that forms in wine casks, used extensively in early chemistry</note> be crushed into a powder, with which you should mix an equal amount of <term>saltpeter</term> <note>original: "halinitrum"; potassium nitrate, used here as a flux to help the combustion</note>; and in an iron mortar, where they have been crushed together, apply fire until the whole is burned. Let the remaining dregs be ground, and once liquefied in <term>lye</term> <note>original: "lixiuium"; an alkaline solution made from ashes</note>, strain it with a small brush; let the lye be dissolved into the air by fire, and the salt will settle at the bottom. Soon you shall boil eggs; take away the <term>yolks</term> <note>original: "boleta"; literally "mushrooms," used here metaphorically for the round yolks of the eggs</note> and fill the empty spaces with the salt. In a short interval of time, they will turn into oil. In this same way, we extract:

### Oil from soda.

We shall dissolve the salt extracted from <term>soda</term> <note>original: "soda"; sodium carbonate or soda ash, often derived from burning maritime plants</note> into water, and strain it through a <term>wick</term> <note>original: "per liciniam"; a method of capillary filtration where a thread or cloth strip draws liquid from one vessel to another</note> so that we may purify it; soon, once dried, we spread it upon marble, and in a damp place it turns into oil, and will flow from the marble into a jar. We also teach the celebrated:

### Oil of talc.

Although oil is sucked out from <term>talc</term> <note>original: "talco"; a soft mineral. In alchemy, "Oil of Talc" was a legendary cosmetic said to whiten the skin permanently</note> by the force of a vehement fire alone, we did not know until now what use it might have. But for the <term>beautifying deceptions</term> <note>original: "mangonia"; refers to the "doctoring" or "faking" of goods, here specifically referring to women's cosmetic arts to enhance or alter their appearance</note> of women, we have made it thus: Let it be crushed into a fine powder in an iron mortar; soon it is placed in a small jar of great thickness and strength, with a cover placed over the work and secured with iron wires. Once you have smeared it with potter's clay, let it be dried in the sun for three days. Afterward, thrust it into the glassmakers' furnace in a place where the flames surge, or elsewhere, provided the fire is most vehement. After three or four days, take it out and break the vessel; if you find it already reduced to <term>calx</term> <note>original: "calcem"; a dry, powdery substance produced by thorough burning</note>, you will have judged correctly; if not, do not be loath to repeat the same and expend equal labor. When the calx has become perfectly white, arrange it upon <term>porphyry</term> <note>original: "porphyreticum"; a very hard, purple-red igneous rock used for grinding and as a non-reactive surface</note> and leave it in a very damp place—either in excavated pits or a well. Allow it to stay for a long time, and you will see it flow out by the excessive humidity; collect it and store it in a glass vessel. It is made in almost the same way.

*A very red oil from sulfur.*
The process is as follows. Grind <term>native sulfur</term> <note>original: "sulphur viuum"; naturally occurring sulfur, often called "live sulfur" because it has not been processed by fire</note> into a fine powder and mix it with an equal portion of the **oil of tartar** already described. Afterward, let it be cooked in a glass vessel for three hours until it dissolves and turns into a liquid. Pass it through a **linen wick** <note>original: "per liciniam lineam"; a method of capillary filtration where liquid travels along a string or cloth strip to purify it</note> so that it may be cleansed. Put it into another glass vessel and dry it with the slow heat of a fire until it turns into a blood-red, clotted mass. This mass is then ground into small pieces, and the resulting powder is spread upon a marble slab in a damp cellar. In this way, it dissolves into a moisture that flows from the marble into a jar placed beneath it. This liquid, having been strained through thin pieces of cloth into a glass vessel, should be warmed in hot ashes until the humidity is consumed; finally, a very red oil will remain. It is extracted by women in this way:

*Oil of Myrrh.*
When eggs have been hardened by boiling, cut them through the middle and remove the yolks. Into their hollows, sprinkle the powder of crushed **myrrh** which has been passed through a sieve. Let these be set out in a clay jar upon longish boards, lest the eggs drink the oil back up again, and let them be enclosed in a damp cellar; you shall find the oil has dripped down into the jar.

### Oil from sulfur.

This is a specific method for extracting oil or water from sulfur. Have a glass vessel with a wide mouth, hollowed in the shape of a bell, which should be suspended by an iron wire. Place a large receiver below it to catch the oil dripping from the bell. In the middle of this, an earthen vessel is suspended and filled with sulfur. Light the fire so that the sulfur burns; while it is being consumed, the smoke rises through the arches of the bell, takes on a body <note>original: "corporascens"; condensing from a gas into a liquid</note>, and flowing back down through the rims, it turns into oil. If the sulfur is consumed, add more, until you have obtained the desired quantity of oil. We can also extract a more abundant quantity by another method. Let a large glass receiver be made, such as we described for the extraction of oil of vitriol and **strong waters** <note>original: "aquarum fortium"; nitric acid</note>. Let it be cut through the middle with an **emery stone** <note>original: "ſmiri lapide"</note>, and let the edges be shaped into teeth through which the smoke may escape. We shall fit this over an earthenware basin, in the center of which the ignited sulfur may evaporate. Above this, another vessel of greater capacity is placed, so that it stands a palm’s length away from the first. Let its edges be cut with deeper notches so that the smoke escaping from the first vessel, swirling through the second, may drip from both vessels. In this way, we can fit a third and fourth vessel above. Pour this oil into another vessel and let the **phlegm** <note>original: "phlegma"; the watery, less potent part of a distillate</note> evaporate over warm ashes; for then it will be made so strong that it will corrode silver—and I would not fear to say gold, if you have worked the process perfectly. The smoke of sulfur is congealed into **sal ammoniac** <note>original: "sal ammoniacum"; ammonium chloride</note>, as we have gathered in the **Phlegraean Fields** <note>original: "Phlegræis montibus"; a large volcanic area west of Naples known for its fumaroles and sulfur deposits</note>, and

## *On the separation of the elements.* CHAPTER XXI.

In a mixture, the four elements are present, but one often predominates; the others, being useless, are weakened. Thus, when we say the elements of a mixture are being separated, we mostly intend to isolate this one dominant part. In the **water lily** <note>original: "nimphea"</note>, the element of water predominates; air, earth, and fire are few. Thus, there is little or no quantity of dryness or heat, but water blunts everything else; the same is to be understood for other things. But because we separate the elements, do not think they are all separated from each other—as if air were absolutely separated from water, and water from fire and earth—but rather by a certain similarity. What we call "fire" is hotter than the rest, and what is more moist we call "water." Stones will have more earth, wood more fire, and herbs more water. We call those things "airy" which, when they have filled the vessels and the receiver, easily burst them, and the air flies out. When the elements have been separated in this way, they themselves can be purified and refined. The method of extraction varies according to the variety of things; for some are **calcined** <term>calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder or "calx"</term>, some are **sublimated** <term>sublimation: heating a solid until it turns into a vapor and then solidifies again on a cooler surface</term>, and others are **distilled** <term>distillation: the process of vaporizing a liquid and condensing it to separate components</term>. But let us look at examples; we wish:

### *To separate the elements of a metal.*

Into **aqua fortis** <term>aqua fortis: literally "strong water," or nitric acid</term>, as we have said, all of the metal is spread so that it may be dissolved. You shall draw this off in a **water bath** <note>original: "balneo"; a vessel placed in boiling water to ensure gentle, even heating</note>, and pour it on again, repeating this until it turns into an oil of a tawny or red color. To this oil, you will pour two parts of aqua fortis and macerate it in a closed glass vessel in **dung** <note>original: "fimo"; decaying manure was used to provide a low, constant heat for slow chemical reactions</note> for a month. Afterward, you shall distill the entire liquid through ash. This you will distill again in a water bath until it rises, and you will have two elements. From the water bath, **Air** is raised; in the bottom remain **Water** and **Earth**; **Fire** remains in the bottom...

### *To separate the elements of herbs.*

In all herbs, some specific element seizes dominance for itself. Take leaves of **sage** and crush them; let them rot <note>original: "putrescant"; putrefaction was a necessary first step in alchemy to break down organic structures</note> under manure in a vessel, and afterward you will distill them. First, fire will ascend until the colors and the thickness of the water are changed. A portion of earth follows, and another remains at the bottom, which is fixed <note>original: "fixa"; refers to the "fixed salt" or solid matter that does not vaporize</note>. Expose the water to the sun for six days; afterward, using a water bath, the water first ascends, then the color varies and the fire ascends until the taste is altered; finally, a part of earth is lifted, while another part remains mixed with air at the bottom. In **aquatic plants**, first air comes, then water and fire.

### *How the virtues of plants are to be investigated.*

There is, therefore, no better method of investigating the powers <note>original: "virtutis"; the inherent medicinal or occult properties</note> of plants than with the eyes and hands, and not by taste. For through distillation, if the hotter part exhales first, know that the plant is hot and composed of thin parts; and so with the rest, you will know from the segregation of the elements whether it consists of more fire, earth, or water. For by first weighing the plant, and then, after the extraction of the water, weighing the dregs of the oil, you will calculate the proportion of them all and thus determine the degrees...

### *How gum may be extracted from plants.*

We are able to extract gum from certain plants. I say "certain," for there are many which lack it, and no one can give what they do not possess. <term>Fennel</term> <note>Latin: *foeniculum*</note> can give it, as can all fennel-like plants, <term>all-heal</term> <note>Latin: *panaces*; a name given to various plants believed to have universal healing properties</note>, and others of a similar kind. ### *To extract gum from all-heal.*

At the summer solstice, the root of the <term>all-heal</term> is dug up at night, lest the heat of the sun’s rays should drain its moisture. Having been cut lengthwise, it is cast into a glazed earthenware vessel and placed upside down in a <term>descensory furnace</term> <note>original: *fornacem descensoriam*; a furnace designed for distillation by descent, where the liquid flows downward into a receiver rather than being vaporized upward</note>. A receiver is placed beneath it to catch the dripping moisture, and by applying a slow fire from the upper part of the vessel, the noble gum is drawn out. This is then purified with other instruments and separated into a more noble form by distillation. We can do the same with <term>giant fennel</term> <note>Latin: *ferula*</note>: the stalk is wounded on the inside at the same time of year, and when placed in a vessel with a gentle fire urging it from above and a small vessel placed beneath, it drips a sticky liquor. Once this has been cleared of dregs, it hardens like gum and is used for medical purposes. In the same way, we can

### How scented water may be made by immersion.

## CHAPTER II.

NOW we shall teach how to make scented liquids, and which ones are able to receive fragrances: for water is poorly suited for preserving scent; oil and wine are better. (We seem able to assign the reason from Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus (c. 371 – c. 287 BC), a Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle, wrote the foundational text *Concerning Odors*</note>: for water is extremely thin, devoid of all scent and flavor, and clear; it cannot take on any odor) and those things which are thick, earthy, or oily are better able to receive them. Wine, even if it is not naturally scented, can draw any odor to itself when placed nearby, because it contains heat within it, which has a nature for attracting; water, being cold by its own nature, can attract nothing, nor can it receive or protect a scent. It is known to be so thin, simple, and meager that any fragrance received into it slips away and, once poured out, vanishes, as if there were no sediment within it by which the scent might be fixed and held together. Indeed, it is understood that only a denser and more substantial body can hold onto a scent, a quality which both wine and oil possess. Oil is the most capable of all at preserving and protecting a scent, because...

->*How oil may be made fragrant.* CHAPTER III.<-

We have spoken in previous sections about how oil might be extracted from fragrant things and aromatics; now we shall teach how to draw scent out of things, either as we reviewed a little earlier, or by establishing an oil as a base in which the gathered scents may reside and linger longer. This is the most fragrant of all, which the Ligurians <note>The people of the coastal region around Genoa, Italy</note> use. Let these be placed in a glass vial, which you shall expose to the sun for twenty days while covered; afterward, you may use it. But let the cover be very well closed: for since the nature of scents is volatile <note>original: *flatilis*; literally "windy" or "breath-like"</note> and fleeting, it quickly vanishes, casts off the grace of its odor, and exhales feebly. In another way,

->*Fragrant oil from flowers*<-

### *How we may extract water and oil from fragrant gums by immersion.* CHAPTER IV.

**W**E ARE also able, by a different artifice than what we described above, to extract fragrant waters from gums through maceration <note>The process of softening or breaking a substance down by soaking it in liquid</note> and expression. For example:

->*A most fragrant water from storax, laser, and labdanum*<-

shall be extracted in this way, one which emits a far most sweet odor. Mix rose water with crushed storax or <term>laser</term> <note>original: *lasere*; likely referring to asafoetida or a similar resinous gum used as a substitute for the extinct ancient silphium</note> so that the water floats two fingers' depth above the solids. Let it be macerated in a water bath <note>original: *balneo*; a "Bain-marie"</note> or a warm place for a week; soon after, you will distill it through the bath and receive the fragrant water. Leave the extracted water in the midday sun so that if any smoky smell remains in the water, it may be cleared away. We can also place the gums in glass vessels and use a very slow fire: for it will sweat out a tiny amount of water of a far most sweet odor, and the gum remains at the bottom of the vessel, which will be useful for other purposes. In this same way:

We can extract oil from storax, laser, and the others, if you crush and mix almond oil, or oil from the <term>balanus myrepsica</term> <note>original: *balanus myrepsica*; literally the "perfumer's acorn," known today as the Ben-nut or Moringa, prized since antiquity for its odorless oil that carries scents well</note>, with these gums. Macerate this in a bath for a month; afterward, let the oil be expressed through a retort, or, what is safer, by a press; for it will fragrance with a most pleasant odor, such that one can hardly discern it from oil extracted from the gum itself by retorts. ### *How scented leathers are prepared.* CHAPTER V.

**N**OW we shall discuss how scented leathers are prepared, which is taught in many ways: either by bathing them in scented waters, or by rubbing them with oils, or by burying them in flowers so that they may adopt their fragrance. We will teach the method using scented waters, and first:

### *How the skins should be washed,*

So that they may shed the unpleasant odor of animals or flesh. The method is as follows. Let them first be washed in what is called "Greek wine" <note>likely a strong, sweet wine like Malmsey used for its high alcohol content to strip away fats and odors</note>; specifically, let them soak for several hours, and afterwards be dried. If a foul odor still troubles the "males" <note>original: *mares*; male animal hides often possessed a stronger, more persistent musk that required extra cleaning</note>, do not be weary of repeating the work again. Once the stench is washed away, let them be washed in scented waters. Prepare four parts of rose water, three of myrtle, two of orange blossoms, one of scented lotus, and half a part of lavender; mix these together and place them in a wide-mouthed jar <note>original: *fideliam*; a large earthenware pot or vat</note>. Let the skins soak in these for a day; afterwards, take them out and hang them to dry in the shade. However, when they are close to being dry, you must work them with your hands and shake them so they do not wrinkle. Repeat this three times until they smell with the sweetness of the waters and no longer breathe any odor of the skins at all. Next, let us say:

### *How skins may acquire the scent of flowers.*

It is necessary that they first be rubbed with oil; for we have said that oil is the "base" of fragrances, as its fatness is able to both attract and retain a scent within itself. This can be done with common oil, but it is better with the ben-nut oil <note>original: *myrobalano*</note> as we mentioned, because it is odorless. However, those who seek to perform the task most excellently rub on "oil of eggs" <note>original: *ouorum oleum*; a thick, fatty oil extracted from cooked egg yolks, used here to soften the leather</note>, the method for making which we have already described. This will be the manner: let us rub the gloves <note>original: *chirothecas*</note> or skins on the inside with a sponge, and especially where they will be worn; once you have completed this correctly...

You will act in this way so that the skins attract the scent of the flowers. First, violets and wallflowers <note>original: *leucoia*; likely the fragrant white violet or wallflower</note> spring forth in the springtime; by collecting these flowers in the morning and leaving them throughout the day with the skins laid beneath the flowers, you will then throw the flowers away—either sooner or later as they dry out—and put in new ones. Do this by removing and rearranging them three or four times a day, so that the skins do not become musty or moldy from being dampened by the dew. When these finish blooming, you shall apply orange flowers <note>original: *narantiorum*; neroli or orange blossoms</note> and roses in the same manner. In this way, the skins or gloves will remain highly scented, but only for the duration of one year; the scent vanishes in a short moment of time and the breath of the fragrance grows dull. However, if you do the same thing a second time, the scent will remain longer and they will preserve the grace of their pleasantness. They especially conserve their fragrance and the scent will have great staying power if they are kept in a closed place, such as in small boxes made of wood or lead; but if they are kept among linens, their scent is absorbed and grows weak and sluggish. ## How scented powders are made. CHAPTER VI.

We now come to the powders, which are made as either simple or composite scents; these are used to fill sachets <note>original: *puluilli*; small cushions or scented bags</note>, and we also use them on skins and in mixtures. Therefore, take note:

### How Cyprus powder is made.

Oakmoss <note>original: *Muscus quernus*; a lichen that grows on oak trees, highly valued in perfumery for its earthy, musk-like base note</note>, which breathes out the scent of musk, should be collected in its pure state. The time for gathering it is during the months of December, January, and February. Let it be washed five or six times in fresh water so that it is properly cleaned; afterwards, expose it to the sun. Soon after, let it soak for two days in rose water and be dried in the sun again. You shall repeat this many times, for the more often you wash it, the more fragrantly it will breathe out its scent. Once dried, let it be ground into a fine powder in a bronze mortar and sifted. Finally, let it be sprinkled upon a sifting-cloth and covered with its lid; beneath it, let coals be kindled, and above, let liquids boil or little cakes <note>original: *placentulæ*; aromatic pastilles or cakes used for fumigation</note> or scented smokes exhale. As we shall describe, the more frequently you do this, the more scent the powder will drink in, and the longer it will retain it. But when you know it has conceived enough of the scent, take a pound of this powder, a little powdered musk and civet <note>original: *zibethum*; a musk-like substance secreted by the civet cat</note>, and a sufficient portion of sandalwood and roses. Let the musk be ground in a bronze mortar, gradually sprinkling in the powder, and let it be ground and mixed in the mortar. Finally, store the powder in a stoppered vial so that it does not breathe out; for if it did, the scent would grow dull and fade away. There are various compositions of this powder, which would be tedious to recount. They are made white, black, dark-brown, and in various colors. The white is prepared from raw gypsum, which is first washed in rose water or scented water, adding musk, ambergris, civet, and other things; in this way, it will breathe out its scent for a long time.

### How to make scented beads
To make scented beads <note>original: *globulos odoratos*; also known as pomanders, these were worn as jewelry or carried to provide a personal scent or ward off disease</note> for very little money so that they appear high in price and give off a maximum fragrance, do this: Take one ounce of Cyprus powder <note>powdered oakmoss, as described on the previous page</note> and one ounce of laser <note>original: *laseris*; likely referring to a resin such as benzoin or asafoetida used as a fixative</note>, one ounce of the "oriental mixture" which is brought from Turkey—commonly called *pasta di levante*—half an ounce of cloves, and a sufficient quantity of Illyrian orris root. First, let gum tragacanth dissolve in rose water; create a mass and form it into beads. Perforate them through both sides and place individual pastilles within each, then fix them upon a board. Soon after, take four grains of musk, soften them in rose water, and with a small brush, smear the outer surface of the beads. Take care to let them dry. By doing this three or four times, the beads will vibrate a pleasant scent far and wide, and they will not lose their fragrance so quickly. If you desire them to be of greater value and scent, it shall be done thus:

->*Another way.*<-

->*Another mixture,*<-

Which will also be useful during a time of plague; it will not only refresh the brain with its scent but will render the contagion of the plague ineffective. ### How to multiply soap

You shall do it thus—for since we have fallen into a discussion of soap, this shall not go unmentioned. When the water begins to bubble and boil, stir it with a wooden spatula. If the lye level drops due to the heat, pour more on top. When the water has been evaporated into vapors, remove the cauldron from the fire and throw in six pounds of well-crushed common salt. Use an iron spoon to set it out on the ground and let it cool overnight. Meanwhile, prepare a brine <note>original: *muriam*</note> so sharp that it makes an egg float high. In the morning, cut the soap into pieces and arrange them within a wide vessel...
