## How fragrant fumigations are composed. CHAPTER VIII.

I see that it remains for me to speak of fumigations <note>original: *suffitibus*; these were aromatic vapors or incenses used to scent rooms or textiles</note>: for they are useful and necessary for providing scents to skins, linens, and powders, and in winter they fill the chambers of nobles with a fragrant breath; they are made from waters and powders. We shall teach

### How fumigations from waters are made.

Take four parts of styrax <note>a fragrant resin from the *Styrax* tree, often called storax</note>, three of benzoin <note>original: *laseris*; while originally referring to the extinct silphium, in this period it often denoted benzoin or aromatic resins used in perfumery</note>, one each of labdanum, aloeswood <note>original: *agallochi*; the rare, resinous heartwood of the aquilaria tree, also known as oud</note>, and cinnamon, an eighth part of cloves, and a little ambergris <note>original: *ambatae*</note> and musk. Let them all be ground somewhat coarsely and put into a small bronze pot with rose water, to the amount of one cup <note>original: *cyathi*; a measure approximately equal to 45ml</note>. Place the small pot over hot coals or warm ashes so that it gets hot, but does not boil, and it will exhale a pleasant odor; if the water runs out, we can add more. We can also add those things which we saved from the preparation of orange flower water <note>original: *aquæ nansæ*; derived from the Arabic *naffah* for orange blossom</note>, for they will breathe out a pleasant scent. It is also made in

### Another way.

Three parts of cloves, two of benzoin, one of aloeswood, as much cinnamon, orange peels, and sandalwood, and an eighth part of nutmeg <note>original: *nucis myristicæ*</note>. Put all these crushed into a pot and pour over it orange flower water, lavender water, or myrtle water, and let it heat. Or

### Otherwise

Extract and strain the juice of lemons, into which you will add styrax, aloeswood, camphor, and empty musk pods <note>original: *moschi vesicas vacuas*; the scent glands of the musk deer, which retained their aroma even after the musk was removed</note>, all of which should be steeped in a water bath <note>original: *balneo*</note> for a week in a very well-sealed glass vial. When we desire a scented room, we shall drop a drop of this liquid into a small bronze pot full of rose water and let it heat over warm ashes, and it will exhale most sweetly. Thus, indeed, they are prepared...

#### *Fumigation.*

If you coat the rinds of citron or lemon with a tiny bit of civet <note>original: *zibetho*; a pungent, musky secretion from the civet cat, used sparingly to enhance other scents</note>, then pierce them with Indian cloves and sticks of cinnamon, and allow them to boil in rose water, the fumigation will fill the chamber with the greatest delight.

Black musk approaching a reddish color is adulterated with a moderate amount of roasted goat's blood or roasted bread, so that three or four parts of the ground material are added to one part of musk, such that they can scarcely be distinguished. ## Devising portentous engines of destructive fire.

### PREFACE.

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'A' set within a square woodcut frame decorated with intricate floral and vine patterns.</image-desc>

Before we move our pen away from Vulcan <note>The Roman god of fire, here representing the arts of the forge, chemistry, and pyrotechnics</note>, we shall speak of that deadly fire, the contriver of marvelous works, which the common people call "artificial fire." Through various devices and portentous inventions, generals and commanders have used this fire to utterly destroy walls and cities from their foundations, and have employed it most fatally in naval battles with great human slaughter, very often frustrating the hostile forces of the enemy. It is a matter both highly useful and admirable; indeed, nothing else more terrifies and strikes dread into the minds of men. God is coming to judge the world by fire <note>original: "Deus venturus est iudicare ſeculum per ignem"; a traditional theological reference to the Last Judgment, used here to emphasize the awesome power of the element</note>. Let us describe the incendiary fires of our ancestors which they used in sieges, and we shall also add those of more recent times—which far surpass the ancients—and finally, our own inventions. ...[various] compositions, fire-vomiting and lethal tubes <note>original: "tubas igniuomas"; likely referring to early incendiary weapons or primitive cannons</note>, inextinguishable fires that rage under water—nay, even in the very depths, like excavated tunnels, with the greatest violence of struggling flames—causing the seas to gape open and be lifted to the stars, so that ships are submerged in a portentous abyss. ### *How various fire-making tools are prepared.* CAP. I.

Vitruvius <note>A famous Roman architect and engineer whose works often discussed the origins of human technology</note> relates that it happened by chance: different trees, frequently shaken by winds and storms, rubbed their branches together with strong friction. This contact and the resulting thinning of the wood drew out heat and kindled fire, from which a great flame followed. Wild and rustic men, terrified by this, took flight. But when the flame died down and they approached closer, they realized the great convenience that came from it for human bodies; they preserved the fire, and thus it provided the causes for urbanity, social custom, and speech.

Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, author of the *Natural History*</note> says it was the invention of soldiers and shepherds. The use by scouts in camps and by shepherds discovered this, since an opportunity for a stone <note>meaning flint or strike-a-light stones</note> to strike fire is not always available. Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and the "father of botany"</note> teaches which woods are suited for this use: although it sometimes happens that the drill <term>drill: a pointed stick rotated rapidly to generate heat (Latin: *terebrum*)</term> and the hearth <term>hearth: the base piece of wood with a notch to catch the sparks (Latin: *conceptaculum*)</term> are sometimes made from the same wood, he judges that one should be made of a part that acts and retains the power of producing [the fire], while the other should be made of a part that suffers [the friction]—one from hard wood, the other from soft. For example:

### *Woods which catch fire by friction.*

There are those that are especially "hot," such as laurel, buckthorn, holm oak, and linden. Mnestor <note>An early Greek botanical writer</note> adds the mulberry, and they conjecture this because these woods immediately blunt and dull adzes <note>a type of cutting tool</note>; they make the drill from all of these so that they may resist more sharply during friction and complete the work more persistently. However, the hearth should be made from soft wood, such as ivy, traveller's joy (or wild vine), and similar dried woods...

...[if they are] completely drained of all moisture. A pot is rejected as unfit if it is filled with fatty matter and excessive moisture. Ultimately, those materials that grow in shady and covered places are inferior for use as fire-starters and are rejected. Regarding this, Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, author of *Natural History*</note> says: "Wood is rubbed by wood and conceives fire by attrition, with a dry tinder material easily receiving the spark, such as fungus or leaves." But nothing is better than ivy, which may be rubbed by laurel, or rub against laurel. Another wild vine, distinct from the *labrusca* <note>the common wild grape</note>, is also approved, which itself climbs trees in the manner of ivy.

We, however, manage this more conveniently: Let laurel be rubbed by laurel and moved vigorously, for it will immediately raise smoke; then, with a tiny amount of sulfur added, you should bring forward tinder or dry fuel. This you will prepare from the material of dry fungus, leaves, or the dried-out downy fluff <note>original: "excocti velleris"</note> found around the roots of coltsfoot <note>a plant (*Tussilago farfara*) known for its flammable, wool-like fibers</note>, for these more quickly catch and retain fire. I have also made the same from ivy wood, cleaned of bark and dried, and by rubbing a giant fennel <note>original: "ferula"</note> with another giant fennel, or—what is even better—with a rope moved quickly over it. The West Indians <note>referring to the Indigenous peoples of the Americas</note> tie two dry pieces of wood together and place a rod into a crack, which they whirl between their hands with a back-and-forth motion, and thus they light a fire.

But since the human mind rarely stops at the same discoveries, but investigates a path further to find new things, by its industry there was found:

### *A Stone that Kindles Fire with any Moisture.*

The method of making this is as follows: Equal weights of native sulfur <note>original: "viui sulphuris"</note> and purified saltpeter <note>original: "halinitri"</note>, and double that amount of camphor, are added to quicklime <note>original: "viuae calci"</note>. All these are ground in a mortar until they are so fine that they could fly away into the breeze. These are wrapped and tied tightly together in a small linen cloth, closed inside an earthenware vessel, and after being smeared with clay mixed with straw, the vessel is dried in the burning sun. It is then placed in a potter's furnace, and when the vessel has been baked, the contents unite and are reduced to the hardness of a stone. Once extracted, they should be stored in a dry place for use. As to why my own experience failed me while making this, I know it has been done without doubt by my friends. However, the pot must not "breathe" <note>it must be perfectly airtight</note>, or else everything is consumed by fire. We have nonetheless seen a flame excited by scattering water over quicklime when sulfur has been moved near it.

### *On the Compositions of Fire Which Our Ancestors Used.* Chapter II.

Before we arrive at our own fire compositions, we shall review those which our ancestors used in naval battles, and in the storming and defending of cities. From Thucydides <note>Athenian historian, c. 460–400 BC</note> it is recorded that when the Plataeans were being besieged, when siege machines were of no use, the attackers fled to fires; for throwing bundles of wood around the walls, and having thrown in fire, sulfur, and pitch, they set the material ablaze. From this arose such a flame as no one had ever seen until that time. Hero <note>Hero of Alexandria, a 1st-century engineer known for his pneumatic and steam-powered inventions</note> teaches that in burning down walls, after drilling holes, pine torches should be placed underneath, and ignited with dry pitch and crushed sulfur, along with liquid pitch, or smeared with oil. 

And elsewhere he teaches how to burn by means of an urn. A clay urn is made, but bound with iron plates on the outside, and filled with tiny coals, pierced toward the bottom where a bellows was inserted; for when the fires have caught the coals, they burn, and the walls are shattered by the pouring over of vinegar, urine, or other sharp substances <note>The "shattering" refers to the ancient practice of heating stone walls and then cooling them rapidly with liquid to cause them to crack</note>. Vegetius <note>a late Roman writer on military matters</note> teaches about combustibles used in naval battles, and uses incendiary oil, tow <note>coarse flax or hemp fibers</note>, sulfur, and bitumen; glowing arrows are fixed by ballistae <note>large ancient missile-throwing engines</note> into the hulls of enemy ships, and they suddenly ignite the boards—smeared with wax, pitch, and resin—with so many fuels for the fire. We subjoin:

->*Fire-bearing missiles which the ancients used.*<-

"Malleoli" <note>fire-darts</note> are described by Ammianus Marcellinus <note>a 4th-century Roman soldier and historian</note> as a type of weapon shaped in this form: It is a reed arrow, joined with a multi-pronged iron between the point and the shaft, which is hollowed out in the shape of a woman’s distaff <note>a tool used in spinning wool</note> on which linen threads are spun, subtly and variously open in the "belly," and in that cavity it receives fire with some fuel. Thus it is emitted quite slowly from a weak bow—for the heat of the fire is extinguished by the faster stroke of a rapid bow—and it is lulled by no remedy other than by throwing dust or dregs of oil <note>original: "amurca," the bitter, watery sediment of pressed olives</note> over it. Livy <note>Roman historian known for his history of Rome</note> [notes]: Some with burning dregs, others with tow...

### On the various compositions of gunpowder.
### CHAPTER III.

**It** would seem we have done poorly, in speaking of fiery compositions, regarding that wondrous gunpowder—the author of all wonders—if we did not first speak of it, since it enters into all mixtures, and everything depends on it; not that it is my heart's desire to treat it extensively, since it is a very common thing, but only those aspects which contain something new or hidden. It consists, therefore, of four parts saltpeter <note>original: "halinitri"</note>, one of sulfur, and one of willow charcoal <note>original: "carbonis salicis"</note>. But it is necessary that the saltpeter be purified from common salt, fat, and earthy parts; for that is the foundation and basis of the rest. For everything must be well crushed, very finely sifted through a sieve, and mixed together as well as possible. Whence it is asked:

*Gunpowder of violent noise and action.*

Add more parts of saltpeter: specifically, to single parts of charcoal and sulfur, add six or eight parts of saltpeter, but let it be excellently purified and mixed. For four parts of saltpeter excellently purified and mixed do more than ten that are foul and unmixed. From the saltpeter comes the force and the roar of the flame; from the sulfur comes the ignition; and from the charcoal comes the rapid burning. Conversely, if it is asked:

*Gunpowder that shoots a ball without noise.*

It is necessary to weaken the saltpeter, but by mixing and remixing it with something fatty—gold glue <note>original: "auri glutinum"—possibly a resin or chrysocolla used in soldering</note> and butter being best—according to the known or proper proportion; this emits the ball without noise, or with very little, so that you yourself can scarcely hear it; and if it does not strike with such violent force, it is certainly only a little less. We do not declare the method, lest we provide an opportunity <note>original: "ansam"—literally 'a handle'</note> for the wicked to do evil.

### *How fire-throwing tubes are constructed.*
## CHAPTER IV.

**Likewise,** Hero <note>Hero of Alexandria, a Greek mathematician and engineer known for his inventions in antiquity</note> advises soldiers about to scale city walls to use portable, hand-held engines <note>original: "tormenta"—meaning devices or artillery</note> that throw fire from a distance against the faces of those defending the city. For those standing upon the walls are so terrified by these monstrous machines—which hurl fiery globes and raging flames—that they cannot even endure the sight of them, let alone the soldiers attacking the walls, and they flee beneath cover as quickly as possible. Furthermore, modern commanders <note>original: "recentiores"</note> use them extensively in naval battles and among squadrons of cavalry; for horses are terrified by fire, just as elephants are, so that they easily turn tail and throw the ranks into confusion. When the people of Megara were besieged by Antipater <note>a Macedonian general</note>, and the Macedonians were attacking most fiercely, the Megarians first set fire to pigs smeared with pitch, and then sent the burning animals against the enemy. The pigs, inflamed with madness and shrieking as they were consumed by fire, ran into the ranks of the elephants; they acted like furies, inciting the elephants to panic and causing grave disorder. But let us describe the device:

->*Tubes that eject fire from a great distance.*<-

Let a piece of wood three feet long be rounded on the outside and hollowed out within using a lathe; the central hole should have a diameter of a palm <note>about 3 inches</note>, and the wood should be a finger’s thickness in solidity. However, the interior must be reinforced with a thin plate of iron, and the exterior bound with iron rings at the mouth, the middle, and the base. The spaces between should be strengthened and tightened with iron wires, lest the violence of the flames struggling within cause the machine to burst into pieces and strike one's friends. You shall fill the hollow with this mixture: three parts of gunpowder <note>original: "Tormentarij pulueris"—literally "engine powder"</note>, half a part of colophony <note>a type of pine resin or rosin</note>, and half a part of sulfur. You must grind the sulfur and colophony somewhat coarsely, and a sprinkling of linseed oil should not be lacking; then mix it by hand. From this, you shall perform a test to see if the mixture burns too slowly or too fiercely: fill the hollow joint of a reed with the powder and apply fire. If it burns so vehemently that it breaks the reed, add more colophony and sulfur; if it burns weakly, add more gunpowder. Then fill the tube, pressing it down in turn with a rod; seal the mouth with linen, wax, and

### How the armed tube is made.

This device, through the perpetual emission of fiery globes and the discharge of lead bullets from iron firearms <note>original: "scloporum"—early handguns or small cannons</note>, will strike the faces of those standing nearby. Take equal portions of turpentine resin, liquid pitch, varnish, frankincense, and camphor; one and a third parts of native sulfur; a double portion of refined saltpeter <term>halinitrum: also known as sal nitrum, the essential oxidizing component of gunpowder</term>; a triple portion of "burning water" <note>original: "ardentis aquae"—distilled alcohol or spirits of wine</note>, and as much naphtha oil and gunpowder <note>original: "pyrii pulveris"—literally "fire powder"</note>. These should be ground together and formed into fiery globes, which should fit loosely within the hollow of the tube. 

Let the first mixture be put into the hollow to the depth of three fingers and pressed down; then add an ounce of simple gunpowder, followed by one of the prepared globes, and then the first powder again. Repeat this alternating series of layers until the whole tube is full, and let the mouth be protected as we described. 

There are some who do not use globes, but rather spread tow <note>coarse flax or hemp fibers</note> wrapped in iron shards <note>original: "tesseris"—small square pieces or dice</note>, which is slow-burning enough that the mixture above can ignite the gunpowder. Some pour coarsely crushed glass into the tow, others salt and lead filings; for if these globes stick to armor or clothing, they cannot be extinguished by water or anything else until they are entirely consumed. 

There are also those who surround the outside of the tube with brass or iron pistols. By making holes through the casing of the tube and filling them with gunpowder, when the fire reaches that point, they discharge lead bullets into the faces of bystanders with a horrible booming sound, one after another. 

We have seen a tube of unusual size—specifically ten feet long and as wide as a human head—filled with fiery globes, stones, and other things, and completely armed with pistols. It was tied to the base of a ship's yardarm <note>original: "antennae"</note> and directed here and there by ropes according to the wishes of the combatants. <header>NATURAL MAGIC, BOOK XII.</header>

It is a recent invention that a larger bronze cannon, or even a handheld firearm <note>original: "sclopus"—referring to an early musket or arquebus</note>, can fire roughly ten balls, more or less, without interruption. To do this, prepare the "slow powder" <note>a gunpowder mixture diluted with other ingredients to burn at a controlled rate, acting as a fuse</note> which we used in the preceding sections, and fill the weapon in this manner: first, put in a measured amount of cannon powder, enough to discharge the ball. Then, insert the ball, but let it be slightly smaller than the bore so that it fits loosely; this allows the powder added from above to reach the gunpowder below. Next, pour in the slow powder to a height of two or three fingers. After this, add the true gunpowder and another ball. Continue this alternating layering until the weapon appears full almost to the muzzle. Finally, add a top layer of slow powder. When you have aimed the machine at the designated target, apply fire to the mouth. It will hurl the balls and fire in succession, with the timing between shots being about the same as if someone were firing a handheld gun in separate instances. Thus, with a single bronze weapon, you can inflict multiple strikes.

### How fiery balls are made, which are projected from bronze cannons. CHAPTER V.

Now we shall teach the compositions for certain pots or fiery balls, which are projected from bronze cannons for various purposes: for burning ships, for illuminating areas at night, or even for being thrown through the air on festive days so that they appear to run about like a falling star. We will now explain how such things are made.

->*Balls running through the air,*<-

This is what is done on feast days. Let there be ground one pound of cannon powder, a third part of saltpeter <term>halinitrum: potassium nitrate, the primary oxidizer in gunpowder</term>, two ounces of sulfur, and an equal amount of colophony <note>original: "colophoniae"—a brittle, flammable resin obtained from pine trees</note>. When these ingredients are combined, sew them into small bags of thick linen in the shape of a ball. These are then placed into hollow semi-circular wooden molds and struck with a wooden mallet until they harden like stone. Next, they are wrapped with cords and dipped in liquid pitch three or four times to create a protective casing <note>original: "loricentur"—literally "to be armored," used here to mean creating a hard shell</note>, so that they do not shatter into pieces from the violence of the cannon's discharge. Finally, let them be pierced through the center with a wooden stylus and the hole filled with gunpowder, then dried, ready to be hoisted or launched. When you wish to use them, choose bronze cannons, or more conveniently a cannon-

### On mixtures that burn in water. CHAPTER VI.

Scholars <note>original: "Philologi" — those who study the records of the ancients</note> investigating the nature of waters hidden above and below the earth, which are perpetually boiling, say that bitumen <note>a naturally occurring, sticky, black form of petroleum</note> is the cause of this thing; for once it is ignited, by its own nature it is not only not extinguished, but it burns more fiercely when water is sprinkled on it. Pliny writes: "Mount Chimera in Phaselis burns with a flame that is immortal by day and night." Ctesias of Cnidus <note>a Greek physician and historian</note> relates that its fire is kindled by water, but extinguished by earth or hay. Likewise, in Lycia, the Hephaestian mountains, when touched by a flaming torch, burn so much that even the stones of the rivers and the sands burn in the waters themselves, and that fire is nourished by rains. The crater of Nymphaeum portends dire things for its people of Apollonia, as Theopompus <note>a Greek historian</note> relates; it is increased by showers, and it will be bitumen, which must be tempered by that undrinkable spring, otherwise it is more diluted than all other bitumen. Now the types of bitumen must be investigated. First the liquid kind, called naphtha, known to our people as petroleum <note>original: "olio petrolio" — literally "rock oil"</note>, which flows from stones, and *kitram* <note>likely referring to cedar oil or a type of liquid pitch</note>. This has a great kinship with fires, and they immediately leap into it from wherever they are seen.

They say that Medea burned her rival <note>In Greek mythology, Medea killed her husband's new bride, Glauce, by sending her a poisoned robe and crown that burst into flames</note> in this way: after she had approached the altars to perform a sacrifice, the crown was snatched up by fire. Another type is found in the city of Samosata in Commagene <note>An ancient kingdom in what is now south-central Turkey</note>, where there is a pool that emits a flaming mud (which they call *maltha* <note>original: "maltam" — a term for natural bitumen or thick petroleum</note>). Whenever it touches something solid, it sticks fast; furthermore, it follows those who try to flee its touch. In this way, they defended their walls when Lucullus <note>A Roman general who besieged Samosata in 69 BCE</note> was attacking, and the soldiers' armor caught fire: for it is ignited by water, and they learned through experience that it can only be extinguished by earth. Naphtha is a variety of this; like bitumen, it draws fire to itself. Pissasphaltum <term>Pissasphaltum</term> <note>a natural mixture of pitch and bitumen</note> is a harder variety of bitumen; there are also types of amber <term>succinum</term> and jet <term>gagatis</term> <note>a type of fossilized coal</note>, but these burn more slowly and less effectively in water. Furthermore, the second substance that burns in water is sulfur, for nothing "fattier" is dug from the earth. To maintain this fire on its own, it neither burns in water nor is it extinguished by water, and it does not last long; but when added to bitumen, it makes the fire last forever, as can be seen in the Phlegraean mountains of Pozzuoli <note>The Phlegraean Fields near Naples, known for their volcanic activity and sulfur vents</note>. And just as fire is ignited if oil is sprinkled on it, so water sprinkled on burning bitumen increases the flame more violently. Therefore, we shall use these materials for those fires which are meant to burn in and under water. But let us offer some examples of how to make:

### A Ball that burns under water.

First, let gunpowder <term>puluis pyrius</term> <note>literally "fire powder"</note> be prepared: for this enters into all these mixtures and provides the others with the power of burning violently. If this is granulated, let it be ground very fine and separated with a sieve. To seven parts of this, let two parts of colophony <term>colophoniæ</term> <note>a brittle resin obtained from pine trees</note> be added, three parts of saltpeter <term>halinitri</term>, and one of sulfur. Let everything be ground together and mixed, not without a sprinkling of naphtha or liquid pitch (*kitran* <note>likely "qitran," an Arabic-derived term for cedar oil or pitch</note>); continue moistening until the powder stays together on its own when squeezed in the fist. They test the strength of these when well-mixed: for if it burns too violently, they add more colophony, saltpeter, and sulfur; if too weakly, they add more gunpowder. This mixture should be wrapped in straw or linen, or placed in small boxes made of the aforementioned materials, and bound as tightly as possible with cords and bandages so it is compressed. Let it be submerged in boiling pitch and allowed to dry, and again with straw...

->**Balls and pots to be thrown at ships.**<-

The ancients wrote that Alexander the Great discovered this composition of fires for burning bridges, harbor mouths, ships, and similar things; now it will work even more violently because of the addition of gunpowder. Or, if you fashion a ball from these and bind it around the head of a mallet—which has a sharp tooth one foot long and a handle three feet long—in a naval conflict, if someone in a light boat pierces the hull of the enemy ships with one blow, it will excite a great fire, unextinguishable by water or any other means.

WE SHALL TEACH how to make brittle metallic balls which, filled with gunpowder and with their vents blocked on all sides, will burst into many pieces by the violence of the flame struggling within, and will pierce the bodies of those in their way.

### Balls projecting iron shards at a distance.

Therefore, let a metal ball be made, a palm’s width in diameter and half a finger's thickness. The metal should consist of three parts copper <note>original: "æris"; likely a brass or bronze alloy</note> and one part tin, so that it becomes so brittle that, when shattered by the force of the fire, it breaks into tiny pieces. So that the ball may be constructed more easily, let it be made of two hemispheres <note>original: "hemicyclijs"</note>; for it is finished with less waste of expense, and let them be joined together like a box, or by one part entering the other by turning it like a screw <note>original: "cochleatim"</note>. Let it be of equal thickness so that it breaks equally on all sides; then let it be bound more tightly by a nail driven through the middle, of a finger's thickness, so that it breaks in every other part before the joints. 

Then let a small tube <note>original: "canaliculus"</note> be made the size of a finger and a palm's length, so that it reaches the center of the ball and stands out above the surface in the shape of a pyramid—with the base on the outside and the cone on the inside—and let it be solidified and glued into the ball. To the nail, which as we said protrudes from both sides of the surface, let iron wires be attached, which should have iron dice <term>taxilli</term> <note>small iron cubes or shards used as shrapnel</note> threaded through them via wide holes, so that each wire holds thirty pieces. Thus, while the ball is shattered by the force of the fire and the iron wires are snapped, the iron dice are scattered and hurled a distance with such force that they seem to be exploded from muskets <note>original: "sclopis"</note> or catapults <note>original: "balistis"</note>. 

Finally, let the ball be filled with simple and excellent gunpowder <term>tormentario pulvere</term> <note>literally "engine powder," used for artillery</note>, but fill the tube with that mixture which burns more slowly. When fire has been applied to it, it may be held in the hand for as long as that slow mixture takes to approach the center, and then it is immediately thrown at the enemies. For it shatters into a thousand parts, and the iron wires, the dice, and the pieces of the ball are hurled a distance with such a strong blow that they penetrate a palm's depth into wooden boards or a wall. These are thrown in the storming of cities and during soldierly assaults, for they can wound two hundred men; and at that time, it will be better to wound than to kill <note>likely referring to the strategic advantage of wounding enemies, which requires more resources from the opposing army to manage than the dead</note>, as military experience proves. But when you wish to fill the tubes, hold one in your hand without the ball, filled with the mixture, and [conduct an] experiment...

### *How squadrons of cavalry may be thrown into confusion.*

Larger balls of this kind are also made, namely of a foot in size, bound with the same threads, but filled with more numerous iron shards <note>original: "taxillis," likely small cubes or metal studs used as shrapnel</note>, specifically by the thousands. These are thrown into the midst of a squadron of cavalry <term>equitum turmæ: the standard tactical unit of Roman and Renaissance cavalry</term>, or into besieged cities, or onto ships, by catapults, or by bronze engines <term>tormentis: a general term for any large-scale projectile-throwing machine</term> which they call stone-throwers <note>original: "petrera," a type of mortar or cannon specifically designed to hurl stone balls</note>, and in various ways. For if they are armed with iron shards, they are exploded by the violence of the fire at their ruptures so forcefully that they pierce through armed men and horses; and with a huge boom, they so terrify the horses that it is impossible for them to obey the spur or the rein without throwing the rank into confusion. They are made with four through-holes and filled with the aforementioned mixture, so that when lit and thrown into the midst of the squadrons, they shoot out flames at a distance with such a noise and crash that they seem to imitate thunder and flashing lightning.

## *How mines may most quickly be dug in level ground and under water.* CHAPTER VIII.

For the making of mines <note>original: "cuniculis," literally "rabbit burrows," the standard term for military tunnels dug beneath fortifications</note>, which are dug to overturn cities and fortresses, there is need of much time, labor, and expense; nor can they hardly be made without the enemy's knowledge. We will teach how to dig them in the sight of the enemies, in that level ground where the engagement of the enemies will take place on both sides, with little labor and in a moment of time. Therefore,

**to dig mines in a plain where a battle will occur,**

If you desire to do this in the sight of the enemies (for they are ignorant of what you are doing), let us be the first to teach: a little before night, or in the twilight, where the engagement, or passage, or station will be, let pits <note>original: "scrobes"</note> be excavated to a depth of three feet, so that one is distant from the other by about ten feet. There you will place balls of a foot in size, or more or less, so that you fill the whole plain. Soon you will dig mines or furrows from one to the other, so that through them cotton fuses <note>original: "bombicea ellychnia"</note> may safely pass within clay tubes or hollowed reeds...

Place this inside a hollowed-out reed and fill the empty space with powder. Or take one part of purified saltpeter <term>halinitri: potassium nitrate, the primary oxidizer in gunpowder</term>, half as much sulfur, and boil them with linseed oil in a new jar. Submerge the fuses so they are soaked through with that liquid; remove them and dry them in the sun. If you wish, however...

### *To make mines in the water.*

You shall use this most beautiful invention. In a place where the enemy's triremes <note>original: "triremes," oared warships with three banks of rowers</note> or ships will come through the waters, you will prepare mines <note>original: "cuniculos," literally "tunnels" or "burrows," a term for military mining used here for submerged explosives</note>. Arrange several beams joined crosswise, or in the manner of a net, on a flat surface. At the intersections, fit and fasten wooden boxes of the desired size filled with gunpowder. The beams should be hollowed out and filled with fuses and powder so that they can carry the fire to the boxes. With great care and skill, smear the boxes and beams with pitch <note>original: "pice," a resinous substance used for sealing</note> and coat them multiple times <note>original: "lorica," literally "breastplate" or "armor," here referring to a protective waterproof casing</note> so that no passage for water remains and the powder does not become damp (for then you would lose both your oil and your effort). Leaving a spot from which the fire can be started, sink the engine <note>original: "machinamentum," a general term for a mechanical device or contraption</note> under the waters with weights and stones, and cover it with mud and seaweed shortly before the arrival of the enemy. Let there be a scout present; when the ships or triremes stand above the trap, and the fire is applied, the sea gapes open and is hurled even to the heavens. It will either sink the ships or shatter them into a thousand pieces, so that nothing is more wonderful to see or to do. We have tested this under waters and lakes, and it achieved an end beyond what was imagined.

## Things that are useful for extinguishing fire. Chapter IX.

We have spoken of setting fires; now we must speak of extinguishing them, and incidentally of those things that remain vulnerable to fire. But first, let us recall what our ancestors said about this business. Vitruvius <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, the famous Roman architect and engineer</note> said that the wood of the larch tree <term>Larix: the European larch, prized for its durability</term> does not catch fire, nor does it burn by itself—any more than a stone in a furnace—nor does it leave behind coals, but is consumed only very slowly. He assigns the reason for this to its having very little air and fire, but much moisture and earth; he claims it is of great solidity and lacks the gaps or pores through which fire might penetrate. He tells how this was discovered: when Caesar had ordered the townsfolk around the Alps to provide him with supplies, they, being fortified in a wooden castle, refused to obey his command. Caesar ordered bundles of brushwood to be piled around the castle and burning torches to be lit, so that when the material caught fire and the flames rose to the sky, he thought the structure would collapse; but when the brush was burned out, the tower appeared intact. From this, Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, the Roman natural philosopher</note> says: "Larch makes no coal, nor is it consumed by the power of fire in any other way than stones." But this is most false: for since it is resinous and oily, it catches fire instantly and burns; indeed, once the fire is caught, it is extinguished with great difficulty. Thus I marvel that this error has been so widely spread, and that the town of Larignum, named for its abundance of these trees, was said to have survived being besieged by fire without damage. Furthermore, we read it recorded in antiquity that liquid alum <term>alumen liquidum: a naturally occurring sulfate mineral used as a fire retardant</term> is effective against fire. For wood smeared with alum and verdigris <term>viridi ære: literally "green brass," referring to the green pigment or copper acetate</term>—whether they be doorposts or paneled ceilings—remains invincible to fire as long as they are covered with some crust of it. Archelaus, the general of Mithridates, gave proof of this in a wooden tower against Sulla, which Sulla tried in vain to burn, as we find noted by Quadrigarius <note>Quintus Claudius Quadrigarius, a Roman historian</note> in his annals. But this liquid alum is still unknown to most of the more learned; our modern alum lacks such a quality and experimental proof. However, there are many who confirm that vinegar <term>acetum: vinegar, used here for its perceived cooling and chemical properties</term> is effective against fire. Plutarch says that no fire extinguisher is more effective than vinegar, for of all things it most suppresses a flame,

...on account of its extreme coldness. Polyænus <note>Polyaenus, a 2nd-century Macedonian author known for his "Stratagems of War"</note> records that when Athenocles was besieged by enemies, he poured molten lead from bronze vessels down upon the approaching *testudines* <term>Testudo: literally "tortoise," a protective mobile shelter used by besieging soldiers</term>, which caused them to dissolve. However, the enemies poured vinegar over the structures, which quenched the lead and anything else falling from the walls. Indeed, they found that vinegar is most suited for extinguishing fire, and the best experiment was performed with it. Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, the Roman naturalist</note> praises the white of an egg for extinguishing fire, saying: "Such is the power of the white that wood soaked in egg white will not burn, and even a garment touched by it will not be scorched." Hieron <note>Likely Hiero of Syracuse or a classical engineer</note>, in covering his siege engines, used the hides of recently killed animals, as these were able to resist fire; they also protected the joints of the wooden beams with chalk, or with ash mixed with blood, or clay worked with hair, or straw and seaweed soaked in vinegar, for in this way they guarded against the onslaught of fires. Carchedonius <note>Referring to the Carthaginians</note> was the first to teach that *vineae* <term>Vinea: a "vine-yard" or light, portable shed used for cover during a siege</term> and battering rams should be covered with fresh ox-hides. We have heard from trustworthy sources that in house fires, even those involving several floors, if a cloth stained with the first menstrual blood of a woman is thrown into it, the fire is immediately quenched by its own peculiar property. Thick and mucilaginous juices are also effective against fire, such as those of the marshmallow <term>Althæa: the Marsh Mallow plant, known for its sticky sap</term>. For this reason, it was not entirely absurd for Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus, the 13th-century philosopher and alchemist</note> to write that if one rubs themselves with the juice of marshmallow, egg white, and alum dissolved in vinegar:

->*The hand may handle fire without injury.*<-

And this holds much truth. But I think that quicksilver <term>Argentum vivum: literally "living silver," or mercury</term>, quenched in vinegar and egg white and then smeared on, can protect a thing from fire.

From there, other doors also smeared with resin began to catch fire and carry the flames all the way to the roof. Once the flame caught the roof, it spread quickly through the whole house, for it had the greatest power of inflammation. Duck fat is likewise highly praised by physicians as being most potent for incendiary fires, because it is extremely subtle, penetrating, and hot. ### Most Inflammable Oil.

When I wished to prepare the most excellent compositions of burning oil, I distilled common oil in a retort with great labor. The resulting distilled oil was thin, easily ignited, and burned so brightly that, once lit, it was almost inextinguishable; it would draw a flame to itself from a distance and was difficult to put out. However, linseed oil is even more powerful, for if you distill it several times, it retains such a miraculous power of burning that it can scarcely be kept in a closed vessel without drawing fire to itself. When the vessel is opened, the oil is so thin that it fills the air with its spirits; if the light of a candle or a fire touches that air, the air itself ignites, and from it the oil is set ablaze, shooting out a flame from a distance so violently that it is almost impossible to extinguish. But it must be distilled with the greatest skill, lest the vessel become too hot and catch fire from within. Furthermore...

### Fire that is extinguished by oil and ignited by water

It is done in this way. We have said that naphtha burns in water, as does its variety camphor <note>original: "caphuram"</note>; therefore, if you mix in sulphur or other substances that retain fire, and then throw on oil or mud, it is extinguished. However, it revives and conceives a greater fire when water is poured upon it. Livy <note>Titus Livius (64 BC–17 AD), a Roman historian</note> relates that certain old women in their games, having lit torches made of these substances, swam across the Tiber to show a miracle to those waiting and watching. For we have said it is the property of bitumen <term>Bitumen: a naturally occurring, highly flammable viscous mixture of hydrocarbons</term> to be ignited by water and quenched by oil. Dioscorides <note>Pedanius Dioscorides (c. 40–90 AD), a Greek physician and botanist</note> writes that the "Thracian stone" is found in a certain river of Scythia called the Pontus; it has the power of jet <note>original: "gagatis," a type of lignite coal</note>, and it is said to be set on fire by water and extinguished by oil, just as happens with bitumen. Nicander <note>Nicander of Colophon (2nd century BC), a Greek poet and physician</note> mentions this stone in this manner:

> If the Thracian stone be burned with glowing fire,
> And afterwards be moistened with water: it will be all ablaze, and yet
> Soon, if oil be poured on, it is immediately extinguished;
> The Thracian shepherd brings this to us from the river by name
> Which is the Pontus.

### Torches that are not extinguished by winds

These are made with sulphur, for they are difficult to extinguish once they have caught flame. For this reason, torches made of sulphur and wax smeared on in turns are carried unharmed through winds and storms. These are useful for leading armies or in other necessary affairs. Others use such methods: they boil the wick <note>original: "ellychnium"</note> of the torches in saltpeter <term>Saltpeter: potassium nitrate, a key ingredient in gunpowder and a powerful oxidizer</term> and water; once dried, they moisten it with sulphur and "burning water" <note>original: "ardenti aqua," likely distilled alcohol or brandy</note>. Then they make candles from this mixture: using one part sulphur, one part camphor and turpentine resin, double the amount of colophony <term>Colophony: a translucent amber-colored rosin obtained from pine trees</term>, and triple the amount of wax. They compose four candles together, and into the empty space in the middle they cast "living sulphur" <note>original: "vivum sulphur," or native, unrefined sulphur</note>; these resist all things most stubbornly. 

Or in this way: boil wicks of hemp or cotton in water with saltpeter. Once removed, see that they are dried. Then melt equal parts of sulphur, gunpowder <note>original: "tormentarij pulueris"</note>, and wax in a bronze pot. Place the wick into the melted mixture so that it absorbs a portion of it. ### *A fuse which, when lit, produces neither smoke nor odor.*

In secret meetings by day or night, soldiers and hunters are accustomed to prepare a fuse <note>original: "funem," referring to a slow-burning match cord or rope</note> which, when lit, produces neither odor (near or far) nor smoke. This is useful because wild beasts, driven away by the scent of a burning fuse, would otherwise gather at the very peaks of the mountains. Take a new earthenware pot and arrange a new rope inside it so carefully that it is entirely filled, coiled so tightly that it can hold no more. Close it with a lid and seal it <term>Luting: applying a clay or paste seal to a vessel to make it airtight for heating</term> very well three or four times so that it does not "breathe," for everything depends on this. Afterward, gradually light a fire around it so that it first grows warm, then boils, and finally glows with heat. If smoke occasionally escapes through a crack, immediately plug it with clay. Finally, let it cool on its own while buried in the coals. Upon opening the pot, you will find the fuse black, like charcoal; when lit, it will give off neither smoke nor stench.

## Fiery compositions for festive days. CHAPTER XI.

Having discussed terrible, horrific, and incendiary fires, it is only right to teach some intended for festive days. These are taught not so much for their own sake, but because they provide a starting point <note>original: "ansam," literally a handle</note> for devising even more advanced things. Let us, therefore, show the method of preparation,

### *so that when someone enters a room, all the air catches fire.*

Take a large quantity of highly refined spirit of wine <term>Aqua vitae: "water of life," a term used by early chemists for high-proof distilled alcohol</term> and throw in camphor <note>original: "caphura"</note> cut into small pieces, for it will dissolve in a short time. Once dissolved, the windows and doors of the room must be closed so that the escaping vapor does not leak out. Let the vessel full of the liquid boil over coals—without an open flame—so that all the liquid is released into a vapor <note>original: "fumum," literally smoke, though here describing a volatile mist</note> that fills the room. This vapor will be so thin that it can hardly be seen. Have someone enter the room with a lit candle in their hand; as soon as the candle is seen, the air itself catches fire and the whole room is set ablaze, looking like a glowing furnace. It strikes great terror into the one who enters. If musk or a tiny bit of ambergris <note>original: "ambara"</note> is dissolved in the liquid, a wonderful scent will follow the flame. ### Concerning various experiments with fire. CHAPTER XII.

We shall add some experiments, outside the class of the others, which I had previously decided would be better left unsaid. We speak of them now so that an opportunity for thinking of higher things may not be lacking.

->*If you wish for the balls of bronze cannons to penetrate more deeply.*<-

You can easily test this with a simple device against a fixed piece of wood or a wall. Let the ball fit into the bore <term>cauum: the hollow bore or barrel of a firearm</term> tightly rather than loosely, but let it be soaked in oil before being put in; once cast into the bore and exploded by the force of the fire, it will penetrate twice as far. The reason is ready at hand: for the oil ensures that any opportunity for the air to leak out is removed. When every vent is obstructed, the flames struggling inside explode the ball with greater violence, as we shall discuss more at length elsewhere. Thus also the balls of bronze cannons <note>original: "Æneorum tormentorum," referring to heavy artillery pieces made of copper alloys</note> will penetrate with greater violence, and even knights in heavy armor are pierced by musket balls smeared with lard. By a certain clever skill, we can also...

->*Pierce a man with a bullet, without a trace of the bullet’s entry or exit.*<-

The human mind is raised so high that it has discovered how to pierce a man through and through with a bullet so that no trace of the wound can be found, even if all the internal organs are crushed and transfixed. Consider those things which are heavy, solid, and yet so subtle that in penetrating they leave no traces of passage; they achieve the same effect whether joined or divided, as if each part acts by itself alone in the same way it would have done when united. I have spoken thus so that the opportunity for sinning is taken away from the ignorant and the wicked <note>The author is being intentionally vague here, likely to avoid providing a recipe for an untraceable murder weapon, though he may be hinting at the use of mercury or extremely fine shot</note>. We have seen...

->*Inflict multiple shots with a gun, without a new refilling of powder.*<-

This is used by excellent soldiers, not only with the larger bronze cannon, but with the handheld gun <term>sclopus: a musket or early firearm</term>. The thing is done thus: around the rod that is inserted into the hollow mouth of the gun, wrap paper three or four times; once the rod is pulled out, fill that hollow tube with powder and a ball. Let the balls be plugged at either end and glued so that no tear in the paper appears. First, let it be put into the gun, but loosely, so that the powder put in from above can reach the lower vent <note>original: "spitaculum," likely a misspelling of "spiraculum," the touch-hole or vent of the gun</note>; then, once the powder is put in...

### To blind eyes with smoke.

This can be very useful in attacks on cities and encounters with enemies. But first, the wind must be considered, so that it hits the backs of our men and carries the smoke into the faces of the enemies. Small jars <term>modioli: small cylindrical containers or buckets</term> are made, like lanterns, of a size that allows them to fit into the mouth of a bronze cannon. Let them be filled with a powder made of euphorbium <note>original: "euforbij," a highly caustic plant resin used as a chemical irritant</note>, pepper, quicklime, ashes of vine-clippings, and sublimated arsenic <note>a toxic chemical compound often used in early "stink pots" or smoke weapons</note>. These are placed cautiously into the barrel after the gunpowder; for by the force of the fire the paper jars are broken, and the smoke of the powder, if it touches the eyes of the enemies, will harass them so much that, having thrown down their weapons, they can scarcely look after the safety of their eyes.

### How it might be done that a candle burns forever.
## CHAPTER XIV.

Finally, before we put an end to this book, it is pleasing to discuss whether it is possible for a candle, once lit, to never be extinguished—a thing which seems most contrary to the nature of the corruptible things of the world and seems to surpass belief. But let us see first whether it was attempted or done by the ancients. It is read in Roman histories that at Rome in the temple of the Goddess Vesta, and at Athens in the temple of Minerva, and at Apollo's temple in Delphi, there existed a perpetual lit fire. But this seems false to me: for I remember reading in very many authors that the Vestal Virgins cared for the continuously lit fire lest it ever be extinguished, as is held from Plutarch in the *Life of Numa* <note>Plutarch was a Greek biographer; Numa Pompilius was the legendary second king of Rome who established many religious rites</note>, and finally in the time of the civil wars and of Mithridates <note>Mithridates VI, king of Pontus, a great enemy of Rome</note>, it was extinguished. And at Delphi it was guarded by widows, and they saw to it with the continuous addition of oil lest it ever be extinguished, though it also failed when the Medes burned that temple. Of this kind was the fire described in the Holy Scriptures by God, established for Moses. The fire on the altar...

...[on] mine it will always burn, which the priest will nourish, placing wood under it every single day. <note>The text likely completes a reference to Leviticus 6:13, "The fire shall ever be burning upon the altar; it shall never go out."</note> Thus, it was not a truly perpetual fire in the temples of the pagan gods. But we read that near the town of Ateste <term>Ateste: modern-day Este, in the territory of Padua</term> in the Paduan countryside, a clay urn was found, inside of which was another small jar, and inside that was found a small lamp still burning; it was broken by the clumsy hands of country-folk who were digging <note>original: "profudentiū," referring to those digging or pouring out the earth</note>, and the flame was immediately extinguished. And in our own times, around the year 1501, on the island of Nisida <term>Neside insula: a small volcanic island in the Gulf of Naples</term>, located in the Neapolitan crater, a marble tomb of a certain Roman was found; when it was opened, a vial was discovered inside in which a lamp was still burning. It was broken, and upon contact with the air <note>original: "viso aere," literally "having seen the air"</note>, it was extinguished, even though it had been sealed since before the coming of our Savior. Others have also been reported by friends, discovered and witnessed with their own eyes. From this we conclude that this is possible, and was practiced by the ancients. Let us see if we too can accomplish the same thing.

There are those who say that "oil of metals" <term>oleum metallorum: an alchemical substance supposed to be extracted from metals, believed by some to be an inexhaustible fuel</term> can last longer, and almost perpetually. But this is false, since the oil of metals does not burn. Others say that oil of juniper <term>oleum iuniperi</term> extracted from the wood lasts a long time, because the coals of that same wood are said to remain burning under ashes for a year; but this is most false, for a coal kept by me under ashes did not last even two days, nor even one; and the oil from the wood burns most violently, and is consumed more quickly than common oil. 

There are those who boast of having squeezed oil out of the stone asbestos <term>amianto lapide: a fibrous mineral known since antiquity for being fireproof</term>, thinking it cannot be consumed by flame, since a wick <term>ellychnium: the wick of a lamp</term> made from it is never consumed, even if it burns forever, provided oil is perpetually added to it. But if it is true that the wick is not consumed by fire, it does not follow from this that an oil extracted from the stone would burn forever without being consumed; and no one has yet been found who has extracted an oil from asbestos that actually burns. 

Others think that oil squeezed from common salt <term>sal commune: table salt</term> lasts forever; for if you throw salt into oil, it causes the oil in the lamp to last twice as long without being consumed, which we testify to be true. From this they argue that if oil were distilled from it, it would burn forever without consumption. However, it does not follow that oil extracted from salt burns forever; and the oil distilled from it burns no more than a stone, or the *aqua fortis* <term>aqua fortis: "strong water," or nitric acid</term> used for the separation of silver and gold, the appearance of which...

...is. But it is the mark of an unrefined mind to imagine that an oil can be found which is not consumed by continuous burning. Instead, something else must be imagined. There are those who say (and their reasoning is not foolish) that the fire does not always burn in the vial, but rather that a certain mixture is stored within the vial which, when it "sees the air" <note>original: "aerem videt," a common personification in early modern science for exposure to oxygen</note>, is immediately ignited; thus it appears to burn only at that moment, having never blazed before. 

This could be true, as it often happens to one performing chemical operations that glass vessels, which were very well sealed and then forgotten after the combustion of their contents—left for many months, not to say years—finally, when opened, are seen to catch flame, burn, and emit smoke. I have forgotten exactly what substances I had burned <note>Della Porta frequently refers to his own laboratory experiments in the *Magia Naturalis*</note>, but they could have been of the same kind as those I heard about from a friend to whom the same thing happened. For when he had boiled litharge <term>lithargyrum: lead monoxide, used in glass and lead glazes</term>, tartar <term>tartarum: potassium bitartrate, a byproduct of winemaking</term>, lime, and cinnabar <term>cinnabarim: mercury sulfide, a bright red mineral</term> in vinegar until it vanished into smoke, he then covered and luted <term>lutato: sealed with "lute," a paste of clay and straw used to make vessels airtight</term> the vessel. After heating it thoroughly with a violent fire, he set it aside until it cooled. After several months, when he wished to open it to revisit his work, a flame suddenly leaped from the vessel, so much so that it scorched his eyelashes, though he expected no such thing—an occurrence which has happened to many others. 

Furthermore, when I was boiling linseed oil for the press, and a flame had caught inside, I covered the pot with cloths to extinguish it; after some time, upon opening the vessel, the oil, having "seen the air" <note>original: "viso aere"</note>, caught flame again and was rekindled anew. 

But experience opposes this opinion; for those who have seen a lamp enclosed in a glass vessel have observed it to hold its flame perfectly and emit light <insert>while still sealed</insert>. For the ancients believed that just as the ashes remained in the tomb, so the soul rested there perpetually; and lest they should lie in darkness, they strove with the greatest zeal to find this light, so that their souls might enjoy perpetual light. 

Therefore, something else must be imagined, and an experiment must be tried. But this must be held as a fixed and certain principle in the "workshop of nature": that the cause of wonders is that a vacuum cannot exist <note>original: "vacuum non dari," the Aristotelian principle of *horror vacui* or "nature abhors a vacuum"</note>, and it is more likely that the machinery of the world would be shattered and all things revert to chaos than that a vacuum could be admitted. Hence, if a flame were enclosed in glass with all air-holes <note>original: "spiramentis," breathing holes or vents</note> blocked, and if it lasted for even a moment, it would last forever, and it would be impossible for it to be extinguished. Many wonders are declared in this book,

## Iron can be made harder through tempering.
### CHAPTER I.

<image-desc>Decorative historiated woodcut initial 'C' containing a profile portrait of a man's face and floral scrollwork.</image-desc>

It is established by a very clear and well-known experiment that iron is hardened by tempering, and likewise softened. When we investigated extensively whether it turned hard or soft due to heat, dryness, cold, or moisture, we found that heat makes it both hard and soft, as do cold and other qualities. Therefore, another cause must be devised from which to hunt for the reasons. We found it becomes hard through "contraries" and soft through "friendly" things; finally, we arrived at the concept of antipathy and sympathy <term>Antipathy and Sympathy: In Renaissance science, these were "occult" or hidden forces of nature where certain substances naturally repelled or attracted each other without physical contact.</term>. 

The ancients believed this happened by a kind of religious or sacred influence. They said there was an iron chain at the Euphrates river, in the city called Zeugma <note>Zeugma, meaning "Bridge" or "Juncture" in Greek, was a major crossing point in ancient Mesopotamia</note>, with which Alexander the Great had bound a bridge; they claimed the rings that were replaced during repairs were infested with rust, while the original ones remained free of it. To Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus (Pliny the Elder), author of the Roman "Natural History"</note> and others, it seems this matter arises from the differences in waters. Perhaps juices or certain minerals flowing beneath them carry "seeds" <note>The idea that minerals grew from "seeds" or "seminal reasons" in the earth was a common pre-modern geological theory</note> by which iron can be made soft or hard. 

He says: "The greatest difference lies in the water into which the glowing iron is plunged." This has made various places famous for the glory of their iron, such as Bilbilis in Spain <note>Modern-day Calatayud</note>, and Tarazona <note>original: "Puriassonem"</note>, and Como in Italy, even though iron mines are not located in these places. Of all types, however, the prize goes to Seric iron <note>original: "Serico ferro"; the "Seres" was the ancient Graeco-Roman name for the people of China</note>. The Chinese send this along with their clothes and skins. The second best is Parthian <note>From the Parthian Empire, centered in modern Iran</note>; and no other types of iron are tempered from pure steel <note>original: "mera acie"</note>...

## How iron may be softened. CHAPTER II.

We shall first speak of how iron may be softened and made workable, whereby we may turn steel back into iron, and make iron as soft as lead. Hard iron is softened by fats, as we have said, and without fat by fire alone, as Pliny says: Iron heated in the fire, unless it is hardened by blows, is spoiled. It is as if he were saying that steel softens by itself if it is repeatedly made glowing hot and allowed to cool by itself in the fire; in this way, the iron will emerge softer. We can also use various methods

### so that iron may be softened.

Once iron is anointed with oil, wax, and asafoetida <term>Asafoetida: A pungent, sulfurous resin from the roots of Ferula plants, often used in historical metallurgy and medicine for its strong properties</term>, and then coated over with mud, chaff, and dung, and dried, let it glow among lighted coals through the night. Soon, once it has cooled by itself, you will find it soft and workable. Or take three parts of sulfur, four times as much powdered clay, and mix it with oil so that it becomes soft. Then let the iron be "armored" <note>meaning heavily coated or encased</note> in this, dried, and buried in live coals. In the same way, as we have said, you can also use tallow and butter.

### CHAPTER III.

We have said how iron might be made softer; now we shall demonstrate tempering <term>tempering: the process of heating and cooling metal to achieve a specific balance of hardness and flexibility</term> methods, and how it may cut more sharply. But there are different temperings for various uses; for a tempering to cut bread, wood, stone, or iron requires different liquids, and also different degrees of heating, and the timing of the quenching in the liquids, so that the result depends on these factors. When iron glows most fiercely in the fires, so that it cannot be heated further and it sparks, they call it "silver" <note>original: *argentum*</note>, and then it is not quenched, because it would be consumed <note>At this white-hot heat, the carbon in the steel burns off and the metal becomes brittle or "burnt"</note>. If indeed it is tinged with a saffron color, or red, it is called "gold" <note>original: *aurum*</note>, or "rose," and then it is made harder when quenched in liquids; this color requires quenching. But it must be noted if the whole iron is tempered, so that the color is blue or violet—as with a sword, or the edge of a chisel or a stylus—in these, because the remaining iron re-softens the metal again with its own residual heat, then the secondary colors must be watched. For example, when the iron is quenched and then immersed, it becomes hard; the last color is that of ash, and after quenching at this stage, it is made the least hard of all. If we look at examples, it is held thus:

->*The tempering of a knife for cutting bread.*<-

I have seen many clever men labor over such a tempering, who, although they had knives prepared for cutting all the hardest things, found it difficult enough to cut bread at the table <note>Hard, brittle steel often struggles with the fibrous texture of crusty bread compared to a more flexible blade</note>. We have fulfilled our wish with such a tempering. To cut bread, therefore, let the steel be tempered softly in this way. Take steel, which when broken shows a body composed of the smallest granules, and is best [worked] from iron...

Once the iron is cleaned, we heat it lightly and strike it with a hammer to shape it into a knife. Next, we refine it with a file, adjust it into the proper knife-form, and polish it with a wheel. Finally, we place it in the fire until a violet color <note>In tempering, a violet oxide layer indicates the metal has reached approximately 270-280°C (520-540°F), a temperature that provides a good balance of hardness and flexibility for blades.</note> appears. ### Tempering of iron for wood.
The tempering for cutting wood should be slightly harder, yet still mild. Therefore, let the iron reach the same violet color and then be dipped in water. It is then pulled out, and when an ash-gray color <note>original: *cineritius*</note> appears, it should be plunged into cold water. A not very different method is used for:

### Iron for bloodletting.
This is quenched in oil and becomes hard; because it is a delicate and thin instrument <note>referring to a lancet used in phlebotomy</note>, if it were quenched in water, it would warp and break.

### Tempering of iron for a grass-hook.
After the iron has been fashioned into a sickle <note>original: *falce*</note>, let it be heated until it glows with a gold color <note>original: *auri colorem*; this indicates a lower temperature than violet, around 240°C, resulting in a harder but more brittle edge</note>, and then let it be submerged in oil or smeared with tallow. Because the iron is thin, if it were quenched in water, it would either become brittle or twist out of shape.

...one part [of the mixture] is to be mixed thoroughly with an equal amount of common salt, crushed glass, and soot from the chimney. Once the powder is prepared, the iron should be fashioned into the shape of a file; then, while the iron is still tender and soft—as we have described—cut the teeth with a sharp chisel in a crosswise and diagonal pattern. Once you judge the powder to be consumed and burnt away, remove the box from the coals with iron tongs, and plunge the files into very cold water; in this way, they become exceedingly hard. This is the common <term>temper</term> <note>The process of hardening the metal.</note> for a file, because we do not worry if a file is slightly warped by the cold water. However, we shall teach a method that is even better.

### Another way to temper.

Take the marrow from the horns of goats, dry it, and turn it into a powder. Then, place the files in a box, sprinkled with this powder, and follow the same procedure as before. One thing should be added, however: two extra "supernumerary" files should be included in such a way that they can be pulled out of the box at will. After you believe the box buried in the coals has absorbed the strength of the powder, pull out one of the extra files, temper it, and break it. If you find the metal inside to be perfectly granulated and pure **steel** <note>original: "chalybem" — iron that has been hardened into steel through the absorption of carbon from the bone/horn powder.</note> and that it has turned out according to your wish, remove the box from the fire and temper the rest in the same way. If not, allow it to remain longer, and after a short interval, take a test from the other extra file until you have reached perfection. In the same way, we can:

### Temper knives to be very hard.

Take a fresh ox hoof, heat it, and strike it on the side with a hammer; the marrow will pop out. Let this be dried in an oven and, as we have said, arranged in a small jar, always adding two extra pieces that can be removed...

...as they are able, by taking an experiment of the best conversion into steel, and by applying the same labor, they are made the hardest. We shall now teach

### *How mail armor should be tempered.*

Seek out a mail shirt <note>original: "lorica"</note> made of iron that is soft and of low price. This should be placed into a pot, with the powders mentioned above scattered over it in layers. The pot is then covered with a lid and sealed with <term>lute</term> <note>A clay sealant used to make the pot airtight.</note> so that the vapors do not escape. Apply a sufficient fire, and then, at the proper time, take up the pot with iron tongs. After striking the pot with a hammer to break it open, quench the entire glowing-hot mail shirt in the water described earlier. In this way, it is made so hard that it easily resists the blows of daggers. The measure of the powder shall be this: if the mail weighs ten or twelve pounds, add two and a half pounds of powder. To ensure the powder sticks everywhere, moisten the mail with water, then roll it in the powder, and arrange it in the pot in alternating layers. 

But because it has been made extremely hard, the rings might break or fly into pieces under a heavy blow. It is therefore necessary to add "sinew" <note>original: "neruum" — referring here to toughness or resilience to counteract brittleness.</note> to the hardness; the workmen call this "returning" <note>Known today as "tempering" or "drawing back," where the metal is slightly reheated to reduce brittleness.</note>. Once removed from the water, let it be shaken in a barrel with vinegar so that it may be polished and its color can be seen. Then, let a broad iron plate be heated in the fire, and a part or the whole of the mail shirt be stretched over it. When an ashy color—which the workmen call *beretinum* <note>original: "beretinum" — likely from the Italian "berrettino," a bluish-gray color indicative of a specific tempering temperature.</note>—appears, throw it again into the water. This blunts that extreme hardness and allows it to yield more easily to a blow. Thus, from a very cheap mail shirt, you will have one that resists every strike. Hardness is granted to iron by the tempering of sharp substances, but with it comes brittleness; unless toughness is added, it will fly into pieces from a light blow. For this reason, it is necessary that they learn most perfectly how to provide this toughness.

## Liquids that temper iron to the greatest hardness. CHAPTER V.

We have said that iron is constricted by <term>antipathy</term> and dilated by <term>sympathy</term>. It enjoys a friendly association with fats, and its pores are opened, which results in softness. On the contrary, astringents and cold substances that constrict the pores render it very hard through an unfriendly opposition. They seem to do this for that reason, not omitting, however, those things which do so by their own inherent property. If one desired

->**Fish-hooks, that they may be made very hard.**<-

The hook is the primary tool for the hunting of fish: for it is necessary that they be small and strong. If they are large, they are noticed by the fish and not swallowed; if they are small but bear a great weight and struggle, they break; if they are soft, they are straightened out, and the fish escapes. Therefore, so that they may be strong, thin, and not able to be straightened by the fish's mouth, you shall temper them in this way. Let iron wires be made from harvesting scythes, or from the best steel, and let the hooks be formed, thin and small. Do not let them glow too brightly in the fire, for the heat consumes them; instead, let them be placed upon a red-hot iron plate. When they turn reddish, let them be thrown into water, and when cooled, let them be taken out and dried. Soon after, let the hot plates be prepared again, and the hooks placed on them once more. But when a cinerous <note>ash-colored</note> or "beretinus" <note>original: "beretinus" — a tawny or brownish-grey color appearing on steel when heated to a specific temperature, known today as a tempering color.</note> color commonly appears, let them be submerged in water again, so that they become tough <note>original: "neruosi" — literally "sinewy," referring to the toughness or resilience that prevents the metal from being brittle.</note>, for otherwise they would be fragile. In this way you have it.

->**Knives, that they may be made very hard.**<-

Albert <note>Albertus Magnus, a 13th-century scholar whose works on nature were widely read, though often questioned by later experimentalists like Della Porta.</note>, from whom others take their cue, says that iron is made sharper if it is tempered in radish juice and the water of earthworms three or four times. However, we, having tempered it many times with the juice of radishes, horse-radish <note>original: "armoraciæ"</note>, and worms, always found the metal to come out as soft as lead. We found his claim to be false, just like his other theories. But in this way we shall make the hardest steel, so that for this purpose alone you may make the hardest knives by tempering. Divide the steel into small pieces, like gaming dice <note>original: "lusorias tesseras"</note>, and let them be tied onto iron rods with iron wire; let them be placed in the fire so that they glow and spark at least fifteen times, and let them be dipped in these powders, which consist of one part black borax, and two parts snail shells and cuttlefish bone. Soon after, beat them with a hammer so that they are joined together as one, and form knives or whatever other tools you wish to shape...

### The tempering of swords.

It is necessary for swords to be tough <note>original: "nervosos" — literally "sinewy," meaning flexible enough to bend without snapping.</note>, lest they break while we are thrusting <note>original: "punctim" — a point-first strike.</note>; it is also necessary that they have a sharp edge, so that when we strike with a cut <note>original: "caesim" — a slashing or chopping blow.</note>, they may lop off and sever. This shall be the method: you will temper the body of the blade with oil and butter so that it retains its toughness, but temper the edge with sharp liquids so that it may receive the strength for cutting. This is done either with wooden channels or with woolen cloths soaked in the liquid; use your own ingenuity and skill.

### On the tempering of a chisel, that it may cut porphyry marble. Chapter VI.

The tempering of the chisel was very well known to our ancestors, with which they cut porphyry marble <note>Porphyry is an extremely hard igneous rock, purple-red in color, highly prized in Imperial Rome.</note> so easily, as testified by the infinite works of art that have come down to us. However, the method has been passed down by no one and is utterly unknown, not without the great shame of our own age, which neglects and undervalues such beautiful and useful inventions. So that we might be free from this fault, we have tested—through anxiety, labor, and expense—whatever came to our hands or to our mind, directing ourselves through various methods and different experiments so that we might achieve it.
