...to attain these and even greater results. Nor will it be a burden to recount those things which we discovered by chance while attempting this work. The difficulty involved these challenges: if the tempering <term>temperatura: the process of hardening and toughening metal through controlled heating and cooling</term> was too sharp and robust, the chisel <note>original: "scalpri"</note> would shatter into pieces under a very heavy blow of the mallet; but if it were too soft, it would bend back and fail to mark the marble. Therefore, it must be made very hard and tough <note>original: "nervosa" — literally "sinewy," referring to the metal's ability to resist snapping under stress</note>, so that it neither gives way under the blow nor <unclear>shatters</unclear>. Furthermore, the juices or water in which the iron is to be tempered must be clear and limpid. If the liquid is turbid, the colors arising from the heat cannot be seen, and the proper moments for immersion will be unknown—and upon this timing everything depends. Therefore, clear and purified juices reveal the moment for tempering. One must pay the closest attention to the colors, for they show the time for plunging and withdrawing the metal. Because it is necessary for the iron to turn out both very hard and tough, the color should be midway between silver and gold. As this color approaches, the entire edge of the chisel should be plunged into the liquor. After a very brief moment, it should be removed, and when a violet color appears, it should be plunged into the liquor again, lest the heat still remaining in the body of the chisel ruin the temper once more. It must also be strictly observed that the liquors in which the chisel is tempered must be extremely cold; for if they are warm, they will be less effective. You should not plunge another piece of iron into the same liquor in which one has already been quenched; for since it will then be warm, it will do nothing. Instead, use fresh, cold liquid, and meanwhile force the liquid to stay chilled by letting its glass vessel float in another basin of cold water, so that it cools quickly and you have a very cold medium for the work. These, however, are 

->*The hardest tempering of iron.*<-

If you plunge glowing iron into distilled vinegar, it will come out hard; the same will happen in distilled urine, on account of the salt it contains. If you temper it in the dew found in the month of May upon the leaves of chickpeas <note>The author refers to the acidic or salty secretions common to chickpea plants, which were thought to have special chemical properties in the early modern period</note>, it will come out extremely hard, for it is salty beyond belief, as we have taught elsewhere from Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus (c. 371 – c. 287 BC), a Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle, who wrote on the nature of plants and minerals</note>. Vinegar in which sal ammoniac <term>sal ammoniacus: ammonium chloride, a salt used historically in metalworking and alchemy</term> has been dissolved will produce a most powerful tempering. Likewise, if you temper iron in water in which the salt of urine and saltpeter <term>halinitrum: naturally occurring potassium nitrate</term> have been dissolved, it will become very hard. ### How we can carve porphyry marble without a chisel. CHAPTER VII.

There are, however, others who have attempted to do the same without chisels, but with strong and violent water <note>original: "valida, & vehementi aqua" — a common term for mineral acids like nitric or hydrochloric acid, which were known for their ability to "eat" metal and stone.</note>. They were prompted by this reasoning: seeing vinegar and sharp juices swell into bubbles when placed upon marble and corrode it, they believed that if they could extract a violent and most powerful liquor from sharp and corrosive substances, it would be possible to perform the same work without labor. Finally, they executed the task in this manner: Take sublimated mercury <note>original: "argentum viuum sublimatum" — also known as corrosive sublimate (mercury II chloride), a highly toxic and corrosive compound.</note> and a little sal ammoniac. Distill these, as we have taught, through glass instruments. Then take verdigris <term>viridis æris: a green crust of copper acetate or carbonate used for its corrosive and pigment properties.</term>, tin reduced to ash <term>calcem: a "calx" or metal oxide produced by heating the metal until it becomes a powder.</term>, and a little pyrite stone. Grind everything together with rock salt, common salt, and sal ammoniac. Distill it, and pour the distilled liquid back over the dregs <note>original: "feces" — the solid residue left after distillation.</note>, and distill it again. Do this a third time, and finally keep the liquor in a well-covered vessel. When you begin the work, smear the porphyry marble with goat suet...

## How iron is cooked, so that it may be workable for various tasks.

### CHAPTER VIII.

There are very many people who most diligently observe and search for how, by some secret art, iron can be tempered to such a degree that it does not break, or is not pierced by the shot of firearms <term>sclopis: an early term for handguns or muskets</term>. But these people ignore what they have in their hands and search for what they do not have; for if they were to consider what happens while iron is being cooked <note>The author uses "coquatur" (cooked) to refer to the smelting, refining, and forging process.</note>, perhaps they would have before their eyes what they seek with such great zeal. 

We say, therefore, that the reason why swords break and shatter into pieces, and why iron breastplates are pierced by the strikes of guns <note>original: "sclopetorum"</note>, is because there are cracks <note>original: "rimæ"</note> in the iron, and it gaps in various places, with the parts being quite poorly joined together. Because the tiny scales <note>original: "squamulæ"</note> are barely visible to the eye, it causes the iron to break when it is bent or struck. For if you observe skillfully, where swords or knives shatter into pieces, you will always find such fissures and cracks, whereas solid parts remain unbroken and always resist bending. 

But when I searched for the cause of these cracks, I finally discovered it in the iron workshops. Where the iron is thoroughly cooked, they pile coals and the dross <note>original: "quisquilias" — the waste or refuse of the fuel.</note> of coals upon the iron, saying that the iron is more stubbornly refined unless it is buried in dross and coal dust. Yet, mixed with the dust there are always small stones, chalk, various filths, fragments of bricks, and other things piled up in abundance. When these melt in the fire, they cause certain bubbly clusters on the surface, or internal voids and fissures, so that the parts of the metal are less able to fuse together. 

Hence, even if it seems a very trivial thing of little consideration, it is nevertheless the cause of these defects. Therefore, so that we may remove this impediment, we have decided this must be done: we throw the coals into a wooden tub full of water, for the coals themselves are carried to the surface (while the stones... <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword "des" suggests "descendunt" (sink to the bottom).</note>)

### *How polished iron may be protected from rust.*
### CHAPTER X.

It is so useful to protect iron from rust that there have been very many who have labored in investigating how it can easily be done. Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), the Roman author of the Natural History, whose works were the foundation of Renaissance science.</note> says: Iron is protected from rust by white lead <term>cerussa: a lead carbonate pigment</term>, gypsum, and liquid pitch. But how the white lead can be prepared for this, he does not explain. However, those who know how to make oil from white lead without vinegar can easily protect iron from rust by coating it. There are some who have kept iron immune to rust by smearing it with deer tallow <term>sepo cervino: rendered deer fat</term>; we, however, have used the fat from the hooves of oxen. <note>original: "pingui unguium boum." This is neatsfoot oil, which is still used today to preserve leather and metal.</note>

### *How the meat of a sheep may become tender.*

The meat of animals killed by their enemies—especially those for which they have a natural hatred and horror—becomes quite exceptionally tender. Zoroaster says in the *Geoponica* <note>original: *Geoponicis*, a 10th-century Byzantine collection of agricultural lore attributed to various ancient authors</note> that the flesh of a sheep killed and bitten by a wolf becomes tenderer, and therefore more pleasant to eat. Plutarch gives the reason for this in his *Symposiacs* <note>original: *Symposiacis*, also known as *Table Talk*, a collection of dinner-table discussions on philosophy and natural history</note>. He says, "The meat of a sheep bitten by a wolf seems to become sweeter because the wolf, by its bite, makes the flesh flaccid and tender." For the spirit <term>spiritus: in Renaissance thought, a subtle, hot substance that carried life and heat through the body</term> of the wolf is so hot that it melts and dissolves even the hardest bones in its stomach; and for this reason, things touched by wolves also rot more easily. 

Hunters and cooks provide evidence that animals being slaughtered are affected in various ways. For we know some who have laid low animals with a single blow, so that they immediately lay motionless; while others have barely finished them off after many strikes. And what you might wonder at more, is that some have left such a force from the iron's wound in the slaughtered animal that it soon became rotten and would not last whole for even a day; whereas others killed them no slower than the former, yet no such quality was left in the meat of the slaughtered animals, and they lasted for some time. 

Furthermore, that some force reaches even to the skins, hairs, and hooves when animals are slaughtered or die was not hidden even from Homer, who, writing about skins and thongs, said: "The thong of an ox killed by violence" <note>original: "Lorum bouis per vim occisi"</note>; for the skin of those animals that died not by disease or old age, but by being slaughtered, is stronger and tougher. Conversely, for those that perish by the bite of animals, their hooves turn black, their hair falls out, and their skins become withered and flaccid. Thus far Plutarch. 

But I think these things are false, for I do not sufficiently understand how the meat of a sheep can become tender from the spirit of a wolf. For the meat of other animals killed by their enemies and those of a contrary nature also becomes tender, even though they do not have a hot spirit. Instead, I surmise that the absence of blood makes the meat in an animal tender, based on these arguments: Quails and pheasants killed by falcons or...

When these are brought to the butcher's stall <term>macellum: a Roman meat market or provision market</term> and butchered, the meat turns out unusually tender. ### Meats which become tender through a hidden property.

## CHAPTER II.

THERE ARE also certain things which, by a hidden property <term>occulta proprietate: a quality in nature that is observed through its effects but whose physical cause is not immediately apparent</term>, render meat tender. Of these, we shall list two miracles of a prodigious nature. One: if it has hung from a fig tree, a rooster’s flesh becomes tender, and so brittle it is a marvel to speak of. The second: roosters, however wild, will become tame and rest motionless if tied to a fig tree. Plutarch, in his *Symposiacs* <note>Plutarch’s *Table Talk*, a collection of dinner-table discussions on various philosophical and scientific questions.</note>, suggests the reason why victims of the roosters’ kind, when hung from a fig tree, become tender and brittle so quickly. During a feast, Aristio’s cook offered a rooster that had been recently sacrificed to Hercules, which was tender and almost crumbling. Aristio attributed such swift tenderness to the fig tree, contending that even very tough slaughtered meat contracts a tenderness when hung from a fig. The sight itself sufficiently testifies that the fig tree exhales a vapor and a breath that is vehement and powerful. Evidence is also found in what is commonly reported about bulls: even the fiercest of them, when tied to this tree, grow mild; they allow themselves to be touched by hand and subdued, exhaling their anger and casting off their spirit as if it were wilting. So great is the power of that sharp spirit <note>original: *spiritus acrimonia*, referring to the pungent sap or "breath" of the tree</note> that it masters the fury of the bull, however much he may rage and grow savage. Since indeed...

The fig tree is more pregnant with abundant milk than any other, so much so that its wood, branches, and fruit are completely filled with it. For this reason, when it is burned, the smoke it belches forth is particularly biting and stings the eyes; likewise, the lye made from its ashes is extremely cleansing and purifying. Cheese is also curdled using the fig milk <note>original: *ficulneo lacte*</note> that the tree emits if you wound the green bark. Furthermore, it is believed to happen by the gift of heat that when this juice is added, the milk thickens, causing the watery parts of the liquid to separate. Thus, the fig exhales a warm, sharp, and digestive aura that dries out and cooks the flesh of birds, making them so tender they practically crumble. In the same way,

->How beef may become tender<-

we shall proceed. If stalks of the wild fig <note>original: *caprifici*</note> are added to the pot in which beef is being boiled, they are cooked through with a great saving of firewood, according to Pliny. We attribute the reason for this to a natural "antipathy" <term>antipathia: a concept in early science where certain substances naturally repel or work against each other</term>. Alluding to this, the Egyptians, when wishing to represent a man disciplined by a recent calamity, paint a bull tied to a wild fig tree; for even if he is bellowing, if he is tied to a wild fig, he is rendered tame. If we wish

->how legumes may become tender,<-

we observe a great antipathy between legumes and broomrape <note>original: *orobanchem*; a parasitic plant that grows on the roots of others</note>, which feeds upon and strangles them. (This is called the "lion’s herb" <note>original: *leonina herba*</note> by others; for just as a lion wickedly and hatefully strangles sheep and cattle, so broomrape strangles legumes.) Because of this, if this same herb is added to legumes while they are boiling, it causes them to be cooked through more easily. They also cause

->edibles to be thoroughly cooked,<-

namely all types of dock <note>original: *lapathi*; a genus of plants including sorrel</note>, even if they are dry and withered; they likewise cause meats to become tender and fit for eating. For this reason, the ancients ate them continually so that they might also digest foods in the stomach and soften the bowels. Even the root of the wild nettle <note>original: *urticæ*</note> cooked together with meat makes it tender, according to Pliny.

### *Peacocks, partridges, and pheasants, that they may become more tender.*

A slaughtered peacock, according to the authority of Isaac <note>Isaac Judaeus, a 10th-century physician and philosopher</note>, is kept for two days in summer and three in winter so that the hardness of the meat is softened. Haly Abbas <note>an 11th-century Persian physician</note> leaves them hanging for three days with stones tied to their feet. Pheasants should be kept for two days in summer and three in winter, slaughtered and hung, before they are cooked for food, according to Arnold <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova, a 13th-century physician</note>; and lest we be too long-winded, I judge the same is to be understood for others. It will be similar

->that birds may become tender,<-

if you expose them to the rays of the moon after they are killed at night; they will turn out more tender when cooked. For the moon contributes greatly to the tenderness of meat, which is nothing other than a kind of putrefaction <term>putrefactio: in early modern science, this referred to the natural breaking down of organic matter or muscle fibers, similar to "aging" meat today</term>. For this reason, wood cut by the light of the moon rots more quickly, and fruit ripens faster, as the physician Daphnis says in Athenaeus <note>a Greek rhetorician and author of 'The Deipnosophists', a massive work on ancient dining</note>.

...to change their shells and cast off their old age <note>The author uses the phrase "senectutem exuere" (to cast off old age), a poetic way of describing a creature shedding its skin or shell</note>. At that time, fishermen searching along the banks of rivers—wherever they see openings and their little burrows half-covered—recognize the sign that the time has come for the shells to be removed. For the more the shell softens, the more tightly they close the little doors of their burrows. This tenderness begins at the feet and gradually takes over the whole body. They are allowed to remain this way for eight or ten days, with the water being changed every day, and each day the shell becomes softer. ->Shrimp, that they may become tender,<-

for just as crabs are stripped of their crust, we can apply the same effort. This is done by nature’s design, for when the shell has become too thick, they are made slower in their movement by the weight; therefore, when the waste materials that used to go into the old shell are consumed by the new interior one, the upper shell is broken and falls away.

->That animals may become fatter and more flavorful.<-
->CHAPTER V.<-

Let us follow with how animals may be made fatter and more flavorful, so that we may serve more savory foods at banquets. Regarding this, the care of the ancients was not sluggish. Hence, many methods are found not only among the cooks, but also among the writers on rural affairs. Gourmets <note>original: "liguritores," meaning those who lick or have a refined, perhaps excessive, palate</note> discovered how to fatten animals so that they might devour them more richly and sumptuously; hence they are called *fatlings* <term>altilia: from the Latin "alere" (to nourish), referring to poultry specifically fattened for the table</term>, because they have been deeply fattened and nourished. Places where all kinds of birds were separated and stuffed were called aviaries. Marcus Laelius Strabo <note>A Roman knight from the 1st century BCE, credited with being the first to create specialized aviaries for fattening birds</note> was the first to establish these, and he added "stuffers" <note>original: "farctores"</note> to manage the business, having written down what was to be given to each bird for stuffing. Fattening is done better in winter than in summer, because birds are better at that time of year, being less exhausted by breeding. Young males are better than females, specifically those that have not yet mated or laid an egg. In summer, they are better when the fruit is ripe and the verjuice <term>omphacium: the tart juice of unripe grapes, used as a seasoning or medicinal base</term> still hangs from the vine. Let us therefore teach...

### *How hens and other birds are fattened.*

A warm and dark place should be chosen; the birds are to be shut up individually in spaces so cramped that they cannot turn around. These enclosures should have holes on both sides: one through which the head may be extended, and another for the tail, so that they may both take in food and void what is digested. Soft hay should be spread beneath them, for if they lie on hard ground, they do not grow fat. All feathers should be plucked from the head, the rump, and from under the wings; this is done so that lice do not breed in the head, and so the rump does not become ulcerated by the dung. For food, they should be given pellets <note>original: "offæ"</note> made of barley flour, sprinkled with water and kneaded. In the first few days, give these sparingly, but soon provide as much as they are able to digest. New food must not be offered until you have felt the bird's throat to ensure that no old food remains. When the bird is satisfied, it should be let out for a little while, not so it may wander, but so that if anything is irritating it, the bird may peck at it with its beak. The time for fattening should not exceed the twenty-fifth day <note>The Latin "quintam, aut vigeſimam" refers to the 25th day of the lunar cycle, a standard period for cramming poultry in Roman agriculture</note>. Sterile pigeons, or chicks, are more easily fattened under their mothers if you pluck a few feathers and bruise their legs <note>A common, though cruel, historical practice to keep the birds stationary so they would gain weight faster</note>, so that they remain still in their place, and you must provide a large amount of food to the parents so they can abundantly nourish themselves and their young. Turtledoves are fattened in the summer; nothing is required but to throw out food for them, especially millet, as they take great delight in this seed, but you should remove it in winter. They are destined for a fattening period of four months; besides barley meal and fine flour three times a day, truly nothing else needs to be given, provided they have a large capacity for drinking but no opportunity for wandering. In this manner, they grow fat in two months, though tender young chicks are often rendered plump in forty days. Ducks grow fat on any abundant food, especially wheat, millet, barley, and aquatic shrimp <note>original: "squillis"</note>, locusts, and marsh creatures. From Columella <note>Lucius Junius Moderatus Columella, a 1st-century Roman writer whose work "De Re Rustica" is the primary source for these methods</note>: Pheasants, partridges, heath-cocks, and Guinea hens <note>original: "numidicæ gallinæ"</note> grow fat when enclosed, so that on the first day they receive food, and on the following day a great deal of water or strong wine is set before them. Their food should be raw barley flour kneaded with water, added little by little; then crushed and ground beans, and pearl barley <note>original: "ptiſana"</note>, and whole millet, and linseed boiled and dried and mixed with raw barley flour. To these you may add oil and make lumps out of them to offer as food, so that they may be satiated and grow fat.

## How quadrupeds are to be fattened.

The pig, of all animals, progresses most easily to fatness; for it grows fat in sixty days, having first been fatigued by hunger for three days, as is done with all others. It grows fat on barley, millet, acorns, figs, pears, cucumbers, rest, and a lack of motion. Moreover, pigs are made fatter when they have wallowed in mud. Figs and chickpeas especially fatten them, and they delight in a change of fodder, according to **Varro** <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a Roman scholar and author of *Rerum Rusticarum*, an influential work on agriculture</note>. The pig is nourished by beans, barley, and other grains, which things not only produce fatness, but also a pleasant flavor in the meat. Olives, wild olives, yellow vetch <note>original: "aphaca"</note>, straw, and grass fatten the herd, all of which are more effective if sprinkled with brine; however, they fatten more fully if the animal is first fatigued by three days of fasting, according to **Aristotle**. Bean pods and stalks are a most pleasing fodder; by providing salt, any loathing of the food is countered, which they lick from wooden troughs where it is placed as a seasoning for the fodder during the summer, and by that taste they conceive a desire for drinking and feeding, according to **Columella** <note>Lucius Junius Moderatus Columella, a prominent Roman writer on agriculture</note>. Oxen grow fat on grain and grass, bitter vetch <note>original: "eruo"</note>, crushed beans, and the bean-stalks themselves. Additionally, they fatten on barley, either whole or ground and separated from the husk; and on sweet things, such as dried figs, wine, elm leaves, and by washing with warm water, according to **Aristotle**. We ourselves raise them at home in Sorrento <note>The author, della Porta, was a Neapolitan polymath and often references his home region</note>, and we provide them with the remains of our food, or we place calves under two mothers to suckle; thus nourished by such copious milk, they can scarcely manage to walk due to their fatness. Furthermore, we scatter blocks of salt in the stalls so that by licking they may become thirsty and drink, and thus we produce a meat of unusual fatness and tenderness.

# *How the flesh of animals may be made sweeter.*
## CHAPTER VI.

NOW, by certain foods and techniques, we shall make not only parts of animals, but the animals in their entirety, fat, tender, and sweeter; and first:

### *How the liver of geese may be fattened.*

Our elders were wiser, says **Pliny**, who knew the goodness of the goose's liver: in those birds that are crammed <note>original: "fartilibus," referring to the practice of forced feeding or 'cramming'</note> it grows to a great size; once removed, it is also increased by soaking in milk and honey <note>original: "lacte mulso"</note>.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of specialized animal husbandry, specifically the production of luxury foods. It transitions from the general fattening of quadrupeds described on the previous page to the ancient Roman techniques for producing foie gras (enlarged goose liver).</meta>

<page-num>510</page-num>
# NATURAL MAGIC, BOOK XIV

And it is not without cause that there is a question of who first discovered such a great benefit: whether it was Scipio Metellus, a man of consular rank, or Marcus Seius, a Roman knight of the same era. The method is taught by **Palladius** <note>Rutilius Taurus Aemilianus Palladius, a 4th-century writer on agriculture</note>. After thirty days of fattening, if you desire their livers to become tender, you shall take crushed dried figs <note>original: "caricas", specifically dried figs from Caria in Asia Minor</note> and, having soaked them in water, roll them into small pellets <note>original: "offas"</note> and serve them to the geese for twenty continuous days.

According to the **Quintilii** <note>The Quintilii brothers, Sestus Quintilius Condianus and Sestus Quintilius Valerius Maximus, were authors of agricultural texts later collected in the *Geoponica*</note>: when the geese have grown, chop dried figs <note>original: "ischadas"</note> into small pieces and, grinding them smooth with water, offer this in their drink for a cycle of twenty days. Some, in order to make the liver large and the goose itself fat, nourish them as follows: they place soaked wheat before the penned animal, or barley in the same manner; for wheat fattens quickly, but barley makes the flesh white. Let it be fed on the aforementioned varieties, either individually or even both together, for twenty-five days, offering dough-rolls <term>collyria<gloss>small, cylindrical pieces of dough, traditionally used in medicine or animal feeding</gloss></term> made from them twice a day. Seven such rolls should be offered each of the first five days, and thereafter the number should be gradually increased up to twenty-five days, so that there are thirty days in total. When these are completed, you shall boil mallows and, while the decoction is still warm, you shall offer moistened fermented dough, and you shall do this for four days. During these same days, you shall offer honey-water, changing it three times each day and not using the same water, and so on in the following days up to sixty days. You shall use crushed dried figs with the aforementioned fermented dough for their nourishment, and it will happen that after sixty days, you will enjoy both the goose itself and its tender, white liver. Indeed, once removed, the liver must be placed in a large vessel containing hot water, which must be changed again and again. Moreover, the bodies and livers of the females are superior. The geese should not be yearlings, but rather from two up to four years of age. **Horace** mentions this in his *Satires* <note>original: "Sermonibus"</note>:

> *A liver of a white goose fattened even more with rich figs.* <note>original: "Pinguius & ficis paſtum iecur anſeris albi."</note>

And **Juvenal** in his fifth *Satire*:

> *Before the host is a huge goose liver, as large as the fattened goose itself.* <note>original: "Anſeris ante ipſum magnum iecur, anſeribus par Altilis."</note>

And **Martial**:

### *How the meat of animals may become bitter and contemptible.*
### CHAPTER VII.

**On the contrary**, if we want the meat to be rejected for bitterness or venom, we shall do the opposite of what we have said; or if we wish to avoid the labor, those times are to be expected in which the animals feed on such fodder that produces it, from which they even sometimes turn out poisonous. For example, if we want:

### *The meat of stags to become poisonous.*

Simeon Sethi <note>An 11th-century Byzantine Jewish physician and scholar</note> says: the flesh of stags caught in summer is poisonous, because at that time they clearly feed on vipers and serpents; from such eating they become thirsty. And they know this by their own nature: that if they drink water before the digestion of those serpents, they die; therefore they endure the thirst, and are parched by it. Thus the meat of stags taken at that time of year is poisonous and very harmful. There are also:

### *times when partridges are at their worst.*

Specifically, when they feed on garlic. The Cyrrhaeans <note>Inhabitants of Cyrrha, a town in ancient Greece near the Oracle of Delphi</note> reject the meat of partridges because of their fodder; since garlic has been tasted, their meat is not at all edible and stinks, so that it is not even used as food by the bird-catcher. Likewise also...

### *Quails and starlings are to be rejected,*

At that time of year when the seed of hellebore <note>original: "veratri"</note> is their most pleasing food. Hence, when quails feed on hellebore <note>original: "elloboro"</note>, they put the lives of those who eat them in such great danger that they become bloated and are seized with convulsions as if overcome by vertigo; for this reason, they must be boiled with millet. There are also

### *Small birds to be rejected, when*

The berries of the yew tree <note>original: "taxi baccae"</note> are ripe, for their feathers turn black, and the people who eat them are seized with a flow of the bowels <note>diarrhea</note>, according to Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD, author of "De Materia Medica"</note>. The eggs

### *of the barbel fish are rejected*

In the month of May because they are harmful; yet the eggs are not harmful by their own nature, nor do they always produce those ills—indeed, they may often be eaten without harm—but they are only harmful at that time when they have tasted the willow flowers that have fallen into the waters. In the same way

### *Snails are to be rejected,*

When they cling to briars and are stuck to thickets; for they disturb the belly and stomach and provoke vomiting, according to Dioscorides. And it is not only the animals themselves that bring these harms, but also their secretions, such as milk, honey, and similar things. For

### *Milk is to be rejected, when*

Goats and sheep feed on green fodder, because it loosens the bowels more; however, goat milk troubles the belly less because this animal feeds on astringent <note>substances that cause body tissues to contract</note> fodder, such as oak, mastic, olive leaves, and terebinth <note>the turpentine tree</note>. In places where the livestock devour scammony <note>a plant used as a harsh purgative</note>, hellebore <note>original: "veratrum"</note>, clematis, or mercury <note>the plant Mercury, not the metal</note>, all the milk upsets the belly and stomach, as is said to happen in the Justinian mountains; indeed, goats to whom hellebore was given as food at the first budding of the leaves will vomit, and their milk, when drunk, creates nausea, and causes the stomach to heave and vomit, according to Dioscorides. There is also found

### *Poisonous honey,*

Which is produced in Sardinia, because there the bees [feed] on wormwood <note>original: "absinthio"</note>...

### *How animals may be cooked so they are roasted and boiled at the same time.*

->*How a pig may be made roasted and boiled at the same time.*<-

> Saying: A pig was brought to us, one half carefully roasted, the other half softly boiled as if in water, prepared with such wonderful skill by the cook that the place where it had been slaughtered was not visible; for it had been killed with a small wound at the shoulder and drained of blood, and all the intestines were carefully washed with wine. Having hung it by its feet and drenched it again with wine, he boiled it. With much pepper, he covered half the pig all over with a thick paste <note>original: "polenta," here referring to a protective dough</note> made of wine and barley meal kneaded together. He then placed it in the oven on a bronze tray and took care to roast it with such moderation that it was neither burned nor taken out raw. For when the skin appeared to be somewhat dry, he judged that the rest was also sufficiently cooked. Once the paste was removed, he served it to the table.

The upper part will be roasted by the heat of the oven, while the lower part will be boiled in the broth. Nor will it be less pleasing to the sight...

### A moray eel fried, boiled, and roasted at the same time.

Before you cook a moray eel <note>original: "Murena," a predatory eel-like fish prized by the Romans</note>, you must debone it so that it is more pleasant to eat, since its flesh is tangled with bones. To do this, grasp two small rods <note>original: "bacilli"</note> in each hand, and by squeezing and wiping down the middle of the fish, you shall remove the spine. Next, cut off the head and the tip of the tail (where the bones have gathered due to the deboning process) and remove the entrails. Fix the eel onto a spit. You will prepare certain parts to be boiled, fried, and roasted: wrap these sections three or four times with linen ribbons. In one section, sprinkle pepper; in the section to be boiled, use crushed parsley, saffron, mint, fennel, and raisin wine <note>original: "passo," a sweet wine made from dried grapes</note> soaked in water and salt or broth. For the fried parts, use oil and order them to be rotated at the fire, constantly moistening them by sprinkling a bundle of oregano over them. When that part has been roasted, remove it; it will be an excellent dish to offer to the banqueters.

->*On the various preparation of poultry.* CHAPTER IX.<-

->*How a cooked peacock may appear alive.*<-

We shall add to these various ways of preparing poultry, which can provide no small amount of delight at feasts. Such as how a cooked peacock may appear to be alive. The peacock is killed either by driving a feather <note>or a quill</note> upward into the brain, or by cutting its throat as is done with young goats so the blood may drain out. Then, the skin is gently slit from the throat down to the tail. Once slit, the skin—along with its own feathers—is pulled from the whole body up to the head; the head is then cut off and reserved along with the skin and the legs. You shall roast the peacock's body itself on a spit, stuffed with spices and fragrant herbs, having first stuck cloves <note>original: "garyophyllis"</note> through the breast. Wrap the neck in a white linen cloth and keep it constantly moistened with water so that it does not dry out at all. When the peacock is cooked and removed from the spit, cover it again with its own skin. To make it appear as if it is standing on its feet, drive iron wires (which should remain unseen) through the legs into a board crafted for this purpose, and run them through the body to the head and the tail. Some people put camphor <note>original: "caphuram," a flammable substance</note> in the bird's mouth and set it on fire when it is carried to the table. Platina <note>Bartolomeo Sacchi, known as Platina (1421–1481), author of the first printed cookbook, *On Right Pleasure and Good Health*</note> teaches that the same can be done with pheasants, geese, capons, and other birds, which we also observe in our own banquets. But it will be a more magnificent spectacle if...

### *A goose cooked while still alive.*

A little before our time, at the tables of the Kings of Aragon <note>The House of Aragon ruled parts of Spain and Italy, including Naples, where the author lived; their court was famous for its lavish and theatrical banquets.</note>, a goose was often served both alive and cooked, as we have heard from trustworthy old men. When we ourselves attempted this experiment, we ended up devouring it before the cooking was fully finished because of the haste of our companions. Yet, the goose was alive, and the upper part of the skin was perfectly cooked. 

Here is the rule for preparing it. Take a duck, or a goose, or another animal that is quite hardy, though the goose is better than all others for this. Leaving the head and the neck alone, pluck the feathers from the entire body. Then, let it be surrounded and walled in by fire—not so close that it is suffocated by the smoke or scorched too quickly, and not so far that it escapes unharmed. Place small cups and little jars filled with water all around it, to which you should add salt and honey. Let the bird itself be entirely smeared with fat and larded <note>The practice of "larding" involved threading strips of pork fat through the meat to keep it moist during roasting.</note> so that it becomes more edible and is cooked more easily. 

Apply the fire, but do not be in a hurry. When it begins to grow hot from the heat, the goose will move about and try to flee, but the fire blocks its path and hedges it in. Thus, the poor creature is forced to drink the water to calm itself, which cools its heart and its other internal organs. The power of the "medicine" <note>The salt and honey mixture mentioned earlier.</note> loosens the bowels and cleanses them, and as the bird heats up, the internal organs will cook. You must continually moisten the brain and the heart with a sponge. 

However, when you see it begin to stumble and falter (for the moisture in the heart is failing), remove it and serve it to the guests. It will cry out as parts are pulled away, so that it seems almost to be eaten before it is dead. If you wish to serve it at the table...

### *A deboned squab.*

This is how you shall debone it. Place a cleaned and well-washed squab <note>original: "pipio," a young pigeon</note> in sharp vinegar for a day and a night. Then, having washed it again and stuffed it with spices and herbs, you may boil it or roast it as you please; you will find it to be without bones in whatever way you prepare it. In ancient times, there was also served at the table...

### *The Trojan Pig.*

The ancient architects of gluttony <note>A playful term for gourmands or professional chefs of the Roman era.</note> devised a method where an entire ox or camel was served, containing various kinds of animals. From this, the "Trojan Pig" gained its fame among the people. It was given this name because it concealed various species of animals within its belly, just as the wooden horse <note>original: "Durius equus," referring to the Durateus or the wooden horse of Troy.</note> concealed the Greeks...

The pig was slaughtered with a small wound under the shoulder (see Dalechamps’ <note>Jacques Daléchamps (1513–1588) was a French physician and botanist known for his translations of classical texts on natural history and dining.</note> version); then, after the blood had been drained off copiously, all the intestines were removed by extraction. After this, it was served on a silver platter of significant thickness, gilded just enough to hold the roasted pig, which was placed on it on its back with its belly bulging and filled with various good things—according to Athenaeus in the ninth book of the *Deipnosophists* <note>A Greek work from the early 3rd century AD that preserved vast amounts of information on ancient food and luxury.</note>. ### An egg that exceeds a human head in size

If you wish to produce one so huge, there is a craft by which one may even hide the eggs of other animals inside the womb <note>This likely refers to the cavity or "interior" of the large artificial egg being constructed.</note>, and it cannot be distinguished from a natural one. Separate fifty or more yolks <note>original: *bolera/boleta*; in this context, the author uses these terms to refer to the yolks which must be separated from the whites.</note> and whites from each other. Mix the yolks gently and put them into a bladder, tying it to mimic a round shape. Put it into a pot full of water, and when you see it swelling with bubbles, or when they have grown hard, take it out and add the whites, arranging them so that the yolks sit in the middle, and let it cook again. Thus, you will have the egg stripped of its shell, which you will then shape in this way: grind up white and raised eggshells until they fly as a very fine dust; let them soak in strong or distilled vinegar until they soften. For if an egg is placed in vinegar for a long time...

### How foodstuffs may be prepared in those places where there is no facility for cooking. CHAPTER X.

It happens sometimes by chance that men find themselves in places where many things necessary for the preparation of a dinner are lacking; but where convenience is absent, these things have been devised by ingenuity. If a frying pan is missing, you shall know

->*how fish may be fried in paper.*<-

Fashion a frying vessel out of a single sheet of paper, in which the oil and fish are placed; then set it over glowing coals without a flame, and you will finish the task more quickly and conveniently. But if you wish

->*that a chicken be cooked without a fire,*<-

so that while we complete a journey, the chickens are cooked: let a small piece of steel be placed in a fire <note>The steel acts as a heat-storage medium; once heated, it provides the energy for cooking away from the hearth.</note>; then let the unplucked and gutted chicken be thrown in with it, and let it be very well covered with cloths so that the heat does not vanish. Even if it is tainted by a foul odor <note>likely from the heated feathers or the steel</note>, it will nonetheless be good for food. If servants are lacking to turn the spit, and you wish

->*that a bird might roast itself,*<-

you may use this artifice, for the bird will move itself. Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a medieval scholar famous for his writings on the "secrets" of the natural world.</note> writes that if you fix a wren—which is the smallest of all birds—onto a hazel-wood spit and place it over coals, it will move about so that it seems to move of its own accord. This happens from the property of the wood, not from any magic. The things the Philosopher <note>Commonly referring to Aristotle, though here Porta is critiquing a folk-belief often attributed to ancient sources.</note> said are false: for if you subject a hazel branch to the fire, it twists and turns so that it appears to move itself; thus, whatever meat you fix to it, provided it is of modest weight, will all be moved by the wood's turning. Likewise

->*Eggs are cooked without fire.*<-

Eggs buried in quicklime <term>quicklime: calcium oxide, which produces intense heat when it reacts with water</term> and sprinkled with water are cooked; for indeed

You shall take a glass flask and, once it has been thoroughly cleaned, let it be filled with spirits of wine <note>original: "aqua vitæ"—distilled alcohol</note>. Put a little musk inside and stop the mouth of the flask diligently so that it does not breathe out. Expose it to the summer sun for two weeks, always shaking and moving the liquid. The use of this will be as follows: if you cast a single drop <note>original: "lachrymam," literally a tear</note> of this into an amphora of wine, the entire wine will smell of musk. Do the same with cinnamon and other aromatics. Thus is it prepared.

->**Hippocras.**<-
<note>Spiced wine, named after the Greek physician Hippocrates.</note>

Take the sweetest wine, among us commonly called *war-eater* <note>original: "mangia-guerra," a potent sweet wine from the Naples region</note>, and into four vials full of it, place two pounds of crushed sugar, four ounces of cinnamon, and an ounce and a half of pepper and grains of paradise <note>A pungent spice from West Africa, related to ginger, highly popular in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note>. Let them steep for a day, then pass them through a strainer. At the very end, add a small measure of musk on the tip of a spoon, and it will be an excellent wine. Or, we may add to the crushed sugar a little spirits of wine in which cinnamon, pepper, grains of paradise, and musk have soaked, as we described; you will have it ready immediately, for it extracts the "fifth essence" <note>The concentrated essence or "quintessence" of the spices.</note>. We shall teach how this is to be done.

->**How wine may be turned to ice in a flask.**<-

Because the primary thing sought at banquets, especially on summer days, is a frozen wine drink, we shall teach how wine may not only be made cold instantly but turned to ice, so that it cannot be drunk except by sucking it and warming it with one's breath. Put the wine into a flask and add a very small amount of water so that it may be converted into ice more quickly. Then, cast snow into a wooden basin and sprinkle over it crushed saltpeter, or the dross of saltpeter, which is commonly called *falazzo* <note>The impurities or refuse left over from the saltpeter refining process.</note>. We shall rotate the flask through the snow, and little by little it will be frozen. For those who keep snow in the summer so that it lasts: let water be boiled in bronze cauldrons, then poured into vats and exposed to the freezing air; for it will turn to ice, and it will be harder than snow and preserved much longer.

->**To make them drunk.**<-

The Egyptians were said to eat boiled cabbage before all other food to prepare themselves for drinking bouts. Many, to be delivered from drunkenness, take cabbage seed beforehand. The Sybarites <note>Inhabitants of Sybaris, a Greek city in Italy famous for its luxury and excess.</note>, says Timaeus, fortified themselves by eating cabbage before they drank. > *Suddenly; for indeed, in a wonderful way, that dissipates it.*

*Such trifles, so that a radish would be no more effective for the purpose.*
<note>original: "Eiusmodi nugas, raphanus ut non magis Ad id valeat." A proverbial expression suggesting that certain remedies are as useless as a radish against a great force.</note>

Some people were accustomed to use a small vessel made of amethyst <note>The name "amethyst" comes from the Greek *a-methystos*, meaning "not drunken"; the stone was long believed to prevent intoxication.</note> before a drinking party, so that they might indulge in wine with impunity, according to Athenæus. If you wish to inhibit the harm of wine by other means, Africanus teaches that this is especially necessary for wine that is somewhat diluted; for people feel a hangover <term>crapula</term><note>A Latin term for the headache and sickness resulting from excessive drinking.</note> more quickly from diluted wine than those who have drunk it pure. If you are going to drink a great deal, you should first eat three or four bitter almonds; these are drying and consume the moisture, thereby repelling intoxication. Plutarch relates that there was a man with Drusus the Physician who, because he would first eat five or six bitter almonds, always emerged the winner in drinking contests. 

Powdered pumice stone <note>original: "pumicis farina"</note> achieves the same effect if the drinker takes it beforehand. Theophrastus adds a warning that there is a risk unless one follows it with a great deal of drink <note>Because of the pumice's extreme drying capacity.</note>. He mentions that Eudemus lasted through twenty-two rounds this way; afterward, having entered the bath, he vomited nothing and dined as if he had not been drinking at all. This is due to its drying power consuming the liquid—indeed, if pumice is thrown into a boiling vat of must <note>Unfermented grape juice.</note>, the heat of the wine is immediately calmed throughout. 

There were also other concerns of the ancient fathers for extinguishing a hangover: they would eat lettuce at the end of the meal, as it possesses a very great inherent coldness. Now, however, we use it at the start of the meal to stimulate the appetite. Hence Martial writes:

->*The lettuce that used to close the dinners of our ancestors,*<-
->*Tell me, why does it now begin our feasts?*<-
<note>original: "Claudere quæ cœnas lactuca solebat auorum, / Dic mihi cur nostras inchoat illa dapes?" from Martial, Epigrams 13.14.</note>

Dioscorides seems to call lettuce "anti-hangover" <note>original: "acræpulam"</note> because it prevents drunkenness. Leeks also dispel intoxication, and anyone who takes saffron beforehand will not feel the effects of wine. There are even herbs and flowers which, when twisted and fashioned into a garland, soothe drunkenness, such as violets, roses, and ivy berries. The ash of a swallow's beak, ground with myrrh and sprinkled into the wine being drunk, will keep one safe from inebriation. This was discovered by Horus, King of the Assyrians, according to Pliny. We have spoken of how inebriation is repelled; now it is necessary to discuss

->**How to make wine-drinkers abstain.**<-

### Which demonstrates how to catch and kill animals by hand.

*We shall speak of fowling <term>aucupio: the traditional art of catching birds, typically involving decoys, lime-twigs, or nets</term>, a pursuit to which the greatest part of mortals, and especially the nobility, is devoted. The objective is to capture animals by force or by guile. Through guile they are enticed, and through death they are punished. By what reasoning this may be achieved is taught by Philosophy <note>Porta refers here to "Natural Philosophy," the ancestor of modern biology and behavioral science</note>, which reveals the natures and peculiar habits of animals. For when their natures and habits are easily understood, one can devise the tricks by which they may be lured and captured. First, we will teach how they are enticed by food, sound, light, fumigation, love, and other ruses; once lured or intoxicated, we catch them by hand or kill them with poison. But let us set forth the examples.*

->*By what foods various animals may be enticed.*<-

## CHAPTER I.

Nothing stimulates animals more than food and luxury <note>original: "luxuria"; in this context referring to physical pleasure or the reproductive drive</note>, or love; therefore, we have decided to begin with these. They are driven to food by necessity, for unless they wish to be killed by hunger, they must hunt for food. But with various—

Just as the foods of animals are varied, we shall describe the specific baits for some, so that by your own ingenuity <note>original: "tuo marte," literally "by your own Mars," an idiom for one's own skill or effort</note> you may figure out the rest. This is

### *Bait for catching the Catfish.*

The Catfish <term>Silurus: the European catfish or sheatfish, known for its massive size</term> is attracted by roasted bull’s lung. The lung is attached to the line where the hook is; when cast into the water, the scent stirs the catfish's senses. Seeking the bait, it devours it immediately and, once pierced by the hook, it is dragged to the shore by oxen, as we learn from Aelian <note>Claudius Aelianus, a Roman author of the 3rd century who wrote extensively on the behavior of animals</note>.

### *Bait for the Seabream.*

The Seabream <term>Sargus: the white seabream, famous in antiquity for its supposed "love" for goats</term> pursues goats with a wondrous affection, as we shall discuss, and they especially delight in the goat's scent. Therefore, the fisherman throws flour soaked in goat broth into that part of the sea where the seabream usually live. Attracted by the scent as if by a love potion <note>original: "philtro"</note>, they approach and are caught by the hook. ## ***How animals may be captured by the allurements of love.***

**T**here are two tyrants of brute animals: food and lust—or rather, love. Neither scent, nor sound, nor fumigations, nor finally anything else stimulates their souls as much as love, so that it may be said not only of man, but of wild beasts: "To what do you not drive mortal hearts, wicked Love?" <note>original: "Quid non mortalia pectora cogis improbe amor?" — a famous quote from Virgil’s *Aeneid* (4.412) regarding the irresistible power of passion</note>. ->*To catch cuttlefish by the lure of love.*<-

To catch cuttlefish <note>original: "sepias"</note>, neither wicker traps nor the snares of nets are necessary, but we fish them out by the allurements of love in this manner: they trail a female cuttlefish on a line, and as soon as the male sees her from even the greatest distance, he immediately rushes toward her with longing, and wraps his flexible knots <note>The male's tentacles</note> around his lover again and again with great care. Meanwhile, in this embrace, they are pulled up by the fisherman's snares.

### *Capturing the Parrotfish*

The Parrotfish <term>Scarus: a Mediterranean fish celebrated in antiquity for its social behavior and supposed intelligence</term> is the most inflamed toward Venus <note>original: "ad Venerem," referring to the goddess of love, here meaning sexual desire</note> of all fish. The cause of its capture is an insatiable desire for the female. Those highly skilled in the art of fishing, being well aware of this, set snares for it in this manner: they tie the upper mouth of a captured female to a thin cord and drag her alive through the sea in a place where the fish usually gather. The males, at the sight of their beloved, are carried away by the madness of lust and rejoice to touch her, seeking a kiss, a playful nibble, or some other secret amorous theft. When they have come close to the fish-trap <term>Nassa: a basket-like trap or weel made of wicker</term>, the fisherman draws the female into the trap, and the males, flowing in at the same time, are caught. This is according to Oppian <note>Oppian of Anazarbus, the 2nd-century author of a famous poem on fishing</note>.

### *Capturing Elephants*

A pit is prepared for elephants, and to entice them, four females are shut inside. When the males come running and enter the pit, the men lying in wait pull away the bridge and capture the trapped elephants. This is from Aelian <note>Claudius Aelianus, a Roman author of the 2nd century who wrote "On the Nature of Animals"</note>.

### *Capturing the Nightingale*

With a female nightingale shut in a cage, the fowlers mock them with a simulated voice. The male is summoned by the sound, and having seen her, he flies around and falls into the snares of the nets.

### *How Sargi are Captured.*

It is a truly mad method of capture. Sargi <term>Sargus: a Mediterranean sea bream, known for its distinct stripes and behavior</term> love goats desperately; indeed, they are carried away by such madness that when the shadow of one or two goats grazing near the shore appears on the water, they immediately leap out for joy. They swim toward the shore with great eagerness and, though they are not well-suited for jumping, they strive to touch the goats with a leap, so much do they yearn to approach them in their delight. Therefore, they are captured by the very thing they desire so greatly. For this reason, the fisherman prepares a snare by putting on a stripped goat-skin complete with horns. Keeping the sun at his back, he scatters flour moistened with goat-broth into that part of the sea where the sargi usually gather. Attracted to this as if by a love-potion, they approach; they are soothed by the sight of the skin resembling a goat and they feed upon the flour. Thus the fisherman catches many of them; this is from Aelian <note>Claudius Aelianus, a 3rd-century Roman author who wrote "On the Nature of Animals" in Greek</note>. Oppian <note>Oppian of Anazarbus, author of the "Halieutica," a poem on fishing</note> describes it most elegantly:

> *A wondrous desire for goats invades the sargi.*

And a little later:

> *But the hunter, covered in the smelly hide of a she-goat,*
> *fits two long horns to the top of his head;*
> *he drops flour mixed with goat entrails and its scent*
> *into the swelling waves of the sea:*
> *the pleasant smell, the pleasant shepherd, and the counterfeit goat*
> *deceive them, etc.*

### *How Partridges are Captured.*

Partridges vehemently love stags, and they are deceived by their skins in this manner. If someone dressed in a stag’s skin places horns upon his head and approaches stealthily, the birds, believing it to be a true stag, look up to him and revere him. They rejoice so much at his approach that they are unwilling to leave him, behaving as if they saw an intimate friend or a companion of their own age returning from a long journey. From this affection, they gain nothing but snares and nets.

### *The Hunting of Bustards.*

Bustards <term>Otis: the Great Bustard, a large, ground-nesting bird known for its cautious nature</term> are considered the most fond of horses among birds; the proof of this is that they scorn other animals, but as soon as they catch sight of a horse, they immediately fly toward it with great joy and proceed to draw near. If someone [puts on] a horse's hide...

### *The Capture of Octopuses.*

Octopuses <term>Polypus: literally "many-footed," referring here to the common octopus</term> are delighted by the olive tree; they are often found embracing its trunk with their arms. They have even been caught at times embracing a fig tree growing near the sea and eating the figs, as Clearchus <note>Clearchus of Soli, a student of Aristotle who wrote on natural history</note> writes. For this reason, when fishermen lower an olive branch into the sea in a place where octopuses live, after a short delay and without any labor, he will pull up as many octopuses as he wants, clinging to the branch. Oppian <note>Oppian of Anazarbus, a 2nd-century poet known for his work on fishing, the Halieutica</note> sings of this quite festively:

> *(wondrous to tell).* And then:

> *seizes him; and the fisherman, skilled in such trickery,*
> *casts a lead weight into the midst, which he binds with*
> *the leaves of Pallas; the fish does not despise the olive branches,*
> *but grasps the companionable leaves and never lets go.*
> *Even when dragged into the boat, he does not loosen his grip on the branch:*

## By What Sounds Animals Are Allured. CHAPTER IV.

Not only by love, but also by sound and music are animals allured, and every animal rejoices in its own particular sound. And first:

### *The Dolphin is Allured by the Cithara.*

The dolphin is greatly soothed by the harmony of the cithara <term>Cithara: an ancient Greek musical instrument in the lyre family</term>, and likewise by the sound of the water-organ <term>Hydraulis: an early pipe organ powered by water pressure</term>. Because of this, the story was first celebrated by Herodotus and later by others, that Arion was carried to Taenarum <note>A cape at the southernmost tip of mainland Greece</note> sitting on a dolphin. For when he was about to be cast into the sea by the Corinthians, he obtained permission to take up his cithara and sing a song before being thrown overboard; but he was caught by a dolphin and carried across to Taenarum, as is recorded in Oppian.

### *The Wolf is Soothed by the Pipe.*

Aelian <note>Claudius Aelianus, a Roman author of the 2nd-3rd century</note> reports that the pipe-player Pythiocharis, when he played intense rhythms on the pipe with great effort, repressed the attack of wolves.

### *Horses are captured by flute music.*

Libyan mares are so captivated by the playing of the flute <term>tibia: an ancient wind instrument, often made of bone or reed, similar to an oboe</term> that they become tame toward men and cease their wild howling through these charms. Shepherds hollow out a pastoral pipe from the *Rhododaphne* <note>original: "Rhododaphne"; likely the Oleander or Rose-bay tree</note>, and with its sonorous breath, they so soothe the horses that the animals follow them. When the shepherd stops, the horses stop themselves from moving forward, to the point that they cannot hold back their tears. Euripides <note>A famous Greek playwright (c. 480–406 BC) known for his tragedies</note> says that shepherds incite mares to "Venus" <note>original: "ad Venerem"; referring here to mating or sexual desire</note> with the pipe, and inflame the stallions to mate with the females.

### *Deer and boars are captured by the flute.*

It is a widespread report among the Tyrrhenians <note>The Etruscan people of central Italy</note> that boars and deer are captured by them most effectively with the aid of music. This is how it happens: once the nets are cast and other instruments for trapping the beasts are set in place, a man skilled in playing the flute begins a soft strain, then relaxes and varies the song. He progresses gradually toward the mountain peaks, the valleys, and all the dens of the wild beasts. Then, while their ears are held by the greatest pleasure, they are caught without any effort. For, soothed by the sweetness of the song, they forget their own homes. Thus, led by the lure of persuasion and bound by the song, they cast themselves into the snares and are caught in the traps. From Aelian <note>Claudius Aelianus, a 3rd-century Roman author who wrote "On the Nature of Animals" in Greek</note>.

### *The stingray is enticed by dancing and music.*

When a fisherman catches sight of a stingray <term>pastinaca: a species of ray or stingray</term> swimming below, he performs a ridiculous dance in his fishing boat and begins to play the flute. From this, the stingray takes great joy and, enticed by this soothing charm, it rises to the surface of the water; then, another fisherman pulls the unaware creature up with his fishing gear.

### *Crabs are led onto land by music.*

Fishermen capture crabs <term>Paguros: likely referring to a specific type of crab or hermit crab</term> through the artifice of musical enticement. Some fishermen hide themselves, while others begin to play an instrument. When the crabs hear this, they are immediately led out of their hiding places as if by a lover's call; indeed, lured by the pleasure, they even climb out of the sea. As the musicians retreat while playing the flute, the crabs follow them onto dry land, where they are captured.

### Fishes are lured by light at night. Chapter V.

Among the various arts of deceiving animals, light is one: for at night, when some fish are resting, fishermen carrying a light above their boats strike the fish lured toward them with a trident, or capture them alive. This practice was not unknown to Oppian <note>Oppian of Anazarbus (2nd century AD), a Greco-Roman poet famous for his didactic poems on fishing, titled *Halieutica*</note>:

> When Phoebus <note>original: "Phœbus"; a name for the sun or the god Apollo</note> stands at equal distance from either goal in heaven,
> Or when he plunges headlong into the western waves,
> Then they subdue the fish; or at the first hour of night
> They drive a boat through the marble-like seas with a lit torch:
> They destroy those resting under the night by a hidden fate,
> The fish, who are delighted by the flame or the clear light.
> While the swarming schools gathered around the boat behold
> The fatal light, they perish by the point of the trident.

For a long time, the anxiety of many has tormented their minds as to how fire or light could be carried under the water so that fish, seeing it from a distance, might come toward it. We have accomplished it in this manner: We constructed a ball of brass or lead, three or four feet in diameter. It was sharp or pyramidal at the bottom so it could be more easily submerged at the base, and fortified with iron rings so that, weighted down, it could be dragged under the waters. Above it, we attached a tube <term>canalis: a pipe or snorkel-like chimney</term> fifteen or twenty feet in length and one foot wide. Let the belly of the ball be opened with many windows, five or six, to which polished glass panes <term>specula: here meaning glass windows or mirrors used to transmit and reflect light</term> are fitted, and the joints stuffed with pitch-based glue so that no water can enter.

Having found a suitable location, let the ball be submerged, weighted down by its mass, but let the mouth of the tube stand at least two feet above the surface of the water. Next, let us lower a lit lamp <term>lucerna: an oil lamp</term> by a cord through the tube into the belly of the ball, crafted with such skill <note>This likely refers to a gimbal or a "Cardan suspension" which keeps a lamp level despite the motion of the water</note> that no matter how it moves, the light always remains standing perfectly upright. The light will pass through the windows and the glass into the waters, and by the reflection made under the water, a great brilliance will be seen from quite far off, to whose splendor a massive swarm of fish will rush; then you will be able to surround them with nets.
->poteris.<- <note>This is a catchword, "you will be able," intended to lead into the first word of the following page.</note>

### Animals may also be gathered by mirrors. CHAPTER VI.

Even if females are absent, mirrors can reflect an animal's own image, whereby the creatures, deceived by their own form, are enticed; liquids can also take the place of mirrors. As follows:

->*The cuttlefish is caught by a mirror.*<-

Fishermen lower mirrors carved into wood and hung from a cord into the water, and they slowly drag them as they float. The cuttlefish <note>original: "sepia"</note> flings itself at its own likeness, wrapping its tentacles <term>flagellis: literally "whips," referring to the long, flexible limbs of the cuttlefish</term> around the wood. While it amorously gazes at the form appearing in the mirror, it is meanwhile surrounded by a small net and pulled up.

->*The jackdaw may be caught by a mirror.*<-

Jackdaws <note>original: "monedulæ"</note> love themselves. The bird-catcher, intending to hunt them, devises such schemes: in the place where he has seen them congregate, he sets out basins full of oil. The curious little bird, having traveled there, perches on the rim of the vessel and, leaning over at the same time, looks down at its own shadow. Because it thinks it sees another jackdaw, it hastens to descend toward it; and as it slips down, it is covered by the thickness of the oil, held fast without snares or nets. As follows:

->*Quails may be caught by a mirror.*<-

Clearchus <note>Clearchus of Soli, a Greek philosopher and student of Aristotle</note> writes that partridges, sparrows, and quails do not only emit seed <note>original: "semen emittere"; an archaic way of saying they are sexually stimulated</note> when they see females, but even when they hear their voice. The cause is an impression made upon the mind, which you will recognize during the time of mating if you place a mirror opposite them, and before this very mirror set the snares of traps. For running toward their own image, which is vainly represented in the mirror, they are caught. This is from Athenæus and Eustathius <note>referencing the *Deipnosophistae* of Athenæus and the commentaries of the Byzantine scholar Eustathius of Thessalonica</note>.

->*The unicorn is enticed by odor.*<-

Tzetzes <note>Joannes Tzetzes, a 12th-century Byzantine poet known for his vast collection of historical and mythical lore</note> writes that the unicorn <note>original: "monoceros"</note> so greatly reveres virgin girls...

Hunters dress a robust young man in the fashion of a girl, and having sprinkled him with perfumes, they place him directly across from the place where the <term>monoceros: the unicorn, a legendary creature often said to be capturable only by the presence of a virgin</term> is known to be, so that the sweetness of the scent may be carried to the beast by the breath of the breeze. ### To gather weasels.

Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman naturalist</note> says that the gall of a gecko <note>original: "stellio," a spotted lizard or gecko</note> ground in water will gather <term>mustelas: weasels</term> together. Indeed, the Plinian Magi write that if the gall of a chameleon is thrown into water, weasels will be drawn to it.

### To gather mice.

If you pour thick dregs of olive oil <note>original: "amurca," the bitter, watery sediment left after pressing olives</note> into a dish and place it upright in the house, they will stick to it, according to Palladius <note>a 4th-century Roman writer on agriculture</note>. Anatolius says that if you pour olive oil dregs into a bronze basin and leave it in the middle of the house, you will gather all the <term>mures: mice</term> during the night.

### So that fleas may gather.

The fat collected from salted hedgehog floating in boiling water, if it is smeared on a stick and that stick is placed in the house or under a bed, will cause all the <term>pulices: fleas</term> to gather to it, according to Rhazes <note>an influential Persian physician and philosopher</note>.

### To gather frogs.

The gall of a goat, placed in a vessel on the ground, is said to gather <term>ranas: frogs</term> to itself, if they find something pleasing in it.

# How drunken animals may be caught by hand.
## CHAPTER VIII.

**W**e have spoken of lures; now let us speak of intoxications. For there are very many simple substances that cause drunkenness, so that animals may be caught by hand while they are fast asleep. Because there are various things that produce this effect depending on the variety of animals, we shall therefore hand down each one in order. And first:

### How dogs are intoxicated.

Athenaeus <note>a Greek rhetorician and grammarian</note> says that crows and dogs are intoxicated by the herb *oenutta*. But Theophrastus <note>the "father of botany" and successor to Aristotle</note>, from whom he took this, says the root of the *oenothera* <note>original: "oenothera," likely the evening primrose, whose name in Greek suggests "wine-seeker"</note> given in wine renders their temperaments milder and more cheerful, whence

The word *oenutta* <note>original: "œnutta"</note> is a corruption; it is actually the *oenothera* <note>literally "wine-seeker," a plant believed to infuse those who drink it with a gentle disposition</note> of Theophrastus, which, as we have said, is the *rhododaphne* <note>the oleander or rose-laurel</note>. In this way also

### *Donkeys are intoxicated,*

and once they are put to sleep, they are not only easily captured, but even if they were to be skinned, they would hardly feel it, much less wake up. This happens because of hemlock <note>original: "cicuta"</note>; for when they have fed upon it, they are weighed down by such a heavy sleep that they seem stupid and deprived of all sensation. In this way also

### *Horses are rendered senseless*

by the seed of <term>henbane: a poisonous plant (Hyoscyamus niger) known for its psychoactive and sedative properties</term>, if you offer it to them mixed in with their barley. They are overcome by such a lethargy that they lie half-dead for half a day. A certain trickster <note>original: "sycophanta"</note>, when he ran out of money on a journey, threw this kind of seed to the walking animals of some travelers. When the animals fell into a sleep like death and everyone was overcome with great distress, he took a fee from them and faked a remedy: by anointing their nostrils with vinegar, he restored them to life, and so they continued the journey they had begun. In the same way

### *Leopards are intoxicated.*

Oppian <note>a Greco-Roman poet who wrote about hunting</note> teaches the method and how they are captured while drunk. In Libya, when hunters notice a spring where leopards <note>original: "pardales"</note> are accustomed to drink at dawn, they bring many jars full of wine juice there at night and sit nearby hidden under blankets. The leopards, burning with thirst, approach the spring; as soon as they have quenched their thirst with the wine—a drink they are very fond of—they first play about with a sort of dance, and then they fall asleep, stretched out on the ground. Thus, while they are sleeping deeply, they are captured with no trouble. If you wish to know how

### *Drunken monkeys are captured,*

Athenaeus <note>a Greek rhetorician and author of "The Deipnosophists"</note> reports that they even drink wine and are sometimes captured when intoxicated. Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, the Roman naturalist</note> says that monkeys and other four-footed animals with fingers will not grow if they are accustomed to drinking undiluted wine. In the same way

### *Swine go mad*

after devouring henbane. Aelian <note>a Roman author of "On the Nature of Animals"</note> says that by feeding on this herb, wild boars are weakened and convulsed; it has the nature of wine and therefore attacks the mind and the head. There also become

### *Intoxicated elephants,*

### *How birds may be caught by hand.*

### *To hunt drunken partridges,*

### *How ducks may be caught by hand.*

If someone observes the place where ducks take their drink, and having drained the water, puts in dark wine, once they have drunk it, they will fall so that they can be easily seized. Wine dregs <note>original: "vini fex," the sediment left at the bottom of a wine cask</note> also perform the same task. There are also caught

### *Drunken ducks and other birds*

For in this way, they will devour the bits of tormentil along with the seeds and, being intoxicated, since they are unable to fly, they will be caught by hand. This is done more effectively when the weather is very cold and the snow is deep. Or, scatter barley grains through a place usually frequented by birds; then prepare a medicine like a porridge from barley flour, ox gall, and the seeds of <term>henbane: a highly toxic and sedative plant (Hyoscyamus)</term>, which you set out for them on a small board. ## **To declare the specific poisons of animals.**

### **CHAPTER IX.**

I would not want you to think that a single poison can kill all animals; rather, each one has its own specific poison. Indeed, what is poison to one is health to another, which happens not by reason of quality, but of its peculiar nature. As, if we wish to list

### **Poisons by which dogs are killed,**

Theophrastus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle, known for his works on botany</note> says it kills dogs and swine when kneaded with barley flour, water, and oil, but with cabbage it kills swine. ### ***On wolf-killing poison.***

Monkshood <note>original: "Aconitum"</note> kills wolves and many other wild beasts; it is named "wolf-killer" <note>original: "lycoctonos"</note> or "wolf-bane" <note>original: "luparia"</note> from its effect. The <term>Agyrtae: wandering practitioners of magic or folk medicine in antiquity</term> prepare the poison in this way: two ounces of wolfsbane, one ounce of yew leaves, an ounce and a half each of beech bark, glass, quicklime, and yellow arsenic, three ounces of sweet almonds, and as much honey as is sufficient. Let little balls be made the size of a hazelnut, which are to be smeared with lard. Others mix wolfsbane, yellow arsenic, and yew leaves in equal parts. There are also other wolf-killing herbs which we omit, so as not to be too long-winded. Near the Nile, Aelian relates, a herb grows which is called "wolf-killer"; if a wolf treads upon it, it dies of convulsions. For this reason, the Egyptians prohibit such a herb from being imported into their lands, because this animal [the wolf] fears it. There are also

### ***Mouse-killing herbs***

Monkshood, which they called "mouse-killer" <note>original: "myoctonon"</note>, kills mice even from a distance, according to Dioscorides and Nicander. <term>Stavesacre: a species of larkspur, Delphinium staphisagria, used historically to kill vermin</term> possesses almost the same powers; a powder made from its root or seed, fried in butter with flour, kills mice when they eat it. They are driven away by the root of asphodel; if their burrows are blocked with it, they die. An infusion of wild cucumber and <term>colocynth: the "bitter apple," a powerful and toxic purgative plant</term> kills mice; spurge <note>original: "tithymalum"</note> cut into thin pieces and mixed with flour and <term>oenomel: a mixture of wine and honey</term>, if the mice taste it, they will be blinded. So also the chameleon plant <note>original: "chamaeleon"</note>...

->*Vultures*<-

Certain animals are killed by those things which smell sweetest to us: vultures are killed by perfumes, and beetles <note>original: "canthari"</note> by roses. The same happens if one either anoints them or offers them food smeared with ointment, according to Aristotle’s book of wonders.

->*Poison for Scorpions*<-

An eagle is killed by comfrey <note>original: "symphyto"</note>, an ibis by the bile of a hyena, a starling by the seed of wild garlic, a plover <note>original: "charadrius"</note> by sulfur, and a hedgehog by pondweed <note>original: "potamogitone"</note>. ### On other hunting experiments. CAP. XI.

NOW we shall add some experiments that seemed to remain, so that you may use them according to your needs and wishes. First:
->*How to change a dog’s color.*<-

Since white dogs are often less suitable for hunting because they can be seen from further away, a method has been devised by which their color can be changed. This will happen if we boil quicklime <note>calcium oxide</note> with litharge <note>original: "lithargyro," a lead-based mineral</note> and paint the dog; for it will turn black. We have taught other methods for this when we described the way of dyeing hair. If you wish:
->*That a dog does not run away from you.*<-

Democritus <note>The ancient Greek "laughing philosopher," often cited in early science for his lore</note> says a dog will not run away from you if you smear it with butter from its head all the way to its tail, and give it some butter to lick. A dog would also follow you if you tie another dog’s afterbirth <note>original: "secundam"</note> in a small cloth and offer it to the dog to sniff. Also, if you desire:
->*That a dog does not bark.*<-

Hold the membrane from a dog’s afterbirth, or a hare’s fur...
