### *So that a dog cannot run.*

If you smear the wings <note>original: "alas," which usually means wings, but in an anatomical context for a dog could refer to the armpits or flanks</note> with oil, it will be hindered in its course; it happens in this way.

### *So that a hawk may be courageous.*

You shall encourage the bird against the prey, so that it attacks large birds; moisten the bait, which it uses during the hunting time, with wine; or if it is a goshawk <note>original: "astur"</note>, give it a little vinegar. When you want it to fly, give it three morsels of meat soaked in wine, or pour wine into a pigeon chick's beak, then make it fly. Thus,

### *You will make partridges more combative,*

If you give them sprigs of maidenhair fern <note>original: "adianti ramulos"</note> in their food, according to Pliny, and

### *Roosters become more combative,*

By giving them garlic in their food just before they are to fight; from which, most wittily in Old Comedy <note>Likely referring to the playwright Aristophanes</note>, they are called *garlic-fed* <note>original Greek: ἐσκοροδισμένοι (*eskorodisménoi*)</note>, that is, seasoned with garlic, a term for one who is vehement and too inclined toward battle.

### *Lest a bird fly high,*

Pluck the tail feathers that direct the course upward; thus it will fly below in a circle. If you wish

### *That a bird cannot fly,*

Cut the upper and lower nerves of the wing, and it remains without further harm <note>original: "sine noxa," implying the bird survives but is grounded</note>; the bird will not fly, and in this manner they do not escape from aviaries.

# BOOK SIXTEEN OF THE NATURAL MAGIC OF GIOVANNI BATTISTA DELLA PORTA OF NAPLES,

->In which secret and imperceptible marks are discussed.<-

### PREFACE.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'F' set within a square frame featuring botanical motifs.</image-desc>
**FOR** secret marks, which the common people call ciphers <note>original: "ziferas," a term derived from the Arabic *sifr* (zero), which by Porta's time had come to mean secret codes or writing</note>, we have established a twofold method. One consists of visible marks, which is a study worthy of a treatise in its own right. The other consists of hidden marks <note>Porta refers here to steganography—hiding a message within something else—and invisible inks</note>, which we have set out to comment upon in this present volume. In doing so, we are looking after the affairs of Nobles and Princes, who must attend to matters in their absence and write to those skilled in such inventions. We shall place a few examples before your eyes; however, these methods and the results derived from them must be kept guarded within a faithful heart, lest they become cheapened by falling into the hands of the ignorant and the common man. These are the matters we have decided to publish.

### Chapter 1: How writing immersed in various liquids may be read.

There are many, and almost infinite, ways of writing where the necessary descriptions remain hidden—the marks being inconspicuous and never becoming visible unless they are submerged in water, exposed to fire, or touched and rubbed with powders. We shall begin with those which are read by being immersed in liquids. If you desire that:

->*Hidden letters may be seen, and visible letters may be hidden*<-

then dissolve vitriol <note>original: "vitriolum," likely green vitriol or iron sulfate, a common ingredient in historical inks</note> in boiling water; filter the solution through a brush or cloth for a long time until the water becomes clear. With this liquid, draw letters upon the paper, which will be concealed as they dry. Furthermore, grind burnt straw <note>original: "paleam," used here to create a carbon-based black ink</note> with vinegar, and write a broad message with this "smoke ink" in the spaces between the first lines of writing. Afterward, let oak galls <note>original: "galla," growths on oak trees rich in tannins that react with iron to turn black</note> be boiled in white wine; soak a sponge in that liquid, and when it is necessary, by gently wiping over the paper and moistening the letters, the black color natural to us will be obliterated and disappear, while the former invisible letters will, upon being rubbed, become visible to us. Now we shall add those ways by which:

->*Letters become visible by immersing the paper in liquids.*<-

As we have said, let chalcanthum <note>original: "chalcanthum," another term for vitriol or copperas</note> be dissolved in water. Soon after, finely grind oak galls and submerge them in water, letting them soak for a full natural day. Filter the liquid through a linen cloth or a brush so the water becomes clear, and with this, write upon the paper whatever you wish to keep hidden. Send it to the recipient, and when you wish the letters to become visible, immerse them in the first liquid <note>the vitriol solution</note>, and immediately the letters will become visible. To ensure:

->*Marks appear by immersing a linen cloth in water.*<-

Let alum <note>original: "alumen," a mineral salt used as a mordant</note> be dissolved in water, and with this, write letters upon white linen—such as undergarments, a handkerchief, and similar items—for when they have dried, they vanish completely. When you wish them to become visible, submerge them in water, and you will see the linen darken—

->*Letters become milky-white by means of water.*<-

First, litharge <note>original: "Lithargyrum," a lead oxide used in pigments and chemistry</note> is ground and placed into an earthenware vessel containing water mixed with vinegar; it is boiled down, and the decoction is passed through a strainer and saved. Then, write letters with the juice of a lemon, or any citrus variety, and as they dry, they are hidden. If you wish:

->*A stone submerged in vinegar to reveal letters.*<-

You shall write letters upon a stone with goat fat; once dried, they are entirely invisible. If the stone is submerged in vinegar, the letters come forth immediately and will stand out as if they were raised from the surface. However, if you require the letters to turn black upon the application of water—so that you may prepare for your journeys more diligently and efficiently—grind oak galls <note>original: "Gallas," growths on oak trees high in tannins</note> and chalcanthum very finely, then sprinkle the powder onto paper, rub it with a cloth, and polish it well. So that it matches the color of the paper and clings more stubbornly, grind up juniper gum (which is called *vernigo* <note>original: "vernigo," likely sandarac or juniper resin used in varnishes</note> by scribes) and add it to the rest. When the need arises, write with water or saliva, and the marks will turn black. Similar tricks exist which would be far too long to recount.

### Chapter II. How letters become visible by fire.

We shall now describe the ways in which letters do not become visible except by fire, or only when light is placed behind them, or when they have been burned. To render:

->*Letters visible by fire,*<-

We can proceed in this way: draw out the letters in the gaps between lines of verse, or in the joins and spaces between syllables. Let the letter contain something trivial, so that they might think the words are placed without order; thus, if the letter is intercepted, it may only be read with the greatest difficulty. If you write with the juice of a citron, a "Median apple" <note>original: "medici mali," likely referring to the citron or a similar citrus fruit</note>, an onion, or almost any sharp juice, and it is warmed by fire, their sharpness—

...[testi]mony is immediately revealed. For there are unripe juices which, when revealed by the heat of fire, show those colors which they were destined to show when mature. If you have written with a sour grape that was to become black, or with a service-berry <note>original: "sorbo," the fruit of the Sorbus tree</note>; when you bring it to the fire, they are cooked and will give that color which they would have borne on the tree when mature in their own time. Cherry juice, if applied with a reed, will mark letters in a green color; if with cyclamen <note>a flowering plant whose tubers were used in medicine and chemistry</note>, in a reddish color; thus various juices of fruits will also reveal various colors by fire. By this method, young girls in love, by receiving and sending back love-tablets, often frustrate the watchfulness of their parents. There is also a kind of salt that they call ammoniac <note>original: "ammoniacum," referring to sal ammoniac or ammonium chloride</note>; this, when crushed and mixed with water, produces white letters for the writer, which can hardly be distinguished from the color of the paper; but if they are brought near a fire, they will appear black. There are also

### *Letters which can only be read when the paper is burned.*

For the mixture will be white, and nothing will be seen; but when it is burned, the scorched paper will be black, while the characters will become white. Take very sharp vinegar and egg white, in which you must dissolve and stir mercury <note>original: "hidrargyrum"</note>; write letters upon the paper with that mixture; let the paper be burned by fire, and the letters will remain unburned. Or letters may be produced on paper with gum, or any kind of salt, or with lime; although these cannot appear through heat <note>that is, simple warming</note>, once the paper is burned and blackened, the characters will shine white. But if it pleases you, let there be written

### *Letters which may only be seen with a fire placed behind.*

It shall be done in this manner. Let ceruse <note>original: "Cerussa," or white lead, a common pigment</note>, or another white color, be mixed into liquefied tragacanth <note>original: "tragacanthae," a natural gum used as a binder</note>; from that mixture, a substance of the same color as the paper will be prepared, so that nothing may be discerned or even suspected from it. Then, when placed between the eye and a light—whether of a star or a candle—the places where the letters were written do not allow the rays of the eye to penetrate; thus they are seen as somewhat dark. This happens by the principles of optics: for that part made of dense material, when held against an external light, prevents the rays from reaching our sight further, and creates for us a visible shadow of the outlines.

### *How letters rubbed with powder can be read.*
### CHAPTER III.

Now we shall employ another device, so that letters rubbed with powder may become visible and can be read, though they were previously invisible—a practice we read was also frequently used by the ancients. It is to be done in this manner:

### *So that letters, when rubbed with dust, may be read,*

Just as on paper, so too may hidden marks be inscribed on some visible part of the body and understood when necessary. Let an inscription be made secretly upon the arm, the back, or other limbs using vinegar or urine, and let it dry so that not even a trace appears. To reveal the writing, let it be rubbed with soot or burnt paper <note>original: "combusta papyro," referring to the fine ash or charcoal produced by burning paper</note>; in this way, the letters will shine through. Or

->*Otherwise,*<-

If characters are drawn with fat, tallow, or some other greasy substance, or with gum or fig-milk <note>the white, sticky sap from a fig tree</note>, and are then sprinkled with the dust of charcoal or burnt paper, they will appear. It was perhaps by this craftiness, as Polyænus the Greek relates, that Attalus used an inscription impressed upon a sacrificial victim. To urge his soldiers to act bravely against their Gallic enemies—who were far more numerous—he thought it would matter a great deal if he presented to their minds the confidence of an indubitable victory. He devised a playful matter, yet a useful one, together with a priest who was about to perform a sacrifice. On the day before the battle, he prepares the victory. While Sudinus the priest was performing the sacred rites, praying to the gods and pouring libations, and was dissecting the victim, the King—using crushed gum—traced this inscription, *The King's Victory* <note>original: "Regis victoria"</note>, from right to left. When the internal organs were being pulled out, the King placed his hand underneath into a warmer and more spongy place <note>likely referring to the liver, which was the primary organ used for divination</note> and wiped the inscription onto it. But when the priest turned over the remaining parts and performed his duties, he turned over that specific part because it contained the inscription *The King's Victory*. This matter being made public was received with great joy and applause by the soldiers, so that they showed spirits more eager and ready for the fight. Thus, led by the hope of a victory that seemed certain, and relying on the promised divine power, they fought fiercely...

## How one may write on an egg. CHAPTER IV.

Since eggs are not intercepted when people are shut up in prisons, or during the assemblies for Papal elections <note>original: "Pontificialium suffragiorum comitijs," referring to the Conclave where cardinals are sequestered to elect a new Pope</note>, nor is any fraud suspected in them, we shall show how characters may be inscribed both on the outer shell and upon the egg white itself. An example:

### so that letters may be written on the shell of an egg.

Smear the egg all over with wax, and with an iron stylus, let lines be drawn through it down to the shell, but let them not damage it; for if you wound the shell with the iron, the stylus, or a knife, there is a danger that the trickery will be discovered. Submerge the egg overnight in "parting water" <term>parting water: historically known as *aqua fortis* or nitric acid, used by alchemists to separate gold from silver; here it acts as an acid to etch the shell</term>. In the morning, remove the wax and peel the egg—or rather, place the shell between a light and your eye: for the shell will be made permeable, and the transparent letters will be seen. The same will happen if you paint the egg with lemon juice, for it softens the shell, so that it does not foul the surface, and you may enjoy the result as desired. If, however, you wish

### that the letters appear upon the egg white

They will appear yellow <note>original: "Croceæ," saffron-colored</note>, and more effectively so when the egg has been cooked. Boil the egg until it hardens, smear it with wax, and carve the letters into the wax with a stylus so that the marks are opened up. Let it then be placed in a liquid made from [oak] galls ground with alum <term>oak galls: tannin-rich growths used to make ink; alum: a mineral salt used to fix dyes</term>. Then you shall place it in sharp vinegar, and the marks will become penetrating; when the shell is removed, you will see them upon the white of the egg. Africanus <note>original: "Africanus," likely referring to the medieval translator Constantinus Africanus</note> teaches it thus: grind galls and alum with vinegar until they have the thickness of ink; with this, write whatever you please upon the egg...

->*How it may be written in different places so as to deceive the readers.*<-

### CHAPTER V.

We have described invisible methods of writing; now those methods present themselves which, by carving letters on various things, will deceive the readers and interceptors through hidden simulation, even though the letters are visible. First:

->*How we may write with a thin thread.*<-

But let us see how our ancestors performed this, as Gellius relates in his books of *Attic Nights* <note>Aulus Gellius was a 2nd-century Roman author whose work preserved many ancient curiosities</note>. When the Lacedæmonians <note>The Spartans</note> wrote to their Generals, they devised this type of writing by industry so that intercepted letters would not reveal secret plans to the enemy—although some attribute the invention of this device to Archimedes. Two smooth, somewhat long sticks <term>surculi: small wooden rods or branches</term>, polished by a lathe, were made equal so that the length and width of both were the same. One of these was given to the General setting out for war, and the other was carefully kept at home by the magistrates. Therefore, whenever the necessity of use arose, a page as large as the matter required was wound around the stick so that it formed a rounded volume, and the edges were so well joined that they adhered to the wood like a strap <term>lorum: a thong or strip of leather or parchment</term>, so that no gaps were left between. Then, the letters were inscribed on that strap, thus wrapped around, from the top end across to the bottom. Once written, the long and narrow strap was removed from the stick and given to the General; for they believed that if it [fell] into the hands of the enemy...

if it should by chance fall into the hands of an interceptor, those looking upon the truncated letters, syllables, and words—with their parts widely separated from one another—would not perceive the writing at all. Nor did this hope fail in its result; for as often as it fell into the hands of enemies, they could guess nothing from what was written on the leather strap, but set it aside as if it were written in an orderly but useless fashion. However, the one for whom it was intended, by applying the strap and winding it around in the same manner as it had been before it was inscribed—so that the continuous sequence of the writing followed—would recognize the message. This kind of writing was called a *scytale* <note>original: "σκυτάλη", a tool used by the ancient Spartans for a transposition cipher</note> in Greek. Plutarch is the authority who relates that a letter written in this manner was brought to Lysander at the Hellespont.

But we have discovered a way to write with a thread. Two thin rods are fashioned, of equal size and roundness; we give one to a friend who is going far away, and we keep the other at home. When we wish to write, we wind the thread around the rod so that the coils sit close together, forming a continuous surface where no wood appears. With the thread thus arranged, we shall scribe the letters along the length of the staff, and write whatever is in our heart. If the rods are wider, they will hold more lines. If you first dip the thread in water in which alum <note>original: "alumen", a chemical salt used here as a sizing agent to prevent the ink from bleeding into the fibers of the thread</note> has been dissolved, the ink will not spread, but being restrained, it will hold the characters more clearly. Then, having unwound the thread from the small rod, arrange it into a ball. Or, to make it most hidden, we sew it into the hems of tunics or handkerchiefs and send it to the absent friend. For a curious interceptor will see nothing on the thread except certain scattered dots. The friend, by winding the thread onto his own identical rod and taking care that the dots come from the upper part and fit together properly, will easily perceive his friend's concept. We shall teach

### *How to write on parchment so that the letters*
### *are not seen.*

### *How letters may be hidden within the edges of books.*

When a book has been very well bound and its edges trimmed and dyed with a black color, if we open it and fan the pages so that they are curved and tilted at an angle, we will be able to write upon the edges of the paper and record the thoughts of our mind. ## Chapter VI. In what places letters may be hidden.

We shall now speak of letters and the places they may be hidden so as not to induce suspicion of deceit, and finally, we will discuss the couriers themselves. We will bring forward examples that we have read in the histories of the ancients and what good may be learned from them. First:

### *How letters may be concealed in wood.*

There occurs a sentiment of Theophrastus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle, often called the "father of botany."</note>, in which he advises that by cutting the bark of a green and still-living tree, and hollowing it out only as much as can hold letters, and then binding it up, the tree—with the passage of enough time—remains closed by nature with the letters inside. He mentions that in this way, people can be drawn into wonder by sacred instructions hidden in the wood through human industry. But I have introduced this from Theophrastus more as a curiosity of the matter than as a practical remedy I would advise, since it would require the passage of a very long time for success. However, one can quite rightly and conveniently imitate this in dry wood, such as fir, by using common white glue to seal the cracks. Also:

### *Hiding letters in sweets*

Our ancestors were also accustomed to hiding letters in sweets <note>original: *bellariis*, referring to desserts, dainties, or after-dinner treats.</note>. Flint stones are ground very finely with bronze mortars and sifted through a sieve; then, after being melted in a bronze kettle, add the powder to colophony <note>original: *colophonia*; a translucent resin or rosin used in varnishes and adhesives</note>—specifically, two ounces of colophony for every pound of stone. ## *Which secret messengers we may use. CHAPTER VII.*

The same diligence of our ancestors sought out deception in couriers; indeed, they used both men disguised in the dress of others and animals. For instance:

-> *To feign the appearance of dogs* <-

It was a clever plan of Josephus <note>original: *Iosippus*; referring to the Jewish historian Flavius Josephus during the Siege of Jotapata</note>, by whose command messengers covered in skins would pass by the hands of guards and sentries unnoticed. If they were ever seen, they imitated the likeness of dogs. This was practiced until the guards perceived the trick and surrounded the valley. Nor was this enough for human ingenuity, unless it also considered the routes themselves, so that messengers would not fall into the hands of guards or those lying in wait. ### To use pigeons as messengers,

And we shall provide messages by means of birds; for this kind of duty we can have reeds <note>likely referring to hollow reed tubes attached to the birds, or perhaps a reference to "reed-warblers," though tubes for messages are more consistent with the technology of the time</note>, pigeons, quails, and other birds as intermediaries. Those birds, greedy for light and food, would fly up and perch on the highest parts of the buildings, and Brutus would catch them. In this way, he was made more certain of the state of affairs, for which reason he would call them back by always placing food in those same locations. Regarding this, Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, the Roman natural historian</note> says: *The rampart, the watchful siege, and even nets stretched across the river were of no use to Antony while the messenger went through the sky.*

By that same method, the victory of Taurosthenes at Olympia was announced to his own father in Aegina on one and the same day. However, some assert this was achieved through a clear sighting <note>original: *perspectum effectum*; perhaps referring to a telescope or signal fire</note>, while others say Taurosthenes, when he was setting out, took a pigeon away from its chicks while they were still wet and in their shells; when he had conquered, he sent it back clothed in purple. The bird, hurrying with the greatest haste to its chicks, flew from Pisa <note>The region of Elis near Olympia</note> to Aegina on the same day, a matter of which Aelian <note>Claudius Aelianus, a Roman author and teacher of rhetoric</note> is the author. Nor are there wanting those who have sought this by means of swallows, so that, being taken from their nests and leaving their chicks behind, they might be sent back to their homes. Some even assert that there are pigeons across the sea toward the East which, acting in the duty of messengers through the midst of enemies when the road is blocked, carry their masters' letters under their wings for a very long distance in a short time. It is recorded in the most ancient monuments of history that there was an Egyptian King named Marrhes, who had raised a crow so mild and completely tame that he used it in place of a "wing-bearer" <term>pterophori; a messenger of high-speed news</term> or a runner whenever something needed to be announced. Indeed, as if it were clearly possessed of reason, the bird would fly where it was needed while carrying a letter; it cleverly knew where to direct its flight, where to perch, and where it ought to rest for a time. Human ingenuity has sought such things out quite skillfully to avoid dangers, but by that same cleverness of wit, it is often provoked into being pierced by its own weapons. 

When the Christian army was besieging Ptolemais <note>The city of Acre during the Third Crusade (1189–1191)</note>, and Saladin had dispatched a messenger pigeon to the besieged in this manner—exhorting them to be of firm mind because of his hoped-for arrival—it was intercepted by our men. A contrary message was tied to it and the bird was sent back out. Consequently, having despaired of that help, the besieged expected nothing further and surrendered themselves. Thus, they came to realize that in human affairs there can be no true security, only deception. 

Themistius <note>A 4th-century Greek philosopher and rhetorician</note> says that among animals, pigeons have a powerful memory because their minds are clear and absolute. Because of this, even if all other animals might flee back to their children if separated from them, no other animal can return if it is carried a long distance away, as its memory would fail it. 

We have seen an experiment concerning pigeons. When a servant was returning late from a country villa, he brought young pigeons <note>original: *pipiones*; squabs or nestlings</note> with me to the house, having taken them from their mothers and wrapped them in a cloak. When we arrived home at night, they were shut in the house; but at sunrise, they flew out the windows. Having caught sight of the distant countryside, they took flight and returned to their own place in the blink of an eye. 

For this reason, in the book of Genesis, Noah sent out a dove and it returned, but the raven did not return; for the raven lacks memory. I also remember reading in the records of Plutarch that a dove sent from an ark during the flood of Deucalion <note>The Greek mythological equivalent to the biblical Great Flood</note> provided proof of the subsiding waters and the ceasing of the storm. # ON CIPHERS.

*How messengers may be sent who do not know they are carrying letters, and in whom no letters can be found.*

### CHAPTER VIII.

There was also another inscrutable technique of our ancestors, devised with barbaric cunning, which Herodotus mentions in the person of the author Histiaeus <note>Histiaeus was the tyrant of Miletus in the late 6th century BCE; the story is a classic example of ancient steganography</note>. This man, born of a noble house in the land of Asia during the reign of Darius, was staying in Persia at the King's court. When he wished to secretly send word to Aristagoras <note>Histiaeus's son-in-law and deputy in Miletus</note> that he should revolt from the King, he feared that if he did not send the message with great care, the discovery of the matter would bring the greatest danger upon him. Thus, he devised a trick of this sort:

He took a slave of his who had long suffered from a weakness of the eyes and, under the pretense of wishing to treat him medically, shaved the hair from his head. He then imprinted the shapes of letters upon the slave's scalp with light ink, in which was written exactly what he had intended to announce. He then kept the slave at home with him until the hair grew back. When this had occurred, he sent the man to Aristagoras, ordering him that when he arrived, he should advise Aristagoras to shave his head just as the master had recently done for him. When the slave reached Miletus and came to Aristagoras, mindful of his master's command, he revealed the matter. Aristagoras, believing that the request would not be in vain (as indeed it was not), carried out the instruction and thus perceived the message.

These inventions of the ancients helped in the sending of messengers, but even that method cannot be considered sufficiently safe—writing letters on a head with shaved hair—since they can easily be erased by sweat, to which the head is prone. Even if the skin is punctured with a needle <note>A reference to tattooing the message into the skin rather than just using surface ink</note>, not even this will be enough to avoid suspicion if the one carrying the inscription is intercepted. For in such cases, the most diligent investigation is made; fear and necessity excel even the greatest vigilance, and searchers do not think they have done enough until they have thoroughly examined everything by which the truth might be unearthed. Nowadays, illicit things are sought out through promises of reward, or terror is struck through threats. If these are of little use, the matter is settled with punishments and tortures. And if even this does not work, to ensure no secret letters are being carried in the meantime, not only are boots and sandals usually searched, clothes removed, and seams ripped open, but searchers do not even abstain from examining the bowels <note>This refers to invasive body cavity searches or the use of laxatives to see if a message was swallowed</note>—so far are they from leaving the head untouched by their investigation.

But we can send letters and write in such a way that they cannot be understood by anyone except those for whom the letters are intended; even if the carrier is captured on the road and questioned through torture, he can confess nothing because he is entirely unaware of the contents, and the letter will always remain hidden. Neither time nor the labor of the journey will erase the characters, nor does it matter if the carrier crosses the sea or rivers, or if the writing is exposed to rain or his own sweat. We leave it to Princes to consider how much this matters, since they especially have need of it when they wish to announce something to besieged friends, for the victory of a city or an army often depends upon a single messenger. 

However, the invention of the ancients was partly good and partly bad: they imprinted letters on the head which the messenger himself could not read, and which could not be washed away by water or sweat because they were imprinted on the scalp and were invisible due to the growth of hair. To ensure the messenger did not know what was written on his head, they took the opportunity of his suffering from an eye ailment to apply a "remedy" that would supposedly bring him health, so they would not make him an accomplice to the trick <note>A reference to the story of Histiaeus, who used a slave's medical condition as a ruse to shave his head and tattoo a message of revolt.</note>. But this trick does not seem entirely secure; for someone suspicious of a ruse could shave the hair and uncover the fraud. Furthermore, if a messenger had to be sent quickly, how could one wait for a month while the hair grew back? And when the letters were imprinted by punctures, how could he not become aware of the fraud through the pain? But let us see how Histiaeus could have done this:

### *To make indelible letters on the head.*

By wounding the skin with the point of a needle, or by opening the skin with a razor and injecting the powder of burnt colophony <note>original: *colophonia*; a type of pine resin used here as a tattoo pigment</note>. Indeed, this is how we are accustomed to imprint indelible letters on the faces of slaves for their masters, which appear green over time. There are also:

### *Subcutaneous and indelible letters on any limb.*

You can accomplish this quickly in this manner: Let Spanish flies <term>Cantharides; beetles used historically as a blistering agent</term> soak for the duration of a natural day in strong water <note>original: *aqua valida*; likely nitric acid or *aqua fortis*, which was used by metal-workers to separate gold and silver</note>, or even faster in "gold-separating water." Then, with a quill or a suitable stylus, you shall trace the characters upon the surface of the skin of the arm or another limb. ## How a seal and writing may be falsified.

### CHAPTER XI.

**In** the sieges of cities, in armies, and in the business of Great Men, it can be of the greatest use to be able to open letters signed by a General’s hand and secured with his own seal, to know what they contain, to unseal them, to write others of a contrary meaning, and the like; we shall teach how we might

->*Counterfeit a seal.*<-

Let sulfur be melted, and into the liquid throw powdered white lead <term>ceruse</term>. Place this mixture over the seal, but protect the edges with either paper, wax, or chalk, and press it down; when it has cooled, remove it, and in it you shall have the impression of the seal. We can also provide the same in another way. Let an earthen pot be filled with vinegar; throw vitriol <term>iron or copper sulfate</term> into it, and a larger portion of verdigris <term>copper rust</term>, and let it boil into bubbles. Submerge iron plates within; after a little time has passed, take them out, and with a knife scrape from the surface a certain residue that it collects, which is like mud, and save it in a small dish placed beneath. Submerge them again in the pot, take another, and scrape it in the same way, and so on until you have some quantity of this thick sediment. Into this, throw quicksilver <term>mercury</term>, and make an amalgam <term>malagma</term>. While this is soft and tender, press it upon the seal and leave it in the open air; for it hardens to such an extent that you will very easily be able to print letters with the seal, as it turns out almost like metal. We can also achieve the same in another way. Take steel filings <term>chalybis scobs</term>, and place them in an earthen vessel over a harsh fire; add those things which accelerate melting, and when liquefied, pour it into a hollow place. Grind it with a bronze pestle, which will be easily done, and do this three or four times; soon after, turn it to powder and mix quicksilver <term>mercury</term> with it. Let it boil in a glass-glazed pot for a quarter of the day <note>A "quarter of the day" usually refers to a three-hour period, based on the traditional division of the twelve hours of daylight.</note>, until it is perfectly mixed; finally, press the seal into it, and let it cool, and it will become extremely hard. It will also be possible

->*To shrink a large seal.*<-

If it should ever happen that we need a smaller seal,

### To open and close letters without suspicion,

Press it with a small weight until it dries; the fraud cannot be detected because the glue is white and cannot be distinguished from the color of the paper.

## How you may speak from a distance. CHAPTER XII.

There are many ways by which we may speak even at a very great distance with absent friends, or those shut up in prisons, or safely in cities without any suspicion, as we shall describe: now two are declared, either by the voice reflected in the open air, or through a tube. We are able

### To signal certain things to confederates by voice carried into the open.

It is truly a marvelous thing to say that, just like light, so also the voice is reflected at an equal angle; we shall say how that can be done with a mirror, but the way in which we can speak through straight or circular walls is almost common knowledge. The voice, sent forth from the mouth, travels through the air; if around a uniform wall,

[Sound] proceeds uncorrupted if it is free; if it is blocked by the obstacle of a wall, it is reflected and heard, as appears in an echo. We, through a circular building of sufficient length and smoothness, uttered words near the wall to a friend listening from a distance, which reached the friend's ears uncorrupted, while those who stood in the middle perceived not even the movement of the lips; and we, in turn, heard what our friend said. In the morning, while I was walking along the edges of the shore, I heard what friends in a small boat were saying more than a mile away; the sea was calm and almost motionless, and the words traveled clearly across the flat surface. I hear that in Mantua <note>Likely a reference to the Palazzo Te or the Ducal Palace, famous for its "whispering galleries" where the architecture funnels sound.</note> and other places, a hall has been built such that one who speaks in a particular corner is heard by an accomplice <term>rei conscio; one privy to the secret</term> standing in another corner, while those standing in the middle perceive nothing. ### To communicate all things to friends through a tube

we shall be able to do so. Let there be a tube of clay, but lead is better, or made of some material very well sealed so that the voice is not weakened <term>exinaniatur; literally 'emptied out' or dissipated</term> by the length. For whatever you speak at one end, the voice reaches the other person's ears uncorrupted and whole, just as it came from the mouth of the speaker. I do not doubt that this can be done over several miles. The voice, not split or scattered, is carried whole through a very long interval. We have tested this over two hundred paces when no other convenience was available, and the words were heard as open and clear as they were uttered by the speaker’s mouth. From this, I took it into my mind to intercept words uttered on their journey within lead tubes, and thus keep them enclosed as long as I pleased, so that when the opening was unstopped, the words would leap out. <note>Della Porta is speculating on a way to "record" or "trap" sound, a common fantasy in early modern science before the invention of the phonograph.</note> For we see that the sound of iron <note>original: "ferri sonitus"</note> takes time [to travel], and those sounds carried through a tube can be enclosed in the middle; and if an extremely long tube should remove the convenience of the device, one could enclose many channels in a small space through winding ducts. We read that a clay head was fashioned by Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a friar and philosopher rumored to have built a "brazen head" capable of speech.</note> which spoke in his time, and I would hope to achieve the same thing by this artifice, though we have not made a trial of these things, except for what we have said. We have heard, however, from friends, that lovers have long spoken together in secret through a lead tube reaching between their far-distant houses.

### *That signals can be sent by fire at night, and indeed by dust during the day.*
### CHAPTER XIII.

It remains for me to show a method by which we can signal our affairs by fire at night and by dust <note>original: "puluere"; likely referring to the smoke or clouds raised to be visible at a distance</note> during the day. This can be accomplished in two ways: either we show something unexpectedly to informed friends by fire, or, as often as we wish, we show a torch according to a system of numbers, representing the letters necessary to denote things, so that those watching from afar may perceive and note down the movements and the counts. Regarding the first method, we read that Medea promised the Argonauts that if she killed Pelias, she would announce it from a lookout point with fire by night and smoke by day. Thus, when the matter had succeeded according to her wish, pretending to fulfill a vow to the Moon by making a fire and lighting lamps in the open air <term>sub dio; literally "under the god," meaning outdoors or under the sky</term>, she gave the signal from the rooftop as she had promised. Upon receiving such a message, the Argonauts invaded the Palace, and having killed the guards, she achieved her desire. We also read that Magas <note>original: "Magam"; likely Magas of Cyrene, a 3rd-century BCE ruler</note>, having occupied Paretonium, arranged with scouts that they should raise a friendly torch toward evening and again at dawn; by this method, a signal was made so that the news traveled as far as where Clius is. The return of friends living outside the city, or the state of the grain supply, can also be announced by the display of fire. It is well known from this art that Hannibal, as recorded by Polybius, when the people of Agrigentum were besieged by the Romans, indicated the intolerable hunger of the army with many frequent fires throughout the night; for that reason, many of his allies, suffering from the lack of provisions, defected to the enemy. The Greeks also made a pact with Sinon that at night, when the Trojans were relaxed in sleep, he would give a signal as they approached Troy, so that the horse, with its barriers loosened, might release the soldiers enclosed within. Whence Maro <note>The Roman poet Virgil, whose full name was Publius Vergilius Maro</note> wrote:

> ...When the royal ship
> Had raised the flames, and Sinon, protected by the 
> Unfair fates of the Gods, secretly loosens the 
> Pine barriers and the Greeks enclosed in the belly.
> <note>These lines are from Virgil’s Aeneid, Book II, describing the fall of Troy.</note>

# BOOK XVI OF NATURAL MAGIC

...so that the torches can be seen from afar, they will provide a great convenience. Let the letters of the alphabet be divided into two or three groups, so that there are eleven or seven letters in each part. If they are divided into groups of seven, the first group is signaled with one torch, the second with two, and the third with three. The alphabet can also be divided into four parts, but in displaying them, we must pay close attention to the variety of movement. For instance, a single torch raised or shown once will demonstrate the letter A; the same shown twice signifies B, and thrice C—continuing in this way seven times until the letter G, which is the last of the first order. Afterward, two torches shown once will indicate H, the same twice I, and thrice L <note>In this period, I and J were often considered the same letter, and the letter K was frequently omitted to fit a 21 or 22-letter alphabet into even groups</note>, and so on for the rest of that order. Then the letter Q will be signaled by three torches shown once, R by the same twice, and finally S by the same thrice; the same logic applies to a division of four parts.

In this manner, a woman from a watchtower <note>original: "specula", a high lookout point used for military observation</note>—by showing three lights five times, then two lights twice, and three lights twice; then again, one light once, then the same four times, then three lights five times, then three times, and finally four times—will signal: *the man is here* <note>original: "vir adest"</note>.

Differently colored lights can also be displayed if friends are close by. We can also use smoke to signal the arrival of enemies or any other news. This is how it happened that, through the trickery of Hamilcar <note>Hamilcar Barca (c. 275–228 BC), a Carthaginian general and father of Hannibal</note>, the people of Agrigentum <note>A major Greek city in Sicily, modern-day Agrigento</note> suffered a great slaughter. While they were drawn far from their city in pursuit of their enemies, the foe hid in ambush and set the forest on fire. When the Agrigentines saw the smoke, which they believed was rising from their own city walls, they thought they were being recalled by those at home. As they turned back toward the city, they were slaughtered by the following Carthaginians <note>original: "Pœnis", the Roman term for the Carthaginians</note> under Hamilcar's command, who had previously been the ones in retreat.

### PREFACE

Now that we have arrived at the mathematical sciences, the occasion requires that experiments in catoptrics <note>original: "Catoptrica"</note> be handed down; for they shine among the subjects of geometry for their cleverness, their marvelous nature, and their usefulness. For what could be thought of more cleverly than that the most certain experiments should follow the imaginary concepts of the mind? And that the true reliability of mathematical demonstrations might also be proven by visual experiments? What can appear more wonderful than that, by the reciprocal strikes of reflections, images might be seen hanging outside in the air, even when neither the object nor the mirror itself is being looked at? So that they appear not as reflections from mirrors, but as ghosts and illusions? Burning mirrors <term>Ustoria specula: Mirrors designed to focus sunlight to a point to ignite objects</term> do not merely cause rays to coincide, but at a very great distance, they hurl not just visions, but terrifying fires and lightning bolts:

BOOK XVII OF NATURAL MAGIC.

*Most useful in military expeditions, not to mention other matters. One reads that Archimedes frustrated the Roman forces at Syracuse with burning mirrors, and that King Ptolemy built a tower at Pharos <note>The Great Lighthouse of Alexandria.</note> in which he had placed a mirror, so that he might see enemy ships invading and plundering his regions from a distance of six hundred miles <note>A Roman mile was approximately 1,480 meters; Porta is recounting a legendary, likely exaggerated, claim from antiquity.</note>. We shall also add spectacles <term>specilla: Early lenses or eyeglasses</term>, by which the short-sighted <note>original: "lusciosi"</note> may see everything perfectly even at the most remote distance. And if venerable antiquity seems to have devised many great things, we shall hand down even greater, more magnificent, and more illustrious things, which will be of no small use to those aspiring to the science of optics, so that loftier minds may propagate them infinitely. Finally, we shall demonstrate how to fashion and polish crystalline and metallic mirrors.*

## Various appearances of a flat mirror. CHAPTER I.

We shall begin with plane mirrors, for they are simpler and require less laborious investigation, even if their appearances are generally common; they will be useful for what follows, and we shall mix in secret matters. The variety of appearing images will result from either the material or the form of the mirror. For the crystal <note>Here referring to high-quality glass.</note> must be clear, transparent, and exactly flattened on both sides; for if either or both are lacking, they will represent various and deformed ghosts to the sight. We shall therefore begin with the material, and we shall teach:

### *How pale, yellow, and variously colored ghosts might appear to the viewer.*

Glass boiling in the furnace is tainted by even the smallest portion of color. If you cast in a yellow dye, the image of the viewer will appear jaundiced <term>icterica: Suffering from jaundice, a condition that turns the skin and eyes yellow</term>; if black, the image will appear lurid with a deformed paleness to be despised; if you add a bit more, it will look like an Ethiopian <note>A historical term used here to describe a very dark complexion.</note>; if red, like a drunkard or someone inflamed with rage; and finally, of whatever color

...rendered images: we have recounted how colors are to be mixed in gems <note>Porta refers here to his earlier work on artificial gemstones and colored glass.</note>. Very often with mirrors of this kind, we have mocked the most distinguished women, when the image they inspected did not correspond to their true form. But many variations arise from the shape itself, namely:

*So that the face of the viewer appears divided through the middle.*

Let that surface of the mirror which is presented to the eyes be flat and exactly leveled; let the other side, at its back, unfold a recessed angle in its middle, so that the part in the middle is higher, while the ends are sharp and lowered. Then, let the foil <term>bracteola: A thin leaf of metal, usually silver, tin, or an alloy, applied to the back of glass to create a reflective surface.</term> be applied. Thus, the image proceeding to the sight will appear split in two where the lines meet at the angle. If you wish:

*So that the face of the viewer takes the form of a donkey, a dog, or a pig.* <note>original: "asinina, canina, vel suilla"</note>

From the variation of the location of the angle and the shape, the viewed image will appear different. If that part of the mirror placed opposite the mouth protrudes backward into a bulge or a blunt boss, the mouth will seem to stretch outward like a donkey's or a pig's snout. If it swells opposite the eyes, the eyes will seem to be cast outward so that they look like those of shrimp <note>original: "squillarum"; likely referring to the bulging, stalked eyes of crustaceans.</note>. If the angle is stretched along the length of the mirror, the forehead, nose, and chin will appear sharp, like a dog's gape. Finally:

*So that the whole face may be seen as varied and deformed.*

If you wish, let the flat mirror deviate from its flatness and straightness. To achieve this, once the mirror has been flattened, let it return to the furnace and be turned by the skilled hand of the craftsmen so that it loses its straightness; then let the foil be applied. Then, the image from the concave part of the mirror reflects that opposite concave part, and so it will present the proceeding image as twisted, swelling both inward and outward. Finally, if in the polishing <note>original: "fricatione," literally rubbing or friction.</note> of the mirror, the rubbing is done from only one side, the image will be shown as long and wide in appearance. It is necessary, therefore, that the strokes be made in every direction so that it shows a perfect face from every side. We shall also teach how:

*To construct a mirror of many images,*

# NATURAL MAGIC, BOOK XVII.

*To show multiple images, one after another, and in various colors.*

Let the solid body of the mirror be cast from glass, half a finger's thickness. Let it be ground in such a way that on one side the thickness remains intact, while on the other, the lines of both surfaces meet like the sharp edge of a knife. Prepare another mirror panel in the same way, or several more; let tin foil <term>bractea stannea: A thin sheet of tin applied to the back of glass to create a reflective surface.</term> be applied to the very last one. Arrange them one above the other, so that the thinner part of one is placed over the thicker part of the next. In this way, the face of the viewer will appear doubled, one behind the other, and the deepest one will always be of a darker color. Thus, if you arrange three mirror panels by the same craft, the image will appear tripled; the further the viewer's face is from the mirror, the further the images of the faces will be separated, but by moving closer, they nearly coincide into one. If you place a lit candle before it, many will be seen at once, which occurs from the mutual reciprocation of the sight and the mirrors. Even if professional mirror-polishers <note>original: "explanatores"</note> are not at hand, we can achieve the same effect with common mirrors by arranging one above the other, but let one be separated from the other at alternating ends. Then, let them be enclosed in a small box so the trick is not revealed. Nor shall I omit

*So that letters to be read may be projected onto a far-distant wall.*

We shall perform this with the same flat mirror, and lovers separated by a great distance will be able to speak secretly. On the surface of a flat mirror, let letters be formed somewhat thickly with black ink or wax, so that the brightness of the mirror is intercepted and clouded. Let the mirror be held against the clear light of the sun, in such a way that the reflected rays falling from the mirror are projected onto the opposite wall of a room. There is no doubt that the brightness and the letters will be seen on the wall—the sun-lit part being brighter and the characters less visible <note>The letters appear as shadows within the reflected circle of light.</note>, so that they are seen clearly as messages.

*So that in flat mirrors the head may be seen below and the feet above.*

If anyone should desire to see their feet above and their head below in flat mirrors (although representing this is properly the quality of concave mirrors), we shall nonetheless endeavor to achieve it with flat ones in this way. You shall place two mirrors according to their length so that they cling together and cannot be easily moved to and fro, and let them form a right angle. When they are properly prepared, let them be placed opposite the face according to the joining of their length, so that half the face is seen in one and the rest in the other. Then you shall incline the mirror to the left or right side while looking directly into it, and the head will seem to be twisted; when they bisect the face according to their width, the image will be made such that the head is seen below and the feet placed above. If the mirror is large enough, the whole man will be seen inverted. This, moreover, happens from mutual and multiple reflection, for the image leaps back from one into the other so that it appears overturned. In this way we can also

*To construct a multi-view mirror from flat ones.*

A mirror is constructed which is called a *polythaton* <note>From the Greek, meaning "many-sighted" or "multi-looking."</note>, that is, "of many visions," for by opening and closing it, it demonstrates twenty or more images of a single finger. Thus you shall prepare it: let two bronze or crystal rectangular mirrors be erected upon the same base, and let them be in a *hemiolia* proportion <term>hemiolia proportio: A ratio of 3 to 2, where one side is one-and-a-half times the length of the other.</term> or some other, and they shall be joined together along one of their longitudinal sides so that, like a book, they can be opened and closed properly and the angles varied, such as are commonly made in Venice <note>Venice was the world's leading center for high-quality glass and mirror production during the Renaissance.</note>. For by placing one face before it, you will see many faces in both, and the more tightly you close it and the smaller the angle, the more images there will be; but by opening it, they will be diminished, and you will see fewer in number as the angle becomes more obtuse. Thus, by showing a finger, you will see nothing but fingers; furthermore, the right parts are seen as right and the left as left, which is contrary to the nature of common mirrors. This happens through mutual reflection and striking back <note>original: "pulsatione"</note>, from which arises the repetition of images. We can also

*To compose a mirror from flat ones, in which one image is seen approaching and another receding.*

### NATURAL MAGIC, BOOK XVII.

You should take two flat mirrors whose length is double or one-and-a-half times their width <note>original: "sesquialtera," a ratio of 3:2</note>, and this is for the sake of convenience; for their exact proportion does not truly matter. They should, however, be of the same length and equal to each other, and joined so they are inclined toward one another upon a rod <note>likely acting as a hinge</note>, and erected perpendicularly upon some flat surface. From there, if the mirrors are moved while fixed upon their mobile side, there is no doubt that you will see an object approach in one and recede in the other; and as much as the object is brought closer in the first, it will be distanced in the second, so that it seems to be arriving in this one and departing in the other at the same time. It also happens

->*that those things happening far away and in other places may be seen with flat mirrors.*<-

In this way, one can certainly observe secretly and without suspicion those things occurring far away and in foreign places, which could not be done otherwise; however, be diligent in the positioning of the mirrors. Let a place be established in the house, or elsewhere, wherever one wishes to watch something, and let a mirror be arranged in the area of a window or a small opening. This mirror should face you and be well-upright if necessary, or fixed to the walls, moving and inclining it in every direction until it reflects the desired place. You will achieve this by moving your eyes and approaching it, and if it should be difficult, you will by no means fail if you use a dioptra <term>dioptra: a classical sighting instrument used by astronomers and surveyors for measuring positions and angles</term> or another instrument. Let it be erected perpendicularly upon a line, cutting the angle of both reflection and the lines of incidence <note>The author is describing the law of reflection, where the angle of the incoming light (incidence) equals the angle of the reflected light</note>, and you will behold the things happening in that place clearly. This will also work for various different locations.

From this it follows that if one mirror is less convenient, you will be able to watch the same thing with several mirrors, even if the thing to be seen is lost to sight due to excessive distance, or if it is cut off by intervening walls and mountains. You will arrange a mirror above, from the region of the other, upon a straight line that divides a right angle; if done otherwise, it will not happen at all, and you will see the desired place. For as one mirror sends the image back into another, the image is struck out through ten or many mirrors and flies out to the eye. Thus you will see those things which first struck the mirrors, provided the image is carried through straight lines and the sight is not hindered by the winding of places or walls; the construction of this is easy. In this way, we have often been accustomed to transferring "simulacra" <note>original: "simulachra," meaning images, likenesses, or spectral forms</note>. But if, on the other hand, some sloping...

### On the theatrical mirror. Chapter III.

A mirror constructed from flat panes, which, if a single visible object is shown to it, will display many images of that thing, was discovered by wise antiquity. This is understood from certain writings of <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the Greco-Egyptian polymath whose work on optics influenced medieval and Renaissance science.</note> that are in circulation. Finally, we shall add what our own age has invented, which is far more wonderful and pleasant. Therefore, to construct the ancient

->Mirror composed of flat panes, in which multiple images<-
->of one thing appear.<-

This shall be the method. On a flat board, or in the place where you seek to erect such a thing, let a <term>hemicylus</term> <note>A semicircle.</note> be laid out. Divide this equally by points according to the number of images you desire. Draw chords <note>Straight lines connecting two points on a curve.</note> between these points, and let the segments be cut away. Then, erect flat <term>parallelogramma</term> <note>Rectangular mirror panes.</note> of the same width and height. Let them be firmly glued and fitted so they cannot be pulled apart, joined according to their length, and standing upright upon the flat surface. Finally, let the eye of the spectator be placed at the center of the circle, so that it has a uniform view of everything. You will see individual faces for each panel, arranged in a circle, just as is often seen in dances <note>original: "choreis," referring to group circle dances.</note> or the theater; for this reason, it is called by them a "theatrical" mirror. For all the perpendicular lines proceeding from the center onto their surface are reflected back onto themselves; thus they reflect the images to the eye, each one bringing forth its own. These are the theaters of the ancients—

<header>IV. ON CATOPTRICS <note>original: "DE CATOPTRICIS" — the study of reflected light</note>.</header>
<sig>Oo 2</sig>

This mirror's composition is simple <note>original: "puerilis," literally "childish" or elementary</note>, but we shall demonstrate one far more delightful and marvelous. In the previous design, images were shown only according to the number of mirrors, but in ours, through the repeated back-and-forth reflections between the object and the mirror, many more—almost infinite—images will be seen. This is the method:

### **How to construct an amphitheatrical mirror.**

Let a circle of the desired size be drawn upon a board. We shall divide this circle into unequal parts. In the place where the object or face is to be positioned, let us leave two sections empty. Along the lines marking the segments, let mirrors be erected perpendicularly. The face presented to the central mirror will reflect back to the viewer; from there, it bounces to another mirror, and from that to the next. Through these many reflections, the faces counted will be almost infinite; the more mirrors used, the more images will be seen. If you place a light before it, you will see infinite lights. However, if the mirrors you erect are of the types already described <note>Della Porta refers to the distorting mirrors mentioned in previous chapters that warp the human form</note>, then from so many various and multiple faces—resembling donkeys, pigs, horses, and dogs—and appearing yellow, dark, or reddish, a far more wonderful and pleasant spectacle will be presented to the viewers. For from the multiple reflections and the various shapes and colors of the mirrors, a delightful medley will arise.

But now we shall construct something far more marvelous and beautiful; for in this device, the face of the observer will not be seen, but rather a wondrous and orderly arrangement of columns, <term>pedestals</term> <note>original: "stylobatum" — the top step of a stepped temple platform upon which columns are placed</note>, and architecture, most pleasant to behold. Therefore, let a circle be made of the desired size, but we judge that a diameter of two and a half feet is best. Let the circumference be divided into equal parts, for instance, fourteen. The points of division will be the locations for the standing columns, but the observer's place should occupy two parts, and the column there must be removed; thus, there will be thirteen columns. Let the column be directly opposite the viewer's sight. Then, let <term>mirrors</term> <note>original: "specula"</note> be erected upon the lines of the intervals—not exactly straight, but tilted. Two mirrors on either side should be placed in a straight line opposite the region, but others should be placed near the start of their connecting parts. This is done for no other reason than to ensure that the observer’s face, if not positioned perfectly, is not reflected, as we mentioned in the previous section. Thus, the mirrors will represent not the face, but the columns, the spaces between the columns, and the ornaments. Because of the reciprocal bouncing of light from the mirrors, so many columns, pedestals, and ornaments will be seen—preserving a true architectural order—that nothing more delightful or certainly more admirable will ever meet our eyes. Let the <term>perspective</term> <note>The art of representing three-dimensional objects on a two-dimensional surface to give the right impression of their height, width, depth, and position</note> be of the <term>Doric</term> and <term>Corinthian</term> <note>Two of the classical orders of ancient Greek and Roman architecture; Doric is known for its sturdy simplicity, while Corinthian is characterized by ornate capitals decorated with acanthus leaves</note> styles, adorned with gold, silver, pearls, gems, idols, paintings, and similar things, so that it may appear more magnificent. Let HG be the position of the observer, with a column appearing directly opposite. In mirror AB or AC, the face of the observer will not be seen; instead, AB is reflected into IH, and IH into BD. Thus, from these **reciprocal reflections** <note>original: "mutuis reflexionibus"</note>, the images are so multiplied that they seem to recede very far into the distance, with such clarity and transparency that no observer (unless they are aware of the secret) would fail to reach their hand behind to try and touch the rows of columns. 

If you place a candle in the center, it will seem to be multiplied by the bouncing images so greatly that you would not see as many stars in the sky; one cannot sufficiently admire the order, symmetry, and perspective. We have also erected this **amphitheater** <note>here referring to the circular, tiered structure of mirrors and columns</note> in various ways and constructed it to show other arrangements: namely, two rows of columns, so that one row is attached to the mirrors, and the other stands alone in the middle, joined to the first by **arches** <note>original: "fornicibus"</note> and various ornaments, so that it appears as a most beautiful architectural perspective. 

In almost the same way, a small box is constructed, covered all around by several flat mirrors; they call this the **treasure** <note>original: "thesaurum" — an optical toy or "cabinet of curiosities" that uses mirrors to multiply a small number of valuables into an infinite hoard</note>. Inside, from the floor, the arches, and the walls, pearls, gems, birds, and coins were hung; and by the reflections of the mirrors, these were so multiplied that the box represented a truly magnificent treasure. ### *Various operations of the concave mirror. CHAPTER IV.*

But the operations of the concave mirror are far more laborious and wonderful than the others, and they will provide us with many more advantages. However, you will achieve nothing perfectly with it unless you first identify the point of inversion <note>original: "punctum inuersionis" — the focal point where the reflected image flips upside down or changes magnification</note>, so that you may more easily:

### *Identify the point of inversion of images in a concave mirror.*

Do this: Hold the mirror up to the Sun, and where you see the rays converge, know that there is the point of inversion. If you find this difficult to see, blow a thick breath <note>creating a mist or fog to catch the light</note> from your mouth, for you will clearly see the meeting point of the reflected rays; alternatively, place a vessel of boiling water beneath it <note>to use the steam for the same purpose</note>. Once the location of inversion is found, if you wish:

### *To see everything larger.*

Place your head below that point, and you will see the huge face of a monstrous Bacchus <note>original: "immanis Bacchi" — the Roman god of wine, often depicted with exaggerated or bloated features; here used to describe the distorted magnification</note>, and it will make a finger look as thick as an arm. In this way, women pluck the hairs from their eyebrows, for they will appear as thick as a finger. Hostius made such concave mirrors, as Seneca relates <note>Hostius Quadra was a Roman citizen infamous for his sexual excesses; Seneca describes him in *Natural Questions* as using mirrors to magnify his debauchery</note>, so that they would render an image larger than life. He was a man of great lust, and he arranged the mirrors in such a way that while he was with a lover, he might see all the movements of his stallion-like partner reflected back, and he would take pleasure in deceiving himself with such massive thickness of the member. Oo 4

### *To light a fire with a concave mirror.*

This mirror seems to possess a quality superior to all others, in that it unites rays so powerfully that it reveals a bright pyramid of rays <note>a focal cone of light</note> when placed opposite the Sun. If one places tinder or any flammable material in the center of this pyramid, it immediately ignites a flame. If left for a little while, the heat melts lead and tin, and turns gold and iron red-hot. I have even heard from others that gold and silver can be melted by it; however, this happens more slowly in winter and more powerfully in summer due to the warmth of the air, and better at noon than in the morning or evening for the same reason. We can also:

### *Make a hanging image appear with a concave mirror.*

This effect is even more miraculous when using a segment of a sphere, for the image will appear further away from the mirror. If you stand beyond the point of inversion, you will see your head upside down. Keep your eyes fixed and unblinking upon that point until it meets your gaze; for where the <term>cathetus</term> <note>a line drawn perpendicular to the mirror's surface from the object</note> intersects the line of reflection, the reflected "species" <note>the visual image or likeness</note> will be seen entirely remote from the mirror. The closer you are to the center, the larger the image becomes, until it seems it could be touched with your hands. If the section of the mirror is large, it is impossible not to be amazed. For if someone approaches the mirror with a drawn sword, they will seem to be attacked by another person and their hand pierced; if you hold out a candle, a lit candle will appear to be hanging in the air. If you wish, however:

### *To make the image emerge further from the center of a concave mirror.*

When you have captured the image of an object at its specific point, if you wish for it to stand further from the center and for the spectrum of the object to be lengthened, then you should gradually move the object to the right or left away from that point along the surface of the mirror. Then the image will emerge further out and reach the sight—specifically at the point where the cathetus touches the line of reflection at the greatest possible distance. This is something noticed by few, yet from this principle, the greatest wonders can be performed. With this known, you will easily be able:

### *To reflect heat, cold, and sound with a concave mirror.*

If someone places a candle in the location where the visible object ought to be placed...

### On the combined operations of concave and plane mirrors.

### C H A P T E R V.

We shall describe the combined operations and uses of both types of mirrors, so that what each could not achieve on its own, they might accomplish through mutual assistance. If we wish

->*To ignite a fire at a distance using a plane and a concave mirror.*<-

It sometimes happens that someone shut in a dungeon requires fire, but the Sun’s rays do not reach there; or perhaps we wish to ignite the powder of a bronze engine <note>original: "ænei tormenti," referring to a cannon or early firearm</note> without a flame, or to set fire to citadels from a distance without danger via tunnels dug and filled with gunpowder <note>original: "pyrio puluere," literally "fire-powder." This describes a common Renaissance siege tactic of mining under walls and using mirrors to ignite the fuse from a safe distance</note>, or even to burn rocks; we can do this with a plane mirror. Just as a plane mirror receives the parallel rays of the Sun, it reflects them in the same way, whereby it will throw equidistant rays a considerable distance. If these are then received by a concave mirror, it unites them so perfectly that they ignite. Therefore, by first making a trial to determine where the concave mirror must be situated so that it ignites the tinder placed within it, one may, at the same hour on the following day, send the rays with a plane mirror to be united by the concave mirror. Thus, without danger or suspicion of these things, we will be able to obtain fire for our use. Nor will the following use be unprofitable:

->*To make the smallest letters appear very large using plane and concave mirrors.*<-

This is for when characters are so tiny that they are barely recognized as being letters at all. For we have seen the Gospel of Saint John—*In the beginning*, etc.—written in a space so small that it would scarcely cover a tiny lentil or a cock’s eye; by this artifice, we shall make it so that the letters appear large and may be read without difficulty. Place a concave mirror against your chest so that its back rests against your breast; directly opposite, within the focal point <term>point of ignition (punctum incensionis): The focal point where a concave mirror converges light rays; here, Porta uses it to describe the optimal distance for magnification</term>, place the writing; behind that, place a plane mirror so that it sits before your eyes. Then the images of the characters will be reflected in the plane mirror—images which are held in the concave mirror, which the concave mirror had already made large—whence you shall read them without difficulty. It will also happen that

->*With plane and concave mirrors, one may see an image hanging in the air from every side,*<-

From this, it is clear to Philosophers and students of optics in what place vision occurs, and the question of "intromission" <note>The historical debate over whether vision happened by light entering the eye (intromission) or rays exiting the eye (extramission)</note>, so long debated by the ancients, is settled; nor could it ever be demonstrated by any other artifice. From here, someone aware of the matter could begin the principles of secret communication of whatever he wished, such as to one shut up far away in prison. ### *How an eclipse of the Sun can be seen.*

I have now decided to set down the method by which an eclipse of the Sun can be clearly noted. During a solar eclipse, close the windows of the chamber and place a piece of paper against the hole; you will see the Sun. Let it bounce from a concave mirror onto the opposite paper, and you may trace the circle of its roundness; thus you shall do at the beginning, the middle, and the end. From this, without damage to your sight, you will note the points of the diameter of the Sun's defect <note>The "defect" refers to the portion of the Sun obscured during the eclipse</note>.

# ON CATOPTRICS <note>original: "DE CATOPTRICIS". Catoptrics is the branch of optics that deals with the phenomena of reflected light and mirror systems.</note>

...by adjusting [the lens], as we said before, but let the light not strike the hole directly, because it hinders the operation; for it is the secondary light <note>The light reflected from the object being viewed, rather than direct sunlight entering the room.</note> that carries the likenesses. We shall not conceal, finally, a matter full of wonder and delight, now that we have entered into this discussion:

### *How a hanging image may be seen in a chamber at night.*

In the dead of night, an image of any likeness will appear hanging in the middle of a chamber, not without terror to those watching. Outside the hole of the chamber, let the image be placed which we seek to represent hanging in the middle of another dark room, and let many torches be lit around it. In the middle of the dark room, however, let a white linen cloth be placed opposite, or some solid object that can receive the introduced image; for to the spectators, since they do not see the cloth in the darkness, the image will seem to hang in the middle of the air, luminous, not without fear and horror—especially if the craftsman is ingenious.

### *How a hanging image may be seen in the air without seeing a mirror or any other visible thing. CHAPTER VIII.*

Before we depart from the sight of this hanging image, let us teach how it can be done so that we see the images of any thing hanging in the air, which will be the most wonderful of all wonderful things: especially without the sight of a mirror or the visible object itself. But first, let us see what the ancients wrote on the same matter. A certain Vitello <note>Witelo (c. 1230–1285), a Polish friar and a key figure in the history of optics; his work was foundational for Renaissance scientists.</note> describes the matter by his own effort in this way: Let a cylindrical segment <term>cylindricum segmentum: a curved section of a cylinder polished into a mirror</term> be fixed upright in the middle of a house upon a table or tripod, so that it stands perpendicular to the floor. Then, let the eye be placed at some hole or small crack a short distance from the mirror, and let it be fixed so that it cannot move back and forth. Then, from the region of the mirror, let the wall be broken and arranged like a window; let it have the form of a pyramid, with the point <note>original: "conus"</note> on the inside and the base on the outside, as is usually done; let a picture or some image be placed there so it can be viewed by the eye, but let it be reflected from the surface of the columnar mirror, so that the picture placed outside, which cannot be seen through the eye-hole, appears to be hanging in the air. This will be looked upon with great wonder. A convex pyramidal mirror also achieves this, if so...

Let all the windows of the house be closed; let a barrier be placed in their cracks so that no entering light penetrates within. In that place where the spectacle is prepared, if the rays of the Sun or Moon should happen to coincide, the entire spectacle will be ruined. Let the reflected ray of the image be adjusted so that it is reflected straight toward the head <note>Meaning the eye-level of the spectator.</note> on the ground.
