## *Composite mirrors, and various appearances of images.* CHAPTER IX.

Now we shall attempt to construct a mirror in which many different types of images will appear; although such a thing may be difficult to build, the diversity and the meeting of images will compensate for the effort. If, therefore,

### *To construct a mirror in which many diversities of images*

you wish to appear, you shall take a circle of either narrow or vast capacity, depending on the mirror you desire. From this, you will cut two portions of an arch: one based on the dimensions of a <term>pentagon<note>A five-sided polygon; Porta uses these geometric shapes to define the specific degree of curvature or "arc" for the mirror's surface.</note></term>, and the other from a <term>hexagon<note>A six-sided polygon.</note></term>, in the manner demonstrated in mathematical studies. Then, let the arc of the pentagon be hollowed out into a certain board or iron plate so that it fits perfectly within its "bosom," appearing as if it were cut from it. The side of the hexagon, however, will be of the opposite arrangement: for its convex measurement should be received by a board so that it projects outward like that arc. 

Then, take a thin plate of wax or lead of suitable thickness, exceeding the hexagon's arc in width and both of them in length. This thin plate is then to be bent so that it sits properly in the hollowed-out wood, ensuring that no gap or tiny crack is left. The protruding convex surface, preserved in its shape, should then be applied inside according to its width, so that the shape of the concavity does not conflict with the convexity, but rather the same thin plate receives both portions without hindrance. 

Once the <term>archetype<note>A master mold or pattern used for casting the final mirror.</note></term> is thus prepared, let the mirror be constructed from a mixture of <term>steel<note>original: "chalybis". At this time, mirrors were often made of "speculum metal" (a mix of copper and tin), but Porta suggests a steel mixture for higher durability and polish.</note></term> or another substance, as we shall teach. Once it is highly polished, it will display many variations of images. First, right things will be seen on the right, and left on the left—whereas the usual property of plane mirrors is that the eye which was right appears here as the left, and the left conversely becomes the right. If, however, you step backward, the <term>image<note>original: "idolum". In early modern optics, this referred to the "phantom" or reflected likeness of an object.</note></term> will appear in its proper proportions and the image will project forward. If you move closer to the convex surface, the image will become distorted, and the more you cling...

### On the properties of the crystalline lens. CHAPTER X.

MANY are the operations of the crystalline lens <note>Della Porta uses "crystalline" to refer to high-quality glass, not the lens of the eye</note>, and we did not think they should be passed over in silence. For they are both concave and convex; the effects of lenses <note>original: "specillorum," a term often used for spectacles or looking-glasses</note> are the same, and they are especially necessary for the uses of human life—yet until now, no one has explained either their effects or the reasons behind them. But we shall deal with these more fully in our work on *Optics*; here, so as not to leave this space empty, we will touch upon a few things. We call "lenses" portions of circles joined together, whether they be concave or convex. We will first teach how

#### *To light a fire with a convex crystalline lens.*
A convex lens ignites a fire most violently, and more quickly and vehemently than a concave mirror; we have given the reasons for this in our *Optics*. For when held opposite the sun, at the point on the opposite side where the rays gather <note>the focal point</note>, it ignites objects, melts lead, and makes metals glowing hot. Furthermore, if we wish

#### *To illuminate a great distance at night with a crystalline lens,*
Let a candle be placed a little behind the point of ignition; in this way, it casts parallel rays very far to the opposite side, so that those passing through the streets, and whatever things may be in rooms far away, are all seen clearly. In the same way, as we said concerning the concave mirror, we can

#### *Read letters in the dead of night with a crystalline lens.*
Let the letter be placed behind the lens opposite the stars, or opposite lights located far away; for at the meeting of the rays, the words on the opposite side are clearly perceived, even in the dead of night and in a closed room. But that which follows brings to you a much more excellent principle of thought, namely:

#### *To see distant things as if they were nearby with a crystalline lens.*

### *How a multiplied thing can be seen.*

Among the games that are passed around, there is no small pleasure in the lens—that glass instrument we apply to the eyes to observe something more conveniently. Indeed, you cannot deceive the eyes in a more effective way than by changing the medium; for once that is changed, everything is changed. Therefore, let a lens be prepared from more solid and thicker glass, so that it may be more easily ground into many faces like a wheel. It should be shaped with many faces and angles, depending on how many times we wish to count the object. However, in their center, the angles should have a focal point <note>original: "metam," literally a goal or boundary mark</note> and correspond to the alignment of the eyes, so that the images are refracted from the various faces to the eyes in such a way that they cannot perceive the truth. 

Once these many surfaces are prepared and placed before the eyes, if we look closely at someone's face, we will see a whole Argus <note>In Greek mythology, Argus Panoptes was a giant with a hundred eyes</note>, or someone entirely made of eyes. If we look at a nose, we see nothing but noses; likewise hands, fingers, and arms, so that you see not a man, but the Briareus <note>A mythological giant with a hundred arms and fifty heads</note> imagined by the Poets. If it happens that you see a coin, you will behold many instead of one, so that it cannot be grasped by the hands, but often mocks the one reaching for it; it would be better to give with such a lens than to receive. If you look at a trireme <note>An ancient galley with three banks of oars</note> from further away, an armed fleet will appear; if at a walking soldier, it will look like an army marching in formation. It happens that a thing seems to be doubled, and you see the double faces of men and twin bodies. From this come various ways of seeing, so that one thing seems like another—all of which are revealed to those who seek and explore.

## How we may see things in a room that are not there.
### CHAPTER 12.

Indeed, we have judged this trick as not at all to be despised: for we will be able to see in some room, if anyone looks in, those things which were never in it, nor will there be a man of such excellent genius or cleverness who would sense he is being deceived. To describe the matter then: Let there be a room <note>original: "cubiculum"</note> into which no other light enters except from the doorway or window through which the observer looks. Let the window be entirely, or a part of it, glass—as we are accustomed to use to keep out the cold—but let one part be polished so that it acts as a mirror on both sides, from which the observer looks in; for the rest of the window performs no function. Opposite this window, let there be paintings, statues, marbles, and similar things; for what things are outside are seen within. Whence those things which are behind the viewer's back, he will think he sees in the middle of the dwelling, receding as far inside from the glass as they recede behind his back, so clearly and truly that he thinks he sees nothing but the truth. But lest the trick be discovered, let the part where the ornament is placed be arranged in such a way that the viewer does not see it—for example, above his head, so that a floor <note>original: "pauimentum," here likely referring to a ceiling or a partition above the viewer's line of sight</note> intervenes above his head. If the worker has operated industriously in this way, it is impossible for the viewer to feel himself deceived.

### On the workings of a crystal ball. CHAPTER 13.

The workings of a crystal ball <note>original: "crystallinae pilae"</note> shall not pass by unmentioned, for there are matters within this study of no small interest. First:

->*Lighting a fire with a crystal ball.*<-

By placing it against the sun, it ignites a fire behind its circumference. Many times, when left upon a bed as the sun begins to shine, it has burned the blankets. For those who wish to burn the positions of enemies at set hours and places, if it is placed over bait or tinder, it ignites a fire without danger and with great certainty. We can also:

->*Using a crystal ball to make a hanging image appear in the air.*<-

It shows a hanging image in the air both in front and behind. Let the object be behind the ball, and let the ball itself be positioned between the object and the eye; the image will appear outside, hanging in the air above the ball, separated from the ball on all sides, clearly and distinctly. If the object is placed between the eye and the ball, the image will be seen behind the ball, as we have described. If the object is highly visible, such as a fire or a candle, the thing will be seen without difficulty and even more clearly; we have explained the reasons for this in our works on optics <note>Porta refers to his earlier technical treatise, *De refractione*</note>. We can also:

->*See many rainbows in a crystal ball.*<-

Let a solid ball be made in a glassmaker’s furnace, about the size of a walnut, and let it be rounded by fire alone in the customary manner of glass-blowers, so that without the help of a polishing wheel, the outer surface is perfectly smooth. Where it is touched by the iron tool, let a small stem <note>original: "pediculus," the mark left by the glassblower's pipe</note> remain. It does not matter if the glass is refined; indeed, impure glass will be better. Let it be held above the eye, with a burning candle placed in front of it; the light refracted by the tiny bubbles <note>original: "vesiculis," referring to small air pockets in the glass</note> will show infinite rainbows and will reflect a completely golden light, so that nothing more pleasant can be seen.

We shall describe those things that have been discovered, and we shall also add our own findings, so that readers may judge how far the inventions of the moderns <note>original: "recentiorum"</note> have surpassed those of our ancestors. Fire is ignited by reflection, by refraction, and by mirrors both simple and composite. We shall begin with simple reflection, and with:

->*Lighting a fire behind itself with a concave mirror.*<-

This has been noticed by few. Know that a concave mirror, from its center point up to the side of a hexagon <note>Renaissance optics often used inscribed polygons—hexagons, pentagons, and squares (tetragons)—to calculate the focal properties and curvature of mirrors</note> inscribed upon the mirror, burns out to a fourth part of its diameter; and from the side of the hexagon to the square <note>tetragonum</note>, it burns outside the mirror from its lower part. Therefore, let that part of the semicircle situated from the pentagon to the square be cut away, like a band of a circle; when polished and placed opposite the Sun, it hurls a fire far from itself, behind it. We add no more here, as we have treated this more extensively in our *Optics* <note>Porta refers to his technical treatise, *De refractione* (1593)</note>. Thus we can also:

->*Light a fire with a columnar concave mirror, and a pyramidal one,*<-

But this happens very slowly, and only with delay and under the summer Sun; it ignites along a whole line, not in a single point, but extended through the ignition point of its circle. The same will occur with a pyramidal concave mirror.

### On the parabolic section, the mirror most combustible of all. CHAPTER 15.

That is called a parabolic section which ignites the matter placed before it in the shortest span of time. It melts lead and tin; though it is reported by friends that it melts gold and other metals, I myself have only rendered them red-hot <note>original: "ignita reddidi"</note>. We read testimonies from Galen and many others that by this invention of Archimedes <note>The famous "death ray" of Archimedes, said to have burned the Roman ships</note>, the Roman fleet was set ablaze when Marcellus was besieging Syracuse, the homeland of Archimedes.

# ON CATOPTRICS.
<note>Catoptrics is the branch of optics dealing with the study of reflected light and mirrors.</note>

Plutarch, in his *Life of Pompilius* <note>Referring to Numa Pompilius, the second king of Rome</note>, says: "The fire that burns in the temple of Lucina <note>Porta likely refers to the Temple of Vesta; Plutarch describes the relighting of the sacred fire using mirrors in his biography of Numa</note> is kindled by this mirror." That is, by vessels constructed from the side of an **isosceles right triangle**; these are concave and face toward a single center from the circumference. Therefore, when they are turned to face the Sun, so that the rays ignited from all sides are forced together and connected at the center, the air itself is thinned and divided; it then quickly ignites the lightest and driest parts of whatever fuel is applied, as the object receives the fiery strike from the ray. In a **spherical concave mirror**, the rays meet at a **fourth part of the diameter** below the center—specifically those rays directed from the surface of the circle within the **side of a hexagon** <note>In Renaissance optics, the "side of a hexagon" refers to a chord equal to the radius of the circle</note>. But in a **parabolic section**, the rays from all parts of its surface meet at a single point.

However, Cardanus <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), a famous Italian polymath</note> teaches how such a mirror ought to be constructed. He claims that if we wish to kindle a fire at a distance of **one thousand paces** <note>Approximately one mile</note>, we should describe a circle whose diameter is two thousand paces. Of this, we shall take a portion so small that the roundness is not hidden—namely, a **sixtieth part**—to which we shall add the diameter for height at one end, and by moving the fixed diameter around, we shall describe a portion of a sphere. When we have polished this, he claims that when exposed to the Sun, it will kindle a very powerful fire at a distance of a thousand paces.

Good gods! What nonsense he commits in these few words. First, he promises a mirror that burns at a thousand paces, which I judge to be impossible even at **thirty feet**, since the mirror would have to be of immense size. For the surface of a cone is so flat that, in order to intercept any curvature, it could scarcely be manufactured at such a magnitude. Furthermore, to describe a circle whose diameter is two thousand paces—what compass, in what plain, and what motors would he use? 

Even if it were true that **Archimedes** burned ships from the wall with a **parabolic mirror**, the distance could hardly have been ten paces. This is evident from the words of the authors themselves, since he lifted ships from that same place and dashed them against the rocks; and the machines were **levers**, the greater part of which would be behind [the wall], and by the logic of the lever, it is certain it could not have been done otherwise. There are other absurdities which we omit, seeking brevity, lest we seem too long-winded; the cause of the error—

### *How to construct a mirror from a parabolic section.*

The method of drawing it shall be as follows. Let the distance at which we wish the mirror to burn be known—for example, let **AB** be ten feet; for if it were larger, it would be constructed with the greatest difficulty. Let the line **AB** be doubled, so that it becomes **ABC**. The whole <term>sagitta</term> <note>Literally "arrow"; in geometry, this refers to the vertical distance from the center of an arc to the center of its base</note> will be **AC**. From point **A**, let a straight line **DAE** be drawn, and let **DA** and **AE** be equal to each other and at right angles with **AC**. Let **DC** and **EC** <note>OCR reads "EN", likely a misreading of "EC" based on the triangle DCE mentioned later</note> be joined to both [endpoints], forming the right angle **DCE** at **C**. Therefore, the triangle **DCE** is right-angled and **isosceles**. If this triangle is rotated around the axis **CD** until it returns to the place from which it began, a **right cone** **EDNG** will be constructed. Its **parabolic section** will be **ABC**, the straight line **DC** will be the axis of the cone, and **CE** will be the radius of the base of the cone. 

Through point **C**, let a line **HI** be drawn parallel to **DE**, of the same length as **CE** and **CD** <note>This defines the width of the base of the parabolic section</note>. Through point **B**, let a line parallel to the aforementioned **ED** be drawn, which shall be **FBG**. Let both **BG** and **BF** be equal to **AC**. Then **FG** will be the <term>latus erectum</term> <note>The "upright side" or parameter, a constant that defines the shape of the parabola</note>, and **HI** will be the base of the parabolic section. If, therefore, a line is drawn through the points **H**, **F**, **A**, **G**, and **I**, it will be a parabolic section, as shown in the following diagram:

If, therefore, we cut the line **BC** into smaller parts, the parabolic line to be described will be that much more precise. 

Let it be divided into four parts, and let the points of division be **H**, **G**, and **F**. Next, let three circles be described which terminate at **A** and the three points **H**, **G**, and **F**: the first **AF**, the second **AG**, and the third **AH**. This will be the desired line of the parabolic section, from which the mirror is to be formed, as we shall explain.

## **How a parabolic section may be described, which burns obliquely and at a very great distance.**

### CHAPTER 16.

We have described the <term>parabolic section</term> <note>A parabola; the specific curve that reflects parallel rays of light to a single focal point</note> which could be constructed with the help of a compass and a ruler, which we can use at a short distance. However, for a greater distance, we must proceed by numbers: such as forty or sixty feet, and not much more, lest the mirror become of an unusual size. The aforementioned mirror burns between itself and the Sun, and if you do not have the Sun positioned as you desire, the operation will be frustrated; it works in this way even from an oblique angle—namely, with the mirror located between the Sun and the <term>combustible</term> <note>The object intended to be set on fire</note>, or from the opposite side. Therefore, you will be able to use it in all positions that suit your purpose, especially since the burning is more vehement at noon.

We thought it necessary to give this warning, lest you be deceived, since those who are often deceived themselves lead others into error. Regarding a parabolic mirror prepared from the vertex <note>The "peak" or highest point of the curve</note>: if the section is taken from the vertex and we wish to burn at a greater distance, the mirror will be so flat that it lacks sufficient curvature and will be of an unusual size. If, however, the section is taken near the base, it will also be very poor, for even at a very small distance it will turn out nearly flat. Therefore, so that we may capture some useful curvature, we shall take the line around the **neck** <note>original: "collum"; referring to the middle portion of the curve between the vertex and the base</note> of the section.

### A parabolic section that burns to infinity.

## CHAPTER XVII.

The Greek historian Zonaras writes in the third volume of his history that Emperor Anastasius resisted Vitalian the Thracian—who had allied himself with the Mysians and Scythians to stir up sedition, plundering the Byzantine countryside and besieging the city with a fleet—through the prefect Matianus. In the naval battle that followed, the enemy fleet was defeated by a machine made by Proclus, a man of most excellent character. At that time, Proclus flourished in both philosophy and mathematics; he not only understood all the works of the most celebrated engineer **Archimedes** but had also invented several new devices himself. It is said that Proclus fashioned **burning mirrors** <note>original: "specula ustoria"</note> out of brass and hung them from the wall directly opposite the enemy ships. When the sun’s rays struck these mirrors, fire erupted from them like a lightning bolt, consuming both the sailors and the ships. This is the same feat that Dion reports Archimedes performed long ago when the Romans were besieging Syracuse.

But I shall hand down a method far more excellent than the others—one never before recorded by any man, ancient or modern, to my knowledge—which surpasses all other inventions. Indeed, I do not believe the human mind could devise anything greater. This mirror does not burn at ten, twenty, a hundred, or a thousand paces, or at any fixed distance, but to infinity. It does not ignite at a single point or "cone" where rays meet, but a **burning line** <note>original: "ustoria linea"</note> proceeds from the center of the mirror of any length you wish, which burns everything in its path. Furthermore, it ignites behind, in front, and on every side. Truly, I consider it a base deed to reveal such power to the ignorant common folk. Nevertheless, let it be brought to light so that the supreme and immense goodness of God may be praised and held in reverence. 

Because in a larger section the ray progresses proportionally, the larger is created from the smaller; let this be achieved by avoiding a parabolic shape and instead using a **cylindrical section** <note>original: "cylindraceæ sectionis"; the author is likely describing a parabolic cylinder mirror, which focuses light into a line rather than a focal point</note>. For this is the middle ground: an axis of both small and large division is established which passes through the middle parallels. This mirror, placed opposite the Sun, reflects the incoming rays to a great distance and perpendicular to the center of the cylindrical section. No logic can be found in this art whereby rays that have converged can be separated again. It therefore receives directly those rays which it transmits obliquely...

A common biblical idiom used by the author to signal that he is revealing a significant trade secret to the initiated.</note>; we have not spoken in a garbled manner, nor could we have been briefer or clearer. But if the small does not correspond in proportion to the large, know that you work in vain: let it be large around the base and small around the vertex, parallel to the first. The mirror should not be made of steel, because it cannot withstand the intensity of the fire and loses its luster in the heat. Let it therefore be made of **glass** <note>original: "vitro"</note>, a finger's-breadth in thickness. Let the tin foil <note>The reflective backing or amalgam used to turn glass into a mirror.</note> be made of purified antimony and lead, as is usually done in Germany; let the mold be made of clay, the glass placed upon it, and melted in a glassmaker's furnace so that it takes the shape. For this is a marvel: that the very thing which causes such a great fire in its operation remains cold, or at least less than lukewarm. If you desire the ignition to occur in front from the section near the base, let a ring be fashioned, in the center point of which the device is adjusted, so that the reflected ray loses nothing in its forward path. We have said this, and we have observed it, so that we might use this artifice for great and wonderful things, and especially for **writing letters upon the disk of the Moon** <note>original: "literas disco Lunae inscribendo". This refers to an early conceptualized "magic lantern" or projection system, imagining the Moon as a celestial screen for messages.</note>. For whatever we have examined with this mirror, as we said regarding the flat surface, we shall be able to send letters a very great distance...

### *To compose a burning mirror from several spherical sections.* CHAPTER XVIII.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating the construction of a burning mirror from multiple spherical sections. Let **GA** be divided into four points, but the more numerous the parts, the more precise the description of the line will be, and numbers should be applied to the divisions. Then, with the fixed leg of the compass placed at **B**, at distance **BC**, or...

...B 4, let a circle be drawn around it, and with the foot of the compass fixed at center B, let another be described always at distance B 3; then a third at B, and a fourth BA, as B 1. Then from point A let a line be drawn, and another from point B, and let them meet at the point where circle L and semicircle I intersect, namely at G; then let a second line be drawn from circle 2, and another from the same center B, and let them meet where the second circle intersects with the second semicircle at H; then from the third circle and from center B, where they meet at I, at the concentric semicircle. Likewise from the fourth, where the fourth begins at K, and let a line be drawn through K, I, H, and G, which will be the section to be described. The same is done on the other side of the fixed circle. 

The reasoning is as follows: The solar ray LI, falling upon point I of the mirror, is reflected toward B, because B 3 and BI are equal, being from the same circle; therefore, angle B 3 I is equal to angle B I 3. But angle B 3 I is equal to angle 3 I L because they are <term>alternate angles</term> <note>original: "subalternus." In geometry, when a line crosses two parallel lines, the alternate interior angles are equal.</note>, for the solar ray LI is parallel to the diameter of the circle; therefore, angles LI 3 and 3 I B are equal, and it is thus reflected to B. The same must be said of rays MH and NG. This mirror is the opposite of a <term>spherical mirror</term> <note>speculum sphaerale: a mirror shaped like a portion of a sphere, which, as the author notes, does not focus rays to a single perfect point, a problem known as spherical aberration.</note>; in those, rays were reflected from various points of the circumference to different parts of the diameter, and all diameters originated from the center. In this mirror, however, the reflected rays converge, though not at a single point, and the various diameters originate from a quarter of the diameter. But of these matters we speak more at length in our *Optics* <note>original: "Perspectiua." During this period, "Perspective" was the standard term for the science of optics.</note>.

Finally, we shall not omit a cone that kindles fire in a circle, whereas up until now these have kindled it in a single point. Let a <term>parabolic section</term> <note>parabolica sectio: a curve formed by the intersection of a cone with a plane parallel to its side; it has the unique property of reflecting parallel light rays to a single focus.</note> be divided by the <term>sagitta</term> <note>original: "sagittam." Literally "arrow," this refers to the vertical distance from the center of a chord to the arc of a curve.</note>, and let the opposite sides meet. That is, let there be a parabolic section CEF, with sagitta DE; let this circumference be cut at E, and let C and F meet together in the manner they stood before, so that it becomes EGFE. Let it be rotated around the axis GH, and a round cone will be produced. Let it be made of steel or metal and polished, and it will kindle fire in the shape of a circle.

->*Fire is more powerfully kindled by refraction,*<-

We have spoken of <term>burning mirrors</term> <note>original: "ustoria specula." These were devices, often parabolic, designed to focus sunlight to a single point to start fires.</note> made by reflection; now we discuss those which kindle fire by <term>refraction</term> <note>The bending of light as it passes from one medium, like air, into another, such as glass or water.</note>. Indeed, they kindle fire more powerfully, and we shall provide the reason for this in our writings on optics. Therefore,

->*To kindle fire with a crystalline cylinder*<-

we shall be able to do so by placing it opposite the sun, though it happens slowly and gradually: for all the rays do not converge in a single point, but along a line. In much the same way

->*To burn with a crystalline pyramid*<-

is our custom; for it also burns along a line. Yet both of these are more powerful than a columnar or pyramidal mirror; in place of this crystal, we may use a cup filled with water. Most powerful of all, however, is a

->*Crystalline sphere or a portion of one,*<-

And if a sphere is lacking, its place will be filled by a round glass vial full of water, placed opposite the sun. If some <term>tinder</term> <note>original: "ignis amicum," literally "a friend of fire," referring to any easily combustible material.</note> is placed behind it where the rays converge near the surface, it kindles fire instantly—not without the wonder of the onlookers, when they see fire being stirred up even from the coldest water. The same is true for portions of a sphere, such as spectacles, <term>lenses</term> <note>original: "lentes." The word "lens" comes from the Latin for "lentil," which shares the same double-convex shape.</note>, and other similar items we have already mentioned.

### *A crystalline parabola kindles fire most vehemently of all*

We shall see that because all rays coincide at a single point, it kindles fire more powerfully than a mirror does. We can also, as we have said regarding the mirror,

### *Kindle fire from a very great distance by refraction,*

And almost to infinity, as is demonstrated by the principles of optics; and all the more so since refractions operate more powerfully than reflections. We shall demonstrate this in more ways than we mentioned previously, not only by logic but through practical experience. Almeon <note>likely referring to the medieval scholar Alhazen (Ibn al-Haytham), a foundational figure in optics whose works were often Latinized.</note> said that it creates parallel lines cut transversely in the same way. We have also said that if perfectly crystalline spheres—as well as spherical and cylindrical portions—are placed opposite a location through <term>convergence</term> <note>original: "coitionem," the meeting of light rays at a focal point.</note>, they cast fire to such a distance that it is difficult to believe, and greater than the imagination can grasp. Behold, we shall provide another even more powerful way of kindling fire. It even emits rays in equal, visible, and parallel paths. Let a uniform section be struck by light, and it will return oblique rays; you will see the fire through a hidden and open ray falling upon a straight surface, and it will arrive powerfully and uniformly in that place where there is the greatest union of rays upon suitable <term>tinder</term> <note>original: "inflammabili," any material capable of catching fire.</note>. For if that flammable thing placed opposite is not dry, it does no good to place a mirror against it, whether a convex cylindrical one or a concave spherical one; indeed, the object will be found quite perforated by the powerful fire, and even if it was not perfectly aligned, it will burn through it, whether the object be large or small. But it matters of what shape the portion truly consists. It achieves the same result whether the object placed opposite is large or small, if it reflects.

## How lenses are made. CHAPTER XXI.

We have seen that lenses <note>original: "specilla"</note>, or crystalline lenses, were extremely necessary for the operations already mentioned, and that without these, wonders cannot be performed. It remains to teach how lenses and mirrors ought to be made, so that everyone may be able to provide them for themselves by their own effort <note>original: "suo marte," a Latin idiom meaning 'by one's own skill' or 'without outside help'.</note>. Glass spheres are fashioned in Germany, whose diameter is a foot long, more or less. The sphere is cut by marking it around with emery stone into many small circles, which are then brought to Venice. Here they are glued to a wooden handle with melted <term>colophony</term> <note>a type of pine resin, also known as rosin, used here as an adhesive.</note>. If we wish to make convex lenses, you must have a concave iron dish <note>original: "clypeum ferreum," literally 'iron shield'</note>, which is a portion of a large sphere—depending on whether one seeks to make the lenses more or less convex—and let the dish be perfectly polished. 

If, however, we seek concave lenses: an iron ball is used, like those fired from the larger bronze <term>artillery</term> <note>original: "vitormentorum," likely a corruption of "tormentorum" (engines of war or cannons).</note>, whose surface is two or three feet wide. White sand, which is brought from Vicenza and commonly called <term>Saldame</term>, is sprinkled over the dish or the ball, and it is rubbed vigorously with the hands using water. This is done until the surface of that glass circle has taken the form of the tool—that is, convex or concave—matching the tool's surface so that it fits against it everywhere. 

When this has been achieved, by heating the handle over a slow fire, the lens is separated from the handle, and it is glued to the same handle with colophony on the other side, applying the same labor so that it receives a convex or concave surface on both sides. Soon it must be rubbed again with <term>Tripoli powder</term> <note>a fine abrasive powder made from weathered limestone or silica, used for fine polishing.</note>, so that it receives the most exact polishing; once it is perfectly polished, you will make it clear in this manner: They fasten a woolen cloth over wood; <term>parting water</term> <note>original: "aqua separationis," usually refers to nitric acid, but used here as a chemical additive for the polishing slurry.</note> and Tripoli powder are sprinkled over it, and it is rubbed most diligently; you will see it achieve perfect transparency. In this way, both large magnifying lenses and spectacles are typically made in Venice.

## How flat, concave, and convex mirrors are backed with foil and finished. CHAPTER XXII.

It remains for me to now relate a few points that must not be overlooked regarding the finishing of convex mirrors, and the application of foil <note>original: "bractea," referring to the metallic leaf or backing used to create a reflective surface.</note> to flat and convex ones, so that we may hand down a complete knowledge of mirrors. First, I shall discuss the finishing of mirrors prepared from crystal and glass, and then the mixtures and polishes of others, so that the skilled craftsman may know how to both recognize and compose them. For although among the many things that reflect the image of an object—such as water, certain gems, and polished metal—nothing reflects likenesses quite as clearly as glass backed with lead <note>original: "plumbum vitro sublitum"; though the author says lead, this usually referred to a tin-mercury amalgam.</note>. Flat mirrors are prepared from crystal and glass; those made of crystal are polished with wheels and require a different kind of labor. But in Venice,

### *How glass mirrors are made,*

We have seen. They draw the liquid glass out with an iron tool, form a hollow column with their breath <note>original: "vento vacuam columnam," describing the blowing of a glass cylinder, a process known as the "muff" technique.</note>, open it from the side with shears, and place the glowing glass upon a flat and perfectly leveled iron plate. They then place it back inside the furnace so that it becomes softer and takes on the exact flatness of the iron plate; they leave it above the furnace to cool gradually. Once cooled in this way,

### *To polish flat mirrors*

they begin by gluing the glass to a flat board with <term>gypsum</term> <note>plaster of Paris, used here as a temporary adhesive to hold the glass during grinding.</note>. Beneath it, let there lie a very highly polished and flat iron plate. They throw on the sand called "arena," and rub it with a weighted stick until it achieves the most perfect flatness. They then separate it from the board and glue it on the other side so that they may polish both faces; soon, as we have said, they bring it to a state of transparency. Now we shall teach

### *To finish flat glass mirrors.*

When the glass or crystal mirrors have been made flat and equalized, the craftsman makes a flat, thin tin foil <note>original: "stanneam bracteam"</note> of the same size, with as much care as possible. For if the crystal or glass were not coated with lead, because of its own translucency and the density of its nature, it would not stop the impressed image but would allow it to slip away; because glass is rare <note>in the sense of "not dense" or "porous to light."</note> and transparent, it would not contain the image due to its own clarity, whence they van-

...one would not recognize the image in it, just as one cannot see an image in the light of the Sun. Next, you shall spread quicksilver <note>original: "vivum argentum," or mercury</note> over this foil <note>original: "bractea," the metallic leaf</note> using a rabbit’s foot, so that the whole surface appears silvery. When you see it adhering to the surface, place a sheet of clean, white paper over it, and then place it upon the mirror—which must first be wiped with a linen cloth and polished, for if you touch it with your hands, the foil will not stick to it. ### *How the foil is applied to a concave mirror.*

Applying foil to a concave mirror is a more laborious task. Therefore, a piece of foil should be prepared to the size of the mirror; you shall place this over a convex surface <note>The author suggests using a matching convex mold to shape the foil for the concave glass</note> and, with the finger of your left hand fixed at the center, you shall stroke and stretch the foil all around with your right hand until it takes the shape of that convex surface and adheres correctly everywhere. Soon, you shall prepare a mold of the mirror from liquid plaster <note>original: "gypso"</note>; by applying the plaster over the convex surface and letting it dry, you will have a "type" or casting mold. Stretch the tin foil over the mold, and it will fit perfectly, because the mold and the foil were formed from the same surface. Sprinkle quicksilver over the foil and ensure it adheres with a rabbit’s foot, as we said (craftsmen say this helps the process). Place paper on top, and by pressing down on the glass mirror, draw the paper out. Once you see it has adhered perfectly, remove your hand and apply a weight, then soon remove it, but with a careful balancing of the hand so that it does not trap air <note>original: "ventum," literally wind or air bubbles</note> and the quicksilver adheres uniformly. It remains:

### *To finish convex mirrors.*

Let a glass sphere be made, but from the purest glass and as free of bubbles as possible—much like the receiving vessels used in distillations. Through the hollow iron tube with which the glass was blown, a liquid mixture should be poured in. This mixture consists of antimony and lead; however, the antimony should be melted and purified <note>original: "defecatum," meaning cleared of dregs or dross</note> two or three times, and you should throw in some rosin <note>original: "colophoniam"</note>. By rotating the mixture inside the glass cavity in this way, pour out any excess, and thus are the convex mirrors of Germany made.

### *How metallic mirrors are made.*

## CHAPTER 23.

BUT there is another way that metallic mirrors are made. If, therefore, a parabolic mirror <note>A mirror curved in the shape of a parabola, which has the unique property of reflecting light to a single focal point</note> is to be prepared, a parabolic line should be marked upon a bronze or wooden board. Whatever lies outside that line should be filed away until it is even, smooth, and highly polished. You shall fix an axis through the middle and fit it to a frame so that it can be rotated easily. Below it, you shall arrange clay mixed with straw and dung <note>original: "paleatum lutum, & stercoratum"; a standard recipe for heat-resistant ceramic molds in the Renaissance</note> so that as the board is rotated, it forms an exact concave shape in the clay; then, see that it is dried. Sprinkle ash over it and apply another layer of clay of a suitable thickness. Let it be dried by the heat of a fire, or the Sun if you prefer. Remove it, for it will separate easily because of the ash. Join the two pieces together, leaving a space between the two molds as thick as you judge the mirror should be. Once dried, bury this mold, leaving the mouth open at the top along with some vents <note>original: "spiramentis"</note> through which air can escape. 

Then you shall prepare the following mixture. Take a new pot that can withstand fire <note>a crucible</note>, coated inside with clay so that it lasts longer. See that it is dried, repeating this twice or thrice. Place it on the fire, and let two pounds of tartar <note>original: "tartari"; potassium bitartrate, used here as a flux to help the metals melt</note> and as many of crystalline arsenic be melted in it. When you see it beginning to smoke, throw in fifty pounds of antique copper <note>original: "æris antiqui"; antique copper or bronze was often preferred for its perceived purity or specific alloy properties</note> that has been worn down by use. Let it be melted six or seven times so that it is purged and the dross removed. Soon you shall add twenty-five pounds of English tin <note>original: "stanni anglici"; English tin was highly prized for its quality in mirror-making</note> and let them melt together. 

Take a little of the mixture out with an iron tool to test it: if it is brittle, add copper; if it is hard, add tin, or let it continue to cook so that some of the tin evaporates. When it reaches the desired temperament <note>The ideal ratio of the alloy</note>, throw in two ounces of borax and leave it until it dissolves into smoke. Then pour it into the mold <note>original: "typum"</note> and let it cool. Once cooled, you shall rub it with pumice; then with emery powder <note>original: "smiri puluere"</note>. When you see the surface is perfectly leveled and polished, rub it with tripoli <note>original: "tripoli"; a fine-grained silica-rich earth used for polishing</note>. Finally, you shall bring out its luster and light using burnt tin <note>original: "stanno usto"; tin oxide, still used today as a high-grade polishing powder</note>. Most people add a third part of tin to the copper so that the mass becomes harder and takes on a greater clarity <note>original: "perspicuitatem"</note>.

### That a heavy object does not descend, nor a light one ascend, within a medium of the same kind. CHAPTER 1.

BEFORE we descend to those things we intend to demonstrate, we have judged it necessary to preface a few matters and set forth some axioms <note>Self-evident principles or starting points for reasoning</note>, without the knowledge of which we can neither prove nor demonstrate anything. We call that "heavy" which descends toward the center <note>the center of the Earth</note>, and we say it is heavier the faster it descends. Conversely, we call "light" that which ascends from the center, and lighter that which ascends more swiftly...

### ON THE EXPERIMENTS OF STATICS <note>The study of bodies at rest and the forces acting upon them, particularly liquids</note>

...ascends. We say that bodies "give way" to one another when they are mixed together by their smallest parts, such as water, wine, and liquids of this kind. Furthermore, we intend to set forth this axiom <note>A self-evident principle</note>: No body is heavy within its own kind—for example, water within the element of water, or air within air. Likewise, a vacuum is so abhorred by Nature that the machine of the world would sooner be dissolved than a vacuum be admitted. From this resistance to a vacuum, the cause of almost all the wonders of the world arises, which we shall perhaps explain in the work dedicated to this subject. Hence, the force of the vacuum ensures that, against the norm of nature, light things descend and heavy things ascend; so necessary is it that in the world nothing exists without a body <note>This refers to the "horror vacui" or "nature abhors a vacuum" theory, which dominated physics before the discovery of atmospheric pressure</note>. Therefore, having prefaced these things, let us descend to some specific examples.

First: **A heavy liquid body, enclosed in a vessel whose mouth is inverted into a liquid—either heavier or of the same kind—I say does not descend.**

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicting a hydrostatic experiment. The illustration serves to show that the liquid in the inverted vessel A B does not flow out into the basin C D.</image-desc>

Let there be an inverted vessel *A B* filled with water, whose lower mouth *B* is submerged in a vessel with a wide and open mouth *C D* filled with water. With the same liquid, or a heavier one, I say the water from vessel *A B* does not descend. For if the water contained in vessel *A B* were to descend, it would have to be heavier than the water contained in the basin *C D*. We have said they are of the same kind, or the latter is heavier; therefore, if it fell, it would be against the first axiom <note>The principle that a substance has no weight when submerged in its own kind</note>. The same would be the case if each vessel were filled with wine, or water; for if the water contained in vessel *A B* descended into the space *C D*, a vacuum would remain in *A*, since there is no place from...

...where air could enter, which would be contrary to the second axiom <note>The principle that nature does not allow a vacuum</note>; therefore, by reason of the vacuum—and because a body is not heavier than its own kind—it does not fall into the basin. If, however, someone were to bore a hole in the bottom of vessel A, allowing a passage for air, there would be no doubt that the water would then descend into the basin. Furthermore, if vessel AB were filled with some light liquid and the basin with a heavier one, they would not be moved from their places. Let vessel AB, therefore, be filled with wine, and its mouth B inverted into a basin full of water; I say that both liquids remain in their place and do not mix with each other. For if the wine were to descend, there would either have to be a vacuum in vessel A, or the heavy liquid would have to ascend from vessel CD, which would be against the nature of gravity and the second axiom—namely, that heavy things would ascend and light things would descend—therefore they are not moved from their places. 

From this comes that which is often practiced by gluttons and drunkards <note>original: *ganeonibus, & bibacibus*—Della Porta often uses colorful terms for those who use "magic" for tavern tricks</note>, who pour wine drop by drop into a cup half-full of water, and do so clearly until the vessel is filled; they cohere together so well that only a single line divides the liquids. And those who seek to make wine cold more quickly submerge a flask full of wine into a vessel full of water with the mouth inverted, and press it down under the water; for when the water touches the surface of the wine and they cannot mix, the water cools the wine quickly. Since it is necessary that the flask be turned over very quickly while being raised to the surface of the water, it may then serve the drink, be refilled, and afterward return to the same place. 

From this corollary, we argue against those who, while drinking, pour water first and then wine; for because wine is lighter and water heavier, they can hardly be mixed. Consequently, they drink the wine pure at the beginning, soon more diluted, and finally water. At the tables of great men, they first offer wine in the cup and soon pour in water, so that the water, mixed with the wine by its own weight, descends and provides a flavor uniform to the taste. Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and student of Aristotle, known for his works on nature and botany</note> commands that wine be poured first, then water.

In a brief moment of time, the vessel is filled with water and the wine vanishes, so that the water does not retain even the slightest taste of wine. For this reason, the mouth of the vessel should be sealed quite skillfully.

## To Separate Water from Wine

Because very often, through the deceits of peasants and vintners, wine is presented to the master of the house mixed with water, we may easily counter their frauds with this invention. Let the lower vessel be filled with wine mixed with water, from which we wish to separate the water. First, however, one must have a vessel that can hold the entire volume of wine that is mixed in the lower vessel. If the quantity is unknown, one should estimate how much there might be, or at least choose a smaller vessel. Then, let the aforementioned vessel be filled with water and inverted over the vessel where the wine is mixed with water. The top part of the inverted vessel should touch the surface of the lower liquid so that no air can enter; for then, the water will immediately descend into the lower vessel, and the lighter part of the mixture <note>the wine</note> will ascend, while the water settles below. If all the wine ascends, or if even a tiny bit of wine remains in the water, you will know exactly how much water was mixed into the pure wine, which can be easily judged by the smell and flavor if you have worked well. Then, take a vessel of greater capacity for that same liquid and place it in the lower vessel until it draws it all out; thus, from the proportion of the ascended wine and water, one can easily know what portion of water was mixed in the wine. For the sake of convenience, let the flask <term>phiala</term> <note>a wide-bottomed glass bottle or vial</note> that contains the water have a round belly and an opening that is not too large, and let the lower vessel containing the wine have a narrow mouth so that the round upper vessel can be joined to it more aptly.

### C H A P T E R IV.

We shall perform the same thing in another way, not by lightness and heaviness <term>buoyancy or specific gravity</term> as we previously described, but by thinness and density. For water is the most subtle of all fluids because it is simple <note>In Renaissance science, "simple" elements like pure water were thought to have smaller or more uniform particles than "mixed" substances</note>; wine, however, since it is colored—and color arises from a mixture of elements—is more corporeal or thick. Therefore, to separate wine from water, we must have a porous material ready from which we may form a vessel, so that wine mixed with water cast into it might drip out. The water slips out through the pores of the material, while that which is mixed and corporeal is kept inside. And although many woods could serve, ivy will be the best because it is porous and open with many small cracks. Hence, if you have a *cyssibium* <note>original: *cyssibium*—from the Greek *kissybion*, a rustic drinking cup traditionally made of ivy wood</note> prepared from it—that is, a vessel turned from ivy wood, specifically green wood—and you pour wine mixed with water into it, the water will drip out in a short time.

I see that all the ancients and more recent writers have held the contrary view, which both reason and experience cry out against. For Cato says: "If you wish to know whether water has been added to wine or not, make a vessel of ivy wood and put the wine you suspect of having water into it. If it contains water, the wine will flow out and the water will remain; for an ivy vessel does not hold wine." <note>Quoting Cato the Elder, *De Agricultura*, 111</note> And Pliny follows him: "The nature of ivy is reported to be wonderful for testing wines. If a vessel is made of ivy wood, the wine flows through, and the water remains, if any was mixed in." <note>Quoting Pliny the Elder, *Natural History*, 16.63</note> From this, both must be noted for a double error: first, for saying this proceeds from a "wonderful power" of ivy, when any porous wood can do it. Furthermore, they say the wine flows out...

Put liquid alum <term>a mineral salt often used as a drying agent or astringent</term> into a jar of wine, then stop the mouth with a sponge soaked in oil, tilt it, and let it flow out; for only the water will flow. For the alum constricts the liquids so they permeate only moderately.

### *To separate a light body mixed with a heavy one in another way.*
## CHAPTER V.

WE CAN also separate the light from the heavy by another device, either wine from water or in some other way. Let a linen wick <note>original: *penicillū*—here functioning as a capillary siphon</note> be made, or one of cotton, and immerse it in the jar which contains the mixed water and wine; let the wick float above the surface of the liquid and ascend upward, then let it hang down outside the vessel. The lighter liquid will ascend through the wick and drip out. But when the lighter liquid ascends, it also draws the heavy one with it. For this reason, as soon as the color is seen to change, remove the vessel: for then the water will flow. For it is clear that since wine is lighter, it will always ascend to the upper part of the vessel and flow out through the wick—even if all the wine-sellers <note>original: *oenopolæ*—wine merchants or tavern keepers</note> say the opposite: namely, that the water flows out through the wick and the wine remains inside.

### *To discover whether water has been mixed into wine*

Place the wine you suspect has water mixed in it into a vessel, and put an apple or a pear in it. If the fruit sinks, the wine will be unmixed; but if it floats on the surface, the wine will be mixed, because water is denser than wine. Democritus <note>Democritus of Abdera, the ancient Greek philosopher</note> set forth the opposite and false view on this, for he says: "It is often necessary for a master to grant wine or must <term>freshly pressed grape juice that has not yet fermented into wine</term> to his stewards and servants. Similarly, it is necessary for a buyer to test whether the wine is pure. Some cast an apple into the vessel, or better yet wild pears; others a locust, others a cicada; and if these float, the wine is pure, but if they sink, it contains water." But if you seek

### *To know whether must has water mixed in it*

The result will be the opposite, for the opposite reason. For pure and sincere wine is thin, but must, when it is fresh, is thick, dreggy, dense, and viscous, because the dregs have not yet settled; but over time it is clarified and thinned. Whence if you put apples or wild pears into must, and the must is very pure, the apples will float on the surface and drift; but if it has water mixed in, the apples seek the bottom and sink inside. For since water is thinner and lighter than must, it causes the apple to sink. This was excellently and quite carefully described by Sotion <note>Sotion of Alexandria, an author of the 1st century BC who wrote on agriculture</note>. He says: "So that we may know if the must has water, cast wild pears—that is, the most unripe ones—into the must, and if it has water, they will sink to the bottom..."

### *To know which part of must diluted with water is better, the upper or the lower*

It is common for peasants, after the wine has been pressed, to throw a certain quantity of water onto the already squeezed grape skins according to a certain measure; in this way, they create a drink to be used by the field laborers <note>This describes the production of *lorca* or *piquette*, a thin, watery wine made for workers by re-pressing grape skins with water</note>. They divide this must: one part is owed to the peasant, the other to the head of the household. A doubt arises: which part is better—the first or the last to flow from the press? But if you remember correctly what we said before, since wine is lighter, it seeks the highest part, while the heavier water always settles at the bottom. Therefore, the first part that comes out is the wine, and the other, which remains and is squeezed from the grape clusters, is watery. When water is thrown onto the grape clusters, seeking the innermost parts of the berries, it draws out the part of the wine clinging to them; having drawn this to itself and mixed with it, because it is lighter, it tends toward the upper parts. Thus, the upper part is better because it contains more wine. But if the tap <term>original: *epistomium*, a stopper or faucet</term> is opened from the lower part, the water will flow out first, followed by the wine as it descends.

### *How we may separate wine from water in other ways*

### CHAPTER VII.

WE CAN also separate wine from water by another principle of lightness: by means of distillation. For in distillation, the lighter substance rises first, then the heavy, provided it is not driven by too great a force of fire. Thus, it is consistent with reason that for a liquid to rise, it must first be thinned into fine vapors and made lighter. Therefore, since wine is thinner than water, if we place it in a distilling vessel in a water bath <term>original: *balneo aquae*, a method of heating a vessel by surrounding it with hot water to ensure gentle, even heat</term>, the lightest vapor of the wine will gradually rise and glide down into the receiving vessel. You will then see "water of life" <term>original: *aqua vitae*, an early term for concentrated alcohol or brandy</term> being collected in the receiver. From the quantity of that, you will be able to judge the proportion of water mixed into the wine. In our own operations, while spirits of wine <term>aqua vitæ; literally "water of life," refers to distilled alcohol or brandy</term> were being distilled in a water bath <term>balneum Mariae; a vessel of water used to heat another container gently</term>, a vessel containing the spirits was accidentally broken and its contents mixed with the bathwater. We put the mixture into a glass vessel and, by applying a gentle heat, the pure, simple spirits first evaporated without any water, and the water remained at the bottom, retaining no scent of the spirits. We could recognize the ascent of the liquid by the "veins" <note>original: *venis*; refers to the visible streaks of condensation, often called "legs" or "tears," inside the glass</note> flowing down from the cap <note>original: *pileo*; the head of the distilling apparatus or alembic</note>. For the sake of enjoyment and subtlety, we will not omit to add—even if by another method:

### *A method for separating water from wine.*

By this device, we shall know how much water has been mixed into a barrel. Let a quantity of wine be taken and put into a glass vial; expose the vial to very cold water so that whatever is in the vial freezes, as we have previously taught. If the wine is pure, it will freeze with greater difficulty and more slowly; if it contains a little more water, it will turn to ice more quickly. When the wine is frozen, let the vial be broken over a basin. The ice will melt little by little; first the wine flows out because it is "warmer" <note>Porta uses "warm" in the Aristotelian sense; in modern terms, the alcohol in the wine lowers the freezing point, so it remains liquid or melts much sooner than the water-ice</note>, and finally the water remains frozen. Separate it from the wine, because it melts more slowly. From this proportion, you can estimate how much water was cast into the barrel.

## *How lightness varies in air and water, and what crafts may be performed through them.* CHAP. VIII.

Now we shall treat of heavy and light things differently than was handed down in the preceding sections—namely, how they behave in air and in water, and what speculation or utility may arise therefrom. First, we shall learn how to identify a metal, whether it be pure or mixed with other metals, such as gold mixed with silver, and in gilded vessels, or even in coins where silver or gold is mixed with bronze <note>original: *ære*; can refer to copper, brass, or bronze</note>. We shall also determine the specific weight of each. This study is useful not only for money changers <term>trapezitis; from the Greek word for the "tables" used by bankers</term> but also for chemists, as they require the testing of metals in the "fixing" of silver or in their other operations. We will endeavor to explain this easily. But let us first see if the ancient writers contemplated anything on this matter and what they handed down. Vitruvius <note>A Roman architect and engineer whose works were rediscovered in the Renaissance</note> relates that Archimedes dealt with this; for when Hiero <note>The King of Syracuse in the 3rd century BCE</note> had vowed a golden crown to the gods in the temple...

...had to be placed, he gave gold to the contractor by weight <term>sacoma; a counterweight or standard measure used to ensure the correct amount of material was used</term>. The contractor presented the finely crafted work to the King, who approved it, as the weight of the crown appeared to match the counterweight. Later, it was reported that a portion of gold had been removed and an equal amount of silver mixed into the work of the crown. Outraged, Hiero asked Archimedes to take this matter under consideration. Then, by chance, Archimedes went to the baths, and there, when he stepped down into the tub, he noticed that as much of his body as was immersed, that same amount of water flowed out of the tub. Thus, having discovered the reasoning behind this fact, he leaped out moved by joy, and running toward home, he shouted "Eureka! Eureka!" <note>original Greek: *heureka*; "I have found it!"</note>. Then he is said to have made two masses of equal weight to that which the crown should have been—one of gold, the other of silver. He then filled a large vessel to the very brim with water and lowered the silver mass into it; as much of its bulk as was submerged in the vessel, that much water flowed out. Thus, having removed the mass, he poured back as much water as had been lost, measuring it by the <term>sextans; a small Roman measurement, literally a "sixth part" of a larger unit</term>, and he found exactly what measure of water responded to that specific weight of silver. Then, he lowered the gold mass into the similarly refilled vessel; having removed it and added the measurement in the same way, he found that not as much water had flowed out, but significantly less—exactly as much less as a mass of gold is smaller in body than a mass of silver of the same weight. Afterward, having refilled the vessel, he lowered the crown itself into that same water and found that more water flowed out for the crown than for the golden mass of the same weight. And so, by the fact that more water had flowed out for the crown than for the mass, he reasoned and detected the mixture of silver within the gold. This was the discovery of the Greek, which deserves praise for its ingenuity, yet it is difficult in practice; for in items of small quantity, the theft cannot be discerned, nor can the reasoning be so clearly obvious to the eye, as it requires the most absolute construction of the vessel. Now a method has been found by which we can test any amount of money—even a small amount—and very quickly, nor do we need many instruments, so that we might say, "Hypereureka! Hypereureka!" <note>original Greek: *hypereureka*; "I have found it even more!" Porta is boasting that his new method exceeds the genius of Archimedes.</note> This is the method:

...of the same metal, but of the purest kind. And when the scales are balanced in the air, you shall place them into a vessel full of water and submerge them under the water, about half a foot deep. Then a certain marvelous thing will happen: for the scales, which were balanced in the air, will change their nature in the water and become unequal. For the impure metal seeks the surface <note>original: "summa petit"; literally "seeks the highest," meaning it is more buoyant</note>, while the pure metal seeks the bottom. The reason for this is that pure gold is heavier in its kind than any impure gold, because pure gold occupies less space <note>i.e., it is more dense and has less volume</note>; therefore, it hangs heavier for the reason stated above. 

Wherefore, if we wish to know how much silver is in that gold, place as much pure gold on the other scale-pan as is sufficient for the scales to be equal under the water; then lift the balanced scales into the air, and the weight that you had added in the water will be the weight of the mixture <term>mistio; the alloy or debased portion of the metal</term>. 

If you wish to know how much gold was used in the gilding <note>original: "deauratione"</note> of any vessel: place the vessel on one scale-pan, and on the other place as much of the purest silver as is needed to balance the scales in the air. Soon, submerge them in the water, and the vessel will descend; place as much gold on the other scale-pan as is needed to reach equal weight under the water. Extract them, and that added weight will be the weight of the gold gilding. You may do the same for silver, bronze, iron, and white or black lead <term>plumbo albo, nigrove; tin or lead, which were often distinguished as "white" and "black" varieties of the same element in antiquity</term>. 

But if you seek to know whether bronze is mixed with silver in coins, or if money has been adulterated by a superfluous addition of bronze, place the coin on one of the scale-pans, and on the other place just as much of the purest silver. When they are balanced in the air, submerge them under the water; let the coin descend <note>The author likely implies the coin is denser if it sinks, though bronze is actually less dense than silver. He may be suggesting the coin is being tested against a standard that proves its weight.</note>. Add as much bronze as is needed for it to be in equilibrium, extract it, and that weight will be the mixture.

*   **Silver** weighs one hundred twenty-five in the air and one hundred thirteen in the water.

### *Whether material statues can be made to speak by some artifice.*

->CHAPTER I.<-

**W**e read that in certain cities there existed a bronze colossus, placed upon a pedestal <term>stilobatum; a continuous base supporting a row of columns or a statue</term> of exceptional height. During the greatest windstorms, when it had caught a great deal of "spirit" <note>original: "spiritum"; referring here to air or wind</note> in its lower parts, this air was carried from its mouth into a trumpet, causing the trumpet or other instruments to sound. We believe this was easily done, as we have seen something similar ourselves. We also read among many men of excellent authority that **Albertus Magnus** <note>a 13th-century philosopher and scientist often associated with legendary mechanical wonders</note> constructed a head that could speak. Although, to confess frankly, I have very little faith in such a man, since everything of his we have tested for ourselves we found to be false, except for a few things he excerpted from other authors. 

Let us see if a statue can be made that speaks. There are those who say Albert achieved such a wonderful thing through astrological timing <note>original: "astrologicis electionibus temporum"; the practice of choosing an auspicious moment based on the stars to perform a task</note>. But, good Gods, how can learned men be persuaded of this, when they have experienced that the stars do not possess such powers? There are others who believe he accomplished it by magical arts. This we believe least of all, since no one has yet been found who professed to know such arts, except for impostors and charlatans <term>agyrtæ; wandering quacks or swindlers who performed "miracles" for money</term>, who deceive ignorant men and simple women. Nor do I think a pious man would have professed such detestable arts; rather, I suspect it can be done by the principles of pneumatics <note>original: "pneumatis ratione"; the study of air pressure and movement</note>. 

We observe that a voice or sound is carried through the air whole, and not instantly, but gradually and over time. We see bronze cannons <note>original: "ænea tormenta"</note> which, by the force of gunpowder <term>pyrij pulueris; literally "fire powder"</term>, roar with a huge boom; and if they are a thousand paces away, we see the flame much sooner than the sound reaches our ears. Likewise, the cracking of handguns <note>original: "manuales sclopi"</note> is carried to us even after some minutes of time over a distance, for such is the nature of sound. Sounds, therefore, travel both with time and as a whole without interruption, unless they collide with something. The proof of this is the echo, for hitting walls while still whole, it bounces back and is reflected, just like rays of light. Furthermore, as we have said in this work, words and voices travel joined together, and when carried through very long pipes, they arrive whole, just as they left the mouth of the speaker. These things being established as true, if someone were to construct very long lead pipes, longitu-

### *Concerning hydraulic organs. CHAPTER II.*

**H**ydraulic organs <term>organa hydraulica; musical instruments that use water to regulate air pressure</term> were held in great value in ancient times, though in our own days their use has fallen out of fashion. We read, however, that **Nero** <note>the Roman Emperor (r. 54–68 AD), known for his artistic pretensions</note> was so delighted by hydraulics that even amidst the dangers to his life and empire, and during the mutinies of his soldiers and leaders, with total ruin imminent, he did not abandon his care and study of them. **Vitruvius** <note>a Roman architect and engineer whose descriptions of ancient technology were famously difficult to interpret during the Renaissance</note> teaches the construction of such an instrument, but so obscurely that what he reports is very poorly understood. We have experimented in many and varied ways, mixing air with water. By placing this mixture at the end of a pipe, or at the mouth where the breath of the opening strikes the air, even if it resonated with a certain pleasant sound, it eventually failed to hold the tone. For while the water swells into bubbles and imitates a nightingale or a tremulous sound, the voice is changed through various tones; one voice is sweet and delightful, but two together make a noise and are discordant. 

In this way, however, it produces a tremulous sound and a soft murmur, and preserves the whole. Let the chest in which the wind is carried be made of bronze and half-full of water. Let the wind be excited by pistons <term>modiolis; the cylindrical pumps used in hydraulic systems</term> or bellows, which should run through a neck <note>original: "cervicem"; a narrow connecting pipe</note> beneath the water. The air, bursting forth from the middle of the water, is shut within the bronze [chest]. Thus, when the stops <term>epistomia; the valves or keys that control the flow of air to the pipes</term> of the pipes are directed by the movement of the keys <note>original: "pinnarum"; literally "wings" or "fins," here referring to the keys of the organ</note>, the tremulous wind entering the pipes creates tremulous and quite pleasant voices, which we ourselves have tested and found to be true.

### Concerning certain pneumatic experiments. CHAPTER III.

**N**ow let us move on to related but varied experiments, also pneumatic <term>pneumatica; the study of mechanical properties of gases, especially air</term>, arising from the nature of air: how it expands and is compressed, how it is thinned by fire and thickened by cold. If you wish that

->An inverted vessel should draw in water,<-

You shall achieve it in this way. Thus seekers of nature <note>original: "naturæ rerum exploratores"</note> say that water is drawn and absorbed by the sun's rays from the hollow places of the earth into the mountains, which is how spring sources are formed. Thus, when brought near a fire, it boils inside, and since it has no other vent, it shoots out a great blast of spirit <note>original: "spiritum"; here referring to pressurized steam or air</note>, though of a damp and vaporous thickness. ### *How we may conveniently make water ascend.*

We can make water rise to the very top of a tower. Let there be a lead pipe <term>canalis plumbeus; lead was the standard material for plumbing in the Renaissance</term>, and let it reach from the bottom all the way to the top of the tower, and from the top let it descend again to the bottom, like a siphon. One part should enter the water we wish to raise; the other part, which should be longer and hang down further, should be glued into a wooden or earthenware cask <note>original: "dolium"</note> so that it does not "breathe" from any part <note>meaning the connection must be airtight</note>. Let there be a hole on top of the cask through which the vessel can be filled with water, and then immediately be most perfectly sealed. Let a cask of smaller capacity be placed at the top of the tower, and let the aforementioned lead pipe be fixed on one side of this cask and exit from the other. It should be in the highest part of the cask, with the pipe divided in the middle inside the cask. Where the pipe enters and where it exits, let the joints be soldered so they do not leak air. Therefore, when we want the water to ascend, let the lower vessel be filled with water and very well sealed so it does not breathe; then, once the lower hole of the cask is opened, the water will flow out. For as much water as exits the cask, just as much will ascend through the other lead pipe over the tower; once the water is drawn out, the upper vessel is filled, and we may enjoy it for our use. By closing that same hole and refilling the lower cask with water again, and repeating the process, we continually force the water to ascend. We can also

Let the upper vessel be heated either by the Sun or by fire; for the air contained in its belly is thinned <term>rarefit; the process of air expanding and becoming less dense when heated</term> and slips out, wherefore we shall see the water swell into bubbles. ## *Description of Water-Clocks <term>Hydrohorologiographia; from the Greek 'hydro' (water), 'horo' (hour), and 'graphia' (writing)</term>, in which pneumatic or aquatic clocks will be described.*

### CHAPTER IV.

In ancient times, they had clocks made from water, and the water-thief <term>clepsydra; an ancient device for measuring time by the regulated flow of liquid through a small opening</term> was their common and famous timepiece. Hero of Alexandria <note>A Greek mathematician and engineer (c. 10–70 AD) famous for his work on steam power and hydraulics</note> indeed wrote books about water clocks, which have since perished; we have established a book concerning these, and so that this part would not seem incomplete, we shall explain two types based on opposite principles: one by blowing air in, and the other by sucking air out. This will be the first:

Inside the bell, a vertical scale is marked with numbers 1 through 10. A tube labeled 'K' enters from the left and curves upward into the bell. Various components and points are labeled with letters A, B, C, D, E, F, G, and K.</image-desc>

### *Vessels are described that throw water by pneumatic principles. Chapter V.*

We shall describe either fountains or various vessels that throw water by the principle of air <note>original: "pneumatis ratione"</note>. Although others were most ingeniously described by Hero <note>Hero of Alexandria, a Greek engineer of the 1st century AD</note>, we shall add some most skillfully devised by ourselves and others. We shall first describe:

### *A fountain that throws water by compressing the air.*

Let there be a vessel or drum <note>original: "tympanum," a cylindrical chamber</note> closed on all sides, **AB**. Let it be pierced in the middle, and let a small pipe **CD** rise from the bottom of the drum **D**, positioned at such a distance from the floor that the water can flow into it. Above the surface of the drum, let there be a tiny opening **C**, closed by a stopper, or let it have, as the Greeks say, a <term>smerismatition</term> <note>a ground-joint valve or precision stopcock used to regulate flow</note>, by which it can be properly closed and opened. In the upper surface of the base, let it be pierced by a small pipe **E**, entering the belly of the drum, and having at its lower mouth a <term>platysmation</term> <note>a flap valve or check valve, literally a "little plate"</note> made of leather or brass, so that it does not allow the air forced in to escape. Therefore, let water be poured in through **E** so that it stands at least three fingers high from the bottom. Soon after, let air be blown in as forcefully as possible; when it is well compressed, let the opening be closed. Then, by opening the mouth **A**, the water will be driven upward until the air pressure is relaxed. When we were in Venice, we constructed a drum with glass pipes; when it shot water a great distance, the Hero of Este <note>Alfonso II d'Este, the Duke of Ferrara, known for his interest in technology</note> marveled that it was driven by no visible force.

### *A device by which a hand-gun may throw a ball a distance without fire.*

Let there be a hand-held engine <note>original: "manuale tormentum," here referring to a pneumatic gun</note> perfectly hollowed out and of remarkable smoothness; this is achieved with a lead cylinder and by rubbing all parts with finely ground emery powder <note>original: "pulueri smire," likely emery or smalt used as an abrasive</note>. Thus, when the lead is placed in the mouth of the engine and compressed inside with a rod using the greatest force and skill, let the hand be removed immediately (you must first plug the small hole at the bottom of the bore). The lead and the rod will descend to the bottom, and by the force of the compressed air, the lead and the rod will be hurled out to a distance, not without causing great wonder.
