### ### That we can use air for many inventions. CHAPTER VI.

We can use air in many inventions; we shall write down a few, so that we may provide an opportunity <note original: "ansam," literally a "handle" or "loop">An opening or starting point for others to build upon</note> for others to discover more, and especially:

->*How wind may be generated in a bedroom, so that guests are cooled*<-

Let river water, or a significant amount of water from some other gushing source, be cast down into a very deep pit. Let the pit indeed be closed on all sides, having nothing but a channel through the walls to carry the air into the bedroom. Let the water be sent down into the pit through a kind of funnel so that air does not escape through the place where it enters; for the air of the pit is expelled by the water <note>This describes a "trompe," a hydraulic air compressor where falling water traps and compresses air</note> and creeps through the channel into the bedroom, so that not only those sleeping in it but even those socializing there grow stiff with cold and become numb. We shall also teach:

->*How air may fulfill the role of bellows*<-

Which we saw in Rome. Let a small chamber be constructed, closed on all sides; let it receive a quantity of water through a funnel at the top. At the top of the wall, let there be a small hole through which air may exit outward with great force. For it is carried with such great momentum that it kindles a fire excellently and easily fulfills the role of <term>bellows</term> <note original: "follium">Traditional leather bags used to blow air into a fire</note> for bronze and iron <term>forges</term> <note original: "fucinas">A smith's hearth or workshop</note>. The funnel should be constructed in such a way that, when necessary, it can be diverted and the water let in.

*WE HAD INTENDED from the beginning of this work to describe all the experiments that might be contained within all the natural sciences, but pressing business weakened our resolve, so that we are less able to achieve what we desire; wherefore, since I cannot do what I want, I must want what I can do <note>Porta is likely referencing a common Latin proverb, "Since we cannot do what we wish, let us wish what we can do."</note>. In this book, therefore, we have enclosed those experiments which could not be confined to any specific categories <note original: "classibus">Literally "classes" or "divisions," referring to the thematic organization of the previous nineteen books.</note>, which were so varied and diverse that they could not constitute a single science or book, and which we have also heaped up here as if they were omissions <term>paralipomena<gloss>A Greek term meaning "things left over" or "omitted," often used as a title for a supplement to a larger work.</gloss></term>—into a chaos, perhaps. God willing, we shall provide a more perfect book at another time. For now, however, you will be content with these.*

-> *How the water of the sea may be made drinkable.* <-

### CHAPTER I.

It would bring no small amount of convenience and benefit to the human race if the water of the sea could be rendered drinkable. In long-distance voyages, such as those to the Indies <note>Porta refers to the transoceanic trade routes to the East and West Indies that were vital to the economy of the 16th century.</note>, it provides the greatest help; for while sailors, forced by storms, remain at sea longer than they had hoped, they face the greatest dangers to their lives due to a lack of water. It is necessary for galleys <note original: "triremes">Ancient-style oared warships, still in use in the Mediterranean during the Renaissance.</note> to seek land for watering almost every ten days; for this reason, they cannot wander for long within hostile regions, nor can they be drawn further away, lest the enemy intercept their route. Furthermore, those settled in maritime cities and on islands suffer greatly when water fails, as in our own times on the island of Malta <note original: "Melites"></note>, and as the soldiers and inhabitants near the Syrtes <note>The Syrtis Major and Minor, two large gulfs on the coast of Libya, known in antiquity for their dangerous shallows and desert environment.</note> have endured, and as many histories also recount. Hence, we have deemed it necessary to investigate more skillfully whether seawater can be made drinkable. 

But it is impossible to investigate how this might be achieved unless we first seek out the cause of saltiness, and what our ancestors have handed down on the matter; especially since Aristotle proclaims that the saltiness can easily be drawn out from the sea, since the sea is not salty by its own nature. Rather, as the Sun heats the water, it raises from it cold and dry terrestrial exhalations <note>Porta is citing Aristotle's *Meteorology*, which argued that saltiness was caused by dry, earthy vapors mixed into the water by the sun's heat.</note> up to its surface, where they are "burnt": this is the cause of its saltiness, as the thin, moist parts are diffused into delicate vapors. We, therefore, by imitating Nature and lifting the thin parts with chemical instruments <note original: "chymisticis organis">Referring to distillation apparatus like the alembic.</note>, can easily render it sweet. 

For in this way, Nature renders the water of the sea sweet for rivers. There are also "veins" of the sea in the lowest parts of the earth heated by the Sun; vapors are raised to the highest peaks of the mountains, where, meeting a cold surface, they gather into drops, and sliding down through the arches of caves, they flow out through open channels. We first fill a concave vessel, like a swollen ball, with seawater; it should have a long neck, to which we fit a cap <term>pileum<gloss>In distillation, the "head" or "cap" of the still (the alembic) that catches the rising steam.</gloss></term>, so that when the coals are placed beneath, the water is dissolved into thin vapors, filling every empty space and being carried upward; these vapid, thick... <note>The text breaks off mid-sentence at the bottom of the page.</note>

# C H A O S. 645

...they leave behind those earthy and dry parts mixed with the soil, and once purified, they slip out as fresh <note>The original uses *dulces*, literally "sweet," which was the standard term for fresh water as opposed to "salt" water.</note> [waters]. He <note>Likely referring to Aristotle, whom Porta often cites on meteorology.</note> asks why salt water cannot flow out as a spring; either because that which is heavy is stable, and salt water is heavy, which is why only warm waters can flow out from salty sources. For they possess a lightness that overcomes the weight of the saltiness, since heat is lighter. Add to this that waters flowing through the earth can be thoroughly filtered; therefore, whatever is heavier and thicker is driven down more and more and settles, while whatever is lighter and purer is separated and flows out. For just as salt is heavy, so fresh water is light, and thus it results that the waters which flow out are fresh. This is the same reason why salt water, when it is moved and changed, becomes fresher, for it is rendered lighter and purer through motion. 

Let us see now if we can imitate nature. We will fill large vessels and arrange them upon steps, so that one filters into another, and thus salt water, slipping through many vessels, will perhaps leave its saltiness behind in the vessel. I have tried this experiment through ten vessels, and the water was still salty. However, a friend said it was fresh after being filtered through twenty. Yet I thought it necessary to warn that not all earths are suited for this purpose. Solinus <note>Gaius Julius Solinus (3rd century AD), a Roman grammarian and compiler of geographical wonders.</note> says that if seawater is filtered through clay <note original: "argilla">A fine-grained natural soil material containing clay minerals.</note>, it becomes fresh, and it is found that salt is removed when it is filtered again and again through the fine sand of a torrent. One must avoid those waters that hide in covered and vaulted places: for they are usually salty, or those where animals are stabled, which Columella <note>Lucius Junius Moderatus Columella (4–70 AD), a prominent Roman writer on agriculture.</note> declares must be avoided for trees, for they turn filtered water salty. Black earths should be avoided: for they have harsher waters; but muddy ones possess waters endowed with freshness, according to Paxamus <note>A Greek writer on farming and kitchen-gardening from the Roman era.</note>. Anaxagoras <note>Anaxagoras (c. 500–428 BC), a pre-Socratic Greek philosopher who sought natural explanations for phenomena.</note> said that the saltiness of the sea comes from rivers, which, by running through salty places, communicate 그 quality to the sea. There are those who approve of river sand for this purpose, and the reasoning that moved them was that fresh waters are always found on the shores; they say this happens because the waters become fresh from the sea by being filtered through the sands. But this is false: for the fresh water found near the sea does not come from the sea, but is water that flows there from the high peaks of the mountains through the hidden passages of the earth.

When I tested this matter, I found it to be false—indeed, it became saltier. The reason is that by heat, the finest vapors of the fresh water are exhaled [evaporated], and the salt settles, and in a smaller [volume]...

### *How fresh waters may be improved.*

### *How one may transform their own face so that they are not recognized even by friends.* CHAPTER III.

For those who have been captured by snares or shut in prisons and are attempting to escape, those who handle the business of the great, spies, and others who do not wish to be known, it is of no small importance—indeed, it will be of great moment—to transform their faces. We shall teach how to do this so precisely that they will not be recognized even by parents or spouses. Secrets of this kind are sought after in no small measure by great men, because by disguising their persons they have carried out immense deeds, and lovers have served their beloveds without the suspicion of parents. Ulysses, attempting to scout the deeds of the Trojans, dressed in false clothes and with a disguised face, accomplished everything he wished while unknown. Homer says:

### To make the face swollen, sunken, and bruised.

Nothing deforms the face so much as the stings of bees. We can induce bruises by applying <term>caustic herbs</term> <note>Plants that irritate or burn the skin, such as crowfoot or spurge-flax</note> and allowing them to remain for a short time. Swellings and depressions are induced by applying the milky sap of the <term>tithymalus</term> <note>original: "tithymali"; the spurge plant, known for its irritating white latex</note> to the mouth, nostrils, and eyes, especially where the skin is broken; by this remedy alone the face is deformed, and likewise the scrotum and testicles. The water of <term>cantharides</term> <note>original: "cantharidum"; "Spanish flies," which were crushed to create a potent blistering agent</note>, when smeared on, immediately induces blisters and swellings. Crushed <term>turpeth</term> <note>original: "Turbith"; a medicinal root used as a purgative, here used topically for its inflammatory effects</note>, boiled and smeared upon the limbs, causes them to swell, particularly the testicles. The powder of the <term>yew tree</term> <note>original: "taxi"</note> so ulcers the skin that it makes men appear miserable and pitiable to the common people. The remedy for this is the juice of the poplar, or <term>poplar ointment</term> <note>original: "vnguentū populneum"; a traditional cooling salve made from poplar buds</note>. Smoking the face with sulfur and burnt straw discolors it, as <term>hypocrites</term> <note>A reference to those who feigned illness or asceticism to gain public sympathy or religious standing</note> do, who disfigure their faces in such a manner. Take one ounce of the dregs of <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>original: "aquæ fortis"; nitric acid</note>, and one drachma each of brine and turmeric; let these be mixed with oil into the form of an ointment and smear it on the face, for they will stain it with a black color. When you wish to wash it off, you may return the face to its former state with cold water. Comic and tragic actors, while performing, smear their faces with <term>amurca</term> <note>original: "amurca"; the bitter, watery dreg of pressed olives</note> so that they may transform their countenances and not be recognized by those who know them. Because the stings of bees, wasps, or hornets change the face wonderfully and render it different—contorting the mouth, nostrils, and limbs, compressing some parts while raising others—if someone washes the skin with a decoction of hornets or wasps, the area swells in such a way that it suggests the suspicion of some sickness, yet it is without pain. The remedy is to drink <term>theriac</term> <note>A famous ancient "universal" antidote made of many ingredients</note> or smear it on the spot; by this fraud, crafty women even simulate the swelling of pregnancy. Grind and mix the dregs of oil, vine-charcoal, and pomegranate peels; if you touch the face with this liniment, you will make it very black, but it is washed away with the juice of sour grapes or with milk.

If a flat piece of porphyry marble, polished on its outer surface, has placed upon it <term>trochites</term> <note>original: "trochites"; fossilized segments of crinoid stems, often wheel-shaped</note> or <term>astroites</term> <note>original: "astroites"; fossilized corals known as 'star-stones' due to their star-like patterns</note>, also polished on their outer surfaces, and then a little vinegar or lemon juice is added, both the trochites and astroites will immediately begin to walk of their own accord toward the lower edge of the surface, with no one pushing them, to the great delight of those watching. <term>Cardano</term> <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), a famous Italian polymath who wrote extensively on the hidden properties of nature</note> said that such stones consist of a thin moisture which is converted into vapor by the power of the vinegar; because it finds no exit, it pushes and moves the stone here and there. He believed the beginning of this thin vapor is what moves them, and therefore one must believe those stones do not have large passages for the vapor to escape. I, however, would judge that air is trapped within the veins of the stone—which is quite plausible where you see substances of different colors. Therefore, because the vinegar is a subtle substance that enters the stone, it expels the air, and as the air exits through the vinegar, it causes the stone to move. But we have found that all stones move of their own accord if they are composed of various minerals mixed together and have various open gaps between their veins. For the vinegar, working its way through the joints, pushes the stone so that it moves. <term>Alabaster</term>, which is commonly called *quince-like* <note>original: "cotogninum"; referring to its yellow, mottled appearance resembling a quince fruit</note>, moves excellently, for it is distinguished by various veins and a variety of stone types. I myself have seen a piece weighing not just one pound, but four pounds, move itself; it had been shaped into the form of a tortoise, and when the stone finally moved, we saw the tortoise appear to walk. That species of marble called *brocatelle* <note>original: "brocadello"; a variegated marble with patterns resembling brocade fabric</note>, which is composed of various mixed parts, also moves of its own accord by the action of vinegar. Even that spotted marble which they call *louse-like* <note>original: "pediculosum"; referring to the small, dark, puncture-like spots on the stone</note>—distinguished by red, saffron, or dark spots and punctures—walks when vinegar is applied, to the wonder of those standing by. The same must be cautioned: it matters not if the lower part of the marble is spotted and the top is uniform and hard, or if the bottom is uniform and hard and the top is varied. For once vinegar or any sharp liquid is cast upon it, it immediately glides toward the lower part, moving now in circles, now 
->leaping,<-
now moving very rapidly.

### How an instrument can be made, by which we may hear from afar.
#### CHAPTER V.

In our works on optics, we have demonstrated lenses <note>original: "specilla"; here referring to magnifying lenses or early telescopes</note> with which we were able to see quite far; now we shall attempt to construct an instrument by which we might also hear through many miles, and we will investigate the type of wood that may perform this more correctly and easily. To discover the form of this instrument, it is necessary that we consider the ears of all animals that possess the most perfect hearing. For it is a sacred rule in the precepts of **Natural Magic** that when new things are to be investigated, we believe that Nature must be thoroughly scrutinized and imitated. To consider those animals that have the best hearing, we must look for the timid ones. Nature has provided for their safety so that those who are less powerful in strength might at least excel in hearing, so they may look out for their safety by flight—such as the rabbit, the hare, the deer, the donkey, the ox, and similar creatures. These animals are long-eared and have their ears open toward the front, and they direct the openings toward where the sounds originate.

According to <term>Pollux</term> <note>Julius Pollux, a 2nd-century Greek grammarian whose "Onomasticon" served as a dictionary of Greek terms</note>, the hare has "high ears" <note>original Greek: "ὦτα ὑψηλὰ" (ota hypsela)</note> or lofty ears; <term>Festus</term> <note>Sextus Pompeius Festus, a Roman grammarian</note> calls it "eared" <note>original: "auritum"</note> because of the size of its ears and its faculty of hearing. Among the Greeks, the name <term>lagos</term> <note>original: "λαγώς"; hare</note> comes from the size of the ears: for the prefix *la-* increases the meaning in composition, and *os* means ear. And indeed, it was fitting that a timid and defenseless animal should be well-eared, so that it might perceive dangers and snares from further away and look out for itself in time.

The Egyptians believed so strongly in this sharp hearing that, when they intended to designate "hearing" in their <term>hieroglyphics</term> <note>Della Porta refers to the Renaissance understanding of Egyptian symbols as mystical allegories</note>, they would paint a hare. The rabbit has the same nature and the same ears. A cow has large and shaggy ears; according to <term>Aelian</term> <note>Claudius Aelianus, a 3rd-century Roman author who wrote "On the Nature of Animals"</note>, she can hear a bull from thirty <term>stadia</term> <note>a Greek unit of distance; thirty stadia is roughly 3.5 miles or 5.5 kilometers</note> away when he is burning most vehemently with the urge to mate, perceiving his lowing as if he were giving a lover's signal <note>original: "tesseram"</note>.

A deer's ears are even larger and longer, as is appropriate for a timid animal. If it holds its ears upright, it senses most sharply, and no snares can be hidden from it; if it lets them drop, it is easily killed, as we know from <term>Aristotle</term>, and from <term>Pliny</term> who followed him. When they have erected their ears, they have the sharpest hearing; when they have relaxed them, they are fearful. And lest we wander through all the other animals that have broad, upright, and open ears, we say (those that have ears of this kind, and when from a distance...

[Those who] wish to hear, raise [their ears] and direct them toward that direction, [indicating they] possess the most perfect hearing. We shall now see, from the opposite cause, that those who have small and hidden ears possess a duller sense of hearing. A large portion of fish lack ears, and those who possess only the internal passages without earflaps <note>original: "auriculis"; referring to the external pinna of the ear</note> must necessarily have a duller sense of hearing; for earflaps were constructed by nature so that sounds might be poured into the ears through them, as if through a funnel. Of this matter, Hadrian <note>original: "Adrianus"; likely referring to the Emperor Hadrian, known for his intellectual curiosities, or a Roman official of that name</note>, the Roman Consul, is a most abundant witness; when he had impaired hearing, he would hold his cupped hands over his ears, facing from the back to the front, so that he might hear more easily. And Aristotle said that horses, donkeys, dogs, and other animals that have large ears always rotate and turn them to perceive sounds and voices, having been taught the use of those parts by Nature. We also find by experience that those whose earflaps have been cut off hear less. 

Therefore, the shape of the hearing instrument ought to be wide, concave, open, and spiraled like a snail shell <note>original: "cochleata"</note> inside, for a twofold reason. First, if sounds were carried straight inside, they would damage the sense; second, because they are carried around through the spiral, and the voice, having struck against the windings of the ears, is multiplied, just as we see happen with an echo. Proof of this matter can be found in the marine snail shell, which, when moved to the ears, produces a certain light noise. It remains for us to say from what material it should be made. I would suggest it be made from porous woods <note>original: "foraminulentis lignis"</note>, for those holes and pores are permeable and filled with air, and they resonate even with a light strike; among porous woods is ivy, and especially <term>smilax</term> <note>a climbing plant, often identified as bindweed or sarsaparilla</note>, the proof being that a vessel turned from ivy wood on a lathe drips water through it, as we have previously stated. For this reason, Pliny, speaking of *smilax*, says: "It is a property of the material that, when moved to the ears, it gives back a light sound." And elsewhere: "We have said that the wood of the *smilax* sounds at the ear." Therefore, let the instrument be adapted so that it may be conveniently placed in the ears, just as spectacles <note>original: "specilla"</note> are placed before the eyes.

## Regarding the lyre, and certain wonderful properties of it.
### C H A P T E R VII.

The lyre retains several properties and observations within itself, which we have deemed worthwhile to bring to light. First, we will speak of certain wonderful effects that are passed down by the ancients; then, in what manner they can be performed, or how they were practiced by the ancients. Since Music now is more refined and noble than it was among the ancients (for then it was ruder and more imperfect), yet in our times it does not achieve these operations. It is certain that rhythms and melodies have power over men, nor is a heart so savage and fierce that it cannot be softened by suitable melodies and songs that soothe the mind; on the contrary, it is distressed and constricted by unseemly and dissonant ones. Musaeus <note>A legendary semi-mythical Greek poet and musician, said to be a disciple of Orpheus.</note> proclaims that song is the sweetest thing to mortals, and it is noted by the Platonists that everything that lives is soothed by Music, and many effects are observed. Drums roar in war to serve as encouragements and to rouse the sluggish, and similar things are found practiced by the ancients. Timotheus the Musician <note>Timotheus of Miletus, a famous Greek musician and poet known for his innovations in the lyre.</note>, as often as he wished, would play a Phrygian melody <note>original: "Phrygium modum"; one of the ancient Greek musical modes, traditionally associated with passion, religious frenzy, and warlike excitement.</note>, and so inflamed the mind of Alexander <note>Alexander the Great.</note> that he would rush fiercely to arms; and when he wished otherwise, by changing the melody and draining away the spiritedness, he would make the mind idle, and having softened it from arms, he would draw him to feasts and banquets. And Plutarch says that when he himself had heard Antigenidas <note>A celebrated Theban flute-player of the 4th century BCE.</note> playing the melodies upon the pipe which are called chariot-songs <note>original: "harmatij"; high-energy melodies intended to mimic or accompany the rushing of a chariot.</note>, he was so inflamed that, rising up together with his weapons, he laid hands on those sitting nearest to him. Cicero reports that Pythagoras [encountered] a certain Taurominitan youth <note>A young man from Tauromenium, modern Taormina in Sicily.</note>, soaked in wine and ensnared by harlot’s love; when he sought to burn down the house with torches because he had been incited by the pipe in the Phrygian mode...

### *A Lyre which, when struck, makes another of the same tone move even though it is untouched.*

Let strings be stretched together so that each reaches the same and perfect melody. If you pluck one of the low strings with your fingers, the other low string echoes and moves; the same happens with the high strings, provided they are at the proper distance. If this is not clearly visible to you, place a piece of straw <note>original: "paleam"</note> upon it, and you will see it move. Suetonius Tranquillus <note>A famous Roman historian, author of *The Twelve Caesars*.</note>, in his book *On History of Games* <note>original: "libro ludicrę historię"</note>, says that on a winter's day, some strings on a lute are plucked by fingers, while others sound on their own. From this, someone ignorant of sound would be able to tune a lyre: if one string is already stretched and brought into harmony, he can leave it at rest and stretch or relax the other string while plucking it until the resting string moves—a sign they are of the same tone. The same applies to the rest. But if you wish

->*That a deaf person might hear the sound of a Lyre*<-

cover your ears tightly with your hands so you do not hear the sound; then, grip the neck <note>original: "capulum," literally the handle or neck of the instrument.</note> of the lyre or cithara firmly with your teeth. Let another person pluck it, and it will produce a harmonious sound within the brain, perhaps even a sweeter one. And one need not only catch the neck with the teeth; even a very long spear that touches the lyre will allow the sound to be heard clearly through it. It could be said that the sound is not perceived by the sense of hearing, but by taste <note>The author is describing "bone conduction," where vibrations travel through the teeth and skull to the inner ear, though he poetically attributes it to the sense of taste due to the involvement of the mouth.</note>. This remaining observation, which I think is by no means unpleasant, is that

->*Lyres, citharas, or other instruments may be played by the wind.*<-

You shall accomplish it thus: When there is a vast storm of wind, set up your instruments—such as citharas, flutes, sambucas <note>An ancient triangular stringed instrument, often associated with a high-pitched sound.</note>, or pipes—facing the oncoming wind. For the approaching wind rushes with force, strikes lightly, and runs through the open reeds; from the sound of them all, a most sweet harmony will be perceived by nearby ears, and you shall be delighted.

->How they pretend to be able to find treasures.<-

The greater part of these charlatans <note>original: "agyrtarum," a term for wandering street-performers or quacks who sold charms or performed tricks.</note>, although they are utterly poor and wretched, profess to be able to find treasures and promise to others what they themselves do not possess. They use four forked rods <note>original: "virgulis bifurcatis," the classic dowsing rod.</note>, the tips of which are held together in a cross, while they hold the lower ends with open hands near their hips. They pretend to murmur certain charms, and the rods fall; and where they fall, they command those desiring treasure to dig. The cause of this is that even if the rods seem to be held firmly in the hands, they are not fixed anywhere and are always on the verge of tumbling; if they are moved even a slightly from their place, they immediately fall to the ground. There is a pulse in the arteries of the arms and hands which, although thought to be immobile, nevertheless moves the hands inconspicuously and affects them with a tremor. 

But there are some among miners who say these forked rods are of the greatest use to them in finding veins of ore. They cut a branch <note>original: "columnam," here meaning a straight shoot.</note> with a knife and consider it more suitable than others for seeking veins, especially if a hazel tree <note>original: "corylus"</note> is found growing above some metallic vein. There are others who use different trees according to the variety of metals: indeed, they use rods made from hazel for silver veins, ash for copper, wild pine for lead—especially "white lead" <note>This likely refers to tin, often called "plumbum candidum" in early modern texts.</note>—and rods of iron or bronze for gold. Then, gripping the horns of the rod on both sides with their hands, they make fists; it is necessary, however, that the compressed fingers face the sky and that the rod is raised at the point where the horns meet. Then they wander here and there through mountainous places, and where they set foot above a vein, the rod immediately turns and rolls, revealing the vein to them; when they step back and move away from it, the rod remains motionless again. Indeed, they say the power of the veins is so great that it sometimes even bends the branches of trees growing near the veins toward itself, as is written more copiously in the works of Agricola <note>Georgius Agricola (1494–1555), a German scholar whose work *De Re Metallica* is the foundational text of mining and metallurgy. <page-num>663</page-num>
<header>CHAOS. <note>original: "Chaos." Here used as a title for a collection of miscellaneous phenomena or "disorderly" wonders.</note></header>

### *Let untouched slips of paper change their position.*

To someone who is completely ignorant of the cause, this cannot happen without appearing miraculous. Let three rather long <term>slips of paper</term> <note>original: "schedulæ"</note> be made, either of paper or linen, and let them exceed each other in size by an equal amount. For if they are all made level at the bottom edge and rolled up equally, when they are unrolled, they are found in different positions. If the longest one is placed in the middle or in the first position, they will swap places; however, if that same longest one is in the last position, they remain unmoved. There is no one who would not think this was done by demons, but it happens for no other reason than this: at the end of the revolution <note>i.e., the rolling process</note>, the longer one remains on the outside, and the edge from which the rolling begins remains on the inside. It seems to me that Aristotle intended to understand this in his *Problems* <note>Referring to the *Problemata*, a collection of scientific queries attributed to Aristotle.</note>: "Why is it that if someone cuts a section of paper by measuring equally from a flat and straight base, it rolls up straight; but if he inclines the cut, it comes out twisted?" Is it because when the circles of one cut are placed in the same plane, that sloping cut is not equally opposite, but partly less so? Therefore, when you unroll it, the circles that are contained in the same plane and have their beginning in the same plane will unfold the line which they create in their own order, and so forth.

It was the error of certain people to believe that this happened by the power of words, and they provided answers to all questions as if from an oracle. For if the papers swapped positions, they believed the omens were properly observed and the outcomes would be favorable; but if not, they were considered unlucky. They were unwilling to exchange their faith for reason and experience, since they had believed this for many years. If you wish—

### *Let a coin roll itself upon a stylus.*

We have often seen impostors use this kind of artifice to deceive simple women <note>original: "mulierculis," literally "little women," used here dismissively to refer to those easily fooled by street performers.</note>, making two slips of paper, or light objects made of other material, rise up from a flat surface and move by themselves. If you search among barley, you will find a small <term>awn</term> <note>original: "aristulam," the hair-like bristle found on grain kernels.</note> of wild oats that is black and twisted, looking like a locust's leg. If you bind this with wax to the point of a knife or a stylus, and scatter droplets by spraying soft water, as soon as it feels the moisture, it will twist itself like a string on a lyre <note>The author is describing "hygroscopy," where certain plant fibers twist or move in response to humidity.</note>, and—

### To discover a theft.

In this way, we can discover a thief and immediately recover the stolen property. There are various superstitions regarding theft which are based on natural reasons, yet scoundrels <note>original: "nebulones"</note> attribute them to the power of words. There is a stone called the <term>eagle-stone</term> <note>original: "ætites." A geode containing loose rattling stones, historically believed to have magical and medical properties.</note>, and it is as if it were pregnant; for when it is shaken, a small stone rattles inside its womb. If someone grinds it up and offers it to a thief—cooked in bread baked under the ashes and seasoned—the thief cannot swallow the chewed mouthful. Indeed, he is forced either to be choked or to be caught as the thief, since he cannot swallow what is cooked with it, as is found in <term>Dioscorides</term> <note>Pedanius Dioscorides, a first-century Greek physician and author of the herbal 'De Materia Medica'.</note>.

The natural cause of this is that the powder ground from the stone is so dry that it makes the bread extremely dry and porous like pumice; it is a substance that can only be swallowed with the greatest effort once it is in the throat. Added to this is the fact that the person seeking to uncover the theft tells those standing by (who are the suspected thieves) that he is doing a wondrous thing, magnifying it greatly. For the throat of the one who actually stole the item becomes parched with fear and terror, and thirst is induced. Thus, he is least able to swallow the powdered bread, for it sticks to his throat—which he could barely have swallowed even if he were not afraid.

There is also another very subtly devised trick: they paste the names of those suspected of being thieves onto small slips of paper, roll them into <term>clay balls</term> <note>original: "argillaceis globulis"</note>, and submerge them in water. As the balls become wet and softened, they open up, and the light paper slips rise to the surface of the water. This thing causes such wonder that those standing by think it was done by nothing but the art of demons. Clay pills are made according to the number of those present, and the names written on the slips are rolled inside the pills. The slips that are less carefully and diligently wrapped in the clay are released by the moisture and are sent forth, held by no bindings. If, however, you wish them never to open, you mix the paper well with the clay, and it does not open.

When I first saw this, I was truly amazed, but when asked, he revealed the matter. There is a certain property of <term>mullein</term> <note>original: "verbasci." A tall, flowering plant often used in traditional medicine; its dried flowers fall easily when the stalk is vibrated.</note> which, when it opens its flowers in the morning, if the plant is shaken slightly, all the drying flowers gradually fall to the ground. There is no one who sees it who would not believe it happens by magical prayers, if the person shaking them off murmurs certain empty words. It also happens

### *that women cast off their clothes and are stripped.*

So that I leave out nothing that is faked by <term>charlatans</term> <note>original: "circulatoribus." Literally "those who move in circles," referring to itinerant performers or medicine-showmen.</note> and necromancers: they set up a lamp engraved with symbols, filled with <term>hare’s fat</term> <note>original: "leporino adipe."</note>. When they light it while murmuring certain words, and it burns in the midst of women, it compels them all to cast off their clothes and willingly show men everything they keep covered. They see this, nor do they stop dancing as long as the lamp burns. This was told to me by trustworthy people. I considered that these effects could only come from the hare’s fat, whose perhaps deadly power, penetrating the brain, excites them to such madness. A similar thing is told about the <term>Massagetae</term> <note>An ancient nomadic people of Central Asia.</note> by <term>Homer</term> <note>The author likely means Herodotus (Histories 1.202), who describes tribes using smoke from certain fruits to become intoxicated and dance; Porta frequently misattributed such classical anecdotes.</note>: that there are trees whose fruit, if thrown into a fire, causes all those nearest the fire to become drunk and foolish; for they immediately leap from their seats and indulge in choruses and dancing. There are also thieves who

### *pierce a chicken’s head with a stylus and dare to say it remains alive,*

and they say it happens by witchcraft. From this, they promise that a man can be made invulnerable; for with certain deceitfully fashioned symbols tied under the wings, they pierce the head of a rooster with a <term>stylus</term> <note>A sharp, pointed tool for writing or marking.</note>. When they have waited for a little while, they pull the stylus out, and the chicken runs away having received no wound, and it remains without blood. When I had considered this and opened the chicken’s head, I found it to be <term>cleft</term> <note>original: "bifidum." Referring to the anatomical structure of the bird's skull which allows a needle to pass between the lobes of the brain without causing fatal damage.</note>, and a knife or stylus passing through those places does not damage the brain—which has very successfully worked for me during frequent experiments. That most great Cato <note>Cato the Elder (234–149 BCE), a Roman statesman known for his work *De Agri Cultura*.</note>, a man of the highest experience in every practice and a master of all good arts, according to the tradition of Pliny, uses certain incantations in his books on <term>Agriculture</term> for the pains of <term>sciatica</term> <note>original: "ischiadū dolores."</note>. He says: "If there is a dislocation, so that you may enchant it and it shall become healthy by this song: take for yourself a green reed, four or five feet long, split it down the middle, and let two men hold it at the hip-bones. Begin to chant in another [voice]: *S. F. motas væta daries dardaries astataries diffunapiter* <note>These are <term>voces magicae</term>, or "magical voices"—nonsense syllables intended to sound like a powerful ancient language to impress the patient.</note>, until they come together; toss iron over them. When they have come together and one has touched the other, take it with the right hand, cut it with the left, bind it to the dislocation or fracture, and it will become healthy." See into what madness this man, so worthy and so learned, has broken out! Nor did he recognize through his many-sided learning that, even without the power of his words, green reeds split lengthwise will naturally curve and join of their own accord if they are held hanging, just as the branches of willow and bramble also do. <term>Theophrastus</term> <note>A Greek philosopher and the successor to Aristotle, often called the "father of botany."</note> gives the reason for this curving in his books *On the Causes of Plants*. Furthermore, one reads in <term>Dioscorides</term> <note>An ancient Greek physician and pharmacologist.</note> that a reed applied with vinegar to the hips heals sciatica; this he performs without words or superstition.

### Regarding certain experiments with lamps.
### CHAPTER IX.

I was not a little delighted when I discovered among the ancients that the philosopher <term>Anaxilaus</term> <note>A Pythagorean philosopher and physician from the 1st century BCE, often associated with "magical" stage tricks.</note> was accustomed to play with lamp-wicks, and by these deceptions showed monstrous heads of men. If one is to believe the assertions of Pliny, by taking the <term>discharge of mares</term> <note>original: "equarum virus à coitu." This substance, often called <term>hippomanes</term>, was frequently cited in antiquity as a powerful ingredient for aphrodisiacs and illusions.</note> from mating, and lighting it in new lamps and wicks, the heads of men are represented to the sight as horse-heads in a monstrous way; and there are other things which, because we do not believe them, we have therefore not cared to try. But take those things which are true.

#### *So that men may appear as Ethiopians.*

Mix ink—though it is better if it is taken from cuttlefish <note>original: "è sepijs." Cuttlefish ink was commonly used as a writing fluid in the Renaissance.</note>—into the lamps, and the flame shines black. Anaxilaus is said to have done this; for often, from the ink of the cuttlefish, he ren- <margin>...dered those standing by as Ethiopians.</margin>

According to Simeon Sethi <note>Simeon Sethi was an 11th-century Byzantine scholar and physician known for his work on the medicinal properties of foods and natural history.</note>. We will be able to imitate this with any color: by removing all other lights so they are not hindered by a different light, and the color emanating from the lamp may be seen and the illusion may not be frustrated; and if it is daytime, the windows should be closed, lest any light breaking in destroy the trick. ### To make a face appear remarkably thin and pale.

You may easily perform the task in this way. Into a larger glass bowl, pour very old wine, or Greek wine; throw in as much salt as a person can take in a fist. Place it upon glowing coals without a flame, lest the vessel shatter. It will immediately begin to boil; bring a candle near, and it will catch fire. Extinguish the other lights then, and it will make the faces of those standing by look such that they strike terror into one another. The same thing happens in <term>foundries</term> <note>original: *fucinis*.</note> where bells and metal objects are cast; for everything there is seen covered in such a dire color that one might be amazed—lips appearing as if smeared with filth, turning from crimson to a livid and black hue. Also, let burning sulfur be placed in the middle of those standing by, and it will work the same effect even more strongly. We have found that the philosopher Anaxilaus <note>Anaxilaus of Larissa was a Pythagorean philosopher and magician who was expelled from Rome by the Emperor Augustus.</note> used to play in this way. For, having put sulfur into a new cup and carrying it around with coals placed beneath, he would cast a dire paleness upon the guests from the reflection of the flaring substance. This has often happened to me by chance while walking at night in the Neapolitan countryside on the <term>Leucogean Hills</term> <note>Now known as the *Colli Leucogei* in the Phlegraean Fields near Naples, an area famous for its volcanic activity and natural sulfur vents.</note>; for sulfur burning spontaneously gave such [faces...]

### On certain mechanical experiments.
### C H A P T E R 10.

There exist certain experiments of no small subtlety, removed from any addition of chemical mixtures, which we thought would not be unpleasant for the ingenious and for craftsmen. There exists a device, which is called by some a

->Flying Dragon,<-
<note>original: *Draco volans*. This is one of the earliest Western descriptions of a kite, which was still a novelty in 16th-century Europe.</note>

Or a "comet star." Its construction is as follows. Let a quadrangle be constructed from the thinner sticks of reeds, so that the length is in a <term>sesquialter</term> <note>original: *hemioliæ*. A ratio of 1.5 to 1, meaning the kite is half again as long as it is wide.</note> proportion to the width. Two diagonals are to be inserted from opposite parts or corners, at whose intersection a cord should be tied; this cord is then joined with two others of the same length coming from the top corners of the machine. Thus, let it be covered with paper or fine linen, so that there is nothing heavy in it. From there, it is to be entrusted to steady and uniform winds from the summit of a tower, a mountain, or some higher place—not to strong winds, lest the machine be broken, nor to light ones, for if the breeze is silent everywhere, it will not lift it, and the sluggishness of the winds makes the labor in vain.

The device does not travel in a straight path, but obliquely, which is caused by the pull of the rope from one end or the other, and a long tail, which you will fashion from ropes at equal distances with papers tied here and there. Thus launched with a light pull, it is to be entrusted to the hands of the craftsman, who should push it neither sluggishly nor carelessly, but strongly; and thus the flying <term>canvas</term> <note>original: *carbasus*, a word for fine linen or a ship's sail.</note> seeks the air. When it has been elevated a little (for here the wind is disrupted by the turns of the houses), it can hardly be restrained or held back by hands. 

Some place a lantern upon it so that it appears as a comet; others attach a <term>firecracker</term> <note>original: *sclopum*, a term for a small explosive or popping sound.</note> wrapped in paper and <term>gunpowder</term> <note>original: *pyrio puluere*, literally "fire-powder."</note>. When the kite is stationary in the air, a lit fuse is sent up the rope by means of a ring or some slippery object; immediately reaching the sail, it applies fire to the opening, and with a great thunder, the machine bursts into many pieces and falls to the ground. Some even tie a cat or a puppy to it and listen to their voices as they are sent through the air. From this, the ingenious man will be able to foresee the principles by which even a man might be able to fly.

...through which, imperturbable and far removed from every downfall <margin>685</margin> and misfortune, it may be able to enjoy eternal and stable joy (which is <term>blessedness</term> <note>original: *beatitudo*. In Renaissance philosophy, this refers to the state of perfect happiness or "the Good" found in union with the divine.</note>). # Front Cover

-> [Front Cover] <-

<note>The cover of this volume is made from a light-colored material, likely vellum or a pale leather. Vellum, made from processed animal skin, was a standard, durable binding material for account books and personal manuscripts during the early modern period.</note>

<note>The binding features "blind-stamped" decoration, a process where ornate designs are pressed into the surface without the use of ink or gold. This includes a decorative border and small floral or leaf-like stamps in each of the four corners. A larger, diamond-shaped floral motif is centered on the front.</note>

<note>Historical wear is visible across the surface, including various dark spots and a distinct reddish stain near the center. The right edge shows the physical construction of the book, with the raised bands of the binding visible where the covers meet the spine.</note>

<summary>The front cover of the manuscript, featuring decorative floral blind-stamping on vellum or leather. There is no written text on this page.</summary>
<keywords>book cover, vellum, blind-stamped, floral motif, foliate motif, binding</keywords>
